title: Thank God
review: It has been done. Finally. A truly good fantasy movie. And this movie is good. And unlike another recent popular fantasy novel adaptation, it stands on its own. Jackson and the crew and cast and especially Frances Walsh, the screenwriter, have not simply parroted Tolkien's words, instead choosing to create a film that can be enjoyed by anyone. The cost of this change is some of the things that make the books so wonderful, the rich history, culture, and language of Middle Earth are sidelined. Instead, Jackson gives us rich, excellently acted, characters immersed in a world of startling beauty and absolute terror. And it can be very scary. The performances in this movie are nothing less than stellar. Even Liv Tyler is surprisingly excellent as Arwen. The first time I watched this film, I was utterly enraptured. The second time, my reaction was no different. In fact, the second time around I saw and heard new things. The distorted, nightmarish voices of the NazgÃ¼l and Sauron, which I could not hear well the first time, became clear. The intense visual and atmospheric detail also became more noticeable. This is an excellent movie, one which deserves to be watched over and over again. The only regret I have is that I have to wait a year for the next chapter of this exciting saga.

title: Huh? WAIT a second....
review:
I know t hat there are some die hard Tolkien fans out there, but this movie needs to be around for about 10 years before it comes close to supplanting any of the Godfather films as one of the great films.

It does an excellent job in giving the audience a crash course in the overall storyline, but its real selling point is the animation.

Interesting story, frustrating ending.

title: Nice scenery
review:
The one thing that everyone learns from this movie is that New Zealand is apparently a beautiful place. No wonder the NZ tourist board is so pleased with the end result. I came out wanting to book a flight there, and I suspect I wasn't the only one.

What I did not come out of the theater with was any sense of having enjoyed myself. For almost three hours I sat through it and at the end all I could think was: What was that all about? I have never read the books, so I had no idea at all what the story was. Maybe in order to drool over this movie you have to have read the books first. That way you can understand it.

At the very start we got a couple of minutes of voice-over narration, telling us in hurried tones that there were these rings, see, and so-and-so got one, and then another lot went to a bunch of people with white beards, and some other rings were given out to other people whose names you don't catch. No one bothers to tell you why, if these rings are so troublesome, anyone went to the bother of making them in the first place. Anyway, some monsters fought each other (why?) and one ring ended up in a river or a field or something, and Ian Holm found it and that was when things rally got bad.

A jolly little scene with Ian McKellern and Ian Holm ensues but then Holm decides he has to leave his home (why?) and we find ourselves cast into what the rest of the movie consists of -- a bunch of people trekking from A to B to C and having to fight various monsters and mutants in a series of almost identical battles. In most of these they are heavily outnumbered but they always win. It may have been allegorical, it may have been full of significance, but by God it was dull! Sean Bean shows up after a while, but his character is as sombre as the rest. Cate Blanchett appears near the end, but she has very little screen time and what she says makes little sense anyway.

And just when you think it has to be over soon, that they couldn't possibly string it out any further, it ends with nothing accomplished, nothing decided, and in order to see how it ends you have to sit through two more episodes, which will probably be just more of the same: walking, fighting, beautiful scenery, joyless acting.

People who have read the books will love this film, because of course they will relive the pleasure they got from the books as the movie unfolds. That will not be much of a reflection of the movie itself. For those who have not read the books it will be an overlong fantasy tale, best viewed in a few years when it comes out on TV.

title: A very good adaption despite a couple of setbacks
review: I mentioned in my one line summary above that this film has a couple of setbacks that detract from this film being a classic fantasy epic.  Since so many people have seen and will see this film and will form their own opinions - and since so many people have already written so much about this film - I will get right into the film's flaws.  In doing so I will leave its positives to be commented upon by others who have already written about this film. In effect I pretty much agree with them about those aspects of the film. Essentially, there are two problems I have with "The Fellowship of the Ring."  First, this is an unnecessarily dark and gory film.  Its joyless action and overbearing heroics take away from the audience's enjoyment of what is intended to be a rousing adventure.  I liken it to a heavy meal whereby one eats too many thick, dense foods and, while enjoying the food when one actually eats it, he regrets doing so afterwards.  It looks like the film makers put too much of a good thing into this film, just like the meal analogy.  In relation, this film takes itself way too seriously, to the point where it does not ask us to delight in hating the many antagonists of the film.  It just plain wants us to hate them, and because of this quality the "bad guys" are too horrific for their own good. Second, the film is rather long.  It does not matter if the film makers wanted to keep to the story line of the J.R.R Tolkien's novel.  What seems like a never-ending yarn of excitement as a book does not directly translate into a similarly thrilling experience as a film.  The film should have been injected with a greater sense of brevity about the proceedings because the film becomes a tad bit tedious after a while.  However, I should mention that the vague homage to the grand Harryhausen epics of the late 50's and early 60's apparent in the fellowship's battles with an assortment of ghastly ghouls in the film's third act is effective and is the best part of the film. Taking into account these reservations (which I should not downplay; they certainly do have a negative impact), "The Fellowship of the Ring" just barely manages to live up to the hype.  Final Grade: B+

title: WOW
review: I just sat there in awe during THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING - no matter how many special effects films I'd seen, I was still wowed by the amazing recreation of Tolkien's most popular and most acclaimed work.  As a child, I read THE LORD OF THE RINGS at least three times, I loved fantasy novels and Tolkien was the king (I also can't wait for someone to make a film of Brooks' THE SWORD OF SHANNARA, and there's nine sequels and a prequel readymade), so I couldn't believe my eyes when the events I'd imagined were materialising right before my eyes.  Of course, effects don't necessarily mean a great film, and this was perhaps slightly overlong and, between the gripping action scenes the lulls were perhaps a little too serene, but hey, this is the best that anyone could have done with Tolkien's novel and full plaudits to director Jackson.  But PARENTS MUST BE IMPLORED, that for a child to see this film, that child MUST BE OLD ENOUGH TO (HAVE) READ THE BOOK!!  It's intense, dark, and downright horrific at times - it's NOT a kids' film, so take 6- and 7-year-olds by all means, but expect to be up all night comforting them!!  Rating: 8/10.

title: The BEST movie of all time!!
review: Omigosh, after waiting a year, PJ, you didn't let us down! This is an excellent film with amazing effects that will leave you breathlessly soaring on a breeze of ecstasy! Dazzeling scenery and a magnificent star-studded cast make this movie a winner. I must admit, I was a little worried about the casting of Elijah Wood as Frodo, but he was superb and now I cannot see anyone else in the role. Boyd and Monaghan were brilliant as Merry and Pippin, and Viggo Mortensen did great justice to the part of Aragorn. Legolas and Gimli were so exactly how I imagined them after reading the trilogy that it was almost frightening! I ADORE THIS FILM and plan on seeing it again many times. 10 *'s.

title: Well worth the lifetime I've waited to see this made into a film.
review: This film is cinema at its best.  Peter Jackson has done what we all hoped he would do....he brought Middle Earth to life.  The effects work is amazing...a far cry from watermelons as exploding heads in "Bad Taste". Highly recommended to Tolkein and non-Tolkein fans alike.

title: Essential for fans and non-fans alike
review:
'Awesome' isn't the word. Truly the best film of the year, and certainly the best book-to-film translation I've seen. I'm a great fan of the book so perhaps I'm biased, but this movie has lost none of the magic of the epic tome.

All cast members are excellent, as are the effects. Minor niggles aside, this film is flawless. Roll on December 2002!

title: Stunning
review:
This was absolutely one of the best films of the year. Many compared it (before it's release) to Harry Potter, which does not do it justice in the least. Harry Potter is a kids film, it will be forgotten in a years time. The Fellowship of the Ring will live on in our memories for a good long time still.

It should be up in the list along with the likes of Star Wars, the acting was brilliant, the visual effects stunning, and the story a timeless classic. It has done the book justice and I am very glad to see Peter Jackson taking up this task. No Hollywood director could have pulled it off this well. I shudder at the thought of Steven Spielberg, Roland Emmerich or Joel Schumacher would have done to it. Well done Jackson, it really shines through that you are a big Tolkien fan, and you have inspired many to finally pick up the novels and read them for themselves. Well done.

title: uh, what? oh, right. movie.
review:
perhaps i had a poor movie experience. sitting in the second row, basically in the isle. surrounded by people, like we were there to see some medicine man or faith healer. plus the people next to me wouldn't shut up, no matter how many exasperated sounds i made and quick quizical glances i shot their way.

not a bad movie, i just found my self coming back to it alot, drifting away in a slow moment and then remembering what i was doing, when the sound track startled me.

maybe my experience is to blame, but i do think that they could have cut out an hour pretty views and sappy sentimentality. and what of the first half hour of exposition? was that needed?

why did they have to go for an oscar? that is what ruined it for me.

i will freely and openly admit that i am a product of this generation, i prefer my movies to be action pack and have the latest hip hop and white boy rap. even some speed metal, but not in the context of john carpenter. in fact nothing the context of john carpenter. so i like jump cuts, cute chicks and bass filled sound tracks. in short, more sword fighting, less story telling.

title: The first part of what will be considered a classic trilogy!
review:
I have been following the filming of this version since its announcement. Being something of a purist about Tolkien's work my initial impression was that of abject terror.

"They will ruin it! Everyone will come to hate the books due to some souless adaptation! The film industry has no care for the work itself or the tale of friendship, and courage overcoming all evil that is at its core!"

However as I followed the online Q&As with Peter Jackson, whose earlier works I was familiar with, that began to change slightly. As production continued I gained even more respect for the project.

I am happy to say my initial impression was absolutely incorrect.

If you have ever wondered where all of the truly passionate films have gone, the films that were a labor of love, see this film. If you have ever wondered if a film can convincingly portray true feeling, courage, friendship, suffering, and redemption, see this film. If you thought that a live action version of LOTR was impossible, see this film. If you think that an adaptation of the book would corrupt the story or weaken its message, see this film. If you know you'll hate any film that is not identical to the books I challenge you to see this film.

I cannot in fact think of any reason not to see this film!

This is the kind of quality film that people want to see every time the lights go down in the theatre!

The rest of Hollywood should sit up and take notice...

title: This is the Reason the Medium of Movies was Invented
review: Completely and utterly breathtaking. If ever there was a use for the silver screen, this is it. You may be aware of the length of the movie, but it's only because you don't want it to end. Every character played an excellent part.

title: Worth the Wait
review:
Peter Jackson has done an excellent job transforming Tolkien's masterpiece into one of the most beautiful and exciting movies I have ever seen. The visuals in this movie are incredible. This movie will be studied far into the future as a monumental piece of work.

Purists will complain about this scene or that being cut, but I appreciate the fact that Jackson carried the essence of the story throughout the film, and make me feel that most of the scenes that were missing happened off screen.

I turned to my wife at times during the film and said that they had just skipped 50 pages from one scene to the next, later we were speaking with another friend (both he and my wife have not read the books), and they commented that they liked that. I feel that Peter Jackson's decision to make a great movie, not to make a word for word translation of the book to film was proper and for the best.

I will be purchasing this DVD as soon as it is released. I am hoping that there will be multiple commentary tracks. I would love one track with the nine, and one with Peter Jackson and Andrew Lesnie (the cinematographer), Howard Shore (score), and Alan Lee (Art direction).

I think that the all of the above deserve Oscars, and I hope that everyone gets the chance to see this movie.

Two things to know before going: 1) there is no resolution at the end, this is not a self-contained story. 2) this is not a children's movie, at least anymore than Braveheart was a movie for kids.

title: A classic book committed faithfully to the screen.
review:
This is one of the few times I have seen such a detailed book epitomized so well on the Big Screen. Most of the charachters and events are faithfully depicted.

There are so many different stories going on at once that it is difficult to film them as the book describes the events. The Hobbits, the Black Riders, Gandalf, Sauruman, elves, and Aragorn tromp through mountains, caves, storms, swamps, forests, plains, and rivers to fight their way to their individual destinations.

So many stories so skilfully seen on the big screen excited me tremendously. I had seen the earlier animated version of Lord of the Rings and was very disappointed. This one did not.

By the way for those of you counting, I read the trilogy 3 times so far.

title: The best movie of all time
review: This movie is the best one that I´ve seen, exept if The Two Towers is going to be better. I recommend that you see this movie cause it´s the best ever. Peter Jackson did great work and I´m really happy that he did this so well. The acting is brillant and Chistopher Lee and Ian Mckellen are VERY good in the movie.

title: Faithful. Epic. Wonderful
review:
There's too much to say about what is so wonderful about this film. I suppose initially you have to say that the effort that went into this project is amazing. From sets to effects and especially to acting this film has it all. Action, love, friendship, special effects, great characters and a feeling of a story of epic proportions. Ian McKellen is a wonder, a disciple of his craft but all in all the performances were striking. The locations, the action, the themes of friendship, sacrifice and the greater good all there.

Is it a perfect film? Well no. So there's a few changes from the book but to be honest most of them are required. But despite the few niggling things like Galadriel being either half asleep or over the top and the absence of any real feeling of how much time has passed, it's a beautiful labour of love.

It's long and the first hour IS slow so don't expect the immediate effect of a blockbuster straight off. When it gets going though, watch out, things really are amazing. From the Mines of Moria to the final heart breaking scenes we are treated to the first classic of the 21st century.

title: Story Takes Main Lead In Tolkien Mini-Series
review: It's terrific to finally see a science fiction extravaganza that relies on story content....rather than special effects alone....to play out its' plot! Some moviegoers may think that 3-hours is too long to sit and see a movie unfold, however with the screen adaptation that the first installment of the Lord Of The Rings brings to the theatre you wish it would go on longer. The "flaws" one might see in the film are so inconsequential that this first film will certainly go down as yet another 'breakthrough' cinematic event much as Star Wars and Alien did when they were first brought to the theater. Caution: Like so many others who have read the warnings for younger audience members who may want to venture into the audience; this film could be disturbing to those who are pre-teen.  It's not like they haven't seen violence and gore before, but this is clearly a fantasy film for adults who should enjoy it most.

title: An earnest, but not entirely sucessfull attempt at filming the unfilmable.
review:
Being a lifelong fan of the book, and having re-read it just weeks prior to the viewing, it is completely impossible for me to give Peter Jackson's FOTR an reasonable evaluation from an artistic standpoint. I couldn't help but dissect the film scene-by-scene as opposed to perceiving it as one cinematic whole. At times it felt like a protracted illustration and little else. Perhaps a second or third viewing will correct that. For now, on first impression, I can only say that the film was uneven, at times frustrating. Frustrating because some of its aspects worked beautifully; and some were pulling it into quite the opposite direction. Frustrating because Jackson does have a strong personal vision, yet he did make some grave and obvious concessions to Hollywood. Here's the breakdown:

* WARNING! POTENTIAL SPOILERS AHEAD*********************************

THE GOOD:

1) Visuals: Landscapes and Architecture. Flawless. Majestic. Alan Lee as design consultant worked miracles. And furthermore, it made New Zealand a lucrative travel destination for me.

2) Certain Actors. Specifically portraying Gandalf, Bilbo, Sam, a few others... mostly dead-on, much like I always imagined.

3) The "creative license" scenes. Surprisingly enough, most of them did not detract from the movie, and even enlivened it a bit. Arwen's involvement did not seem out of place, and her "flight to the ford" scene is easily one of the finest setpieces of the whole 3 hours. In fact, I would have liked to see even more of her. The allusions to various chapter titles were in good spirit, and the comic relief for the most part worked decently, although it was somewhat upsetting to see Merry and Pippin reserved strictly for that purpose. The subtitled Elvish was a nice touch, in part because it eliminated the prospect of listening to Aragorn's and Arwen's romantic dialogue in English (!)

4) Action Scenes. Nicely staged, esp. the entire Moria sequence.

THE MEDIOCRE:

1) Heavy Cuts. It's true that the film is rushed. The only clues to how much time elapses between various scenes are periodic edits to the transformation of Isengard, and that is insufficient. Many scenes feel shortened in order to meet the 3 hour obligation, especially those of Lorien and I would hope the more complete version makes it to DVD.

2) At times, overdramatic. Some of the players' approach is not very authentic, overly self-aware, Elrond most of all. Aragorn and Boromir overact on occasion, but sparingly. Saruman and Gandalf, bellowing spells at each other across mountain passes come off as a pair of grand opera singers.

3) Derivative Effects. While impressive in their own right, the Wizard duel scene, Cave Troll, and Balrog seem to be inspired by latter-day videogames rather than by Tolkien's descriptions.

THE BAD:

1) Frodo's cleanliness. While Elijah Wood's undoubtedly put his heart and soul into the role, his physical appearance was just a tad bit overpolished. He resembled a CGI model rather than a living, breathing hobbit. And throughout the film, not a speck of dirt seemed to have touched him - does being the ringbearer automatically merit a daily bath in wartime conditions?

2) Prologue. Cheezy and unnecessary. Much of it is repeated through subsequent flashbacks anyway. Could have done without it and went on straight to the original storyline. The initial shot of Sauron holding up the ring is laughable, straight out of a grade-Z flick.

3)The Soundtrack. Atrocious, absolutely atrocious. The single element of FOTR that tipped the scale toward the negative for me. If it was used half as much, the movie would have been greatly eleveated in my mind. But this generic tripe...too closely reminiscent of Titanic for comfort. Remember that scene in South Park where a character is tortured by Enya's music? - well, that's precisely how I felt.

title: Incredible movie.
review: Anyone who read the books should see this movie.  I loved it.  If you haven't read the books but have even a marginal interest, see the movie also-- then read the books too.  It's worth every minute you spend.

title: Good Film
review: I wish I didn't read the book because if I didn't know what the story was about I would have enjoyed the movie even more. If you haven't read the book my advice is go see the movie first. This is a great film but I'm sure this first wave of excitement is going to die out pretty soon once all the Tolkien's fiends see it. I'm sure they are going to be upset about many things as it doesn't quite follow the book's narrative and interprets it freely in some instances. But I am also certain that The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring will receive an Oscar this year for the best motion picture. However, I wouldn't rush and push over The Godfather from the first place of the all times charts.

title: Amazing!
review:
I have to admit I was slightly worried when I first heard that a Lord of the Rings movie was being made. I couldn't see how a film could do Tolkein's masterpiece of a book any justice whatsoever. I initially thought that the special effects would be lame and the acting would be over-done. I thought that a film version would be naff and would butcher my favourite book.

However, after seeing trailers, reading interviews etc. I started to get excited. I could see that the huge team behind this film had obviously worked very hard in getting it just right. The casting sounded perfect (Ian Mckellen as Gandalf - genius) and the location, beautiful (New Zealand with its strong contrasts of terrain.)

The excitement of this movie began to grow and grow and after re-reading the book just in time, I knew that this was going to be one hell of a film. The cast was strong, the effects team were doers of the impossible and lets face it, the story in question is the greatest one ever told...I just hoped it came across that way.

I went to see it last night. I was speechless. It didn't seem like 3 hours - the whole thing was a joy. Tolkein would be so proud of a film like this one. It does the book justice and more - Peter Jackson, you are my hero.

I was worried about Liv Tyler (I'm not her biggest fan) but I needn't have been. I thought that Elijah Wood may have been too American, but he wasn't. I was worried that the effects would be too unbelieveable - they weren't. They were completely awesome. The whole experience was great.

This is a film that will go down in history. This is a film that will rival the classics such as Star Wars (In my mind last night's film was far superior!). Roll on the Oscars - this film deserves the lot!

I just hope the next two will be as good. I'm sure they will.

10/10

title: the best fantasy film ever made
review: You don't need the book to understand the film. The  history of the  story is well explained in the first 5 or 10 minutes the history is told, so you now the what, the who and the where. Although it's a fantasy film, computer animated graphics seem's only a small part of the film. The landscape scenery's are great. The problem of that this is only part one was for me no great problem. Part one ends where it should end, afterwards i can already imagine what the next two episode's will be like. I regret that we should wait so long for part 2 and 3 although these are already filmed

title: A Classic already
review:
I was hesitant as i watched it the first time. But as the movie rolls on it draws you in even more. I cared less about how faithful an adaptation it was, and moreso on its own merits. As most people are saying its a beautiful movie that begs to be seen again and again.

The second time i saw (12 hours after the opening on midnite no less!), i noticed it had an elegiac quality for an epic movie that oozes with style. Its dreamlike yet palpable in its portrayal of evil (Sauron) and there is a theme in the movie of an undeniable evil that corrupts absolutely, even moreso that the books when i read them. Theres more to this movie than just a fantasy flick for the family.

Also of note is the complexity of the shot selection particularly with the closeups of the characters. I've never seen a big budget movie show as much depth and character with its onscreen closeups as Lord of the Rings... and when you couple it with the fact that its a special effects epic thats a great feat!

etc

title: Nice movie, nothing more
review:
I really can't understand where the long list of 10 votes comes from, the movie id good enough but to get a 10 the movie would really have to be of superb quality in all aspects and in my opinion it's not. I have a feeling (I can even see it in my surroundings) that a lot of people just won't allow themselves to see any flaws in the movie made about their favorite book.

The story stays very close to the original but of course due to time constraints it lacks the depth the book has. It also shows how difficult it is to put something on the screen that can only exist in your imagination (elves are supposed to be so beautiful that looking at them almost brings tears to your eyes).

The special effects are mostly quite good, never exceptional and at times a bit "unnatural" (being able to see ropes that orcs are using to pull down trees in the middle of the night from very high up).

But for the rest an enjoyable movie and I'll go see parts 2 and 3 for sure, the movie at least deserves that much.

title: Very good - but not perfect by any means
review:
OK - so it's good. I don't deny that. It's beautifully put together, well shot, well directed, and really well acted. Viggo Mortensen has been dying to be in a role like this - and makes the most of it. He is the best thing about this movie by some stretch. Elijah Wood's accent grates, but his facial expressions are perfect, while the other hobbits are, to be fair, useless and not funny.

The problem I had with the film was its lack of depth. It felt like one long chase sequence ("Quick, let's make it to the bridge", followed by "Quick, let's make it to the river"). All I ask is that the second and third films don't follow this narrative thread - we've had enough chasing and monsters - give us some story and some dialogue!

I still have to recommend it though - but don't expect it to be as earth-shattering as some are suggesting...

Although Liv Tyler and Cate Blanchett look sent from heaven....

title: So is it? Yes it is!
review: And by that I mean that everything you have expected from the film has come true, most of the good and some of the bad. Yes, the bad, because now 2 days after seeing it there are some things that seem to keep bugging me. I didn't care about the fact that large parts of the "slower scenes" were left out, the larger role of Arwen (10 minutes of screentime isn't all that much) didn't bother me either. Both these changes made the story even more exciting so why bother. It were more the small details that were changed without a real reason tha bother me. Why let Merry & Pippin trow rocks in the lake near Moria and not Boromir, why remove the explosion (made by Gandalf) at the disappearance of Bilbo and most of all Why doesn't Aragorn carry Narsil? I don't believe that these changes really make this a better film. Not that it in in need of improvement, mind you. What I've seen was absolutely thrilling from the first apocalyptic scenes to the last, the shortest 3 hours of my life later. Most satisfying was probably the cast, Jackson has chosen the best possible actors for each role, after seeing the film it has become impossible to think of anyone else playing the characters. The one actor that springs most to mind is of course sir Ian McKellen as Gandalf but the others are equally good choices. 10/10 Casting is one thing, acting an other and here again everything works out splendidly. One beliefs the fears, the hopes, the desires of the characters even if they are forced to use a language that should feel a bit archaic. 9/10 Photography: the best ever, you have to see it to believe it: 10/10 Special effects: I could well use the previous line and be equally right but these effects have earned a bit more text. They are not just extremely well done, they actually feel right. At no point in time you go yeah right I know how it's done. Instead you have the idea that Elijah Wood is in fact 3 foot tall and no it is not a good idea to meet the Balrog after dark. 11/10 Respect for the master: this category is more or less for the Tolkien buff who wants everything to be right. Well the atmosphere is there, the main storyline is there but ... some parts are left out, this is of course inevitable but because of this i'll just give him a 7 out of 10 on this thing (still more than I expected 6 months ago) To conclude: go and see this film if you've read Tolkien you'll recognise all the works beauty and if you haven't it'll be the visit of a lifetime. By the way Sam is the servant of Frodo, just so you'll know why he keeps calling him Master "Frodo".

title: Simply Incredible
review:
After reading the books more than 25 years ago, I remember thinking this would've made a great movie.

My only complaint (and there's nothing else about this movie that is at fault) was the level of volume. Hugely loud, almost deafening. There again, it may have been the theatre's volume control and not the film itself.

title: This is how you make an epic adaptation!
review: What can I say that hasn't been already said.   Wow!  Peter Jackson has managed to do what other directors have failed miserably in doing, ie. adapting a wonderful novel to the big screen (butt out next time Mrs Rowling).  LOTR will rake in all of the Oscars having anything to do with cinematography, makeup, set design, etc - ALL of them.  All of the actors cast in the movie are almost just as I'd imagined the characters when reading the book.  Liv Tyler is astonishingly beautiful, sexy and literally luminous as Arwen.  The horse chase scene where the wonderfully costumed Ringwraiths are pursuing her as she carries Frodo is literally breathtaking. I think I held my breath for the entire scene. Orlando Bloom as Legolas is dead on.  Viggo Mortensen and Sean Bean as Strider and Boromir are also cast very well.  And what can you do but heap praises on the casting of Ian Mckellan as Gandalf and Christopher Lee as Saruman - perfect.  I do have one complaint, however.  Hugo Weaving as Elrond???  Sorry, but that just didn't do it for me; all I kept thinking as I saw him onscreen was, "Goodbye, Mr. Anderson."  Slight miscast aside, the movie was absolutely splendid despite the minor changes in the adaptation. 10/10!!!

title: Good movie but parents should take caution!
review:
I read the book in the weeks preceding the movie and I'm glad I did. Even though the movie is 3 hours long, most of the characters cannot be developed to the degree they are in the book. For example, the relationship between Gimli (a dwarf) and Legolas (an elf) evolves in a very significant way in the book and you don't pick up on it in the movie. Other characters in the book were left out completely. Some of the names of people and places are confusing and the distinctions are easy to miss in the movie. For example, Sauron and Saruman sound alike and are both evil characters in the story.

As a parent, I would caution you against taking a younger child. I took my 15 and 13 year old children, but not my 10 year old child. There are a lot of scary looking creatures and much violent fighting. Overall, the movie has a dark feel to it. Although the movie portrayed scenes that were in the book, I think we spent too much time viewing some of the evil characters and not enough time on some of the lighter elements of the book.

Overall, I rated it an 8 out of 10 and would recommend it to others with the above cautions. I will not buy the video/DVD because I have young children who do not need to see some of the images. But I will read them the story because their own imaginations will not be nearly so violent and graphic.

title: A Beautiful and Heart-Breaking Movie
review:
Here are a few words that describe this movie for me: audacious, tragic, memorable, infuriating, beautiful, and heart-breaking. Let me start with audacious. How dare Peter Jackson! How dare he change the Tolkien's sacred text. Where is Glorfindel? Where is that wonderful scene of Sam confronting Strider? And why wasn't Sam present at the Mirror of Galadriel? It's like making a movie of the birth of Christ and inserting a scene where Joseph and Mary are pursued by an army of Roman soldiers, until finding a hiding place in a cave. Hey, it may be an exciting episode, but it aint scriptural.

On the other hand, the Lord of the Rings is a work of fiction. It's a great work of art. When a movie is made from a book, there are two things that must be considered:

1) How does it compare to the book? 2) How does it stand by itself, as a work of art?

Let me tackle the first question. Simply put, the book is better. But then again, how could it not be? Was anyone really expecting that the movie would outshine the book? Simply impossible. That being said, there were some choices that Peter Jackson made that simply mystify and/or infuriate me. Let me start with the areas that I think the movie moved away from the book to its detriment:

1) The flight to Rivendell was too hasty and jarring. Merry and Pippin are never "officially" enrolled into Frodo's quest. They are simply caught up in the flight to Bree. This makes their presence seem like a mistake rather than an act of friendship. A similar problem occurs with Strider, who joins the company without that wonderful scene where the hobbits (and Sam, grudgingly) accept his presence. I can't understand why anyone would take these scenes out when they add so much depth to the characters.

2) What happened to the Elves? Rather than appearing high, fair, and noble, they often appear as petty and quarrelsome. Elrond is no better than any other man, he's just gifted with long life and a good memory. Heck, it appears his only concern is getting the ring out of Rivendell as fast as possible so he can finish packing on his way out of Middle Earth.

In the same vein, we see Lady Galadriel as Boromir might have seen her. But we have to see Galadriel also as Frodo sees her. We have to understand why Frodo would offer her the ring. In the context of the movie, it seems that he offers the ring because he's afraid of the quest, rather than because she is "wise and fair" and would be a "better" keeper than Frodo.

3) What happened to Lothlorien? I just finished reading the Lothlorien chapter to my son tonight and it bore no resemblance to what was presented in the movie. I want Lothlorien to be a place of surpassing beautiful and stillness; instead it look like a place with a bunch of tree houses in someone's psychedelic dream.

There are a few other areas that I cringed at, but these were the ones which made me shake my head in disbelief. People, people, people, WHAT were you thinking?

Ah, but now let me turn to question #2. Divorcing the movie from the book, and accepting it as a work of art on its own merits, it is a stunning achievement. When the Return of the King was published, a reviewer called it "beautiful and heart-breaking", the same words apply to the movie. Peter Jackson paints a vivid picture of a world in decay. The great cities and towers of the past have fallen. The Last Alliance has been sundered. The Elves are weary of the world and desire only to leave it to rot, and the Dark Lord has risen again.

And into this world comes a token of doom, the ring, and the one who seems chosen to rid the world of this evil is a simple hobbit. Frodo does not desire adventures or glory. When he learns of the ring, he first wants to hide it forever and then he wants, no PLEADS, for Gandalf to take it. Finally, because there is no other way, he reluctantly takes it to Rivendell, where he hopes that his job is finished and he can go home. But he soon realizes that there is no one would will take his burden from him, so he must continue. The cost is great. Bilbo is tempted to seize the ring, Gandalf perishes in the Mines of Moria, Boromir betrays him, and so, step-by-step Frodo becomes more and more isolated from the world. Frodo's haunted look as he watches the Fellowship fall apart around him, will stay with me a long time.

So too, will the friendship between Gandalf and Frodo. Ian McKellen's portrayal of Gandalf is perfection. He portrays a vulnerable Gandalf, one that knows there are indeed greater powers than himself in the world, and yet he forcing himself to go forward. His courage may even exceed Frodo's since he fully knows the dangers that awaits him, and Frodo does not. Mixed with his courage is a tenderness for the hobbits. When Frodo agrees to take the ring, Gandalf's face expresses both amazement and sadness. It's a wonderful characterization.

And finally, there is Aragorn, who in this movie, really is Strider. He is the man that we know will become the King of all Middle Earth, but he is not ready yet. He must grow into his Kingship. I was greatly moved when he let Frodo go into Mordor alone because he knew that could not trust himself to be near the Ring any longer. It was perhaps, his first kingly act. An act that Isildur could not do. The development of Aragorn may be one area in which the three movies will exceed the three books. We shall see.

I finished watching the movie eight hours ago. A part of me still dwells in the Middle Earth of Peter Jackson's invention. No, it is not as good as the book; but it is a great and heart-breaking movie, and after I recover, I intend to see it again.

title: A dream come true.
review: I close my eyes and still see that majestic introduction, always my favorite, the back ground, the legend that lays behind the tale. I have been expecting this movie for two long years and it did not let me down for the slightest moment. It revived that fire i feel inside of me whenever i read the book. I remember how depressed i felt when i read it the first time. I wanted it all to be real, i wanted it to be the story of our own past and i wanted to be part of it. This movie has been a dream come true and in the most inexplicable way because the soundtrack includes music by Enya, my favorite singer and whom i listened to when i read the book. Every time i read it i hear her, every time i hear her i remember. I hope this sensation stays with me forever and can only add that it is utterly unfair that we have to wait a whole year to see The Two Towers.

title: Jackson's "Fellowship" Seems Fairer, Feels Fouler
review:
Do you like medieval fantasy, but hate to read? Do you find character development and exposition are annoyances you are forced to tolerate between action scenes? Then this may be the film for you. Peter Jackson's `The Fellowship of the Ring' rips out all the subtlety from the novel that gave birth to the fantasy genre and leaves you with a pumped-up, over-simplified caricature of J.R.R. Tolkien's masterpiece.

Okay, I admit it. The scenery is breathtaking. The costumes and make-up are inspired. The casting (with a few exceptions) is divine. But just like a teen pop-star, underneath the eye-candy, there's no there there. Yes, there are some excellent performances, and a handful of characters and scenes are right on target. But that just makes the plot skimming, gross character distortions, and over-indulgent action scenes stand out all the more.

Ralph Bakshi's `Lord of the Rings' film from the late 70's, as ugly and inaccuracy-laden as it was, at least understood most of its characters and made an effort to stay true to the text. Jackson, on the other hand, seems to delight in taking credit for triumphs great or small from one character and bestowing them on another, for no apparent reason. He also either skipped or botched almost every pivotal or memorable line of dialogue. The impact of Frodo's heroic and poignant, `I will take the Ring, though I do not know the way,' is lost when Jackson turns the Council of Elrond into a shouting match--the first half of the line being drowned out, and the second coming after so long a pause that audiences actually laugh at it.

If you read `The Lord of the Rings', you will recall how Tolkien drew you into his world rich in cultures, language, and history with a subtle thread woven through your imagination. Jackson apparently decided this task would be better accomplished with a sledgehammer. In an effort to get to the next hyped-up, over-the-top fight scene, Jackson seems to have decided that every nuance of the book should be painted in bright primary colors with a flashing neon arrow pointing to it. Where Tolkien gave us evidence of a wary mistrust between dwarves and elves, Jackson gives us a Gimli who shouts, `No elf will lay his hands on this ring!' When Galadriel probes Boromir's thoughts, Tolkien tells us only that Boromir would not speak of the experience. In film, this could be shown in elegant simplicity by having Boromir look quickly away when under scrutiny. But in Jackson's version, we instead are subjected to a long shot where he sweats profusely and his breath echoes in our ears. UmPeter, we got the point. We are capable of thinking for ourselves, you know. And as if that weren't enough, in a subsequent scene Galadriel herself proceeds to bluntly spell out Boromir's thoughts for Frodo and the audience, leaving little suspense to his pivotal scene near the end of the film.

Even the action scenes are overdone. Where Tolkien (and even Bakshi) gave us terse, tense combat, Jackson pulls out all the stops in every fight, and seems to have set himself the goal of trying to outdo every Jerry Bruckheimer film ever made. I kept waiting for him to work in a car chase somewhere. The `Crouching Hobbit, Hidden Wizard' battle in Orthanc was painful in ways I can't even describe. Having seen and enjoyed Jackson's horror/comedy classic `Brain Dead', I knew he had a penchant for going way over the top, but I foolishly assumed that he would realize that what is appropriate for the horror genre really has no place in high fantasy. And the ironic part is that, instead of making them more intense, Jackson succeeds only in causing the action scenes to be the slowest, most dragged-out parts of the film.

You may think I'm being too harsh. I admit I'm a purist when it comes to this story, but I'm no fanatic. If these sacrifices had been made simply due to the fact that the source material is so rich that there was no time to spend on every nuance, they would be a little more palatable. I understand that, even with three 3-hour movies, there is no way to deal with everything in the books. Traditional omissions like Tom Bombadil's chapters are concessions we have to make to the exigencies of filmmaking. But when you bite your tongue at the fact that the entire journey from the Shire to Rivendell is presented in almost summary form, and then have to sit through a 15-minute rancor-oops, I mean cave troll-battle in Moria, or shake your head at the complete omission of the wonderful blindfold scene in Lórien only to be subjected to an all-out melee by the Falls of Rauros involving the entire Fellowship, you find your patience begins to wear awfully thin. Hey, Peter, uminteresting new scenes, but don't you think the time could have been better spent showing things that ACTUALLY HAPPENED IN THE BOOKS?

If you have never read LotR and you like fantasy movies with lots of action, you may enjoy this film. If LotR to you is `that book about the elves and stuff' that you read when you were younger, you may like this movie as well. But if you truly loved LotR for all the richness and subtlety with which Tolkien infused his saga, you should be gravely disappointed if not incensed by this all-too-Hollywood caricature of a classic novel.

About 2 hours and 45 minutes into the film, Frodo whines, `I wish none of this had ever happened.' So do I, Ringbearer. So do I.

title: Thank you all for this dream came true...
review:
A long time we have waited, and a long time we have feared what would happen if the greatest novel of our time will be brought to the screen. Now it finally happened! Weeks ago we have started searching for available teasers, trailers, making of's, interviews, pictures, sounds,... watched and listened to them with open mouths and eyes. We hoped, hoped so badly that it hurt until the day of truth came and we sat in the cinema: The night from Tuesday to Wednesday, 12 o'clock, midnight. I read the book, several times. I watched the animated LotR from Bakshi, more often than I can remember. It has to be good, it has to be the best movie ever. I heard these words out of hundreds of mouth throughout the last month and I did no better. Sitting in the best row of our cinema, next to me my girlfriend, gripping my hand so tight that it hurts. I feel her tension, I feel mine. Then the curtain opens for the last time and there is no way back.

We left the cinema gently crying and stood in row to buy tickets for the next 5 showtimes. I think there is nothing more to say. But I do it, because I hear those guys, running around with their special edition leatherbound mastersigned books, complaining about this leftout and that change. Sure, everyone of us would have made it a bit different and better, no question. I myself would have stretched the movie to 6 hours and put in all the small details that I have missed, but I tell you, what Peter Jackson has created is so great that I am lacking words to describe my feelings, watching this film. What Peter Jackson and all of the crew has accomplished is unbelievable. Capturing the atmosphere of the book, with all their character developing details etc. and in the same time do a great fantasy movie for everyone, knowing the books or not. I love this movie. ********** 10 stars! Deserving every one of it!

title: As a movie: 10. As an adaptation: 9.9. As compared to book: .1
review:
I had to go see it a second time before writing a review. It seems I left my jaw on the floor of the theater.

For those who see this movie without first reading the books or knowing much about the doings of Middle Earth, there is much to like. Great acting, a nice score, fantastic scenery, and a depth and scope that has not been seen in Hollywood, by my own eyes at least. Not to mention a Balrog and the Nazgul and the Tower of Orthanc, of course, which were beautifully and faithfully reproduced. It is doubtful that anyone who sees this film will dislike it, when being analyzed simply as a movie.

Then there's the case of the written word being adapted, transliterated one might say, to film. Never before have I seen this done with such skill, nor as much dedication to getting it right. Peter Jackson is to be commended. To be fair, there are a few groans that nearly escaped my throat during the movie, when certain things were changed or added or removed. Most of the alterations were due to time/resource limitations, and those were properly done and did not harm the story. There were a few though which were done simply to please the average movie-goer, and for myself as a serious Rings admirer they were annoying. Mildly so, though, and what can we expect? This movie could not be made just for the avid readers - it is after all a Hollywood production with the goal of entertaining wide audiences and generating profit. As it were, the latter form of alteration is perfectly acceptable - but when I consider that if it were not for this wider audience's ticket purchases, I would not have this film to watch, those alterations are perhaps even welcome. None were too bad, there were no glaring missteps. Except one, which was an editing problem, not a storyline issue, and was not even noticeable to anyone who hadn't read the books a half dozen times. Without spoiling anything, there was one shot of one character approaching a landmark that was quite important in the books, you see him stepping toward it, and in the next instant they're not just off on the journey, but already to the next destination, which as I remember was a full day's travel from the landmark's position. In any case, this is quite simply the finest book-to-movie translation I have ever seen.

Now we get to the nitty-gritty. The text vs. film. There is nothing much to say, actually. The books are the finest, most beautiful, and terribly, deeply satisfying work I have ever read. The movie falls not too short of that mark, in regards to films I have seen - but in comparison to the movie, it is nothing. It was never expected to be, at least by me. It did, however, far exceed all expectations save one: the movie is not as dark or grim as it might have been. That is my one true complaint - a mild change of tone would have made the movie perfect, a tone to match the books, of great, sad, passing beauty. Something so overwhelming and powerful... that as it progresses, and fades away, you cannot even feel much bitterness. It is enough to simply witness it.

In the end, I suppose the movie does live up to this expectation in one manner: Commentary be damned, this is a fantastic and wonderous movie. It is enough to simply witness it.

title: Exceeded Expectations
review:
The film is excellent. After having read all of the books (LOTR, Hobbit, Silmarillion) and read all of the great reviews the movie has been getting, my expectations were ridiculously high for this movie. Still, it surpassed them all. It is visually stunning. The score is breathtaking. The action leaves your heart beating like a drum for several hours after you exit your seat. Still, it is not overwhelming as the rising conflict is interlaced with moments of calm. In other words, the film is quite well paced. There goes the Oscar for best editing. In fact this movie will (and I am certain here) be nominated for the best picture Oscar. I haven't seen 'A Beautiful Mind', but up to now, this has been the best film of the year in my opinion. The critics seem to agree as there have been mostly positive reviews. I even enjoyed it more than the book, because the book at times seems like it should have been trimmed down. For example, in the book, people sit around a fire several times and talk about what they have done and what they will do. This takes pages and pages and happens over and over again. It seems redundant at times. The film does away with all of that and retains the core of the story. Those who have read the book may miss some characters like Bombadil, but if you think about it, the story flows just fine without them. In fact, meeting Bombadil in the movie and having him sing his songs would have simply eroded the rhythm of the film.

All in all, I recommend both the book and movie to everyone.

title: Better than I hoped!
review:
I read all of the comments. I heard all of the hype from friends who hadn't read the book. I half-expected to come out of the theater disappointed.

However, after watching the movie, I now wonder when the crowds will thin out enough for me to go again. I loved it. What was changed, to me, seemed to fit in the spirit of the original novel. Although my two favorite characters (Tom Bombadil and Glorfindel) were worked out of the movie for virtue of time, it did not impede my delight at the craftsmanship of this excellent piece.

I suggest it to everyone who read the book. I suggest it even more to everyone who hasn't. (Though I would then suggest you read the book :)

This was the only movie I went to see in the theater this year. I wasn't disappointed.

title: An excellent depiction of the book, but hard to judge on its own
review:
Warning: Some spoilers inside

The movie starts with a prologue, lining out the context of the story: the story of the Rings of Power, of Isuldur and how the Ring was forgotten, and came into the hands of Bilbo. A nice and useful addition, especially for people unfamiliar with the books. Of course, the story is at many places shortened, leaving out many details. To accommodate for this, the story has also been altered at quite a number of places: events have been merged. Sometimes, this has gone too far. One case I'd like to mention is the new role Arwen has been given, rescuing Frodo from the Dark Riders by taking him to Rivendel. She has been portrayed as a here as a very strong, almost warriorlike women, when in the book she is not. It would have been better in my opinion not to change characters like this, and thus have Glorfindel rescue him instead. The time needed to explain could easily have been taken away from some scenes at Bilbo's farewell party, where in my opinion a couple of useless scenes have been added. Another problem is in my view the early discovery of Gollum. I don't understand the need for this modification, and I therefore think it is a shame it has been modified at all.

The bigger role for Saruman is a good thing in my view, as it reduces the need for flashbacks and clears up a lot of potential problems later. The palantir should not have been shown that early however, and certainly not to Gandalf. It is an essential part of the story of The Two Towers, and giving away the link between Sauron and Saruman, even suggesting a joining of powers between the three wizards, is a useless modification to the story.

The ending of the story is in fact part of book two, thus creating a more logical point to stop than it is in the books.

Overall though, I find the movie a great addition to the book. Apart from a few mistakes, it is as good as a depiction as you may reasonably ask for in the time this movie runs (which is already long). The footage of the landscapes is awesome, and the characters are in general well portrayed. It is difficult however to judge this movie by itself, as it is an unfinished story. The ending as is now presented is of course unsatisfying, and we will have to wait for part II and III before a good judgement can be given about the this movie. For now, I give it the benefit of the doubt.

title: spectacular
review:
The absolute best movie of the year, stunning both visually and emotionally. The scenes in Moria and of the Argonath are breathtaking. I can't believe I have to wait another year to see the next installment.

One disagreement on interpretation though: Galadriel and Lothlorien were *so* much darker than in the books. I did not get the impression that Lothlorien was a place the Fellowship would not want to leave and Galadriel was very ambiguous. Also, I just can't make myself like Liv Tyler.

But beyond this, a wonderful and thrilling adventure. Can't wait to see the Ents! Oh, and to the guy with the really long comment on the combined details page: Girls do NOT need a romance to make us sit through a movie. We just need an Aragorn ;) kidding!

title: not nearly frightened enough...
review:
"Three Rings for the Elven-kings under the sky, Seven for the Dwarf-lords in their halls of stone, Nine for Mortal Men doomed to die, One for the Dark Lord on his dark throne, In the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie. One Ring to rule them all, One Ring to find them, One Ring to bring them all and in the darkness bind them In the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie."

As I write this I'm enjoying a cup of fine Ceylon tea. Why tea, you ask? Why not and ale, or `something stronger'? Because, I am afraid, when there's serious business to discuss and matters are everpressing, tea is the drink of choice. I sense the presence of evil during these dark times. The Nazgul are afoot. It is not a time for Merriment, or for catching up with old friends. It is a time for action. The ring is near.

Back in the days of the Shoppe, in the quaint village of Isla Vista, we lived an easy and simple life, free of adventure. We knew this would not last for long. My friend Phil often spoke of the ring, saying that any day we may find it, then our paths would be clear. But find it we did not. And, since this time, our lives have become disjointed, muddled, and un-focused. But the forces are amassing in the east. Sauron has again become active. A foreboding sense of turmoil has come to the forefront to my thoughts. Dark creatures lurk in the shadows. Our conversations are not our own. The holidays are upon us but don't be lulled into thinking all is comfortable. You say that you are frightened, but you are not nearly frightened enough.

New light was shed on this last night whilst viewing Peter Jackson's new film, Lord of the Rings. The film chronicles the first third of that great adventure which took place many years ago, before the ring in our story was even conceived. Back then, there were other rings, that were all powerful, until one ring was forged that could rule them all. It is a story of tragedy, hope, and heroic deeds. It is a story that should not be joked about or taken lightly, because it's our history and, as you all know so well, history has a way of repeating itself.

Jackson's re-telling of this epic is about as flawless as could be imagined. Save for the edits that needed to be made for brevity's sake, he has not missed out on much. The film looks shockingly beautiful. The choice of New Zealand was a stroke of genius. For one, it matches the books. But, more important, it's scenery that most of the world doesn't know, so we can't ever feel like it's being shot somewhere that we have pre-formed memories about. It looks, if possible, even better than I imagined it. The acting is so good that it's really beyond even a mention. For these are the characters of the tale: Gandalf, Frodo, Aragorn ... as if they have been brought to life. There will be no George Clooney as Frank Sinatra substitutions here. What we see it how it was. How it looked, sounded, and felt to be there.

If there is one problem with this telling, it's that it still feels a little rushed. The hobbits' journey out of the Shire didn't allow them time to slowly realize the situation that they were getting involved with. Of course, we all knew that Tom Bombadil would not be taking part. Even still, they stumble upon Bree a little too quickly, and the Nazgul are a bit too ever present at their heels. Still, it is remarkable to be able and capture the story as well as it did, because an unabridged LOTR's would have to be 30 hours long!

In Bree, we have what has always been my favorite scene. Where the serendipitous adventures meet the reticent king. It's the gateway to the real world, where life is not going to be easy or simple any longer. We see the rogues of the world. It's like the bar scene in Star Wars, or any number of port scenes in historic tales: The Prancing Pony or Rick's Cafe American. The meeting with Strider is the focal point to me. How this is handled will give insight to the way in which the tale will unfold. Aragorn is a complicated man living what is, on the surface, an uncomplicated lifestyle. Because of this he is misunderstood and feared. A king living as a ranger; a conflicted man; a man full of the deepest torment: a man that is regal and confident, yet scared and torn. This scene must be able to show this, without words or actions. Jackson pulls it off. It is brilliant. Bravo to Viggo Mortensen for understanding this about him, but didn't I say we are above critiquing the players of this performance.

A lot of folks had trepidations about Arwen. My only comment is that she was great. Tyler not only holds her own, but also treats the role with the highest reverence. Ditto for everyone at the Council of Elrond. This could have easily become a melodramatic Hollywood mess, with cliched characters hamming it up for advertising dollars. But it didn't. It remained serious and restrained. Sure, Sam, Merry and Pippin are funny. But that's how life is: always a touch of humor in even the direst of circumstances. And Rivendell: it was even more glorious than what was conjured in my mind's eye.

The final act may have had too much action. Certainly, this is important for audience numbers. It is also important because this film's aim is to visualize a book. We already have the words. But, still, the story is at its best when dialogue, or Tolkien, is being spoken. The action is part of the story, for sure, but the story is in the words and the ways in which they are uttered. Galadriel seems a tad too conflicted and loses a bit of her airiness but, really, she isn't around long enough to make this judgment sound. Boromir, on the other hand, is played and handled beautifully. I think that a little too much torment is caused with the wearing of the ring but, again, it's just a personal feeling about it-after all, it's `my precious' so there has to be some good feelings associated with it. However, maybe it is all caused because Sauron is closing in on it. Perhaps it doesn't always cause such anguish. But, when all is said and done, I am just nitpicking. This piece transcends the art of filmmaking.

In the words of Professor Arthur Ayers in the cult film Icarus Descending, `It is tale I will not tell willingly. A tale that requires, what was it Coleridge said -- ah, yes, a tale that required the suspension of disbelief'

Suspension of disbelief? Perhaps that will work as an excuse for many. As for me, it's a tale every bit as real as my life; it is the world around me in which I live.

"All that is gold does not glitter, Not all those who wander are lost; The old that is strong does not wither, Deep roots are not reached by the frost. From the ashes a fire shall be woken, A light from the shadows shall spring; Renewed shall be blade that was broken, The crownless again shall be king."

title: Thank You Peter Jackson!
review: I first read "Lord of the Rings" when I was a teenager (early 1980s).  It is hard to overstate how much I enjoyed the story or how much it influenced my imagination.  I read the books, but somehow Peter Jackson read my mind.  If I made a movie about this greatest of all epic stories, it wouldn't be too much different from what I saw last night!!! Everyone in the theatre I was in last night would have gladly stayed right in their seats to see it.  Frodo Lives!

title: Excellent
review:
Considering the time and budget limitations of the movie format, this is a really good adaptation. It seems like it would be an impossible task to turn these books into films and include 100% of everything, "The Fellowship of the Ring" easily could have been two or three three-hour films. One can't help thinking that the director must be completely mad to take on the task. Where the movie excels is in bringing key scenes from the books to life, many uncannily close to what I and others I spoke with imagined would look like. Also, the various components that made up the film, costumes, props, music, special effects, speech, editing and "laws of physics" flowed together naturally without drawing attention to themselves.

It would be impossible for me to be objective about a film about "Lord of the Rings", such a beloved story to so many. I probably would have been happy just to see the characters on screen even if the movie had been awful, and would have given it a high rating anyway. If I wasn't so familiar with the storyline, the motivations, actions, and relationships of the characters in "Fellowship" might have been very confusing. I had high expectations and was not disappointed. I was surprised at how the film effectively conveyed the changing moods of "Fellowship" as the story progressed through the key acts. "Fellowship" is probably the slowest of all three books, leading me to think that the other films will be even more fantastic. I will view this film many more times. I hope this film does very well so that New Line will be more willing to release longer versions of the following two films to theaters.

I was surprised at the amount of screen time given to Bilbo's "back story", there's no way that "The Hobbit" won't also be made into a film at some point, because these films are going to make a lot of money.

title: A good movie, but I'm a Tolkien fanatic
review:
SPOILERS, and I mean of this film adaptation, not just of the story.

Also, if you don't know and love the story, then you probably wont want to waste your time reading my comments.

I just saw the movie last night, and I have to go see it again in order to determine what I think of it. This is because when I saw it all I could think of was, no, that's not right. I understand that in 3 hours you can't recreate and entire story, but where his recreations are unfaithful to the vision are where I have my problems.

First off, Gandalf is not always portrayed correctly. Gandalf, in the books is always a wise, super-human being. Heck, if you really follow Tolkien you know that he is not human, he is of a race that was created before the world itself was created (as was Sauron and Saruman). This is not a being that would bump his head in Bilbo's hole (home), tell of the Ring's location to Saruman or need Frodo's help to solve the riddle of opening the door to the Mines of Moria. In the books he also had a lot more real power than was displayed here. I can only guess that Jackson doesn't want to show too much too soon or we would not be wowed in the future films.

Merry and Pippin seem to have gone along almost accidentally. You are not even given over to know that they are close friends with Frodo, nor do you see their serious side, but rather they are shown as comedy relief.

The Ringwraiths in the movie are a joke. The hobbits were able to fool them and get away from them over and over again without even trying. In the book I was truly terrified of these beings, they were evil incarnate, and only great power could drive them back. The only reason Frodo got away from them on Weathertop is because they had already stabbed him and they figured it was only a matter of time before he was theirs, but in the movie you actually are given the impression that Strider is able to fight off a whole group of them, singlehandedly.

The ring itself, and the world the wearer enters, is also modified. In the books the wearer enters the world of the Ringwraiths (thus is invisible in the normal world), but just because he is in that alternate dimension, does not mean that the Wraiths can automatically see him. They would have to be in his presence in order to see him, but in the movie, Sauron himself, all the way in Mordor, was able to see Frodo in Bree. Heck, if that was the case, then why didn't he see Bilbo at his party, or for that matter, all of the other times that Bilbo wore the ring?

Finally, though I could go on and on, the Council of Elrond is a joke. The movie makes it sound like all of the attendees were summoned, whereas we know that they were all there for their own reasons, reasons that could have been explained without adding too much length to the film, while definitely keeping to the spirit and making other things easier to explain. I have no idea how the rest of the story is going to unfold with Boromir not seeking Elrond because of the dream/riddle. It makes no sense that he would have been there, especially considering the war that was going on. Boromir also treats Aragorn with disrespect when he finds out who he is, something that he would never have done in the book, jealousy maybe, but not disrespect. He wasn't even supposed to know that the line of Isildur still remained, yet his only comment when he learned who Aragorn was was that "Gondor needed no kings."

I'd better stop now. In general I thought the movie was good. I plan on seeing it again, soon, as now I am prepared to accept the modifications, so maybe I'll have a better chance of enjoying the movie for what it is, rather than for what I wanted it to be.

title: Being a big fan of the book I was worried how hollywood would handle the movie
review: But WOW! Of course they left some stuff out, but they kept in all the goodies I always thought 'That would look SWEET' in a movie. Best three hours I've spent in a long time.

review:

But then I realized that it's a movie and as such the pacing needs to be different.

The second time I went I could really enjoy the movie on it's own merits and thus have to say that in my opinion it's the best movie ever.

title: a dream come true
review: as a long time Lord of the Rings, I was full of hope yet skeptical as I sat down to watch the Fellowship. All doubt was blown away as soon as Cate Blanchett's intro to the world of the Ring set the stage for the film. What followed was three hours of, dare I say it, Perfection. Everyone of the nine members of the Fellowship are right for their roles. Ian McKellen and Elijah Wood both shine. The action scenes, immaculate. The music, haunting and majestic. The vistas, well let's just say that after watching this, you'll want to visit New Zealand. The villains are all great, particularly the dark riders and their screeching. And prepare to drop your load when subjected to the Balrog. This is a movie that everyone, and I mean, EVERYONE, should see. Forget movies made by producers with dollar signs in their eyes, this is a movie with vision and it deserves to be huge.
