title: The film I've been waiting my whole life for.
review: At last someone has done it.  Finally a real version of The Lord Of The Rings.  Everything about this film is spectacular.  From the script to the acting to the effects.  It was probably the best movie going experience that I've ever had. The characters are just as I imagined they should be.  Ian McKellan is the perfect Gandalf.  It would be a crime if he doesn't get an Oscar for this film.  Elijah Wood IS Frodo.  I could not believe how well he handled such a difficult role.  As far as the rest of the fellowship, my two favorites were Aragorn and Legolas.  Viggo Mortensen really captured the spirit of the reluctant heir to the throne of Gondor. Aragorn is flawed but he fights for what he knows is right,  Orlando Bloom was a huge surprise as Legolas.  He was just such a real joy to watch.  He was just one hell of a character.  Probably the biggest surprise was Liv Tyler as Arwen.  She handled the role exceptionally well.  She didn't even sound like herself. Probably my favorite location  was Moria.  The gloomy atmosphere and the perils they faced, chiefly the cave troll and the Balrog, were excellent.  It was also in Moria that we are teased with our first closeup of Gollum, just in the shadows.  His eyes really freaked me out. I can't wait for the Two Towers so that I can see more of him. I only have two problems with the film.  First, it was too short.  Even at three hours I wanted more.  I didn't want it to end. Second, I have to wait a year to see The Two Towers and another year after that to see The Return Of The King.  What can I say, it's going to be a long year.

title: Better than Star Wars!
review: One of the best films in our generation.  A magical and enchanting experience.  Never thought anything could come close to Star Wars - but this one surpassed it! I can hardly wait for the next two episodes to be screened.

title: Outstanding
review:
First of all let's say that this film (and the ones to follow) will unquestionably be the standard by which all future fantasy films will be judged. Given the less than glorious history of fantasy in cinema that may sound a little bit like calling someone the world's tallest midget but, fortunately, this is also a film that transcends its genre. It's a flawed but ultimately thrilling film that flashes enough of the brilliance of both Peter Jackson and J.R.R. Tolkien to keep most movie-goers hungry to see the next chapter unfold in twelve-months time.

I saw FOTR with a group of eleven that was composed of two people who had read the books multiple times, three casual fans who had read the books years ago, and six people who were Tolkien virgins. At the end of the film all of us had the same major gripe - that we would have to wait a year to see more. That's the sign of a filmmaker who has hooked his audience.

It's not a perfect movie. The first half is unevenly paced (a trait it shares with the book) and those who have said that Jackson is better at portraying the dark than the light are right. Rivendell and the Council of Elrond in particular come off awkwardly. Ironically, it is Arwen and the infamous Ford scene which are the highlight of the first half of the film. Liv Tyler has an undeniable screen presence and a feminine voice comes as a welcome change to the relentlessly male-driven story.

The need to dole out exposition and backstory in large measures also causes the film to drag at times in the first half. But when the Fellowship enters the heart of darkness in Moria, Jackson is finally in his element and the film soars from that point on. Moria, quite simply, will go down as one of the great action sequences in film history. From Moria, to Lothlorien, to the breaking of the Fellowship, Jackson explores the dark side of Tolkien's epic brilliantly and the film reaches it's peak in the final act.

Peter Jackson's greatest accomplishment was that he made Middle-earth feel real - it felt like a real place, at a real time, with a real history. This is what Tolkien himself accomplished so brilliantly and if Jackson had failed at this, the film itself would have failed. He didn't fail.

The acting was superb, the cinematography stunning, and the CGI was extraordinary with only a few brief jarring moments.

All in all, a damn good film. Bring on The Two Towers.

title: Good but Hyped
review:
First, I'd like to say that I have NOT read the novel, this is my views towards the movie ONLY.

The first half (1:30) of the movie is all about boring (interesting? not me) Hobbits life. Instead of focusing on important events with smooth transactions of others, this movie seems spending too much time on unimportant ones. I have NOT read the novel, but from what I've heard, it's sort like quest after quest, meeting interesting people, exploring new worlds, and goes on and on. I just don't see that in the movie.

Yes i do understand the director is trying to show that it's a long journey, however the National-Geographic-Explorer-type shooting of scenery needs to STOP after like 10 times. I'm annoyed after seeing it for 10 times, it's tiring. Not as much action as I'd like to see, but maybe that's true to the novel, which I haven't read. Not as true to the spirit of the internal struggle faced by the characters, I can't feel the emotion.

To conclude my words, this movie is good but it loses the fine point of balance. I wouldn't recommend people to see unless they are interested in the D&D setting. It is WAY TOO LONG, cut the first hour completely then I would feel better. I give it a 7/10 for such production but I believe I submit a 6 due to my fast itchy-trigger finger.

title: Truly amazing.
review: Faithful to the book and dazzling to behold, Lord of the Rings is the beginning of an astounding epic! Though I have only read the Hobbitt and the Fellowship of the Ring, I can tell that this film was made BY fans FOR fans. Do NOT miss this movie on the big screen, or you will regret it.

title: Never read any of the novels, but was blown away...
review:
The only real attempt I've made to read any of the three Lord Of The Rings novels was the back cover which gives a preview...so I didn't know what to expect from this film.

Often film adaptations from books end up dramatically horrible, when I saw 'The Fellowship of the Ring' with a few others who had read the trilogy, they of course ranted about missing pieces and the short span of the story when compared to the real thing.

Honestly, the ending scene w/Sam and Frodo continuing to Mordor was a cliffhanger..nobody expected it to end right then and there and I think they didn't want it to. It really is a brilliant thing to make these three books into three films separately, rather than to compact them all into one - Most definately will I see 'The Two Towers' and 'The Return of the King' but one year between each flick...that's a hard wait..

title: Brilliant!!
review: This is possibly the best movie I've ever seen. I was a major Star Wars fanatic when the first three came out. The Fellowship of The Rings blows Star Wars out of the water. The cinematography is breath-taking;the special effects and computer animation couldn't be better. And you won't see finer acting than in this movie right down to the subtle nuances of a sudden shift of the eyes. Emotions run the gambit from comedy to sorrow. And scary?--WOW! I saw it twice on opening day. There is so much to visually take in,you have to see it more than once. The three hours fly by leaving you wanting more--NOW. This part is just for Peter Jackson-Peter,are you reading this? We can't wait a whole year!! In short-great movie!Go see it--go,go,go.

title: One film to rule them all
review:
The most powerful and elegant fantasy film of the year is Peter Jackson's "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring," the first of three films to dramatize J.R.R. Tolkien's beloved trilogy.

From the film's compelling, visually stunning prologue, it's clear that we're in the hands of two master storytellers: Tolkien and Jackson.

Jackson's film is a triumph of casting. It's nearly impossible to imagine a finer choice for the role of Frodo Baggins than Elijah Wood. As the young hobbit who answers a life-changing call to adventure, Wood combines wide-eyed innocence and a deep sense of wonder with innate intelligence and warm humor.

Ian McKellen is superb as Gandalf the wizard, clearly relishing the role that is great grandfather to "Star Wars'" Obi Wan Kenobi and "Harry Potter's" Dumbledore. This wizard is no mere guardian mentor, but a heroic participant in the adventure with fears and demons of his own.

The spirit of Tolkien runs deep in the performances of Ian Holm as Bilbo Baggins, Viggo Mortensen as the tarnished hero Aragorn and Cate Blanchett who brings a stunning intensity to the elf queen Galadriel.

The characters' inner lives are as rich as the film's spectacular production design and Jackson's direction moves effortlessly from quiet moments of intimacy to scenes of operatic grandeur and heart-stopping adventure.

An approaching flock of black birds hasn't been this ominous since Alfred Hitchcock was around, and the heroes' escape from an underground cave is like nothing this film fan has ever seen.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" is quite possibly the best fantasy adventure film ever made. At the end of its two and a half hours, I sat stunned, dazed and hungry for more.

title: UTTERLY FASCINATING!
review: FINALLY! After DREG such as: Tomb Raider, Mummy Returns, Ghosts of Mars, Evolution...comes a fantasy film to end ALL fantasy films! This movie is so engrossing, I didnt even know 3 hours went by! I have never read the books, but one doesnt need to familarize themselves ahead of time, because the beginning of the film supplies a GREAT backstory prologue to let the viewer know the required info. Incredible SFX, writing, directing, and acting...I actually BELIEVED there was a Wizard named Gandolf...thats how GREAT Ian is in the role! Run....or drive....but do NOT hesitate to see this FILM!

title: FINALLY! A fantasy done right.
review: If you have, like me, long been awaiting a fantasy movie that lives up to the scope and vision of a fantasy novel, it's finally here! I have never even read any of Tolkien's books and yet was completely captivated by this movie. Peter Jackson and his crew have done a magnificent job of bringing a fantasy world to life--breathtaking views of ethereal cities, convincing special effects, and a whole cast of characters the viewer actually cares about, topped off with music that will make your heart pound. Brilliant! I was very impressed and cannot wait to see the next two. (You'll ESPECIALLY appreciate it if you've ever suffered through the animated movie, or had high hopes for Dragonheart or Dungeons and Dragons....)

title: A Film That Touched My Soul.(contains plot spoilers)
review: I will start with this, I have never seen a movie that touched me in a way this did. Peter Jackson has outdone himself in directing this piece of cinematic magic. The other actors are outstanding as well. Viggo Mortenson's Aragorn is the true action hero I imagined and Elijah Wood is Frodo. No one could have done it better. The scenery and buildings were wonderful. No doubt most of the movie was computer effects but stunning none the less. My heart dropped as Gandalf fell from the bridge and I cried as The hobbits shed tears for their dead friend. I jumped as creatures attacked my heroes and I lept for joy everytime Legolas sent an arrow into an orc or Aragorn skewerd some monster with his sword. Now if the plot alone doesn't grab you the music will. The composer (Howard Shore) has outdone himself. In the end of the film the song "Breaking of the Fellowship" made me cry because I knew with a song like that the end was near. I only hope that people watch this movie and feel the same way I did. That you are not watching a movie but that you are watching the struggle of a people and their hopes resting on a fellowship of nine Frodo,Samwise,Merry,and Pippin the hobbits. Aragorn and Boromir the humans. Legolas the elf. Gimli the dwarf and Gandalf the wizard. I hope you will be touched and amazed and that the characters will not seem like characters to you, but people.Be prepared Tolkien fan or not this movie will grab you and bring you along for the ride. From the Shire to Mordor you will be amazed. Hang on and enjoy this movie. I can only hope they decide to release the other 2 early I don't know if I can wait!

title: An Excellent Companion to an Excellent Book!
review:
I think it was in October that I decided I wanted to read the first book in the Lord of the Rings Trilogy, by J.R.R. Tolkein. I became enthralled in the story and was very excited to see the movie. Even after having incredibly high expectations, I was not disappointed. This movie truly delivered, and is the perfect companion to the book.

Frodo Baggins (Elijah Wood), a little hobbit who lives in the Shire in Middle-Earth, has just received a seemingly harmless gift from his uncle, Bilbo (Ian Holm): a simple gold ring. Frodo soon discovers from his friend Gandalf (Sir Ian McKellan) that this is no simple ring. It happens to be the one ruling ring, over all other powerful rings, that once belonged to the evil Sauron. Now Sauron is trying to find his ring, which will give him power over everything, and the ring is trying to find Sauron. The only way to keep this most terrible thing from happening, is for the ring to be cast into the fires of Mount Doom from whence it came. And it seems our dear Frodo will have to lead the way to Mount Doom, in the heart of Mordor where Sauron resides.

To help Frodo along on his journey is a fellowship: the heroic ranger Strider (Viggo Mortensen), his hobbit friends Sam (Sean Astin), Merry (Dominic Monaghan), and Pippin (Billy Boyd), the emotionally tortured Boromir (Sean Bean), the wize wizard Gandalf, Legolas the elf (Orlando Bloom), and Gimli the dwarf (John Rhys-Davies). They will form a bond as they travel towards Mordor, passing through breathtaking lands, like Lothlorien, and unspeakable terrors, like the Mines of Moria.

Considering I finished the book the day before I saw the movie, I knew every tiny discrepancy between the two. And, I must say that every discrepancy was called for. There is absolutely no way the movie could have followed the book exactly--it would have been 10 hours long. Omitting characters from the movie that were in the book--Glorfindel, Tom Bombadil--did not take too much away from the actual story. However, I do feel that it is so important to read the book before going to see the movie. Then, when the fellowship visits exotic lands, like Rivendell or Lothlorien, the moviegoer knows the history of the lands and what makes these lands so special. I would also recommend to anyone who has read the books to see the movie. It gives an excellent visual for Middle-earth, and helps personify the characters, who were by the way perfectly cast! In my opinion, the movie and the book are companions and one should not be seen or read without the other being seen or read. It makes the whole experience much richer.

I will have to agree with everyone who has commented about the wonderfulness of Ian McKellan as Gandalf. He was Gandalf--it's as simple as that. Wood did an excellent job as Frodo, having no problems portraying the inner turmoil that he feels when the ring takes him over, but also showing the innocence and naivity in the hobbit. The special effects crew did an excellent job with the height differences; the shortness of the hobbits never bothered me, although I found their feet really gross. I was most impressed with Viggo Mortensen as Aragorn (aka Strider). It's probably becaused I admired his noble, loyal character in the book, but I just fell in love with him. Everyone should have an Aragorn to look after him or her.

One of the only characters that I wasn't impressed with in the movie was Elrond (Hugo Weaving). I guess I just had a mental image of Elrond being this truly wise and wonderful elf, who really wanted to help Frodo find a solution. In the movie, I thought he just came off as a jerk, demanding that Frodo get the ring out of Rivendell as fast as possible. Other than this, I absolutely adored this movie and can't wait for the next installment. Congratulations Peter Jackson! You've created a masterpiece.

title: Speed bumps ahead.
review: Since 1969, the year I discovered J.R.R. Tolkien, I have tried to read The Lord of the Rings twice a year. I have read everything I could find on Middle Earth and consider myself a dilettante-amature expert on Tolkien and Middle Earth. The movie, Fellowship of the Ring, was by any standard a wonderful film. And yet . . . well, we will get to that in a minute. But first, the good stuff. Mordor transferred from book to film better than the book described it. My deepest, meanest imaginings of Mordor did not compare to how absolutely dismal Jackson made the place look in FOTR. Ringwraiths: right on! Hobbit society: perfect. Elves: noble and genteel warrior-poets. Of the nine members of the Fellowship, seven made the transition to film perfectly or almost. The best were: Gandalf, gentle but quick-tempered; Legolas; Gimli (this WAS Gimli!); Boromir, brave warrior with a human's weakness. Aragorn was very good, although less woods-crafty than I had pictured him. Sam was also very good, better than I was expecting. Still, he was not as subservient as I had imagined Frodo's employee would be. As for Frodo, I had imagined Elijah Wood playing the role long before any casting announcements were made. The Merry and Pippin characters diverted from The Book more than any of the other characters, by far. Even so, they were fine. The non-Fellowship characters were all well-represents and well-played: Galadriel; Elrond; the Orcs. The CGI graphics of the troll and the Balrog were perfect. Perfect! They were all as they should be, but . .. But. I took my wife and my adult children to see the movie with me. None of them have read The Lord of the Rings. As the movie progressed, I was delighted with Jackson's adaptation. But I was very aware of the modifications he made to the story to bring it to the screen: Frodo's ignorance of the existance of the ring or Bilbo's plans; the suddend escape of Frodo from the Shire (hardly the 17 years that passed from Bilbo's 111th birthday until Frodo's 50th birthday); the nature of the Council of Elrond; and so on. I was aware of the differences. Those small changes were like speed bumps to the flow of the film's story. It was MY awareness of Tolkien's work that disrupted my attention to the film, not any flaw in the film. The rest of my family was totally absorbed in the movie. I realize that my knowledge of the novel keep me from getting into the film as much as they. Even so, the film was totally faithful to the spirit and story of the book. My minor complain is, the film is NOT the book and such differences as existe are distracting. Does it mean I will not see the film again? No. Does it mean I won't purchase the DVD when it is available? No. I give this movie a 10 out of 10. Non-readers will probably find this movie more fluid than I did, but that does not mean I don't LOVE this movie. It fulfills my 30-year-old wish.

title: Well Done
review: I have been looking forward to seeing this movie for sometime now. I was concerned whether the film-makers would stay close to the story or turn it into some commercial junk to sell stuff in the stores. The "making of" program did a little to alleviate that. I found the movie very good. Although a few things were changed in regards to the story. Fans of the book might be a little disappointed with some of the artistic liberties taken, but the movie does a pretty good job of catching the essence of the story. The images of such places as Hobbiton, Rivendell, and the mines of Moria, were spectacular. My image of Lothlorien is brighter than they portrayed but the film could not spare the time to linger there as the fellowship did in the book. Was it worth a couple bucks per hour to sit through this? Yep!I've paid more and got much less in return . That D&D film last year was as bad as this is good. At least it's only a year until the sequel!

title: Is this what Tolkien envisioned?
review:
If you have never read the book you will LOVE this movie. If, however you saw the movie and are now planning to read the book then you have lost something. No, I didn't say that backwards. The book is fifty thousand times better than the movie. If you see the movie and THEN read the book then you lost out on the hands down most incredible piece of fiction ever written. In your mind Kate Blanchett will always be Galadriel, Elijah Wood will always be Frodo and so on and so forth. I feel sorry for all the fans of the book that claim that this is what they imagined when they read it. No offense ,but they must have the worst imaginations in the world. Lothlorien was supposed to be a restful place of light, happiness and peace ,a place where all cares are forgotten. Instead it's dark and dreary,(aren't mallorn leaves supposed to be gold?) and Galadriel is stern and frightening. Where was the box of soil she gives to Samwise? Isn't that kind of crucial to the end of the story? I can see why they cut out Tom Bombadil and the Barrowdowns, but would it have killed them to cast Glorfindel or explain Caradhras? What about great moments like Gandalf telling Saruman,"He that breaks a thing to find out what it is has left the path of wisdom." The only scene that was good was Gandalf facing down the Balrog. That was pretty awesome.

Tolkien was never typical fantasy which is why I love his work. There is a spirit behind it, a pureness that I have not encountered elsewhere. They took it and turned it into your ordinary Dungeons & Dragons/Willow fantasy poop. However:) if you don't compare it to the book at all it might be the best movie ever made. That's the genius that is Tolkien.

title: The Fellowship: The Rediscovery Of Movie Art
review:
I was one of the "Pre-read" arriving with a racing pulse(4000 rpm), dark (to middling gray) anticipation, and a smattering of dread. I had initially read that the intro was turgid and would be dropped, and that the music was occasionally "wishy washy" and "out of place".

Ah.

Ahem.

Please excuse me as I clear my very vocal pipes.

I was instantly engulfed in a Smorgasbord of Pre-History, clearing things up for those new to the Middle-Earth scene (Once you know who the bad guys are, you know when to throw popcorn AND eat Scandinavian food?)

Lesson One: Tame, this film is not. Agreeably, it has a minor rating, but when did this discount those of us who need no imagination to understand the bloodiness of war? From battlefields teeming with the dead and dying we fly to the innocent and innocuous farmstead, from sky piercing, avalanche laden mountain, to the ethereal, tranquil yet foreboding abode of the elves. From delightful heart-warming scenes of friendship, to sometimes shocking, always stunning images of the workings of Sauron's evil, you are presented with the best of both classical dialogue, original sets and values, while simultaneously being bombarded with what feels like set piece after set piece of sheer cinematic excellence. And yet in no way does it become negligent to our interest in the people we observe.

Lesson Two: The books' characters become flesh: The dichotomy of Boromir, and indeed Strider, coupled with the warm friendship between the Hobbits, is portrayed with the care and attention it deserves, and you can't help but feel the on-screen emotions reciprocated within yourself.

Pardon?

A fast action movie where you genuinely care?

Care you do, and fast it is. From enthralling camera pans over sprawling, warring hordes, from lofty tower to mining pit (thus the minor rating) in seconds, and sumptuous glides over steep river valley, lush forest and cool blue glacier, the viewer feasts upon the natural beauty of New Zealand (Last Minute Middle Earth Stand-in), and the digital glory of the finest computer-rendered graphics to grace the screen. Subtle, human-to-hobbit-sized shrinking effects (with other great camera tricks for the same big-small illusion), to the jaw-dropping sight of thousands of individually rendered creatures navigating, in discrete, personally flavoured fashion, across a huge virtual canvas, seamlessly (really) blended with the "Actual World Footage".

Again, really.

It's that good.

What I cannot convey is the way 3 hours slip away from you; how deeply you feel for the characters, understand their fears and their desire to hide, to return to their former, safer, lives; why you want to charge in and take control, oust the evil for yourself; and why, overall, you leave the cinema filled with excitement, hope, and perhaps, as I did, that feeling that something profoundly important and magical just happened.

Thank you to all those talented people for bringing us something special to the screen, where pervading, enduring human values meet contemporary technique in harmony. An outstanding cast, never underplayed, nor heavy-handed, slowly unfold their inner conflicts, strengths, and wants, and you realise that, for those who will survive, you will discover much more. It could have been so easy to ruin this for all. I believe that Mr Jackson and the vast crew of imagineers have created something beautiful.

Something poetic and something enduring.

And the Balrog kicks ass.

title: Well, not the exactly THE masterpiece we waited for...
review: The movie isn't (as I said above) the masterpiece we've been waiting for all the time. The has some quite boring scenes (The love story thing at Elron's House and those stupidly long traveling-parts) that make this movie a bit too long (if you cut this scenes it would be half an hour shorter). Also some of the scenes (especially the one with the ringwraiths in the bedroom) looked like a direct copy from the old animated movie. So, this movie isn't true to the hype that was made about it, but it is still a good but long movie.

title: Excellent Start
review: It has been a very long time since I was able to walk away from a movie and be shocked at the amount of time I have spent in the theatre.  I was that engrossed.  The acting is superb.  The storyline (though not completely true to the book, does not deviate much) draws you in and pulls you along. (Keeping you on the edge of your see most of the time)  The cinematography is gorgeous, and the costuming is perfect.  If you enjoy a great fantasy movies (this surpasses Willow and LadyHawke and is probably neck and neck with Legend in my list of all time favorite fantasy movies)you must see this in the theatre.  I will be there on opening day again for the second one.

title: Great Movie
review: This movie has it all, romance, action and non-stop adventure. I have only read the books once and I did not take the time to develop a definite picture in my mind about all the characters and places. I now have that picture and it's beautiful. I am so happy for all the Lord of The RIng fans, they have done a great job in creating this world. I loved this movie and will have to see at least two more times!

title: An epic film on a scale the world has not seen before !
review:
I was pleasantly surprised by this film.

My hopes for this film were very high, and I was almost certain they couldn't be met. The film starts strong, with an epilogue which blew me away ! The battle scenes are truly spectacular and the special effects work brilliantly. From the trailers I saw I was worried the comic side of the Hobbits would be underplayed, but Peter Jackson has really hit the mark in this respect. Bilbo , Pippin and Sam get some great laughs. Bilbo's farewell party is great. The fireworks are brilliant, the Hobbits endearing and the antics of Merry and Pippin hilarious.

On the down side I was a bit disappointed in the elves. In my mind the elves were more striking, taller with an unworldly beauty. And the journey through Lorien seems a bit rushed (but then would you want to have an extra half hour added to the film !) Galadriel had some moments which looked a bit weak to me. The scene where she envisions, what would happen if she takes hold of the Ring is very powerful though. That makes up for a lot. And she is beautiful ! Elrond works for me. He has a strong presence. Legolas too. Swift. The way that bow just keeps going on...

The cinematography is breathtaking. New Zealand couldn't have had a better way to promote itself. The sweeping camera moves combined with the excellent cgi added to the epic scale of this film in a manner which sent chills down my spine !

title: Amazing Journey
review:
Power can be held in the smallest of things.

This film is the best I have seen so far this year. I remember when I was eleven years old I watched a cartoon with the weirdest animation at that time which completely fascinated me. The cartoon was called The Hobbit.

J.R.R.Tolkein wrote the books which this film is based on. This film is the beginning of the trilogy. The second and third films will be released the week of Christmas in 2002 and 2003 respectively (The Two Towers and The Return of the King).All three films were filmed back to back to back. In the years between releases they are doing re-writes and editing.

The Lord of the Rings is a very complicated yet simple story told very well by director Peter Jackson, best known for The Frighteners(which flopped). The subject matter is the most imaginary, creative, far fetched fantasy world ever attempted to be put on film. There are elves, dwarves, hobbits, dark lords, humans, dragons, you name the imaginary character, it's in this film.

Elijah Wood heads the cast as a hobbit on a mission. Wood turns in a fine performance as he has in his previous work(The Good Son and Deep Impact). Sir Ian McKellen and Viggo Mortensen are probably the best known supporting cast besides Liv Tyler. They all do great jobs in this movie. The acting is not what makes this a great movie, believe me it does help. However it is the storyline and the way it is presented, the excellent direction, the enormous set designs, the landscape(filmed entirely in New Zealand), music score, wardrobe and the lastly the special effects. Peter Jackson covers and takes care of the little details which Tolkein purist should appreciate. When you combine all of those qualities used in this film, you believe Tolkein's characters have been brought to life.

I'm not a Tolkein purist by any stretch. I'm sure there are those that will say after seeing this film it variates from the book some, if it didn't the movie would be 6 hours instead of 3. It did not matter to me, the film is a true escape from reality. To me movies are meant to do a few things: Entertain (make you laugh, cry or both Enlighten (make you think) Make you forget your troubles(take you to another world)

Obviously all films don't do this, but this one does film does all of the above.

It is not for anyone under 13, there many violent battle scenes and disturbing images for the faint of heart.

RC

title: A flawed masterpiece
review: There may be niggling details I would have changed, but taken as a whole this is the finest piece of epic filmmaking that I have ever seen. Particular favorite moments included Gandalf and Frodo's conversation in Moria, Boromir's swordwork with Pippin and Merry, and the fight with the Cave Troll.

title: A landmark film!
review:
Made with passion, intelligence, imagination and skill - this IS a landmark film. The acting is superb, especially for a film of this genre. I think this is the first time since the original Star Wars trilogy that I have found the main characters to be so compelling and this is the reason why the film works so well. It was always going to be near impossible to include every aspect of the book and I think Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens and Peter Jackson have written a very courageous screenplay.

FOTR features a lot of computer-generated effects, but they have been used in such a way that they do not distract the audience from the main storyline. I do feel however, that the greatest visual effect' was created by the New Zealand landscape itself. The makeup is very good  the Orcs' and Uruk-hai' are genuinely terrifying. Howard Shore's score is also very effective.

If parts II and III are even half as good as this one then I think the LOTR trilogy will surpass even the original Star Wars films in terms of achievement. Roll on Christmas 2002.

Rating: 9/10.

title: Blasphemy!
review: What a great movie! The acting was top notch, the special effects were better than anything my imagination could have ever come up with and the sets were fantastic. Don't get me wrong, the special effects and sets aren't what make the movie but they are a strong influence on the overall scope of the picture. The cinematography was breath taking. I never saw such a wondrous place while reading the novels (which I loved) and I never felt the depth of emotion that the movie brought to the characters. That in my opinion is what really makes the movie. In many ways the movie was better than my memory of the book. Some may say that is down right blasphemy but that's just my humble opinion. Now that I have seen Middle Earth in this way I am going to re-read the novels and perhaps see them in a different light. The one and only thing I found disappointing in Fellowship of the Ring is the knowledge that I have to wait a whole year for the sequel. I have to admit that I was a little wary about the movie when I learned that Peter Jackson, the same guy that brought Bad Taste to the world, was directing but he has made one of the best movies I have ever seen. My hat goes off to him for having the vision and imagination that I obviously lack and for bringing this enchanting world into being. I have seen many, many movies, science fiction and fantasy are at the top of my favorites and Lord of the Rings now takes the place at the top of that list. Go see and then go see it again. What a trilling adventure!

title: It was like the book WAS the script Tolkien wrote for a PERFECT movie
review:
I have to say that I've seen the theatrical trailer about 100 times. I was so looking forward to this extravaganza. And it was worth the wait.

There is a quote about the readers of J.R.R. Tolkien's works, that goes: "There are two types of people in this world: Those who read Tolkien's world and those who will." I guess I'm one of those "who will". I have begun to the The Fellowship of the Ring and only finished about 1/3 of it. Somehow it sadly flowed out of my mind. I loved it but just one day I seemed to forget about reading some of it and forgot to finish it. Coincidentially, I heard about the movie almost the same week I stopped reading. As soon as it was confirmed, I picked up that book and didn't stop reading until the end of the first volume.

I decided that I should wait about reading The Two Towers (which is not a good thing to do because you should be fully aware of the trilogy), until after I've seen The Fellowship of the Ring. And boy was it REAL.

The story just came to life, so believable, so realistic, so intriguing. I have to say that it was the best adaption if a trilogy I've ever seen. The casting, the crew, the scenery, the script - all so perfect and "commentless" (nothing to improve). However, I do miss the scene with Tom Bombadil and the Sleepy Forest but those were most likely cut due to time constraints.

Now I have to admit that for people who haven't read the book it might seem a bit confusing and slow. But I myself, after watching it, got the book again and skimmed some of the scenes of the story. It was like reading the book for the first time, only now I knew what was happening, where and with who, thanks to such a WONDERFUL adaption of the novel.

For those of you who have seen the movie without reading the works and didn't like it, I tell, I URGE you to get the book and AT LEAST skim some of it and the descriptions. I say "at least" because the best thing would be to read it fully. It would be a good way to understand what the movie was about. For me, it was like the first time I played the N64 game "GoldenEye" and THEN only saw the movie. To me, the movie was like "Wow, this is just like the game" and that's because the game was so accurate like the movie. Same idea would apply to Lord of the Rings; After watching it and THEN reading it, it would seem so clear and awe-inspiring.

Salutations Peter Jackson! Thank you, merci, gracias, arigato, spasibo for such a wonderful book-to-screen transition. With it, the world of Middle-Earth that Tolkien created with his brilliant mind came vividly to life. I give it a definitive 11 out of 10. The extra point, however, does not exist on the voting (hence I put a 10), for it is for the believable and breathtaking translation of the literature world into the visual-audi one.

P.S. I think I know why the movies have a 1 year difference between them: it is so that each one would get a chance to be nominated for Oscar AND win it. For you see, if they are all released in the same year then only ONE of them could win a category of the Oscar nomination. Brilliant thinking Mr. Jackson!

title: Simply, a great movie.
review:
I read LOTR multiple times during the 70's and 80's, and have looked forward to a fully realized film version for a long time. I wasn't disapointed. Peter Jackson did as good a job as anyone in bringing LOTR to the big screen. I look forward to the next 2 films.

Regarding the IMDB ranking of FOTR as #1, how can anyone take this site as a definitive ranking of the best movies of all time? At best, it ranks the best movies at this time. Most users are of the internet generation with limited cinematic perspective. This ranking system generally reflects what is currently popular with over 30% of the top 100 movies made in 90's to present, and 45% made since 1980. With 100 million books in print,(and likely, fans)and only 17000 plus voters so far in just the last 7 days of its release, FOTR will likely finish in the top ten at worst.

No, FOTR may not be the greatest movie of all time, but in many minds it is right now(IMDB #1), so who is to tell them otherwise? As a body of work only time will tell. Not all are LOTR geeks, or have read the books, though it seems most negative criticisms are in the minority of either not having read the books, have a perspective limited to Star Wars and video games, has an attention span of a 2-year-old, or just bitter and hateful of people who simply enjoyed it. There seems to be a backlash of people trashing FOTR for the sake of trashing it, and it shows that there are some very, very unhappy people out there needing attention. If you didn't like it, just say so. It doesn't have to take 1000 words to justify why you didn't like it.

FOTR was a labor of love for Peter Jackson, and it showed throughout. As Gandalf told Frodo in the mines, "...it is what you do with the time given to you..." Peter Jackson has chosen to devote these many years to make this epic, and I, and many others, have chosen to enjoy the 3 hours given to us to experience it.

title: Good job with difficult translation of book to film
review:
This is from the Tolkien fanatic's perspective. I've read the trilogy at least a dozen times and know the story by heart. However, unlike other die-hard Tolkien fans, I'm not going to complain about the movie version cutting out several big scenes, eliminating characters, and basically taking every shortcut they can to keep the story moving. They had to do it. The movie is long as it is and there are too many characters. Because of this, I'll say straight off that Fellowship is not going to be a super blockbuster. The much simpler (and far inferior) Titanic is safe with its record.

Cutting out some characters was essential. Giving Arwen the added role of Glorfindel was absolutely necessary. Did we really need another elf? How could they possibly have gotten Liv Tyler to do the movie when her role in the first book would have been trivial.

I also agree with most of the scene cuts. Did we really have to see Tom Bombadil? Do I mind that Farmer Maggot is reduced to a passing reference? Does it really matter that Frodo leaves immediately rather than waiting around in the Shire for many weeks first? These are all wisely chosen scene cuts to shorten the movie. Even cutting out the Barrow Downs is OK, although it does seems funny when Strider suddenly throws weapons at the hobbits out of nowhere.

And this is the main flaw of the movie. Because there is so much story to tell, the movie seems choppy in places. The editing is weak. Plus, they've made an attempt to put the story in chronological order, meaning that they had to bring some scenes from later books into the already long Fellowship. It doesn't quite fly. I think they really needed four movies to perfectly render the three books. Fellowship, for example, would have been far better off ending after the escape from the mines.

Worse, they've botched a few important scenes. We see Aragorn giving Frodo his tacit permission to leave the group before he sneaks out. This has got to be incomprehensible to fan and novice alike. Since we later have a scene with Aragorn restraining Legolas from giving chase to Frodo and Sam, the earlier added scene is unnecessary. They should have just left it with Strider refusing the ring to contrast him with Boromir.

Another big botch is at the Prancing Pony. We never hear about the letter that Gandalf gave Butterball. So how in the world do we understand why the hobbits eventually learn to trust Strider?

OK, we've gotten the picky bits out of the way, on to the positive side. The art direction is absolutely fabulous, quite possibly the best I've ever seen in a movie. Every location -- Shire, Isenguard, Rivendell, even the difficult Mines of Moria, are wonderfully brought to life. An amazing achievement! Plus they've handled the special effects well, including the tricky task of making the hobbits look small.

As for the acting, McKellen's Gandalf is getting all the advance press, but really, almost everyone in the cast does an admirable job. It's hard for the actors to not be overshadowed by the effects, and they are to some extent, but most of them get the essence of their characters to come out.

While this is not a perfect Fellowship, it is almost certainly about the best Fellowship they could have made today, and that far exceeds my expectations. The first book of the Rings trilogy is the hardest to translate. Two Towers, with it's three part parallel story lines, will be much more cinematic. Return of the King will be easier to render since it can get by without so much introductory material and will be easier to condense. With that in mind, I'm very much looking forward to the next two films, which are already in the can and coming out one per year.

title: Thank you Peter Jackson.
review:
Wow. I wish that I could give Peter Jackson a great big hug. Although Tolkien was a professed enemy of Hollywood, I'm sure he would feel honored at the tribute that was paid him in this film. Everything about the film was simply amazing; I was amazed at the Balrog and am now rereading my favorite parts of The Silmarillion directly because of that image, I cried when Boromir died, and I grinned like a five-year-old when Merry and Pippin stole one of Gandalf's fireworks. More than anything, Tolkien's books capture in my mind a true sense of creation, of the wondrous power that literature can hold over the minds of readers, and of the beauty that is capable of being created in darker times.

This movie is without doubt the best movie I've ever seen. I love movies, I love the art of cinema, and my friends and I go out of our way to see as many independent and foreign films as we can, usually only excluding "Hollywood" blockbusters which are sure to be trash. I had some fears that someone like Steven Spielberg might end up with the project, but three years ago when I learned of how Peter Jackson set these movies into motion, I knew that Tolkien's works were in good hands. In conclusion, I would just like to extend a heartfelt thanks to Peter Jackson for bringing to life what has been in my heart and mind for years.

title: An adaptation worthy of every success it achieves.
review:
While I don't believe that a motion picture could ever do complete justice to Tolkien's work of sheer genius and live up to one's expectations totally, I can say that I came away more than satisfied that the movie is worthy of every success it achieves.

Perhaps the main concern I have is that, while it could not possibly have been done in less than its three hour duration, too much was packed into too short a period. But, in rating the film, I really cannot find enough fault to afford less than the highest rating.

The choice of cast was superb; Ian McKellen fitted the role of Gandalf perfectly, as did Viggo Mortensen in that of Aragorn.

I was impressed and surprised with the quality of the special effects employed; almost always they are so unrealistic they detract from a film, but here they were used wisely and complemented the story well.

I can't help but wonder whether my interest in The Lord of the Rings would have been greater had I not already been familiar with the trilogy. Bring on the next two films!

title: Awestruck
review:
I must say I walked into this movie with the greatest reservation. I had read TLOTR multiple times; and just pondering the amount of effort it would take to translate this epic foundation of Fantasy was mind boggling. I was afraid that either it would not look anything like it was discribed in the book(IE; the world, races, language) or the story would be hopeless corrupted for the sake of the corporate buck(can enyone say Episode 1, or as I sub-titled it: the longest commercial ever filmed?)

after 3 hours of watching this movie one thing was abundantly clear in my mind; THIS WILL GO DOWN IN HISTORY AS ONE OF THE GREATEST FANTASY EPICS EVER FILMED. While I understand why Jackson made Frodo tell Aragorn his motives for breaking the Fellowship, I personally beleive that the Original ending from the book was more dramatic and would have been a perfect cliffhanger for the next movie(after all int he end of book one Aragorn, Gilmi and Legolas don't have any real idea what happened to all the hobbits.)

But in the end I have only one thing to say; eat your heart out George Lucas, Peter Jackson made a better movie with more hassle than you did you hack. You should sit that man down and learn from him on how to make a real fantasy epic.

title: A triumph of visuals over victuals
review:
J.R.R. Tolkien was a professor of medieval literature at Oxford University when he wrote the `Ring' trilogy between 1937 and 1949 and, since their publication in 1954/55, apparently some 100M people have consumed them. I've never read a word of Tolkien and have no desire to do so, but I'm always up for a fantasy film because today's special effects are so brilliant in realising strange, new worlds. Director Peter Jackson shot three films in one mammoth undertaking, taking 15 months and $300M and deploying 300 crew members and 20,000 extras.

Certainly there is much to admire here: an eclectic cast, some fine acting from veterans Ian McKellan (Gandalf) and Christopher Lee (Saruman), magnificent sets, wonderful prosthetics, stunning special effects, terrific battle scenes, soaring camerawork, and the splendidly varied terrain of the director's New Zealand.

But there are many problems too  most of them inherent in the novels themselves. For starters, how can one believe that the saviour of Middle Earth can have a name like Frodo Baggins (played by pop-eyed Elijah Wood)? Indeed, for viewers not familiar with the books, there is a bewildering array of strange names and it's not always clear what's going on. Then there's the lack of female characters, just brief appearances by the ethereal Queen Galadriel (Cate Blanchett) and the elf Arwen (Liv Tyler). Next there's the utter ponderousness of it all  this is a work that takes itself so seriously and `Harry Potter' was much more fun. In short, one could say that the film is a triumph of visuals over victuals.

Most seriously of all, there is the poor pacing. The bladder-straining three hour movie is one set-piece battle after another, with no real plot development or build up of the tension. Then, to cap it all, suddenly the film ends in mid air, leaving us to wait for 12 months before we can pick up the story (`The Empire Strikes Back' did this much more successfully). However, real fans will stick it out and Christmas and the `Ring' is set to become a hobbit.

title: This has made me happy
review:
I've just got back from seeing The Fellowship of the Rings.

Before I go into how I felt about the film, I want to give you a little background info on me.

Most of you don't know me that well, I'm pretty much a non-entity of these boards, I only post when I feel like I have something to contribute and it's not that often that I do. My life pretty much revolves around me trying to become a filmmaker. I have dedicated my life to movies and I made the decision when I was very, very young to do this. I have seen thousands upon thousands of films, some I loved, some I hated and some were just average  but all I can remember.

I have never seen ANYTHING like this.

The way I felt after the first 10 minutes or so is indescribable, I kinda felt like crying and kinda felt like laughing at the same time.

I don't want to mention any of the plot here because it will ruin it for anyone who read the book (but there are some minor differences for anyone who HAS read the book, which I liked).

I think what I loved about this film is that (unlike most Hollywood blockbusters) everyone involved seemed to CARE about this film. You could literally see Peter Jackson's dream being painted in each individual shot. It made me smile.

This all may seem a little sad a geeky to most of you, but this film has affected me greatly  it's given me hope for my future and my dream, it makes me want to make films more than ever before.

It's made me happy.

And in the end that's all that counts for any of us.

title: Insert [Superlative] Here
review:
I went in with trepidation. Fellowship of the Ring is the slowest book in the trilogy, and I couldn't see how they could turn it into a successful movie. After 30 minutes of TV commercials and the 6th cell phone going off I realized that I was surrounded by morons and that if the movie started to drag it would get very ugly.

That didn't happen. Everyone was spellbound. No talking over the movie, and almost no one got up throughout the entire thing. For a three-hour film in a theater full of cell-phone wielding morons drinking giant sodas, that's saying something. During Boromir's fall one of said morons was so engrossed, even, that she let her phone ring for a full three minutes.

So, the film is absolutely the best adaptation anyone could have done. The sets, effects, and performances were great, and the attention paid to the book itself was more like homage. They even included the cloud of bird spies that caught up to them in the mountains. Sure, they excluded Tom Bombadil but Tolkien fans themselves have always argued about his relevance. And, yes, they introduced the Arwen/Aragorn love story two books early, but the changes they made were clearly for a reason and clearly with due respect for the Tolkien opus. They turned a wonderful but slowly evolving book into a movie whose pacing built and built and built.

I know the story by heart, but when they were cornered in Moria by the orcs I said, "they're screwed," and when they were confronted by the Balrog, I said, "they're really screwed," and when Aragorn turned the corner at the Gates of Gondor and saw the horde of orcs and uruk-hai, I said, "now they're definitely screwed." If I have any complaints at all it would be that Rivendale was like a ghost town, when in every book it was always overflowing with song and laughter. But seeing Lothlorien and watching Legolas mow down charging orcs like a chain gun made up for it.

Frankly, this is one of the best movies ever made, and to the people who are slamming it here, you must have really pathetic and bitter lives that you can't recognize a tour de force when you see one. Go refill your prescriptions of thorazine or prozac and shut the hell up.

title: How Peter Jackson Butchered a Classic
review:
J.R.R. Tolkein's Lord of the Rings is THE definitive epic of the fantasy genre. His story telling is clever and subtle, his imagined landscapes grand and immersing, and the entire story is a complex and subtly weaved pattern that culminates to the sharpest, most finely hand created needle point of a climax that the many generations who have read the book, since its printing, will ever know in the fantasy genre....and maybe other genres. And Peter Jackson has ruined it for all to come.

Here's how he ruined it:

1. Storytelling

Peter Jackson took Tolkein's wonderfully suspenseful, subtle and intricately designed plot, dissected it and laid it out open with all its innards disgustingly displayed for all to see. The mystery of Gandalf's capture, and his failure to meet the hobbits is thrown out into the open. The mystery of the Palantiri, part of the cause of Saruman's corruption is thrown out to the audiences a whole movie too early, and not even told properly (Saruman is in contention with Sauron, not in league with). And what really smacked it to home that Jackson was not leaving anything to suspense was in the Mines of Moria, when Frodo suspects they are being followed, where in the book the reader is left to suspect and guess at it being Gollum...Gandalf quickly reveals this fact with a quick "if you were at all in doubt, let me ruin it for you and tell you 'its Gollum' " blurb.

The one part where Jackson's tendency to tell things before hand may have been good was the prologue and the story of the ring. Granted the prologue was very good, and was a good introduction to the whole story line, and especially informative to those who have not read the book. The audience would have received the same information as it was meant to be, through the hard earned efforts of Gandalf' investigative efforts. Remember you have a captive audience for 3 hours, your allowed to keep them questioning and in suspense, and the story of the ring is a big piece of suspense that the reader/watcher really wants to know about and will sit through some storytelling to hear. And it doesn't change the length of the movie and it doesn't drag it on, it's a simple rearrangement of scenes movie wise.

2. Gandalf

Gandalf is a noble, overpowering character of great stature in middle-earth, even so that many are scared of or dislike him. He is of the mysterious order of wizards; he does not cower in the corners of Bag End in fear. He does not sit at the Council of Elrond in confusion or self-doubt, and he does not leave crucial decisions of the fellowship to Frodo. He is a man of authority, dignity and strength and even some times cruel in an importantly leader like way. He faces the Mouth of Sauron himself, when all of his most subtly laid plans are thrown out in front of him and almost proven to have failed (meaning the possible destruction of middle-earth as he knows it) without barely a shudder. This is the Gandalf of the book, not the cowering, fearful, self-doubting character Ian McKellan plays. And for those that argue that Ian portrayed a more human/realistic character, remember this is fantasy, we didn't come to see reality we came for quality entertainment, we came to see Gandalf in all his power and glory. The only way that this mistake would be offset, is if after he comes back in the second movie Ian plays his character properly so that there is a contrast between the old and the new Gandalf. Given the part in Bag End where Gandalf appears large and terrible to Bilbo is good, it is lost in the weakness of character he is portrayed with in the rest of the movie. A better portrayal would have been compared to Li Mu Bai in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon....quiet, cold, powerful, grand and authoritative but yet a sense of something more underneath his outer character. Even Magneto in X-men would have been a better portrayal of Gandalf than in this movie.

3. Elrond

Elrond is another grand character that was "humanized" and poorly portrayed in the movie. Here is a 3000+ year old Elf of great wisdom and experience. He is one of the oldest elves alive on Middle Earth and was there when Isildur cut the ring from Sauron's very hand. Hugo Weaving plays him as a panicky stressed out man who sounds like he might lose his job and has no idea as to how to win this war of the ring. Given Elrond in the book does not know how to win this war, and does not know that they will win, but he has focus and composure and maintains his dignity, as does Gandalf. They are both grand characters that may not know everything but always maintain their composure with the recognition that they are role models and leaders of the highest order in this world of middle-earth.

4. The Council of Elrond

The Council of Elrond is probably the most important meeting of people in their Age. It is a meeting of many, with many important elves present to say the least. Not a meeting of a handful of people. The importance and stature of those present at this meeting is downplayed by the childish bickering they get into in the movie. These are mostly representatives sent by those races who have had problems very recently, and many important stories are told here. Some very important background of the fellowship is told here and there should have been more effort to show the council accurately, even if time did not allow. Again, the full story of the ring is told here, the story of the mines of Moria are told here, all of Gandalf's efforts are revealed here, Saruman's betrayal is revealed here, it is a mini climax in the book after a long hard journey to Rivendell, not a squabble-fest between the races.

5. Galadriel

The scene where Galadriel turns horror like? Come on, she is the most beautiful of all the elves, the most elegant and again one of the oldest remaining on middle earth. The explanation of why she could not take the ring could have gone without tarnishing her character. Another grand character butchered....are we seeing a trend yet?

6. Move time vs. Middle Earth time

Part of the grandness of this epic is that it takes place over many many years in middle earth. This sense of time is lost in the film. I know your first argument is "its a 3 hour movie", but time can be quickly and concisely depicted with narration and scene collages and labels like "50 years later..." etc. The way Gandalf travels in the movie makes everything seem like he's in the same city and is only a horse ride away from the nearest wizard. It takes 50+ years for Gandalf to finally find out the full story of the ring, between Bilbo's departure and Frodo's departure. The journey from the Shire to Rivendell is a long hard journey. Understandably it is hard to convey time in a limited length movie, but it is possible, and the value of conveying this properly is important to this book to give it that epic feeling.

7. The Reforging of Narsil

This was left out along with the prophecy of the return of the king. Sorry, this is a critical part of the story and unthinkable that it was left out. Sure they showed the sword, but nothing else was said edgewise. Maybe Jackson means to bring it up later on, but if not....shame on you Jackson....shame on you. Does he remember the name of the third book? I think not.

8. Arwen

Yes, Arwen's character is little seen and heard of in the book. I agree that maybe expanding on Aragorn's love interest is in the best interest of moviegoers, because it is nice. But is that what he has done here? I don't think so. He hasn't told more of the story of their love, he's just put her in the movie more than she needs to be. It isn't that bad, but the whole part from the stabbing of Frodo, to the Flood at Rivendell is butchered so that she could have more screen time. Okay, parts need to be cut out to shorten the movie, but the more times that a single character takes on the 5 Ringwraiths and wins takes away from the dread the Ringwraiths should bring to the story (remember Strider fights off all 5 Ringwraiths....unheard of in the book, in the book the Ringwraiths pull back of their own accord). The whole horse chase could have been shortened or made to incorporate the other elves that come and help the hobbits go that last bit to Rivendell, rather than have Arwen ridiculously outrun, for a fairly lengthy time, all the Ringwraiths on her own.

9. The test of the ring

Again In case we were all too blockheaded to realize that the ring is a temptation to even those that are striving for good in middle-earth, and can never be wielded by any but Sauron without falling to the taint that the ring carries with it, because it was made by the greatest evil of middle-earth, Peter Jackson has kindly depicted the gist of this message in several easy to understand, explicit tests for most of the main characters of the movie. Thank you Peter, otherwise I would have missed out entirely.

10. Meriadoc and Pippin

Meriadoc and Pippin are not along for the story simply for comic relief. They are close friends to Sam and Frodo, and they forced themselves into the trip out of a deep friendship with Frodo and Sam. Would have taken that much longer to replace the useless scene where they are running from Farmer Maggot with the proper depiction that Pippin and Merry were spying on them and knew the whole story and forced themselves along through a sense a friendship so that there is some importance of them being there and some friendship and closeness between the hobbits? I think not. Don't even get me started on the lack of story with Sam.

Of course there are many other things that could have and did irk me, but these I listed above are the major ones.

So now your asking, how does this ruin it for those to come? In the present day, when most people are willing to go see a movie over reading the book, many of this generation and the following will form their opinions of the trilogy on the movie rather than on the book, and even for those who watch the movie but then take the time to read the book, the way the story is sculpted to keep you in suspense to find out about things throughout the book and earn the knowledge that is acquired, is lost on those who have seen the movie and were force fed everything that you were meant to wonder about and strive to read about. This is my biggest qualm, Peter Jackson could have kept as much of the master storytelling intact as possible, but instead has turned this story into an okay tale at best.

So enough of the whining, here's the pluses. Overall the movie was visually pleasing, the effects were very good, some strange glitches, like the part where they are running out of the tomb room in Moria to the bridge (got a little Charlie Chaplinish there). But generally Middle-Earth was shown in incredible and accurate detail. The orcs left something to be desired, but the Balrog....Amazing! And the scene at the River Bruinen(?) was as I imagined it. Even the Prancing Pony was accurate. The movie was good, but could have been much better.

Its understandable that there are only 3 hours in the movie, and stuff like the story of Boromir's horn, or the relation of Arwen to Elrond, or the whole Tom Bombadil sequence, or the full stories behind every major player at the council cannot be told. But what I'm saying is even in the given time, the story could have been told in such a way as to capture why this saga is an epic and not just another fantasy trilogy. But instead, what could have been an incredible film, turned out only to be a good film. Those that have never read the book, think that this is an amazing movie, and maybe it's just me, but I'm sure if more thought was put into the proper storytelling and character portrayal, both those who have seen read the book and those that have not could have both benefited equally.

title: The Big Screen Theater Experience

title: Totally enthralling; probably the best adaption possible
review:
Having waited for several years in nervous anticipation for the release of the first installment of Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings trilogy, I perhaps went into the screening (opening night -- God bless ATMs!) with a more critical eye than most.

An avid fan of the books since my teens (although, I like to think, not to fanatical lengths -- no pointy hats or hairy hobbit feet in my wardrobe), I recently re-read all three books in the lead-up to The Fellowship of the Ring's release. As a result, my mental images of the places, characters and situations were still very clear.

So, armed as I was with my own personal interpretations and a critical eye developed through four years of waiting, Peter Jackson was going to have to come up with something pretty special to impress me.

And boy does he deliver the goods.

From scenes of heart-pounding action (the Black Rider chases, the cave troll and Balrog in the Mines of Moria, the attempt on Caradhras, the duel of the wizards) through to heartfelt moments of friendship and love, the New Zealand born director and co-scriptwriter (with his wife Fran Walsh and Philippa Boyens) handles every element of J.R.R. Tolkien's fictional Middle-earth realm with a deftness that it's hard to imagine could come from any other director.

There are problems with the abridged nature of the story, of course, and not just for purists. The arrival of the Fellowship at the Golden Wood of Lothlorien, for example, is swift, with their journey in the wood starting out among what look like thin beech trees. But suddenly the travellers reach the huge trees of Caras Galadhon in the heart of the wood, with a whole city in their branches. In the book, the trees gradually get bigger as they move deeper into the wood. In the film, however, this sudden leap seems to offset the pacing a little.

Nevertheless, this is only a minor quibble -- a necessity of keeping the audience interested for the whopping 128-minute running time. And if viewers are not already familiar with the books, it's likely that these things will go unnoticed.

As for the acting, it is universally superb, with Ian McKellan (as Gandalf the Grey) the show-stealer. It must be a real challenge to portray someone who wields such awesome power and yet is equally capable of gentleness and kindness beyond measure. The performances of the entire fellowship, and the film's supporting players too, are a tribute not just to the actors themselves, but to Jackson's always-impeccable casting.

An overall opinion is difficult to decide upon, since the film should probably be judged as part of the whole when the other films have been released. But, on the strength of this first episode, I think we can look forward to gripping Christmas viewing in both 2002 and 2003, when The Two Towers and The Return of the King respectively head our way.

The crunching goblin noises were good too...

title: Good movies are good.
review:
Finally, a movie based on material with a huge cult following that doesn't resort to stupid in-jokes. This is one of the first movies in a long time that just tells its story without trying to be hip, or be hugely ironic. Peter Jackson has pulled it off. I was not disappointed, even though I expected to be.

The acting was better than I expected it to be, too. The movie allowed for much more depth in the performances than most adventure movies ever do. Sean Bean's performance is so brilliant, it's a pity he probably won't get any awards for it. It's easy to understand why Peter Jackson wanted Bean for this part. Ian Holm is also great as a Bilbo we have never seen before. He is, at times, a much darker, scarier character than we are used to. Ian McKellen's Gandalf is, of course, great, and Viggo Mortenson does a fine job as Aragorn.

The camera work is stunning, as well. Jackson's horror roots are evident here. The camera rarely stands still, but it is never too much. It is always fluid, and exciting when it needs to be. The battle sequences use some incredible crane shots that make you wonder where the crane could possibly be positioned.

Suffice to say, December 2002 seems like a long way to go.

title: An excellent movie
review: Time flies when you're having fun. I never thought I could enjoy a film this long. Boy was I wrong... The story is, of course, very good and very reliable to its source. The acting and the soundtrack are very good as well. What do you possibly need more?

title: A wonderful disappointment.
review: I realize that a lot will be said about this film and that my comment may not matter, but I'm going to say a few words nonetheless. I, too, had been waiting for months, biting my fingernails in anticipation and I, too, sat in the theatre with a pounding heart waiting for the film to start, and I can't say I didn't enjoy watching it.  But in all, I was disappointed.  I had seen 'Dungeons and Dragons' (an apparent failure) a few months earlier, and I seriously couldn't find anything that set 'Lotr' apart from that film. (besides some possibly better acting and more expensive - though not always better - special effects).  Things I liked were Christopher Lee, who gives away a classic performance, bringing back memories of his glory days, and the breath-taking design of Isengard and the Shire.  Things I didn't like were Liv Tyler's ridiculous British accent, long scenes that weren't going anywhere, jokes that weren't funny and the fuzzy (if impressive) battle scenes.  If you've read the books, you should of course still see this film, and if you haven't... well, I guess it's inevitable anyway.

title: One that is flawed, falls short of the greatness of the novel, but none the less quite good.
review:
Peter Jackson's 'Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Rings' is indeed not J R R Tolkien's 'Lord of the Rings'. I went into the theatre a few hours after having set down the literary masterpiece that is LOTR:FOTR. I have yet to finish the following volumes. In the case of the film, it is hard for me to admit I was disappointed. I am not saying the film was appalling however, if one compares it to the novel, it comes nowhere near the brilliant world of Tolkien.

My first concern was a sense of 'realism'. I read the novel feeling and learning and eventually knowing the world. There was political conflict, racial differences, class systems, and vast and deep culture. Lord of the Rings was simply a disguised comment on our very own society. Those condemning a 'good v. evil' plot and saying that we should concern ourselves with fighting the 'real evil' in the world fail to recognize that the story is simply taking us from reality and putting us into a façade of what we know we are living, all it has is different names, different landscapes, and different creatures. It seems this is a lot to ask for from a film, yet this is the single most important thing that must be accomplished, a sense of 'Realism' Tolkien proved he could do it in a novel. Jackson failed to translate this.

Another important aspect of a Film's success is creating a sense of Time. The duration of events in the novel LOTR:FOTR spans almost a year (from what I recall) The film seems to play out the sequences within a matter of days. There is no sense of journey, no sense of development, by the end of the film we don't really care that the fellowship is broken (the fact that something like "we have failed, the fellowship is broken" is an actual piece of dialogue is another matter) because to a general audience these faces don't know each other. Of course one would argue against my claim of time being important by saying that Jackson was limited, but I would just say even with limitations, one must establish a pace. Jackson's translation was too fast in pace all that he needed to do is show wear and tear, the slow demise of food, the change of season, Tolkien used these in his novel, weather, clothing, and food, and a sense of time was created. Even if wearing is implied is enough to slow the pace of the film. Rather then inserting and unnecessary scene between Arwen and Aragorn, add something that would aid the simple STRUCTURE of the film, which then aids the plot itself. The journey of the story is as important if not more important then the action and mounting climax itself. The Novel explores the human' condition (with time!) the film explores New Zealand, and as a result failed to allow character development and ultimately restricts the film to a shallow rendition of Tolkien's and surely Jackson's intention. Rather then cramming Jackson should have attempted to slow the pace down.

Relationships are seemingly non-existent and sadly this is a result of pace and action. Limitations of course will ultimately become the excuse, yet some things cannot be excused. Relationships are vital, and the lack there of makes it difficult to feel for the characters, and secondly makes it difficult to imagine a continuing development in an established relationship. Legolas and Gimli. No, they do not only become buddies, they allow us (as a metaphor) to see political and racial tolerance, the change in attitude between races, which leads to a newly founded allegiance. That is the strength that Tolkien was trying to celebrate, not that of a sword, bow and an axe. Rather then promoting their physical attributes, Jackson could have at least included something deeper that would be of use. Again, the excuse is that of limitations.

The acting was quite well done. I did gain a sense of the characters surfaces indeed, Again screen time was limited and thus names like Cate Blancett were wasted in misinterpreted scenes (Galadriel is not a cold witch) The actors looked their part yet hadn't had enough dialogue to completely play their part save Gandalf.

Direction, Peter Jackson's vision was wonderful, again limitations brings the film down. Cinematography was quite impressive, visual effects were stunning. The script was true to Tolkien dialogue yet there was not enough.

The Novel was the Book of the Century; I've read that the film is the film of the century. If that were the case, the book being so acclaimed and all, the film would have worked even if it toned down the minor action sequences, toned up the major and necessary action sequences, and finally it would have worked even if it included something OTHER then the action sequences. Yes they were just an excuse for making pretty' lights and monsters dance, and congratulations for the special effects, well done I've seen special effects carry a film before (Star Wars Ep1.) Thankfully Lord of the Rings has much MUCH more then just its special effects, and it's hard to say after all that, that it is decent film. It just lacks a greater sense of realism, journey, growth and humanism that made the Novel so great.

I offer this collection of comments after my first viewing of the film, I only hope my second viewing will all me to see more. People must come to their senses and view this as NOT Tolkien's Lord of the Rings, but as a Film firstly, then as Jackson's Lord of the Rings.

Again it is merely AN adaptation, yet it is one that would only make the Global Village squirm with satisfaction, Tolkien might have been impressed with the look, perhaps the feel. But ultimately it misses something, then again, what film doesn't.

8/10 (might seem a contradiction, but like I said, this is not a bad movie, simply one that is flawed and falls short of the greatness that is the book.)

title: In the clash of the titans---
review:
Peter Jackson is running with two points, leaving Chris Columbus with 1, and George Lucas with zero.

Let me not praise this film too much, but just reassure you, that this is a good film. If you don't like the action, you'll love the scenery.
