Rivendell was just as I had imagined it. Hobbiton was as it was described in the book! Isengard (yeap that's an addon in the movie - a very good addon imo) was perfect! All the places where so close to Tolkien's descriptions that you could actually feel they were true. One who has read the book won't be disappointed, actually he will say as I said: That was the book in graphic novel format :-)

The characters in matter of appearance where also just like if they were taken out of the pages of the book. When I saw Aragorn in Bree, dressed in the dark green cloak, smoking his big pipe and having a huge mug of ale in front of him it was just like reading the paragraph in the Fellowship of the Ring (in chapter Strider) describing us for the first time that amazing hero. Legolas and Gimli where perfect also. Both of them dressed and equiped according to the book. The hobbits, Boromir, everyone was perfect. But imo the ones who where the peak of the show where Galadriel and the Wizards!

Blanchett was just Galadriel. McKellen and Lee were just Gandalf and Saruman. So close, that one thinks they were raised to play those parts in their life.... Oh and Gimli's Axes ruled! Especially the bloody huge one he holds in the last Battle next to river Anduin (where the Orcs and Uruk Hai atack and steal Pippin and Merry). Gimli was indeed a perfect dwarf!!!

As for the acting and charater impersonation in general... well here one could have his obections. Characters where more humans than in the book. For instance Gandalf, Aragorn and elrond are always concerned in the book but there is never an implication that they don't know what to do. They rarely question their desicions or stand thinking "ok what's next?". In the movie all characters are in agony and fear, they seem like they want to rush, to do whatever possible even though they are not sure. Not a bad aspect for the movie imo (it made you feel the chase, the importance of the problems they were dealing with). However it sometimes allianated me from the film.

Those who have read the book and loved it, will feel at home. It's Tolkien feeling 100%. But what about those who don't know the actual story? Well here there might be some problems. Although everything is being explained as much as possible, there are some things left deliberately in the dark, else the movie would be over 4 hours. A viewer with no contact with Tolkien's books will see an amazing scenery with a good dark fairy tail story, but he will propably won't understand exactly what he is watching. He will be thrilled as if he was watching Braveheart or the Titanic, he will be enchanted by the photography and the scenery but he won't be able to understand everything from the movie.However propably he won't notice that as he will be already captured by the action and the power of that movie.

I could go on and on and on talking about the Lord of the Rings. But I will stop here since I have to work a bit :-P. In overall the movie was great, it will be a blockbuster, it will be the new king of the Cinema and it will propably sweep the Oscars :-) DON'T MISS IT!!! :-))

Cybertroll

PS: Oh I forgot to talk about the amazing soundtrack! Perfect binding with the scenery!!! :-)))

title: Oh, my word, this is simply the greatest spectacle on film
review:
One film to rule them all, One film to find them, One film to bring them all, and in the theater bind them...

**POSSIBLE SPOILERS (but if you've read the books, what the heck!) **

Spectacular, abso-bloody-lutely spectacular. An excellent cast and mind-boggling special effects thrust you into the center of Tolkien's first Lord of the Rings book. The danger, evil, and heroism are not merely portrayed, they are palpable, surrounding you at all times. The three hours will pass as but a few moments of the day to all but the most churlish, the least imbued with a sense of wonder.

As a LOTR (and Tolkien) buff, I noticed several departures from the book, notable but not major. First, Frodo is supposed to be quite a bit older than Sam, having reached his forties or so when his adventure begins; Pippin and Merry are younger, and Sam should be the youngest. Frodo's manner of leaving the Shire is wrong; it was well planned and Pippin, Merry, and Sam secretly plan to go with him, not as chance as the movie shows. However, all of that would have required a much longer first installment. I don't believe the Riders come that close to Frodo before Bree in the book, either. The Council did not behave badly in the book, and of course much less time was spent on Saruman in the book as well.

So what? It works in the film, and the most important themes are beautifully drawn. CGI usually gums up films, with a few exceptions, but here it is put to brilliant use. The cave troll and the Balrog look as though they were filmed right alongside the actors in the scenes. When Frodo puts the ring on, the imagery conveys the same sense I had when reading the books. And the scenery! New Zealand is displayed in beauty and splendor; more than once I wondered why this spectacular scenery isn't used in more films.

I've only seen this film the one time, but you can be sure I'll be heading back -- very soon -- to see it again. Go see it ... film history is calling you.

title: Gobsmacklingly stunning
review:
Simply put, this film will leave you begging for more. It packs an unbelievable punch - the battle scenes are utterly realistic. Its also filled with an eery sense of dread.The sheer evil contained within the Ring reverberates throughout the film - from Bilbo desparately trying to kick his "ring habit" as if it were crack cocaine, to Frodo who is tasked with destroying the ring - even Gandalf can't take the ring due to its corruptable powers.

Peter Jackson's landscape panning is utterly utterly mindbogglingly awesome - no 30 second CGI clips here mate, oh no. You want to see an Orc mine? - well Jackson obliges with a full panning , swooping camera that floats above and then dives deep right down into it. Want to see a massive battle between Orcs and an Elven/Human army - again, the panning camera shot, almost as if taken from an imaginary helicopter comes in. When the scene deserves a "big" shot, by God does Jackson deliver. This alone should convince you to see it on the big screen - dont want for it to come out on VHS or DVD - this film was simply MADE for the big screen.

This film deserves a multitude of Oscars. Not only for the cinematography and special effects , but more importantly for the character performances. Everyone here acts incredibly well - so well, that you really get into the characters and emphathise with the plight of Middle Earth.

This is the best thing I've seen since Star Wars , way back in 1977 when i saw that film as a kid. Awesome awesome awesome.... 1 year for the sequel to come out is too long - i want to see it next week please!

title: Wonderful adaptation, plan to see it again in the next few days.
review:
To adapt one of the most important books of the 20th century is no simple task, but Mr. Jackson has done so. With spectacular visuals, emotional soundtrack and perfectionist directing, this movie is one of the best I have ever seen. The acting is exactly right, the sets are spectacularly detailed and the costumes look truly authentic. The first few scenes of the show grabbed me and hauled me into the movie. I spent the next three hours in Middle Earth. Well worth the price of admission, and well worth a second visit,

Note to 'True Believers': Yes, there are parts of the book that have been removed, and yes, parts have been changed. But the sacrifices were worth it (and lets be honest, some things had to go -- there is not enough celluloid in existence to fully capture the book). The only omissions I objected to were in the forest of Lothlorien. However, I got over it, and so should any other critic; the rest of the movie is perfect. The other additions, changes and omissions allow a perfect book to become an almost perfect movie. The BIG flaw? It ends. Just as when I read the book, I was disappointed that I would have to wait for the next installment. Years ago I just bought the next book in the series, now I have to wait a year for my next fix.

title: Amazing.
review: Peter Jackson is a genius. He's really done it, he has filmed the unfilmable. Every change from the books works, every scene works. The special effects are stunning. The acting is top-notch. And the landscapes, ruins and towers are just incredible, beyond belief. My only complaint is that it's too short, it needed at least 20 minutes more spent on camping on the way and Lothlorien. But that's a minor complaint. Amazing!

title: Brilliant marriage of narrative, film, and technology...
review: I don't think I've ever seen a greater marriage of several mediums to tell a story.  Superb acting, a director who so obviously has a vision, beautiful cinematography, and special fx, that bring the first part of Tolkien's own vision to the screen.  I was inspired and engrossed from beginning to end. Thank you to everyone who brought it into being.

title: A great movie, but was it a 10?
review:
Well, I finally saw LOTR:FOTR last night. A great movie, but was it a 10? I scored it a 9.

I think my experience started off poorly as we were in a small cinema. That was REALLY annoying -- the screen was not much bigger than my TV at home! I really must remember to check that next time. So, I guess I will just have to see it again, but make sure I am in the main cinema!

The movie was certainly darker than I thought it would be; this is definitely no kids movie. Regardless of what the ratings say, I probably wouldn't let my kids see it till they are 15 or so. But as a dark portrayal, it was very, very good.

The acting was great, the special effects were great and there were parts that made me laugh and smile and jump with fright. And the story line was well adapted I thought. title: Disappointing
review:
So there I was, these last few days, getting myself ready for the new Lord of the Rings film. Read the book, watched the documentaries and gathered thoughts and opinions from industry types. I was almost ready to write a review before the film even started; all I needed to do was fill in the blanks. I could have talked about the flaws, the highs and the lows of the book, how Middle Earth came to be and why Tolkien only agreed to sell the movie rights to help educate his grandchildren.

And so, on opening night, I watched The Fellowship of the Ring. All my preparations were in vein. Sadly, the film just isn't good enough to talk about any problems with the book for the film has many problems of it's own. Peter Jackson's film is certainly an ambitious project, and one that will both amaze and disappoint in equal amounts throughout its 3-hour running time.

It is understandable that changes have had to be made to the film, many minor characters from the book have been dropped completely (Tom Bombadil) and some scenes have been cut surprisingly short (The Barrow-downs get about 2 seconds). The first book of The Fellowship, the journey from The Shire to Rivendell is told at breakneck speed. While the book made it clear that it was a long trek, the film made it seem more like a short stroll. Also the characters of Pippin (Eric Idle Jr.) and Merry (Dominic Monaghan), the token comedy duo of the film, are woefully 2D and more irritating than funny. Because of this, the film feels too rushed in its early stages, losing much of the depth of Middle Earth.

Peter Jackson and writer Frances Walsh agreeably wanted to make a coherent film while keeping much of the detail of Tolkien's world. Many subplots have been cutout, but strangely their conclusions remain. This means only those who have read the book will the spot any subplot at all and will most likely only pick-up on its shallow representation on film. Perhaps most obvious is the friendship between Sam and the starved pony, Bill. In the book Sam brings the pony back into good health after its poor beginnings in Bree before having to leave it behind when the path was no longer suitable. In the film, a pony appears from nowhere after Rivendell and soon disappears again (at the same point as the book). Sam still appears to be upset, but the audience is given no reason why and no reason to care.

To me at least, Fellowship of the Ring seems like the result of an unholy marriage between Tolkien's imagination and Hollywood intervention. In their need to make a coherent film, Jackson and his team have created something that feels more like a string of set pieces in a series of impressive backdrops than the sprawling epic it should be. The need to remind us that Mordor is evil after almost every scene with a quick flyby is irritating and the time wasted here would have been better spent expanding the characters or adding depth to the ground they stand on.

But that isn't to say the film is particularly bad. It is, at times, an amazing spectacle, showing off Jackson's talents admirably and the action scenes are occasionally exceptional. The acting too is impressive, with the veterans giving the best performances, especially Sir Ian McKellen's Gandalf in an almost certain Oscar winning roll (whether there are better or not).

Perhaps it is because the book is so fresh in my mind, or because my expectations were so high, but this first part of Lord of the Rings is a bitter disappointment. The lack of depth and bastardization of Middle Earth is the films undoing, while the action and the majority of the characters are likeable enough to raise the film above the usual Hollywood yarn. It is hotter than Potter (itself a film with similar problems, but without the imagination) and a film that everyone can enjoy, but I'm left confused when seeing what lofty praise the film has been gaining recently.

7/10

title: My faith in the power of film is restored!
review:
I had been looking forward to this film for a while. I have been a big fan of Peter Jackson's film work. This year has been a monumental disappointment for movies. Well, my friends, this year has been redeemed by an astounding, thrilling, beautiful and, surprisingly, very moving film.

"Fellowship" is a transporting experience. I cannot remember the last time a film took hold of me like this. Just about every element in this film was nailed!!! From the amazing prologue to the heartbreaking, yet hopeful ending three hours later, I felt as if I was actually in Middle Earth.

Peter Jackson's direction was top notch. His ability to contrast breathtaking visuals and action sequences with quiet, character centered scenes was deft. Sure, I will admit the scenes in Lothlorien were a bit weak, but that is very minor.

The cast was very, very good. Elijah Wood, Ian McKellen and Viggo Mortensen's performances were 100% convincing. I was particularly taken aback by Sean Bean's Boromir. The scene in which he teaches Merry and Pippin sword fighting told more about his character than 10 pages of dialogue could have.

The cinematography was utterly beautiful throughout the film. Let's just say that I wish I could catch the next flight to New Zealand.

I think the best special effects are ones that propel the story and don't make the watcher ask, How did they do that? When a story is told as well as this, I just accepted everything that I saw onscreen. I can't pay a higher compliment to WETA, the effects company, than that.

All told, I will be seeing this movie several more times.

9/10 By far the best film of the year.

title: Some improvements
review:
In a lot of ways, I was pleased with how Middle Earth was brought to the screen visually. The visuals are very similar to a lot of fan art and the previous animated feature, and I think that Peter Jackson borrowed a lot of this imagery. I can't say that this is a bad thing, because fan art helps the LOTR community converge on a singular vision of the universe. This movie is a multi-million dollar addition to the collection of fan art, and will definitely influence the visions of many.

If one doesn't take the movie too seriously, or as canon, or as if Peter Jackson is Tolkein's heir, then you shouldn't be disappointed. For the most part, the film is extremely well done but standard Hollywood fare.

To sum things up, I enjoyed the movie greatly compared to most movies in the theater, but it does not transcend to the level of art, art-house, or even just complete immersion.

Warning: The following is spoiler-ish.

With the fact in mind that I thought the movie was fun, some things that I think would make it better:

* Even though the costumes and computer graphics were well-executed and convincing, the monsters seemed to be typical Dungeons and Dragons - a bit more stylization would be nice, especially with the Balrog. I think I've seen him in a couple of movies before.

* The fellowship seemed to be somewhat weak, with the Gimli the dwarf and Legolas the elf not being fleshed out.

* The fight scenes were too chaotic, with flashes of legs, arms and swords taken with a shakey camera. I find general battle scenes boring, and instead like some physical narative, even at the micro-level of blow by blow. Perhaps they could have hired a martial-arts choreographer and kept the camera still during the fight scenes.

* The music was extremely generic (oxymoron?), and could have been lifted from any action movie soundtrack. The music made a huge difference in Star Wars. Imagine if the Darth Vader march was a generic orchestral piece, instead of synchronized with his steps. Better music could have, if I may borrow from Emeril, kicked this movie up a notch.

* Stylization. As I eluded to, Peter Jackson may have been a little too fearful of stylization, but Tolkein was vague enough in his descriptions to add a little more uniqueness to the characters and scenery. I didn't feel a kind of mystery or magic (you know, that sickly-sweet feeling you get that you wish you were up there instead of sitting down in the movie seat as a passive observer) with the look of the characters. The look was too derivative for me to think that the characters actually existed, instead of being actors in costume.

* Tom Bombadil is one of the more playful characters, and a great mystery in the Lord of the Rings, and may even be one of Middle Earth's deities. His inclusion would have added a nice incongruity and more lightheartedness to a movie that is darker and more driven than the book.

You shouldn't have read this far if you've already seen the movie. In fact, you shouldn't read reviews before you see any movie. But if you haven't seen it, don't let my criticism stop you from seeing the movie. Everyone else is covering the positive aspects. I just pointed out a few negative ones.

This film is about one man braving seemingly unsurmountable odds to accomplish his mission. Yes, he is accompanied by a diverse fellowship of strong individuals, but I'm sure he must have felt the immense responsibility a whole world put on his shoulders.

The man is, of course, Peter Jackson. He embarked to do the undoable. And he succeeded. From the birthday party (which reminded me so much of Ireland) to the Nazgul, from Moira to Mordor to the Balrog's whip, everything simply felt right - dirty fingernails included.

Go see it. No, I mean, again. After all, this is the very first fantasy film in which the spectators aren't seen as kids. No Jar Jar, no human chess game. The hobbits could have been cute, playful - but they aren't. Tolkien is treated with respect. I, the thirtysomething year old moviegoer, am treated with respect. It's been a while.

Martin

title: An imperfection worth seeing.
review:
It has been a slow development of late, but with films such as "The Matrix", "Eyes Wide Shut" and with the latest development of "LOTR: Fellowship of the Ring", the truth is evident: the EPIC is back.

And thankfully so. Many of us had long feared the destruction of the attention span, but now we have help in the form of the cinematic adaptation to the most important fantasy book series of all time. While I must admit that I am not an expert on the series, I will spare legions of fans from a shortsighted review of the series and focus on the film itself.

First and foremost, the story is very well done. The epic scope and the complexities of Tolkien's world are kept very much intact (save a few embellishments here and there), however, the film is damaged by an overlong opening narration that condenses the magnificent history into a montage. If spared until lull periods of the journey, the exposition could be much more effective and not feel so rushed. Considering that the film is unafraid to take its own time, the compression of the story seems unnecessary.

Secondly, the technical accomplishments are marvelous, although with reservation. While there are many beautiful shots (the computer-generated landscapes are SPECTACULAR) overall, the cinematography seems a bit unimaginative; the setups and the lighting, while appropriate for mood, diminish the detail of the sets, and take away from the extravagance of the production values. Perhaps a more depth-oriented approach like Kubrick or Tarkovsky would be more appealing (however, I must admit my own bias towards these two artists, and therefore, this is not an objective opinion). The accentuated highlights of certain scenes are beautiful, but the film suffers from a bit too much filtration, and the computer-generated traveling shots are quick and run-of-the-mill, framed and shot with all the care of a tight-budgeted weekly sci-fi television show, and not a mega-budgeted epoch.

All this notwithstanding, I have NO complaints about art design and set decoration, all of which are wonderfully detailed and expertly constructed. Not to mention the perspective effects created for the Hobbits in comparison to the others. I imagine that Tolkien himself would be proud.

It is also wonderful to see many great and favorite actors of mine (and many others) all together in the same film. It almost brings a tear to my eye to see Christopher Lee plucked out of the miserable Hammer film purgatory and into grade-A projects, where he belongs. It is also quite a treat to see Ian Holm and Ian McKellen, two of the best actors still living, work together with the skill and ease that only the Royal Shakespeare Academy could produce.

In closing, "LOTR: Fellowship" fails to completely enchant due to the perils of script condensation and subdued framing, however, it is anything but a failure overall. I enjoyed my time spent in front of the screen, watching this epic unfold, and I must say that, despite its flaws, the strengths of the film and the intention of the film to remain loyal to the source material make it, if nothing else, an overall success.

title: Never has a story gained so much in translation to film
review:
I was fortunate enough to catch the midnight show of THE LORD OF THE RINGS: THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING Tuesday night. I can almost guarantee Peter Jackson's name has already been engraved on this year's Oscar for Best Director. And I would be willing to bet that THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING will be named Best Picture. (It would seem Michael Mann picked an unfortunate year to release ALI.)

In Hollywood, it is hardly difficult to find an entertaining, big budget, multi-market-franchised blockbuster. However, it is almost impossible to find such a movie that is actually a good film, let alone a great one. THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING is nothing less than a great film, astonishingly faithful to the books. This story world is brought to life in grander fashion than any fan could dare to hope. Any time a beloved novel is brought to the big screen, fans wonder what will be lost in the translation (e.g. HARRY POTTER). With the LORD OF THE RINGS movies, I think what fans will be most surprised by is what is gained in translation, the vision Peter Jackson brings to the telling of the story. I would argue this is the best film adaptation of a novel since THE GODFATHER, and I don't make that comparison lightly.

If you've read the Lord of the Rings trilogy, you'd know it isn't really a trilogy but rather one story published in serial form, three volumes comprised of 2 books each.. So, the first of the three movies is not the full story. THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING is the first of 3 volumes. The worst thing about this film is that it does leave about 2/3 of the story unresolved. But because volume I is in and of itself a gripping tale, this is still likely to be the best 2 or 3 hours of movie-watching you spend all year. Your greatest frustration, like mine, will be that you have to wait a year for THE TWO TOWERS (volume II), and another year on top of that for RETURN OF THE KING (volume III).

If I thought it was bearable, I'd advise you all wait 2 years and watch all three movies back to back when the 3rd comes out in 2003. Instead, just get to a movie theater as soon as humanly possible and see the first installment of what is likely to be the most beloved cinematic experience since STAR WARS.

title: This flick is a hands-down, three thumbs up WINNER! "Now let's go hunt some Orcs!"
review:
Director Peter Jackson has created an absolutely winner in this truly visionary cinematic masterpiece of J.R.R. Tolkien's fantasy _The Lord of the Rings_.

If you are a diehard Tolkien fan (like myself) you'll find yourself more than happy to grant him all the artistic license that Jackson used (and I dare say he took some liberties, but never missed the essential theme and motif) and you will forgive him when he strays from the text here and there, for any such meanderings are a thousand times compensated by his pristine portrayal of such Middle-Earth wonders such as The Shire, Rivendell, Saruman and the Tower of Orthanc, the assault on Redhorn Pass, the awesome and mind-boggling Mines of Moria and the Battles in the Chamber of Records and the Bridge of Kazad-dum, and Lothlorien and Queen Galadrial, and the astonishing Gates of Argonath and the carved and crumbling yet still majestic images of Isildur and Anarion, Tol Brandir, and Rauros falls. And the fall and salvation of Boromir the Brave, and the dreadfully awesome Eye of Sauron and His Dark Tower -- Baradur.

I do not doubt that J.R.R. Tolkien would have approved of this film. Long time fans of Tolkien will marvel in its delights, and for those who have not read, or have read only superficially and cursorily Tolkien's epic fantasy, well, this movie will undoubtedly spawn a whole new generation of readers.

Three thumbs up and HOORAH!



~revlove

"Now let's go hunt some Orcs."

title: Enjoy three hours in another world
review:
Watching this film is like planning a great birthday-party (like the 111th birthday of Bilbo)for almost 20 years (that's the time that has passed since i've first read the books)and looking forward to the day when all the guests you are waiting for with great expectations will arrive. And yes, for the next three hours, almost everyone of them came and almost everyone (the only one i've sadly missed is Tom Bombadil) was just as i've imagined after reading the books. The only exception for me was Elrond; casting Hugo Weaver as Master of Rivendell was in my opinion the only mistake among the otherwise excellent chosen actors. Outstanding: Ian McKellen does not play Gandalf, he seems to incarnate as the old, sometimes funny, grumpy and very mighty old wizard as he is portrayed in Tolkiens books.

Okay, this is certainly no objective critic, not even a comment it's more or less a love-letter but this film deserves it. I'm quite sure that almost all who love the books will love this film for the pictures do not destroy the fantasy that lies in the heart of the readers but engage it and even make them love Tolkiens world more than before. Enjoy three hours in another world, called Middle-Earth, long ago gone in the mists of time.
