Love it- its all unique, Well done Peter Jackson-U rule!!!!! Vexa

title: Wonderful
review: After seeing the midnight showing at the Cinerama in Seattle, I wanted more. I cannot say what it was that took this film over the top other than the brilliance of Tolkien.  He created a world that has been fantastically adapted to the big screen.  Elijah Wood surprised me as a very believable Frodo.  Humor avoided being cheesey.  The score, including 2 Enya pieces were moving.  Liv Tyler and Kate Blanchet were enchanting.  Action sequences told stories.  Story is really what its all about, and in this trilogy, the story has only just begun.

title: so unbelievable impressive
review:
i was seated in 3rd row in one of the best cinemas ... and i really felt being part of the fellowship.

this film is a MUST for everybody, who doesn't know the books and a PLEASURE for everybody who does. i will definitively go again.

a tip: prefer cinemas with huge silver screen and a good sound system.

title: Cooooool movie
review:
It is lovely to watch a movie, which are true to its genre - in this case the adventure genre!!!!! Lovely instruction by Peter Jackson - my new hero in the movie business - distancing himself from the stereotypes in Hollywood.

WATCH AND ENJOY ..... :-)

title: Breathtaking - Left the cinema enthusiastic
review: Ok. I'm a fan of the books and I was sceptical. I saw what happened to DUNE, another masterpiece of a novel that was not properly adapted. What Peter Jackson did here though surprised me in many ways. I did not expect so much emotion in it. My pulse went up as soon as the hobbits left the shire and from then on the movie was absolutely thrilling. Even though I knew the plot by heart I was continually surprised by details and excellent emotional acting. All the characters had great depth, the dialogue was close to the book but matched the flow of the action. The special effects were probably the best I've ever seen, and even though the movie was FULL of them you never had the impression that this was an effect driven movie. So many scenes looked totally natural and realistic...it must be the landscapes of New Zealand that just look more beautiful than anything a computer could render. The ending is perfect. I can't remember when I left the cinema with such a broad smile on my face. Possibly a runner for the best film of the year Academy Award. And George Lucas should watch this. It shows what his recent Star Wars attempts are lacking: Depth.

title: The Ultimate Fantasy Movie Based on the Ultimate Fantasy Book...SPOILERS AHEAD
review:
It was almost 1,5 years ago that I saw the first trailer of "The Fellowship" and I remember looking my friend in the eyes saying: "I just cannot wait that long". And last night the moment was there. I was extremely nervous and also afraid that I had already seen the most impressive shots in the trailers. Well folks, for those who hasn't seen the film yet...none of the many, many highlights were in the trailer. I was completely overwhelmed by all the visual surprises Peter Jackson came up with. He really made the ultimate fantasy film based on the ultimate fantasy book.

Here are some of my favourite moments...*SPOILERS* ahead!

The Prologue...look at Elrond's face when he is standing there in front of this huge army...WOW!

The Weathertop...very scary and intense.

Arwen...believe me...she is absolutely fantastic and mysterious. And what a first entrance she has...

Seeing Bilbo again in Rivendell...with a very frightening and unexpected moment. Ian Holm was so lovely...

The fight in Moria...the music stops and there is this incredibly agressive fight with some orcs and a troll. Not for the kids...

The Ballrog...Does it have wings...I still don't know...

Boromir's death...very moving and realistic...

Reading the books, I created my own images. And the visuals in the film reached beyond my imagination. It was all even bigger then I had in mind. Thank you Peter Jackson for this magical adventure. This film takes you to another time in another world. And after September the 11th...who doesn't want to spend three hours there, just to forget it all for a little while.

title: Great eye candy, however story lacks peaks and valleys
review:
Just got home from seeing this movie. Let me start off by saying the cinematography is fantastic, and the special effects are awesome. But that's pretty much where it stopped impressing me.

With all the hype about this film, the storyline has all but been fully revealed, thus not leaving many surprises. The plot never really took me up very high and failed to drop me to any depths. I felt that it lacked any highs and lows, and rather continued on a flat journey. (visually, a very impressive journey - but as far as the storyline went, I wasn't all that impressed) What I'm trying to say is that I really didn't become very attached to any of the characters, and therefore couldn't really have sympathy for them during their losses and didn't feel very rewarded during their triumphs.

I do feel that the high ratings it has received is largely due to the spectacular special effects, very impressive computer animation, and breathtaking scenery. (which is why I gave it a 7/10) While it's certainly no Star Wars (New Hope, Empire, and Jedi all get 10/10 in my book) or Braveheart (another 10); VISUALLY it is an excellent film.

I will be anxious to see what they give us in the next two...

Just my $.02 so please keep the flames to a min. =)

title: Very Good and mostly faithful to the book
review:
I was a little afraid to see this movie since I thought it wouldn't measure up to the book or take liberties and make the books seem cheap. I was very happy to find that it measured up excellently.

There were a few moments where the acting was a little over the top (like maybe 30 seconds or a minute out of the 3 hour movie) and Lothlorien was a disappointment because it was cold and sterile (the blue lighting?) instead of being green and full of life. Overall great, though. Ian McKellin was amazing as Gandalf.

The art direction was mostly excellent and they didn't cheapen things by making people look stupid or exaggerated. None of the UPN crap of having cheap costumes or blue people or anything outrageous and dumb. Some of the vistas in the movie were breathtaking and everything was incredibly believable.

title: Summarized Perfectly
review:
Obviously leaving a bit out of the movie version of this incredible story, this is a visible summary. However, the accuracy at which this movie reflects Tolkein's original story is outstandingly great. The most important parts of the story were captured, and the less important were scrapped for the sake of keeping the story three hours long, even though seeing the dwarf beg the Lady of the Woods for a strand of her hair would have been amazing, as well as having the dwarf blindfolded on the way to see her.

Anyhow... I most definitely suggest you see this movie, but ONLY after reading the book by J.R.R. Tolkein. You may enjoy it more if you only read the first book (Fellowship of the Rings) before seeing the corresponding movie rather than reading the Two Towers and/or Return of the King. Well, I'd love to tell more about this spectacular piece of filmography, but I just saw the movie four times since 12:05 this morning, so I really cannot stay awake much longer. Take care, and see it!!!!

title: Fellowship is a stunning new invention in cinema - a 'companion' film to the book.
review:
Fellowship was a new experience in cinema - perhaps the beginning of a genera or at the very least a 'format'. Fellowship was not a 'movie', it was a 'companion'. Oh, and what a companion it was.

Never before has written description been translated so completely and perfectly to the screen. The settings and characters leap from our imaginations and onto the screen with such force and unity that one might go so far to say Peter Jackson was channeling the spirit of Tolkien himself.

That said, if you haven't read the books, you haven't a hope. As I said, this is a companion, NOT a film. It could not, and should not, exist alone. It uses the base of a wonderful book as building blocks to open up a new way to experience the horror and wonder only hinted at through the words. Where Tolkien's words somehow lack, Jackson's vision takes over. The image and sound compliment the words, interpret it, draw us farther into it - but it does not replace it. It could not dare to replace one of the greatest written works of fiction, and it does not intend to. Wide swaths of narrative are cut from the film because they wouldn't play well on screen, and for that matter they don't need to be visualized - the words work just perfectly. That doesn't, however, mean they're not important to the narrative - you need to have the background of the book to fill in the film, to complete the story.

If you have read the books, drop what you are doing to see the film and experience the book. It is one of the most satisfying entertainment moments you will have. If you haven't read the books, by all means, DO NOT see this film. Do not let anyone TAKE you to see this film. Do not let anyone TELL you about this film. DO read the book... In fact, read all three. It is some of the finest writing ever. Then, and only then, let the spirit of Tolkien draw you again into middle earth through this wonderful new invention - the "Companion Film" to Fellowship of the Ring.

title: Wonderfully adapted from the novel
review: The movie remained true to the books in every plausible way. Although some points were circumvented and a few characters shifted from here to there, the spirit of it was phenomenally in place. The characterization was nearly flawless; the characters came to life in a very vivid way that, in my opinion, is very true to the intent of the text. The hobbits seemed as though they'd leapt from the pages as did the rest of the fellowship, straight down to Legolas and Gimli. The visuals were also phenomenal, landscapes, scenery and special effects. She shire in all its simplistic complexity was beautifully rendered. Absolutely a wonderful transition from print to film. Perfectly lovely.

title: Utterly Amazing
review: I'm sure many other moviegoers are raving about this film as much as I am. I just want to congratulate the cast and crew of "The Lord of the Rings" and wish them success in any other ventures they pursue.  You guys deserve it. And to all the movie studios out there, this is how to make a great picture. Give more control to the director and allow them to make the film as good and it can be.  Mr. Jackson, you blew me away.  Thanks so much for giving the world such a wonderful addition to Tolkien's legacy.  Now, when will the DVD's be release.  I got my check book out already.  Thanks again!!!  This movie should win the Oscar for best picture and director, without a doubt.

title: Great Stuff - just Great Stuff
review:
This movie is THE movie.

My favorite scene is when we see Arwen for the first time (that is also the first time we see an elf in the film) - that's art. But the whole movie has a kind of artistic feel to it. This is very much caused by the digital effects - but I must say that the effects are a part of the story, so you don't see the effects as just special effects - but you see it as a "natural" thing in the world which the movie describes - so it's not a "look what we can do" film (as we have seen plenty of times), but a movie where the effects are used to tell the story - that's rare.

All the actors were, without exception, excellent. Especially McKellen - the number of different facial expressions he is using...wow! There is something very wrong if he dosen't get an Oscar for best actor.

The overall impression is that the movie is massive, epic, ranging from ultra closeups to wide perspective shots - from good to evil - horrific to the cosy - sad to the fun etc. etc. We get the whole package.

And that's it - great stuff - just great stuff. All there is left is to

thank all crew and cast for it all. Cheers y'all - well done.

title: Unprecedented in the History of Cinematography
review:
If you have been searching for a purpose in life... search no more.

This lone gem proves to be a masterpiece of art, history, and entertainment. If you wish to see a mere movie, do not venture forth; but if you wish to experience a truly majestic marvel of our time, then view with eyes that do not blink. You would not want to miss a second of cinematographic perfection.

title: Great movie, been waiting for this since Star Wars.
review: Great movie, thats sums it up.  Special effects were awesome; most of the landscape is computer generated or composited with real footage.  The only way I knew that these were not real was by the breathtaking beauty of some of these landscapes (such as the city of the elves) or from watching The Making of the LOTR.  The fight scenes were incredible, the hits looks very real.  With the speakers of the theatre, I felt the hits.  Even the end of this movie got me pumped up by showing true friendship and honor; I am so ready to see the next LOTR movie.

title: The most anticipated movie of all time?
review:
20+ years of longing for it to be made... 2+ years of anticipation of its release once I learned it was being made... The trailers... The hype... The TV ads... The makings of...

One question is on everyone's lips. Does the Fellowship of the Ring meet it's expectations? To put it bluntly...

No. It exceeds them.

Words cannot do justice to how I felt walking out of the theater last night. I wanted to run back in and see it again. Peter Jackson has captured the very essence of Tolkien's vision and placed it on the silver screen for all to revel in.

The sets and scenery were simply breathtaking. For three hours I did not just view the events that transpired in Middle Earth, but were a part of them. I felt as if I was actually there. The Shire was warm and cozy. Isengard was grim and sinister. Rivendell was beautiful and serene. The Mines of Moira were dark and foreboding. Lothlorien was ethereal and majestic. The world was alive.

The characters were dead on. Every single one of them.

From Frodo to Aragorn. From Gandalf all the way down to Merry and Pipen. All exactly how I pictured them. Not only were the leads all superb, the supporting cast was every bit as amazing, Saruman and Galadriel especially. Yes there is the controversy of the Arwen character and her increased role in the movie. It is negligible. The put her in one scene that should have been another character and she had an extra scene in Rivendell which I do not remember ever happening in the book, but added so much more depth to the Aragorn character, it was easily overlooked as a discrepancy.

The script was outstanding. Obviously parts of the book are left out. All the most important parts are there and while the dialog may not always be word for word (it is in some very crucial parts though) the actual events were all as I remember them.

For three hours I lived in Tolkien's dream. I was reminded that even the smallest person, has it within himself to stand up to the greatest evil imaginable. That even the simplest person has it within himself to do the most heroic and courageous deeds.

I cannot recommend this movie enough. Thumbs up. Four Stars. 10 out of 10. A+. Three of the most magical and enthralling hours I have ever spent in a theater. The only downer is having to wait a whole year for The Two Towers.

Whether you have read the books or not. Whether you like epic fantasy or not, do yourself a favor and see this film.

title: Incredible!
review:
To say that this is visually stunning and more gripping than a roomful of new lock-wrenches would be like saying that Shakespeare wrote a little, in other words, a gross understatement.

The scenes are amazing, the acting magnificent, and the visual effects peerless.

The monsters... have to be seen to be believed.

A heart-felt 11 from me. :-)

title: Jaw dropping splendor
review:
I have to say that when I went to the theater, I didn't know what to expect, but while watching, I can recall the novel and this is what I see when reading the book. Each race excellent in their own fashion and the scenery was magnificent.

This is what a real epic fantasy movie should be. Thumbs up all the way around.

title: Amazing!!!
review: I watched this movie on the first day it came out, the line up was huge, the theatre was packed, and for a damn good reason!!  This movie was amazing. The story was awesome and the action was incredible.  I read the book in the summer, and this is the only movie based on a book that I have read, that actually comes close to the book!  I gave this movie a 10, and recommend everyone see it!!

title: Middle-Earth just as I imagined it
review:
I am a long-time fan of the Tolkien books, having re-read all of them at least three times. Tolkien spends a lot of time in his books helping the reader visualize the Middle-Earth, so naturally I was curious whether the movie would portray something completely different from what I had imagined. Surprisingly, I found the visualization completely consistent with what I had portrayed in my mind.

One image that really stood out for me was the initial battle scene against Sauron and his orc army. I had never imagined seeing such an epic and glorious battle, especially not in those proportions. To have this scene stand out is completely consistent with Tolkien's style; his reverence for epic historical events resonates througout his books.

title: Peter Jackson, get your Oscar speech ready...
review:
Wow! Great flick. I went into the theatre today ready to pick this movie apart. I was ready to slice and dice through all the hoopla.

Did they follow the book to a tee (most excellently conceived story of all time, thanx Professor Tolkien...)? No, of course they didn't. They couldn't. It would have taken nine hours to fit it all in, for the Fellowship installment only. The entire Lord of the Rings would have to be at least 27 - 30 hours in all.

Were the special effects the best of all time? Perhaps. They were certainly better than those done in the last installment of the famous "Space" franchise.

The ensemble cast was perfect. The acting was superb.

The direction was absolutely perfect. For example, I'll try not to give anything away to those who don't know the story (are there really people who haven't read the books? What planet are they from?), Peter Jackson is one of very few directors, who even when practically EVERYONE knows the outcome to a particular sequence, can get the tears to well up in the eyes of the most stout emotion-quellers.

Enough said. This is the reason I go to the movies. This is what I have waited for all these years. Oscars will go to this movie, and rightfully so. Peter Jackson certainly deserves one. If he doesn't get one, he was robbed. Sir Ian McKellen should receive one as well.

10/10

title: Comparative discussion on the fantasy dilemma
review:
I must say that Lord of the Rings the movie is a complex, astounding, and a bloody brilliant work of art (pardon my English). The movie takes the book and repairs the faults it had. The book is a bit dry and tedious in places which slows down the pace of the thing, but in the movie you can see how close evil snaps at frodo's heels. The closeup of the ugly and gory orcs and goblins is a mark of Peter Jackson, he's not afraid to use ugliness to get a reaction from a crowd.

I also just like the concept of the thing, there is only elementary magic which the highest magicians can use, basic telekinesis, and influential magic can be seen used, and gandalf uses a plain horse to get from one place to another (and horses are expensive so not a lot of people have them). The world created by J.R.R. Tolkien is not a world of fireballs, and flying brooms, it is a world where the most powerful item in the world is a small ring, which can at first sight make you invisible and in the end corrupts your soul.

I would not try to compare Harry Potter with Lord of the Rings. Yes they both have magic, but that is the only obvious similarity they share. If we take it out, then Harry potter is generally just about a geek which finds school life to be rewarding (and in a school of geeks he is the coolest geek of them all), and helps defend a priceless stone from being captured into the wrong hands (and ***diminutive spoiler*** the same guy who tries to capture the stone is the guy who killed his parents). Lord of the Rings is then generally about a small geek who is thrust out of his normal cosy life into a violent and perilous adventure in which the whole world might stand or fall with his actions. The difference is quite a large one if you take the magic out of them both.

People who will fall in love with Harry potter but not Lord of the Rings are people who like plainly obvious plots, simple conversations and other safe and predictable movies.

People who will fall in love with Lord of the Rings, but not harry potter are people who have grown up out of the kiddie movies and want some "real" fantasy plots (real meaning fantasy movies which are finally taken seriously) with great actors, polished storyline, superb CG and some bloomin' heck to boot.

Generally people will like and love them both, Harry potter as a great children's movie, and Lord of the Rings as a great film classic.

title: Simply Amazing !
review:
This movie was worth the long wait ! It has the most heart touching acting and equally matched, no one out does anyone else. Superbly Directed with fright and beauty! The score suits each scene with a unique sound! and The graphics and set design are at the top of the line. THIS MOVIE IS BEST OF THE YEAR!

For sure seeing this again

title: Prepare to stay in your seat for the full 3 hours, you don't want to miss anything!
review:
At two minutes under three hours this is certainly a long movie. Take my advice, plan ahead, use the washroom before the movie begins, don't buy a drink at the concession stand, because there is nothing in this movie that you can afford to miss!

I was gripped by the movie for its full length and like most people who'll see this movie I already knew what was going to happen. I congratulate the director and cast on producing a film that most fans of Tolkien will love. The aching knees, stretched bladder and sore back are more than compensated for by the quality of the storytelling.

The choice of New Zealand's rich and roughhewn landscape as the backdrop for Middle Earth was excellent. I was pleased to see the very landscape that Tolkien's words evoked when I read the books. All the characters in the film are faithfully portrayed by the actors involved with Ian McEllen and Viggo Mortensen being the two high points in the film for me. My only disappointment was that I saw Strider as being much bigger than Mr. Mortensen but I can't fault his portrayal in any other way.

In general, I've found that movies made from books don't often do justice to the books. A book is limited only by the imagination of the reader but films are constrained by time, budgets, and technology. This film does justice to the book and that is high praise.

This film hits a home run. My only worry is that the succeeding films now have a high standard to adhere to, I hope that the bar is not set too high as I want to enjoy the next two as much as I have enjoyed this one.

title: Best Movie of All Time...
review:
This is the greatest movie of all time PERIOD!

Nothing even comes remotely close to this cinematic masterpiece.

The Fellowship of the Ring makes The Godfather look like a cheesy episode of Sopranos and Star Wars look like Pokemon trash.

The acting was superb, the settings amazing, and the special effects top notch. The Balrog is the greatest moment ever seen on screen in the young history of CGI.

Am sure there are few people who wont like it because its 3 hours long, but those are the type of ignorant people who like movies like scream and scary movie, and enjoy 90 minutes of trash with no character development and useful dialog. So pay no heed to those types.

This movie has Oscar written all over it.

Gollum was everything we hoped for and Liv Tyler was perfect for Arwen. The best moment of the movie aside from the Balrog was when they showed Gollum being tortured by Orcs in Mordor. Brilliant.

The Soundtrack was also superb. Chalk up another Oscar in that department.

The combat scenes were some of the best ever seen on screen, sword fighting and archery at its best. Moria was worth the price of admission alone.

My only complaint "and its a small one" is that the movie moved too fast at times. This movie really need to be 4 hours long, as lots of little things were left out from the book, and not enough time was spent in Rivendale and Lorien. Some scenes needed to be played out slower than they were. But the good news is that Jackson has promised 27 minutes of additional cut footage to be included on the Dvd this summer. This movie will just get better and better....and then next year we have part II! Pure Bliss.

Bottom line...

GO SEE THIS MOVIE!!!!!

First timers will like it just as much as fans of the book do. Cinema does not get any better than this.

This movie is so great that is pushes Empire Strikes Back from a 9 to a 7 because ESB is not worthy enough to be one number below FoTR's 10.

10/10 Stars!!!!

title: Incredibly well done film of classic fantasy literature
review: Having read the trilogy 14 times over the past 25 years I had high expectations for the movie. I was not disappointed.  Much of the dialog is lifted directly from the novel.  The characterization, background scenery, action sequences are done impeccably.  I'm just your average Joe Blow, not some well known talking head movie critic, but I give it two thumbs up. Enjoy!

title: Spectacular!
review: After waiting months for this movie, I am happy to say that Book I of the Lord of the Rings lived up to the hype. Great acting by well cast characters, unbelievable special effects, and a script that was able to remain true to the spirit of Tolkien while fitting into a three hour timeline make this my film of the year. I can honestly say that few other movies had me walking out of the theatre as excited as did FOTR. My only regret is that I will have to wait two more years to finish watching this masterpiece; however, it is appropriate that all three movies are released during the holidays, for they are truly a Christmas present like no other. This was the easiest 10/10 I have ever given.

title: Brilliant!
review:
I have never been so blown away by a movie in my life! Despite the plot changes (which I recognize as necessary for the sake of storytelling and seamless flow in both the film and it's pending sequels), I thought the film was brilliant. There were numerous times when a character or location would be presented and the only response that I could come up with was "that's just perfect!" It was as if Peter Jackson cracked open my brain, poured my imagination onto film, and then made it better than my mind could even conceive.

It was better than 10 Christmas mornings combined......

title: excellent!
review: The Lord Of The Rings is the most wonderful movie in the century! Elijah Wood is perfect and pretty faced actor! ^_^ It's great movie from awesome trilogy.... personally I'm already waiting for other parts too. The effects are very great.....absolutely the greatest movie in the history!

title: One of the best book to film transitions ever!
review:
Forget what you've heard about the changes in LOTR coming to the big screen. Sure, some things are left out and minor (and I do mean minor) changes were made to make an entertaining movie, but it also leaves the viewer realizing that have seen one part of a gigantic film. If the other two movies do the book half as much justice, this may be the best 8+ hour film ever.

I feel that while some diehard fans (I'd like to think I'm in that category) will pigeonhole the movie to death, we should all keep in mind that this is one of the best book adaptations ever. Name me a book to movie that didn't lose at least SOMETHING in the move and I'll tell you a movie that probably doesn't watch all that well.

So, with all this being said, keep in mind that this is a movie and that Peter Jackson or whoever you want to "blame" for your nitpickings did not come to your house and rip up the original text, but created a beautiful movie based on the favorite book of the 20th Century. The books will always be there if you need them.

title: Great movie, too short for the real fan ;) Hope to see a Directors Cut soon!!
review: There´s no scene where I would say "I know how to make this better", of course the are some scenes which are not-so-perfect, but I couldn´t imagine who could do it better than P.J. did! For me there is too much left out (the discussions about entering Moria or Lorien, the Legolas-Gilmi talks, Gandalfs letter introducing Strider in Bree, etc.) But, anyhow - these left-outs are very well chosen and don´t leave a hole when you watch the movie (except for the gifts of Galadriel which appear without mentioning, Lorien is IMHO the weakest part) --- for me it´s just the feeling that I want to see more; it´s over ways to fast. I wouldn´t mind sitting six hours ;))

title: Awesome
review: Extremely well done movie, although there are many changes from the storyline of the book it manages to stay true to Tolkien's original spirit. In terms of production values, flawless.  Go see it - again and again and again ;).

title: I don't want to wait a year
review:
It's now 10 hours ago since I came out of the local cinema. I've sleept like baby after the enormous tense about the movie has left me amazed and confused...

I don't want to wait another year...

PJ, GIVE US THE OTHER MOVIES RIGHT NOW... please... :-)

I can't bare to wait to see the rest of the storyline...

title: It was awesome
review: This is the best movie ever made in the film History. The only thing to complain on, is that Tom Bombadil not is included. Gandalf looks a litle bit too much like a bum, but wtf. Legolas is the King, he rules middle-earth!

title: An amazing journey
review: This was just a wonderful film.  For 3 hours the audience is transported to the most fantastic and magical place. A lot of the people writing comments have complained that it isn't always totally accurate and things have been left out but they are totally missing the point.  You shouldn't go into a film looking for failings because you will always find them.  Anyone taking on Tolkein's world could not please everyone and it was inevitable that some changes would be needed.  Instead of moaning let the amazing sights and feelings that you are treated to take over your mind for a while.  You will be very impressed.

title: Quite literally the best film I have ever seen
review: Only the Star Wars films could give me even half the amount of giddy anticipation I had for seeing Fellowship. As a longtime Tolkien fan I was counting the minutes until I could walk in, sit down and see if Peter Jackson had the capability to translate Tolkien's epic to the big screen. Well, not only was I so impressed I was left speechless, but I found myself thinking, for the first time, three hours is not enough. This movie left me so hungry for more that the wait for The Two Towers will be the longest of my entire life. I cannot say enough good things about this movie. Everything, EVERYTHING is so masterfully done that even those who know nothing of Tolkien and care nothing for fantasy will be impressed. I always knew Jackson was a good director (The Frighteners is one of my favorite movies), but here he has outdone not only himself but every director in the biz. Even Spielberg can't hold a candle to him. The production design was mind-blowing, and the CG characters SO realistic they put all other CG characters in all other movies to great shame. The actors were all beyond awesome, especially Ian McKellen and Christopher Lee. Elijah Wood makes the BEST Frodo any Tolkien fan could ever ask for. Liv Tyler surprised me; she was excellent as Arwen. The action in this movie was awe-inspiring. I went in knowing exactly how the story progressed, yet sequences like the trek through the Mines of Moria still scared the crap out of me, they were so well done. And the Balrog -- words do no justice! It truly has to be seen to be believed, and it will be believed! And we get to see just enough of Gollum to get an idea what he looks like... scary little creature, my precious! Everything about this movie is true magic. TRUE MAGIC. Never has a film captured me so completely before. I didn't want to leave the theater. I'm going to see it again tonight. I'll see it as many times as I can manage. If you haven't seen it yet, you honestly don't know what you're missing. I could pour my heart and soul out, and it would still pale in comparison to how much this movie blew me away. Do I sound like I'm exaggerating? I'm not. It's that good. This movie deserves a 10 out of 10, though I would have voted 11 were I so allowed. Go see it. Even if you don't like fantasy (and how could you not after seeing this), go see it. This is Tolkien done right.

title: Uncompromisingly Good
review: The American viewing public has never been shown an epic film that could touch this.  I'll say without batting an eye that it is my favorite film of all time.  The only glaring flaw was that it was about 3 hours too short. Lets hope the DVD has ridiculous amounts of extra footage.

title: As good a flick as the best of 'em!
review:
This is rant - so don't expect too much.

You know, seeing all these reviews about Lord of the Rings - The Fellowship and all the people slamming those who were struck by it appears odd (Hey, snobbery is good and alive I guess). It appears that 50,000 plus people were affected by this movie enough to write about it. Oh I know, the masses are all wrong and I am enlightened because I can analyze plots, acting, direction, music score, lighting, etc.(Which always makes me wonder about who is enlightened about the enlightened people?)

I will quote one of my favorite professor's of poetry - Prof. Moon. It is not what a poem says that is important but how it makes you feel. I believe this applies to films too. Sure to many LOTR is over-rated. So is the Jabberwocky, but it makes me feel good. It is a great movie that takes you somewhere else. So this then, is a top notch film, and if it makes number one then so be it. (Actually, I enjoyed it more than The Godfather.)

Now the review of certain elements ;)

Ok, now that I have read the book again, I still love the movie. This is coming from a person that helped his brothers paint their room with a HOBBIT mural - all without permission from mom of course. My family, from my mother on down to the youngest of us were enraptured in 1974 with Tolkein and his works. Middle-earth has been a favorite character of ours - like a welcome neighbor that pops his head in every once in a while. And when Mr. Jackson decided to come out with a movie version with actual actors on a screen, I cringed. How can a movie match a child's imagination. (It does rather well, but you must remember that it is an adaptation!)

The story has a simple premise, good vs. evil. But how fearful the evil!! All creatures, small and great, tremble at the mention of MORDOR - think of a fallen angel and you'll have a good idea of his history. And the movie gives us many a good suggestion of his might. But the power of evil and Mordor lies in its focus - it wants one thing and it consumes all in its path. The world has changed and many powerful allies have disappeared. Good's former strength is diminished.

The story then is about how good regroups to form new leadership, alliances and powerbases while evil has no such problems. It is the story of the changing of the guard, from one age of wonder to a different and more pragmatic one. If this interests you then these three movies will grab you. If you read the book(s) though understand this: Mr. Jackson changed parts here and there.

Things that could have been changed:

I would have included the trip to the Lady Galadriel. Sorry Mr. Jackson but it would have given us an idea of what the world was like before Mordor stained and tired it.

The representation of the elves. To me they come across as cold and not that important. This story is their swan song. They are passing out of the world of magic into the world as we know it. I expected to see more warmth, wisdom and a sadness from having seen too much evil.

Things that I enjoyed:

The Shire - In the movie the Shire is well... the Shire!! The Hobbits are good people all around if you spend the time to get to know them.

Gandalf, Bilbo and Frodo Baggins - Okay, you know they did a good job when you read a book and you see Ian Mckellen there instead of the wizard you imagined before. IMO this is far far better than a silly Oscar.

Even though many lines are changed I still enjoyed the characterizations of Sam Gamgee, Merry and Pippin. They should be in their 50's as hobbits, but hey - it's Hollywood. Nevertheless, they really are Hobbits.

Arwen - She did not need to take Glorfindel's role to be introduced earlier on but it works and she is great. Really she plays a much more important role later in the trilogy.

The dark riders, Moria, the Balrog - Mr. Jackson understands how to communicate evil - brrrrr - it really is that good. The Balrog is primal and epic in stature!

I didn't write this to convince the naysayers but to interest those fans of Middle-earth that are standing on the lines. It is a great film, see it and if it is good - it will entertain you. It did me. You did notice that I did not say it was the best film of all time - I am reserving judgement until my eighties when I can snort at all you young whipper snappers out there and give authority to the phrase, "I remember when I was a young man..." (Or until they make a film with Marisa Tomei, Winona Ryder and...never mind 8-)

title: A+ mazing!!!
review:
When I saw Bad Taste in 1988, I told all my friends that this guy (Peter Jackson) was more talented than Spielberg (most of them laughed at me), but I never guessed he would be this good. Even though I'm not a big fan of fantasy films about dwarfs, wizards and elves, I was absolutely amazed by what I saw. When I came out it fell like three days had passed since I went into the cinema, so much had happened. This was cinema at it's best!

I'm not familiar with the books but I can understand it if people are a little bit disappointed because they wanted the film to be more thruthfull to their own experience of the book. But I dare anyone who says that Peter Jackson did a bad job to make their own version and do it better or Rest in Pieces!

title: Boring
review:
What it reminded me of more than anything was the old computer

game 'Lemmings' where a bunch of chirpy little chaps progress

through increasingly hostile environments and severe attacks.

That's why it was so boring - very much like watching over

somebody's shoulder while they play a computer game. It would have been more fun if you could join in and help destroy

the little twerps yourself. I kept nodding off - difficult, as this was one of the noisiest films

I've ever seen.

title: Epic Videogame
review: Academy Award nomination? You gotta be kidding me? Wake me up from this silliness. Fellowship was one long passive video game. Overcome one level and you get to the next. OK, Ian Holm's Bilbo Baggins provided a little interesting drama before the epic game got started. And, yes, the scenery, sets, and special effects were excellent. Of course, we enjoyed the great masks and costumes. But Academy Award? Artificial Intelligence had equally spectacular visuals, and a much more emotionally compelling and intellectually challenging story. Even the Harry Potter movie was better than this. Why not nominate a superb old-fashioned drama such as Charlotte Ray? or the ingenious Amelie?

title: Wonderful addition to the book
review:
THE IDEA: I am the one who read the famous book at the appropriate age and still believe it's one of the best books. It was some time since I last read it when I saw the movie in cinema, at the end of 2001. My first impression: not close enough to the book, but the feeling it leaves is the same, just a bit fainter - it does leave the noble longing to stand on the light side, whatever evil we must face, and first of all the evil that acts from within us. For those who treat it as childish fantasy, have too little imagination to see that it is all about real things we face everyday, and our time is also a difficult time of changes and many dangers to the world, in which we live. It is true however that it is much more evident in the book. But it is hardly wise to expect a movie based on a masterpiece to be one too. And the only courage of the director who dared to put it into a film is to admire.

THE PLOT: Lately, I read the book again and to my surprise I found that the film is much closer to the book, than I first thought. As to the omitted things, they are many, but some of them are impossible to put into a movie, and also, the film is long enough like this. Nothing of most important things is omitted and there are good inventions to put an image to some of important things which cannot be rendered the same way as in the book. There ARE few commercialized moments like Gimly being slightly a clown and Pippin and Merry - two fools, Tolkien is gentler to those youngsters. But we have to not forget that the whole affair IS commercial, whether we want it or not, making movies cost money which have to be repaid and repaid double for someone to put money at all in the thing.

CHARACTERS: Reading the book again after seeing the film has done magic - it put faces to the characters and almost all of them fit so well! The best is Gandalf and the worst - Galadriel, the actress had a wonderful voice, but her appearance can hardly put in awe everyone despite the wonderful light-from-within effects. Elves could be more elvish and hobbits also less alike to men - in our time of special effects! What's done good is height difference between heroes and Legolas shooting arrows. Elrond is disappointing too by appearance although he's not purely Elf, neither is his daughter Arwen - that is so far the most betraying point of the film to the book. And I was happy to read that Viggo Mortnsen replaced another actor as Aragorn - the other's face isn't half so noble.

--------------- After reading the book I've seen the movie over again and my opinion of it improved much.

VISUAL RANGE: The landscapes are wonderful and outlandish, I guess the place was very good chosen. The work of sculptors and builders and animators for the craft-made places of dwelling is also above all praise.

AUDIO RANGE: At first I scarcely noticed the music, but after seeing the movie over and over again, I cannot help but praise it apart - it is a light magic woven into the film and it renders so very well the particularity, the powers and the moods of Middle-Earth created by Tolkien. It is not the least part in creating the special atmosphere of a world that binds into it so many people who have read the famous work

Everyone keep talking about the book and I'm not the last, but we must not forget that this whole world with its history and races was created by Tolkien over long years, a world almost real, especially now, thanks to the courage of the film-makers.

RESUME: The film does not replace the book. It might be very good for children to see, and later in age they might read the book and discover its depth. And the film COMPLETES the book by video-audio ranges.

Do not even try to see it or to comment on it, if the child within you is dead and you laugh at romantic, courageous and noble hearts, even if a bit naïve - you do not understand the message, that's all. But if your heart beats more soundly on reading about great deeds and evil defeat even in fantastic worlds, then among the fantasy-films, this is the best so far, as John Ronald Ruel Tolkien's book is among the fantasy-books.

Namàrië!

title: Hey dol derry dol, where's tom bombadillo?
review:
heh, the BBC radio drama left him out too, but thats ok I dont mind much.

I can't even begin to describe how wonderful the movie was. I read through the book again a few weeks ago and I came to the conclusion that no movie could ever touch the expanse of the book. A certain John Travolta movie recently made had put doubts into my head that LotR could be done. But its been done. I am a hardcore Tolkien fan but the screenplay was put together so nicely that I really didn't care about the changed/added pieces, they fit in very well. The mood and emotions were captured along with the sheer visual magnificence of it. Sure there was some little annoying things, but oh well, they don't even begin to detract from how incredible this movie is. I came out of the theater and my hands were shaking and my eyes were teary. I am still speechless after the second time seeing it. I think C.S. Lewis had the best description of the book; "...here are beauties which pierce like swords or burn like cold iron; here is a book that will break your heart..." All it needs is to have book replaced with movie.

title: Fantastic! My precioussss!
review: As a very lucky reviewer it was great to watch this probably most highly anticipated movie ever. In three hours we get to see a very impressive look at what Middle earth must look like. Peter Jackson has done an incredible job of bringing to the screen the emotions I had felt while reading the book. The characters may or may not be what you've imagined, but they really look fantastic for LOTR-fans as well as movie-fanatics. There are, in my opinion, no essential parts of the book missing on screen and that must have been hard to do, since the book is very descriptive. People who have not read the book might be at a slight disadvantage while watching the film, but all the more reason to read the book as well. It will only deepen the characters even more for them, but even without that the film will be great to watch too. The movie leaves the audience with the desire to see the other movies and after watching a three hour movie that has to be a great compliment to all concerned. Great scenes, excellent acting, powerful music. No adaption of LOTR could have been better.

title: I'm of the "excellent but overrated" opinion
review:
I do grow weary of the googly-eyed folks on IMDb, in the way they respond to the "dazzling" new/recent releases. I imagine that these are predominantly the same folks that in the last couple years vaulted _American Beauty_ to #6, _The Matrix_ and _The Sixth Sense_ into the top 30, and _Being John Malkovich_ and _Magnolia_ into or near the top 50. I do often find myself going against popular opinion on all sorts of subjects and it is tiresome to do so, but obviously what is popular isn't necessarily what's great. This is often compared to _Star Wars_ but at least _Star Wars_ is in the top 10 on this site rather than top 3. (And I don't consider _Star Wars_ top-10 material, either....)

Let's not get ahead of ourselves. Yes, there is technical wizardry here, there are gorgeous vistas, a tale of epic scale containing a classic story of good vs. evil with the fate of everything at stake. All in all, I can grant that it's probably quite the achievement to be able to put the story contained in the book up there on the screen. I imagine that many of the folks rushing in to rate this so highly hold the STORY near and dear to their hearts. That's understandable, but this is a *movie* site, so I judge the film by how it succeeds at being great cinema. And by that standard, I'll just say that I found this well worth my time to see it the first time, but not worth my time to see it twice. (Yes, I saw it twice before reaching that conclusion.) I can say that I'm glad they hired a director like Peter Jackson to direct the project, and even then there was a pervasive "Hollywood" feel throughout. I came out of the theater feeling unfulfilled (moreso the second time than the first), mainly because it's so heavy on the presentation but only "pretty entertaining" in terms of storyline. Maybe there is too much in fantasy-stories that makes them exceedingly difficult to succeed as great cinema, at least by my standards. To each his own, I guess.

I don't care to "knock" the film beyond this. It's excellent. Go see it at least once. Aside from the incessant ear-piercing shrieks of the Cloaked Horsemen of the Apocalypse, you'll have a fun time. But I figured it bears mentioning that it doesn't merit the ranking it's attained on this site, and I don't feel at all that it was robbed at the Oscars given the other nominees for Best Picture. (_Mulholland Drive_ was the best achievement in cinema in 2001, anyway. Hey, what's right ain't always what's popular -- almost certainly so in this case.)

title: Good cast, effects, Acting, Action but bad screenplay and script.
review: I didn't saw it on cinema which makes a big difference. I saw the movie after reading the first part and the hobbit and i think as one of the critics from Yahoo said: LOTR is about going places, that's why there'a map in the end of the each book. It would have been much better if they could incorporate the use of maps in their travel! they could use narration in some places. Movie was good but it was not close to LOTR novel - it seemed like it was made in bits and pieces. One minute they r in Bree and second in rivendel. But i guess it'll take a long TV series with good production to illustrate it properly.

title: This is the way to do fantasy
review:
If anyone asked me what's the game Dungeons and Dragons like, I wouldn't point to that ridiculous piece of garbage that came out in 2000. I would point to the original source, Lord of the Rings. This is the best film of 2001. This is a blockbuster mainstream flick that doesn't insult the audience's intelligence, like every mainstream blockbuster flick over the past couple years. George Lucas should take note. This is how you do a movie that everybody can enjoy. I've been a fan of Peter Jackson ever since I saw "Dead Alive".

I really liked "The Frighteners" as well, but this is leaps and bounds above those.

title: Maybe not the best ever... but still very good
review:
I'm not sure this movie would appear in the list of my 50 best films, but it's still a very good piece of entertainment.

Call me an illiterate, but I have to confess that I haven't read Tolkien's work. But I was still able to enjoy the movie. And to enjoy I did! It's a magnificent epic adventure in a world with strange inhabitants. The acting is very good, Elijah Wood is radiant as Froddo, Ian McKellen excels in his role. I found Liv Tyler and Cate Blanchett to be very good too.

The cinematography is superb. You feel that you're there. You feel that you're the one being pursue by the darklord with the terrible black horse. Amazing what technology can do for the image. But amazing to see that a lot of the film was actually shot in New Zealand and Australia. Just fabulous scenary.

I'm waiting for the Two Towers!

Out of 100, I gave it 85. That's good for ***½ out of **** stars.

Seen in Toronto, at the Regent Cinema, on April 21st, 2002.

title: Satisfied, but not amazed
review: I read LOTR ten years ago, but still remember most of it. When I left the theatre, I thought that I had seen a good film, with certain scenes quite stunning, but in total nothing breath-taking. Concerning the characters I was pleased with everyone, but Saruman. In my imagination he more represented the evil side by his look and speech, that most of all. He is supposed to seduce anyone merely by the power of his voice, which simply does not happen in the film. Also I was disappointed by omitting Tom Bombadil, the Master of the Old Forest. He is THE ancient character, as a matter of fact, far more powerful than Gandalf, for he does not vanish when wearing the ring, for instance. He precedes even the Dark Lord himself in age. And-he wins by song. On the other hand, Arwen and Galadriel "took" me really. When Arwen whispered to the river to save her and Frodo from the Nine, I hardly breathed. She was natural! The way she cried:"If you want him, come and claim him!", with her sword brandished high, that was SOMETHING. The other moment of this sort was Gandalf stopping Balrog at the Bridge of Kahazad-Dum, with all his might:"You shall NOT pass!" These moments, together with the temptation of Galadriel ("they shall all LOVE ME AND DESPAIR") and few others made me see the film three times already. Despite the fact that the structure of the film is not exactly excellent, following a scheme: talking-journey-battle... I can't wait to see the Two Towers.

title: The power of words and legend
review:
Starting off, this film is good as adventure films go. I never really got bored or anything, even though it was a full 3 hrs. I believe it's faithful enough to the book to get by all but the most rabid of fanboys as well. Apart from one thing. This movie has been nitpicked by lots of people, as well as praised, but I still feel I have one issue to press. That is, the power of word, history and names.

The Anduril (the blade of Isildur) is a highly potent token in the books. In the movie its just a broken sword. All through the great tale, the name of the enemy is hardly ever uttered. In the world of the book, a single name (Aragorns real one, for instance) has the power to rally armies. The importance of legend and history is really pressed on, even though some of these characters still walk amongst mortal men, their names and deeds are part of myth. Why take away from that grand atmosphere just to dumb it all down.

I guess people (read: americans, and yes I'm thoroughly prejudiced on this one, feel free to chastise me) are just plain stupid.

title: I know, but it IS the One Film to Rule Them All
review:
It is astounding to me that you could watch this movie and not be moved to tears, impressed beyond words, and in some basic fundamental way, changed.

The Fellowship of the Ring is, quite simply, the best movie made, ever.... so far. Will the next two movies match or exceed it? I hope so.

Can you find flaws? (*possible spoiler in this paragraph*) Yes, there are a few minor niggling CG errors that can be safely ignored. But, the scene with the giant statues looks like it was filmed, not generated. The Balrog was awesome, the loss of Gandalf was stunning. I had real tears in my eyes, as did others around me.

If I had to, under duress, find any flaw at all in casting, it would be with the dwarf... but then, we haven't really done much with him yet.

I have a new love, and it is this movie.

The last time I read the books was a few years ago, so it wasn't so fresh in my mind that I was annoyed by the few variations of book-to-script. Maybe it was better that way.

I feel like they went on location in Middle Earth and filmed there. The film is gorgeous. I want to visit.

Are you reading this to figure out if you should see the movie? If so, the answer is absolutely, positively, definitely, and without question, YES.

title: Good, but not nr 3 on the all time list.
review:
Let me start by pointing out that this is a good action/ adventure/ fantasy film, but it does have it´s flaws.

I read Tolkien in my teens and was really excited by the his work. I have since then read his books over again and do still find them enjoyable. I had no real expectations when I went to see the first part of the upcoming trilogy. I was at first truly impressed but I also felt that something was missing. I could just not put my finger to it.

After seeing the film I started to think about what I really thought of it. My humble conclusion was that while it is a technically brilliant and visually impressive film it lacks in character depth. If you think about you have to agree. The thing that makes Tolkiens work so much better than every other fantasy is that he gives a great deal of effort to explain and develop the characters and their motives.

I do realise that it is impossible to have long voice-overs to explain every single character that appears in the film but it also means that you don´t get the kind of emotional attachment to the characters as one would need to really feel immersed in this great tale. Now you don´t really care whether somebody lives or dies. And this is especially true when it comes to the Orchs, Saruman and Gollum.

The Orchs are reduced to a homogenous group that get killed in the dozens. It seems that these "fierce" creatures are so weak that the only way they can overpower the heroes is by huge numbers. But what I am most confused over is that Sarumans action are hardly explained. Why he acts the way he does and how it comes that he develops the way he does. And don´t get me started on Gollum. When I saw this film with friends (who have not read the books) they all wondered over what that creep was all about.

It´s not a bad film, but I think that in a couple of years it´s position as the third best film of all time will not be as obvious as it seems today.

title: This is NOT the #3 movie of all time!!!
review:
After seeing this movie rated as #3 in the history of movies worldwide on the IMDB rankings, I had to post a reaction (this happens to be the first time I have posted on this site).

I have generally agreed with the user ratings of movies on this site, but #3 all time?!?!? I don't think so.

Arguably, this movie is not even in the top 3 for 2001-2002 and it is definitely not in the top 3 for the last decade (Schindler's List, Pulp Fiction, Fight Club, Being John Malkovich, Life is Beautiful, Traffic, Memento, Magnolia, Fargo and Billy Elliott are just among the handful of superior films that were released in the past decade). This movie doesn't even belong in the top 50 all-time.

That being said, this is a movie that deserves all the "technical" awards it won for special effects, editing, sound, cinematography, etc., but lacked in several critical areas including acting (the only performance worth even mentioning for any awards was Ian McKellen) and character development (I haven't read the book, but the movie could have used more character development...and, no, we shouldn't have to wait for the sequels to see more development).

I agree that this is a good movie, but #3 all-time is giving is way too much credit. If one goes in to this movie expecting one of the best movies of all time, one will be sorely disappointed. Go in without any expectations and you will see a very good movie that was arguably one of the top 3-5 films of the last year (personally, I think The Royal Tenenbaums, In the Bedroom, Moulin Rouge, Amelie and A Beautiful Mind were all better films...but that's just my opinion...).

title: I film, while exciting, is not the vision of the book.
review:
Perhaps I have come to expect that this film would mirror the book, but instead the book has been "hollywoodized". About 2 hours in, myself (and my son) continued to ask "when is this over? Is it over already?"

Ian and Elijah give good performances, and the special effects are excellent. However, I expected more from one of the childhood tales that I will never forget.

title: Tolkein really is Hobbit forming
review: Now with this many posts someone's probably mentioned this already but.... Can you believe the amount of stoner references they crammed in to this flick? From Saruman repremanding Gandalf for his "love of the halfling's weed" to Sam. Merry and Pippin getting all excited over some special mushrooms to Bilbo and Gadalf toking on the hill. Of course I exaggerate, there's probably very little danger of Cheech and Chong turning up as a couple of Orcs in the next installment, still I do wonder. Story wise I reckon Sean Bean is man of the match, he gave the character of Bormir a real sense of tragic heroism , and expanded on what we know from the book. I approved of all the deviations from the novel, especially Aragorn getting the chance to say G'bye to Frodo. It made the story much more satisfying as a cinematic experience.

title: A Masterful Epic
review: I have seen The Fellowship of the Ring a few times now, and it only gets better.  This film is truly an epic, and captures the blend of humanity and fantasy that Tolkien probably envisioned.  I was deeply impressed by the cinematography, artistry, acting, and also the music/sound.  I was especially surprised by Elijah Wood.  At first, I was a little skeptical. Within minutes of meeting the character Frodo Baggins, I was immediately charmed.  All of the acting in the film was spot-on.  Also, I think that Howard Shore's score for the film is brilliant, which contains some gorgeous moments and expressive themes - the film wouldn't be the same without the music.  The whole experience is a feast for the senses.  Not only that, there is a lot of playfulness in the film in contrast to the serious moments.  I eagerly await the other two films in the trilogy.

title: Really brings to life a whole world. Incredible.
review: The acting was superb, the sets and scenery were simply stunning or stunningly simple, the music was apt and well incorporated, the special effects were as amazing as you would expect from such a filmmaker as Peter jackson, who has used CGI very effectively in at least two of his previous films (Heavenly Creatures and The Frighteners), and the story is fascinating and absorbing.  The Fellowship of the Ring puts to shame many a fantasy film that has come before, but also has an indescribable flavor of its own and the method of storytelling is as purely entertaining as it is well conceived.  Already one of my favorite films of all time, and my only complaint was that at its 3 hour running time it was too short.  I like some really long movies and would gladly sit through a 6 hour version of this film.  Alas, it is still nearly perfect!  Ian McKellen is Gandalf, he's that good.  The rest of the cast is fantastic as well.  My highest recommendation.

title: It's great, it's great, it's great, it sucks
review: Lord of the Rings. What can I say? Pearl Harbor was suppose to take the year 2001 away, like that. with no sweat. The movie that ended up being the Titanic of 2001 was Lord of the Rings. And its really everything that people said it would be. It's funny, intense, breath-taking, a nail biter, heart racing, scary, and sad. The graphics and special effects. Let's just say I'm still in awe. How do you take normal people and shrink them so they appear to be hobbits? but not only that, in the same shot, there is a normal person who appears to be a giant. How do you create a population full of grusemely gross creatures that just can't seem to die out? How are the fire-cracker ideas thought of? It's amazing, and as a member of the audience I guess these questions will never be answered, but that's fine, because I'll just let them amaze me, and i'm ok with that. The story line is great. I haven't read the book, but I heard it differs in many ways, unlike harry potter which follows the book's story line 100%. I have to give the author credit. His ideas are different from Harry Potter, yet similar as well. However he must have the best imagination, because the story line was amazing. It always kept you guessing what was going to happen next. And you were never let down. Everything that happened was always a suprise. Nothing was left given. That's why everyone can enjoy it. However, for the girls, there's also the sappy part. The part that made me cry along with the characters in the movie. But I guess you'll just have to watch the movie yourself to see why I cried. Trust me it's worth it. But now, we've gone through the it's great. it's great, it's great. it doesn't seem like it could suck does it? Anyways, it did. The climax kept on building and building and building, until the 3 hour long movie seemed like nothing. And you want to keep on watching the movie, but it ends, and it just leaves you hanging, when the movie is at the top of its climax!!!! At some points the movie seems long, but at the end you don't want it to end. And you don't believe it has ended until you see the credits. Well at least that's how it was for me. That's why it got a 9. But there are two more sequels coming out, so maybe its good that i was left hanging. Because I am definitely watching the next movie. And if that movie leaves me hanging too, I am definitely watching the third movie.

title: Middle of the road Middle Earth
review:
I've watched the fellowship 3 times and I'm sorry to say it really doesn't impress me that much. It's a good film but it lacks the final few brush strokes that could and should have turned the 20th century's greatest piece of fiction by a Much copied (I'm thinking of George Lucas) writer Mr Tolkein.

I'd like to say that I think it was really brave of Peter Jackson to try to make Rings and I feel he did his best but it was not good enough.

It had the distinct feel of a Hollywood no brainer (eg. Legolas firing a arrow about 600 meters across a cavern and low and behold hitting an Orc square in the nose.) Do me a favour Mr Jackson!!! It really does insult ones intelligence and education, which my parents spent their hard earned money one.

It had no feel to it, no style. I like films to have a Recognisable atmosphere, if you've seen the cartoon version of Lord " " " I think you'll agree that it did have a wonderful atmos unlike Jacksons "BIG BUCK UP"

The acting was good from the lead men, the friendship between Frodo and Sam is the Pivotal part of the saga and I was Satisfied with the convincing performances given. The supporting cast was held together by Mckellen and the BRILLIANT Christopher Lee, plus a heart warming performance by the Mr Ian holm. I thought the part of Aragorn was miscast, but you have to have someone with an American accent in these big movies or they get upset.

title: Wonderful movie, even for a non-fanatic
review:
Wow, where to start? Firstly, this movie is so well put together it's hard to nitpick on anything other than the long-ish running time. 3+ hours is needed to try to fit in the huge scope of the novel. Having not read the book for over 2 decades, it was hard sitting through at first. You feel like you've been plumped on your seat right in the middle of the movie already partway in progress. But once you start taking in the wonderful acting, you get truly acquainted with Middle Earth and its denizens. My one big complaint was I didn't remember Frodo being this wimpy. He was basically the biggest coward in the Fellowship. The special effects were well-placed and not very "brazen." The cinematography is first-rate, the actors are well-cast and the lines are well-written. They even managed to put in a few welcome comedic scenes along the way. Put it this way: this is one of the best 3 hours you are ever going to spend in a movie theatre (unlike *cough* Pearl Harbor *cough).

Even if you don't know Middle Earth from the Shadow Lands, come and see this event movie. Kudos to everyone involved in the trilogy. You have done excellent work and should be very proud of yourselves.

The screen adaptation doesn't live up to Tolkien's work, though I don't suppose that any film ever will. Even so, I still loved the film.

title: the Chinese Food of films
review:
I liked the movie. I did, really, all three hours of it. I didn't find it humorless, though my incorrigible husband made it easier to find the laughs (Gandalf re going to Moria: "Frodo must decide..." Husband, coyly: "I dunno, what do YOU want to do?"). The scenery and sets were breathtaking, Moria was in itself worth the price of admittance. Most of the actors did a fine job. The CGI was only distracting a couple of times, which given the sheer volume of special effects in the film is more worthy of lavish praise than complaint. And I doubt anyone can come away from this film without a hankering to personally explore New Zealand's incredibly gorgeous landscape.

If the characters or events didn't look or play out as I'd always imagined them, they at least made sense within the context of the books and/or the movie, so I took no offense; the vision of the film was pleasingly consistent. Tolkien himself doesn't spend a tremendous effort in development of characters, really... he's much more concerned about the sweep of history and the environment in which the action takes place. Jackson has made some changes to the story, and although I might quibble with some of them and wish he'd spent more time on character development, overall he has kept very closely to the adventurous spirit of the tale. The books are largely (with apologies to Mr. Ebert) a hop from one threatening moment to the next battle, with explanatory councils and lectures peppered liberally about. Jackson takes full, colorful advantage of those skirmish-ridden passages and (understandably, given his filmatic background) makes hay with the darkest and ookiest of Tolkien's beasties.

I admire Jackson tremendously for bringing this film to the screen in the face of the overwhelming pressure inherent in depicting one of the most well-known and rabidly loved classics of our time. It's a perilous landmine-strewn task he's taken on, and he's done an excellent job of it. My mother enjoyed the film tremendously. My eleven year old, to whom I read the books aloud this year (as my mother read them to me, when I was eleven), held my hand throughout the entire three hours, something I can't remember him having ever done before. He loved it, and can't wait to see it again. The incorrigible husband, who has never read the books, gave it two thumbs up. I can't complain at all.

And yet... and yet... I can't put my finger on it, quite. Although I enjoyed the movie very much, I'm left feeling still a bit hungry, a bit unsatisfied in some small and nagging way.

There is a bright thread that runs through most of the literary trilogy that keeps us in touch with the tenderness we see but briefly in an early scene between Gandalf and Bilbo in Jackson's film. Tolkien paints vividly in nearly every passage an admiration for the flawed but passionate races of man and dwarf, a strong sense of nostalgia for the innocence of the Shire and a yearning for the purity of the Elvish hames. It is this admiration and tenderness that inspires Gandalf and Aragorn to self-sacrifice, that binds Sam to his erstwhile employer and keeps Frodo foraging ahead on his increasingly burdened and seemingly impossible quest. In spite of the charming Hobbiton beginning and the occasional reference to the Shire and Hobbits by Gandalf et al, I think that perhaps my sense of nagging Something-Missing stems from some slack or occasional break in that thread in Jackson's vision, a small but essential neglect of that element which elevates the books from a list of battles, flights, and passages of historic exposition to the place of near reverence it holds in the hearts of generations of readers. I can only hope that Mr. Jackson makes up for this small but essential lack in the next two installments, which I am bound to see. After all, the first film is very good, though somewhat unsatisfying, and it has left me hungry for more...

title: A film for readers, not for film-addicts!
review:
I had not read the trilogy before watching the movie, which I deeply regret (because now I'll never be able to take E. Wood's face out of Frodo). But I'm not very fond of fantasy stories since I was ten. So I went to the theater feeling curiosity but expecting nothing specially exciting. And what I found was a poorly directed movie with poor and too noticeable computer effects. Lack of suspense, less locations that this high budget production should have (replaced with computer-made landscapes, like the disturbing fake Rivendel), lack of female strong characters (for which we should blame Tolkien, though) and the film taking too much to get nowhere (for those who hadn't read the books, the film ends almost where it starts).

However I must say that it struck the reader that lives inside me and made me rush to the bookstore. It was good enough to make me want to read the trilogy. I was sure that the books would be far better than the film. And I was right. Though it's not my favorite genre I must thank the movie for leading me to the books.

One more complaint about the FX quality. The size of the hobbits seems to change depending on the camera position. On general shots, half a man. Close shots, hardly smaller than men and definitively taller than dwarves! This incredible mistake kept disconnecting me from the story. Come on, this has been made before. Hadn't the producers ever seen "Willow", for example?!? Hadn't they heard about chroma-keys?!? This film won't be mentioned in film-making history for it's quality but for it's box office all around the world.

There's still a chance to make a much better translation of those books into film, maybe within the next few decades! I hope I can see it!

title: What can I say that 3000 others have not said before?
review:
Only 1000 words? Oh dear. So much for the five page essay.

First, let me be up front - I LOVED FOTR! It certainly would be included on a list of my PERSONAL top ten. Whether it should be listed as one of the top movies of all time is a question I will address a later.

Are there flaws in this film? Yes. As with all films, there were moments that fell short of perfection. However, one must be careful to separate matters of personal taste from actual shortcomings with the movie.

There were badly edited moments. There were drawn out and/or repetitive slow motion scenes. And I can understand those who felt this movie was an endless, monster infested, three hour chase scene - part of the difficulty lies in trying to condense hundreds of pages of detailed text and a time frame of years into one movie. Had Peter Jackson been able to include all he wanted, this film would have been far longer than three hours. Some things had to be sacrificed, and much of what was lost were the restful pauses and conversations that would have lessened the frantic pace and helped define character relationships.

That having been said, I think Jackson still managed to do an excellent job of establishing the characters within the parameters he was allowed. Some reviewers felt that the film lacked characterization. However, during one's initial viewing, there is so much occurring, it is easy to miss the subtle glances and facial expressions that mark much of the character interaction in this film. This is a movie that should be seen multiple times in order to get the full impact. Perhaps there is merit in the idea that a movie should convey its entire message in one viewing, but even I had trouble telling some of the characters apart the first time, and this from someone who *read* the book!

There seems to be controversy over whether LOTR deserves to be a top rated film. Admittedly, I have never studied film and would not know a gaffer from a gopher if it bit me  but in this I am not unlike MOST of those who contribute to the IMDb top 250 Movies of All Time. We vote based upon mainstream films we enjoy. However, as taste varies, so will those films that reach us at that most elemental level. Personally, I go to the cinema looking for movies that will show me new vistas, open new worlds and appeal to my active imagination and creativity. The films I enjoy run the gamut from westerns, to comedies, to quirky offbeat flicks that defy classification. Some of `good' filmssome are not so good. But they all generally share two of the elements that appeal most to me, characters to whom I could relate and a setting that tickled my imagination. LOTR had both.

I have seen many of the movies that others considered `the best.' Some are favorites of mine, but others I found exceedingly tedious. Does this mean I think they are bad films? No. Do I purposely go out of my way to give them a 1 in order to lower their ratings? Of course not! I am not so egotistical as to assume that, just because I do not fully appreciate a film, it must be horrible.

Perhaps those who protests the presence of LOTR as a top film do not understand that `fantasy' fans have been waiting for a movie like this for years! Any given year usually has a least a couple quality dramas, but really well crafted fantasies are a rarity. Most fantasy movies are generally targeted at children, or never rise above the level of your typical B-grade popcorn flick. Not so with LOTR. Here is a film, part of a larger epic, which is made for adults. It is dark and far more complex than some, `silly little movie filled with fairies and wizards.' Furthermore, it garnered critical acclaim, including 13 Oscar nominations, of which it won four. Its success can be seen as vindication that fantasy is indeed a viable genre, and can be well executed by someone who really cares.

So you see, LOTR is more than a `movie' to most of us  it is a step towards legitimacy for a genre we love. Thus we are passionate about its success. Of course, the fantasy genre will not appeal to everyone, and if someone genuinely dislikes this film for legitimate reasons, that is valid. However, I have read more than one review for LOTR where someone blatantly bragged that they gave the film a lower rating that they really felt it deserved because they either don't like the fact it is so successful or they don't like the fans. This says a great deal more about the reviewers' own prejudices than it does about the movie.

Which brings me to my final comment. I do not understand WHY some of those who did not like the movie feel obliged to insult those who did. Calling the movie a `geek-fest' or referring to its fans as `nerds' is totally unnecessary and does not add any weight to your opinion. In fact, it only makes those who resort to such tactics appear foolish and petty. Comments about `fanboys who have no lives, no girlfriends and live in their parent's basement' are not clever. There are tired old cliches that those of us who enjoy fantasy and sci-fi had been listening to for years I suspect that some of the nay-sayers actually enjoyed the film, but are so fearful of being labeled a `nerd' that they feel the need to assert their `superiority' by tearing others down  humanity at its worst.

In the final analysis, this film will appeal to many. Others will dislike it. This is true of any film. My recommendation is that you see it and make up your own mind.
