title: It's good (possible spoilers)
review:
SPOILER WARNING

This is a pretty solid film, but its not perfect.

The make-up, costumes, and props are wonderful; this film really succeeds in the close-up details. However, many of the large-scale special effects sequences don't hold up to scrutiny; Lothlorien & Moria look great, but Isengard & Barad-dûr suffer from that cgi/miniature 'look'; the automated tracking shots of these locations don't help either. The cinematography is mostly fine (some great lighting), but the pilots are flying much too fast during most of the scenery grabs.

I skim-read the book after seeing the film, and I can understand why fans were frustrated by some of the changes. Whilst I have no problem with removing whole episodes and upgrading Arwen's role; it's sad that some of the key exchanges in the books (the meeting of the Council, Galadriel's mirror) were shortened considerably. This was probably done to include more action sequences, but to be honest these are the not the things that I look forward to when I re-watch the film.

The confrontation between Gandalf & Saruman borders on the comical, and the Redhorn Pass, Watcher in the Water, and Cave Troll sequences are just action/monsters-by-numbers. The staircase in Moria is exciting enough, but its far too contrived. Funnily enough, the best action sequences are those which significantly advance the plot (Frodo's wounding, Frodo's rescue, Gandalf's fight with the Balrog, Boromir's death, and the capture of Pip & Merry). I would have quite happily jettisoned the rest in favour of more character development.

The acting is generally good (especially Gandalf, Boromir, & Aragorn), but Frodo, Elrond & Galadriel are let down by some seriously clunky lines. The worst thing about this film is probably the script; it's just inconsistent. The score is inconsistent too; it's fine overall, but has annoying lapses into "Titanic" style sentimentality.

However, it IS a good film - not worthy of all those 10s, but definitely an 8.

title: Dull and uneventful
review:
After all the hype of this film, one easily has great expectations, and it is easy to be disappointed. And I was. Maybe it is unfair, because I have seen similar films earlier, loosely based on the LOTR world. Nevertheless, there are several reasons why this film was truly disappointing:

Lightning was inconsistent. Some scenes had bright and Disney-esque colours, others had washed-out near B/W effects. Other scenes again looked like they were made in the 70's. Maybe it was deliberate, but I failed to see the brilliance.

Plot was dull. I have not read the book(s), and maybe I therefore missed some points. The background for the rings' existence was incoherently explained, but the the plot thenceforth was so straightforward I was bored to tears. No surprising twists, no suspension; very predictable.

Repetitive and inane dialogue. How often did I not hear Frodo state "I did not want this to happen"? Too often. And the references to myths and traditions popped up like fungi but contributed precious little to the plot as it did not bring in any element of suspense or explanation.

Seriousness. The film was pompous - both in terms of directing, acting and dialogue. The only relief was Pip, the "Irish" Hobbit. In Willow (in my opinion, a comparable film in terms of genre), humour was more prevalent. Lack of any lighthearted situations in LOTR contributed to my boredom.

Directing and editing sometimes seemed to be deliberately fragmented in order to cover up poor special effects. In this day and age we should be able to expect focused cameramen. I have no plans seeing the next "instalment". But if LOTR had been cut down to two hours, I might have enjoyed it.

title: Seeing the movie without reading the book.
review: I was really glad I saw this movie without having read the book first. The gorgeous scenes add to the magic of what truly is a great movie. Strong characters held the story together, and the cinematography, music, action...it was all to die for. A triumph for a local director taking on the Hollywood big-guns.

title: A solid adaption worthy of praise
review:
To be fair, I should state that I read Lord of the Rings before I was a teenager, so I knew what was going on before seeing the movie. I had not read the book recently, so didn't know the specifics, but knew the general plot line. Certainly, this prior affiliation afforded me the luxury of knowing the plot line, yet also not getting caught up in the differences between the book and the movie, which I discovered when I re-read the book after seeing the movie.

I was very happy and impressed the first time I saw the movie and felt it very accurate to the book, or accurate to the feeling of the book at least. Upon re-reading the book I found that there are significant differences between the movie and the book, but differences are unavoidable adapting a good sized book to a movie, even a three hour movie.

Is this movie complicated? Not really. Neither was Tolkien's work. At least at one level. The movie is true to the book in this respect: at the surface level there is a struggle between good and evil and a quest that the heroes of good embark on to overthrow the forces of evil, with the enemy creating numerous obstacles to foil the heroes' efforts. There is not a lot of nuance or subtlety. The story is the adventure of the characters trying to destroy The Ring. There aren't really any plot twists or characters struggling with some big moral dilemma or any betrayal. I don't think Tolkien meant for it to be complicated; I think he meant to create a good story. There is depth to the story in the relationships among the characters, but not so much in the plot line itself. If a quest of good versus evil where good triumphs in the end is not your style, don't bother watching.

My general feeling of the movie: the acting was great. I felt the emotion of the characters and that the emotions they felt were real. Evidence to back that claim up? Can there be evidence of convincing acting? I think one is either convinced or not, but I don't know what one can point to say, "That made me believe." because another could point to the same thing and say, "That didn't work for me." Casting was great and captured the spirit of the book. That's what it should do, right? Yes, I think a movie should be able to be enjoyed without ever reading the book, but the movie should be some sort of representation of the book, right? The scenery and settings were fantastic and fit the feeling of the book as well--and better than I imagined them myself at times, especially concerning Mordor and Isengard. Some of the CGI was great, some very obvious and ho-hum. Most importantly for me, at its best it enhanced the movie, at its worst was passable, but at no time prevented the movie from advancing the plot. Costuming was great on the whole, though I felt the orcs to be not so interesting. Sound was good, but I would have liked more usage of all 6.1 channels (could have been a theater thing, though). That said, let me address some specific complaints I've read in other reviews, and these very well may be "Spoilers", so if you don't want anything to be "spoiled", stop here.

The "no-ending" complaint. Tolkien wrote one book that publishers split into three for economical reasons. Jackson created a much better "ending" than the way FOTR "ends." Be glad it's not spot on accurate to the book. It would be much worse. Jackson should be applauded for manufacturing a reasonable stopping point one-third through a 1000+ page book. It's not really a trilogy. As one comment criticized, "it's basically a nine hour movie." Well, yes, it is. =)

One reviewer claims that the costumes were rags and the scenery wasn't anything special. The hobbits and Aragorn wore little more than rags. I guess that person didn't notice Sauron or all the men and elves in armor or dwarves or hobbits or orcs who weren't wearing rags. As for scenery. Well, if some of the more beautiful landscapes on this planet is nothing special, then there is no really special scenery on this planet. I feel, however, that huge expanses of mountains and forests and plains are very special.

As for hero invincibility. There is good reason that the heroes are so invincible, but it is true that the movie does not convey why this is. Basically, all the characters have some level of supernatural power. Boromir the least, and he does die. What the movie is not so clear about is that Gandalf and the elves are immortal, Dwarves generally live to 250, Hobbits over a 100, and Aragorn is about 90. These aren't normal people; there is good reason they kick so much butt, but the movie does not relate this well, unfortunately. Watching the movie I wondered the same thing, but in the book one expects the heroes to make mincemeat of the enemy. All in all, I don't mind criticism, I just get frustrated when people criticize yet cite no proof, and especially when I can look at someone's criticism and quote a line from the movie which debunks the criticism. Feel free to criticize, just back it up with evidence, otherwise you make yourself look like an unintelligent, baseless, mud-slinger.

Moral of the story: FOTR is not one of the best films of all time, but is very well done on the whole and does an admirable job of bringing to screan a beloved story. It has more ups than downs. It is a very different movie to those who know Tolkien's work as opposedto those who don't.

Above all, pay attention and have an open mind. And be fair in understanding that changes had to made from the original book.

title: A Generally Excellent Film
review: While perhaps not the best movie of the year, and certainly inferior to Peter Jackson's earlier film, Heavenly Creatures, The Fellowship of the Ring is nevertheless an impressive film.  I have met very few people who find it perfect, but I also don't know anyone who actually claimed to dislike it. For the most part, its virtues are hard to deny. The spectacular set pieces such as the pursuit of Arwen and Frodo by the Nine Riders or the concluding battle between Boromir and Sauruman's orcs are such that very few viewers could remain unmoved.  I find it difficult to explain why, despite these scenes, I did not like the film more.  I only know that the friends and family members with whom I have discussed it share my feelings to one extent or another.  Perhaps Tolkien's book should not have been made into a film. Even so, it is worth seeing for the spectacular visuals alone.

title: The ultimate epic?
review:
It's LOUD! Man was it loud. It's long. And it's BIG! I mean massivebig. Ian McKellan's face takes up the whole screen. And it's very, very good. It's Star Wars good (and the comparison with SW doesn't just stop at 'good'. Watching LotR just shows how incredibly derivative Lucas was) People will be dissapointed, there's been a lot of hype, everyone that's read the book holds it dear to their heart (and there simply isn't enough cash in the world to budget a film to equal one person's imagination.)

You can only judge the film on it's own merits, and by that standard it's simply one of the most breathtaking pieces of cinema i've been lucky enough to see. It's so richly and meticulously detailed that you don't have to *try* to become involved, to believe. You just do. Everything just works so well. The towering, powerful but vulnerable Gandalf. The innocent, brave, resiliant Frodo. Classicly heroic Aragorn. Fiercely loyal (and clearly gay) Samwise. The grace of the Elves, and the beauty of their language. The characters are so deep, so full of life.

Be patient. It starts slow. Once the history unfolds, the pace starts to gradually rise. And rise. And before you know it, hell's breaking loose and you're being whisked along for the ride. Visually, you've never seen anything like it. I just walked about 4 miles to get home (serious lack of taxis) and it was all i could think about. Indellible images. Leave work right now, go to the local cinema and beg them to give you a ticket for the next performance.

title: Truly Remarkable
review:
After seeing an early press screening of LOTR:TFOTR, I was left with very few words floating in my head... epic. fantastic.

This is the reason the movies still exist. This is why we make movies. This is why television will never outdate the silver screen.

LOTR is an epic fantasy that has range and scope greater than any movie I've ever seen. Don't get me wrong, I don't feel it is the best movie ever or even of the year (Memento seems to have a lock on this year's best), but LOTR is an event film in the purest form.

We needed that now. Peace.

Myself not having read the classic fantasy novels by tolkien hope that all of the LOTR fans were as amazed by peter jackson's rendition of a classic. The movie had something for everyone there was mystery, romance, humor and of course more then it's fair share of action.  I don't know when the DVD will be coming out, probaly after the other 2 sequals do, but i know that when they do i'll be first in line to pick them up

title: You can always put a book down...
review:
Of course, you can always put a book down... which is the only reason Tolkien's work is even remotely bearable. Peter Jackson attempts to please the legions of people who have forgotten that they put 'Lord of the Rings' down at least twice per page and swore they'd never read it again have resulted in 3 hours of turgid nonsense. What follows would be SPOILERS, but pretty much everyone on the planet has to know the plot by now:

'Fellowship of the Rings' is the emptiest 3 hours I have ever spent. What actually happens? Cute hobbits, birthday party, nasty ring, take it to Mordor... ooh, Black Riders - run away!... ooh, orcs - run away!... ooh, more orcs - we can't run away! But here comes a Balrog... RUN AWAY! Let's cross some mountains, wander through some mines, have the entire story explained to us by some fairies. Hmm, dramatic tension ebbing a bit... ooh! Look! More orcs - run away! Oh, we can't. OK, we'll have a fight then, and lose instead. But off go Frodo and his light-relief sidekick, cos the poor little hobbits can't trust anyone not to steal their ring. When Aragorn, son of Arathorn, son of somebody else ending in 'orn' announced that it was 'Time to hunt some orc' I was on the verge of standing up in the cinema and screaming, but fortunately it was the end. At one point my girlfriend, who hadn't been paying attention, noticed Frodo was walking through a bleak landscape and whispered 'Have I missed something? Has he got rid of the ring already?'. Oh no, no, no, my little innocent - you've got to sit through another SIX HOURS of this nonsense before that happens.

DO NOT WASTE YOUR LIFE. Don't bother reading the book instead - you can get on with other things at the same time, like watching paint dry.

title: One of the best films of 2001
review:
My rating: 8 out of 10

I must admit, I was a tad wary about seeing this movie for I am not very fond of the fantasy genre. But I gave it a shot and just recently saw it in the theatre and was left speechless. This has easily got to be one of the best films of 2001. There are so many wonderful things to say about it but I'm not sure where to begin. The special effects were simply astounding--the best I've seen in years, the cinematography was extremely impressive, the acting was superb and flawless (McKellen was badly cheated at the Oscars), and the musical score was gorgeous. It is so sad to see that it only won 4 Oscars out of 13 (especially losing to "A Beautiful Mind" for Picture and Adapted Screenplay). This film ranks up there with "Gone with the Wind," "E.T.," "Apocalypse Now," and "Casablanca." Unfortunately, I do have one little complaint. For some reason, an idea has materialized that in order to make an epic film, it HAS to be 3 hours of length or longer. Why filmmakers hold strong to this philosophy, I do not know. There were some scenes that just seemed to badly drag. For example, there is somewhat of an "intermission" between the two climactic parts of the film that just goes on and on. Had it been trimmed, it would not have affected the film in any way. Further down the line, all the combat scenes become a tad mundane and could have easily been shortened. And in the final combat scene, it takes like 10 minutes for a character to die and I got the feeling that I was having emotion that wasn't there shoved down my throat. About 5 minutes into all the grief that this character was doomed, I was saying to myself, "Will you just DIE already?" However, these problems are strongly offset by the rest of this spectacular film and appear miniscule in the long run. I recommend LOTR very highly. It is truly a wonder to behold and will not be forgotten anytime soon. I rate LOTR:TFOTR as a 8 out of 10

title: YO, THIS MOVIE IS FANTASTICAL!
review: I really really liked the thinking of a epic movie with mitey heroes and legendary evil forces kicken butt all over the place.  It's like, hey, that's incredible!  The way the good guys just team up against the evil magic of the dark powers was well thought through, and way cool.  Seeing great movies like this always reminds me of my favorite flick, Rocky, since the magic in this film is similar to the dark forces, both internal and external, that Rocky Balboa has to confront.

title: Slow as the feloship's journy.
review: Let me start by saying that I never liked the book Lord of the Rings. Happy memories entwine me from when I was about 12 and would sit and draw while listening to The Hobbit. The Hobbit was ingenious and clever, while Lord of the Rings felt like a dreary old history book. Now we come to the movie, what can I say? I saw it in the theaters the first week it came out. Did I like it? This is not the question; more precisely let me state that, yes, it did, so far as I could tell, follow the book, perhaps not only that, but it had the feel of the book. It flowed as the book does, and it was every bit as boring. Just as in the book it started out charmingly with the little Hobbit village, quivered on the edge of being intriguing for a moment, but soon wound its way into a tireless sickle of attacks, runs, and frustratingly predictable sentimentality. Yes I fidgeted and yawned, but finally gathered myself to sit though and enjoy, just as the movie uncompromisingly, frustratingly, ended. So this is one idea I propose. PUT A STOP TO MULTI PART MOVIES!!! Yes I can understand making a movie that is complete in of itself, it has a beginning and and end, such as Star Wars episode one, yet you know there are three coming up, but The Lord of the Rings did not even have the climax in the movie, all it had was the meat usually found in the second third of the book. As sorry I am to say, even the nice effects did not make this movie more then just another average; that could have waited for my home screen.

title: Very good, but not great.
review: It seems, now days, that a movie can be mediocre, or average, yet be praised because next to all the other horrible movies out there it seems to shine. I don't think this is fully the case with LOTR, but what's it have to compete with today? While 70%-80% of this movie had me awestruck and anxious for the next scene, the other 20%-30% had me wondering if I was watching the same movie. The casting was excellent Liv Tyler's Arwen was very disappointing however, and I kept expecting Elrond to call someone Mr. Anderson from behind a pair of shades. The cinematography was as one would have viewed it from there own eyes. I noticed some difficulty relating the eye contact in some of the generated scenes ,much like Liam Neeson's eye contact with Jar-Jar in the Phantom Menace. My biggest complaints; 1.there seemed to be much more fighting scenes then in the book 2. the generated faces lusting for the ring (facial expressions are the key to acting, let me see the want in there face, don't express it for them)3. the lack of certain situational, relationships. For example, the brotherly love between Frodo, and Sam; the hate that bleeds to love between Gimli and Legolas; and the master and apprentice-like union between Gandalf and Aragorn. I was slightly disappointed of the decision to exclude Tom Bombadil, too, as that was a favorite section of mine. And of course the Hollywood like approach to force a love interest into a story. A love interest that not only doesn't exist (in this chapter) but is awkward and unnecessary. I hate to be so critical as I did enjoy this movie very much, but it for no reason belongs in the top 3 movies (or even 50 for that matter) of all time.

title: A Good Start; let the waiting for parts II and III begin!
review:
"One film to lure them all, one film to woo them, One film to bring them all and in the darkness glue them."

Well, maybe...

I found it pretty well impossible to think about this film without considering the book.

If you've read it recently enough to remember it, then you'll probably find the film an almost entirely satisfactory rendering of Tolkien's flat, detailed, humourless, occasionally superficial narrative prose style (there were a few little muckings-about, cuts and additions but these were mostly harmless). But as with Potty Harry, you might still think (as I did) that a film should be a lot more than merely a cinematographic rendering of a linear sequence of words; then again you might think that suitable homage has been paid to a book that brought the idea of the mythic epic narrative form back into the mainstream (thereby unfortunately spawning an orc-ish horde of poor imitations that didn't bother with Tolkien's attention to sub-structure; remember that The Lord Of The Rings was just skimming the surface of the complete mythology that The Silmarillion revealed more of).

If you haven't read the book but the idea of "a mixed bunch of adventurers who don't really like one another but have An Important Mission to carry out" appeals to you then you'll probably enjoy Our Heroes' struggle against overtly Evil forces and covertly Disruptive influences; you might even find the brief nod to "Back To The Future" amusing rather than cheesy and pointless.

If you haven't read the book and you don't fancy the film, then ask yourself this: did you like Star Wars? Because if George Lucas didn't find inspiration in the likes of Tolkien then I'll eat my light sabre.

Regardless of where you're coming from, it's certainly a visual feast. Spectacular computer animation plus the lovely New Zealand scenery (not been there? Go!) mostly managed not to distract from some fine acting and excellent costumery. (I said *some*; the ubiquitous Cate Blanchett got a bum deal here: looking soulful and sad didn't really capture Galadriel's sense of impending loss of her own power, but perhaps the fault lay more with the dialogue and direction at this point.)

Oh, you want a rating? Sorry, you'll have to wait a couple of years until I've seen all the installments. It's all based on one big book really; practical considerations of time and economy are what have split it into three films.

title: Peter Jackson was robbed!!
review:
Now more than ever I am convinced that the Oscars are a sham. Peter Jackson DESERVED to win best director. He orchestrated the making of three epic movies simultaneously, directing thousands of actors, extras and crew. He made a movie that was believed untranslatable to the big screen, and satisfied thousands of Tolkien fans in the process.

I never expected the Academy to vote LOTR for best picture (too much fantasy, no Russell Crowe and without a neat and tidy Hollywood ending) but Jackson definitely deserved the honour of best director.

title: It has a few flaws, but is still the finest fantasy film of all time.
review:
It lives up to the hype. It's magnificent - the best fantasy film I've ever seen.

O.K, so it is not as great as the book. Even in three hours, set against the gorgious New Zealand landscape and featuring some lavish sets and costumes, it cannot hope to match the richness of detail and historical depth that Tolkien could fit into the 500 or so pages of The Fellowship of The Ring. Nor does it have the pacing of the book - without slashing more parts of the story director Peter Jackson simply couldn't spare the time to make the transitions between the major events as smooth as Tolkien did. At times we seem to jump from one big scene to another in 'Greatest Hits' style; for example, the shift from Moria to Lorien is too sudden.

Having said that, the screenplay by Jackson and his collaborators is an excellent adaption of the book, retaining almost all of the best scenes and lines - 'many who live deserve death, and some who are dead deserve life. Can you give it to them? Do not be so quick to deal out judgement.' - while keeping the plot tight and even improving on Tolkien (blasphemy! the fanatics cry) in some ways, such as by showing more of Saruman's rise to power, adding the big badass orc Lurtz and bringing out several laugh-out-loud moments, particularly with Merry and Pippin, which the book lacked.

Jackson's best achievement though is how the film looks. As with 'Harry Potter', my imagination generally topped what was on the screen - but to the filmaker's credit there were plenty of things that were even better than I had envisioned. I cannot emphasize this too much - 'Fellowship' looks AMAZING. Seething hordes of goblins, an idyllic, waterfall-bordered Rivendell, hellish labyrinths of mines and tunnels, thrilling, chaotic battles, and the Balrog. Oh my God, the Balrog. I spent a lot of this movie with my jaw unhinged.

In terms of the acting, the casting is just about perfect. Sir Ian McKellern as Gandalf, Viggo Mortensen as Aragorn, Sean Bean as Boromir and Sir Ian Holm as Bilbo are outstanding, and pretty much everyone else hits the mark. To act in this kind of high-flown mythic style and not be melodramatic is tough, but they pull it off - with the exception of a few moments.

Yes, it's not perfect. A few shots of Arwen and Galadriel - all angelic and glowing - are overdone, some of the lines are delivered sentimentally, and the music, which generally excellent, also goes over the top at times. And, reluctant as I would be to do it, if I was editing the film I'd cut out the whole Lorien chapter. It's pretty good but compared to the rest of the film it doesn't add much, has a couple of those creaky moments I mentioned, lengthens a long film and does upset the pace. Again, Jackson couldn't afford the time to give the forest enough of the feel of a wondrous, magical sanctuary that Lorien had in the book.

Rating: 8 1/2

title: a comment worth viewing
review: I have read the books and absolutely adore them. Was the movie satisfying??? Well, I don't know how hard it would be to make some scenes as they are in the book. I know how much Jackson loves the books so I will give him the benefit of the doubt. I will not focus on what should of happened, but what happened. Elijah Woods as Frodo Baggins: I've always been fond of Elijah's movies. I was a little skeptical at first, but when given the chance to show his skills he delivers. Ian McKellen as Gandalf the Grey: Top notch, who else can deliver such a touching performance as a wise wizard then Ian. Enough said. Viggo Mortensen as Strider/Aragorn: This is the performance that will catapult Viggo's career. WOW! What a king he will make. Everyone else shows how weak they are when confronted with the ring. Frodo offers it to him and he closes his hand and pulls it towards Frodo's heart as if it didn't even phase him. Viggo was in my opinion the most memorable character and actor in this movie. He rivals Russel Crowe's character in Gladiator. I believe he saved this movie from being average. Sean Astin as Samwise Gamgee: Good performance and very satisfying. Sean as Sam will come full circle in the Two Towers. Orlando Bloom as Legolas Greenleaf: I am convinced he is an Elf in real life. I don't think their will be anyone out there who will say Orlando's performance wasn't anything but perfection. Sean Bean as Boromir: He is in some sense a bad guy and I'm upset that we realized this so strongly in Rivendale. He ended up realizing his errors by contesting for the ring. I admire his performance and he will be missed. Liv Tyler as Arwen Undomiel: So she had too many lines and too many scenes for Arwen. Don't blame her. She did OK and I'm not upset with her role, but that the writers didn't stick true to the book. I really do feel a strong bond between Aragorn and Arwen in the movie and can't wait until their love brings tears to fans when they finally unite. I think it's great that Aragorn speaks Elvish to her. I also enjoyed how well Aragorn spoke Elvish and damn I can't say enough about viggo Mortensen. Cate Blanchett as Galadriel: A solid performance. Could of been better and more magical however. Of course they should of showed more of her and her gift givings to the Fellowship. So I won't blame her for it. I like Cate Blanchett and she did just fine, but I would of enjoyed her more if she wasn't so dark and hard. Gollum: Good. Can't complain at all. All in all I will say that the movie is nothing short of an experience!!

title: good, but not great
review: Apart from the visuals, there is nothing about this film that lifts into the realms of the fantastic. It's good entertainment - nothing more, which is fine of course. To champion this film as some kind of cinematic masterpiece however, is ludicrous. Although Oscar nominations/awards are not a sign that a film is any good (hello Good Will Hunting, A Beautiful Mind, and so on and so on)suggesting Lord of the Rings is one of the five or six best films made in 2001 is crazy. I like dumb action movies, but why wasn't something like Die Hard showered with Oscar nominations when it is actually a much better film?

title: Truly great
review:
I have been waiting to see this movie for ages, listening to all people have to say.

I have read the book a couple of times, and thought the visualisations brilliant, just as I imagined

The three hours whisked by, I was spellbound. Can't wait for the next one, saw the preview trailer now attached to the end of the movie.

Will buy on DVD

title: More than acceptable
review:
Decent acting, decent costume design, decent music... quite a fair

treatment for this fable of good and evil thus far. Toward the close

of this installment it's a bit difficult to follow the separation and

reuniting of the various fellowship members in the forest - but

then, there's a lot to follow in the books as well. As in the Di

Laurentiis DUNE, the questions I'd have of the film would be

questions of the book.

title: There is hope for story driven effect films...
review:
I feel this could be appreciated as a stand alone piece, but I think a small understanding of The Hobbit or a brief introduction to the mythology of Middle Earth could help. As far as die hard Tolkien fans are concerned, I think that they will have no problem with this adaptation.

It's been quite some time since I read these books, but it didn't seem to matter. Immediately this film presented an interesting introduction and back story without burdening the viewer with useless detail.

And it only got better. Although a few (very few) of the effects were not completely desirable, Peter Jackson created a landscape of a scope I have not seen in quite some time. He presented Middle Earth as a reality. He maintained a continuous story of interest, with characters that came to life. The cinematography was tremendous from the close-ups of characters, to the sweeping vistas. The battle choreography was so realistic, it left me wondering how many deaths they covered up. And last, but by far not least, the acting was magnificent! There wasn't one performance I found lacking.

BRAVO!

I hope the award committees take note as well as filmmakers of all genres.

I would compare this to Star Wars The Phantom Menace, excepts, that George Lucas has a lot to relearn about Fantasy Film Making. LOTR will stand as a milestone to be surpassed as the first Star Wars Trilogy once did.

title: The Ending..
review:
Not only is this the best movie of 2001, but it is clearly one of the greats of all time. What a difficult movie to make! And a huge risk! I don't rightly understand some of the reviews on here. Maybe I had an advantage going into the theater because I have read the books several times over the years. Because of that, I have a difficult time imagining the movie experience without my already developed love for the story and characters. Maybe Jackson primarily created this film for those who have read the books.

I see people criticize the non-ending and I get confused. Did somebody actually expect a different ending? I see people criticize that the heroes were too successful against astounding odds, and that "at least Boromir died." Did somebody actually expect others to perish? The ending is not a cliffhanger! The story has been around for about half a century and are among the most read books of all time. The Fellowship of the Ring has had the same ending since its creation. After pondering the different reviews here, I can only conclude that this movie is an entirely different experience for those who have read the books than for those who have not read the books.

My only gripe against this movie is that many of the fight scenes were filmed too closely. I did not like some of the camera angles during the more intense battles, and believe more could have been done to enhance the battle's impact on the viewer. Because of that and because movies are never as good as the books that inspire them, I rate this movie a 9/10 instead of 10/10.

title: What´s the controversy about?
review:
First of all one has to see this movie for what it is. An epic fantasy movie (the first of it´s kind). Every effort to compare it with other great movies like Citizen Kane is just a waste of time. And all of you who are irritated that this movie is so popular at the imdb´s top movies list don´t waste your energy on such a strange, out of the blue list where ok, well handcrafted movies like Shawshank Redemption is getting such ridiculous high ratings.

Now, what do I think about the movie? Well I like it. Like it a lot. And here are my main reasons:

1) Peter Jackson direction is a unusual mix of shakesperian actors giving weight to lines no american actor could pull off, some almost childlish scenes of hobbits (where for example Gandalf takes Pippin and Merry by their ears), and of course the thrilling, gory action scenes.

2) The use of the New Zealand scenery.

3) The efforts that has been put into details.

Am looking forward to The Two Towers. And especially Gollum. I just hope we don´t have antoher Jar Jar Binks on our hand.

title: Believe the hype
review: I was concerned after reading all the positive reviews that this movie wouldn't live up to my growing expectations. But it did. LotR is a wonderful movie and its so good I'll probably go back a few times to see it again. The three hours flew by and I am so ready for the Two Towers. Sure, Jackson couldn't put everything from the book in the movie, but trust me, by the end you really don't mind. In fact you'll just want to thank everyone who made this movie for staying true to the book and one-upping it. What you get in Jackson's LotR is a satisfying, visionary adaptation. And, if that doesn't make you want to see it, go for Orlando Bloom's Legolas, he is such a cutie.

title: Almost there...
review: I had hoped that such a well-known story would command strict adherence to the story line from the director.  Any changes should have been justified and understandable.  The conversation between Aragorn and Frodo at the end of the movie should have never happened.  Arwen replacing Glorfindel in the ride for the ford, I can live with.  Ignoring the development of the relationship between Gimli and Legolas is not acceptable.  Do not be swept away with the grandeur of the cinematography -- brilliant as it is.  And don't buy into the ridiculously expanded fight scenes -- like Saruman and Gandalf.  Here's hoping the next two capture more of Tolkein's essence.

title: Great movie!
review: It is rare to see a movie better than the book in which it was based. Well, "The Lord of the Rings" is certainly the case. In the movie there was certain details that I didn't understand in the book and the story is told in a much more simple way. There are, of course, things that were taken of the movie and others that were altered, but the things that are important to love the story are still there. This film is perfect in every way: great actors and actresses, great special effects, great soundtrack. I wasn't a bit disappointed when I saw the movie. I can't believe that this movie lost the oscar for best picture for "A beautiful mind"! How can that be?!!!!!!!!!!

title: (visually) impressive
review:
OK, this comment is not going to add anything dramatically new, but I recently had a discussion with somebody about why "A Beautiful Mind" won all major Oscars instead of this movie. I still think that is unfair.

OK, in term of story this movie is very shallow: It's basically a very long chase. But that's mainly because it's so true to the book, and the book is many times more boring then the movie. Some people claim also that this movie has a lot of cliches, but don't forget that those things weren't cliches when the book was written and might have never become cliches without the book. In terms of character development, I've seen much better movies but also a lot poorer movies. Some characters are underdeveloped, but in order to develop them properly the movie would have had to last 10 hours...

What is left is a visual and technical masterpiece. Everything, from the costumes to the make-up, from the landscapes to the CGI and the cinematography, looked simply perfect. Yet even in some of these categories Lord of the Rings didn't win the oscars. And, contrary to my expectations, the movie was also really exciting and suspenseful. True, there are some parts were everything succumbs under too many effects (the Mines of Moria), but it's not nearly as problematic as in Episode I for instance.

When you look at the sheer size and scope of this production, you have to be deeply impressed. Even though it's lacking in story and character development, it should have easily won the "Best Picture" award, let alone the "Best Male Actor in Supporting Role" for Ian McKellen as Gandalf.

***1/2 out of **** stars

title: Lord of the BoRing
review:
Seen as a illustration of the book, I guess this movie has some merit. The scenery is amazing, the make up astonishing, the music is just perfect... but behind the perfect production, something is lacking.

For some reason, the movie fails to captivate the viewer. After the intro, it all ends up in a series of "Aaaargh, something is coming, let's run". And some set of characters run, pursued by some set of monsters either riding or on foot. And then the same thing again. And again. And again. And maybe some conflict over the ring, but then it is time to run (and maybe kick a little orch butt) again. And then it ends, and we need to suffer another two movies of three hours before the hobbits have defeated evil, saved the world, and they can stop running and walk home.

Seen as a movie, WITHOUT considering the background in a world famous seried of fantasy books, it is just to shallow. THe characters are never given time to develop, they are basically paper dolls of known types paraded before the camera. The evil is too pitch black without nuance, and the good guys (especially the elves) are too boringly good. It is nice to see that they do have the guts to kill of a few heroes, but even this does not really create any real suspense.

Even action movies should manage to grip the audience for more than half an hour, but this movie does not.

I'm looking forward to the promise of some big battle scenes in the next part, and might see it because of the visuals, but as a whole the ring series does not merit much excitement.

title: A magical tale of extreme proportions
review:
There truly is no other movie like this. The fantastic epic tale is breaks barriers in many ways and for three hours or so I was really able to live in the world only Tolkien could see and knew existed. The beauty of this film lies not only in the scenic world or the visual effects, but comes to life especially due to the actors who bring a magical and wonderful atmosphere to the movie and thus also bring believability of their roles to the maximum.

The scene that I most remember is when the Fellowship arises, because the film makers truly captured the moment. If there is a downside to the movie it's definitely not it's length because the movie never lost its tempo - it's those blasted seats in the cinema that made my but ache and fall asleep. And there's that "Titanic"-y feel to the score when Frodo and Samwise head off in the canoe. Bhhhhhhhhhh.

And the ending, if I can even call it an ending came very suddenly and I left the cinema feeling cheated of the rest of the movie. Oh well, "The two towers" next year then.

8/10

title: Beautifully crafted and an overall delight to watch
review:
The acting is fantastic and the scenery filmed in New Zealand creates a visual feast for the audience, keeping them on the edge of their seats the whole time. Director Peter Jackson has put to screen a classic novel with style, receiving numerous Oscar nominations including best picture.

I am personally not a fan of fantasy whether it be literature or film, yet I thoroughly enjoyed The Lord Of The Rings: The Fellowship Of The Ring and I eagerly await the next two in the trilogy to appear in cinemas. It is definately a movie that must be seen on the big screen to fully appreciate what it has to offer - a wonderful tale with superb performances and visuals all round.

title: There seems to be 2 problems that makes this movie away from perfect
review:
(Slight spoilers) Ah, yes. The perfect movie. Is there such a thing?

No!

Even CITIZEN KANE has it's flaws! There's a pterodactyl in KANE, for crying out loud.

The main problem with THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING the beefing up of the role of Arwen, played by Liv Tyler. She is only slightly mentioned in the book, but now she is Xena's more-covered Elven Clone! And she talks as if she has learned to live with something stuck in her throat! One of my friends, who did not read the book, commented that this part of the story could have been better, but since it never existed in the first place, we can see why Fellowship of the Rings couldn't win Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay.

The other flaw is that, after the Council of Elrond, the story's pace becomes faster, but at what cost? In the second half the Hobbits (and Frodo) seem to be deminished from their roles by Aragorn, ogres, orcs, elves, and only seem to be some kind of irritation. Making it longer by twenty minutes could help.

(I'm the only person who wants this longer)

And the balrog, despite being wonderfully done, dissapointed me because he looks like a run-of-the-mill demon.

Other than that, the movie's fine.

title: Impressive work
review: I'm a long time Tolkien fan and I remember when cast lists were being drawn up on USENET five years ago. I don't think any of my cast list made it. I felt that the Shire was too rustic. The first half was a little too lose with the book for my taste, but the second half was wonderful. The Balrog will be in my nightmares for a while. The story does seem to move slow. It is definitely worth the big screen and I will spend a lot of time pausing the video to look at the background effects, which looked amazing in the small amount of screen time they got.

title: fellowship of the NERDS
review:
I know I may be hated by thousands of IMDB fans, but... whatever!. This movie is only for the lovers of sci-fi or fans of the Tolkien book. LOTR has great special effects, and a good original music score, but that's it!! There's no good acting, I can't believe Ian Mc Kellen got nominated for Best Supporting Actor. This film is almost dedicated for nerds, those who think that this is the best movie of the year, or even worse, the best movie of all time!!!! Don't get me wrong, this movie is entertaining, but it's not the 8th wonder of the world.

---Minor SPOILER--- The ending! what about it??? It's like a soap opera's Friday episode it lets you guessing what will happen on the next episode,... the difference is that in a soap opera you know what will happen on Monday, and in this movie, you'll know it until late 2002!.

title: Way too long
review: A somewhat interesting story, doesn't hold your interest a lot of the time. Three full hours long. By the end of the of the first hour I was thinking "GOD!, ARE THEY FREAKING THERE YET?" [Minor Spoiler] * * * * * * Even after three hours, everything still hasn't been resolved and it has a cliffhanger ending.

title: The good, the bad and the reason for not overdoing the music
review:
The movie follows the book pretty well, although naturally some parts are missing. I particularly missed Tom Bombadil and I think that part could have given the movie extra flavor. Some things are added; Arwen, played by Liv Tyler, quite successfully increases the female part of the otherwise male dominated story. All in all, I was positively surprised of how the difficult script was handled. From a movie point of view the story is not a perfect one, since there are many similar parts where the book is able to add something new while the movie is locked repeating the same theme; They are traveling and suddenly they're hunted by evil of some kind and they barely make their way to a free haven. This cannot be helped without rewriting the story and I don't find it annoying. However, I have problems with the following issues:

The music - Why not let it be quiet sometimes, silence can really build tension and suspense. Especially when you have good actors giving an excellent performance, why cloud a good dialog with strings? Is it not possible to let the viewer develop his/her emotions or do directors need to

aid us with sentimental music. This is a major problem for american movies that accelerated during the 90's and it unfortunately got to Jackson. Check out all the classics from whenever and you will miss silence in contemporary american films.

I'm not too content with Legolas and Gimli, but it is not the acting. Legolas looks carved out of plastic and silicon and he has the same stupid look on his face the whole movie through (like he is trying really hard to look attentive). Gimli, played by usually excellent John Rhys-Davies, simply don't get through to me, but I cannot put the finger on the reason. Ian McKellen (Gandalf), Elijah Woods (Frodo) and Sean Bean (Boromir) are excellent as well as the brief appearances of Cate Blanchett(Galadriel) and Christopher Lee (Saruman). I have no major complaints on the acting.

title: WOW!
review:
Peter Jackson has done what many thought impossible: bringing to the screen the most popular, most imaginative, best-told novel of our time. In the interest of length, there were certain parts that were eliminated or abbreviated, but the feeling is definitely there. People familiar with Tolkien will not be disappointed, and those who have not been introduced to these enchanting tales will be no less spellbound. The dialogue quite often comes directly from the book, which was also a big plus to me. I am anxiously awaiting the next two installments.

One word: BRAVO!!!

title: Loved it!!!!!
review: This movie is incredible!  The first battle scene had my mouth gaping wide in disbelief and pretty much stayed that way through the whole movie.  I could not believe how realistic the acting and SFX are.  The casting is flawless, esp. Gandalf.  The fight scene with the cave troll is one of the best. The balrog scene was damn scary!  Its a shame this movie got the boot at the oscars, it really deserved more than what it was dished. Go and see this movie if you havn't yet, you will not be disappointed.  I can't wait for the DVD,I'm buying a surround sound theatre system for it!!!

title: People who rip it off: "Don't Know Jack!"
review: I watched the movie twice last year, and I was very pleased with it. I admit that my expectations were in a way dashed, because I had raised them WAY to high. The LoTR are my favorite books, and I think that Jackson [the director] did an awesome job with "keeping to the books". There were a few parts in the movie where I actually understood it more clearly then I had before. This movie is a most see. The acting was good, but some of the actors I would have picked differently. The movie [in my mind] gets a 4 and a half out of 5 stars! Two  thumbs WAY up! And for the people who detested the movie...it's because they can't read the subtitles, can't understand the plot, and are eagerly looking foward to the next Rambo or Rocky movie. Another reason is that they are so filled up with movies where Bad wins. Get a grip you losers!

title: Fine effects and a whole lot of setup
review:
Its quite remarkable how well the first installment of the Rings trilogy works as a stand-alone epic, considering how much screen time is devoted entirely as exposition for the next two movies. Basically, Rings 1 is just a series of ante-upping battles with abominable creatures as our fellowship of heroes sets of on their journey to save the world and meets all the important players. I will admit that I am one of the deprived few to have never read Tolkien's trilogy and therefore fully expected the "Fellowship of the Ring" to conclude with Frodo casting that ring into the depths of hell from whence it was created. Imagine my surprise when I realized this finale would be delayed until the end of movie three!

The glaring lack of a proper narrative arc in this story throws down a daunting challenge to the film trilogy. Is it possible to make theater entertainment by offering a 9 hour epic in thirds, one segment every year for three years? I'd say yes, as long as the movie fills the narrative pleasure gap with something else -- in this case special effect shots. The make-up, costuming, and art departments on this film should be proud of their work, but it all pales in comparison to the jaw-dropping computer generated work that fills out every frame. Truly engaging and thrilling to watch, but I wonder... Will I care by hour 9 of the trilogy about the completion of the story, and if not, will the effects be enough to get me to shell out 9 bucks? So far, The Lord of the Rings is just excellent popcorn fare.

title: I think the very best it could be. Exceptional
review:
A number of people will not like this movie for quite a few reasons. Some of them will think it too long and boring without pausing to think about what they are watching (one third of an epic story) while others will complain about what isn't in the film (without seeing that everything cannot be included). I thought it was amazing and enthralling. The running time was not a factor to me and I can't recall the last time three hours flew by that fast.

It's good. It's complete to the extent that this story will ever be completed on film. It's excellently cast and acted. The effects are outstanding without being the entire focus of the picture. The story is fluid and understandable. Peter Jackson has made the picture in such a way that I think he's going to manage to please as many of us as he possibly could and what more can we ask of him?

I've read a number of the reviews posted thus far and those in the negative don't appear to have understood what it was they were going to see. I add this because frankly this is a story that you shouldn't walk into blindly. It's not a hour and a half roller coaster and it's not a movie you should confuse with Harry Potter. One writer complained about nightmares? Sounds to me like Peter Jackson nailed the Ringwraiths, Orcs, Balrog, and other nasties pretty well doesn't it?

If you like fantasy and want to see it done well see this film. It's not for little children and it's not for those with shorter attention spans. Shrek was great but this ain't it. This is what you wanted when you went to see The Phantom Menace and walked out of the theater shaking your head in disappointment. This is a fantasy story told in a serious tone and has more in common with Braveheart or Zulu than Harry Potter.

It's amazing. I've been waiting for this movie since I was 13 years old. I'm 36 now and it's lived up to 23 years of building expectations.

title: Definitely one to catch in the theater!!!
review: To sum it up quickly, I thought it was awesome! The costumes and makeup were great, and I loved the fact that there were so many good-looking guys in one movie. (Hooray!!!) The only reason I'm giving this a 9/10 is because I didn't understand why the dudes in the black riding the horses (I forgot their names) couldn't find Frodo and his friends, even when they were right in front of them. Possibly cuz they had no eyes? Dunno... anyway, I'm not a major fan of fantasy movies, but this one completely rocked! It could've been five hours and I still wouldn't have left my seat for anything!

title: He got "IT"
review: Middle Earth has existed in my mind for thirty-five years. Within ten seconds of the movie's opening, I had slipped totally into that world, with absolutely no "cognitive dissonance."  Peter Jackson has achieved what Tolkien would call a true "sub-creation' - a world entirely valid in its own terms. My jaw is still on the floor. I once (1970!) taught a course in the literary antecedents of LOTR, so I can nit-pick with the best of them. But why? As has been said, this film is in a category of its own. I simply have no understanding of the people who didn't like it.  The set design and conceptualization were beyond hope. The acting, especially Sirs Ian & Ian, Elijah Wood (to my abject suprise), Cate Blanchet, Viggo Mortensen, and the incredible Sam of Sean Astin, was inspired. You can feel the bonding and duty. Tolkien's gift to humanity has been made manifest for the new century by Peter Jackson. Laus tibi Deo.

title: Good, but Looooong! (one spoiler)
review:
In some ways, this film suffers from the same flaws as the book. Though the producers do (thank goodness!) cut out the ridiculous Tom Bombadil episode, the story meanders and there are too many scenes where you're left wondering what they were for.

With that gripe out of the way, it has to be said that the acting and characterization are great, the music is fine and the special effects are simply awesome.

At the end, though, I was vaguely dissatisfied, very much aware that I'd watched a long film. A truly great film wouldn't leave that feeling.

Maybe parts 2 and 3 will do better. Rating: 7/10.

title: Captivatingly imaginative!
review:
*Note: *SPOILERS* abound throughout this post, but many of you have already read the books, so it only matters to those who haven't.





Okay, I have to say that my favorite movie of this year was not unseated. What I will say is that I now have a second favorite movie this year. LotR was pretty damn good and worth seeing, despite its over-ambitious pace and washed-up cast.

First of all, the good. Ian McKellen was tremendous. He steals EVERY scene he's in. His wizard was so believable. Near the beginning, when Bilbo is contemplating keeping the ring for himself instead of passing it on to Frodo, McKellen really shows why he's been dubbed Sir Ian by the queen. As Magneto, McKellen wasn't given the chance out-act his coworkers because of the shoddy script, but he has many lines and stands as the most important, best acted character in the movie.

Elijah Woods' portrayal as Frodo is decent. He's shown up by John Rhys-Davies and Billy Boyd (two of his Hobbitt friends) though. Sean Astin's Samwise Gamgee was really disappointing, however, and proves why Astin hardly makes any movies anymore; he can't act very well. Astin and Woods spend most of the movie crying or whining about something, as do Boyd and Rhys-Davies, but at least the latter two are hilarious.

Upsettingly, Cate Blanchett and Liv Tyler weren't given enough screen time to do anything with their characters. This was one of the biggest shames. Tyler's love scenes with Viggo Mortensen's Strider were touching and believable. Blanchett, as an Elf queen, is absolutely beautiful. She is the most beautiful on-screen actress in recent memory. Too bad the girls didn't get much screen time, but perhaps we'll see them in the next two movies.

Sean Bean (Boromir), Viggo Mortensen (Strider), Orlando Bloom (Legolas), and I believe Andy Serkis (Smeagol) were great. Next to Gandalf, they were the best characters in the movie. I hope for big things out of each of their characters in the next movies (except for Bean's Boromir, who dies heroically).

Most reviewers have slammed the film for its incredible length, and I'm going to be no different. It is too long. Some scenes (such as the scene where the evil Saruman destroys a mountain to block off Frodo and company and another where Frodo is attacked and stabbed by a ringwraith and is saved by Tyler's character Arwin, which I believe wasn't even in the book) were just unnecessary. I have no major complaints, just that that these scenes interrupt with the pace of the movie, making it seem somewhat clumsy and laborous. Had it been cut to a more lean 2 and a half hours, it may have been better.

However, some scenes which were fantastic were cut waaaay too short. The opening scene, which tells of the forging of the evil ring was too rushed, as was the end battle. I just felt kind of disappointed, because the battle scenes in the middle of the movie were so well-done and their timing's were just right, but then the end battle is abruptly cut short.

Despite minor complaints, I felt this movie was absolutely terrific. Many movies claim to the be the next big Star Wars Trilogy in the making, but Lord of the Rings is really going to do it. Forget about the kiddiness of Harry Potter. The wizards, orcs, dwarves, elves, and hobbitts of middle earth are much better peoples. Simply put, I can't recommend this movie to all of you enough. It's the second best movie I've seen this year, and the BEST fantasy movie of all time.

5 stars out of 5

I can't wait for the next one.

title: From Someone Who Didn't Like the Original Books
review: At least it was better than the books. I hated the books. What this movie did for me was reveal how closely the story follows "The Wizard Of Oz" (L. Frank Baum's book, not the movie), although I guess most quest stories pretty much follow a similar formula. What I find interesting is how the most recent comments seem to be somewhat negative; perhaps that is to be expected from latecomers. So, if you haven't seen "Lord of the Rings" by now, chances are good that you won't be too impressed by it.

title: Great movie, worth the price to see it in the theater
review:
All I can say is, wow. This is a great film and the start to what looks like an awesome trilogy. Even with it being 3 hours long, it wasn't drawn out or anything. The scenery and the fight scenes, especially the beginning one, were spectacular. This film is definitely worth the price to see it in theaters.

I know people said that the ending was bad, but when you realize that the film is part of a trilogy, that the ending doesn't look as bad. I never read the books, but from I hear they kept most of the storyline the same as how it was in the book. 9/10

title: If you haven't read the novel -
review: the movie won't make alot of sense.  "Rings" is an action adventure all the way, forsaking the mythologic middle earth of Tolkien's novel for a "Star Wars:  Phantom Menace" style wanna be epic. title: good, but nothing special
review:
This is not a bad movie.Agreed.But I don't understand what all this hype is all about.I have certainly seen many better movies.I must admit I heard about J.R.R. Tolkien only recently, but I like these kind of stories, and yet LOTR failed to inspire me. First there are too many characters, both good and bad,but none is aptly developed.Time and again ,when a new character makes an appearance, we expect something better but they too fades away as if they are making way for something big in the end.But there is none,nothing. Elijah wood does a good job as "Frodo", who is supposed to be the protagonist of the movie.But as I said earlier ,too many characters shifts the onus from him and spoils the movie.As a result we fail to feel with him.The other characters are also played well.I enjoyed the characters of Aragon and Samwise Gamgee very much.

The special effects in the movie is also not that special. In fact it is below par.It certainly should have done better, with the technology available today.None of the creatures in this movies looks real, except Gollum.But then he is not shown fully.

Having said this, this movie has a couple of impressive scenes,like a river in the form of horse riders washing away the nasguls, the 9 dead/living kings.Then there is a fight between Gandalf, the grey and his mentor Saruman.

One more thing, the sceneries in this film are excellent.

I give LOTR a 7 out of 10.The movie has a lot of good things but they fail to produce a whole that is greater than the sum of the parts, a feature that is the hallmark of truly great movies.

title: Point-blank, the best film I have seen.
review:
I have been a longtime fan of Tolkien; I've read The Hobbit, the entire Lord of the Rings trilogy, and The Silmarillion many times. So of course, I have been looking forward to this movie for a long time. Since I was such a fan, I was hoping that the film wasn't a total botch. The excellent reviews from professional critics were a real boost, as was the movie's quite good web site, but I just had to see it for myself.

WOW!!! This movie surpasses everything I have ever seen. The original "Star Wars" movies don't even compare. Having been immersed in LotR, I can't really speak for those who go into the theater without having read the books, but I have not spoken with anyone who thinks the movie leaves them confused. The opening scenes tell the history of the Ring clearly, and the rest of the movie is just as simple to follow.

Purists may possibly object to scenes in this movie that are told about by characters in the book but are actually shot in the film, but I think it is a more-than-acceptable adaptation for a movie to do this. Instead of having a character just telling about something that happened to him, the action is shown (sometimes during the telling).

The film is beautifully shot and edited, with a grand sound track to fit the imagery. The parts where Frodo the hobbit has put on the One Ring are truly eerie -- especially one toward the end (**possible spoiler**) where he is rushed to the Dark Tower in Mordor as soon as he puts the Ring on. The battle scenes are not gory at all, and very little blood is shown in the movie. The battles are effective because of the intensity of the pictures and the sounds -- they work because they work on the mind.

This movie is 3 hours long, but it was worth every minute and every penny. That may seem long, but after you see it, you won't want to cut anything out of it to shorten it. If you see "Harry Potter" and skip this film, you have missed out on the best movie of the year -- and, quite simply, the best movie I have ever seen. 10/10!
