title: Ive got to be the only one 2 say it but: it was only ok
review: Yes ok it was a brilliant movie in all ways possible but i can assure you the book has got to be better than the movie. I dont know why or how i can say this but ive got to. Yes the sets were designed brilliantly, the actors were first class, the special effects were great and the costumes and props were very good but the book was better. So all in all ive got to say, do yourself a favour and read the book instead. Id give this an 8 out of 10 as it is quite thrilling and quite a nice 3 hours to sit through.

title: Star Wars? Potter?
review: This film was amazing. It combines spot on performances with beautiful locations and thrilling action sequences. Could this be bigger than Star Wars? I hope it won't be but y'know, I think it's got the potential. As for that Potter boy? Well I've forgotten bout him. Roll on The Two Towers.

title: A breath-taking screen adaptation (which is a revolution of the fantasy film genre)classic which gives us the viewing public what we have been waiting for. December 2002 bring it on !!!!
review: Now I have to admit that I am one of those people who has read the series about twice and so I had some very reasonable expectations for this movie. But what I saw was a gigantic improvement on the underachievement of so many fantasy based movies of the past and despite some small omissions to the plot and characters it stands out for me as one of the greatest of its genre. I will have to admit I was a little taken back by the depiction of Bilbo and Galadriel's (over dramatized) seduction by the power of the ring but apart from that there are all the important ingredients of the fellowship which include loyalty and sacrifice and one of the highlights for me which really made this film feel familiar is the use of Stephen Tolkien's maps (I know it sounds a bit sad but who cares) Now I just can't wait for the next two films to come out as the BBC's radio 4 is doing reruns of the stage production and it has just reminded me again of what a grate work of literature it is with all its many intricate and engrossing characters and if anyone can translate this to screen I'm sore Jackson can.

title: Good, but not that good
review:
I have to give Lord of the Rings credit. Despite running almost three and a half hours, it kept my attention all the way through to the end. There have been a lot of movies I've seen that are significantly shorter but I end up checking my watch every so often anyway (most notably every Kevin Smith movie I've been forced to sit through.) But I wouldn't consider it to be the #2 movie of all time, I wouldn't even consider it to be Oscar worthy. I found a lot of movies ranked lower on the top 250 (Raiders of the Lost Ark, The Matrix, The Shawshank Redemption, Snatch, Seven, and Glory just to name a few) to be a lot more entertaining than Lord of the Rings. The acting was good enough, Peter Jackson did a fine job of directing, but there is nothing really special about it. Maybe I'll change my opinion after I see the two sequels. It's definitely worth seeing, but don't expect it to be a world beater.

I think a 7.5 is a more accurate rating than 9.0.

title: WoW!!!!!!
review: All I have to say is WOW! This was an amazing movie! If J.R.R Tolkien was alive today I think he would be please at this movie. The words from th book finally came to screen even a better way of what one might have pictured! The actors were perfectly chosen and the screenplay was beautifully written!! I would be so pleased if this movie made it to the Oscars because it has what it takes! One of the most imaginative and just plain good movies ever made! Go see 'The Fellowship of the Ring' you will not be disappointed!

title: What a joke...
review:
It's quite apparent you can trust the IMDB fanbase about as much as your pedestrian local film critic. I mean...63% of them rank this movie a 10 out of 10? It rates higher than Citizen Kane on the overall list? What a joke!!! Are you telling me that 63% of the people that log on to this site are 13-years old?

This movie was a fine piece of entertainment that was respectful of the source material. It had wonderful sound and visual effects and a decent cast of performers. But great cinema it is not.

I found myself looking at my watch about halfway thru the film (never a good sign). The script, while faithful to the storyline, is filled with one hackneyed Hollywood cliche after another and never captures the mysticism of the original material. The cinematography is far from creative. Anyone who thinks this film was beautifully shot is confusing the naturally beautiful landscapes of NZ and CGI effects for great camera work. And between the script's and the director's inclinations to draw out every emotional moment far beyond it's natural life, you could almost read the trilogy in the time it takes to unfold on screen.

As I say, I would recommend this film. It is a fairly entertaining adaptation of a great piece of storytelling. But spare me the hyperbole. This is NOT the "greatest film of all time". It's "Tomb Raider" with elves and dwarves, ok?

title: Expected to see a kiddie movie, was instead delighted!
review: I have never read the books and had no interest in them, but my children wanted to see the movie, so I took them.  I expected to see a kiddie show, a cute fairy tale about cuddly little creatures and the like, but was I ever surprised.  The movie was wonderful and held my interest throughout.  Good chracters, comprehensive plot even to someone unfamiliar with the books, great FX!  I can't wait to see the next two.  (And as a Star Wars fan, I can see where Lucas got some of his ideas.)

title: Sir Ian McEllen deserves Supporting Actor Oscar
review: Have seen movie 5X. Read books dozens of times since middle school. So...Gandalf the Grey is now the archetype once in words, now in (movie)person. Twinkle of the eye. Butterfly fireworks for hobbit children. The dragon Smaug roaring over Bilbo's birthday guests. You Shall Not Pass! Looking @ Elrond slyly (as if to say that he was happy to see Isildur's heir taking up the quest and also his inheritance as it is linked to the Ring) as Aragorn offered his assistance and sword to Frodo. Talking with Frodo in the Mines of Moria about not choosing to be a ringerbear but that it was reassuring to know that it was meant to come to Frodo--a vote of confidence for Frodo and for his mettle). Gandalf's support in general of the smaller peoples of Middle Earth. His knowledge and affection for hobbits in particular. A Maia of great sympathy. Gandalf represents the Wizard order with such aplomb and personality. He cares. He is worried. He is magnificent. He has hidden powers. He enjoys his pipe and a joke. I've always thought that J.R.R. Tolkien created Gandalf as one of the Inklings members. Gathered at the Eagle and Child, drinking their pints, smoking pipes, enjoying poetry in languages from long-ago, song--both silly and serious, academic Oxfordian discussion with tomfoolery mixed in. He is such a perfect Gandalf--Sir Ian. Academy members---Give him the golden guy! :-)

title: Whodathunkit? They did the impossible...
review:
RATING: ***1/2 out of ****

I don't need to tell you how much of a classic J.R.R Tolkein's "The Lord of the Rings" series is. I don't need to tell you that its influence has been felt all over, from "Star Wars" to Led Zeppelin. I also don't need to tell you what a huge undertaking it is for anyone to adapt it to the big screen, something which many considered impossible. But lo and behold, here it is, a well-acted, respectfully scripted and incredibly epic film that only years ago would have been considered a fanboy's pipe dream.

Frodo Baggins (Elijah Wood) is an unassuming, happy little hobbit (little people for those who aren't Tolkein-initiated). His uncle, Bilbo Baggins (Ian Holm) is preparing to leave his home in the Shire (someplace in the Middle-Earth) for some peace and quiet. Years before the start of the film, he found a ring that allows people to disappear in the hideout of a creature named Gollum. He doesn't know that it's really a "Ring of Power" that would give Supreme Evil Guy Sauron the strength he needs to take over the world. Silly Bilbo. Well, anyway, after a huge birthday party in his honor, Bilbo leaves the Shire and the ring behind him. His residence and many of his possessions (including the ring) go to Frodo. Wizard friend Gandalf (Ian McKellen) comes to tell him all about the ring, who's searching for it and what Frodo has to do: bring it across Middle-Earth to Rivendell, where it will be temporarily safe. Frodo leaves with three of his hobbit friends, Pippin (Billy Boyd), Merry (Dominic Monaghan) and Sam (Sean Astin) to do his duty. The ring proves to be a real pain in the ass, with nine seemingly immortal Ringwraiths (I'm not gonna explain these things anymore, so just go read the books, OK?) on their tail. Some protection comes from Aragon (or "Strider") who helps them out of more than just plain ol' good will. Some may consider this a spoiler, but the four hobbits + Strider get the ring to Rivendell, where we learn that the ring has to be destroyed at the center of Mount Doom. Always the brave one, Frodo agrees to take it there, and a fellowship of elves, dwarves, hobbits and men will protect him. From there our adventure continues.

It's not too much of a stretch to call "The Fellowship of the Ring" the most ambitious Hollywood offering of the year (don't even talk to me about "Moulin Rouge", which played it very safe thank you very much). New Line took huge risks enlisting a relatively unknown director (Peter Jackson) and trusting him with about $350 million and one of the most revered fantasy epics of all time. All three films were shot at the same time, so if this one failed, there'd be trouble for New Line. But thankfully, "Fellowship" is a success, containing its fair share of magnificent moments. The last time I enjoyed a purely fantasy film this much was the original "Star Wars".

The beginning of the film is where I found the most faults, and it's a rare case of the omission of details from the source actually being distracting. That is a little nit-pick, and very soon, the film had me under its spell. "The Fellowship of the Ring", unlike another wildly popular fantasy film (*cough* "Harry Potter" *cough*), is not a slavish mirage of visual interpretations. Rather, this film is it's own. Jackson has done a terrific job in making everything seem real and natural. I got the feeling that each set has a magnificent history behind it, like the film was merely there documenting one quest in the long life of the Middle Earth. There is some magic afoot here; I really believed that the Middle Earth existed.

The cast of "Fellowship", for the most part, does a magnificent job. I enjoyed the hobbits, and Elijah Wood, who isn't exactly the first person one would think to play Frodo, but does a very good job. I wasn't as impressed with Ian Holm, whose performance was unfortunately the low point of the film. He was all fine and good while playing the hobbit in his quieter moments, but when it's time to get serious, he plays Bilbo so fiercely that it was simply unpleasant to watch him. But fortunately, he is given little screen time and is given less dramatic moments, so that is a small quibble. The women of "Fellowship", although we see them just as much as Bilbo, do good. I enjoyed the little twist on the original flight to Rivendell that helped us get to know Lady Arwen (Liv Tyler) a little more, and Cate Blanchett is (literally) luminous as Galadriel. A few of the characters in the fellowship go undeveloped, but most people do not want to sit through a four hour director's cut, so unfortunately Jackson did have to cut a few corners. But out of the entire cast, it is Ian McKellen who is most memorable. He is more than completely and totally believable; I was convinced that he was the only one who could ever play Gandalf.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" is a solid, sometimes mesmerizing work. This seems like a movie that will be remembered for a while, and I hope that the next two films can follow suit. We are going to be a spoiled bunch of moviegoers these next two years, if we get this kind of present every holiday season. Finally, here we have a finely made film to add to the list of enduring cinematic fantasies. The tagline says "Power can be held in the smallest of things." It's a good thing Hollywood realized this, and trusted the small New Zealand team that brought this epic to life. At least someone these days knows how to get bang for their buck.

title: What did I miss?
review: I suffered through three hours watching this movie only because I went with someone else. I constantly checked my watch hoping it would be over soon. I can't for the life of me understand why this movie was nominated for so many Academy Awards including Best Picture.  All I can say is what am I missing? To me, the  characters seemed to be thrown into the plot through the manipulation of the story and not by their own motivations.  Frodo is a completely reactive character and I didn't understand why he was chosen for this quest and I couldn't root for him when he went through a laughable series of disasters from avalanches to monster attacks coming oh so close to dying but no, he pops back all healthy again.  The movie that constantly talked about evil failed to climax with good overcoming evil.  I guess we have to wait for the second sequel for that to happen. Characters seemed to die or be carried off by monsters to suddenly appear unscathed later with no explanation.  Please!  There were only two women with lines in the movie and I'm not sure their importance to the story.  I think we could have left out the scenes with them and not missed a thing.  In fact, I thought it was such B movie trash that it made "The Mummy" look like a masterpiece by comparison.

title: Stunning performance!
review: The Fellowship of the Ring was an intense 3 hour ride through the world of J.R.R. Tolkien!  The movie didn't skimp on Tolkien's actual work, and the brilliance of the filming and acting helping to give a true portrayl of Middle Earth as J.R.R. Tolkien might have imagined it.  This is by far one of the greatest films that I've ever seen.

title: Best novel ever. Best movie ever.
review: I can't tell you how, but I saw the first installment of the Lord of the Rings and it literally blew me away in every aspect. The actors were all perfect (Ian McKellan, Chris Lee and Viggo Mortenson were dead on). The shrinking of the hobbits and dwarf (let's not forget Gimli) were done to perfection you never even considered that they weren't the same height. It never looked phony. The cinematography and art direction will win hands down at the Oscars. So will Peter Jackson for best director. The only complaint I have about this movie is, as a Tolkien fan, it was too short. I completely agreed with the cutting out of scenes and the 'refining' of others to give the story more appeal. I had no problem with Liv Tyler's acting or her replacing Glorfindel. I think it is essential to the later movies. The ringwraiths are very frightening and I guess my only complaint (well more like a comment) is that young children WILL be afraid... I have no complaint because unlike Star Wars 1 and Harry Potter, this movie IS made for adults and not children or pre-teens. I give it a 10/10. It will be very hard to wait another year for the two towers, and maybe even harder to wait another week to see the film again. Kudos to the actors, director, WETA and everyone else who took part in this epic movie. JRR Tolkien would be proud.

title: Astounding
review:
I intentionally waited until I had a chance to see this movie for a second time before rating/commenting on it -- my first viewing left me with such a jumble of impressions that I wanted time to sort them out and gain some persepctive.

Let me first say that this movie did not change my life -- I am neither taller, smarter, nor better looking for having seen it. And in fact I can not even in good faith give this movie a "10" because it DID have flaws (some over the top effects as the ring tempted people, some scenes and sequences and characters which felt rushed and not fully developed despite the movie's three-hour running time, the (entirely necessary) lack of a true climax/ending etc.). But with all of that said, make no doubt that this is an absolutely astounding movie -- probably one of the most remarkable things ever to appear on film. There are a handful of scenes in this movie that are not only jaw-dropping, they are so absolutely perfect that it brings tears to your eyes. And the sheer scope of the project, its incredible imagination, stunning special effects, and just as critically, a series of casting choices and performances which could hardly have been better, make this not only easily the best fantasy film ever made, but a movie destined (likely with its sequels) to go down as one of those cultural milestones people will still be talking about in 20 years. Its that good.

P.S. Kindly ignore the small minority of people who felt compelled to give this movie a "1". For anyone who has humiliated themselves in this fashion, allow me to suggest a couple of titles: "Hercules in New York" and "Santa Claus with Muscles". Watch them, and then answer me this question -- if LOTR is a "1", what on earth are these films?

title: A Win in a seemingly No-Win situation.
review:
Everyone has their own ideas about this story. We all have

visualized the Hobbits , Dwarves, wizards Orcs etc, so there was a

good chance that Jackson would offend most of us some of the

time with his portrayal of the characters. Even given the sections

left out, I though he did a stirling job with this monumental task,

and I think its a good job it was released after Harry Potter and the

Philosophers Stone, as that film would have seemed even more

release of film number two!

review: "The Lord of the Rings" from John Ronald Reuer Tolkien is not A fantasy, it is the FIRST fantasy of the modern literature of science-fiction and fantasy. At last, we can see it. However there are many novels what weren't so good and somebody made a film about it, the Lord of the Rings is a unique masterpiece, the eternal story of the fight of good and evil. The film (directed by Peter Jackson [Dead Alive etc.], starred by Elijah Wood [The Faculty, Armageddon, Forever Young etc.] is the BEST movie of the year of 2001 (and not the Harry Potter...) A must see show, 10/10!

title: Damn good movie, but not #2
review: I thought that this was the best movie I've seen in about 2 or 3 years.  I can't wait for the next one.  I think that the amount of work that went to it is unbelievable.  But it's not the second best movie of all time, that's for sure.  Sorry.

title: One ring to bring us all
review: A three hour long film about elves, dwarves and hobbits didn't appeal to me at first, I preferred Harry Potter, but after seeing Lord of the Rings, Harry Potter was spoilt.A brilliant film. I started to read The Hobbit a couple of years ago, but failed, after seeing Lord of the Rings, I've started the trilogy. The film is a brilliant adaption of the book, the characters are exactly the way you imagine them. I think that Elijah Wood was brilliant, he acted so innocently and you almost imagine him being a hobbit in real life.Pippin and Merry made us all chuckle, and they reminded me of my friends (no offence to them!) Strider was outstanding, his sword fighting brilliant and Viggo Mortensen portrayed him so well, and Orlando Bloom as Legolas, well..... his archery and delicate footwork made him one of the best characters in the film, but that has to be beaten by Sir Ian. A magnificent actor, playing the part of Gandalf as it should be- strong and fierce. After the first time, I went to see it again, twice! This will always be one of the best films, a classic.

title: Definitely worth it!
review:
I've been waiting to see "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" ever since I heard about the trailer being available for download on the Internet. I'd never read any of Tolkien's novels, and I had heard great things about them. On December 16th, three days before the movie was to be released, I found myself running up to a local bookstore and purchasing a copy of "The Fellowship of the Ring" for seven bucks and planning to read 500 pages in three days!

Of course, I didn't finish in time, but I saw the movie on opening night. Right from the opening scene, I knew right away an instant classic was being shown right in front of me. If you loved "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" (me being somewhat of a fan of Rowling's books), you'll most likely love "The Fellowship" even better.

The special effects in this movie were stunning and pure eye candy throughout. The long running time is definitely a drawback, but don't be fooled! What surprised me the most about the movie was Elijah Wood's performance. I remember seeing him in "North" in which he was pretty wooden. But he was perfect as Frodo Baggins. Liv Tyler was much of a disappointment, though. She was credited as one of the main stars, but she's only on camera for at least twenty minutes out of 180 minutes! She seemed quite amateurish and didn't quite fit the persona too well. McKellen (who plays seven-foot-tall Gandolf) is also very good and most of the time stands out more than anyone else on screen.

Don't feel bad if you find yourself fighting back some tears in certain parts of the movie because I did too. You get to know the characters and feel sympathy throughout their journey that when they're scared, you're scared, when they're happy, you're happy.

All in all, this film was definitely worth the money. I can't wait until the second and third films come out!

title: I walked out.
review: I couldn't take this movie.  I loved the books, read them all, including "The Hobbit."  I even liked the animated version that came out in the '70's. There were some lovely things in this film, liked Elijah Wood, liked the sets, costumes, etc. My major problem with this movie was that it was very cold in tone.  It went from battle to battle, and the scenes in between the fighting were little more than "whew!"  The books were emotional, the books were involving, evocative.  This was awful.  When the characters emerged from the underground dwarf mines, and I realized that they had at least two set-piece battles remaining, I was out of there. It was a shame to waste such a talented cast.

title: Ignore everything anyone writes about this film....
review:
...and go to see it without any preconceptions.

Hype is a double edged sword. Some believe that positive word of mouth precludes anyone other than themselves and some discerning fellow travellers from making an objective assessment of a film's qualities. Others write off the fact, that some film-goers fail to enjoy the film as much as they did, as a cynical reaction to huge popular acclaim.

There is probably some grain of truth in each point of view, but in the much larger middle ground there are people who simply enjoy this film because it appeals to them, or they don't because it doesn't.

If you take my advice you won't read any further, but if you choose to ignore me (many do) and colour your potential enjoyment of this film, here are my 2 pennies worth.

In my opinion, FotR has the potential to be a great film, but whether it meets this potential is down to the viewer.

It has inherent flaws such as the uneven pacing, and a repetitive stop-travel-stop-travel formula.

It also has features that can be viewed as pluses or negatives. These include the balance in favour of progressing the story over developing our familiarity with some of the characters; a number of frantic fight scenes which some people find exhilarating and others compare unfavourably to the highly choreographed style introduced by Hong Kong cinema; a score that is either highly dramatic or gratingly distracting depending on your perspective; and a tendency towards the epic which people may find either profound or pompous.

Finally it has major, almost indisputable achievements, most notably in the visual department, but on the whole for bringing to life the equally magical and sinister world, characters and story of Tolkein's book (regardless of whether you have read it or not, or whether you enjoyed it when you did).

Personally, I found the experience to be very enjoyable, so much so that I've since spent a lot of time thinking and talking about the film. The strongest recommendation I can make is that there were moments of heart-stopping beauty that literally did move me to tears and while I didn't miss the flaws in the film, they seemed trivial at the end of the day.

As I've already said though, that's a personal view. In the end it's up to each film-goer to decide how the negatives and positives stack up for them, and whether other people liked it or disliked it shouldn't matter a jot.

title: Peter Jackson is a brave man..
review:
I took my wife along to our local multiplex to see this knowing that the signs were not good. She had struggled through Tolkiens prelude to the LOTR Trilogy,The Hobbit and I shuffle like an 8 eight year old in my seat at any film longer than 2 hours.

Three hours and five minutes later we were both amazed at the time that had passed and were in awe at what we had just seen.I take my hat off to Peter Jackson in tackling what was obviously such a difficult project.Given the fact that some minor changes have been made to the plot it follows the book very well.The actors were well chosen and in my view no one put in any less than a good performance.

I would recommend this film to anyone (including those of a shuffling disposition) and my only gripe....I have to wait 10 months to see part 2. Go see it on the big screen now.

title: I think I am in a minority.
review:
Before I begin let me just say that I did like this movie. However..I did not think it was worth all the high marks that it has been getting, this site not excluded. Visually it was stunning but one can only take so many stunning vistas and panoramic landscapes. The special effect were impressive (although by 2002 standards they may only be considered normal.) Casting was good. Ian Mckellen was the only person who could pull off Gandalf.

You will love it if you see it. But I think time will not be kind and many will watch it again or spend oodles of money to own a copy or two and be disappointed after repeated viewing.

title: If you haven't seen this movie, go. Now!
review: Well what can I say? I've tried not to get too excited by the hype surrounding this movie. I've even avoided watching the trailers, as I didn't want anything to spoil this. Nothing was spoiled. I've just spent three mesmerising hours in a packed cinema. I've never been with so many people, who were all so taken in by what was up on the screen. I wanted to look around and gauge the reaction of the other cinemagoers, but I just couldn't take my eyes off the screen for one second. In summary, this is a great movie, a fantastic movie. But don't take my word for it, go and see it for yourself. I certainly will be again!

title: Very Good, Best of 2001
review: I saw this film the first day it came out and I must say that I had very high expectations for it. I was not disappointed. The performances are all top notch and the cinematography is superb.  Ian McKellen deserves the Oscar for best supporting actor; he literally does no wrong in this film. I have a few small gripes about the repetative nature of the film. They travel over tremendous landscapes, rest and fight off an attack. Then... they do it again and again. I know that this is how Tolkien wrote the book, but the battles seem to lose a little intensity each time. Still, the best film of 2001. I can't wait for the next two to be released.

title: The Hobbit
review:
The hobbit and the trilogy of the rings were my favorite books growing up! Now, after seeing this movie, I am eager to reread all of them. Peter Jackson, the director of the Fellowship of the Rings, did an excellent job in portraying the magical and mythical nuances of the books (and everyone else involved in the movie). It is a movie I don't think I would ever get tired of seeing. I've already seen it 3 times.

The question that comes to my mind is, 'Does Peter Jackson ever plan to make a movie about The Hobbit book?' The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring was done so incredibly, that I'm certain he could do equal justice to The Hobbit.

title: It was brillant.
review: It was brilliant. I was overwhelmed. "...And in the darkness bind them" in the opening of the movie still gave me chills the third time seeing it in the theatre. The actors were perfectly cast, bringing to life the personalities of all the characters in the book exactly how I had imagined they would be. The sets were absolutely stunning (especially Rivendell and Lothlorien); the scenery (the beautiful New Zealand countryside) was breathtaking. From the armies of orcs, Gollum and the Balrog, to the details of hobbit feet and elf ears, the effects and costume and makeup were amazing. The film retained the integrity of the book and stayed true to the characters and the events.  I couldn't believe they fit so much into only three hours, yet I was left wanting more. Now I wait patiently for The Two Towers...

title: can't wait the other two.
review:
I must say, this film filled all my expectations, because frankly I did not have them. I'd never read the book, never played the games. Was not even sure if I was going to watch this, which now seems ridiculous This is movie-making at it's best. The one thing that really caught my eye was that the cast was so well chosen. They fit into their roles like gloves. The elves are a quite rare species but I definetely would not mind if one looking like Legolas would come by. He's a man of my taste: brave and quite a traditional hero. I hope his role get's a bit depth in the other parts of the trilogy. Peter Jackson's directing work, though is, fluent of course, quite traditional adventure.(remembering his other work) The fighting scenes are of course very important but at it's best this film is when it comes to quiet moments. My favourite is right after passing the Brigde of Kazad Dum.

Just realized that maybe the originality of Jackson does not show in his directing but in the way he has bought ( with his crew of course)this package alive.Thanks.

title: Tolkien's Middle Earth has come to life!
review:
I've seen this movie seven times and will see it again next month when the the trailer for the next movie is added to ending of first one. New Zealand is perfect for the locations. The Shire is just as I pictured it and Bilbo's house is so real. The cast was well chosen and each one fit his/her roles beyond imagination. Yes, there were some parts left out and scenes changed, but on the whole the movie is gorgeous! I can accept the deletion of Tom Bombadil, but think the scene with the barrow wright's cave should have been included. Aragorn didn't give the hobbits swords. They got them from the barrow wright's cave and Merry's sword is particularly important later on. Oh, well, this is how it goes!

The Elves are beautiful, eerie, and majestic! I loved the line about "The dwarf breathes so loud, we could have shot him in the dark!" being included in the film. Poor Gimli, he is the greatest dwarf I've ever seen and he is so full of life & boldness that it nearly tired me out watching him! Elijah Wood is the quintessential Frodo Baggins. He knows all too well what being a Ring Bearer is going to entail, yet takes on the role because he realizes that somehow he has the strength of will that it's going to take to carry the ring all the way to Mordor.

Ian is Gandalf through & through. He is both wise and merry. He understands about sacrifice of self and yet manages to come across as guide, protector, and friend of the soul. Aragorn appears to be a little weak in portrayal at first, but then he develops more strength of character when Gandalf falls in the chasm of Moria. Pippin & Merry are made to look like idiots in a lot of ways and hope this changes drastically in next film. I think that the two of them should have been seen as they were in the book since they willingly left the Shire with Frodo in a carefully arranged plan. Frodo didn't flee wildly into the night as shown in this version of the film. Indeed, he took 17 years between Bilbo's leaving and his own departure from the Shire.

Samwise Gamgee is incredible! He starts out as an apparently simple hobbit, but he shows frequent bouts of wisdom, common sense, and practicality to whatever challenges life brings to him & his master. I hope that the courage, passion to protect Frodo, willingness to take on the Ring at one point, is further developed in next two movies. I've heard complaints that the film is too long, but I thought it was too short!

The underground city of Moria is magnificent! I could imagine it as the way it had once been when filled with busy dwarves. The Balrog was exactly the way I had imagined him, all flame, terror, and power. The Orcs are like something out of nightmares, but perfectly created. The Nazgul/Ringwraiths were true horrors. Their unending pursuit of the ring and quick disposal of anyone who got in their way was spooky. The Nazgul's cries both in Bree and the Wilderness are enough to collapse the back bone. The sudden flash flooding of the Bruien with the foam disguised as fierce, white horses was exactly the way the book desribed this incident. I do think that Gandalf should have mentioned that the illusion of white horses was his doing.

Arwen was great in her defense of Frodo. Calling upon the river to flood and her determination to take on all of the Nazgul was well done! I loved hearing her in particular speak Elvish as she gave the language a lilting, musical tone. I didn't think it was right for her to be shown giving the slightly glowing, white pendant to Aragorn as she gives this to someone else in order to give them the gift of immortal life in her place.

The opening scene with Sauron against Elves, Dwarves, & Men was the best teaser to introduce rest of movie. Isildur was not especially intellingent keeping the one ring, but then, without him doing so, there wouldn't be any further story so... Elrond played by Hugo Weaving was excellent in his somber, grave approach to the future disposal of the ring. He also had a nice flair for sarcasm which is really evident in how he talks to Samwise who lets everyone know that his master isn't going anywhere without him!

Sean Bean as Boromir is well portrayed as the complex character he is. I think that Sean captured the essence of Boromir just right in his desire to find a way to save his people in Minis Tirith and yet struggle with honor's/duty's demands even when running contrary to his wishes. If ever redemption was needed by Boromir, he obtained it without a doubt defending Merry & Pippin until no longer able to do so.

I don't want to spoil next film for those who've never read the books, but I'm gleefully anticipating the consequences for Saruman's having the trees all chopped down. The scene for this sequence is again the way I imagined it from reading the book. Saruman was an idiot to think that he could both imitate Sauron's stronghold and perhaps even rival him.

For those who haven't read the books, please don't hesitate any longer! Go out there and get them from a library, new bookstore or used bookstore! Reading them will make the next two movies even more enjoyable!

title: Superb adaptation of the book and an OK movie
review:
Warning: Spoilers

Let's face it. Any truly faithful adaptation of Tolkien's classic (especially FOTR) is destined to make a lousy film. Much of what makes the book an epic can't be contained within the commercial limitations of film (even if the film runs close to three hours). Given this limitation, The FOTR was masterfully done, and it took just enough artistic license (Arwen saving Frodo, etc. Dropping Bombadil, etc.) to improve the movement of the story.

I was a little disappointed with the treatment of Galadriel who came across a bit too menacing in my opinion. The score could have been better also. Other than that, FOTR is a great film worth watching many times over.

title: IN MY TOP 10 OF 2001
review:
Although 2001 was a weak year for the movies, there were at least three films that managed to be very good (not great). Lord of the Rings is one of them (In the Bedroom and Mulholland Drive were the other two in case you were wondering). Peter Jackson does absolute justice to the first installment of the beloved trilogy, confidently choosing which passages to include and which to discard (otherwise we would have a ten hour film on our hands). The $109 million budget can be seen in every frame as the movie progresses and it actually becomes more impressive with each passing sequence. The actors do a credible job particularly Ian McKellen as Gandalf the Wizard. Many people are complaining about the non ending but they have to realize this IS a trilogy and the second one will pick up where the last one left off. Overall an entertaining and satisfying film going experience. I look forward to the next installment.

8/10

title: 13 Oscar nominations? Give me a break!
review:
I have never read Tolkien's books (never enjoyed the genre to begin with) and did not go to see LOTR when it was released last year. But when I heard about 13 Oscar nominations I told myself that I have to give it a chance.

Unfortunately, there is nothing remarkable in the movie for the rest of us who don't worship Tolkien's novels. Whether you look at acting, camera, special effects or music, everything is so-so. I would even rank LOTR below "Harry Potter" because the latter is not so deadly serious.

Overall, it's a good movie for kids between 9 and 12 or grown-up fans of "middle-earth" world. It will most likely have the destiny of "Titanic" who grabbed lots of Academy Awards but is already forgotten.

And oh by the way, people were leaving the theatre in the middle of the movie... Bad sign, huh?

title: Lord-y, Lord-y, look who's eleventy-one
review:
Define Hype. My definition? When, nine days after it's release, the Arklow cinema in Co. Wicklow (Ireland, for you uneducated swines) is FULL, cash register overflowing and people sitting in the aisles. Now, usually films with this much hype I find sickening, yet having read the books and seen the trailer, I had no choice but to go see it.

After hearing people say that it was only good for people who'd read the book I decide to bring along two guinea pigs who hadn't read the book (not litrelly guinea pigs, although their views might have been more interesting). When I say brought them, I mean they paid for themselves. Another problem some people feared was the fanatics with notebooks of maps and the like, but the only things I feared in Arklow was my feet getting stuck to the floor and that people wouldn't shout "What the F**K is a hobbit?" too loudly or often. Where was I? Oh yes, the film.

Story Okay, so I'm biased as I'm a fan of the book, but I think it's an intriguing if a little simplistic story. A brief outline: Rings are made to rule each empire. 9 rings for the men, 7 for the Dwarf-lords and 3 for the Elven-kings. Yet there is one ring which has far stronger powers, the ruling ring. This was made by Sauron himself, the Dark Lord.

The film starts off with a huge battle scen which sets the pace for the film. In this Sauron wears the ring, and is cutting through the troops like a knife through butter and seems invincible. However, one man manages to cut off the hand that bears the ring. He decides that he must keep this ring, yet it is soon lost and found again by a strange creature called Gollum. It then reaches the hand of Bilbo Baggins and this is where our story really begins.

The Shire is the home of the hobbit called Bilbo, and also his adopted heir Frodo. It is Bilbo's eleventy first (111th) birthday, a very old age indeed. However, at this party Bilbo dissapears forever and leaves the ring to Frodo. Yet Gandalf the wizard soon finds that this is the ruling ring, and of the terrible powers it possesses. Sauron is coming back to power, even though he has no physical presence, just in spirit (Voldermort, anyone?). He tells Frodo that dark powers are heading for the Shire with the name Baggins in mind searching for the lost ring and that he must leave and destroy the ring.

And that's where I'll leave it, at the basic story. Hope it wasn't too complicated. Anyway, on to...

Visuals What can I say? The setting is absolutely magnificent. Every landscape is meticulously created and everybody agreed they were stunning. Just for good measure every few minutes they would take a camera swirl and show us the beautifully crafted mountains or the huge statues. It is breathtaking. There's not much more I can say, except that Middle Earth looks far better than I ever imagined it could, and that was one thing I was very doubtful about.

As for the costumes, they were perfect. From the hobbit's round tummies and furry feet, to the perfectly straight white hair of the elves, it was immaculate. The orcs are terrifying, the elves are mystical and the hobbits are... well hobbits. Even the biggest Tolkien fan will find it hard to fault the intensive pursuit of perfection in the costumes. The best however was rerserved for what little we saw of Gollum. He is going to be seen more in the later films, and I can't wait. He is part-lizard, part-man kind of. Whatever he is, he's pretty scary.

As for the special effects, they are as you would expect from a film with a budget of this amount, incredible. I'm not going to spoil the film by telling you some of the moments it is used in, just trust me, it's excellent.

Sound I usually don't write about this in a film review, but I think it deserves a mention. The music is so atmospheric you can actually feel yourself drawn into the screen. As for the numerous battle scenes, the grunts from the orcs, the clashing of swords and the dark battle scene music made me duck for cover (which was slightly embarassing and meant that I had popcorn thrown at me for the rest of the film. A short mention, but a mention nonetheless.

Acting Hmm...my first complaint. Elijah Wood (Frodo) obviously knew he was picked for his wide-eyed, innocent look because that is all he does during the entire film. Orc going to kill me: wide-eyed look. Talking to a friend: wide-eyed look. Eating...etc. I felt his acting was wooden. Hold the phone... wooden? His acting was Wood-en! HAHAHAHAHAHAHHAHAHAHHAHA! God I'm good.

I also felt Ian McKellen(Gandalf) could have shown more emotion at times, yet he at least has more range than Wood. Ian Holm (Bilbo) gave an excellent if brief performance, and I also thought Sean Astin (Sam) was good in parts. Besides that, the acting was average. Believable, but nothing to get worked up about.

Bits I disliked The fact that Frodo is about as heroic as a can of sardines. People keep saving his life and then telling him how brave he was. Yes, you truly are a king among hobbits. I also hated the way Frodo kept showing us the ring in the palm of his hand. We know you have it, there's no need to keep doing that. As I said Wood's acting is atrocious. They also left out the fact that Sam loves the elves and the scene where they meet them which I thought was a pity (not to go all fanatical on you). That's about it.

Layman's view The two people I brought with me felt that the story was boring in parts, there were too many battle scenes, too many different characters but they both agreed that the visuals were amazing. They said they would give it three stars, which isn't bad (they're very critical).

Overall Battle scenes are slightly long, and all the other bad bits I mentioned, but overall it is a solid film with stunning visuals, great atmosphere and a sturdy story. I liked it a lot, so five stars it is. Basically, if you've read the book it's worth a look, if not... I don't know, Harry Potter?

title: A Heck of an Enjoyable Film
review:
I saw a midnight showing on opening night, and it was one of those great audiences that applauds at all the right parts. I've never been a Tolkien fanatic, and I only recently finished the first book, so it was still fresh in my mind when I watched the movie. There were some changes from the book -- some necessary for pacing and length purposes, and then some minor ones that bothered me, but didn't really detract from my enjoyment of the film. All of the actors put in exceptional performances -- especially Ian McKellen, Elijah Wood, Sean Bean, and Ian Holm -- though, really, probably everyone deserves accolades. I just named them because they were all my personal favorites.

The movie looked perfect, visually; Hobbiton, Rivendell, and Lothlorien were exactly as I pictured them; many of the panoramic landscapes may as well have come from a painting, and the characters and costumes were right on-target. Scenes such as the Fellowship sailing between the two great stone kings were just breathtaking, and I'm looking forward to getting the DVD already, just to savor all those shots I didn't get enough time to enjoy in the film. Nothing was skimped on, and you can tell that the creators really put in the effort to render Middle Earth as Tolkien had written it.

All in all, I hope this series of films will show future directors what fantasy movies *should* be.

title: Absoluetly Fantastic!!!
review:
When I saw Lord of the Rings, it was the first time I had been to the cinema since November 2000 when I saw Little Nicky. Although I enjoyed it and thought it didn't deserve the treatment it had received, it does not even compare to this wonderful epic! I haven't read the book so I don't know how different it is from that.

There is no point of me explaining the plot so I'll just say how good it is. I've noticed this film is even similiar to Star Wars! Gandalf's demise and extreme emotion from Frodo echoes Obi-Wan's demise and Luke's unhappiness from Star Wars. Also, both Alec Guiness and Ian McKellen have received oscar nominations. LOTR has received 13 nominations. I hope it wins them all.

The only negative point is the ending. Although I know it is a long saga split into 3 films, I was hoping for a better ending. I'm not saying the ending was bad or anything but it was a bit of a dull way to end it. Throughout it's 3 hour length, the film has enough endings for 6 films!!

If you have not seen this film, then I advise to see it at once! This is one of the best films I've seen in a long time and is a promising start to what looks like being one of the best movie trilogys of all time.

Breathtaking.........

title: Very well done
review:
If you'd have asked me a year or so ago which book is the most difficult to make into a film, I'd have almost definitely said Lord of the Rings. When I saw the film, I was taken aback. Firstly, it looks visually stunning. What's more, it fits Tolkien's descriptions very well; the appearance of the scenery in the film was strikingly close to how I'd imagined it on first reading the book, and the mixture between the beautiful scenery of New Zealand, indistinguishably blended with stiking computer-generated imagery.

Many of the negative comments I've read about the film stem from the director's interpretation of the book: specifically the sticky subject of turning the first third of what must be truly an epic book into a film which is watchable -- and enjoyable -- by all. I think Jackson has got this truly right. By all accounts, the book starts off slowly, and much of this needed to be cut in the film to make it appeal to all. And I think that's been done incredibly well.

title: fantastic movie, 4.5 stars out of 5
review:
I came out of Lord of the Rings very happy. I will mention now that I never read the books, however I went to the movie with two friends who read them all at least three times. They had given me the the plot-line of the book so when I did watch the movie I knew when certain incidents were to occur.

Going into the movie: I was excited, but also worried that it would disappoint the book fans, also if the were showing the balrog would it really be that authentic? Reaction: It was great. Jackson's Balrog was quite well done, especially since illustrating fire through computer graphics as being real is one of the hardest to do. The action sequences were very entertaining and kept me at the edge of my seat. The 3 hours went by fast. Then I asked my friends, who actually read the books, they said it was great. The few parts left out in the movie, as well as the Tom Bombadil character, were not essential to the primary story. One friend said that if Bombadil was in the movie, his character would have confused anyone who hadn't read the book.

Overall: this is a must-see movie, leaving this person the anticipation of December 2002.

title: Great Creation, Ruined Plot
review: I was absolutely blown away by the world that was created in the movie. The settings, costumes, and appearances of the characters greatly surpassed my expectations, and really brought to life Tolkein's Lands of Middle Earth. Far and away the best movie I have ever seen in that respect. However, some of the changes in the plot to me were unacceptable.  While I understand that people have different interpretations of the world Tolkein created, there comes a point where changing things due to one's interpretation starts to destroy the original vision.  While I do not think the vision of Tolkein's world was destroyed, I do think that several areas of it were weakened.  The most obvious is the politically correct additions concerning the role of women.  First, there's the decision to have Frodo saved by Arwyn.  While she may very well have been capable of this, I think having her do this ruins her role in the story.  Tolkein's trilogy already has a warrior princess who saves the day, therefore it doesn't need Arwyn to be one to show how capable she is.  Elfin women are often more powerful than the men, but the power is reserved.  Which is also why I disagreed somewhat with the portrayal of Galadriel.  The audience never got the sense of absolute awe at her beauty that the characters should have, and the portrayal of her awesome powers looked more like a freak show.  Women are powerful characters in the books, but their powers are often hidden, even though they may be more powerful than the displayed powers of men, and I think that is an important theme that was missed.  However, the most important problem was the shifting of focus from the story being a struggle of hobbits to being a great tale of a king and a wizard.  Having Frodo ask Aragorn permission to leave changes the entire scheme of things, which I disagree with. Otherwise, great casting, great acting, great movie.  I just don't know why they had to change those few things.  I understand the character cuts and restrictions, but changing things from the original story that didn't need it kept this movie from being the greatest of all time.  Ian deserves an Oscar.

title: A sense of perspective
review:
LOTR:FOTR is a very fine movie. It is not perfect, but let's be honest.. there is no perfect movie. I have recently re-seen the Godfather and Shawshank Redemption. Both are great films but also flawed movies [although I do find SR to be rather trivial even though it is hugely entertaining]

FOTR is also a great movie.. it has finally brought to the screen the world of Tolkien in a way that does not greatly offend the original source. Obsession with IMDB rankings is not what a love of and a critical appreciation of movies is about. LOTR deserves a place in the top 50 movies... it is innovative, perhaps as faithful to a very complex text as can be achieved in three hours of film, has some very good acting, and a score that is neither intrusive or manipulative.

Some people left feeling cold. I found that time flew but it was not the WOW movie that Gloomy Sunday or Fitzcarraldo were to me. It is, for me a very good movie, a good 8 bordering on a 9. There are many other movies that reach this level but for different reasons.

We will all await the next two movies which offer a lot more in terms of the narrative potential.

title: i'll keep this short. [SPOILER FREE]
review:
look i love movies, i watch tons of films, i even someday hope to be in some way responsible for making films.. i'd like to think i know a good film from a bad film. title: I honestly wanted this to be great. It was horrible.
review:
I hate to see bad reviews, especially if it's a movie I'm looking forward to, so I hate to write this since I know that a great number of people are looking forward to this film. I also hate it when people are angry that a movie doesn't perfectly reflect a book, movies are a different medium and will inherently be different than a book.

Having said that, I'm sorry but they really destroyed a perfectly good story. I know that 3 hours isn't enough time to cover everything that happens in the fellowship of the ring, but they took out too much detail and then rushed everything else. The characters DID have depth and the acting was (for the most part) better than good (but never really great) but this was overshadowed by unnecessarily dramatic camera work and sound effects applied to voices (worst was what they did to the elves voices).

On the other hand, like I said the acting was mostly good, and the characters had depth (at least I thought so). The special effects were nice (although used inappropriately sometimes) and the fight scenes were great. A lot of the landscapes looked right to me, and well most of it looked great.

All in all, I enjoyed watching it, but if I hadn't read the book first, it would have ruined it for me. I think they left out too much detail and tried to compensate by using camera work to make the scenes dramatic when the story would have done that for them if they had let it. Maybe they could have left more out and instead replaced it with narraration and then concentrated on certain scenes, drawing them out more, taking more time on each rather than rushing every single one. I hate to see stuff cut out of a film, but its worse when every bit of it is rushed just to make sure it all gets in, even though you end up leaving some out anyway.

title: Brilliant. Where can they go with film making next.
review: I don't think I have heard a bad comment from anyone who has seen this movie.   My wife and I sat in the theatre absolutely spell bound by the sheer grandeur and magnificence of this masterpiece.   Never having read the book, it took a little time to associate with the characters, but once I had time to piece it together I was hooked.  Parents of younger children be warned; there are quite a few frightening looking characters who try to do their worst to our heroes.  Teenagers up would be the suitable and appropriate ages to see this movie.  It is a lengthy film and is of course the first in a trilogy, so be prepared to be left hanging in midair at the end.   Hurry up episode 2!

title: Wake up people!
review:
For Pete's sake people! 9.1, Top 2 of all time! What's happening?

Honestly... has three hours of squashing orcs become a universal idea of a cinematic masterpiece? Remember there once were some niceties like complex characters.. their development.. their feelings.. uh.. unexpected and beautiful turns of the story.. some nice camera work.. interesting evil? Anyone?

Is it strange to want good guys explained and endeared to me before I even start to like them? I know they're some of them good looking but sadly I'm not a teenage girl. Is it too much to ask bad guys also explained? One of them has a really big black stick and is proficient in using it - that should be enough? Oh, then there's the little eventuality of being, like, born out of mud and having a wee bit of a weakness for black in dress - and so not having very good looks... But hey the All Blacks might be scarier and lots of people even like them! Oh the nicest looking is the good one? Doesn't it sound a bit fascist?

Is it cheeky to ask for a few shots in a 3hr movie that could make good art when stilled? The circling camera sweep routine has apparently been burnt into the firmware of WETA's computers somwehere right down Mount Doom - it's been used I've lost count how many times.

What of a story? I'm sure if you tried to recount it to anyone who hasn't read the book or seen the movie you were having a hard time. Seems to me that the screenplay misses a lot of messages from the book.

My greatest actor grudges are Frodo, and Elrond. McKellen is definitely getting his Oscar for best supporting role - that Frodo needs a hell of supporting. Don't know if Wood would be playing well, for he has very little to play. Hugging Gandalf and pulling faces when hit by a spear - not much room for an actor's feat. And 'have you not heard nothing Lord Elrond has said?' He said 'My name is Smith. AGENT Smith'.

Now, hey, hey, don't throw stuff at me! The movie's beautiful and yeah, it's based on a great book, and yeah it tries hard at transferring it on the screen. Whether it manages is a big question tho. Stop for a moment. Inhale. Count to three. Exhale. Is this movie head and shoulders above Casablanca... American History X... Fight Club... The Usual Suspects... any great film you still remembered before Christmas 2001? I hope there's still sanity in many of us to say NO.

7/10

title: Best Adaptation Ever
review:
The Fellowship of the Ring...J. R. R. Tolkien's first volume of a trilogy of the grandest scope and imagination. It almost single-handedly created the modern fantasy genre, influencing Dungeons and Dragons, Star Wars, Magic the Gathering, and much more.

I first read the book one year ago. I was an instant fan. I recently reread the trilogy in anticipation of the movie's premiere. Then, three weeks ago, I saw Harry Potter, a perfect picture of how NOT, and I say NOT, to do a book-to-movie adaptation. Harry was so faithful to the book that when time constraints arose and parts had to be omitted, it was extremely obvious and ended up ruining it (at least in my mind, though the chess scene ruled all).

Fellowship is different. Peter Jackson fudges a few parts, merging roles, shortening parts of the journey, changing the circumstances of Frodo's departure at the end, but here's the major difference--it feels natural. Fellowship is still extremely loyal to the book (the scene where Bilbo leaves Frodo the ring is line-by-line form the book), but it moments of disloyalty give a strength that is lacking in Potter. In short, Peter Jackson has taken a book and a world that seems impossible to do justice to, and does it, just like that...in 2 hours and 58 minutes...but well worth every second.

title: Oscar contender...NOT!
review: This was an overlong experience.  While some (SOME!) of the effects were excellent, the acting seemed stilted to me.  Of course, having read the trilogy, the expectations for myself were probably very high.  Still, though I did like (not love) the movie, I was disappointed.  I'm only hoping the next volume raises the bar a little bit.

title: good action flick
review: THe opening sequence of battle scenes was the high point and the rest ain't too shabby either, but it does drag in places, there's only so much sword fighting i can take. it starts at bilbos party and goes up to the point where gandalf and boromir are killed, i think it covers the start of book 2.

title: A work of art
review:
I really don't think LOTR could be called the greatest movie of all time, but certainly the greatest fantasy movie. Is it better than Star Wars? I don't know, it's hard to compare a space opera to a pure fantasy. I do know that Lucas was "heavily influenced" by LOTR. I won't say he stole from it, but just look at the similarities..

I am a fan of the trilogy. I read it first in the 8th grade, then in my twenties, then again last year because I knew Peter Jackson was making it into a series of films. I had forgotten a lot, (I'm 40 now) and reading it this last time was the most enjoyable of all. LOTR is truly an epic, grand tale. I know a lot of people find the books boring in parts. Yes, Tolkien could spend ten pages just describing a forest, but it really makes you feel like you are there. People must have the attention span of gnats nowadays.

LOTR-THE FILM is definitely not boring. It is an action film. If you want the full backstory and character development, read the book, it has plenty. I actually like the slow parts in the book, they break up the chase\battle

scenes. A lot of people have complained that the movie is just chase\battle\pause, over and over. This is a story about a perilous quest, what do you expect? And it is a LONG quest, Frodo has a lot further to go at the end of this film. If you haven't read the books, believe me, it just gets better! The film has quite a few scary images, but LOTR is not a children's book, it's a serious story about the corruption of power, filled with horror, war and despair but with an ultimately uplifting ending.

**possible spoiler ahead ***

I loved everything about the movie, with the exception of the giant crumbling staircase sequence in Moria. That wasn't in the book and just seemed like something out of an Indiana Jones flick. Other than that, Jackson's vision of Middle Earth was pretty much exactly like what I pictured in my mind. And I didn't miss Tom Bombadil a bit. I've seen it twice now and enjoyed it just as much on the repeat viewing. Acting, special effects, costume design, cinematography, and especially sound are all top notch. Jackson and crew truly did Tolkien's work justice, and accomplished what many thought to be an impossible task. I'll be buying the DVD for sure.

I can't wait for "The Two Towers". It'll be interesting to see how they bring the Ents to life.

title: Empty characters, go see a real movie, please!
review:
I just saw the Lord Of The Rings and it was NOT what I hoped for. Not even a quarter of it. OK, special (&sound) effects are pretty astonishing, as well as the marvellous landscapes, but that's not all that makes a movie. What about a story for example? I think you are much better of reading the book (which I have not read) to get more into the characters, which are totally empty in the movie. The movie was very slow and that's the only reason why you have to sit three hours, not because it's exciting. The end was just so silly that I was looking around if I was dreaming or missing the point. Yeah, I think I just missed the point. I hope.

So, I guess I am part of negative of the two parties; it seems people either hate or love this movie. But let's be real, #2 in the Top 250? People, get a life and go see a real movie.

title: Not the best Jackson's film, but the best fantasy one
review: All my hopes to see another great extreme-styled Jackson's movie were failed. But another side of my hopes - to see a great screening of THE Great Book - was reached at impossibly high level. And today I got an real shock to my nervous system. Three years ago it was absolutely impossible for me to dream to see as PJ nominated for 13(!!) Oscars. And he deserved it, deserved for each sequence in this 3-hrs movie - one of the most quick and most terse movies I ever saw.

title: If you think you've got a favorite movie already, then now you've got a new one!!
review:
OK, anyone who says this movie isn't any good is, to put it simply, an IDIOT!!!! As for people who say the plot is no good and lacks development, you have to remember that the director had to put a entire book into three hours, he will have to miss some details!!

The movie is by far the best, most epic movie I've seen in a VERY long time. I don't usually go see movies in the theater more than once, especially a 3 hour movie, but I WILL be going to see this a FEW more times! The SFX are flawless, the acting is nothing short of perfect, the cinematography beautiful, there isn't a single thing about this movie I didn't like! BTW, I never read the books so this isn't a review by a "Tolkien Freak" as I heard it but in earlier reviews.

title: A well done recreation doesn't mean it's a great movie
review: The Lord of the Rings is a good movie, especially for this year, but it is in no way above classics such as Citizen Kane or Shawshank Redemption or even Momento. Just because Jackson did a good job at capturing the book's character's appearance and personalities, doesn't qualify it to be the second best movie of all time. It has no message, it's just a very well told fantasy story. So stop giving it praise it doesn't deserve. It's an 8 not a 9 or a 10.

title: I was stunned by the movie when I left the theatre.
review: If you have ever been in a dream that you just did not want to wake up from, this movie was IT!!! From the moment I saw Gandalf riding in his horse drawn cart, I was transported to Middle Earth. When I saw the map of the Lonely Mountain on the table at Bilbo Baggins hobbit hole, I was completely gone. I became mesmerized by every character that came on screen, in the shortest 3 hours of my life. The script changes from the book to the screen just flowed and even when the movie was over and I had a couple of days to digest them, I DIDN'T CARE. My imagination had been taken while I was sleeping, and Peter Jackson had made it into a movie. Emotionally the movie drained me and if Mr Jackson wasn't stopping your heart with the scenery and action, he was breaking it with the relationships of the nine companions. If I could add up all my vote points for all the movies I have voted for here in the past, I would give them all to "The Fellowship of The Ring". But I can not do that, as I will need some for the next two "Lord of The Rings" movies. I won't say that this is the best movie I will see in my lifetime, as I know twice more I will be transported to Middle Earth and although I know what happens in the end, it is the JOURNEY, that I will take that will make all the difference. Mr Peter Jackson, I read the LOTR's trilogy 20 years ago and twice more since, but you bought back a twelve year old boys imagination. I thankyou and can't wait for the "Two Towers" and "The Return Of The King".

title: Impressive in scope and depth.
review: The adaptation of Tolkien's classis trilogy has started off on the right foot.  A long time fan of Tolkien, I was impressed with the way in which the epic tale was compressed to fit into a movie-length format.  Undoubtedly some fans will feel slighted by omissions and aggregate characters, the movie held my spellbound for all three hours.  It is too bad the others are still a year and two years away.  For good measure I watched the 12:01 AM showing with friends whom had both read the books and those whom had not. One friend who had not declared that she would not see another movie until next Christmas.  The score is amazing and doesn't seem overbearing, but rather delivers the emotional elements well.  The dialogue seems a bit rushed in places, but the film lingers when it should to take in the scenery and the emotion.  The battle scenes are graphic and the tension is powerful and under no circumstance would I recommend this for a child too young to separate a movie from reality.  The actors are strong and I believe this to be among the best movies yet produced.  It stands on its own merit, but as an adaptation of a beloved book, it is in a class by itself.

title: This Would Be So Much Easier If There Was No Ranking System...
review:
I remember walking out of the theater on December 19th. I had just witnessed a movie that I had waited for almost my entire life, and eagerly anticipated for 2 years. I was flustered, amazed, and I was for once, excited over the fact that after seeing movie after movie surrounded by hype, that 2 months from then, no justification about how I liked it then as opposed to now would be needed. It's been about 2 months now. How do I feel?

The exact same as I walked out of that theater for the first time.

Since then, I've gone back 3 more times, and I plan to see it once "The Two Towers" footage is added. Despite the nearly 3 hours running time, despite the slow moments, and despite the liberties that were taken with the story, I did, and still do love it. For once, I saw a movie that has still lived up to the hype that was injected into it. Fantasy, was alive; Middle Earth was there. I witnessed the Shire with my own eyes. The dwarves were real; I knew it, because I saw their great castle in the depths of Moria. Elves and Maiar; they were there. I saw Gandalf's fight with the Balrog, and I saw Rivendell in all its glory.

So why the ambiguity in my summary?

Because trying to rank this film is one of the hardest thing any of us can do. A lot of fans were quite enthusiastic when it came out, and quickly put their mouse key over that "10" button in the vote. This made Fellowship's rating soar, and because of that, it polarized people about how they felt about the film. People who had merely liked it now loathed it because of this, and tried to bring it down with ratings of "1." I understand that people grew tired of seeing LOTR at number 1, and saw this as more hype for the movie, but honestly; do people think this is as bad as "Hobgoblin" or "Cop and a half?" This ain't an Ed Wood movie. Despite how you felt about it, I seriously doubt all of you think it's that bad. Likewise, the ratings of 10 are also flawed; this is by no way the best movie ever made, or even in the top 10 or so. Despite how much you loved it (and I do love it) I really think that there are better movies out there; maybe not as entertaining ones, but there are better ones.

I loved "Fellowship" and I can't wait for the other two. However, trying to big-league this in the same ranks as "Shawshank," "Schindler's List" or "The Godfather" is in my mind, not something we can do yet. I remember waxing greatness about "Pay It Forward" until realizing how completely manipulative that ending is. Likewise, I remember ranting about "Unbreakable" because I wasn't happy with the advertising campaign, but learned to realize that it's well made, and not as bad as I initially thought. "Fellowship" is still too fresh, too new. Trying to give an impartial rating on it is something that none of us can do yet. Wait until the third one comes out, and then wait a couple years. Then we'll see.

title: Visually Perfect!!!
review:
Once again I find myself leaving a review for a film that has so many reviews that it is unlikely that many will see it. The reason I am leaving it is because this film is so good on so many levels. First let me begin by informing readers that I have been a fan of Tolkein and his Middle Earth since I was about 8 years old and saw the television version of THE HOBBIT. As a child I was drawn to the story line and fantasy world so much that while in grade school I read THE HOBBIT and while in junior high school read THE LORD OF THE RINGS. This was one of my first introductions into Fantasy based books. I am not a big fan of Fantasy based books and that's basically because it seems to me that most other authors have plots so similar to LOTR that I get bored and would rather read LOTR. Two exceptions would be the authors C.S. Lewis and Terry Brooks, although I think it's safe to say that Brooks's material borrows heavily from Tolkein.

One draw back to Tolkein is that I, especially when I was younger, found it hard not only to pronounce some of the names that he uses for people, places and things but I found it hard to follow the story line because I would become confused while reading. The film eliminates this problem. It is so much easier to follow the story line while hearing the proper names used effortlessly.

I think that this film gives the viewer an excellent depiction of what middle earth would look like. The scenery is beautiful. I found towns such as Hobbiton and the Shire more beautiful and real than I had imagined. I especially liked Rivendale(sp) the elvish town. I did enjoy the fight between Saruman and Gandalf. Seeing these two wizards duke it out with such power despite their frail appearances was a visual treat.

Of course the story has been altered and but not to the point where it detracts from the original story or alters the meaning or ending of the story. I read one review that indicated the movie left us hanging and should have bought some sort of conclusion to the ending so that if the viewers who are unable or choose not to see the following films would not be left hanging. If that reviewer had read LOTR he/she would know that the books don't bring an kind of conclusion until the end of RETURN OF THE KING. In fact I don't know how this movie could have had a clear cut ending without ruining the story line. What I like about this movie trilogy is that all 3 parts were made back to back unlike the original STAR WARS trilogy that spanned over 6 years. By filming it this way LOTR ensures that it's actors won't noticeable age or in case of some of the elder cast die before the series can be completed. Also, all 3 movies will be released within a 3 year time frame. Even though it may seem like a long time it's a lot better than waiting 3 years between sequels like SW.

Lastly, LOTR has just been nominated for many Oscars this year. I personally would love to see it get best picture and director. My guess is that the academy will give the director award to Ron Howard for A BEAUTIFUL MIND. I believe this will happen because he has been nominated several times before and the academy will figure he is due an award. However, given LOTR fan base, excellent box office receipts and almost universal praise from fans and critics I don't see how they can not give it to LOTR. If it should win Best Picture this would represent a win for director Jackson in case he is passed over for Best Director and it would honor and pay tribute to Tolkein the "father" of modern mythology and fantasy.

title: Adequate rendition of Tolkien´s Masterpiece
review: J.R.R. Tolkien´s "Lord of the Rings" is the Grandmother of all classic fantasy - generations of role playing gamers would confirm this. It was said a long time that it is not possible to make a movie out of Tolkien´s 1200p-novel. But in my opinion Peter Jackson succeeded in doing this. Of course there are some details missing - but these are details which are in principle not that important for the story per se. Hardcore fans perhaps wouldn´t like these slight changes, but I felt comfortable with them. LOTR:TFOTR is thrilling, has well-made action scenes and SFX, does not lack some humor, has well-playing actors and is a nice movie even for them who didn´t read the books. 9/10

title: boring to say the least
review:
Umm yeah #2 on IMDB for this crap is ridiculous. I was falling asleep by the time the third hour was going by. It's dull, the lines are horribly cliche, and the plot is very predictable.

The scenes throughout the whole movie reflect the cliche lines by the banal characters. From the fighting to the rescuing to whatever, it's all very childish. I was laughing during most parts: Hobbits killing orcs? They had some long description of how elves turned into these fighting machine that were orcs, and then they come and all these hobbits that have never touched a sword are killing them left and right. Insanely stupid.

The scene where one of their party members was being hit with arrows and dying - that scene was absolutely laughable.. Oh my. One arrow hits him.. he falls.. gets up.. second arrow.. same thing.. oh so dramatic I wanted to puke.

I was screaming, die already.

Usually when a movie has sequels coming I want to see the sequels because there is some suspense in the plot, not here. I really could care less for that ring being burnt. I'd prefer him to fail and all the evil to take over, would definitely make for a more entertaining experience.

title: Not as great as I was led to believe...
review:
Perhaps I'm in the minority... OK, yes, I am definitely in the minority, but I just saw "Lord of the Rings" yesterday and am still wondering what all the fuss is about?

Yes, the movie is technically brilliant, from special effects, to art direction, to cinematography. But the story didn't move me at all.

I admit I am NOT a fan of fantasy - "Star Wars" left me similarly unmoved. But to say that "Lord..." is one of the greatest movies of all time is confusing to me. And it's not just IMDB voters but movie critics alike.

One thing I noticed in the film (and since I have not read the book except for "The Hobbit" I don't know if this is similar) is a lot of homoeroticism. I wonder if I'm just reading something into it or was my mind wandering so much that I had to think of subtext, or what?

Did anyone else notice this? From the opening "smoke rings" sequence (Gandolf's smoke boat goes into Bilbo's smoke ring) to the lack of female characters, to the womb-like "evil eye", to men convincing other men to stay with the men and not go with the women...

Anyway, I give the movie 7 out of 10 stars (normally I'd give it 8 but it's overrated here so it needs a bit of reality).

title: The ideal motion picture
review:
Three people make this film sublime: Tolkein, Jackson, and the shadowy guy at AOL Time Warner who had the bravery to give the licence to a comedy splatter-movie maker from New Zealand.

The music is effective but unmemorable. Apart from that, every aspect, every frame of this film is solid gold. The casting is flawless, and each cast member gives everything under Jackson's passionate, intelligent guidance. Frodo and Gandalf in particular are mesmerising. You will see not just the finest special effects ever (to be expected) but their most moving and artistic use. And don't forget that this is the adaptation that for fifty years Hollywood said couldn't be done.

This movie fills you with a passion from about five minutes in until long after the credits; an enchantment worthy of Gandalf himself.

title: There, but not so there!!!
review:
Ok then, for the record, I am a huge Tolkien fan, have read and studied the books many many times in my life, needless to say I love them and still after all these years I read them and I enjoy them, it gives me time off to delve into an imaginary world, unfortunately thats exactly what the movie does not do.

I was extremely excited when i got to travel to London, that meant I would not have to wait eons to watch the film in Asia, but was I sad or was I angry, I actually could not make out.

Peter Jackson is no doubt a brilliant filmmaker. The film was ripe with lush images of Middle Earth, remarkable production design, decent acting and even a pretty good score. One thing that I feel Mr. Jackson lacked was the ability to tell a story. Most of the people whom i know who have not read the book were completely left out in the cold as to a great many things.

The film spent too much time on petty sequences i.e. interactions between Frodo & Sam, the Boromir dying sequence. The film also spent too much time panning and flying across endless Middle Earth.

I feel all this time added up could have been used to better introduce the characters and the plot to many people who simply came to see the movie without reading the book.
