title: Oh, the fine line between spectacle and travesty!
review:
Minor spoilers

Have you ever heard that song about Tolkien's trilogy by the rock group Styx? In it they ebulliently intone, `All hail to the Lord of the Rings, to the wonder and mystery it brings'. Nope I'm not kidding. It stands as a perfect example of how rock musicians should not try to incorporate classic books about fantasy worlds into their music (at least Led Zepplin had enough sense to only dally in self-indulgence by inserting a pithy, enigmatic reference to the LOR in `Ramble On'). So how would Hollywood fare in the quest to apply the LOR saga to another medium? WellÂ…

Ultimately it comes down to the dividing line between those who have read the book and those who have not. Those who are acquainted with Tolkien's world will appreciate the attempt at faithfulness that the filmmakers have made. They will be able to fill in the lacunas that are engendered by the time constraint involved in movies (though this a rather long one for weak bladders). They will be familiar enough with the characters, locations and situations to become as enthralled as one can with a film, that for all its effort cannot perform the impossible; that is live up to the book(s).

Unfortunately, those who have not read the novel(s) will be benighted of the intricacies of Middle Earth and become easily confused. The lack of in-depth explanation, offered by the novel, will leave those audience members wondering about many aspects of the film such as why the Fellowship members should be scared of Ringwraiths and Orcs when they are so adept at slaughtering their numerous, pullulating masses, ala Rambo and his respective commies. If they can kick their evil butts so easily why sweat it? But that's just one item among many that makes this seem much like numerous other `quest' adventure films, where the protagonists battle one baneful threat after another.

Another note: I am not a big fan of special effects, but in this case the wonders of modern computer technology lend themselves well in creating a stunning visual landscape.

title: Great & fantastic
review:
*MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS* *MAY CONTAIN SOPILERS*

The arguments against and for adaptation of book are always the same. It starts with the question what kind of adaptation is the best for the book? A loosely based on a the book or a faithful one. There are enough examples of success and failure for both approaches and the arguments about it would always be here. "Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" will be used as a good example for those who are in favor of a middle ground between both approaches. It is not a 100% faithful adaptation but it is not a loosely based one. The film is a very good example that even a popular book, as this one, can be translated to the big screen without loosing any of its strength in the way and not forgetting that this a film a not a book.

Peter Jackson(director and co-screen writer) has managed to keep me interested all through the film 3 hours run. He knew that there is no way he could put the whole book(and each part of the 3 books is a huge one)into the screen so he decided to be faithful to the main core of the story. He got rid of characters and plot lines that seems to him unnecessary and told the story with passion that gave the film an extra bonus. The result is a great film which looks fantastic(and you could see how good it look when the trailer came out). I admit to have a vague memory of the book. I have read it long time ago, but during the film I found my self remembering the book more and more. The film actually refreshed my memory. By the end of the book I knew that I have to and want to read the book one more. For me that alone is a sign for a good film. A one that make me curious about the original material.

Jackson could not have done it without a cast that can bring the characters to life. In most case he had success in his choice of actors. Elijah Wood(Frodo Baggins) and Ian McKellen(Gandalf the Gray) are leading the excellent cast(I do have some reservation for Liv Tyler's presence, but her part is so short and at this point unnoticeable). The combination of known an unknown,English and Americans actors work well. New Zeeland looks terrific and serve as a very useful background. The decision to film there gave us a fresh and unknown landscape, one that looks like Middle Earth that we imagined. Howard Shore's score is nothing short of brilliant. At time quite and at time operatic(always when needed) and give the film the right atmosphere.

I liked the film, very much. I was very sad when it ended because I knew I have to wait another year for part 2. The film is the best of 2001. And it deserve any recognition it get. Even people who have not read the book will enjoy it. It has everything a good film have: good script, excellent score and vision, very good acting and it have passion. All the above should convince you by now. Go and watch it.

title: It needed to be 5 minutes longer.
review:
NOTE: This review is aimed at those who have read the book and contains comments on the movie in relationship to the book. For those who have NOT read the book, there will be spoilers.

The Fellowship of the Ring is a wonderful movie that needed to be 5 minutes longer to be perfect. But, before I get to what is wrong, let's deal with what was right.

This is the story of the Ring of Power, the One Ring forged 2500 years ago to be the master ring for 19 other rings given to the other races of Middle Earth (9 to Men, 7 to Dwarves, and 3 to Elves). The Ring was forged by the evil power Sauron (an ancient evil not explained in the original trilogy but fleshed out in the Silmarillion). This first book contains the discovery of the Ring after its loss 500 years before, its identification, the councils on what should be done with it, and the first part if its journey to ultimate destruction.

I first read these books, all of them (Trilogy, Hobbit, Silmarillion, Tolkien Reader, etc.) 25 years ago and have, periodically read them several times since. Needless to say, I was ready to be disappointed in this movie and I am happy to say I wasn't. It was almost perfect (I gave it a 9).

That isn't to say that things were perfect. The Shire, Rivendell, and other scenes and characters were not as I had pictured them in my mind. That beind said, they still felt right. The photography was right, the casting was well done even if I though the Hobbits were a bit skinny. Even the additions to the move, the things not in the book, were right. The major rewrite was the harrowing ride to the ford at Rivendell. But even this, although completely different from the book, felt right and Tolkien would not have been disappointed with the change.

Also, the way in which the One Ring was quite sentient added to the story and it was very nice to see the way they gave a history of the ring, covering parts of the Silmarillion and the Hobbit in 15 minutes.

The sound and visuals are incredible and the fight scenes suitably horrific without being gory. I think New Zealand needs to give the makers of this film some royalties because I very much want to go and do some hiking in that country now.

What was done well? The Balrog (although they slipped a bit in the Mines and referred to Goblins once before switching to Orcs) was great. The battle with the Nazgul was perfect. The flood at the ford even had the white horses. In fact, far more was done right than wrong and made up for the ommissions.

What was left out? Well, Tom Bombadil does not appear (poor Tom has yet to survive outside the book), the Barrow Wights have disappeared, and the scene in the Prancing Pony where the Hobbits meet Strider is cut short so you don't get the full mystery behind him. These cuts were all appropriate and maybe some will arrive in a longer version of the movie on DVD.

So, why 5 minutes longer? There was two very major ommissions to the movie that will have a profound effect on the following movies. Galadriel never shows Frodo HER ring so Frodo's offer of the One Ring doesn't have as much impact nor does her refusal. Also, other than the crystal vial, Galadriel never gives the other gifts. The party is seen wearing the cloaks but the presentation never occurred. Nor is the waybread, Sam's dirt and seed with which he replants the Shire, nor any of the other gifts. All of these have a profound effect on following books and detracted from the impact that Galadriel had on the quest.

But even a blunder as large as this couldn't do more than add a chink in this movie. I liked it alot. Not perfect, but very, very good. I hope that they go back and do the Hobbit in the same style after the last of the Trilogy is released.

title: Better than expected
review:
I've read and re-read the book several times, and love it more with each reading, so was apprehensive about what might have been done to it, but on the whole I thought Peter Jackson had done a really good job in adapting it as a film. Some of the performances were excellent - Sean Bean, Ian McKellen, Hugo Weaving and Elijah Wood were all superb; I also liked Sean Astin's Sam (whom Tolkien saw as the real hero of the story) - but the film really diminished the roles of Merry and Pippin, cast as the village idiots. I also thought Viggo Mortensen had too little gravitas as Aragorn - I hope he improves in the next installment (Hugo Weaving would have been a more interesting actor in the part).

All in all, the film is worthy of its origins, and I hope it inspires more people to read the book itself, which is so much greater. I would also recommend that anyone who liked the film search out the BBC radio dramatisation of "The Lord of the Rings", which is available on cassette tape and is being reissued on CD - it is faithful to the book and has wonderful actors (including Ian Holm as Frodo), and uses a lot of the book's poetry (something sadly missing from the film) set to superb music by Stephen Oliver.

title: They're Alive! Thank you.
review:
I first read LOTR in 1967 and, like so many others, was afraid to see the movie lest it disappoint. The casting of Ian McKellan convinced me that the film was not being made by idiots. Indeed, it was not.

Peter Jackson has made an epic a bit long on battles and short on meals but one must admit that meals, however dear they are to Hobbits, do not make interesting visuals.

This was a very fine film, extraordinarily well cast, beautifully shot and perfectly acted.

Frodo lives!

Thank you, everyone.

title: Inspired Movie Making
review:
I had often wondered why I had never read The Lord of the Rings books. I was always amazed at the enthusiasm, dedication and loyalty of the countless people I know who absolutely adore these tales. I said to myself 'what's all the fuss about? They are only silly childern's books!!

Well I could not have been more wrong!! The LOTR is a tremendous story, which totally captivated me for three very short hours! It paints a huge canvas of a totally alien world filled with Hobbits, Elves and giants! An alien world but at the same time a world which has many similarities to our own. There is Good V Evil, Friend V Foe, Love V Hate. And at the centre of all is the most unlikely of hero's, a four foot tall Hobbit!

J.R.R. Tolkien was inspired to write a beautiful tale of friendship and loyalty in a harsh world of betrayal, death and damnation! With the odds firmly stacked against them, this fellowship of unlikely companions (four Hobbits, two warrior humans. a dwarf, an elf, and an old Wizard called Gandalf) battle the Evil Saruman and his forces of darkness.

It is a tribute to this fabulous story that I have not yet mentioned the special effects, which are truly outstanding! Director Peter Jackson has made a wonderful film co-ordinating what was a massive project! Three films made back to back!!!

The cast we are all excellent, especially Elijah Wood as Frodo Baggins (Our Hobbit hero). I particularily liked Sean Bean as Boromir and Ian McKellen as Gandalf the Grey!

There is not much left to say only **DO NOT MISS THIS FILM** It is the movie experience of the new millennium!! Roll on next Christmas and The Two towers!!

One Ring to conquer them all, has been rewritten to one film to conquer them all!!

title: Lots of disappointments
review:
OK. I am a huge fan of the books. That's the main reason I have to say to anyone else who loves the books as much as I that they changed WAY TOO MUCH!. I don't want to give spoilers, but critical character development points in the story are altered, and change the feel drastically.

That being said, the movie is brilliant, with fantastic cinematography. Hey, just cause it's not as good as the books doesn't mean it's not worth seeing. It's still a good ride in spite of their changes.

title: This is how an adventure should be told
review: Wonderful, what a great movie ! I enjoyed watching this magnificent movie. What a great special effects and what a story. I can't wait for part II & III

title: Grim, epic, and powerful
review:
As my friends and I were waiting in line, we argued about whether

this movie or The Phantom Menace had been more anticipated,

finally noting that no one had camped out for The Lord of the

Rings. Someone commented, however, that since the Stars Wars

movie had been such a big disappointment, the fulfillment to

anticipation ratio would probably be much higher with LotR.

And they were so right.

I think this may well be the best fantasy movie I've ever seen. The

special effects are excellent -- very little of the distractingly obvious

CG that detracted from The Phantom Menace -- and the sense of

immersion in the world is very strong. What I was not prepared for

was how frightening the film was. I mean, okay, ultimate evil and

all that. But it frightened me more than any horror movie I

remember seeing. The grim despair of Middle Earth in time of war

was absolutely overwhelming, and I understood why the artist who

did the LotR poster on my wall used only browns, greys, and wan

pastels. In addition, the acting was excellent -- Ian McKellan's

Gandalf being especially memorable. Cate Blanchett's Galadriel

was also surprisingly disturbing -- the sense of power she

radiates is a considerable accomplishment both in terms of acting

and in the appropriate use of special effects.

If this film has any flaw, I think it might be insufficient emotional

variation. It is almost unremittingly dark, suspenseful, and scary,

and neither the characters nor the audience get to rest and recover

often. I know there were a few cheerful stops on the journey that

didn't make it into the film, and I have to wonder if that wasn't a

mistake. The stop in Galadriel's forest, which I remember being a

relief in the book, was too creepy to provide the kind of comfort I

was craving at that point. Only the Shire and Rivendell provided

bright spots in the narrative.

While I think retaining the grimness of the books is important, I

also think exhausting the audience is a bad idea. Although Merry

and Pippin provided a little bit of comic relief, a few more scenes in

which the audience can relax might be a good idea, if only to keep

them from becoming desensitized.

title: Great, Can't Wait For The Next Installment
review: Just like The Phantom Menace, TLOTR generated high expectations. The Phantom Menace disappointed me somewhat. Perhaps it was too kid-oriented and simple. However TLOTR satisfied me more. The atmosphere was great and the characters appealing (Ian McKellen is great as Gandalf). It was maybe too long  and at times dragging (especially the first bit) but I know that the story is complicated for a 1 1/2-hour movie. However, well done to Peter Jackson and co. I hope The Two Towers is even better. I expect so.

title: Over-hyped
review: Good movie but completely over-hyped.  This should not be anywhere near number 1.  Far more violent and far less spiritual than the actual book. It was beautifully shot and of course it's a great story, just over-hyped.

title: LOTR is an adult film worth watching
review: Read the book bought the tee shirt now see the film! Here is a film that tells the story of the little hobbits Frodo and his friends. For three hours, you are taken on a journey and at the end you are left wanting more. I sat beside someone who as the lights came up looked shell-shocked. Overcoming my own visualization of the characters and settings, (BBC Radio adaptation and reading the book) after a few moments they all appeared totally natural. The acting is never overshadowed by the plentiful special effects. At times LOR is reminiscent of a Ray Harryhausen film. I did feel however that some of the settings a little over the top, this being the ever dominating modeling software, as well is the constant swooping through the virtual settings. Will I be sitting in the cinema next year for another three hours? The answer is a definite yes.

title: nice, and the mistakes are mostly Tolkien's own
review:
*spoilers, maybe. but everyone's seen it by now anyway.*

I love & respect those books. I also think that general-plot- & motivation-wise the first film actually makes a whole lot more sense than the book does, without drifting into amusing, but frankly, pointless side-stories.

so, I liked the film. but I'm pointing out the aspects of it I didn't like.

a fair part of the things that bothered me were Tolkien's, not Jackson's idea. the question of women, that remains despite the amends. the irritating "noble master-humble/loyal servant" relationship between Frodo and Sam, whereas everyone else in the gang appears equal. (well, I know that if they'd been just friends, it would probably have appeared more than slightly homosexual, but still.) and last, but by far not the least, the *One* plot flaw OF ANYONE WISE NOT EVEN CONSIDERING USING THE NICE AND NOBLE AND HELPFUL AND FAST, ETC. EAGLES TO CARRY A HOBBIT WITH A RING TO THAT MOUNTAIN IN A DAY OR TWO and back safely. (mind you, while making plans at Rivendell, the Council didn't yet know about the nazguls being able to fly, even if they already were by then, which I'm not sure of). Could have saved all the corpses-to-be and spared everyone else of the general trouble and mess.

anyway. we wouldn't have two more films coming then, would we.

I too found the presented PACE of events a bit TOO FAST... glad to hear the rumours about the dvd cut with an extra half hour. because out of the Fellowship, only Boromir gets the chance and screentime to develop a full character, 'cos he won't be seen again. the two funny-sidekick hobbits, on the other hand, don't justify dragging them along at all, at least not in this film.

everything LOOKS QUITE AS I IMAGINED, apart from the "golden" elf forest, which appears way too blue and heavy and gloomy on the screen. but as they only trot straight through it anyway, nevermind. but also, some of the elves, namely Celeborn and the talking border guard of the forest, just don't have that "tight skin over an amazing delicate bone structure" -look. my apologies to the respective actors, but I consider them miscast. (but Legolas is gooood...)

the only seriously DISAPPOINTING part for me was the SOUNDTRACK. it simply didn't create the extra depth and dimension to back the visuals, as for instance the amazing Gladiator or Crouching Tiger soundtracks did. instead of brilliance, it was something "usual", and occasionally worse, since hearing those sickeningly overpopular fake-celtic new-ageish sounds created by Enya seriously disturbed my personal suspension of disbelief. GET A NEW COMPOSER, PLEASE!

but I'm seeing it again, nevertheless. and buying the dvd as soon as it comes out. and the Special Edition dvd-box, that will undoubtedly follow in a few years. and re-reading the book.

title: Need we heap more praise upon this masterpiece?
review: Well, everyone else has called this movie the second coming, so I'll just toss my hat onto the pile.  I really see this film as being the best combination of actors, effects, and direction that it could have been. There is no slice of the Multi-verse with a better version, my friends!  My only criticism is the music, because it was just so transparent, I would have liked more of a distinctive tune as opposed to Howard Shore's fitting but "safe" score.  Oh well, John Williams can't do them all!  Anyways, who care about that, I'm nit-picking.  Ian McKellen is absolutely perfect, as is Christopher Lee.  Lee especially is just so wonderful to see here, as he is a true Tolkien fan who says he re-reads the trilogy every year.  You just get the feeling here that you're watching the work of true nit-picking fans like yourself, who agonize with every element they must cut.  The mines of Moria alone are worth the price of admission, the Cave Troll is the most impressive and transparent integration of CG to date, bar none.  Legolas is an incomparable badass, as is Aragorn, just as they both should be.  There's just so much heart in this film it's unbelievable, it washes any bad Hollywood taste from the last couple years right out of my mouth.  Thank you Peter Jackson, the cast, WeTA et al.  You've made my year!

title: Visually stunning
review: ***SPOILER ALERT IN THESE COMMENTS*** OK, let me first say that it was an amazing movie. The acting was remarkable, the effects incredible, the scenery lovely (NZ - one of my all-time favorite holiday destinations), and the story overwhelming. BUT there was simply no resolution to ANY of the central issues or conflicts. Talk about sucking you into coming back for the sequel!!! Now I haven't read the books (I did read the Hobbit) and I did know it was part of a series, but I expected there to be some type of conclusion at the end. I was simply left hanging! That for me was sufficient to see my score go from a 9 to an 8 out of 10. If the next episode does the same it will drop from an 8 to a 7!

title: Excellent Movie and Excellent Adaptation
review: I give this excellent movie a 10 out of 10. I need to mention something important.  Tolkein, who wrote The Lord of the Rings, was also a good calligrapher and talented artist.  He rendered many scenes of the Lord of the Rings and of Middle Earth and Marquette University, here in downtown Milwaukee, Wisconsin, has purchased many of them and they are on display here in Milwaukee.  This is important because Mr. Jackson, the director, and others, made alot of the sets look alot like how Tolkein wanted them to look like and drew them.  Examples include Rivendell, Bag's End (Bilbo's hobbit-hole mansion in a hill, a glimpse of Minas Tirith (the white city) and Isegard where Saruman stays. This authenticity extends to the characters as played by the actors (you can look them up) including Gandalf the Grey, Frodo, Bilbo, Sam, Pippin, and Merry, Saruman, Sauron, Aragorn, and others.  They were very well done likenesses and close to how many pictured them while reading the books. I have read the books several times over the past 15 years, most recently last year, and I can tell you that this movie is an excellent adaptation of the plot and events and details of the movie.  It follows it really well and only really cuts out one sequence of events of about three chapters between when the Hobbits cross the small ferry across the Brandywine River and when they arrive in the run down town of Bree.  In this missing part of the story (you should read the book as it is a classic and is much more exciting than the movie) they have an adventure in the Old Forest and a plain of mound tombs called the Barrow Downs.  This is not a crucial element for a movie but added to the suspense of the quest in the book.  Mr. Jackson and the others who made the movie stuck to the book really, really well and you can tell that they had a great love for The Lord of the Rings and tried to do NOTHING which would offend Tolkien.  Also, this movie has ground breaking special effects.  Battle and fight scenes are wonderful.  Tolkien thought the movie could never be made but that was before computer graphic technology.  Every creature is based on drawings and descriptions by Tolkien.  They really respected his intent alot and he would be very proud of it, I believe. The soundtrack was wonderful and heroic and perfect and I give it a 10 out of 10.  The cast was awesome and I give it a 10 out of 10.  The effects were awesome and were a 10 out of 10, they fit what you imagine when you are reading the books!  The adaptation is a 9.5 out of 10 and the plot, which is all Tolkien, is a 10 out of 10.  Please remember that Tolkien reinvented the genre of fantasy writing in the 20th century and millions have read his books.  The scenery, it was filmed in New Zealand, was a 10 out of 10. Overall, the movie was a 10 out of 10 from the Shire to Moria to Rivendell to Lothlorien to Gondor and beyond.  (I just wish they also had the Old Forest and Barrow Downs and Tom Bombadil in there but they probably had to keep the time, it is three hours long, in check.  I HOPE those scenes were shot and there is a Director's cut with them in there on DVD when that comes out some day!!!!).  Excellent, 10 out of 10 movie!!!!

title: Amazing...
review: This is one of the best movies I have ever seen!  There is nothing that I would approve upon...  It's a brilliant realization of one of the all time classics of the fantasy genre- J.R.R. Tolkien's world lives and breathes in this movie...  I feel like a little kid again...I've seen this movie 7 times so far and will see it again this weekend!  I recommend it highly to ANYONE!!!  (Notice to all heterosexual women and gay men...Elijah Wood has the bluest eyes in the ENTIRE WORLD and is sexy as ALL GET OUT as Frodo Baggins!!!  Go see LOTR's NOW!!!)

title: Strong on scenery, mood and effects, weak on hobbits.
review:
I've read about as many viewer comments on this film as possible, and for the sake of me cannot declare it as "the" greatest movie ever, but perhaps I might have had I been born after 1995. It is, rather, a very good movie. The acting is excellent, the cinematography superb, the sets and effects which set moods are very effective. Disappointing is the fact that the hobbits in this movie are not the true center of the story, as they should be and as they certainly were in the books. Unfortunately, the hobbits in this movie are portrayed mostly as hapless and almost unbearably vulnerable little pawns in the grand scheme of others. The wizards, humans, and elves in this movie come across as the strong and important elements, which is quite unfair to the spirit of Tolkein's hobbits. And, something must be said of the special effects make-up for some of the creatures -- we've seen similar such make-up as far back as "The Lost Boys", and even for the past few years on T.V.'s "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" (please do not confuse my comparison of make-up with any type of praise for the T.V. show!) -- I mean, check out the giant Orc foreheads, noses, and eyes!

So, definitely a movie that should be seen and enjoyed, but I didn't see "greatness" in the film itself.

title: Strong on background & scenery, weak on hobbits
review: The cinematography of this film is magnificent, and the full-size characters quite engaging (wizards, elves and humans).  But we never quite see this story from the viewpoint, and action-point, of the  hobbits, who should be most central to the experience.  Rather, the hobbits are played mostly as happless pawns in some grand scheme, when in fact the original novel has the hobbits as the doers and actors that affect the world around them.  Lastly, a comment is needed on the make-up effects in this movie -- sadly, a few of the creatures' faces in this movie are not as original as they should have or could have been; the first place we saw such similar faces was way back in "The Lost Boys", and ever-so-recently about every week for the past few years in T.V.'s "Buffy The Vampire Slayer" (check out the vampire foreheads, noses and eyes!!!!).

title: The magic and spirit makes up for the flaws
review:
As a long -time Tolkien geek I spent the first time I watched the film in shock. Both in 'Wow, that looks *awsome*' and in 'hey, what the hell happened to..' ways.

The second time I went to see it I could enjoy the film for what it was without comparing it to the book all the time - and I had a most enjoyable time.

No, it did not get everything exactly right. I missed certain things from the book (though not, I have to say, Tom Bombadil). I missed certain plots from the book. I thought the hobbits were given rather less credit than they deserved (Frodo spending half of the film dead/ill/having to be carried/etc). I wasn't happy about the portraying of Galadriel (I'd have liked to see more of the good-Galadriel).

I felt that a lot of scenes had been cut (no doubt at great pain for the makers) that were needed to form a good image of the situation.

Yet still, it got a lot right. Most of the characters were spot on (to me at least), there was some _great_ acting, and most of all, it managed to capture the magic of Tolkien's writing. Not everything could be included, but there was a story below the surface. Little details put in just for the sheer hell of it - even though maybe 5% of the viewers would notice/recognize.

That showed to me that there was someone on the team who not only knew about this pretty obscure bit of Tolkien-lore, but also felt it was somehow important enough to include. And that is the strength of this project - there's heart in it.

title: It's not that good
review:
After learning that Lord of the Rings manage to beat my favorite movie - "The Godfather" on IMDB ratings, I couldn't wait to watch this film.

But today, after around 1.5 hours of the movie (knowing that there's a lot more to come..), I got a feeling that this is the most over-rated movie of all time. The movie shows great scenery and good performance from Ian McKellen but the script is just so boring and repetitive.

Step 1: Group of monsters are approaching. Step 2: Fight...Frodo almost got killed. Step 3: He's saved. Step 4: One of his companions got killed fighting the monster. Step 5: "we have to move on"

Repeat Step 1 to 5 a few times, possibly in the upcoming sequels as well. (which I am NOT going to watch)

6 out of 10 is a generous score.

title: A fantastic movie
review:
I am a bit of a movie snob, and not usually one to give raving reviews. But this is one of those rare times.

I was simply awestruck, as in - mouth open in amazement - not once, but multiple times. The trailers just do not do this movie justice.

And I plan to do something I've never done in my life - I'm going to see this movie in the theater again...at least one time, maybe more.

In my opinion, we have a new film by which all others (at least in the fantasy/sci-fi genre) will be judged.

Was it perfect? No...not perfect. But awfully close.

Thank you, Peter Jackson and crew - you have given us a wonderful gift. I can't wait for parts II and III.

title: expected more
review: Camera work and special effects great as was the New Zealand scenery, you must come. but I found the story simplistic (as the book when I once tried it) It was hard to remember a characters motivation even withall the male bonding and the sound a bit mushy didn't help. Not one for the kids. Not a #1 memory, try the ship approaching space station to the sound of the 'Blue Danube' for that.

title: One (movie) to rule them all
review:
When I read somewhere (I think it was Wizard magazine) that a live action movie based on the 'Lord of the Rings' was being planed, the first thing to come to my mind was 'How ever are they going to manage that.? Either this is going to be a huge flop.or the greatest epic ever made.' Well, after seeing the first movie I have to say it came close to the second option.

When I was inside the theatre and during the entire movie, all I wanted to do was cry. Not because of the movie, but because of the shear idea that it was actually done.and might I add, beautifully so. The visuals are amazing, of course, nobody could expect any less, but the story and the whole ambience of the books was very well portrayed as well. The casting was perfect because rather than finding big names to fill the screens, they found 'big' actors.No one could ignore the magnitude of Sir Ian McKellan's Gandalf and the gorgeous innocence of Elijah Wood's Frodo.

I was especially amazed at the way we could see what was it 'inside the ring': it was more that just becoming invisible, it was exactly that other world that the ring invented for itself and the emergence of the bearer's inner self, the confrontation of what you are most afraid to release in fear of corrupting your own morals for the gift of power. It is rarely seen: a motion picture that combines action and depth in such a complete way, you easily find yourself caring for these people (the Brotherhood), and even though I can't personally abide to this, I vehemently believe this occurs even amongst those who haven't read the books. For the rest of us (except for the more purists whom I'm sure will have loads of criticising to do) it's a dream come true.

One could not, EVER, expect this story to be collected in one movie; it would never be possible. Undoubtedly it leaves a bitter taste of 'unfinished business' in you, personally, the wait for next Christmas is the longest I have ever experienced. But it does make sense that this was the chosen way to complete this first movie, because it has to be accessible to every one, not just the legion of Tolkien fans. The death of Boromir is the closing key to the story (even if it only happens in the second book); it gives you the notion that the ending makes sense, but Frodo's and Sam's escape definitely makes you salivate for more. And I am. I doubt this movie will get any of the 'big' Oscars, simply because the Academy doesn't value this kind of thing.but maybe (hopefully) I'm wrong and it will be given it's worth. This one is definitely in my top 5 forever. Maybe it's even the One.

title: A True Motion Picture Epic
review: This movie not only deserves to be one of the highest grossing movies of all time, it also deserves to win the Oscar for Best Picture.  This is easily one of the greatest motion pictures of all time.  The movie was one of the greatest all around motion pictures with great performances, amazing special effects, and some of the most breathtaking cinematography ever seen. Thanks to Peter Jackson's creative direction, the Lord of the Rings trilogy is easily the next Star Wars trilogy.  His vision of hobbits, humans, elves, dwarves, wizards, orcs, and many other creatures are the epitome of what motion picture epics should be like.

title: Oh come on
review:
What the hell? 9.8 with 20000 votes than dropped suddenly to 9.2

I never read the book and could barely enjoy the movie, i mean, yeah, it got the visuals and audio and all that. I am a big fan of matrix, and so this movie does not strike me as one of the BEST visuals.

Now to the plot, that's where I think is is kinda weak. I mean, oh yeah you got a bunch of ppl who doesn't like each other on a quest. United by the little boy, they go fight evil. Isn't the "good v evil" thing so DONE with already. I mean come on, the movie was so long and you just give me that good v evil quest with all those little sub-plot so done with also. Like your boy being poked at with the beast by its stick, and saved by the jacket. I personally have seen that too many times. Before that, some morons as the main boy's friends followed him with the quest and dropped something down the well and woke up the monsters, I mean, the whole thing hasn't really got some plot to me.

Don't get me wrong, I like the matrix and eager for more. But at the end of the movie session I heard ppl yarning its a pretty good suggestion that the long 3 hrs plot with good v evil and no other engaging sub-plots is obviously requiring people who are really really into the story. For ppl who don't care to read the book, which I think is quite a lot, the open-ended conclusion is even more to the blow. 3 hr of ongoing good v evil with normal fightings like all those we have seen before, swords, arrows blah blah blah. They should show some cool magic scene just for the sake that this is kinda like a sci fic genre.

title: Fellowship follows Tolkien's genre
review: I have been waiting for years for a film based on the Tolkien books that actually captures the feel and subtleties that Tolkien produced. This film is close and far surpasses all others who have tried, yet I left feeling little sympathy for any of the characters and attribute it to too much reliance on special affects and hard-hitting action (which it excels at) and not enough on the character development aspects.

title: beautiful jet flight through the works of JRR Tolkien
review:
Peter Jackson finally accomplished what no director ever thaught to be feasible. Beautiful, rich, glorious, amazing, overwhelming ... screenplay and great actor achievements!!

Just one flaw in this success story, though ... those who read the trilogy will certainly agree when stating that Jackson at some times seems to rush through the more depicting, but still vital, parts of the book.

I guess that's the price we all have to pay in order to step into the dazzling world of JRR's imagination.

By the way ... you better write Jacksons name down for the Academy Awards this year!

title: An Exquisite Epic
review: Having read the book, this is everything I had ever hoped for in the film version. Great acting, epic sets, fantastic effects and an enthralling plot - what more could anyone want? Well... I want parts two and three already! This must be the film of 2001 without a doubt. Ten out of ten - top marks - second to none...

title: Boring
review: It's not a bad movie, but it doesn't live up to all the commotion. "Lord of the rings" has great effects, the cast does a great job (mostly) and all those dollars were well spent. The problem is that the movie takes itself way too seriously! It's too dense and too long. I was about to fall asleep when the 235th seven-headed monster came out of the dark spitting flames to (once again) try to kill everyone. You know, they should have given Godzilla a little part! Boring, boring, boring...

title: Perfection!!!!
review:
LotR: FotR was not only better than I thought it would be, but it far surpassed what I thought it COULD be. If Peter Jackson doesn't win the Oscar for "best director," I'll lose faith in the Academy. The movie was brilliant and inspired, and managed to capture the grandeur and vision of Tolkien's work. And I'm sure that I wasn't the only one in the audience who cried at the "death" of Gandalf and the passing of Boromir.

Now, the most trying part of the trilogy will be waiting another 12 months to see "Two Towers!" I say bring it on now!! :o)

title: fantastical
review: I didn't know this film had such an abrupt and cliffhanger ending. I saw that the characters were getting slower and more emotional but I was ready for at least afew more hours more of chase. And what a masterful chase it was. Although feeling like a tired formula where as soon, like clockwork, one enemy or difficulty is overcome, another ensues. This, we have seen in Star Wars and many a follow- on. Don't forget Tolkien is the master of this and it is quite clear that the film should have been made along time ago, I heard that the only reason it was not was for the reason of a dispute between Tolkien and the film rights. But luckily it was not, because now us audiences have a feast of state of the art digital manipulation, and what a sight we have. Didn't make me laugh or cry though, or feel angry or moved by some political or moral obligation. It's for the moviewatching extravaganza that we will all buy it on DVD or buy a DVD to watch it on.

title: One movie or 3?
review:
This movie was awesome in the true sense of the word. Every aspect of it was tremendous - casting, acting, location, cinematography, music. From what I've read, heard and seen on this very website, the people who did not like this movie 1) went into the movie expecting to hate it (probably because it is "fantasy") and therefore spent the whole time looking for things to criticize, 2) cannot sit through a three hour movie, or 3) cannot open their mind enough to appreciate a "fantasy" movie, even though I don't consider this "fantasy." I consider this closer to historical fiction. I think most people who have read and understood LOTR feel the same way.

I have also read reviews by popular critics like Roger Ebert, who gave the movie a lower rating because it failed to show him things that he mistakenly took from the book - where did he get the idea that in FOTR Frodo was a leader of any sort? He claims the movie made Frodo out to be a follower, carried along by bigger, stronger people, and he felt this changed a basic theme in the book and therefore lessened the movie in his eyes. Otherwise he loved the movie. Go back and read the book again, Roger, because the movie was not off base. Frodo did nothing on his own (and in fact repeatedly got himself into trouble and endangered the mission without Aragorn or Gandalf around) until The Breaking of the Fellowship.

Is it the greatest movie of all time? Fellowship cannot be the greatest movie of all time. Nor can The Two Towers, nor can The Return of the King. But what about "The Lord of the Rings," as a movie, taken as a whole? The Lord of the Rings is one book, not three. Just like the movies, the book was split up solely for marketing's sake. Fellowship is not such a great book. But the Lord of the Rings is considered by many to be one of the greatest books of all time.

When The Two Towers and The Return of the King are released, all three should be considered as one movie when debating whether it may be the greatest of all time. So far the first movie lived up to my expectations. The next two books take the story farther than people who have not read them could have imagined. When the final credits roll on Return of the King, I predict that the trilogy, as a whole, will have been one of the greatest things to be portrayed in cinema to date and will not be topped for decades to come.

So I suggest viewers wait until all three movies are released to pass final judgement on any of the movies.

title: There aren't many films that move me - and this is one of them.
review:
Leaving the theater I was so - shell-shocked, so spellbound that remarks about the portraying of characters or the resolution of key scenes of the book would seem a bit petty and childish.

I'm willing to give it a shot however, so here goes (minor spoilers included).

Concerning omissions: what I thought was rightly left out were the sequences with Tom Bombadil and the Barrowdowns. They would have contributed nothing to the main storyline, and would have pushed the duration well beyond the three-hour boundary - which is simply too long. What WASN'T omitted however, and in my mind could have been, was the Lothlorien scene. I'll probably skip that one when I get my hands on the DVD, much like the Ewoks in Star Wars.

The score was - I immediately noticed this when I rushed out to buy the soundtrack afterwards - very good. the only minor annoyance for me was the main theme, which vaguely reminded me of the poorer-quality movies in the genre. Very good I thought was the mood of the score; the dark and unsettling undertone that is one of the themes in the movie. And I must say that the Moria sequence brought a tear to my eye.

The camerawork and CGI more than make up for whatever small failing. If I have to attach a percentage to it, I would say that at least 75% of the imagery portrayed corresponds with what I made up reading the book. And from speaking with others I know I am not alone in that assumption.

It has been said that the story misses an 'arch villain' with clever dialogue, like Agent Smith in The Matrix (SPOILER: although he does make an appearance as a grumpy Elrond) or Darth Vader and The Emperor in the original Star Wars films. This is true I think, even if you take into account that the Ring itself is the real villain in this story. Sadly, rings don't have James Earl Jones' voice. Evil is a lot less convincing if it doesn't speak.

You should go see it however, even if you have read the book many times (like myself). Jackson in my view really has captured the essence Tolkien wanted to convey with his masterpiece, and added a puff of magic for himself.

Oh and please book me a flight to New Zealand. Now.

Rating: 9.5/10 (I'll keep the 10 for the sequels.)

title: The best movie of the 21st. century
review:
The Lord Of The Rings: The Fellowship Of The Ring is, by far, the best movie of the current century. I know the 21st. century is wearing diapers, but it is kinda stupid to say that it is the best movie ever, 'cause the last century brought to the silver screen countless masterpieces, which can't be compared to a single movie that needs other two to complete the best fantasy story ever written.

I hope days passes quickly, 'cause I can't sleep right now...

title: You can't please everyone
review: Two thousand plus reviews and counting. I won't go on and on about what a great film this is, as so many have done that already. I won't gripe about those who found it terrible to watch, since they're entitled to their opinion, no matter how trite. I personally loved this film, but required a second viewing to fully realize it. The movie seems to be getting the same sort of love it/despise it response as the books themselves. As to those who don't feel it deserves to be number one on the all time list, you can't please everyone. No movie on that list is without its detractors who feel it has no place there. After the first thousand or so votes, I thought it was just the legions of Tolkien fans stuffing the ballot box. But at thirty thousand and climbing, it's more than just hard core fan enthusiasm at work. The mark of a great film is the level of contoversey and passion (both good and bad) that it generates. After only three weeks, this movie has generated so many votes and so many reviews that it bears the mark of a truly monumental work. Go decide for yourself, but definitely GO!

title: 3 hours in a Fantasy World
review: Well, I haven't read the book and watched the animation movie - which I didn't like - when I was a kid, but I like Peter Jackson's work and also a good adventure flick. I have to say that the first 30 minutes of the movie disappointed me and I was starting to agree with my wife, who did not see the movie because she got bored reading the book and left it. She probably stopped reading it before Frodo starts his quest, because that's where the adventure begins. After 30 long minutes I almost could not feel the other 2 1/2 hours pass in front of my eyes. It was a pity the movie ended in "only" 3 hours. I wanted more ! At that time I was so captured by the movie that it could goes forever. Everybody in the theater claimed for more but we will have to wait one year to see this great adventure continues.

title: Closer to my own view of the book than I thought possible.
review:
While we all see and percieve things differently while reading texts, I must say that Jackson and myself were on the same wavelength when we read FOTR. Much of that must be attributed to Tolkien's lengthy descriptions and interpretations of person and place. Whatever be the case, for me personally that was what surprised me the most.

I found the film to be great, even as one who got caught up in the hype. I was worried that my expectations were too high, as has happened with a lot of other films. But this did not happen this time. I was thrilled with what I saw, and look forward to seeing it again as well as buying the DVD when released. We still have 2 more to go, and I think that the filming of all 3 films at once was a great idea that some have criticized. Jackson was in the same frame of mind when filming all 3 segments, whereas he more than likely wouldn't have been if he had filmed them with a significant time frame between.

To rebuke other criticisms that this movie followed along with the book too closely, and while doing so spoiled some of the cinema magic - I say to them not to post any more comments. Tolkien is long followed by many LOTR freaks (myself now one), and that is what drew many people to the cinemas. Tolkien is also of the great fantasy writers, and to rewrite any part of his work would be a great insult to him, and to his followers.

If I have any criticism, it would be that some parts were changed, or left out altogether. Tom Bombadil? Why not? To me he was a big part in creating the mood for me as I read the book. A ray of hope in a dark world he was. And I speculate that Arwen's part, which was played by Liv Tyler, was extended more out of demands from the movie industry in some form or fashion because of her name. One comment that I agree on wholly is that the cast worked together so well because there were no "huge" stars in this film. The focus of this film was on the characters and not of the actors, which is how all movies should be.

All in all, a great movie in my mind, and one of the greatest I've seen. There is no such thing as a 10, but I'll give it a 9.8 or so. I can't wait to see the other two, and I hope with them that my expectations aren't too high because of the prescedence that is set by the first one.

title: That is how you make a movie
review:
There are certain moments in life that lets you know why it is you do certain things. The first time you meet and fall in love with a girl lets you know why you brave the bars or clubs every week, piling on rejection after rejection. The first time you get that big raise and huge promotion lets you know why you go to that run down, neon lighted hell called work everday, and the first time you hear a song like "Stairway to Heaven" lets you know why you turn on your radio every morning, surfing through such ear bleeders as Britney Spears or N'Sync. Well, for me, watching Fellowship for the first AND second time has let me know why, after a year filled with monkeys and morons driving cars, I still go to the movies. Because something extraordinary can happen.

Lord of the Rings: Fellowship of the Rings follows Frodo Baggins, and his other 8 counterparts, on a quest to destroy the one ring, a magical and evil ring, that could bring darkness to Middle Earth. Leading this quest, with his wit and wisdom, is Gandalf the Wizard, played by Ian McKellan, who leads this band of hobbits and elves and dwarves and men to the Mountain of Doom, to destroy the ring once and for all in the fires from whence it came. Of course the path to this mountain, and the evil which is bent on returning the ring to the Dark Lord who created it, make it a perilous trip in which death is a distinct possibility.

If I were paid, as I am not yet, to share with you this movie and my opinion of it, then I would tell you how much I enjoyed all of the performances of the film. Elijah Wood is fantastic and, for anyone who loved the books, fits the picture of Frodo perfectly. Sir Ian is amazing in bringing all of the aspects of Gandalf, argueably the most famous character of the books, to life, and the rest do equally wonderful jobs. But the magic of this movie, in my mind, is in the effect it has had on myself and many who have seen it.

It is a transportation, and escape of epic proportions. You believe from the moment the movie starts that you are indeed peering in on Middle Earth. That hobbits do in fact exist and are as cheerful and robust as the books say they are. You believe that evil can and does exist in pure form and that your heroes are being hunted by that evil. You believe everything you see and you lovce the fact that you are there. After 3 hours and 15 minutes you are ready for more, ready to watch your heroes finish their mission, ready to see good triumph over evil one more time, and you are ready to live in Middle Earth again, if only for another few hours.

I have seen movies more then once at a theatre. I have loved movies, cried at movies, laughed at movies, and seen certain movies to the point of memorization that both astounds and annoys friends when watching the feature with me. I do not know where this movie rates on my all time list, since the experience of it is far too new, but I can say this. I have already seen this movie twice and I would venture a guess that 2 will not be the final answer to my viewing equation. I am in love with Middle Earth all over again, having been so from the moment I first put down The Hobbit, Tolkiens first novel of the like, to the time I began reading the trilogy. It brings many of us who loved the books back to that place that, before now, I was convinced only books could bring us to. It brings us to a place we do not want to leave, a place so different then the one we all woke up in today, but still so similar as to not be completely foreign to us. It is magical.

I do not know if those of you who did not read the books will have as magical an experience watching this film but having been there with people who have not read the books I can say that enjoying it does not hinge on that fact. Some have made a point of being upset by the voting on this site but it is a simple reflection of the love most of us have for this story, for these characters, and for the world that Tolkien and now Peter Jackson have created. It is why we buy DVD's, it is why we still go to the movies, and it is why many who grow up watching films like this decide they, in fact, want to make them. It is why movies are made, and if it is not recognized by the Academy then, well, the Academy is lost for good.

review: this is truly one of the films that difines cinema- inspiring, breathtaking, exhilirating, enchanting. it pulls u into it's world and invites you almost to be a character. it's also kinda scary. not in a horror film sort of way, but you feel so immersed in the world your in (and you will feel like you are there) that when a monster chases you, you feel the fear of being caught, of the quest lying in ruin, of evil dominating the land. and this is after i read the book, and i know excatly what's coming. it's that kind of film. it's not a striaght translation of the book, some bits are missing, others changed, but all to the betterment of the film. and have no worries, the book will remain intact for you to read after, spoiling nothing. the characters are perfectly cast and perfectly acted. the battle scenes are gripping, and the entire enterprise is on a mammoth scale. you have seen nothing like the sheer scope or scale of this film, nothing in cinema history has prepared you for peter jackson's clarity of vision and the exacution really should grab Oscars intrest. oh yes, this is the film of the year, and no doubt. nothing in the last twelve months can match it. it truely is cinmea at it's finest

title: Why the 'stair' scene?
review:
SPOILERS Very well done, but I found the "stair" scene in Moria (just before kazadh-dun bridge) extremely poor. Does the screenplay writer think viewers are THAT stupid? Also, this scene has no impact whatsoever, they could have used these 10 minutes to shoot a ride in the Maggot's wagon in the night or almost ANYTHING that has some atmosphere.

Anyway I did enjoy the movie, although it is sometimes being too majestical and a bit over-stuffed with effects.

7/10

title: Excellent, but not totally convincing
review:
I went to see this movie with someone who never read the book, whereas I must have read it about 25 times as well as every other book on the subject of Middle Earth/Tolkien. We both came out the movie a little bit out of breath. The last three quarters are so full of action that one hardly has the time to blink the eyes. For sure: there is a lot of cruel fighting in the books as well, but we both thought it was slightly overdone - especially the scene where the Uruk is trying to kill Boromir and Aragorn comes to the rescue. There was no need for this, nor is it in the book. The cast was very good, although I am not sure if Frodo and Elrond were played quite correctly. Frodo seems a bit too amazed all the time (and why does he remind me of Michael Jackson all the time), whereas Elrond clearly was cast wrongly. Why is Sam calling his Master 'Frodo' all the time? Is this a case of political correctness? I thought that was a grave mistake, one that Tolkien would never ever have allowed, had he been alive. On the other hand I thought the landscapes, the Shire, Rivendell, the Golden Wood, Orthanc, and Moria were just brilliantly done. My partner got lost quickly in all the names and side stories - but that is something that happens when you read the books as well. I, on the other hand thought some scenes - the handing of the Star-glass of Earendil to Frodo, Galadriel not being seen wearing the Elven Ring etc. were omitted needlessly as there was time enough to explain. Instead that precious time was used for the action scenes - and I am afraid it will be the same in the following parts, as there is still a lot violence to follow.

But I wouldn't miss them for the world.

title: Thumbs up
review:
Far, far better than I had dared to expect. It is one of those rare films where blockbuster action and a fine artistic vision blend seamlessly. You could not mistake this for the work of any other director than Peter Jackson - his visual style is all over the film. Excellent art direction (even if the Elven dwellings seem like cheap Charles Rennie Mackintosh knock-offs) and wonderful cinematography. Good acting (although I had a few problems with Sean Astin and Cate Blanchett) and the script is good. I've read the books and I was pleasantly surprised to see how the scriptwriters had managed to recover the _story_ underneath Tolkiens stylistic mannerisms.

In short: I liked it. A lot.
