review: I think that this film is so overestimated that it hurts. I saw it, without the greatest of expectations, and jet I felled that "This is definitely not the final version of the ring"!, my main critics of the film is, that it totally lacks soul and humor. without that one can have as many special effects and as many battle scenes as one desires, but it will still not be a great film. No charisma at all.

title: How fortunate we are that it all came together!
review:
It's impossible to compare this film with the pantheon of great movies after only seeing the first of three chapters of the story. It's like reviewing "The Thornbirds" or "The Jewel in the Crown" after watching only the first Sunday night installment. So I won't cast my vote until at least December 2003.

However the love of film making and appreciation for J.R.R. Tolkien's magnum opus already shines through Peter Jackson's "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring". I thank director, producers, cast and crew for elevating the art of motion pictures to new heights in the post-Lucas era.

Howard Shore's astounding score is a case in point. I once thought that the only music that could truly capture the heroic dimension of "The Lord of the Rings" was Richard Wagner's masterwork, "Der Ring des Nibelungen", the opera cycle concerning another great ring of power. Wagner's `musical dramas' combined the most inspired elements of music and poetry into visual spectacle created to deliver an unprecedented emotional impact to the audience. In a real sense Wagner was the minstrel who

"Sang to them...until their hearts, wounded with sweet words overflowed, and their joy was like swords, and they passed in thought out to regions where pain and delight flow together and tears are the very wine of blessedness." (LOTR, Book VI, Chapter 4)

But would Jackson overlay Wagner's music about German myths and legends onto Tolkien's Anglican-inspired mythology as John Boorman had done for Arthurian legend in "Excalibur"? Jackson eventually trusted LOTR's quality to inspire artists to achieve their greatest potential, and he wisely decided to have Shore compose a unique score for Tolkien's universe. Shore delivered on the promise and captured the essence of Middle-earth. How fortunate we are that the `inspired elements' all came together!

Minor spoilers:

Consider the scene where the fellowship, after departing Rivendell, crosses the mountain pass. The film speed slows down slightly as all nine members advance, one after the next, as Shore's triumphant Fellowship theme blasts forth. (Some audience members take a bathroom break at this point in the film and so miss one of the movie's most sublime scenes.) Here Jackson delights in the *realization* of the Fellowship of the Ring. Look, everyone! he seems to say, after all these years our old friends are up there on the silver screen for all to cheer onward!

Not long afterwards we are swept across the rim of the tower of Orthanc as Shore's music swells to a frenzy. There stands Saruman in a rage, screeching incantations in Black Speech into the sky. I am reminded of one of those old film clips of Hitler babbling and gesticulating his hatred to the crowds. Of Christopher Lee's appearances in more than 200 films I can think of no personification more frightening, more gothic, more magnificent than this.

Later, in the aftermath of Khazad-dûm, the companions spill out of Moria onto a gray and desolate plane that reflects their state of mind. Colors are washed out and time slows to a crawl. Faces are twisted in grief, confusion, shock. Sound is cut off except for a solitary voice singing a plaintive theme.

And for me, this is a point where pain and delight flow together.

title: Very close
review:
I read LOTR when I was 13, some 20 years ago now. I have read it many times since and as with all books got the image in my head what the world of Tolkien was like.

After seeing the film today I can honestly say I was nearly there, a few niggles aside.

I have waited 20 years to see this film and I am not disappointed.

LOTR is one of those books that will never be perfect on the big screen because of it's size and detail, and you will never please everyone, but all I can say is thanks PJ for doing such a superb job in try to realise Tolkiens masterpiece.

title: Peter Jackson did it - slightly flawed but still a masterpiece
review:
Firstly let me congratulate Peter Jackson on making a great adaptation of "Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Rings" and, in the process, making the greatest fantasy movie so far.

Let me tackle some of the negative comments people have commented first. "It's not completely faithful to the book" - Well of course it isn't. It's an adaptation, it's using the source material of the book to create the movie. Imagine if Jackson had left Tom Bombadil in it? We'd have had the return of Jar Jar Binks. People who complain too much about deviating from the source material (which I read and enjoyed) need to sit back and just enjoy what he has done with the movie: He could have done a lot much worse and very little better. "It's too long" - No it isn't. It needs the length of time to give the book a decent treatment. Elements such as the council of Elrond or other Elvish bits all add to the texture of Middle Earth that Jackson is building up. Despite the length of the picture there's little in the movie that I would have cut out as it all adds to the viewing experience. "Some of the dialogue is hammy" - For those who complain about some of the script recall that this is a fantasy epic and these lines have place here. It's part of the genre.

What's good about the movie? Script - Generally well paced. The points where the pacing slows are due to the neccessity of being faithful to the original and manage to add to the rich background (whatever you may think of the moments of the elves they sure look gorgeous).

Acting - Well done! I had mixed reservations hearing Elijah Wood would be cast as Frodo but they proved groundless. Everyone was pretty much perfect for their part and I too must single out Ian McKellen for exceptional praise. Perfect casting.

Directing - What can I say? Jackson I love you. You did something which we feared nobody could do. He starts with an incredible intro as he recounts the history of the One Ring - a great way to get the blood pumping because he knows it will be awhile after that before we see some large action. But when we do see action we see it on an epic large scale. LOTR:TFOTR needs a cinema screen to be screen - watching as the camera pans around huge landscapes. I remember watching one scene, thinking how I would really love if Jackson made the camera plunge off the side of the tower and into the grounds below... and then he did it. He was making the movie exactly how I wanted it. That's great stuff.

Does the movie have flaws? Sure it has but a lot of those rest with the conventions of adapting from a book. It's hard to get characterisation in for example so we find out, and care not much, about Pippin and Merry for example. There's certain pieces which work well in a book - such as the Council of Elrond - which can slow the movie down sometimes. There's the obvious fact that the movie leaves us hanging but since this is but a third of the total picture I can forgive that.

In the end "Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" succeeds. It's not the greatest movie of all time in my opinion - but it is damn good. It's one of the best of 2001 (competing only with "Amélie" and "Moulin Rouge!") and far and away the best fantasy movie ever. It's got the epicness of Lean's "Lawrence of Arabia" and the intense action of Spielberg's "Saving Private Ryan". Whatever you do make sure you see this in the cinema. More than once. And then buy the DVD. This is why we have movies. 9.5/10

title: Awesome, definitely worth your time!
review:
Those of you out there who didn't like the movie, I don't know why, too picky I suppose, are a little messed up. You're entitled to your own opinion, but mine is that the movie was awesome. I can't wait until the next one comes out! I don't want to wait a whole year. I thought it was really well done and the acting, despite the picky peoples opinion, was really good. I haven't read the books, so I don't have anything to compare it with. I've already seen it three times and can't wait to go again. I hope everyone out there can at least enjoys it as much as I did.

I give it a 11/10. Very good. Definitely worth three hours of spare time.

title: This Movie gives the book Justice
review: Wow this movie blew me away. I am a Lord of the Rings..Geek and I am proud of it. I really enjoyed this movie. All the characters are just how I imagined them to be. Elijah made an awesome Frodo, I was afraid that the movie wouldn't bring out the true friendship of Frodo and Sam, they are my most favorite characters in the book, This movie hit the mark I was hoping to see. I have gone 4 times now to see this movie and I have not had enough yet! I give this movie a 10+ It is my most favorite movie it did the book justice. It really took my breath away. I was raised on this book it was read to me by my Mom and I read it 3 times a year. All the Actors did wonderous in The Lord of the Rings. The only part that was bad was that it ended. All you Tolkien Fans keep up being Geeks like me!!

title: Great movie, but it ain't the book.
review:
This was a great movie! I can't believe my eyes... But I am not totally convinced:

First, the good things: The scenery was just as I imagined it, the acting was good, the visual effects were amazing, and the music was breathtaking.

Now the ONE MAJOR bad part: It missed out too much. I know it's 3 hours already but I can't sit comfortably without Tom Bombadil, The Old Forest, Buckland, a good look at Lothlorien, and who on (Middle-)Earth is Lurtz. Leaving out things is one thing, but creating new things is not acceptable.

On the whole a better movie tan Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone but no a better book-movie (if you get my saying).

7/10

title: True to Tolkien's Vision
review: This movie for me is a representation of unconditional love.  Not the kind that goes along with loving something so much you love every thing related i.e. Star Wars 1, or the mediocre intelligence of the statement 'I loved the book so I must love the movie'.  The film version of Tolkien's mind shattering and earth changing novel is not to be loved for what it is in book form, but for what it accomplishes as a movie.  All book related comments aside, this movie is tremendous.  Rising action, blindingly powerful scenery and cinematography, lovable and somehow real characters. Wonderfully rendered and detailed cinema. Now back to the book.  If you, personally, had the oppurtunity to make a Lord of the Rings movie, you would probably say no.  No way.  Well, Jackson had the courage to attempt it, and using his knowledge of the books and a keen mission statement  'I will stay true to Tolkien's vision' he accomplished the unthinkable.  He made a great movie out of a great book, without sacrificing the beauty and majesty of either.  Argue all you want about the subtle changes, but the film industry is so very different then the ever fading species of the book worm that it would have been impossible to translated the book exactly, and still hold the wide spread audience. And in this case, the audience was as wide spread as I've ever seen.  This movies proves that there are still people out there who simply know 'what's up' in terms of artistic integrity and respect.  Bless them.

title: GREAT MOVIE EXPERIENCE
review: To tell the truth, I was not eager to see this movie and to sit in a theater for 3 hours.  Once the movie begins, however, you are transported to Middle Earth and feel as if you are part of the Fellowship.  The movie is amazing. I have gone back to see it 2 more times (this is very rare for me).  I have only read The Hobbit, but will soon begin the trilogy.  I highly recommend this movie.

title: pretty great really
review: Being a bit of a cinema geek, I can safely say that my heart has never beat so fast as when the Balrog appeared in all it's glory. But then, it had been palpitating from when the Newline logo appeared. And I thought the ending with Frodo and Sam was incredibly touching. Can't wait for the next one.

title: An excellent movie from an excellent book
review:
This movie is up to what we expected. Although some parts of the book were cut, and other were cut in the final version; this movie still claims the title of "Best movie of the year". I cannot wait to see the next two installments and this movie's Director's Cut.

Go to see the Movie!!!!

Thanks Peter Jackson

title: Excellent movie, but only considering the task
review:
I've tried to seperate myself as a fan of the book and a viewer of the movie, but I can not do so completely, especially Having recently reread the Fellowship. They did do a creditable job of tackling a book that simply does not translate well to a moive. The series built a world, not just a few characters. There are books and books to explain things behind people and events mentioned in the main four books. How could a movie realistically handle that for the non-readers in 3 hours ? I think that some items were left in the movie that were never explained. Some of the recent and past tensions were not mentioned that explained the attitudes and actions characters had. One negative comment said that the hobbits were like this, the humans that, the dwarves like the other thing, and so on. Really, that comment was completely right, but the movie didn't help explain why they were like that. Unless you know Hobbits main pastimes were eating and smoking, then you may find their 'cuteness', as many called it, annoying. But they were a naive people whose cares were not too great.

Again - given the task a great job, but I think the task was too great to make a movie all could enjoy (although most seem to have enjoyed it, so, uh... not sure where that leaves me :-)

title: Outstanding
review:
The spirit of the trilogy is captured more excellently than I had hoped. The Ring Wraiths are truly terrifying, as are the Orcs. True to the book, Orcs are easily killed, but always numerous.

The better-known actors, Liv Tyler, Christopher Lee, Cate Blanchet, are used in less prominent roles to make their characters more memorable, while the acting of the main characters is first-rate.

The balance between action, suspense, and dialogue is full of care and steady. The visual look is breath-taking and true to the imagination of the books. Go see this film, but be sure to read the books first!

title: Good film, good treatment, good job well done.
review: A very good film that dealt well with some of the problems of filming this book - thousands of years of history, dozens of important characters, and the consequences of being up against my imagination, and that of everyone else who has read the books. The characterisations were, in the main, spot on, many of the scenes were very faithful, and the movie can be forgiven those parts that were skimped or missed on the grounds that very few people would sit through a six hour film just to check everything was there, page by page. Some of my favorite parts weren't done quite the way I was expecting, such as parts of the third chapter and Lothlorien, while Moria was far more open space than I had expected, especially at the western end. The setting was superb, and fitted the book well - care has obviously been taken in finding the right spot for each shot. Even the outside scenes that looked as though they were shot in studio had a feel of wide open space around the setting. Of course, the big problem is waiting two years for the end.

title: Good, No Terrific
review: Being 15 I never until recently was familiar with the Lord of the Rings Trilogy, my father spoke about it before but I never got the acual idea of reading the books. When I saw the trailer for the movie I gave a "sigh" thinking it would be another STvideo release. (Note, I did not know the superb storyline) My brother dragged me to the theater one day and I was amazed, not at the special effects, or the acting (witch was perfect, it gave great justice to Tolkens characters) but at the entralling story. The minute I got home I ran to the store and picked up the book, I'm near the end and I can't believe someone could create so rich a world, I thought George Lucas was the only one who could do something like that (Star Wars 4-6) Tolken is a genius. See this movie, but if you haven't read the book do that first, but quickly! The movie will be such a greater experience to you. (The Gollum Story, etc.)

title: Not Bad
review:
Much has been written by others about Lord of the Rings. As a rapidly approaching old foggy, I am hard to please. Was this a good movie? A great movie? It is hard to call this a great movie. Good, yes. Most impressive from my point of view was the stunning visuals, which hardly let up throughout. Moria was truly breathtaking and I could see a whole movie built around just that set alone.

Otherwise, I am seldom satisfied with movie story lines and character development anymore, and this film was no acception. Frodo was cute, but uninteresting. Bilbo reminded me a little of Dudley Moore somehow. Why, I don't know. The other characters worked fairly well and Gandalf was the star. But like most sci-fi or fantasy films, directors are too afraid to bore people with dialogue. What they don't realize is that if the dialogue was truly inventive, people would not be bored by it. But unfortunately, fantasy films like this one always have grand, universal themes, and that seems to make for uninteresting dialogue. Does it have to? No, but it always does.

As I was watching Lord of the Rings, I kept flashing back to "The Wizard of Oz" because of similarities in the story line. Why don't they remake "The Wizard of Oz" with today's special effects? That would be worth seeing. As for "Lord of the Rings", I look forward to the next movie in the series, but doubt that it will captivate me like the orignal "Wizard of Oz" did. You have to look back a long ways in order to see the rut that Hollywood has fallen into with this genre. "Lord of the RIngs" is better than most, but a breakthrough film its not.

title: the emperor's buck naked
review:
After searching this film on IMDB I found that it has been voted #1! Number one? Sorry people, this movie is not the best film of all time. Actually, it is fairly mediocre.

Uninteresting two dimensional characters plod along for over three hours, engaging in one boring special effects battle after another. It occurred to me that you could string most of those scenes in any order you wanted and it wouldn't matter. I didn't care about any of the characters. They were more interesting in the book - more charming and more humorous (though the novel is overrated as well).

Hopefully, as time passes, and marketing budgets disappear, this undeserved ranking will drop slowly to the depths of other average and common films.

title: Great entertainment!
review:
The people who made the movie of The Fellowship of the Ring put their all into it, and it really shows. There is such a sense of love and enthusiasm for the material. I got completely engrossed in the movie -- I had to go see it a second time, and will see it a third time. It has been almost 20 years since I saw a movie multiple times in the theater (and that was before I had a VCR, let alone a DVD player). This is why I say it is great entertainment!

I read The Lord of the Rings several times as a teenager, and again a few years ago out loud to my nephews. They are great books to read out loud and I recommend it to any family with kids old enough to follow the plot (probably 10 or 11). A great substitute for TV.

Before seeing the movie, I had lots of pictures in my head from the books. Some things in the movie are different from how I pictured them, but I really enjoyed seeing Peter Jackson's vision of the book. I still have my own pictures. It's great to have both. I thought the casting was terrific. I especially liked Ian McKellen as Gandalf, Elijah Wood as Frodo, Orlando Bloom as Legolas, and Christopher Lee as Saruman.

If you haven't read the book, you can read the book first and see the movie, or see the movie first and read the book. I don't think the movie ruins the book at all. In fact, I think that if you see the movie, you will want to read the book, if nothing else to see how it ends. Tolkien wanted to publish it all in one book, but the publisher insisted on splitting it into three volumes. So you are really seeing part 1 of a very long, wonderful movie.

Three cheers to Peter Jackson, cast and crew!

title: A fantastic epic with no equal - but tragically Kid-friendly too
review:
Kind of like an experience rather than a movie - "epic" permeates this entire film - and the feeling of wonder stays with you long after leaving the cinema.

The casting is perfect - everyone is exactly right for their characters - Gandalf has all the poise and power you'd expect - Elijah Wood is a wide eyed revelation - the Orcs.. Well they're not at as charismatic as they were in the cartoon version - but then again - the film is only book 1 so by the time it ends the quest is only just getting underway. Big assed, big headed dudes with dreads, big gums and little teeth. I guess I'll have to see how they fare in full scale scenes of slaughter in the next movie though - before I can comment on whether Jackson orcs are as good as Bakshi ones.

The most interesting emphasis is the power of the ring itself- and this icon of dangerous temptation really crystallises the whole quest into a sustainable narrative drive over the relatively short 3 hour running time. There is always an impressive sense of urgency, which motivates the characters - a believable through line of action that modern films have long forgotten. (eg Any horror film of the last 18 years - If there's a monster killing people - why isn't everyone acting scared when they deliver their lines - instead of just lamely posturing and making "Halloween" references? shows how good a director of actors Jackson is.)

The action scenes needed to last longer I thought. I'm a fan of Peter Jackson - he is a master of the amusingly violent black comedy action sequence. A lot has been mentioned about the lack of time devoted to character development, but I'd argue that consumes the most screen time by far. When the action does kick in though, the monsters are generally good -the fights with bows are excellent - computer graphic arrows really kick ass: even better than Crow out of Hawk the slayer - and the skirmish at the end at least has some dramatic impact, but I'd have liked to have seen more comedy amputations in line with the splatter of his other work.

I think there's a bit of pandering going on to the 8yr olds of this world by the studio (Or rather the deep pockets of their parents) which makes me almost rabid with anger. (No one STAYS 8 yrs old for gods sake! They'd get to see it later anyway) Film is more important than an age demographic, and the resulting dilution of adult content that occurs. I am a grown up, and my tastes largely differ from that of an 8yr old - why then should I have to accept their standards?

Justification for violent sequences:

You have a commendably realistic film in every other sense, and then you have battles where burly enemies are felled by a slap with the flat of a blade: nothing rams the artifice of film making home worse as a noticeably unrealistic fight scene. If you fight with a sword - bits of your opponent come off - It's a simple fact. Yet it hardly happens here. I'm hoping that they get the black blood bags out for the second movie and plump for a more exciting film, rather than sucking up to film censors and delivering a children's movie from an adults book (Jackson should do an adult version of the Hobbit after this - with Goblins being hacked into chum - to redress the imbalance of putting in kiddie-safe fight scenes in Lord of the Rings)

Maybe the revenue generated will release some of the pressure on Jackson in terms of contractually delivering commercial diluted violence for the next two movies, and let him put out the best films possible. If Braveheart could achieve it - an unrealistic film in every other sense - then why not this! I realise New Line cinema stress they have taken a huge gamble in making such an ambitious project - but with source material so good and Jackson at the helm - there was never any doubt that it would be a success

Gripe over. fight scenes are entertaining enough - particularly the Mines of Moria sequences, and I'm sure I'll forget my initial disappointment

Overall though, it's a stunningly impressive achievement. jackson keeps it moving briskly and even manages to wring pathos and melodrama from the impressive cast. Plenty of weepiness to cater for the ladies, just enough fighting, hacking and arrows zinging around like gunfire, to satisfy the action fans. jackson has tried to keep everyone happy - from the moron in the street who goes to the cinema because he's programmed to, to the English Scholar who knows the books by heart

Much has been made of the FX - nothing special in this day of CGI proliferation - almost as good as ILM - especially since so much of it is virtual scenery and compositing, ILM's speciality.

The film starts with a cracking fight sequence, and ends on a bit of a downer (I know what's coming next though and the prospect of seeing entire warring armies is extremely enticing) and in between there's just under three hours of the kind of film making that is a delight to watch - it's imaginative, exciting, epic and inspiring. Just what a fantasy film should be.

another 10/10

As an afterthought - It's a far less laughable statement than suggesting some cack like "The Godfather" is number 1 film ever. Surely every cinema goer knows Star Wars (the 1977 film) is the best - it re-invented the motion picture as we know it and it's story is distilled from every archetype known to man - it's no longer my own favourite film - but it's easily the best film ever made. No other film will (or can) ever have such impact again. Ever.

review: Not only this thing with the LOTR´s story hasn´t ended with this movie, but the movie itself seems endless. It seemed to me there were too many things to be shown in the movie, and they were just packed in one after the other, with no regard for story-telling at all. Best movie ever? review:
There is the Lord of the Rings book, a masterpiece of storytelling and there is the movie trilogy. It comforts me that they have reviewed the entire book and tied up a few links in this one to the next two, re-working I think it's called. title: Despite some shortcomings, a success
review:
Those familiar with Tolkien's book will recognise the enormous challenge which the director and production crew faced in bringing the book to the screen. Overall, I think this challenge was met pretty well.

In my view, the film version manages a satisfying portrayal of most of the book's characters, and especially of Gandalf and Frodo. I had some reservations about the portrayal of Merry and Pippin, who come across as buffoons in the film. In the book they are young and brash, but they aren't stupid. It's hard to see the reason for the change, unless it's to get some cheap laughs at their expense. The visual portrayal of places and characters worked successfully, although some of it (Isengard, and the portrayal of the orcs, for example) was a bit over the top for my taste.

The director did an excellent job of selecting which parts of the book to include and which to omit. The difficult challenge of conveying the history behind the quest was dealt with in the best way possible, using Isildur's defeat of Sauron as the key historical event.

The treatment of many of the battle scenes did not appeal to me. A number of these (such as the one near the end after Boromir tries to take the Ring from Frodo, and the fight with the cave troll in Moria) were changed from the book, often lengthening them or making them more complex for no apparent reason other than to increase the amount of limb-hacking, possibly to appeal more to a juvenile male audience.

(SPOILER ALERT)

I was disappointed by the treatment of the Council of Elrond, which is the turning point of the Fellowship of the Ring volume. In the book, the decision to send the Ring to the fire is taken after a long debate in which all the participants are involved. In the film, Elrond makes the decision in advance of the Council meeting, and the meeting descends into an unseemly squabble which Frodo resolves by announcing that he will take the Ring. Also, those in the audience who had not read the book must have been mystified by the sudden appearance, with no explanation, of Boromir, Legolas and Gimli. In the book they are introduced at the Council meeting and the reasons for their arrival in Rivendell are properly explained. This is particularly important in the case of Boromir, who comes after a dream in which he is enjoined to `Seek for the Sword that was broken', etc.

I found at least one change from the book to be an improvement - the treatment of Arwen. I had wondered before seeing the film what Liv Tyler would have to do, since in the book Arwen is no more than an ornament and marriage fodder for Aragorn. In the film she is given a role of greater action. This changes her character somewhat, but is I think it is an improvement.

Overall, despite some shortcomings, most of those who enjoyed Tolkien's book would approve of the way that Peter Jackson's film version has accepted the enormous challenges of bringing this story to the screen, and will look forward to seeing The Two Towers. 7/10.

title: To Male and female, young and old alike, this is a masterpiece.
review: When I first entered the theater, I was somewhat skeptical as to how the movie would turn out. The reviews were A+'s across the board, the critics were wowing at the mere mention of the film. But without a doubt those reviewers were readers of the original novels. I, myself, have never read any of the books my Tolkien. I felt that I had no grasp as to the story line, and probably wouldn't be in the loop for all three hours. But you know what? I never blinked! I was completely, utterly, and totally engrossed in the sites before me. The images were breathtaking, the acting superb, and the sounds were astounding. Some of the images actually brought tears to my eyes, it was that great! And as I peered across the theater, I saw the same reaction on the faces of everyone. This is a beautiful film, and I recommend you to see it at all costs.

title: kicks ass
review: Lords of the ring is a non-stop, 3hours, rollercoaster of a ride! Is is very true to tolkien's work and an enjoyment for the family to see. Before the movies it was hard to get my son to read books other than comics, now he has just finished the Hobbit and can wait to read the Trilogy!

title: Will become a true classic, by every definition of the word
review:
Thirty years from now when I sit down with my children, I can say that I watched Lord of the Rings at the theater. This movie is a true event. If Fellowship of the Ring is any indication of the quality of the next two films, this trilogy will be remembered by generations (maybe even hundreds of years from now), I'm fairly certain of this. This movie has a mythic quality to it that transcends generations, much like Star Wars. Yet this movie is so much more than Star Wars - difficult to put into words - it's not your formulaic Joseph Campbell-ian fare, that's for certain. While you can't really call it a true classic yet (it's only been out for a short period of time, and there are still two more films), it very likely will become one. Do not miss out on movie history in the making. Score: 11/10!

Every bit deserving of whatever awards it receives.

title: 2 more years?
review:
I have to wait two more years to see the rest? I can't possibly wait that long and I hope PJ will give me a private screening.

I was cautiously hopeful when I heard they were making the trilogy into a trilogy of films. I followed the newsgroups and websites through the whole process of pre-production, production and post-production. I stood in line opening night with my heart in my throat. Why? Because these books have been my favorite books as long as I can remember and they are a huge part of my life. I have to say that Peter Jackson and his entire team have far exceeded my expectations.

Of course I was disappointed by the many cuts that were made to the story, but I understand why they did it. Many of my favorite parts of the book are not particularly visually exciting. They did keep some of my favorite dialog (such as Bilbo comparing himself to butter spread over too much bread). What was really important to me was that the movies express accurately the themes of the book. Love, honor, and in particular, duty. As I see it that is the real theme of the book- duty to self, to community, to family, to friends, to the world. And I thought the single minded focus on the ring helped to express the power and terror of that thing.

Most of all, I thank Peter Jackson and his entire cast and crew for giving me a vision of the world. I first read the books at the age of 8, and ever since I have had an 8 year old's vision of the story. What is scary or beautiful or awesome when you are 8 is totally different from what is scary, beautiful or awesome to an adult. I have been stuck with seeing the story on a small-scale and was totally unable to picture battle sequences at all. So, thanks to Jackson, I have been able to see the story through someone elses eyes, through his imagination. And what an imagination it is!

title: The best book to film ever
review:
Well, this is the first time I've ever been inspired to write in with a review for a movie. I've been a huge Tolkien fan since I first read the books when I was ten, and although I don't think he's the best storyteller around I think the sheer scale and imagination of his writing is incredible. What is amazing about the movie is that so much of this has been retained, and even better has been brought to vivid life by the stunning special effects.

This is the first time I have really enjoyed a book to film. Always before I have walked out saying 'it was ok, but the book was much much better'. This time I feel like the film has enriched the whole experience and added a greater sense of reality to Tolkiens fantasy world. I loved it. I've only seen it once so far, I'm planning at least two more visits to see it on the big screen.

It's a complete movie experience - everything is there for me, good acting, great plot, stunning visuals, fast and furious action mixed in with the occasional break just to allow you to catch your breath!

This movie sets new standards in fantasy storytelling, compare it to the The Phantom Menace for example. Enough said.

My score: 10/10

title: True to the spirit of the book.

title: Different - and one of the best I've ever seen
review:
(This review contains some spoilers)

When I took my seat at my local cinema at midnight, I thought I was quite prepared for what to come. For little less than a year now, I've been part of the Internet-LOTR hype, downloading every image, preview, trailer and interview I could possibly find. (Naturally, I've also read the books a couple of times). However, the real experience turned out to be something quite different. Visually stunning beyond belief, and in ways that I couldn't possibly imagine, and have never seen before. And the acting... This is one of the few movies I've seen where the actors really _were_ their characters, not just playing them. Initially, when I saw the first pictures of the actors on the web, I must admit that the only one I had some doubts about was Elijah Wood as Frodo, (he was a little younger than I imagined Frodo to be, and perhaps too "cute") but oh... now, after seeing the movie, I realize how wrong I was. Now I really understand why he even is named "The Chosen One". He is the perfect Frodo; and the spirit of his character is the true spirit of the Frodo we know from the books. Wood really makes you care about him, he just feels so genuine, through and through. When Frodo is standing on the shore of Anduin, making the final decision to head for Mordor alone, and the tears are running down his face... For me, I think that was the most moving scene of the entire film.

The only thing that I found slightly disappointing was that evidently, a lot of scenes had to be cut down to make the three-hour limit. I would gladly spend another 30 minutes in my chair, (or more!) to stay a little longer in Rivendell and Lothlorien, to see more of the wanderings of the Fellowship and hear more campfire-conversations. It also felt like Merry's and Pippin's screen-time was a little limited, which removed a little depth from their characters. I have no doubts, however, that this will change with the second and third film. And I _really_ do hope that we'll see at least some of these missing scenes on the DVD, as soon as it comes out.

Oh, yes, this movie was really worth waiting for. It is absolutely one of the best I've ever seen - and I'm already counting the days... no, the hours, until Dec 18 of 2002, when I finally will take my seat in the theatre again, to see The Two Towers...

title: "Best Picture of the year"
review:
I've been waiting for this film a long time. This is the best film of the year. I had my doubts when I first saw the ending but have since made up my mind that this film is the best of the year. The directing was beyond my expectations. I anticipated lyrical beautiful directing as David Lean did with "Lawrence of Arabia" but instead Peter Jackson made The Lord Of Rings a cross between "Gladiator" and "Saving Private Ryan." Elijah Wood did a great job holding his own in this film.

I've notice that Ebert and Roeper said the film was too long but it didn't seem too long to me; 2 hours and 58 minutes is not that long if the movie is good. I've seen almost every movie this year and at first it was a toss-up between "A Beautiful Mind" and "Lord of the Rings" for best picture of the year. But I thought about it while longer and I must say that Lord of the Rings is it for me this year. A friend of mine asked me whether Lord of the Rings was better than Star Wars. But there is a fundamental difference between the two movies. And because "Star Wars" is a Sci-Fi epic and "Lord of the Rings" is a fantasy epic, there is no comparison. I am not about to say that Lord Of The Rings is a better movie than Star Wars. Besides Peter Jackson took this saga from a book and George Lucas created Star Wars on his own. I have not read the book yet so the ending took me by surprise. Mr. Jackson said he's going by the book to make this film and I've only seen the animated version. I'm not going to spoil the ending for anyone.

I love the film so much I need to say it again "Lord Of The Rings." I recommend this film to anyone. I give it a 15 out of 10.

title: Great movie and my theory on it's #1 ranking
review: I don't really have a lot to say about this movie beyond the fact that I did think it was quite enjoyable and very good.  However as many before me have said I don't think I would consider this the best movie ever made and here is my theory as to its ranking: The past oh say, 2 decades or so, has been an age of horrible incompetence on the part of the movie industry as a whole.  So as a result when the occasional competently made film like Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon, Memento, or Lord of The Rings comes out its greatness gets somewhat blown out of proportion, because it's the only movie around at the time that's even decent. Then if it IS good enough to be considered a "great" film it ends up in the top 10 of all time when instead it should be in the top 10 of the last 5 years.

title: As faithful an adaption of Tolkien's works as could be expected in a film
review:
A film of any of the LOTR novels could never approach the literature it is based on. The novels are so detailed in developing the history, legends and lore of the middle earth, so much of which cannot be filmed. Peter Jackson probably is the best director for this film, although Neil Jordan or Tim Burton in their better years could have done a pretty good job (Thank good it wasn't Lucas, Speilberg, Cameron or god forbid Bruckheimmer doing this film!). What I liked:

  • The landscapes and visuals, both natural and digitally created, and the charaters were incredibly faithful to Tolkiens vision (then again, the novels are very detailed in their description) Rivendell, Isengard, Misty Mountains and Minas Tirith exactly how I pictured them, although I pictured the Shire as being more wooded.


  • From the novel, I pictured middle earth as a largely desolate brooding haunted place with a few isolated communities, depopulated by millenia of conflict, with reminders of ancient great civilizations everywhere. The film went to lengths to capture this.


  • Great performances, again faithful to Tolkien's vision


  • Battle scene in Moria one of the best around, must be seen. the balrog looked great


  • Some Tolkien purists were complaining about Arwen's expanded role. All that happened were to minor characters were combined into one still minor character, her scene actually enhanced the story.


Some (very minor) criticisms:

  • What's with the glow-in-the-dark elves?


  • Some minor details not well explained ie. Legolas is a different type of elf from the high elves, and he and Gimli hate each other's guts.


  • The final collapse of the staircase in Moria was very fake looking.


  • I pictured Moria as a more spooky, haunted place, so much that the travellers were terrified of it.


  • Was the cave goblin in the original story?


All in all, the best (mainstream) movie in years. 9/10

title: Great, borderline Excellent
review: I loved this movie.  I never read the books.  I made sure to not read them when I heard they were to be made into films for fear that I would like the movies less.  I gave this movie an 8 out of 10 because it does not stand up as a movie, as one story, on its own.  I understand that it is part one of three, but it still does not stand alone well enough to deserve a 10. Each of the Star Wars movies, so far, has been a movie in and of itself. A New Hope, Empire, Jedi, and Phantom each could stand alone as one movie. Each had a goal, each achieved that goal. A New Hope was to show that the little guy can defeat the big guy.  Empire was to show that no war can be won with a single blow, the big guy will come for you.  Jedi showed that persistency and friends will win a war.  Phantom showed that there is always evil among the good and that it will rear its ugly head (and it was pretty ugly) at any time. The Lord of the Rings story is to show how good triumphs over evil, how everyone needs faith and faithful friends, how the little guy is as important as the bigger guy, and how consistant persistancy is the key to winning a war.   Fellowship only begins these goals, it does not prove them or finish them. I anxiously await the Two Towers.

title: The film is unlike the book, but both are great!
review: When I next read "The Lord of the Rings" this year, it will be the 40th time that I have begun the great and timeless adventure. I never thought that the gigantic work could be reduced to its barest essence and translated onto the screen with any kind of success. I was happily, ecstatically wrong. When I first read "The Lord of the Rings" some 25 years ago, I was stunned by the literary quality of Tolkien's writing. I hadn't thought that any creative writer could tell a story about weather and time better than Tolstoy, perhaps the greatest writer of naturalism, ever. Tolkien is the Russian master's superior in this regard. Since the New Line Cinema tease began early in 2001, I have waited with the greatest anticipation for "The Fellowship of the Ring." I shall not insult those who may read these lines by passing myself off as THE Tolkien expert, but I know every scene in the three "Rings" book by incident, if not by heart. I was ready for the absence of Tom Bombadil and Goldberry, as I was for that of such minor functionaries in the book like Fredegar "Fatty" Bolger, and Farmer Maggot. Peter Jackson got it right. He distilled the essence of the first book to make it watchable, and interesting, to those who may not have read the book, or may not have had a prior interest in Tolkien at all. As a dedicated reader of the book, I have my regrets. We'll have to wait almost a year until "The Two Towers" is released, but "The Fellowship of the Ring" revealed no clue as to whether or not Gimli and Legolas will become friends. I always thought the burgeoning comradeship between the prickly dwarf and the haughty elf, made possible by Galadriel's magnanimous and compassionate behavior towards Gimli when the bedraggled, demoralized Fellowship reaches Lothlorien, was one of the book's singular highlights. While I was disappointed that this was not explored in the film, the movie is a magnificent work. The casting is well-nigh perfect. I could not think of an improvement upon Sir Ian McKellan's Gandalf, Christopher Lee's Saruman, Elijah Wood's Frodo, Viggo Mortensen's Strider/Aragorn, or Sean Bean's Boromir, if my very life depended upon it. While every Tolkien reader has his/her ideas of what certain locations must look like, the Chamber of Mazarbul in Moria struck me as a superb rendering of the ominous, stone-walled room. The computer graphics wonderfully displayed the Gates of Argonath and the Seat upon Amon Hen. Actually, the cinematic differences between Tolkien's words and Jackson's celluloid are many; however, Tolkien's lyrical prose is the payload for readers, just as film was for those sitting in the theater. This, finally: as I watched the film, the entire theater, full almost to bursting, was silent, engrossed. People didn't leave their seats for the bathroom or the popcorn stand. When credits began to roll, the audience sat silently for a moment; some burst into embarrassed, brief clapping. It seemed that the audience was indeed a fellowship, and an ennobled one, at that.

title: "Star Wars" pales in comparison!
review: All too rarely does a movie match the inspiring book in both spirit and text.  The Fellowship of the Ring does so far better than I'd dared hoped. Thank humanity for modern technology!  Thank Peter Jackson for his sweat, his time and his heart!  Thank J.R.R. Tolkien for setting the bar so high!

title: Will become a true classic, by every definition of the word
review:
Thirty years from now when I sit down with my children, I can say that I watched Lord of the Rings at the theater. This movie is a true event. If Fellowship of the Ring is any indication of the quality of the next two films, this trilogy will be remembered by generations (maybe even hundreds of years from now), I'm fairly certain of this. This movie has a mythic quality to it that transcends generations, much like Star Wars. Yet this movie is so much more than Star Wars - difficult to put into words - it's not your formulaic Joseph Campbell-ian fare, that's for certain. While you can't really call it true classic yet (it's only been out for a short period of time, and there are still two more films), it very likely will become one. Do not miss out on movie history in the making. Score: 11/10!

Every the bit deserving of whatever awards it receives.

title: Exceeded ALL Expectations - A "Raiders" for OUR generation!
review:
Indeed, this is a film for the ages. Truly marvelous, with exquisite cinematography, awesome visual effects, splendid acting, impressive storyline - Uh....

Dang, I'm running out of adjectives. There isn't a thesaurus made yet that will help describe how well made this film is. Just a joy on all levels. Sean Bean and Ian McKellen are completely Oscar worthy. If Peter Jackson isn't even NOMINATED for best director, then there is no justice in this world (and then if he's nominated, he BETTER win). The artistic merits are on a scale not seen for decades of film making. The attention to detail, the embroidery on the costumes, the grotesqueness of the orcs, the way the camera flew through towers and canyons. Incredible, breathtaking. The interaction between the four hobbit actors is wonderful. Elijah Wood and Sean Astin have such splendid chemistry together, it's not funny. And Gandalf's death scene - I hadn't cried at movie in such a long time, until then.

Go, see, experience. You'll never forget it.

title: Lock, stock and barrel...
review: Hype is the name of the game, and even the best of us sometimes fall for it; I did, when I read the plethora of glowing reviews of this movie. Did no one else notice the cheesy effects, the deadening performances, the often lackluster direction...? The movie has its moments, but mere moments do not a three hour film make. When it's not dragging along like a crippled animal, it's dashing headlong like a video game gone haywire. And that, I think, is the audience at which this one is aimed: the "shut-in" kids who spend most of their time (and tons of money) on video games and the ilk. Certainly it's not geared toward mature viewers, who quickly grow bored with the paper-thin plot (Tolkein has never been mistaken for a writer of great literary worth) and the even thinner film-making sleight-of-hand that Jackson employs. (I was genuinely shocked by some of the downright dunderheaded things the filmmakers tried to get away with when it came to fx- from incorrectly aligning composite images, to cheesy video game fx that never even come close to passing muster, to the use of what are quite clearly children in wide shots showing hobbits and humans and elves together.) I could go on, but there's really no point: the film is a financial success, and that's all that Jackson and company are concerned about, anyway. (Reminding me in that respect of Ridley Scott, a once promising director reduced now to making movies like the godawful HANNIBAL, who boldly proclaimed in one nationally televised interview, that he no longer cared what anyone else thought of his films.) One would do well to remember one thing: even if a million people say a stupid thing, it is still a stupid thing.

title: I was impressed with the passion and humanity this fantasy is filled with.
review:
Never having read the books, it was with wide-eyed naiveté that I went to see Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring. Three hours (that didn't feel anything like three hours) later, I left the theater awestruck and speechless (and anyone who knows me will tell you, that is a rare thing indeed). What I had seen was a movie full of passion, care, and more humanity than I had seen in a long time. The cast was superb and the direction invigorating. LOTR is JRR Tolkien's classic tale of a hobbit named Frodo who inherits a magic ring from his Uncle Bilbo. Gandalf, wizard and friend to both hobbits, discovers the ring's evil history and sends Frodo on a quest to get the ring to a safe haven and ultimately to destroy it. Frodo is wonderfully played by Elijah Wood. Wood, best known for childhood roles like Huck Finn, has really matured as an actor and is perfectly cast as the everyman hero. It is easy to empathize with his plight and to care about what happens to this young hobbit. Ian McKellen is perfectly cast as Gandalf. There is no other actor alive who could have played Gandalf so brilliantly and with as much warmth and caring. Viggo Mortensen as the ranger Strider, Cate Blanchett as the elf sorceress Galadriel, Sean Bean as the easily tempted human Boromir, and Billy Boyd and Dominic Monaghan as hapless hobbits Pippin and Merry are all standouts. Likewise Christopher Lee brought his years of experience to fruition as the evil sorcerer Saruman. Newcomer Orlando Bloom plays Elf bow-man Legolas. Bloom's cat-like movements, mild manner, and lightning like handling of the bow and arrow make Legolas one of the most memorable characters in the film. It is surprising to know this is one of Bloom's first film roles. However, the biggest surprise in the cast was Sean Astin as Frodo's best friend, Samwise Gamgee. Astin has come a long way from the boy who sought treasure in `The Goonies.' Having put 30 pounds on for the role, Astin brings loads of emotion and humanity to an otherwise otherworldly tale. Director Peter Jackson's passion for this material and dedication to Tolkien's work is evident in every frame of this, the first film of the trilogy shot back to back in New Zealand. Nowhere is there a wrong step or missed shot. Jackson uses the camera as another character in the story and therefore draws the audience into the story all the more deeply. LOTR has changed to face of films. The special effects never really look like movie wizardry, thereby allowing the viewer to forget them and just accept them as part of the story. No other fantasy film has been this real and this magical at the same time. And never has a film left me with such a feeling of warmness and caring. The only problem is, how am I ever going to wait till next Christmas for part 2?!?

(In fact my mother was beating me when she found out part 2 won't come out till then. I guess I should have warned her before hand, but I thought she knew!)

title: A fun movie, and a good adaptation of the book
review:
I'll freely admit that I am a Tolkien fan (and proud of it). I've read the Hobbit twice, the Lord of the Rings at least six times, and the Silmarillion twice as well -- in addition to much of the "unfinished" work.

I went into this movie hoping for the best, but expecting the worst.

Thankfully, the movie exceeded my expectations by quite a large margin. Peter Jackson has created a truly wonderful adaptation of the first book. I'm not going to call it a masterpiece, but it's a very entertaining and engaging movie. Most importantly, Mr. Jackson managed to stay, for the most part, faithful to the source material. There were some liberties taken: the role of Arwen (Liv Tyler) was expanded, the true impetus behind Sarumans evil machinations, the "magic fight" between Gandalf and Saruman, the reasons for Merry & Pippin joining Frodo and Sam on their adventure, etc, etc.

Most of this, IMO, came about because there is really no way that a single 3-hour movie can capture the staggering amount of "history" and back-story that forms the core of the the series. If Mr. Jackson had adhered strictly to the books, most of the audience would have been buried under obscure references and left the theatre scratching their heads in bewilderment (not to mention the runtime would have been, at least, 3x as long). You have to read the books many times, in addition to voluminous amount of related material, to truly understand the epic scope of the history of Middle Earth and the War of the Ring.

And, most importantly, let's not forget that Mr. Jackson (and the studio involved) has to make a movie that will appeal to those who know nothing about the world created by J.R.R. Tolkien. Hence the reason for many of the "changes" and the amped up action sequences.

In short; Mr. Jackson managed strike a respectable balance between the works of Tolkien and the avarice of Hollywood. Will it replace the books? Not by a long shot. It is, however, an entertaining movie from beginning to end, and it's a shame that we have to wait a year to see the rest of the story unfold.

title: Amazing.
review: It's just a crying shame the Academy will never recognize the sheer brilliance of this watershed film. Okay, I'm sorry - it will probably garner an insane amount of nominations for cinematography and "special" awards for technical achievement. If you ask me, the only thing "special" here are the members of AMPAS come decision time. They're the kind of special that rides on the short bus if you get my meaning. Fellowship of the Ring (along with its forthcoming sequels) is a film with the ability and charisma to define a generation of moviegoers, young and old alike. But really, if you'd rather go see the Royal Tennenbaums because you want an "intellectual experience" instead of the popcorn flick you heard Rings was going to be, that's fine: you can burn in hell too along with the Academy for all I care. Fellowship of the Ring: 10. AMPAS: -2

title: Brief Comment
review: I believed that the Lord of the Rings was one of the best movies of the year and surpassed Tolkien's actual book. (Die hards are going to be seeking my head now.) I loved Ian McKellen's outstanding performance as Gandalf- he was most excellent!!

title: Books to film
review:
Every movie that I have ever seen that was originally a novel, I read prior to seeing the movie. For the most part, this disappoints me a great deal, but not in this case.

I am truly amazed at how well the book was followed. I must have read the books a dozen times, so I knew the story very well. Normally, a movie completely demolishes the storyline of the novel...this is the first time that the movie acts as an enhancement to the book. No shortcuts taken, no punches pulled.

My only wish is that a clearer view of the Balrog was possible. However, there are some things in the book that were simply too fearsome, and had we gotten that clearer view, the movie probably would have been rated R.

Still, in my personal opinion (which, along with a quarter could buy a newspaper...maybe), I believe Tolkien would be proud.

title: It's great but there are faults
review:
I went to see LOTR today (all the more enjoyable now that the annoying school kids are chained to their desks once more):-).

This is the second time I have seen this film (and the second time I have reviewed it). My original thoughts still hold true - Lorien & Galadriel are totally wasted in this film. Jackson should have been ruthless and cut them out. Compared to the detail shown to the other scenes Lorien seems half-a***d and allows the plot momentum to falter badly.

On the whole though this film is well worth the ticket fee.

However, best film ever? Don't think so. Let's let the hype die down and look at it in the cold light of day.

What does strike me after reading the comments on these pages is that this is a film made by Tolkien fans for Tolkien fans. The difference in the reviews posted here by Tolkien fans and those with little or no knowledge of the books is striking. Us Tolkien geeks have to bear in mind that, of course we're all going to enjoy watching seeing the characters we read about years ago brought to life but the uninitiated do have a point. This film contains many of the flaws the books do and so will engender the same emotional extremes as have been generated by the text. For those who were less than impressed by the film I have to say that this film does a lot of scene setting. The next two parts really do gather pace and will probably be shorter.

This trilogy shouldn't be regarded just as three movies but instead as the most expensive and risky experiment in movie history. It has begun promisingly but lets wait until it is completed before passing judgement. After all this is one long story and we've only seen the first third.

The overall feeling I have though, is that for the first time in a long while Hollywood has taken a risk and has devoted a big budget to a cult novel and to a director who cares about the story more than pleasing the widest possible audience (eg Chris Columbus) and has avoided meddling too much in its production.

8/10

title: For those of you who...
review:
For those of you who bash this film, I have a few very brief comments. First of all, are we talking about the same movie? Lord of the Rings, right? I've actually seen comments that it is "boring." That's the most insane thing I've ever heard.

To those of you who think it is "trite" or too "Hollywood" or overcommercialized, I must ask, do you not realize that Peter Jackson filmed in New Zealand? The entire film was both physically AND artistically well out of Hollywood's evil grasp.

To those of you who stand so firmly behind the book that you condemn the movie, consider this: Peter Jackson LOVES this book. He's probably read it as many times as you have, maybe more. His choices have all been brilliant.

As for the movie itself, ***possible SPOILERS ahead***

What can I say but wow. This was easily one of the best movies I've ever seen, maybe THE best. (I said maybe.) The casting is inspired, the actualization of Middle Earth is astounding. I was as frightened by the Ringwraiths as I was enchanted by Rivendell. And like I said, Jackson did an excellent job putting the book to film. After all, do we really need Aragorn to stop and sing a little chant after Frodo is stabbed with the Morgul blade in the movie? Do we really need Bombadil? (Although the Old Forest would have been cool.) True, there could have been more between Legolas and Gimli, but I'm willing to overlook that.

In terms of casting, wow. Ian McKellan, wow. And I'm convinced that Aragorn has slipped out of Middle Earth and is wandering around secretly disguised as an actor named Viggo Mortensen. But my favorite is the hugely UNDERrated Elijah Wood. Not only is he beautiful, but I never once saw that he was acting. His eyes are so large and luminous that they bring a quality to Frodo that is both other-worldly and very compellingly human (or Hobbit). I can't say enough about how wonderful he is. I was also very happy to see Sean Bean. I've seen a few reviews ragging on his death scene, and I have to disagree. Give the guy a break! He had an opportunity to play through the kind of enormous and valiant death scene most actors dream about, and he went for it. Bravo!

Anyway, if you have any doubts, do yourself a favor. Go see this movie. As I saw another viewer write, my only complaint is about the length: at 2 hours and 58 minutes the movie was just too short.

title: Great by itself
review:
What makes "Fellowship of the Ring" so successful?

Tolkien's fame and story telling genius? That may be, but one should remember that a great story doesn't necessarily make a good movie. In fact, it usually happens otherwise: great and especially well-known story gets smashed up and stumped into dust by horrible movie-making. Sad but true. The story may be compelling, and very well suited for modern times (people are getting tired of machinery and technology, as Tolkien once predicted), but nevertheless Tolkien has much less part in the film's success than many think, simply because movies are not books. The gap between those two arts is vast and impassable. A movie maker, of course, should honor the writer's work, more so if the book is as influential as "The Lord Of The Rings", but that makes his job even more difficult. More difficult than, say, Lucas' work on "Star Wars", where the story was generally unknown before the movie's release.

Jackson did it brilliantly. He managed to combine the book's own virtue with his creative approach, in a perfect proportion. The movie certainly appeals to much wider audience than Tolkien's books. I do not doubt that many people who have never being able to get through Tolkien's somewhat lengthy and somewhat boring (at least for some, let's admit) volumes, and never intend to try again, would be completely blown away by the film. It's just so good. Good on it's own, let me emphasize that, not just because it's based on a well-known story. Editing, directing, casting, location settings, cutting - Jackson really deserves praise for what he did. Simply outstanding.

In the second place, actors, being carefully chosen, kept up to what their looks had promised. Another incredible achievement, and something I have not seen for eons. All of them, with the possible exception of Hugo Weaving as Elrond ("Mr. Baggins, we kept an eye on you quite for some time now..." - just can't keep myself from quoting this joke, thanks to whoever invented it!) have played their roles exceptionally well. I bet several of them will be nominated for Oscar, and I am not quite sure who exactly (which I think already says a good deal about my impression on their performances).

CG department did a great job, too. I am not going into details here, but the special effects in the film are just superb. I don't think ILM has been put into shame, though, simply because all CG departments do what director tells them to, and it's really a director's part to decide how and where to put SFX into the footage. The special effects in the "FOTR" are on the level with the rest and blend seamlessly, which is great. Not a slightest bit of overexposure.

Soundtrack is good (worse than I had hoped for, given the name of Enya, but very good)

My only complain is about camera work in some battle scenes (too erratic to my taste), but still it's adequate, if only barely.

Let me summarize, I think the movie is great in itself, not just because it's based on Tolkien's work.

And that is why it smashed the box offices.

P.S. There's certainly a huge number of fans and admirers of the book out there, but their contribution to the general praise of the Jackson's work is, I think, questionable. Many might have been actually distracted from the movie which, being "only" 3 hours long, inevitably couldn't capture all the detail of the 300-page book it was based upon, and left some minor and major plots intentionally omitted. I can easily imagine such people (well, at least some of them) being blindly infuriated by Jackson's cuts and twists. Those of them who actually liked the film in no way could make a significant percentage of satisfied viewers Jackson could count on.

title: Great. Tremendous. Should have been longer.
review:
Seeing that there are already 1967 reviews already posted, it might not make much sense to add any more, but here goes.

I approached the movie with a bit of trepidation, having read the books some 5-6 times starting in college (but not in at least 10 years). Would the movie be faithful to Tolkien? Would it be painful to watch like the animated version done in the early 80's? I had hopes but was ready to be disappointed.

Right off the bat, I found this first installment of LOTR exhilarating and stupendous. Through much of the movie I was in tears, choked up at the thought of seeing old friends from the book brought to life in such a lifelike way. Acting? These characters lived their parts. I came away thinking it would be nearly impossible to make a more faithful and compelling cinematic version of Tolkien's epic.

I do have a few caveats. With the concentration on battle scenes (all superbly done), the movie comes off quite a bit more dark and intense than the books. This is not all bad; much of what makes the books such a reading pleasure might not translate into a good cinematic experience: the long descriptions of countryside and weather, some of the songs and conversational banter.

Nevertheless, a bit more balance could have been brought in at least in the Lothlorien sequence. Basically this whole scene was far too short. In the book, the Fellowship's time in Lorien provided a welcome and healing respite after the shock of losing Gandalf in Moria. The trek through the forest is described at length with wonder and joy growing, and the time with Galadriel and Celeborn is a marvelously refreshing encounter. There was the testing and the anxiety at the mirror, but in the movie these darker elements became almost the sum of the experience in Lorien. In particular, Galadriel came across much darker and foreboding. My wife, who has not read the books, asked me in a whisper at one point if she was evil. That seemed amazing to me, but from the movie's depiction alone some could get that impression. I would have added 10 more minutes to the movie (didn't want it to end anyway) to round out this episode. The change in Gimli's attitude toward the Lady (hostile at first) needed to come through, the gifts to the whole Fellowship should have been shown (including the provision of the lembas), and more effort to provide the sense of respite that Lorien represented, as did Rivendell.

I definitely want to see it again, and like many others, will have a hard time waiting for The Two Towers.

title: Unfounded apprehensions
review: Having read and dissected the Tolkein classic over and over again for 30 years, it was with considerable trepidation that I made my way to the cinema on Dec. 19th. After 30 minutes, I feared that my apprehensions and reservations would be justified. There were huge liberties taken with the original text in this period of the movie. But the remaining two hours plus more than allayed any fears. It was as if a new, yet strangely familiar, epic was unfolding before me. I had many times to remind myself that I knew the story, because what transpired was awe-inspiring in its own right. I was simply speechless at the end. A masterpiece.

title: No words
review: This movie made a thing that I believed impossible: the same feelings that I read the book. The universe that I made in my mind It was on the screen and I feel like I was a part of the fellowship of the ring. It was magic. I think Tolkien can be rest in peace now.

title: The movie is 10 times better than the book!!!
review: Finally someone has put together a movie adaption of a book that is far superior to the original literary work. When one takes into context when the Fellowship of the Ring was published, it is a big deal because it and the Hobbit started the genre of Fantasy literature.  However, when compared with the Fantasy novels of today, The Lord of the Rings Trilogy simply can't compare.  Peter Jackson has taken the majority of the good elements of the book and cut out a lot of the boring aspects and created a wonderful story superior to the book.  A must see!!!

title: Greatest Movie Ever?
review: This movie is just plain incredible.  The emotions it evokes run the gamut from deep sadness to pure exhilaration.  I have never experienced anything like it in all my life.  I do not claim to have seen every movie, but this is the by the far the best I've seen.  Wow, a movie that not only lives up to the ridiculous hype, but actually exceeds it!  Can you say Best Picture 2001!

title: Excellent film, excellent performances
review:
Others here have said all the great things about this movie that I would, so I won't reiterate them here except to say that as a long-time fan of the books, I'm now a fan of the movie as well and eagerly awaiting the next one.

What I've not seen enough people comment on is Sean Bean's portrayal of Boromir. Wow. In the book, the character seems flat and unsympathetic, just a cardboard cutout meant to show us Man's Corruption, but in the movie, he's fully realized. Sean Bean brings an emotional and wholly human depth to the character, making real the conflict within Boromir's heart, and his terrible regret at the end. In his confrontation with Aragorn at the council - indeed, from his first appearance - you see it clearly: his fierce love of Gondor, and the conflict he feels upon discovering who Aragorn is; his need to save his people like he needs to breathe; and an inner desire for power that seems to shame him even as he reaches for it. To say much more I'd have to give away plot points, so I won't, but Boromir is a complex and very human character, and it's thanks to Bean's performance that we finally see it.

title: The best adventure film of all time
review: I haven't read the Lord of the Rings since grade school and I probably wasn't as hyped about this film as most of the people at the theater. I wanted to see the film mainly because I'm a big fan of Peter Jackson. After seeing the film it is hands down the best film of the year. The story telling was epic. The script exceptional. The acting wonderful. I would rank this among the top 10 films I have ever seen.

title: OUTSTANDING!
review: I went to see the movie this Saturday (1/5/02) and, must I say, I'm trying to drag everyone I know back with me as much as I can! The movie has EXCELLENT special effects with the best casting I've ever seen. Elijah Wood played Frodo superbly, as an example. Every actor seemed to fit their roles perfectly. One of this movie's best elements was the characters. It was made so that you developed a feeling for the characters. You actually felt for them. This movie definitely deserves nomination for several different Academy Awards and the like.

title: One hell of a ride
review: So many people have delivered the same glowing praise of this movie that I'll restrain myself from gushing too much. I don't think this is the greatest film of all time, but it hits a nerve with me that no other movie has. In 3rd grade when I was sick w/the chicken pox my mom sat on the couch and read me The Hobbit over the course of a week. The next 2 years were occupied w/reading the LOTR trilogy, chapter by chapter, night by night, w/breaks in-between each book. It was a wonderful experience, and when my family went to see it together, it was a terrific bonding moment, as well as a well-acted, beautifully realized movie. Not flawless...but a terrific interpretation. Does anyone else out there think Dominic Monahan (Merry) did a fantastic job? Everyone is wonderful, and Sean Astin is also a pleasant surprise, but Monahan has such an intelligent and expressive face. Truly wonderful to watch. I agree w/those who say that 12 months will be a long time to wait for the second installment. At least we'll be able to get the DVD of FOTR before then, to tide us over.

review: After seeing this film, every time I close my eyes I imagine these amazing tiny creatures hiking across a huge, fantastic landscape trying to save the world from a horrible darkness.
