title: A CLASSIC FANTASY MOVIE (FINALLY) OF GOOD OVER EVIL
review: I'm just beginning to read JRR's books from the Silmarillion to the LOTR. Actually, I'm still in the appendix for LOTR -- that's how in depth JRR's world is.  Director Peter Jackson did a wonderful job adapting the book to screen.  Since most who were involved in the project were avid fans, it's no wonder the movie came out wonderful.  Read, watch, and immerse yourself into Tokien's universe!

title: Answering those who had problems with some aspects of Rings
review:
I'm not a fanatical LOTR fan - I've read the books about twice in total (once all the way through, and then parts of it again, several times). I've seen the film twice (so far). Several of the problems some reviewers have with Fellowship... need dealing with.

Firstly, there are NOT "endless fight scenes" - there are in total only 4 in the whole film, 3 if you don't count the attack of the Killer Tentacle (Weathertop, the Cave Troll battle, and the forest battle with the orcs being the others). Other scenes involving enemies are frequently not fights as such (or even that fast) - the Balrog, the wizard duel and the scene where a the huge crowd of goblins surrounds the heros are NOT fight scenes in any traditional sense. As for the editing of the fights, the problems with them are down to film goers getting used to endless carefully choreographed Kung-fu fights such as the Episode I light-saber duel, where the combatants can pull off absurdly balletic moves without any effort at all. The actual fight scenes in Fellowship feel like the combatants are performing REAL improvised attempts to kill each other, instead of slow motion 10 foot leaps and silly speeded up show-fencing moves.

Secondly, to those who didn't like Elrond, I was pleased there was an elf in the film demonstrating an emotion other than nobility. If you can't stop thinking about Elrond as Agent Smith from the Matrix, uh, I think you must have seen that film a few too many times.

If you hate the open-ended conclusion to this film (and if you know it's a trilogy I think it's a bit sour of you, really), you'll DIE when you see the ending of The Two Towers. Hur hur. You'll go ballistic. But anyway, what's the problem? The Empire Strikes Back is the best Star Wars film, and that's completely open-ended. If it's frustrating, it shows how emotionally involved you were with the film. And that's a good thing.

Character development wise, I think those who didn't think there was enough of this are underestimating how much is shown rather than demonstrated with dialogue. The other two films will provide ample time for all the development needed.

Showing Sauron too early - it had to be done. When you're watching an action-adventure, good vs. evil type film, you just HAVE to know what the good guys are up against, if only so you can cut between the goodies progress and the baddies evil scheming. It would have been impossible to get across the importance of the quest to destroy the ring without showing how powerful it would be in the wrong hands.

All in all, Rings is a fantastic visual feast which, though in a few ways flawed, manages to make those flaws somehow not matter and diminish in importance with each viewing. It's interesting how critisisms have been both that the plot is non-existent and too difficult to follow, that the ending is to ragged and that the film is too long, etc.

title: short but true
review: I want to make it short because I think people have already written how they feel about what Peter Jackson has created. I just want to say so much: The Lord Of The Rings is one of the greatest books ever written and has become one of the greatest films ever shown. With no doubt 10/10

title: Amazing movie
review:
I went to see LotR not really knowing what to expect. I have not read any of the books nor am I a fantasy fan. I had heard many great reviews and hype about the movie so braced myself for disappointment.

It was amazing. From start to finish I was drawn into an unbelievable world that seemed to be real. The effects were totally seamless and seemed to belong to each scene. The acting was faultless and directing and editing was tight and kept you enthralled.

The thing that stops me from giving this movie a perfect score is that it had no closure. Not having read the novel, I assume that it stayed true to the ending of the book, but does that constitute an entertaining movie? A documentary about ant farming might score highly with ant-farm enthusiasts, but it doesn't make it appealing to documentary lovers.

All in all, it is a visually pleasing feast and one that I will be adding to my DVD collection as soon as I can.

title: LOTR I excellently done, Mr. Jackson!
review:
Most movie adaptions of famous books are subpar or terrible, but not so with Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings: Fellowship of the Ring (1st of 3 movies). Peter Jackson, director, producer, and screenplay writer is a genius, and my long and pointed hat off to him! Each of the cast members is exactly what you'd expect Frodo, Gandalf, Bilbo, Aragorn, etc. to be like. I especially loved Ian McKellan as Gandalf, and Elijah Wood as Frodo, who play their characters with such heart and soul. I've seen many comments on the length of this movie, which is nearly a hefty 3 hours. But the movie has a fast pace, and the time whizzes by. Trust me, you won't be looking at your watch while this movie is playing.

The cinematography in this movie left me gasping, especially the mountain scenes and grasslands. New Zealand, where the trilogies were shot, is a beautiful landscape, and I am even more eager to visit it now. My only gripes are the moments that were left out, such as the hobbits' encounter with Bombadil (who I really wanted to see onscreen), and the creative liberties taken with the script at various moments (though I suppose the changes don't impact the movie negatively). All in all, I'm excited about this series, and look forward to the next two adaptions.

title: Number 1 at the top 250 list...?
review:
I still can't believe that this film is at the very first position at the IMDb top movies list. This film has very good special effects, but it has (of course in my opinion) several weak points. Firstly, the music, which is a bit boring and very similar to Titanic's soundtrack at times. Secondly, there's a lot of stuff like "Oh, this is the son of...", or "I remember when I was at this or that place, which was marvelous and blah blah blah...". This kind of lines in the script (something you don't know a priori but you have to accept although you haven't seen it with your own eyes) often gets me angry. Thirdly, this kind of movie can only fully satisfy people who like this kind of stories, and, unfortunately, I am not one of them. In any case, this movie MUSTN'T be above The godfather, Schindler's List, and even Star Wars. I can't believe that more than 30,000 people have voted an average of +9 points over 10. It's simply incredible. I am sure that this rating will go down a lot in the future. This ISN'T the best film of all time... let's be serious about this.

My rating is 7-8 out of 10, of course trying to be objective, as I don't like this kind of stories, as I said before.

title: Best Fantasy Movie To Date
review: This was an excellent movie... although not the best movie I have ever seen. The picture painted of middle earth was incredible.  Many of the children in the theater were scared by the dark images portrayed, but I thought it was fitting for the story.  I am now eagerly awaiting the sequel.

title: No fear of length
review: Like many others, I believe that the film could have been somewhat longer. Length is no problem here. It's almost expected really. In spite of it's flaws in condensation, FOTR is a worthy attempt as a cinematic transformation of a classic piece of literature. Much praise to Peter Jackson for his creativity and vision. Looking forward to the next installment.

title: A way of showing fantasy.
review:
Many fantasies have been made showing nice special effects and a good story line. This one (of course based on a book)gives us the chance to refresh our minds in the fantasy genre but still keeping us interested in old ways of the genre.

Despite the length of the film which does bring us to get a bit tired, you know you have to stay awake to see better parts of the film. It doesn't disappoint. Everything, from small battles to giant monsters are shown here and because the director keeps everything under control, none of it gets silly or farfetched.

This film is not for young children, yet it is a family film and has no sex or nudity or bad language. The violence is there but is entertaining all the way through.

I've got to mention the plot. I'm sure you know it but it's great and every actor does a terrific job bringing extremely difficult characters to life.

I will just say that this movie is one the best ever made and if you stick with it you are really going to enjoy. Those who don't read or find anything and everything funny, will want to pass as it does get confusing as you may probably laugh at a few things and find yourself asking yourself "What's going on". 4 out of five.

title: One of the all time greats
review:
The "Lord of The Rings" series of films will, no doubt, go down in history as one of the best and most popular of all time. What Star Wars did for science fiction, "Lord" does for fantasy.

Rather than hire in a lot of big name Hollywood stars, thus ensuring a large audience, the filmmakers found an exceptional bunch of character actors and smaller stars. The necessary work and money was put into developing the stories and establishing setting, and so the movie is thoroughly satisfying as many modern big-budget action movies often aren't.

While the coming of the first installment was probably most drooled over by readers of Tolkien's original books, it may actually be a bit more popular with those who have not read the book, or at least aren't too picky about the details (as I am, somewhat). Hardcore fans will be sure to notice two or three minor discrepancies within the story, as I did. Most notable in its absence is the Tom Bombadil episode which added a very dreamlike sequence to the original book. While it, of course, isn't essential to the basic plot, it was a pleasant diversion and is missed somewhat. I've thought of several actors who would have been perfect as Bombadil, if only in a small part.

Notable also are the outstandingly subdued special effects. The filmmakers could have gone completely overboard in this film with stupid animated creatures and cutesy little pets at every turn, but the very tasteful animation is blended seamlessly with live action and superb makeup. Even the Sauron animation, which I expected to be completely overblown, really DOES look real (which is a first in computer animation for me).

In the end, "Lord" is an outstanding movie. Show up expecting one that will leave you shocked that you really sat there for over 3 hours and still don't want it to be over.

title: Visual Aspects
review: IN today's world of computer technology, the 100 million easily built the cities, creatures, and effects in Lord of the Rings.  But clearly Lord of the Rings stands out, as a film, against the technology-ridden films we are embarrassed with today.  Most films are reliant on their computers, and therefore limited by them.  The strength of this film, however, is not found on its dependence on computer technology, but on its independence, leading to its most innovative use.  Indeed, Lords of the Rings stands out today was being unique because it relies heavily on the (old) tricks of the trade. Camera angles, miniatures, re-shoots, costume design, make-up, and the latest in computer animation all combined made this film to produce a visually stunning experience.    I was awed at the beautiful use of color throughout the movie.  For the first half-hour, as we are emerged in to the Shire, the greens and yellows of the hills are shot with amazing clarity and realism.  As the story line travels darker, so too does the film.  Many scenes that could not be created by hand, contained some of the best use of computer technology to date.  The scenes seem so real, the depth-perception so well done that I found myself in many of the shots on top of the high tower feeling like I was going to fall, a feeling I do not feel that often.  Indeed, I didn't know I was afraid of heights untill I saw this movie. The vision of this movie is surreal and it is extremely well done.  A monumental visual achievement.

title: Only Disappointment is waiting a year for the second movie!
review: Only Disappointment is waiting a year for the second movie and another for the third! Excellent movie, lots of action, great sound track..... Great visual affects I am very hooked this movie.

title: Amazing, Truly Amazing
review:
This if the greatest movie I've seen in years. It was an outstanding piece of American Cinema. This movie had it all; romance, action, drama, comedy, suspense, it's got everything. The special effects were mesmerizing, the acting was very convincing, and the story itself is probably the best story ever told.

At first I was sceptical, simply because it said Elijah Wood in the credits, but I was surprised to see that he did a great job. The characters in the movie go through so many adventures and hard ships that you are not board for one second the entire movie. The power of the Ring over everyone who comes across it makes you wonder who will be the next to fall under the Ring's seductive curse.

I can't see how anyone could go to this movie and utterly enjoy it! This movie will inspire many to read the book, and from what I understand, the movie followed the book as closely as possible. I think this movie should win some Oscar's, because it is the best film in recent years, and it has become a favorite of mine. I just can't wait until the other two come out. 10/10

title: ... a Tale becomes Legend, Legend becomes Myth ...'
review:
... and myth becomes movie.

In this ambitious working of the J. R. R. Tolkien classic there is much to be admired.

Yes, there are a few errors and omissions but how can a screenwriter (or a director for that matter) possibly condense the complete `Lord of the Rings' masterwork into three films and perfectly translate it into comprehensible film and still achieve the kind of quality that is seen here.

I would have preferred to see four shorter films (released in both the summer and winter peak film seasons) rather than the three, three-hour films that we get. It would not have been so overwhelming.

Sir Ian McKellen is precisely what one would imagine Gandalf the Grey to be -- he does his usual outstanding job. He is a genius at transforming written words into a real creature.

Christopher Lee (Saruman the White) proves that the bad guys don't always wear black -- he is as capable as Sir Ian is. Their `duel of the wizards' is a gripping scene that will leave you breathless.

The special effects are over-the-top though at times they can be subtle -- hinting at what is to come rather than attacking the audience. However, there are times when it does get to be too much -- the roller coaster effect is unsettling, at best.

Creature makeup -- while probably mostly computer generated -- was horrifying, intense and shocking while the makeup on the actual actors was at times inconsistent.

This is a huge film and will probably not translate well to the small screen; it should be seen in all its glory on the big screen. Oscar nominations will probably go for sound effects editing; it was inspired and brilliant. So, if at all possible, see it in a good theater with a full range of Dolby Digital and DTS sound equipment.

`Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring' is certain to become as classic as are the books upon which it is based.

title: Not impressed...
review:
It's been hailed as the 'first epic of the millienium', and also 'the greatest fantasy film ever made'. Needless to say having finished the first part of the book (which the film is based on) literally 30 seconds before I stepped out the door to go see the film I had pretty high expectations. Almost everyone I know who had been to see it has said "brilliant", and that included those who had read the book... so I was really looking forward to seeing it, but...

I wasn't really impressed... and I soooo much wanted to be. It IS a stunning film, with some good believable character acting, and some amazing locations. The cinematography is excellent. But nothing much happens - it's just an introduction for the other films, and I don't think it works at all as a film in it's own right.

The whole problem was the film was too rushed. It *did* manage to fit in all the important bits to tell the story by juggling a few things and rewriting here and there, but it was all thrown in your face too fast and you never had any time to stop and take a look around.

Saying this tho I have every faith that when the next two parts are released and the film is viewed as a whole it will work a lot better. But until that time I must judge it on it's own merits - and those only get it 5 out of 10 on my scale.

title: Hype creates disappointment. *Minor spoilers*
review:
Forget the fact that it is an adaptation. Middle-Earth is going to be something different for everybody. The question is does it stand up as a piece of entertainment?

In a large sense 'Fellowship' does. It is exciting, admirably paced and in my view, exceptionally well cast. However, you can read a lot of uncritical reviews of the movie both on IMDb and in the press. Is it really THAT good? In a word...no. Although not particularly technical minded, the movie suffers from sound problems. at least 50% of what Gandalf says is inaudible. The New Zealand landscape is fantastic, and makes for some beautiful photography, yet a lot of the CGI 'sets' seem to be over dark, and over busy. Two indefensible problems for a movie of this magnitude.

Other complaints. The humour is often lame, and wildly misses the mark. And I'm sorry Tolkien fans, but the movie is too late. People have spent the last 15 years making fun of the kind of people that play Role-Playing Games and this seems to be a movie made squarely for them.

I have been sucked in however. Jackson made a very clever move by ending the movie exactly where the book ends and leaving the viewer wanting to know more. The viewer knows that they are going to get more...in a years time. Now that is what I call building anticipation. Just please Tolkien fans, contain your excitement. Hype hurts the viewers experience.

title: Different from the book, but excellent
review:
I have considered "The Lord of the Rings" to be my favorite novel for over 25 years, and have owned a collector's edition for 15. I have read it to others, including my sister and husband. I have even set some of Tolkien's poetry to music. You might say I'm a fanatic.

What I find interesting about people's reaction to the film is that those who have read the books and those who have not seem to view the film through entirely different lenses. Along with others who have read the books, I missed: Tolkien's character development of Merry and Pippin that occurs when they are introduced at Buckland, Tom Bombadil and Frodo's clowning at Bree that hastens his introduction to Strider/Aragorn.

There are changes that I thought worked well, however. Arwen's transporting Frodo across the Ford of Bruinen to Rivendell worked for me because it allowed a little more development of a strong female character, showed the partnership between Arwen and Aragorn, and eliminated Glorfindel, who was a minor elf-lord anyway.

To sum up: those of us who are real fans missed our favorite parts (and what about Galadriel's gifts of the grey cloaks with the leaf clasps that are shown after Lothlorien, but not mentioned, and her individual gifts, especially the one to Sam?). If I am honest, though, I must say that Jackson gets the scope, scenery and the landscape's impact on the characters just right. It must have the FEEL of the book. And it does.

Those who are disappointed who have never read the book don't understand its mythic feel and its ability to strongly move the reader. It has a depth that Jackson struggles to portray, but those who have never read the book should not expect the film to be a simple, fast-moving story with lots of action and a pat ending. It is not any of those things. What it IS is a story of sensitivity, a mythic-historical feel, and the height and depth of emotion. If movie-goers get it, they should laugh, cry and feel tremendous yearning throughout much of it.

It ends as the book did, and sets the stage for "The Two Towers." As one who first read the whole trilogy in three days, the waiting will probably seem unbearable. But do I question its 9.2 out of 10? Keeping the big picture in mind, absolutely not! Thanks to Peter Jackson and all of the cast and crew! This is an incredible film and a monument to Tolkien's Middle Earth!

title: Best film ever
review: I have never seen such a good movie I just love it, I can´t wait for the next one, I am now reading all the books and they are so much fun. I think that Lord of the rings is going to get the Oscar for best movie, best makeup, best graphics, best actor: Aragorn or Gandalf, and probably more. I am going to buy it on DvD I like it so much.

title: Incredible...
review:
It's a great movie. I went to see it twice and still wish to see it again...that's rare for me. Even my other favorite movies I only wanted to see once. This is probably my 2nd or 3rd movie I had to see it more than once. This film is different from any other you will or have seen. Don't miss out on this phenomenon. It's visually stunning and beautifully acted. Peter Jackson (casting director [s]) took his (their) time in casting the characters--you can tell; they were made for the parts. I can't imagine anyone else playing any of the characters. I can't believe I have to wait a whole year!

Note: considering the length--3 hours!--Jackson did an awesome job of cutting out what was needed and left was needed. Although, some die-hard fans will be disappointed. The development and history of the characters and the relationships are left out or briefly noted. It makes the movie a little more impersonal. You may not notice it because they beefed up the romance between Aragorn and Arweyn. STILL--I loved it.

title: Best fantasy film yet - Absolutely!
review:
I am normally an (avid) film watcher, not an ersatz reviewer, but having read other reviews/comments on the IMDB, I felt that I had to air an opinion, too!

Firstly, I loved the film. It is the best presentation of a fantasy story ever brought to the screen, and I am counting the days until the next film.

Yes, it's not a word for word translation of the book. Yes, there are flaws - (the only major one being IMO the frenetic pacing) - but come on people, film and literature are two totally different media, and deserve to be treated as such.

I have been a Tolkien reader from the age of 7, and was terrified that this adaptation would ruin my cherished feelings for the book.

It didn't. The film is a beautiful adaptation, and much credit to all involved in the production.

It certainly exceeded my wildest expectations - amazing casting, (particularly the two Sir Ians, Elijah Wood and Viggo Mortensen) cinematography, FX, the list goes on. I thought it was an inspired and inspiring film, and deserves those 10/10 in my opinion.

Its only flaws- for me - were a rushed feel to the second half of the film and lack of proper introductions for the non hobbit/human members of the fellowship - but these are minor niggles in a film I have now enjoyed seeing twice - oddly, for me it actually felt substantially shorter second time round.

A lot of comment has gone into the fact that it is currently on the top of the IMDB "chart". Why are people so upset by this? If it is the truly great film that devotees (including me) believe it to be, then it will stay there, if it is only "hype", then it will slip.

Why all the vitriol?

I agree that there are other great films, but for me, at least, The Godfather would be struggling to be in the top 10. Everyone's entitled to their own opinions...

In summary - for me this was not only the greatest fantasy film yet, but also a fantastic, beautiful and persuasive visualisation of Middle Earth. The Two Towers beckon...!

title: Unimaginably, the film completely does justice to the book.
review:
I'm a pragmatic realist, as well as a LOTR fanatic of 22 years who re-reads the books every six months, so it was too much to expect that their essence could be captured in three hours. My most optimistic wish was that those who haven't ever enjoyed Tolkien before would all catch a glimpse of the depth of imagination, creativity and sheer wonder he injected into this tale.

In fact, I was simply overcome by the movie, despite already knowing the plot intimately and therefore exactly where it would take me next. Even if the story didn't capture my interest, the variety of scenes, visual imagery and incarnate creativity had sufficient impact to exhilirate all but the most sceptical critic.

I went back the very next day and enjoyed it more than the first time, because I no longer made comparisons back to the books. This film stands in its own right, but is also loyal to its origins. I don't know how they managed it.

I'm actually grateful they made the movie.

title: A rave review
review: Amazing. Brilliant. Subtle. Precise. Moving. Faithful. The list of words that you could use to describe The Fellowship of the Ring is endless. A masterpiece of a book was adapted lovingly into the epic film that it is. The stellar casting helped somewhat and Elijah Wood's Frodo deserves recognition and admiration. Sir Ian McKellen as Gandalf was an inspired choice and the two of them together were electric. Hugo Weaving and Orlando Bloom as Elrond and Legolas were brilliant and Viggo Mortenssen as Aragorn was truly magnificent. If this film doesn't wipe the board at the Oscars I don't know what will. Roll on December!

title: I preferred it to the book!
review:
Perhaps I'm not in a position to pass judgment on this movie and say that it is better than the book because I have only read it once. And I sped-read it at that! But I wanted to have at least a bit of an idea of what was going on before I saw the movie. It was a bit of a struggle to get through it. I found Tolkein's language quite dry and exhaustive. But the movie takes that language and gives it color and dynamic zing. I preferred it to the book, no question. And I find no problem with the alterations that Peter Jackson made to Tolkein's story such as enlarging the role of Arwen and dropping Tom Bombadil completely. I think that Arwen's strong character, bravery and courage in the scene outrunning the Black Riders would only illustrate why Arathorn loves her so much. Her willingness to endanger herself to help the forces of right echo his own principles.

I went into this movie with an open mind because I didn't have any expectations and that served me well. I was receptive to whatever Peter Jackson wanted to tell and, yes, I was suckered right into it. I haven't ever seen such a movie that captured my imagination and wouldn't let me go for 3 solid hours. I wanted to go right back into the theater and see it again (but, alas, it was sold out!) All the actors appeared to be channeling the roles. They were completely and utterly believable. The standouts in the cast were Ian McKellan and Elijah Wood, but in truth everyone did a phenomenal job. Cate Blanchett's voice, haunting and aristocratic, sends shivers up and down my spine. And Orlando Bloom's archery work was quite notable. That such an epic film should sit on everyone's shoulders so well and so naturally speaks volumes about their dedication and Jackson's ability to hold it all together.

Although I'll read the other 2 volumes in time before the other movies are released, it is just to have an idea of what is going on. But reading them will be made easier by having in my mind the breathtaking visuals, scenery, sounds, and crackling performances already supplied by Jackson in this first movie. The DVD can't get here fast enough!!!! And neither can the next 2 Christmases!

title: Is this "The Lord of the Rings"?
review:
I was in a very interesting position while I watched the film. I had read only the half of the first book of Tolkien. And I could clearly realize all the changes that the director made in the plot. Sometimes they were so major changes that I started to feel extremely uncomfortable.

In the other half, which I had not yet read from the book, I had great joy, since I could not tell whether the director changed the plot or not.

I have got to say that the movie is actually a very good movie. It captures you and takes you to the fantasy world. The players play their role very well. The places are just like you have imagined while reading the book. The battle against the evil and temptation... The journey that makes one find its own true self... The essence of the book is there for sure. But having read all of the book now, I've got to say that ONLY THE ESSENCE is there. The changes that were made in the plot actually makes you see some of the characters differently. The hobbits for example. Their characters are changed in some ways. They are not only little, children like characters like shown in the movie. Frodo and Merry are more grown-up and brave characters in the book. The same thing can be said for Aragorn. And some of the changes in the movie are only made in order to put some romance, and make the average American viewer satisfied.

The movie is a good fantasy movie, but it is not "Lord of The Rings". It is something else. The story is changed. Can the essence be enough to make the movie of a book? Especialy if some of the changes are even against the Essence.

title: A beautifully filmed rendition of a classic series.
review:
This is perhaps the pinnacle of fantasy movies. Well, shouldn't is be? The series of novels upon which it is based is generally considered to be the greatest fantasy story ever written. To be completely honest, there are many details missing from the movie, but overall, I think Peter Jackson has faithfully recreated the excitement and wonder surrounding the fantasy world of Middle Earth. Any all too relevant scene in the book is included in this film and you will not need to worry about critical parts being excluded as the running time clocks in at about 2 hours 50 minutes.

The wonderment that I first experienced upon reading the novel for the came rushing over me all over again during the opening title. Little have I anticipated a movie premier as much as this one. I even took 4 hours off in the middle of a workday to see it, so there was a lot of expectation riding on this one. I have to tell you, it lived up to the hype and more.

The most incredible camera work gave this movie a real sense of motion. There are a lot of digital SFX, but they are so seamless that you mostly won't realize that it was an effect. The costumes and makeup are top notch. The hobbits even have big hairy feet. The offset perspectives used to make the hobbits appear to be smaller than the rest of the Fellowship is great. There are also some really great panning camera action shots of the Fellowship being fired upon with arrows in the mines. But again, SFX are what the masses want to see, and it provides plenty. The two of the best rendered scenes include the orc battle in the mines and Galadriel's temptation of the ring.

If you liked the series by J.R.R Tolkien, or loved it, you will surely not be disappointed. This is worth every cent you pay for your admission and then some. I think I will go see it again tonight.

title: No doubt in my mind that this film will amuse, amaze and entertain both fans and Joe Average alike.
review:
Immense! Unbelievable! A tale that exceeds every single tale in it's genre. The sheer grandeur of this film is amazing and will easily be able to hold you in a tight grip during the almost three hours it lasts! Although I am equally blow away as my Scandinavian colleague, I am still able to put the pieces together. I will not have to many spoilers in my review, you must go and see all that is Lord of the Rings for yourself.

The story must be quite clear by now. Sixteen rings have been made to be able to let the wisest of people of different races rule their people and country with great wisdom and kindness. What the dwarves, elves and humans did not know, was that the evil Lord Sauron made a ring for himself to rule the other rings. The One Ring!

The film begins and must not be missed for those who do not know Tolkiens work. In a clear voice, both Ian McEllen en Cate Blanchett tell the tale of the rings and the great battle between good and evil, a couple of thousands of years before our tale starts. Amazingly grande battles unfold before our very eyes, with great detail, powerful visuals and incredible amounts of actors and CGI effects. But, for the CG (computer graphic) haters, do not be alarmed. Almost every single piece of CG is either unspottable, necessary, or overwhelming. The story then shows us Gandalf who visits his old friend Bilbo on his eleventy-one birthday in the Shire. The party commences and at the end, Bilbo disappears and leaves the One Ring in the hands of his nephew Frodo (a masterperformance by Elijah Wood). Gandalf then tells Frodo that this Ring will only answer to Lord Sauron, no-one else, and must therefor be destroyed in the fire in which it was created. The fires of Mount Doom (sorry Tolkien, but that's a really cheesy name for a mountain). Frodo sets for Mordor, the evil land of Sauron, with his hobbit friends and later Gandalf himself, a dwarf (Gimli), an Elf (Legolas) and two humans (Aragorn and Boromir). LotR commences.

Lord of the Rings is beyond anything I have ever seen before. I do not dare to say that it is the best film I have ever seen, but it is most certainly up there with in the Top Ten of Great Cinematic Masterpieces. Every single actor was convincing. No, let me correct myself. Every single actor was his/hers character. There were, obviously, some actors that surpassed even my boldest expectations when it came to the realism of the famous Tolkien characters. Sir Ian McEllen, for example, did an amazingly good job on Gandalf. It would not surprise me if he told us that he had been wearing his costume every single moment of the day, because he wore his cloak with the great pride, kindness and wisdom that made Gandalf one of the most favourable characters in the books. Chapeau, Sir McEllen. Another remarkable appearance was that of Sean Bean as Boromir. He impressed me sincerely, when he showed us this man, who still finds pride in being a human, but becomes emotionally troubled by lack of hope and the power that the One Ring holds over him. Other amazing appearances were those of Liv Tyler (yes, LIV TYLER) who most certainly was able to prove that she CAN act and be extraordinary beautiful at the same time. But that goes for almost all actors who played Elves: Hugo Weaving, Cate Blanchett and Orlando Bloom as the straightforward, ultracool Legolas. Tough, magical and beautiful.

Even Viggo 'Jake from Melrose Place' Mortensen was intense as Aragorn. The only actor who was slightly disappointing, was our Dracula playing friend Cristopher Lee as Saruman, who had a bit too much 'Disney' in his character by waving around a golfball on a stick and coughing up some evil laughs or gazes.

Although LotR is pure cinematic lust for both eyes and ears, an epic of unrivaled magnitude, it sure had it's flaws. For one, it was slightly too long. Understandably so. It had to be rough for director Peter Jackson to cut and keep certain scenes, but my butt DID hurt when I left the theater. Another disappointing part of the film was the ending, which was a bit of an anticlimax. Though (thankfully) true to the book, it will leave moviegoers with an unsatisfying feeling when movie finally ends. We are used to films that have boombastic endings and if this lacks in a movie, we will easily write it down as a 'so-so' film. A shame really, because you have been watching an amazing movie. Helas, most movie-goers frequently judge a lot of films by their ending. Let's just hope they will not do this with LotR. Other flaws were some CGI scenes. When we see Saruman building his evil army for Lord Sauron, the camera swoops over his castle, then swinging down into the ground, revealing millions of Orcs hacking in the ground, using primitive wooden machines to help them with their evildoing. But the whole film is filmed quite reserved and when we see the (obviously) CGI sequence with the camera swooping back and forth and Orcs stepping away to 'let the camera pass', it will leave you with a bit of a 'thrillride' feeling. Odd, just a bit odd. Talking about CGI. Some sequences were never done before and Weta Digital pulled most of them off perfectly. Gollem and the Cavetroll for example, were done incredibly realistic and you will no doubt forget that it was done with computer. Other parts of the film, however, still have that 'fake' feeling. It will not bother you though, most of the time it's just a minor detail. I have to admit though, that I am not willing to see anymore grande panning shots of villages and buildings (Star Wars Episode 1-stylee) with a couple of CGI birds flying by to set the mood. It's getting a bit ridiculous now people.

So, although it has some flaws and a bit of an anticlimax ending, it is still a piece of filmmaking that kicks the crap out of big productions we have seen so far. And for people who like scares: there are at least two scenes you will definitely like, for it will scare the hell out of you.

Episode 1 is now nothing more than a CGI joke and Harry Potter nothing more than a long advert to sell books, Potter underwear and other Potter 'useless, but it has Harry on them' things.

No doubt in my mind that this film will amuse, amaze and entertain both fans and Joe Average alike.

9,5

title: Magic
review:
*spoilers* This has to be one of the best films I have seen for a long time. It stays so faithful to the book and all of the characters are just how I pictured them. Its no good people saying that it was a waste of time and that it was boring,all of the scenes were in the book. And whats with all the complaining about the traveling? its a journey!

They cut out Tom Bombadil (and with good cause)because if they hadn't then the whole film would have been turned into a musical and his shoes were filled in with Liv Tyler,who's character appears in the third book (The Return of The King) anyway. I think it was a work of art and I can understand that people who have not read the book might find 3 hours of talking and walking and a little fighting quite overwhelming. title: Summary on Lord of the rings

title: A movie woth seeing
review: I have been waiting for the movies since I read Tolkien's trilogy. I'm not a hard core fan of Tolkien's world but still I liked many aspects of his creation such as the detailed description of the settings in which the story takes place. I see Tolkien as a fiend who spent numerous hours in spinning details to a world which in it self is an endless task. Although his story was a bit longwinded at times it had a wholesome picture of his imaginative world. Not only is it picturesque but also full of references taken from various literature works and folklore. In my opinion this picturesque complexity makes his books an ideal movie material although difficult to handle. As with other great literature graphic images have been developing threw artists such as painters. The legacy of Tolkien's books has been great on other fields such as fantasies and computer games. I consider it luck that a movie wasn't made earlier on Tolkien's trilogy, which could have ruined the image of Tolkien's books. It looks like the movie script was written under influence of former matured ideas of Tolkien's work. I think the script is well written. There are a few unexplained instances in the movie which only those who have read the books would understand such as when Sam is saying goodbye to his horse at Minas Tirinth which came out of the blue and when Arwen suddenly used her magic on the ringwraths. I don't agree with others that think that every person should be introduced in the beginning such as the Hobbits Mary, Pippin and Sam. There is only time to introduce Frodo and Gandalf who play the key roles in this story. The introduction of the others must come as the story enfolds. Some say that to much attention is on Ian McKellen, Gandalf, even more than on Elijah Wood, Frodo. I don't agree with that argument, firstly Gandalf plays a big part in the book and secondly Frodo seems to be more on the screen than old Gandalf even though Ian McKellen is very memorable in his role. Some say that the role of John Rhys is cut to short, maybe, but still his personality shines in those scenes where he speaks and his attributes are clearly seen. All in all the manuscript is well written with few minor debatable flaws, which are understood if you read the books. The décor in the movie is superb. I've seen the movie three times and the last time I spent in examining the well-crafted props. All the little things make a difference such as the three ravens sitting on the scarecrow, the superb home of Bilbo Baggins with the cut bread on the table, and papers everywhere. The computer graphics worked well, better than ever before. In my opinion it is because that the images were often shown from distance and in darkness so the obvious characteristics of computer animation was faint. The blend of computer animation with real actors also shift the attention of the animation details to the real actors. I agree with some others who say that the troll was the worst animated creature of the film, It was too obvious. Before I saw the movie I was worried about the animation of Gollum, which in my opinion is the most exiting character in the books. I was hoping he would be played by an actor, not animated. Well he came out well but was either seen from distance or hiding in the shadows. I'm concerned with how he will be displayed in the coming movies. The top of the computer animation for me was animation of the mines, Minas Tirinth, what an atmosphere. I may be wrong but someone must have taken an idea or two from the computer game Ultima Underworld. In my opinion every frame in the movie is a work of art, landscape, animated castles, scenes full of prop, actors and computer animation. The music in the movie was well made. There was no catching theme played over in the movie as was done in Star Wars, Indiana Jones or Titanic. In stead it was atmospheric for every place shown on the screen. The music was often symphonic but often it bore resemblance of Irish folk music. Music was used to get some of Tolkien's poems through and that was a good idea for those who want them in the movie. If a catching song would have played over and over I think the atmosphere of each place would have been lost. Though I would have preferred a well-written theme which would have been played at the end with a small hint of it in the beginning. The movie is well acted, not unexpectedly. The actors are well chosen and fit their roles nicely. My highest applause goes to Ian McKellen, who played Gandal flawlessly, Christopher Lee who was born to play Saruman, especially in the dramatic scene upon Isengard when he is casting a spell on the fellowship, Ian Holm who played Bilbo well especially when he put on his addictive face  every time he saw the ring and finally Cate Blanchett who is extremely memorable in her role as the fair telepathic elfin queen, especially when she is tempted by the ring. Other memorable performances are Elijah Wood who plays Frodo very well and you can see how he changes from a cheerful behaviour  in the beginning into a more grave and sad appearance when the story progresses, just as in the book. Sean Bean's portrayal of Boromir was very good and he was able to create sympathy with his character. Other good performances were made by Liv Tyler, Sean Astin, Hugo Weaving, John Ryhs Davies, Orlando Bloom and Wiggo Mortensen though there is one lame scene with him where he is comforting Sam before they enter the mines. Marry played by Dominic Monaghan and Pippin played by Billy Boyd were portrayed as clowns and were mostly associated with misadventure and they seemed alike, their act was also good. In all the actors in the movie did a good job and so did the Peter Jackson the director. The action scenes were good even though some don't agree. The first scene of the classing armies is one example, it is magnificent and the scene where Gandalf and Saruman fought. The piercing arrows in Minas Tirinth and well co-ordinated sword combats. Though there is one thing which could have gone better, when a battle is fought the tempo of the editing suddenly increases and the camera movement also as if this was a dogma. This is just the director's style but not an attempt to hide details of the battle. It is though good that he didn't show the action scenes in slow motion. The fellowship of the rings has all the elements of a good movie: good manuscript, good directing, excellent acting, excellent filming and animation, excellent props, atmospheric music, good lighting and exciting action scenes.

title: It's not the novel. Get over it!
review:
Okay, Christopher Tolkien was correct.

You cannot make Lord of the Rings into a movie and remain 100% faithful to the book. You'd wind up with something utterly unwatchable if you did. Not only that, you'd have to break down each of the 3 volumes (Fellowship, Two Towers, Return of the King) into their component books (Fellowship is books 1&2, TT is books 3&4, and Return is books 5&6), or you'd be watching 16-18 hours of LOTR.

And, quite frankly, none of the individual books would be capable holding up as a self-contained movie.

While Jackson is a fan of the books, he also knew that, were he to do a literal production of the books, he'd never finish it. Nobody except a VERY hardcore section of the movie-going population would watch it. Seriously, how many people today would actually sit through the meeting with Tom Bombadil (*singsong* Tom Bombadillo!)? And while I regret the omission of the Barrow Wights (now the hobbits swords were given to them by Aragorn), it again tied into the diversionary Bombadil subplot.

Another area is the betrayal of Saruman. In the books, this happens completely in an after-the-fact narrative by Gandalf. Yet it's MIGHTILY important to the main plotline of the book. So it was expanded upon in the movie. Or would you rather Jackson just put the main plot on hold while Gandalf goes into a rambling 15-minute monologue?

What he's done is NOT give us a literal translation of the books. He's given us a movie that we can actually watch, and enjoy as something that evokes the awe and admiration we felt for the novel.

If you went, expecting a syllable for syllable translation, you're BOUND to be disappointed. If you went, expecting an adaptation of the novels, and reminding yourself that it wasn't going to be the novels, but on film, then you should have found it to be a fairly enjoyable (if slightly lengthy) film.

I went and saw it in IMAX. And I was blown away.

I give the film an 8 of 10. Mostly because I would have handled some of the initial character interactions differently.

Instances:

1: Boromir having already heard of a nameless ranger named Aragorn.

2: Gimli's rather "abrupt" introduction.

3: An explanation of Frodo's familiar relations to Merry and Pippin.

4: Gimli's interaction with Lady Galadriel.

Oh yes. And the Xenarwen thing. It irked a bit. But hey, most people who'd never read the books would have been like "Who's this bimbo?" at the end of Return of the King, since she has only a VERY small mention in Fellowship.

Things I DID like:

1: The visualization of the Shire (and Hobbiton in particular).

2: The visualization of what one sees when putting on The Ring. Especially during the scene on Weathertop.

3: The gates of Moria.

And one last thing. Do you ever think we'll see Hugo Weaving get a part where he actually LIKES humans?

title: Unlike anything seen before in cinematic history
review:
Peter Jackson's meticulous adaptation of J.R.R. Tolkien's tome will validate the fealty of acolytes while delighting apprentices with a sense of discovery. Newcomers may also feel just a little dazed and confused. Those who know little of Middle Earth and connect the word Elvish with a feet-of-clay rock-'n'-roll god may on occasion wish for a handy copy of Tolkien for Dummies. The film contains a great deal of new info to sprinkle throughout even a three-hour running time.

Yet, under director Jackson's baton, it all comes together with exhilarating, if occasionally solemn, majesty. The film presents a world of dark enchantment. The Lord of the Rings is not the lark that Harry Potter is. It's filled with sprawling battle scenes that are spectacular in scope but frighteningly intimate in detail. And the mood is largely serious. The saga of the One Ring is a primal battle between righteous good and terrible evil, with only a few gray areas allowed.

At the center of all this hubbub is vertically challenged hobbit Frodo Baggins (Elijah Wood), who is somewhat baffled to find himself anointed as the keeper of the One Ring. He must begin an odyssey to keep the ring from falling into the hands of wicked Dark Lord Sauron, who will use it to assure himself world domination. Frodo and his fellowship of dwarves and elves must head straight for Sauron's ominous living quarters and personally watch the ring perish in the fires of Mount Doom.

Along the way, our heroes are attacked by various bats, dragons, and other unsightly beings determined to retrieve the ring for Sauron or use it for their own benefit.

Mr. Jackson's visual flair was flawless in 1994's Heavenly Creatures and 1996's less successful The Frighteners, not to mention 1992's cult horror fave Dead Alive. Many a promising director has been stifled by the responsibilities of big budgets and sprawling logistics, but Mr. Jackson retains his vision. The film's pastoral scenes are ripe with gentle beauty, and the overall color scheme darkens as the mood demands. Like all great adventures, The Lord of the Rings is located in a land of enchantment, and the director and his large crew have an enchanted spirit.

Although the film aims for a different emotional impact than Harry Potter, both ventures share the same structural handicap. Each film's first half superbly establishes the right emotional and physical atmosphere. But their second halves flounder somewhat under the weight of too much plot development. Each scene brings a fresh crisis before audiences have had time to digest the previous one. The ongoing avalanche of plot elements makes the film seem no less (and yet, no more) than its 178-minute length.

Mr. Jackson's Heavenly Creatures provided Kate Winslet with a spellbinding feature debut, while The Frighteners contained one of Michael J. Fox's best performances. Even amid the sound and fury of The Lord of the Rings, he remains an actor-friendly director.

Twenty-year-old Mr. Wood is an appealing, convincing Frodo despite the fact that, with long locks, he bears an uncomfortable resemblance to Winona Ryder. Also, in the Tolkien world, real men do shed tears, and during the film's second half, Mr. Wood's Frodo weeps more copiously than Meryl Streep in Sophie's Choice. Still, it's a performance of depth and growth.

As the wise wizard Gandalf, the renowned Ian McKellen is majestic but not haughty; he's a wizard all hobbits would want as their own. Cate Blanchett's Galadriel possesses equal measures of serenity and urgency. Viggo Mortensen's Aragorn is a brooding and (at least in the movie) love-struck warrior viewers will take to heart. The film expands the character of Arwen to be the object of Aragorn's adoration, and Liv Tyler delivers the proper spirit. The entire project contains no misstep, even if some of the right steps are accomplished in a slightly plodding manner. The Lord of the Rings is a major achievement of mystical spirit and high adventure. For many, it is the film that Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace should have been.

Final Verdict: 9.3/10

title: To answer some people's problems with this film...
review:
I'm not a fanatical LOTR fan - I've read the books about twice in total (once all the way through, and then parts of it again, several times). I've seen the film twice (so far). Several of the problems some reviewers have with Fellowship... need dealing with.

Firstly, there are NOT "endless fight scenes" - there are in total only 4 in the whole film, 3 if you don't count the attack of the Killer Tentacle (Weathertop, the Cave Troll battle, and the forest battle with the orcs being the others). Other scenes involving enemies are frequently not fights as such (or even that fast) - the Balrog, the wizard duel and the scene where a the huge crowd of goblins surrounds the heros are NOT fight scenes in any traditional sense. As for the editing of the fights, the problems with them are down to film-goers getting used to endless carefully choreographed Kung-fu fights such as the Episode I light-saber duel, where the combatants can pull off absurdly balletic moves without any effort at all. The actual fight scenes in Fellowship feel like the combatants are performing REAL improvised attempts to kill each other, instead of slow motion 10 foot leaps and silly speeded up show-fencing moves.

Secondly, to those who didn't like Elrond, I was pleased there was an elf in the film demonstrating an emotion other than nobility. If you can't stop thinking about Elrond as Agent Smith from the Matrix, uh, I think you must have seen that film a few too many times.

If you hate the open-ended conclusion to this film (and if you know it's a trilogy I think it's a bit sour of you, really), you'll DIE when you see the ending of The Two Towers. Hur hur. You'll go ballistic. But anyway, what's the problem? The Empire Strikes Back is the best Star Wars film, and that's completely open-ended. If it's frustrating, it shows how emotionally involved you were with the film. And that's a good thing.

Character development wise, I think those who didn't think there was enough of this are underestimating how much is shown rather than demonstrated with dialogue. The other two films will provide ample time for all the development needed.

Showing Sauron too early - it had to be done. When you're watching an action-adventure, good vs. evil type film, you just HAVE to know what the good guys are up against. If only so you can cut between the goodies progress and the baddies. It would have been impossible to get across the importance of the quest to destroy the ring without showing how powerful it would be in the wrong hands.

All in all, Rings is a fantastic visual feast which, though in a few ways flawed, manages to make those flaws somehow not matter and diminish in importance with each viewing. It's interesting how critisisms have been both that the plot is non-existent and too difficult to follow, that the ending is to ragged and that the film is too long, etc. It indicates the fine balance of the film that those that didn't like it dislike it in contradictory ways.

title: Great fantasy film with a few...kracks
review:
The acting was good. McKellen, Holms and Lee were fantastic, as was Elijah Wood, although I didn't connect fully with him during the movie. The supporting cast were ok. I did have trouble assigning or remembering some character motivations; I suspect this is a symptom of losing the background from the books. Movies like this are difficult not because of the special effects undertaking, but rather with making a functional movie within a limited running time. More of Gollum would have been a treat, but I'm guessing he will materialise in the second movie. To me the wizardly Gandalf was perfect.

I LOVED the darkness. Peter Jackson, who has given us a fair share of horror and the macabre in the past, delivers my favourite moments of the film. And yes, it follows that I found the nice aspects and characters a bit dull and tedious. The lust everyone had for the ring added a nice thread of doubt which deepened the 'good' characters. The monsters were fantastic, especially the big 'boss' creatures like the Balron, Kraken and the grey giant in the mine. The orcs were goofy in the climactic battle, my least favourite part of the film - how could they catch up so fast?

The film dragged in places, mainly due to the many (necessary) shots of the Fellowship travelling through countryside. An unavoidable liability since this is supposed to be a 'road movie', but I kept hanging out for the next adventure. I also didn't understand Kate Blanchet's character. Some of the dialogue was not intelligible in my Cinema (Palace, Brighton, Melbourne Aust).

Overall I enjoyed LORD OF THE RINGS. This is certainly not The Best Film Even Made. I think Jackson and Co. would be the first ones to refute that claim. The action is fine, although a tad fast, and it also takes time out to allow the audience to drink in the world(s) of Middle Earth, warts and all. The movie is a well-crafted collision of goodness, evil, determination, wisdom, betrayal and commitment, friendship, greed, hatred, a touch of romance, and a good dose of 'Just do It' ethos.

title: Firing up your imagination
review:
Fellowship of the ring is the first out of three movies telling JRR Tolkiens incredible story The Lord Of The Rings, continuing where The Hobbit left off. This is a fact, and you should know it before you enter the theater. If you have problems relating to fantasy, this film is NOT for you, if you don't like elves, orcs and dwarfs, this film is NOT for you, and if you have problems following a long intricate storyline, with a lot of characters, this film is NOT for you. And it lasts for three full hours. All that aside, this is, without a doubt, the greatest film I have ever seen. The hype was big, the movie is even bigger. Spectacular scenery, great and believable acting, filming better than in any other movie, and the greatest story ever told. Could you wish for more? Well, more is on the way.

There are no high-speed car-chases here, there is no Tom Bombadil, no naked women, the songs from the book have been left out almost entirely, and the main character is a ring. A lot of things to p*** off almost everyone who are either fans of Tolkien or fans of Hollywood-blockbusters. I am both, and I'm still immensely pleased. I have read the books by Tolkien, and I have seen most of Peter Jacksons movies. Some say it can't compete with Star Wars... Of course it can't compete. Can the Godfather compete with Police Academy? Can Indiana Jones compete with the Shawshank Redemption? We're talking different genres, different universes. The Fellowship of The Ring is a huge, epic movie, almost flawlessly done, depicting the evil and horror that could lead Middle-Earth to its destruction. But the most important thing this movie shows us, is that it's really all about hope. If hope is lost, ALL is lost. You can see this movie as a political statement, but please don't. It's a fairytale. It's the greatest of all fairytales, and you're never too old to enjoy it. You may be too young, however, or you may be too set in your ways and expectations to enjoy it. Forget all other movies, this one is beyond comparison. Forget the regular 90 minute timeframe, forget the stereotypes, you have to dig a little deeper. What will you find? Solid gold. Pure and simple. And when all three movies are out, I hope they give us moviegoers an opportunity to see them all in a row, as they were meant to be. It's a ten out of ten, expect nothing else.

review: I wasn't eager to seeing this movie until I saw the trailor on TV one day about a week before opening.  But after seeing this movie, twice, already, I can truthfully say it's my favorite movie of all time.  There's not a thing about it that I  could complain about.  With non-stop action the whole movie, it's just incredible.  Usually parts of movie where there is all talk and no action, I can get very antsy, but figuring that the only way to understand the whole movie was to listen to every word said.  I truthfully can not wait for the next two movies to come out.  I said it before...if this movie isn't up for a "Best Movie" at the Oscars...I'm not even going to watch.

title: Good but to loud
review: Great attention paid to costumes, sets, etc., but the movie was mostly about fight scenes and little time spent on developing any of the many sub-themes. If I hadn't have been warned in advance and brought my ear plugs with me -- I would have had to leave the theater!   I'm planning on seeing parts 2 and 3 but this movie could have been better.

title: Praise be to Peter Jackson
review:
My god. I will never have to go to the cinema again. I have just seen the ultimate film of all time. I am talking about The Lord of the Rings: the Fellowship of the Ring. Absolutely riveting adaption of the Tolkien classic. Words almost fail me. I have only been out of the cinema for an hour and my head is still spinning with the great scenes that Jackson somehow plucked out of my brain. I saw on screen tonight what I had seen in my head when I read the book. I took my wife, who hates this type of thing, and all she did on the way home was talk about it and she is going to start reading the book tomorrow to find out what happens. She loved it. I have read some reviews here moaning about the lack of an ending to this movie. I can't understand it. Didn't they know it was part one?-------SPOILERS----- What the hell do they want? For a special bit to be tagged on at the end of this part showing gollum biting the ring from Frodos finger etc? Get a life!--------END SPOILER.

The amazing use of colour throughout the film gives great effect to the story. The vibrant warmth of the shire, to the greyness and monotone of the Dwarf mines of Moria, the best part of the film.

The CGI was completely realistic. Better than anything that has been done before. Anyone who says it's not as good as Star Wars is talking out of the rectum. The Cave Troll and Balrog are mind blowing. In fact the effects are so good you don't even notice the main one, that's the size of the hobbits compared to the humans and elves. Completely seemless.

For reviewers here who say they were bored, well obviously this isnt for you. Go catch a Ben Stiller flick. But for fans of film that want to see a great story, fine acting, superb cinematography, top notch action and be transported to another time and another place, then you can't go wrong. As I said at the begining, I never have to go to the cinema again. Not until the Two Towers comes out this time next year!

I give this film 10/10. Best film in years. Best fantasy film of all time. It's going to clear up at the Oscars. It's just fabulous.

title: Yes, I agree that it is the BEST movie I've seen.
review: First of all I want to tell you that I am a huge movie fan! I feel that the Godfather and Shawshank Redemption deserve to be at the top of the list. Some of my other favorites include: North by Northwest, Doctor Zhivago, Shawshank Redemption, Star Wars, The Great Escape, The Shining, It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World, Alien, Titanic, The Matrix, October Sky, etc.... The reason that I've mentioned some of my other favorites is to show a wide range of appreciation for different types of films. I STILL feel that "The Fellowship of the Ring" is superior to all of them. Some of the others are VERY close, of course, but the acting, scenery, special effects and overall mood of the film is fantastic. I've watched the film only TWICE thus far and desperately await the DVD!!! The second time watching I was joined by two close friends of mine who seemed bored during some of the slower segments. I felt sorry for them because I assume that they would prefer an effects laden film that has to be fast-paced. This film is NOT a fast paced "Speed" type of film and anyone that needs to be constantly kept on the edge of their seat may find "Fellowship" plodding. I, on the other hand thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it! *** :)

title: Amazing Movie Finally Done Justice
review: Finally movie makers have had technology worthy of creating movies based on Tolkiens magnificent books. If there is a film that everyone must see, this has got to be it. Smashing into the IMDB's number 1 position, overtaking "The Godfather," LOTR can safely be described as "The Single Best Motion Picture Ever Created." And that's some bill to live up to. This movie is better than every other movie EVER made. It is simply that good. Whether your a fan of action, comedy, fantasy, drama, or ANY genre it's all incorporated into this. In what can only be described as a Masterpiece the Directors have also included fantastic backdrops that photographers and Artists around the globe should be jealous of. If it's 3D animation that's your thing there's plenty of that too, using a 3D engine called MASSIVE millions of onscreen people were reproduced from a few images, making the battles seem infinite. This movie can be summed up in two words, "Absolutely Amazing."

title: WOW!
review: I had read many many comments about the movie before going to see it last night and I was expecting a great adventure movie. Wow did it deliver. Just amazing and surprisingly emotive. It had a few not so great parts but still a very good movie. I now believe the next movies will be better. The only people I saw leaving were parents that had brought their five and six year olds to see, what they thought would be a willowesk fantasy. I couldn't help laugh at them ;) taking a young child to this movie is like throwing a puppy into blender, just plain silly. Can't wait to see what that the quirky Peter Jackson will do next.

title: Amazing, Amazing, Amazing
review: Amazing!!!!!!!!! That is my first reaction to this movie. My second, when I had time to think about it a little, take in everything I had seen, and really analyze the context of the movie was AMAZING!!!!!!! If you don't like the story, or never cared for the story and especially hated those obsessed morons who always talked about it, then this movie is not for you. It is a 3 hour movie and it is not a Hollywood type, in your face for 2 hours, half the world blows up experience. If that is what you are looking for, and I enjoy that as much as the next man, then you had better go somewhere else. This movie is remarkable, and if you love fantasy, far away places with strange and mystical creatures and amazing adventures, then this, in fact, is the movie for you to see.If you are scared off by the running time, let me just say that as with many great movies, Braveheart and the Godfather, the time flys by. If you are avid fan of the books, as I am, then you may be scared off by the fact that Tolkiens masterpieces can never truly come to life, except in the minds eye. Well, I agree, yet this movie fits and stays to the book as well as any movie ever has. The effects are amazing, the acting tremendous, the fight scenes astounding, just flat out great. Don't be scared off, go see this movie. I will be, again.

title: Perfection
review:
The Lord of the Rings is an amazing journey. It's characters, plot, scenery, emotion and power enthralled me. It is a life-changing epic that should be cherished by millions. It is rich and deep and wondrous. Words cannot describe the emotions felt within me regarding this movie. I had to recover at the end of the film as I felt it had entered into my bloodstream and taken over me.

Every character was perfectly cast. Viggo Mortensen's Aragorn was exactly as one should expect. Orlando Bloom's Legolas was astounding. Perhaps my favorite was Sean Astin as Samwise Gamgee. His determination and loving admiration of Elijah Wood's Frodo was touching and real. Though honestly, it is far too difficult to hone down on one single performance. Each actor exceeded my expectations by far.

The cinematography of a film has always been extremely important to me. I felt the cinematography was as close to perfection as it could get. The score was gorgeous. Costumes and make-up were wonderful. Every single piece of the movie seperate and together equalled one thing: Perfection.

title: Excellent!
review: Probably the best interpretation of a classic book I've ever seen to date. The movie captured Tolkien's vision so vividly.  It was as if they painted the picture as I saw it in my mind.  Definitely a must see, again and again.

title: Very well done
review:
The casting for this movie was well done, and the acting was good. Though some of the early emotional scenes were a trifle overdone, it seemed the actors fell into the story more as time went on.

I was a little disappointed in a few of the pieces that were left out. I didn't feel like there was enough there to provide ground for the bonding of Gimli and Legolas later on, and I was surprised that Bill Ferny and Sam's relationship with the horse were left out, leaving the audience (I imagine) wondering at Aragorn's comforting of Sam when they had to let it go.

The other thing that bothered me was leaving out the blindfolding of the party (particularly Gimli) in Lothlorien, and the lack of covering any of the gifts given other than Frodo's. Most especially Gimli's gift, as the time there and the exchange that occurred where a large part of Gimli's character development.

Regardless, the movie was very enjoyable. But I warn you, if you have small children that you are interested in taking, the PG-13 rating is well deserved. Some of the scenes may be more than a small child can handle.

title: Translates the poetry of words into the poetry of music and film.
review: J.R.R. Tolkien's epic fantasy of Middle Earth tells the story of a ring of power forged by the Dark Lord Sauron that has been lost for many centuries but is finally found. Unless it is destroyed in the fires of the very mountain in which it was forged, the forces of the dark lord will overrun Middle Earth. The task falls to a short human-like halfling called a hobbit and the fellowship that accompanies him. This is the first of three films based on one of the richest and most poetic tales ever told. The film version is nothing short of a masterpiece as it retains the meaning and power of the original work by translating the poetry of words into the poetry of music and film. With exceptional performances by all, a brilliant directorial vision and a dynamic and suspenseful screenplay that happens to be one of the most faithful translations of a great work of literature, this film will become a classic to rival the great films of all time.

review: I have little time. Therefore I shall be brief. The first installment of The Lord of the Rings proved enormosly entertatining when placed against Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone as the young magician's first adventure was: - Poorly executed - Unimaghinatively Directed - Atrociously Scripted - Shockingly Scored (Williams's 'mush' (RollingStone) is truly a diabolical piece) - Acted without proper conviction in some areas - I have already made the point, but may I say again how CATACLISMICALLY DREADFUL the angles of camera proved in this deeply unfortunate adventure. title: Two in One: Best movie and Best Fantasy movie EVER
review:
Going to see this movie, I felt as if I've been waiting for it all of my life. After the first few minutes, I knew what I thought and felt was True. When it ended, I said to afraid of mine, "Forget STAR WARS, this is IT!".

The movie is two in one: One: It's an amazing portrayal, true in essence and in form, of the first part of "The Lord of the Rings" trilogy, one of the most renowned literary works ever. Two: It's the best fantasy film to have ever been produced. Aside from "Willow", every fantasy film was either a Comic Romance or a kid movie - this was genuine Fantasy, and not just GOOD fantasy, but a good movie! This might be the breaking movie for others of its kind - Serious and good fantasy movies (I can't weight to see the Dragon Lance Trilogy, The Dark Elf Trilogy and other famous and renowned fantasies on screen.

And, at long last, it put "Harry Potter" in it's rightful place. Saying "Harry Potter" is a good fantasy film, or comparing it with "The Fellowship of the Ring", is like comparing Sesame street with Shaekspeare.

FORGET STAR WARS: THIS IS IT!

title: SEE THIS FILM
review:
I was slightly disappointed with Harry Potter, but this film really does live up to the hype. Unlike a lot of people I actually like the 1978 animated version, but agree that it is woefully flawed, something which cannot be said of this version. Visually I don't think there can be any doubt that it is the greatest film ever made - it surpasses even The Matrix in that particular area - but it is a great film for other reasons as well. The danger with huge-scale action films is less focus on the actual performances, for example in The Matrix, but this wasn't relevant with Peter Jackson's film at all - the casting was absolutely spot on, and the performances, particularly Ian McKellen's, were first-class. There is another link with The Matrix, that being Hugo Weaving, and Elrond did remind me of the 'chief agent' somewhat, but better that than Weaving's character in Priscilla.

The effects have been talked about a great deal, and with good cause, as they were simply stunning, as was the photography. I think die-hard Tolkien fans might be a bit miffed at some of the changes, but I thought they worked well, for instance Arwen meeting the Hobbits before Rivendell, and not Glorfindel, a character who never appears again, as it is in the book.

Actually I found it slightly surprising that it was only PG-rated: the black riders and the Balrog were pretty damn scary, the latter being a superb realisation of Tolkien's rather simplistic description of 'shadow and fire'. All in all, you MUST see this film.
