I also have issues with the timing of Frodo's departure. Gandalf was to have visited him months before he left, and the only reason Frodo got out in the nick of time (as opposed to having months to spare, as Gandalf would have had it) was because Barliaman Butterbur (the bartender/innkeeper in Bree) didn't forward a letter that Gandalf left with him months before Frodo's departure telling him to get the heck out of the shire no later than July. It was at this point that Gandalf left for Saruman's place (and we know what happened there) but it was Butterbur's oversight, not Gandalf's, that caused Frodo to almost get captured. Still, this only makes the difference between a 9 and and 10, and a 9 is an amazingly high score for a movie from me.

Aside from that, this movie is amazing. The camerawork was superb, as was the scenery. The portrayal of the characters was fantastic. I do wish that Merry and Pippen had been introduced more as friends of Frodo rather than just folks that they happened to come across, but the characters themselves were perfect. I'm willing to accept the under-development of Legolas and (especially) Gimli, because they're going to have huge roles in the next movie. Gandalf is perfect, as is Elrond. I actually liked the enhancement of Arwen's character, because that didn't affect any of the key elements of the story. And once the story hits Rivendell, it hits right on the mark as far as the storyline goes. I can't wait for "The Two Towers" next Christmas.

title: Filmed on Location in Middle Earth
review:
(Very mild spoilers)

This film works because director Peter Jackson brings his vision of Middle Earth to the screen in a vividly realistic manner.

That is why this film's reviewers - amateurs and professionals - can give long lists of flaws in character development, plot, computerized effects or fidelity to the book and still give the film a stellar rating.

To borrow from Orson Scott Card, LOTR is not a character story - so Jackson can be granted a certain (though not unlimited) license with character interpretation. (If one doubts this, try to think of more than a handful of specific ways in which Tolkien himself distinguished Legolas from other elves or Gimli from other dwarfs (or Merry from Pippin, for that matter)).

And it is not an event story - so Jackson can be granted a certain (again, not unlimited) license with the events in the book. (If you think LOTR is a plot-driven story, then ask yourself why the book's story continues for over a hundred pages after the fate of the ring is resolved!)

The Lord of the Rings is a milieu story and in a milieu story (of this genre) what counts - in the final analysis - is the ability to present a believable and fascinating secondary world.

And Peter Jackson's Middle Earth is 'realistic' in character, event and setting. In the course of three hours the balance of script, acting, costumes, special effects, cinematography, etc. work together to move the audience from mere spectators to involved participants. I care about Jackson's Middle Earth (and its inhabitants) as I care about Tolkien's.

As a Tolkien fan (though hardly a fanatic), I found many flaws in the movie version of Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring. Most of those flaws are posted in other reviews on this site.

But, bottom line, the cast and crew have lovingly and successfully created a compelling Middle Earth in which dwarves and elves, hobbits and wizards, Gondor, Rivendale and Barad-Dur are real.

If you're looking for a wooden rendition of the book in which the root cause of Merry and Pippin's decision to follow Frodo into exile is presented in depth, you will be disappointed (though the movie shows an extraordinary respect for its literary source).

And if you're looking for a hack and slash action movie, you will be disappointed (though the movie is certainly eventful).

But if you are the kind of person who can sit back for three hours and let Jackson's Middle Earth unfold (and walk away contented and at peace after the movie ends in the middle of nowhere! :-), then this movie is for you.

It's going to be a long two years...

Ten out of ten stars on this one.

title: This is a Movie, Not the History of the World!
review:
What an extraordinary movie! I was visually stunned, shocked, soothed and in utter awe of this adaptation of Tolkien's work. I freely admit that I have not done more than a cursory scanning of the first installment. This, however, does not disqualify me from expressing my impression of this film. While I harbor no disagreement with the opinion of others on the film's lack of acute detail to the written work, I think it only fair to state the axiom of any movie of this magnitude: I have never seen a film reproduce what was originally put to paper that will satisfy everyone. It is virtually impossible to convey every nuance, creature and custom which Tolkien has endeavored to create due to the following constraints: Time, locations, replications of all things which are not a part of our world, and the most vital, the power of imagination. Tolkien delved into his mind, created a world that does not exist today, and Peter Jackson has illustrated that on the big screen for us.

The concept is simple though not easy: Accept that what you will see will be in part a portion of the world Tolkien has created and that's it. His work had such great scope and detail, to put it on celluloid would take countless installments.

What I will say is that I must see this movie a number of times. To absorb it all in one sitting is asking the impossible. My senses were stunned and could absorb the fundamental plot, the characters and the emotions. It is a violent, emotional and dedicated story. Any film, I believe, based on literature is essentially a moving Cliff's Notes. We see the foundation of the books, but it is up to us to go beyond that. If we are dissatisfied with what we see on the screen, especially for those who are Tolkien purists, then it is essential to separate the literary form from the movie. And for myself, I believe only in one thing: READ THE BOOKS!

The Lord of the Rings was a spectacular visual guide for me to start reading and let my imagination find Middle Earth as I "see" it. Other than that, the performances by Wood, McKellan and Lee were outstanding. The Aragorn as portrayed by Mortenson was noble and had integrity. The others, for me as a naive Tolkien reader, did not have the import that I think Jackson put forth. "Adaptation" is just that, and with close to three hours time, I felt the essence of the book was wondrously brought out. I was left wanting--the virtual goal of every filmmaker--and will wait for The Two Towers with impatience and toe tapping.

This is a spectacular movie, but it's not the history of the world, where I would indeed demand, nay expect, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. I take the movie as it is: A visually and conceptually presentation of a truly amazing world, its forces at work for good and evil and cultures not of our own. It is worth the three hours and worth the stirring of curiosity to crack open the books by Tolkien and do my footwork. Peter Jackson can only whet out appetite, open the pathway, he cannot do the reading for us. And, in my opinion, he has done well.

title: Blew me away.
review:
The science fiction and fantasy genres are not generally taken

seriously; this is not without justification. It is all too easy to distract the non-discerning moviegoer from a bad film with beautiful actors, formulaic plots, strange weapons and gadgets, plenty of action and/or sex, and the odd latex prosthetic and weird, yet revealing, costume.

Fellowship of the Rings is not such a film. In fact, in the first draft of this review (which I lost), I realized that it is better off being compared to a film like Casablanca. I know some of you are cringing, but let me elaborate.

For me, a good film does not require an original plot (or even a plot), nor must it be very intellectual or difficult to grasp. It should have something in it for nearly everyone - maybe a little action, maybe a little adventure, maybe some romance, some subtlety and sophistication, and something to say. There should be layers of enjoyment and meaning, and each time you see it, you should find something new or interesting about it. There should be a careful attention to detail that may not be obvious except after repeated viewings. A great film has all of these, and then it blows you away. All aspects of the film show the same excellent care and attention as the others - none are shortchanged.

Casablanca never was meant to be the film phenomenon it became. It was one of those films that was thrown together after World War II was over and filmed a relatively short period of time with not a lot of money. However, like all great films, it just outdid itself.

Here we have the story of a few previously insignificant people who are now sucked into a situation of gargantuan importance. The hero knows that doing the right thing will mean a loss of comfort and familiarity, someone he loves, and quite possibly his own life. Doing the wrong thing means a victory for a great evil and unimaginable suffering for countless others, both strangers and friends. He has also never done this sort of thing before, and it's the hardest choice he's ever made in his life. In spite of all this, he makes the right choice. One of the subtler points of the film in my view is how even the least of us have the capacity for greatness of heart.

The film itself hits us where the heart is. We are compelled by the humanity and context of his situation. The actors take a script that is not particularly profound and give it impact and meaning through their delivery. We forget who they are in real life and for awhile see the characters as real. There is a chemistry among the players that makes this easy for us to do. After the film is over, we realize that only a great director could pull a performance like this from everyone, and create such an irresistible vision. Only a great film crew could get the shots the director needs to complete his vision. Only a great casting director could put together a group of people that well-suited for their parts and each other . We realize that the cinematography was so good and so fitting a part of the story that we didn't notice it until the film was over. We must see it at least once more to catch the things we barely noticed, or missed completely, the first time. We didn't notice we had been sitting down for this long.

I could have written those same two paragraphs about Fellowship of the Ring, almost without alteration. I didn't want it to end. I must see it again. The Balrog was more terrifying than I ever imagined, and the dire circumstances of the Fellowship was illustrated so well that I found myself almost wondering if they would make it. This is one of the hallmarks of a great film - it's just as compelling and hard-hitting every time; __it doesn't matter that you know the story__.

Peter Jackson has outdone himself, and in that, he caused his actors and crew to do so as well. I went into the film expecting it to be good, even excellent, and my expectations were surpassed by far. I have no problems with the liberties taken with the story as part of transferring it to the filmic experience. I do not think that these differences disrupted the story. I actually liked better the interaction between Sam and Frodo, as I have always had a problem with the subservience and deference that Sam shows in the book. The scenery was magnificent, the colors, stunning. Boromir's inner conflict was exceptionally well played - I sympathized more with him in the film than in the book. Everything was fantastic, yet not so much as to seem wholly unreal. Jackson thought carefully about the psychological impact of color, lighting, costuming, and other aesthetic elements, before choosing anything, and also he cared about getting Tolkien's original intent across in the film. Any change that was made was made with this intent in mind, and it shows.

The omission of the Tom Bombadil thread is unfortunate, because it's fun, but it is certainly not a required part of the tale. Tolkien himself said that the point of Tom and Goldberry was to show how some in Middle Earth were not only completely unaffected by the main events of the Trilogy, but also uninterested, so we don't really have to care about them, either.

Fellowship of the Ring is a great film. I think that with time, it will probably be listed as one of the best. Even if it isn't, I don't care. I loved this film so much that I would write this exact review even if I were the only person who loved it, even if Roger Ebert called me personally just to berate me for comparing it to Casablanca and to tell me what horrible taste I have, so I'm giving it a ten anyway.

title: The film will only add to the enjoyment of the books.
review:
After what seemed an endless wait I have finally seen the first installment of the Lord of the Rings, I am a big fan of the book and have followed developments on the production of the film since it was first announced. My expectations were high although I did my best to play them down to avoid disappointment but that really wasn't possible with all the hype surrounding the project.

However it wasn't until I started to watch the film that I realised there is just too much material in Tolkien's original work to be covered in three hours. Instead Peter Jackson has remained faithful to the story but out of necessity omitted some the detail which Tolkien developed over the best part of a lifetime. Therefore elements of the original story are glossed over or ignored and many of the main characters are not introduced and developed in a satisfactory manner.

But while I was aware of these omissions I couldn't help but be drawn in to the fantasy world that this film creates, it is so well realised that I really believed in it. At last we have a film which treats fantasy seriously. It is a wonderful spectacle, a visual feast, the landscape is massive, both beautiful and terrifying which truly brings Middle-Earth to life. The special effects blend in seamlessly and don't overwhelm the picture which is often the case.

The cast is excellent and without a doubt Ian McKellen offers the star performance as Gandalf, you really appreciate that there is more to him than meets the eye. Hopefully we'll get to learn more about the others in the second and third installments.

But above all this is the corrupting power of the ring seducing all who come near it whether they are great or small, powerful or weak, it is a brilliant achievement.

A great story, at times very moving and a wonderful cinematic experience, it's a blast.

This film does not disappoint.

title: Maybe this Movie is Overrated...
review:
I went to see this movie with high expectations. I had never read the book, and therefore, I was not worried about watching the movie with any book bias gnawing at my mind. I had skimmed through several reviews prior to seeing the film, not one of the reviews, had said anything significant to detract from the film's incessant buzz. It seemed as though this movie might single-handedly counteract what has been a disappointing year at the movies.

Maybe, like so many my age, I carry with me the bias of the indomitable Star Wars trilogy in my mind. Maybe, the movies this year have been so bad that critics have forgotten what a truly good movie is and should be. Maybe, the book provides too much story for the world of film. Maybe, I need to go see the movie again before I am so critical of the film. Or maybe, I have forgotten what it feels like to watch a movie for the pure enjoyment of it, because so many movies suck these days. No matter, while the Fellowship of the Ring does much in the way of special effects, set design, and Sir Ian McKellan's career, it fails on so many other levels, namely, I did not give a rat's a**e about what happened to the characters.

There are just too many characters to get to know in this movie. There isn't enough time to get to know them. When the end of this movie finally arrived, it felt abrupt and incomplete. Excluding Mr. Sir Ian McKellen, the characters were no more complex than characters in a porno.

Sir Ian McKellen is masterful and commanding in his portrayal of Gandalf the Wizard. He alone is the movie's saving grace. Is it surprising that, with the exclusion of Frodo, he is given the most screen time and thus we care more for his character's fate. Unfortunately, where he succeeds, the other characters fail miserably. Elijah Wood plays Frodo with the depth and reaction of a smiling deer-in-headlights. He is vacuous and boring. Viggo Mortenson, though he certainly has the chin structure to be a swordsman and reluctant king, comes across as a flat character among many paper dolls. Liv Tyler's character, I couldn't even understand the name, appeared so quickly, during a chase scene no less and an inexplicable love scene, that her only noticeable attribute was the ability to speak Elvish or Elvin or whatever. This years Jar-Jar Binks clones were played by Frodo's annoying buddies, Rudy, Merry and Pippin. I understand they were intended to be bumbling fellows, but they come across as just plain stupid. The other Fellowship members were no more than guys with different weapons and costumes. Who cares if they're good fighters. If we don't know them, we don't care.

I won't go on. I don't know if I've really made any point, other than to say that this movie has been overrated by fans and critics alike. I guess moviegoers have become bleary-eyed by an increasing succession of s***ty movies. Yes, amazing settings were created for the screen, but the inhabitants never breathed life into their world. Ultimately, you can only love a movie when you actually care about the characters, whether they are good or bad guys, who make up that movie. One more thing, the score sucked too. I've heard more rousing music in a nursing home elevator.

title: Good movie, not the best
review:

I had just read all of the books (NOT a trilogy, as the forward says in the books!) within the last 6 months, so they were fairly fresh in my mind. I loved the books, but only liked the movie. The action and scenery were the best I have seen, but the acting seemed to be lacking. It seemed to suffer the same fate of any book-to-movie, in that the actors were acting in regards to the book and the movie, and not just the movie. So they alternated between reacting to events that happened in the book and not in the movie, so you felt lost if you hadn't just read the book; and not reacting to key events in the books, so if you had ever read them you felt like they forgot about something that shaped their character.

Also, it seemed to rely too much on the sweeping, beautiful landscapes. At times I felt like I was at a documentary about New Zealand. But, all in all, a good movie, definitely NOT the best of all time.

7/10 rating.

title: No complaints necessary...
review:
OK, enough of all the Star Wars: Episode I disappointed like complaining about The Fellowship of the Ring. I saw this movie last night, and my only thought after seeing it was lining up right away to see it again, despite it's length. This is the best movie adapted from a novel that there has ever been, period. Even though I have read Tolkien's books five times, and knew exactly what was going to happen, the movie had me on the edge of my seat with suspense. Of course, some things were changed from Tolkien's novel. The major changes that get complained about are the removal of Tom Bombadil and the insertion of Arwen. These two modifications are really one in the same. The filmmakers, despite the novelistic purists complaints made an excellent decision here. Let's be realistic, the only reason Tom Bombadil is in the novel at all is to connect us all back to The Hobbit and Bilbo's story, so it works well in the story to establish that connection in the reader's mind. However, it has no greater purpose in the story of The Lord of the Rings, and in the end is rather insignificant, even in the novel. Now, perhaps if they had made four movies, starting with The Hobbit, the Tom Bombadil character should have been included. In essence, what the filmmakers have done is to drop Tom Bombadil's screen time in favor of modifying and incorporating the Arwen character more. Now, if anyone has read the entire three books, they should have also read the touching appendix on Arwen and Aragorn. Peter Jackson certainly has read this and decided to take slight interpretive liberties to expand the story of this appendix back into the main screenplay. I see nothing wrong with this. Yes, the novel was modified - slightly. Let's give credit where credit is due and congratulate Jackson for getting in 95% true to course.

There have been some other complaints, such as seeing Gandalf's time in Isenguard while the Hobbits journey to Rivendell. But this is simply to make this part of the story work cinematically - it would be a bad thing for the movie to have Gandalf arrive in Rivendell and drone on in flashback mode about what happened. It is much better for the action and the pacing of the movie to show the audience what is happening, as it is happening, not where it is the novel. And it does tell the story presented in the novel.

There have also been complaints about lack of development for Merry, Pippin, Boromir, Legolas, and Gimli. Give me a break, what do you want, a five-hour movie with endless character bios read in a droning voice over of some historical shots? You've really got to remember that what we have here is one story in three parts. In the novels Boromir is a significant character and the movie does a good job of fleshing him out in the time allowed. Legolas and Gimli are underdeveloped in this third of The Movie. But even in the novels the first book is more about Frodo and Gandalf than anyone else. I suspect and hope that, just as in the novels that Gimli and Legolas will have a more prominent role to plan in the second act out next Christmas.

Let's give Peter Jackson credit - the casting is dead on for every character in this movie. Even Boromir, who I had fears about, considering he is described by Tolkien in the books as someone of larger stature than Sean Bean can pull off. However, Sean Bean takes on this role with good acting presence in his allowed screen time so well that Boromir does have the presence represented in the novel, if not physically, at least dramatically. Along with the casting all the roles are well played with no overacting whatsoever.

Other complaints have been filed that the beginning drags a bit, but first time readers of the novel have also had the same complaint. I know many people that tried to get through The Fellowship of the Ring more than once and put it down in frustration right before it starts getting really good. But, when the do pick it up again and get through the beginning they have all said it was well worth it. So it is with the movie. This is another reason why the exclusion of Tom Bombadil is a positive for the film version of the tale, add him back in and the beginning would begin to drag more than a little bit, detracting from the rest of the movie.

Certain people have also complained about the fight scenes, that you cannot tell precisely what is happening and they are rather darting and frenzied. Well, this isn't The Matrix, where every detail is laid out and choreographed so slowly that you can distinguish every move. Jackson makes the fight scenes darting and frenzied on purpose, because it puts you in the midst of the battle, closely identifying you with how the characters feel at that point in time, and adds significantly to the thrill and suspense. You begin to really feel like you are in the fight and not watching some fight/dance on a movie screen. By making this choice, Jackson draws you into the fights at a frenzied pace, and makes a three hour movie seem much much shorter.

There are the little touches as well, such as with Legolas when he is walking so lightly due to his elven nature that he doesn't sink into the snow, while the others in the Fellowship have to plow through it. Such attention to detail has made this movie an outright excellent film adaptation of one of the greatest stories of our time. Let's face it; this is a more than adequate, no excellent, film based upon the greatest fiction novel of the 20th century, and the greatest fantasy novel of all time. For all you complainers, just remember Star Wars Episode I and remember that this movie could have sucked just as badly after all the hype too. Thank God it didn't, it's an 11 on a scale of 1 to 10, and lived up to all the hype and more. Go see this movie, I don't have to tell you to see it more than once, you'll do that all on your own.

title: Peter Jackson should thank George Lucas
review:
I have to thank Lucas for preping me to see LOTR. I was so excited to see Episode I after waiting 20 years that I didn't really appreciate the movie. Episode I is really a good film, it just didn't satisfy 20 years of anticipation.

Hence my expectations for LOTR were much lower than had Episode I been as good as the original Star Wars. As a result I was blown away by the excitement and intensity of LOTR. IT WAS TERRIFIC!! 22 years have passed since I first read FOTR (in fourth grade) and I thought the movie fulfilled and surpassed my expectations. It is difficult to think of anything I would change in the film: maybe the party standing still while the Balrog approached and Frodo being the last hobbit over the falling bridge in the mines; nothing significant.

This film reaches into your soul and scares you then touches you with nobility, humility, and awe. I was moved to think of September 11th and to consider that even though the threat creates fear, we need to take up our ring and/or stand with those who carry the burden despite any fear. The willingness to put aside differences because of a common cause and remembering that we are really all on the same side. The petty differences we focused on six months ago I hope will never seem as important. Finally, my original comments were not meant to be an attack on Lucas. The Star Wars movies were incredible, they literally changed film making and I can't expect ever step up to the plate to be a grand slam home run. Episode I was still a double or a triple even though fans wanted a home run (especially after Titanic).

LOTR:FOTR was a home run and maybe a grand slam, depending on TT and ROTK.

title: As good as it could be in 3 hours ...
review:
I saw it last night at 12:01AM. Keep in mind that I've read the book 18 times, the Hobbit 6 times and the Silmarillion twice. As such, I'm not the easiest fan to satisfy.

All in all, I was very pleased. A few of the characters could have been truer (although, it's possible that _my_ interpretation of them is wrong). Elves are tough to portray. Legolas was amazing -- really amazing. Undaunted, mysterious and aloof, he might have been my favorite IN THE FILM. Galadriel and Elrond were too ... harsh, in my opinion. They are stern and cold in the book, but not harsh. The hobbits were perfect, especially Samwise. Gandalf was as perfect a depiction as anyone could imagine.

The effects were downright amazing. The balrog and mountain troll were just as I had imagined them. At no point in the movie did I feel like the effects were overbearing.

My only REAL complaint was that I sat down in the theater, and before I knew it, the film was over. Through the whole thing the film felt like it was on fast-forward. So many things were compressed. However, this said, Jackson did a really amazing job keeping the storyline with the sacrifices that he made. I really wish that it was 6 hours long.

title: One movie to bore them all
review:
First of all, as I´m from Spain, hope you´ll forgive me if I make some mistakes with your language.

I´ve been looking forward to read the book for years, and I haven´t done it yet. Maybe next summer.

As I haven´t read the book, I´m not sure what should I expect from the movie. An epic history like "Cleopatra" or "The Ten Commandments"? Or merely a thrilling film like "Mission:Impossible 2"?

Despite what I expected, I have to say that this film really bored me to death. It´s too long for the little it has to tell (well, three hundred pages -I think so- are one hour and a half movie, not three!!!). The acting is horrible: Elijah Wood thinks he´ll get somewhere acting with his two unique facial expressions (smile and fear), and Liv Tyler, though she doesn´t appear much in the movie, tries to fill all of us with her sex appeal and hermetism that so well did Liz Taylor in "Cleopatra". But Liv is not Liz. Disgusting, really.

It seems to be a videogame. Really, it seems so. They find a problem: they solve it; they find a problem: they solve it, and so on.

Peter Jackson has made the same as many other bad Hollywood directors: to try in a film the ecuation: "violence + special effects = people looking". This is very insulting for the seventh art, the only ecuation that there´ll ever be when making a movie is "good actors + good script + good direction + good soundtrack + good photography = good movie". But, painfully, "The Lord of the Rings" had none of those elements.

On the other hand, it does have great special effects and great sceneries. God, they´re really wonderful!

The soundtrack is not memorable, sure it´s not. It´s not even good. It doesn´t create the mood it has to create many times.

Since I saw this movie, I can say wonders about how in Hollywood they shoot from helicopters. But shooting so much from helicopters won´t make it a good movie. And it won´t make it more spectacular, either.

At the beginning of the movie, we can see thousands of creatures fighting among them. That is very spectacular. Yet I can´t stop thinking that the scene of "Gone With The Wind"(1939) where Scarlett walked over all those soldiers, though technically was worse, it was more dramatic.

In conclusion, it bore me to death. I hated the movie, I really did.

title: Great Movie - Still, you need to read the book
review: I've been waiting for this movie with a combination of anticipation and dread.  Now that I've seen it I'd have to give it a 9 as a Tolkien reader and a 10 as a movie viewer. If you really love Tolkien, you will be somewhat dissapointed.  There are some scenes that just don't cut it.  Galadriel is way way over the top, and misses what I though was the book's best line ("Wise the lady galadriel may be, but she has met her match in courtesy..") and one of it's best scenes; sam looking into the mirror ("I'll go home with master frodo or not at all").  However, the cinemetography is excellent, and I think that any reader of LOTR will be thrilled with the views granted them. The charactures?  Well I was somewhat dissapointed, but I'll be honest with you.  None of them will overcome my own visualisations of them (ok ok, Gandalf probably will, but the portrayal is sooooooo close to what I'd imagined, there's little difference...).  My only real beef is that Gandalf is not quite the lore master the book had him as (the door of Moria for example, where he was the one who figured out the riddle). **************** OK... Here are some SPOILERS!!!!  If you haven't read ALL of the books yet, go away now!!!!!!! ********************** I was a bit concerned with the doing away of Tom Bombadil's chapter.  Not because I'm a huge Bombadil fan, but because of the chapter in the Barrow. My big questions was how would the hobbit's get a Numenourian Sword?? Well, when Aragorn gave them to Pippen and Merry, I was satisfied.  Not that I was pleased to do away with a critical chapter of the book, but at least the shortcut made sense.. Aragorn should have access to such swords, one would think. I will withold judgement on Awren.  Now mind you I think Liv Tyler is an excellent choice ( I still have her role in That thing you in mind). Getting rid of Gorfindel is a bit of a bummer from a Simarillion sense, but honestly, he's not critical to the story line.  I also thought her actions at the river with Frodo will come up later (when she gave him her "life's grace"), and was a clever move on Peter Jackson's part. Boromir I though was done very well, considering the constricts, but the slight change in his outlook (considering Gondor above his himself) will cause some changes in the rest of the story.

title: disappointed but not disgusted
review:
Jackson has made a good film, not a great film.

Probably the single thing that ticked me off the most is Jackson's fear of a slow spot. For example, instead of having Gandalf describe to Frodo some of the history of the ring, we see a flashback of ancient history. A chance is lost for interaction between Gandalf and Frodo. A chance is lost for the audience to understand Gandalf better, and to appreciate the relationship between Gandalf and Frodo.

The characters of the film are strange people, not easy to identify with. Only slow spots can build this identification. When Gandalf ran into trouble near the end of the film I just couldn't see why everyone was so upset; I hadn't seen any fierce personal loyalties develop.

I've also got some minor quibbles: (spoilers ahead) like: why did Jackson have to let a black rider get about a foot away from Frodo before being distracted by someone throwing a stick? why did Jackson allow the fellowship to be surrounded by goblins in Moria, only to have the goblins all run away when their friend the balrog showed up? why did we have to have that dumb wizard's fight (at the time I thought it was neat, but later I thought: better if they hadn't actually fought), couldn't the plot condensation have been done a bit better so that Gandalf didn't abandon Frodo five minutes into his flight to Rivendell?; why did the black riders have to get within arm's reach of Frodo in the last desperate ride to Rivendell? and why, o, why did the black riders have to be such wimps in battle...Aragorn fought off five of them that easily?

The first book was done badly. However, Jackson's style will probably shine brightly in the next two installments because they are more action-oriented. So far, the fight scenes have been fabulous, and I look forward to the battle of Helm's Deep and the great battle in Gondor.

title: Close enough to get the cigar I think
review:
I've just seen the film this evening, read the reviews on IMDB and probably had the great advantage of having completely reread the book within the last month during a bout of 'flu. I went along prepared to be disappointed and yes, there were casting flaws, (Elijah Wood could have made a great elf but he's just too "pretty" to be a Hobbit) and plot changes from the book. Some of the characterisation does need to be further developed but hey, there's two more films. However, for me at least, the key is that Peter Jackson has managed to retain the soul and intent of the book in a way that I wouldn't have thought possible and I think for most people, most of the time, his vision of places such as the Shire, Rivendell, Moria, Mordor etc will match what the viewer will have built up in their mind while reading the book. For those who haven't read the book then just enjoy a cinematic masterpiece (and then go and get a copy). Apart from the above what worked best for me was that the casting (or most of it) was superb, the acting of the highest standard and the choice of location a spark of genius. I also loved Elrond casually dropping into the conversation about having been in a battle 3000 years ago!

Roll on the next two films, although no doubt the critics will pan the second before claiming the third to be a return to the high standard of the first - or am I just an old cynic! Any guesses on the number of Oscars?

title: Superb vision of a fantasy masterpiece.
review:
I read Tolkien's Lord of the Rings as a teenager and was completely enthralled. It is a masterpiece of imagination and wonder, and was the novel that sparked in me a lifelong interest in fantasy literature. Therefore, I was somewhat apprehensive when I learned about this film version because of the very rare instances when a film matches its original source material. However, after the first five minutes of viewing, my fears were scattered like Orcs before the Riders of Rohan! This is a wonderful, uplifting, and exciting film. To the filmakers' credit, they have been completely faithful to the source material: the story, characters, dialog, action, and setting are all exactly as I had imagined while reading the book. An epic story, brilliant acting, incredible action sequences, mind boggling special effects, achingly beautiful natural and fantasy landscapes...... it's all here. And, it is not necessary to know anything about the story in advance...... the film, through an exciting and visually stunning prologue, does an excellent job of introducing the "backstory" and will appeal to both beginners and experts in Tolkien's world of "Middle Earth".

Please see this film. You will not regret it. In the field of epic adventure films, it is easily the best ever made, far surpassing a certain film about crouching tigers and hidden dragons that for some incomprehensible reason (perhaps political correctness or trendiness) received unjustified critical praise last year.

title: WHAT THE HELL HAPPENED???
review:
So, they finally made LOTR into a movie, now what do I think? As an avid moviegoer I think that the film was pretty good, I think most of the actors played very strong roles and the storytelling was great. But, as a lifelong hardcore Lord of the Rings fan, I have to wonder, when does Peter Jackson get taken to Mordor for his torture? I was looking forward to seeing this for the most part, but when I found out that Glorfindel wasn't in the movie and Arwen was taking his place I almost didn't see it, and that's just a minor change. I understand that when adapting a book into a movie some sacrifices have to be made, but when you start changing how the characters act and speak you might as well write your own piece. For instance, when we first see Gandalf in Bag End with Bilbo, he bumps his head on a beam of the ceiling, Gandalf has been going there for well over 60 years, you think by now he would have realized hobbits houses are shorter than mens. Also they portray the King of Gondor a.k.a Aragorn son of Arathorn as a weak unsure of himself person. My understanding from reading these books at least 100 times is that he is very sure of himself and doesn't need anyone else helping him to make choices. I am sad that some of the hardcore fans that I know couldn't have made these movies, maybe Tolkien would have been proud of them that way.

title: The Best Book-to-Film Adaption is not the Most Faithful
review:
Let's face it: The Lord of the Rings is one of the world's sacred texts. It has probably enjoyed a more attentive, faithful, and glad readership than readers of the Bible, the Koran, you name it, since it's publication. The numbers of people who have read it speaks for itself. You don't hear too many readers of Tolkien disparage his works in any fundamental way. People not only like these books, in the way they might like Harry Potter. They take Tolkien pretty seriously. Is this despite, or because of, the huge amounts of whimsy and lightness Tolkien padded his very dark tales with?

Now in putting this epic onscreen the makers were doing something on the order of filming the New Testament with hearty helpings of the Old thrown in for exposition. To accomplish such a thing in any watchable form is a work of great magnitude, to make a good film of it is genius. The movie is far from perfect but that in itself seems part of it's mission: In its imperfection it simply makes one turn to the books with refreshened reverence. Personally I never thought Tolkien had it completely right to begin with, but they are an astonishing accomplishment, themselves corralling vast amounts of pre-existing material. Tolkien himself was editing and reshaping source material for the eyes of a new century. To fault Jackson for doing the same is senseless. It is merely necessary to realize that Lord of the Rings the movies are not synonymous with Lord of the Rings the books. The places, characters, and events are not the same. They should not be, either, because an exact transliteration would be both unwatchable, and more likely to supplant the imagination of the diehards who could sit through it.

The Ralph Bakshi LOTR was among the first films I ever saw, and I saw it, and the other cartoons, before I ever read the book. Plus I heard the book discussed by the adults in my family. When I finally read the novels in my adolescence, I discovered that I had many misconceptions about the way the story played out. But this did nothing to diminish my enjoyment of the novels and in fact surely strengthened it. If the new movies are thin in spots and apocryphal in others, so much the better for that watcher's future career as a reader or re-reader.

title: A couple of criticisms...
review:
Since there already seems to be a good million comments on subjects like how well the movie followed the book, if it's the best movie of all time... etc. I won't go into detail on that.

I thought that this was an excellent movie. I watched Harry Potter a couple of days before I saw this movie, and I certainly think that there is no comparison. I've read both books, and while the Harry Potter movie was simply inferior to the book, I think that the Lord of the Rings movie does a great job of complementing the book. It does a great job of conveying the fear, anxiety, tension, and the excitement of Frodo's adventure that the book seems to lack - a result of the fact that Tolkien is so careful in developing the plot. One simply can't read fast enough to feel excited when the party stops every other chapter to get a nice bath and a great meal in a warm, comfortable house. Seeing the movie, to me at least, seemed to make the book more exciting because I could feel the way I did when I watched to movie while I read corresponding parts. I think this sets a new standard for adaptations.

However, there are a couple of criticisms that I haven't seen touched on. One of them is the lack of singing in the movie. The book has so many seens where the characters sing amusing or informative (as far as Middle-Earth lore goes) songs, but the movie is completely devoid of them. Although one could argue that these would take away from the pace and the excitement of the movie, it seems to bad that we don't have the "cow jumped over the Moon" scene and such.

Along similar lines, I'm not entirely pleased with the music in this movie. The problem is not quality; it is the fact that it seems highly cliche and repetitive. Even though the music "worked," I couldn't help but to think of this everytime I came upon some scenes.

Overall, however, this movie was absolutely wonderful. Even though it is not perfect (what movie is?), I still give it 10/10.

title: It live up to the hype. What more can you say?
review:
I've been obsessing about this film for two years, checking out for news on the net on a weekly basis. I had incredibly high expectations and I'm relieved to say that it didn't disappoint. Every time I start thinking about this movie I want to go back and see it again. I've only seen it twice thus far and, if possible, it was even better the second time (the audience nearly spoiled it the first time). I cried like an 8 year old when Boromir died and the Hobbits were taken away (I was also on the verge when Gandalf fell).

I was also relieved to discover that my friends and family loved it too. I was worried that only Tolkien fans would enjoy it but at least three of them who haven't a clue about the story thought that it was better than Star Wars (no idle boast for my generation who grew up with Luke and co.). I was also happy to discover that a lot of the girls I know thought it was very good. Even my Mum liked it (but that could have a lot to do with the presence of Aragorn). It's going to be a long and agonising wait until Christmas 2002.

I've read several reviews and there seems to be hardly any mention of the brilliance of Viggo Mortensen's portrayal of Aragorn. The subtlety of his performance made you forget that this was an actor acting (an accusation that could be charged against Sean Bean at some points). In some ways I think Aragorn will become like Han Solo: the kids and the blokes will think he's cool, while the women will fancy him like mad.

As for the other characters, I didn't have a problem with any of them (even Arwen, who I thought could have been a potential weak point). Special mention should be given to Ian McKellen. He just was Gandalf (and to think they were going to give it to Sean Connery at one point). He should get an Oscar nomination at least. Sam and Pippin (great comic relief) were great and the rest of the Fellowship did a good job with relatively little screen time. As for Elijah, he was rock solid, but I think greater performances will come in the next two instalments.

The greatest praise of all should be levelled at Peter Jackson. A masterful display of direction which used real emotion rather than the usual cheap Hollywood sentiment. Lucas should go and see this movie and take some notes.

I just hope that the Academy will acknowledge this film in March (it should get at least 5 including Best Picture and Best Director).

P.S. I'll also just mention that the Uruk-hai were cool.

title: A difficult one to judge
review:
First of all, I went into this film with far too much baggage, the over hyped expectations were bound to be a let down, and having read the books many times over the last ten years (although not in the last 3 or 4) it would have to be something incredible to live up to my expectations/hopes.

I think I needed to watch it a few more times before I can really judge it, but after the first viewing I was left slightly annoyed, this is why.

Annoyed that it was so very good in many places, but let down by naive almost typical Hollywood direction in several places.

the first hour was almost faultless, but the first uneasiness I felt was with the hobbits first encounter with the black rider; the atmosphere, look style tension was perfect, the scene was laughable. The rider seems incapable of catching a few unarmed hobbits while on horseback... he's almost got them, cut to scene hobbits are suddenly 10 meters ahead again, cut to another shot, he's almost got them.. Repeat, repeat... It took all the fear the black rider's image had generated and made them seem harmless.

However it was the Rivendell sequence where I first felt really annoyed, I could put up with the minor plot changes with Liv Tyler; that was done nicely. As soon as they arrived in Rivendell it felt wrong, it seem too beautiful, too cgi, there was no life in those scenes, no people, I always thought Rivendell was alive with people and music, I would have expected a beautiful but more rustic surroundings, I think of the Indoor candle light scenes in Kubricks Barry Lyndon.. Then the meeting was skimped over, no large gathering of people, no real discussion, no long table, it was like this whole chapter was rushed and pushed under the carpet, the only redeeming feature was the excellent Bilbo scene.

I put this all down to time constraints, put it to the back of my mind and tried to enjoy the rest of the film.

Then the Moria sequence, this started great, the imagery was awesome, the atmosphere was good, everything was perfect until the fighting started.....

Why in movies does everyone fight like they are in a movie?? You might think that's an odd thing to say, but fight scenes are cliché, the goodies wield their swords/bow perfectly, can do unbelievable moves, they fight like I do when dreaming.

I again think back to the great director, Kurosawa and his film Rashomon. it probably has the best fight scene ever, you see first the samurai's recollection of his noble fight, crossing swords 20+ times before the final kill, then later you see a witnesses account of what really happened...

When people fight for their life's they stumble, are scared/terrified, make mistakes are desperate, sometimes have flashes of brilliance, its a hard brutal thing and not a 'he shoots he scores' extravaganza time after time.

I could live with the flashy fast cut direction of Jackson, but it just seemed like he was going through the motions, no imagination to move away from the norm.

Then it got worse... the escape to the bridge why do we have to have the Indiana Jones style/dues ex machina c**p that we see in Hollywood films... before they get to the bridge the stairway collapses, they get split up.. ah but its ok because the other stairway falls into the other one saving them... why did we even have that scene, it added nothing, people in the theatre laughed, let them just walk down the stairway for god sake.

The stand on the bridge however was done well, as was the aftermath.

I distinctly felt the whole lady of the woods sequence was rushed, and not given the attention it deserved, it was like Jackson wanted to get to the next fight sequence as soon as possible.

** SPOILERS **

The last fight sequence, was again handled well, the imagery was excellent as was the acting, up until the Boromir's death.

First of all more dues ex machina The hobbits are about to be taken, at last second Bormoir arrives to save them, literally 1 sec before they are about to be killed/captured.

He took far far far to long to die, was it Monty Python?? 'he's dead!'.. No I'm not, 'he's dead'. I'm getting better??? Then as he's about to take his 4th arrow at point blank range more dues ex machina... a split second before the arrow is released Aragorn arrives and saves them again, some more Hollywood fighting, at least Boromir's death speech was well done.

Then finally Sams terrible drowning scene... Why oh why... it was probably some of the worst cinema I've seen in ages. It served no purpose, it was badly done.

** END SPOILERS**

There was some very good imagery in this film and very good acting, the script was good (obviously a sound base) but I think the direction was let down by either a rushed approach, studio pressure or naivety.

This certainly isn't the best film of all time, or even in my top ten, but its a solid top twenty, I gave it a 8/10.

title: Expert film adaptation of the Book
review:
Absolutely incredibly. My family members, none of whom have ever read a bit of Tolkien's work, absolutely loved this movie, as did I, and they are also fond of such hollywood garble as the common person. A very unique experience, and as my brother puts it, "it's like Harry Potter but for smart people."

They picked exactly the right details from the book to enhance upon, and usually, the perfect ones to remove, such as Tom Bombadil. Granted, he's a wonderful character, but he's something right out of a children's book. Like stated before, the Hobbits being eaten by tries and then magically let go through the singing of a strange goofy being about his Goldberry is just not something people accept nowadays, Elijah Wood or not.

The most common complaint is that coupled with the removal of certain scenes, the alteration of certain events(like having Arwen bear Frodo to Rivendell rather than Glorfindel), and the like. The casting was great, and it's amazing to see how closely the characters come to my mental images from the story and indeed, the images many of my friends also pictured for them. That just goes to show the skill of Tolkien in giving you 'detail' without 'going into detail', so to speak.

I have a few gripes however, which could easily have been remedied by the filmmakers and wouldn't have caused much problems. In fact I'm surprised no one noticed these particular peculiarities.

Gimli, where the heck is Gimli in the movie? The Legolas/Gimli relationship in the book, which was well on its way by the end of the Fellowship, is now 90% Legolas and 10% Gimli. Hopefully this was somewhat intended and they will pick up more on this in the next film. It was really sad to see such a great actor as John Rhys-Davies get so little lines in the film, when all his life he's been stuck with horror films and B movies, and now at his first chance to inspire awe in millions, they give him a whole 2 lines in the entire film!! Ah well, I just hope he gets more spotlight in The Two Towers, which Legolas certainly has had enough of!

Second gripe: the fight scenes. I think my eyes really started to ache at the end of the Moria battle. What is with all the camera action?? It was just way too fast; perhaps they wanted to show off the fact that "yes, we CAN have a computer image stay still when the camera is experiencing 10 on the Richter scale! YAY TECHNOLOGY!!" Sheesh. Anyways I hope they're a little easier to follow in the next film. The filmmakers could, for a change, take a few pointers from the Hollywood fight scene choreographers. Brave Heart, First Knight, and a slew of other Hollywood films, despite their flaws, had wonderful battle-filming techniques, which Fellowship seemed to completely ignore.

Third and last, yet the most minor: the fight between Saruman and Gandalf. Though no such fight took place in the book, or at least was said to have taken place, I'll say this once: if you're going to add brand new stuff in, do it right!! They accomplished this with the Riders chasing the hobbits throughout the woods and to the ferry, and with Arwen at the Fords. But with this fight scene, I'd say it was a bit off. Keep in mind that Gandalf has a ring of power, and that Saruman is the most powerful of all the wizards. This makes for a great contrast of powers combined with Gandalf's surprise and Saruman's jealousy. All we get is a few seconds of wall-crashing and that's about it. Ah well, my sanguinism was appeased at the Moria battle at least.

Overall, a great fantasy film despite its flaws. I've never seen one film without flaws, and this one at least has a chance to correct them in two future films!

title: Simply brilliant, I say!
review:
Others have already praised this movie so much that I will settle on some points that made it perfect for me and give some criticism for details that bothered me. (Minor spoilers ahead, so don't read if you haven't seen it yet.)

First, the acting and the camera work (incl. special effects w/ computer renderings) were stupendous. Second, the plot of the classic story was followed very well and the makers had avoided the trap of 'updating' the plot (like in Costner's Prince of Thieves). There's not much one could have done to make this movie better, but some details come to mind: The omission of Tom Bombadil is one of them, although I understand the reasoning behind the decision. Another lacking detail was the scene where Gandalf escaped from Saruman: there was no explanation of where the bird came that took him away (wasn't it supposed to be Radagast the Brown?). Including some explanation of the Istari might have been useful here to tune in those watchers who have not read their Tolkien (sacrilege, I admit).

All in all, I suspect that those who have not read Tolkien's work or studied the maps of Middle-Earth may have been left a bit baffled by the fast recap of the history in the beginning of the movie and the references to geographic locales when the fellowship is discussing the various routes that they could take when travelling to towards their goal. Perhaps the characters could have pulled out a map of some sort to make those discussions clearer.

Another thing that bothered me was the amount of action the movie threw to the viewers faces: the book offered descriptions of the nature and the journey as well as discussions between the characters that alleviated the scenes between action sequences, whereas the movie seems to rely heavily on the action part of the story. Perhaps too much.

But, despite my critique, I think this is The Best movie that I have ever seen and I expect that the second and third part will follow the same excellent route and take the trilogy into the annals of history. And, perhaps, then a prequel about Isildur might be in order...

10/10 for this one.

title: Great film with some comments on Jackson's interpretations
review: Peter Jackson's LOTR series is a fantastic adaptation of Tolkien's famed writings.  I do disagree to some extent with some of Jackson's interpretations of the books.  First, Tolkien makes a serious effort to develop the relationship between Gimli and Legolas--this is never addressed in the film.  Second, many people have complained that Arwen has much too big a role in the film.  I think there is a need (to appeal to a wider audience) to introduce the love story between Arwen and Aragorn, which is only subtely addressed in this first installment of the books (thought the story is told fully in the book's Appendix).  Third, Jackson has seriously tried to make Frodo the "driver" of the fellowship whereas in the books, Gandalf and Aragorn are more in control.  Finally, towards the end of the film, I think Tolkien does a much better job of presenting the ring's control of Baromir than does the film. In addition, I want to note that having read the books (several times in fact, I must admit) I think gives a much better feel for the film. Criticisms that the film ends without any sense of "closure" may be true but that is because Tolkien wrote the Trilogy not as 3 distinct books but really as one whole work. I think Jackson did a great job and can't wait for the next installments.

review:
I love Star Wars. I love most science-fiction films in General. So when I was invited to see 'The film of the year', I was slightly skeptical.

title: Superb! The visualisation is spot on 99% of the time...
review:
I am a HUGE fan of the book, and like many similar people I was worried about what might have been done to our beloved epic.

Firstly, there are changes (some good, some not) and many omissions (by necessity). But - it doesn't matter. The changes are mostly for story flow (I don't think it will surprise anyone to discover that Tom Bombadil has gone on the missing list) and many other changes are small. The important bit is - it's Middle Earth. Not exactly as I imagined it, nor exactly how you did either, but the ESSENCE is there, spot on.

Some of the casting is inspired, and this helps enormously. Ian McKellen is PERFECT as Gandalf, and the rest of the fellowship isn't far behind. The baddies are really nasty - the Orcs (especially the Uruk-Hai) are just great, but the real star of the bad guys is the Balrog. There is a heat haze rising from his furnace-like mouth that just sent a shiver down my spine...and as for the locations, well, they filmed it in Middle Earth, didn't they?

If you like the book, go open minded. It isn't word for word (though there are sections of dialogue lifted straight from the original - "Fly, you fools!") but once you get past that you will really enjoy it.

If you haven't read the book, I guarantee you will want to buy a copy on your way out of the cinema...

I can't wait for 'The Two Towers'.

title: Peter Jackson Scares The Living Breath Out Of Me
review:
This is an incredible film. Three hours of dazzling adventure, knuckle-chewing suspense, powerful action, and majestic sceneries.

Especially the effects were amazing. Not because they were more advanced than in other movies this year, but because they were so damn...tasteful. It´s easy in this sgi age to overdo effects and digital animation (Can u say "Phantom Menace"?). But here every animated frame was just a little extra touch to twist reality that made every added creature or edited landscape seem totally natural. Real life scenery and props still did most of the work. That makes it much more beliveable.

The cast is almost perfect. Elijah Wood IS Frodo Baggins, although both Liv Tyler and Hugo Weaving seemed a bit displaced at first, but it only took a few minutes to forget about who they are. (I kept thinking of Weaving as Agent Smith or Mitzi Del Bra from Priscilla!) But the wizards are the true gems. Seeing old geezers Christopher Lee and Ian McKellen hurling eachother against the walls of the Isengaard tower like two martial arts titans with Big Fat Magic Staffs was too cool to describe. And totally beliveable.

One of the best stories ever told finally has a worthy silver screen adaptation. More than worthy, actually. Incredible

But still, there is one thing that I just can´t understand. THIS IS A MOVIE BY THE MAN WHO MADE "BAD TASTE" AND "MEET THE FEEBLES" FOR CRYING OUT LOUD!!! Who did he sell his soul to to be able to make films like Lord Of The Rings (or Heavenly Creatues, for that matter)?

title: Another Dune, and another ambition unabated
review: There are two books I'd like to turn into films; two fantasy worlds that are so fully realized that I want to try to get them onto celluloid: The Lord of the Rings: Fellowship of the Ring and Dune. I'm a big fan of both, and have read the books, related books and books about the books, so I have certain expectations of films made from them. And, since I have yet to see a film that does a good job adapting them, I'd like to see if I could take the very complete vision I have of them and make a movie. FOTR, much like the two adaptations of Dune I've seen, does nothing to lessen these desires. Most of the comments I make refer to David Lynch's version of Dune, since I'm much more familiar with it, and I don't think it's fair to compare a six-hour miniseries to one-third of a trilogy (though LOTR will be twice as long as the Dune miniseries at its present pace). Let me say that I don't have a problem with adaptations that are well done. Interview with the Vampire, The Stand (it even matched that dead spot in the third quarter of the book), Gone with the Wind, The Grapes of Wrath, Titus, William Shakespear's Romeo and Juliet and Lawnmower Man (even as far afield as the last went from the source material) are all excellent adaptations of written works that incorporate more or less of those works and are effective. Sadly, Dune and FOTR don't fall in that category, but this isn't to say that these aren't very good films in their own right, each with great moments. But even that's skewed by their attachment to the books. In both cases, there are times when the director and/or screenwriter is trying to throw a bone to the books' fans and it just doesn't fit in with the rest of the film; that's what caused Dune to have more loose plot ends than an angora sweater has loose hair ends, and it's what made every ham-handed use of a chapter title in FOTR jar me from any semblance of the suspension of memory I needed to enjoy the film. Another problem both films share is the jarring changes from the tone of their source material, tones that preclude an easy transition from page to screen. The Dune series has very little external competition; Dune has the most battles, and these are presented as small-scale affairs of knife parry and thrust. LOTR (both book and film) has more swordplay, once you get into The Two Towers, but it's not very central to the plot. Tolkien's handling of time in relation to plot is almost Swiss, and changing any part of it would necessarily have far-reaching effects. Therein lies my first major problem with FOTR: the changing of Book I into a John Woo western. I guess I could stand to see Arwen taking Glorfindel's place, though the strange "let my grace" scene didn't do anything for me. The treatment of all the elves, with the exeption of Legolas, really disturbed me. I mean, sure, Galadriel bugs bad boy Boromir, but she isn't creepy! Hugo Weaving kept reminding me of Ronny Cox as Dick Jones in Robocop with his portrayal of Elrond (I do have to admit that it took a while to figure out that he was Agent Smith in The Matrix, so it wasn't a bad performance). The plot and dialog made me think of dadaist experiments with cutting up a source and pasting the clippings back together in random order. How else could an entire scene from the chapter Shadow of the Past move from Bag End to Moria? The use of exposition, both in direct dialog and in voice overs, really made the filmmakers' attempts to make comprehension by those unfamiliar with the books obvious. These unnecessary (to my mind) changes make the story a shallow version of its former self, and are much the same sins Tolkien derided himself for succumbing to in The Hobbit This isn't to say there aren't good points: it's probably the prettiest movie I've seen since Oh Brother Where Art Thou or The Apostle; Ian McKellen as Gandalf and Orlando Bloom as Legolas are great, and Viggo Mortensen, while not my idea of Aragorn, does a fine acting job; the orcs, uruk-hai, hobbits and dwarfs are all great looking; and the sets are nothing short of amazing, even if, again, they don't match my personal vision. In all, this is another film lightweight fans and non-readers will enjoy, but I suspect the wholesale (and meaningless) plot and dialog changes will be too much to ignore for Tolkienphiles.

title: Wow
review:
Well, it seems that everyone bows in awe to this movie, and I am not one to differ!

I watched it on the opening night, and then again the following afternoon. It is a blast of a movie!!!

Naturally, there are some discrepancies between the movie and the books, but show me the person, who could bring John Ronald Reuel Tolkien's thoughts to life! Peter Jackson has done a job more admirable than most, but on behalf of the few faults that can not attributed to artistic liberty, I have to award him a 9. I am loath to do it, but it is not in my power to award him a 9.9!

title: 13 time Reader of LOTR finds an unexpected treasure
review:
I first read the Lord of the Rings in 1975, and I have revisited it 12 times in the years since then. Obviously, I am fan of Tolkien's monumental work of, dare I call it, fiction. Tolkien's works seem too true to not be real (the mark of a great fantasy). So you can imagine my fear at what might happen to this treasure in the hands of Hollywood. Fortunately, New Line and not Hollywood got the rights to do this movie. Burger King light up goblets aside (RANT: This is Tolkien for goodness sake, not Harry Potter - and the Search For Marketing Mammon), I found nothing major to take issue with in this production, and I'm not going to blame Peter Jackson for some corny cups one might find in ye olde dumpster behind a Renaissance Festival.

The bones I do have to pick with Jackson's adaptation are small ones; Where's Tom Bombadil and the Old Forest, or the Barrow Downs? What's up with Glorfindel being ousted for an uberArwen. I do understand from the perspective of film making, why this huge work must be cut and reconstructed somewhat, but I enjoyed this movie too much to dwell on these types of omissions and changes. Let me say that the film left me wholly satisfied. It was true to the spirit of the book and the visual style was so right, I almost never found myself saying, `oh, that didn't look like right, or that can't be how Tolkien meant this to be'. I'm guessing they actually went to Middle-Earth to shoot this and just told everyone they where on location in New Zealand. The casting was inspired, Cate Blanchett was Galdriel, and Woods and McKellen nailed their parts. Sean Astin as Sam came right out of my minds eye, and Legolas the elflord, well, my wife said he was the most beautiful man she had ever seen. And Sean Bean this man is an under rated actor, in everything I see him in he is good. The sad inevitability of the Elves, the stubborn determination of the Dwarves, the soulless evil of the orcs, the tragic conflict of the Men, and the surprising courage and humanity of the Hobbits all come from Tolkien's mind out of his books and through this movie, to the enraptured viewer. This film is a true wonder. Can anyone who has seen The Fellowship of the Rings not be counting down the days til the release of The Two Towers (Which will set all box office record next December)? The Fellowship of the Ring will win the Oscar for best picture. I just took a peek at Amazon.com and 3 different sets of Tolkien's are in the top 10. Harry Potter was an appetizer; The Fellowship of the Ring is the meal.

title: Almost perfect....... nitpickers beware
review:
Film, to me, is entertainment.

Sometimes it can also educate or even allow me to let my thoughts take me to other places hitherto forgotten.

But when it comes right down to it, was my 5 quid well spent? In many cases, yes, because unlike many of the complete film nuts in this world, who cannot help themselves but disassemble, analyse, and criticise all material, I go to HAVE FUN.

LOTR: Pt1 succeeds in almost every way it could, and for that alone, I cannot bring myself to nitpick.

Casting was, like Harry Potter, inspired and perfect; the scenery was incredible; the atmosphere truly other-worldly and the music superb.

It was all I hoped it could be, and simply can't wait for December 2002, when this will all happen, all over again.

10/10..... of course

title: The most awesome cinematic experience I've ever had
review:
My mind is in a daze right now. I have just seen the film that I've waited all my life to see. This was the big one, the movie that delivers everything I ever wanted from a film. My impossibly high expectations were actually not impossible at all. I have just had an experience I will never forget.

Peter Jackson, I love you dearly, but you almost killed me. You see, I had a very frightening experience during my first viewing: twice during the film I got so overwhelmed that I had pins and needles over my entire body, my hands, my feet, even my face. I was really scared, as was my girlfriend, who kept telling me to calm down. What I was seeing was just too much. The first time it happened was Weathertop.. after Frodo puts on the ring. When Aragorn jumped in I had to try really hard to calm myself, and didn't pay attention to him fighting the nazgul. The second time was the Balrog, and was even worse.. I just had to avert my concentration from the film. When I came out I couldn't remember a thing about the Balrog other than it was totally mind-boggling.

I came out amazed at how much I had just seen, trying to absorb it all. Usually with a movie you come out and talk about it with whoever you went with for perhaps half an hour. But with this movie, you could talk about it for hours, there is just so much in it. At first I was numb, and couldn't think clearly about it.. but an hour after seeing it I knew I'd just seen the greatest film ever made and couldn't wait to see it again in the evening. My 2nd viewing was just as enjoyable, as I was calmer and could take more in. My girlfriend (non-fan), while she did enjoy the first viewing, said she had been really worried about me so perhaps didn't get into it as a result. But the 2nd time, when I was calmer and she fully concentrated on it, she totally loved it, and cried 3 times.

The effort and love and technical skill put into this movie is astonishing, and I could see it in every shot. I am starting to feel lost for words even typing this... just the cinematography, the way the shots were set up, the lighting, it was all so beautiful. Seeing Gollum in his cave in the prologue sent shivers down my spine. Middle-earth just felt living and breathing right before your eyes. It was the little things as well as the big things that got me.. such as the short montage of the black riders before they set out from Bree.. all so beautiful and so cinematic. Any quibbles would be so minor that they are not worth mentioning right now.

I was very pleased to see that virtually every evening showing at the two main Cardiff cinemas tonight were sold out. After my 6.00 pm showing, which was nearly full, there were a few cheers afterwards and I couldn't help joining in. I have never seen a film twice in a day before, and I don't think I could have done with any other film, but this blew me away both times. I am still awed by what happened today. It felt very strange arriving home to a quiet house after having been immersed in Middle-earth for 6 hours. I was expecting to be sad after seeing the films because all the anticipation has gone.. but I'm not, I'm on a real high because the film met my expectations and I know I will have it with me for the rest of my life. The world has truly been blessed.

:)

title: Finally, a good epic movie for the masses!
review:
After a year of bad movies, "The Fellowship of the Rings" is such a delightful and satisfying experience. Even at three hours long, I enjoyed this epic adventure immensely, and I believe that most any viewer will enjoy it too. Peter Jackson's interpretation of Tolkien's book has great entertainment content for both adults and children alike, and it also has taken appropriate creative latitude with the book in order to keep the boring parts out.

(Yes, call me blasphemous, but I thought Tolkien's book was boring. Despite its many rave reviews, the dragging narrative of that novel made me yawn repeatedly. Thankfully, Peter Jackson has converted that grievous Tolkien tome into a masterful and well-paced 175 minutes of epic adventure on-screen.)

Before I go into the highs and lows of this movie, I want to publically acknowledge director Peter Jackson, screenwriter Frances Walsh, and the WETA special effects team for bringing Tolkien's book to life in such a crafted and compelling way. Beautifully done, guys... I think that James Cameron (Titanic) is probably feeling threatened now because another film has just rivaled "Titanic" for all-time best epic adventure.

====================================> LOW POINTS OF "LORD OF THE RINGS":

1. They could have cut an extra 15 minutes out of the initial Shire narrative sequence (those darn Hobbits drinking was actually kind of boring).

2. There could been an extra 15 minutes of battle scenes for us adventure fans. (see point 1 above)

====================================> HIGH POINTS OF "LORD OF THE RINGS":

1. This film is so well-told, you don't need to read the book to enjoy it as a 3-hour epic adventure.

2. The battle scenes that were included were absolute fun! As a nice change from exaggerated Jet Li and John Woo combat, these sword fights and ball-and-chain melees are juicy entertainment. There are about five really memorable scenes, including the opening sequence and final sequence, where every guy in the theater is riveted by the action.

3. The battle scenes, although graphic, were tastefully done. Unlike "Braveheart", the gore is really toned down without diminishing the anxiety and tension. This makes "Fellowship" friendly enough to take the kids to.

4. Sir Ian McKellen is absolutely perfect as Gandalf the Wise.

5. Elijah Wood plays a pretty convincing Hobbit.

6. The special effects outdo Titanic and Aliens. The Hobbits are cleverly "shrunken" on-screen to appear as small men, the sweeping landscapes and panoramic New Zealand sets are breathtaking, and the Orcs and Trolls are convincingly nasty.

7. The underground mine scene alone is worth the price of admission. Splendid action and SFX!

8. Liv Tyler's Uriel character was a nice creative touch by Peter Jackson. 'Girl Power' was something the original book lacked, so it is thankfully added to the movie interpretation in the form of butt-kicking Elfen Uriel.

9. The Ring Wraiths and horse scenes are unparalleled. Big points to the stunt riders who staged those scenes.

10. The ending will leave you craving for more... and will drive you to the store to buy the second book to satiate your craving.



==============================> Thank you, Peter Jackson, for renewing my faith in Hollywood. I spent $12.50 to see your movie in the big-screen IMAX theater here in Edmonton, and I got my money's worth.

I look forward to seeing the sequel.

Five stars out of five.

title: CU's Film Critic reviews "LOTR"
review:
I read `The Hobbit' in fourth grade, loved it, and then proceeded to ignore the rest of the Lord of the Rings series for about 13 years.

That is, until I realized I had three days before screening the first of three new films based on the trilogy, `The Fellowship of the Ring.' Luckily, I had a little time, and knocked out the first book in exactly enough time. I finished it, in fact, roughly seventeen minutes before the screening began.

Some of you, I would imagine, have been living in a cave for the past fifty or so years, so it rests on me to give you the basic rundown of the story in question. Keep in mind, I'm not exactly a Tolkien scholar, so you'll be getting the Cliffs Notes version.

In the fantasy world of Middle Earth, there exists an ancient ring imbued with evil by the Dark Lord Sauron (imagine if Christopher Walken and Jack Nicholson had a kid who grew up listening to a lot of Danzig), which is lost, then through a series of chance conincidences, finds its way into the hands of the quiet, fun-loving Hobbit Frodo (Elijah Wood). Hobbits, you ask? Short people with fuzzy toes who would rather be eating and hanging out with their amigos than, say, slaying dragons and such (under this definition, it appears I could also be considered a Hobbit).

Whatever the case, the whole ring situation is just a bad scene all around, and someone's got to get rid of the thing. The esteemed wizard Gandalf (the guy from the `Sorcerer's Apprentice' minus the brooms), played by Ian McKellen, shows up with good news for Frodo: All they've got to do is put together a crew that can haul the ring down to what is basically hell itself and destroy the thing without going mad or becoming possessed.

The film is great not because the acting is great (though it is), not because the special effects almost caused me to soil myself (which they almost did), and not because the screenplay was virtually perfect (which it was). `The Fellowship of the Ring' works as a film because the story is just THAT entertaining.

Little gems of wisdom abound. Sauron, for example, is the Dark Lord and basically the thorn in everyone's side. The thing is, he's not really evil; when it comes down to it, he's just mean. He hates and destroys good things because they're good. But beyond that, we don't know a whole lot about his motivations.

The movie (or book, for that matter) doesn't give us any insight whatsoever about this, but we soon realize that evil or not, Sauron's not really the issue. Where instead do we see the real evil? In Frodo, his uncle Bilbo (Ian Holm), and the members of the Fellowship. Their internal corruptions and temptations are hundreds of times scarier than anything we get from the `bad guys.' Still, that's not to say the film doesn't have its share of creepy antagonists. You're gonna have to see those for yourself.

Need more reasons? Viggo Mortensen, Liv Tyler, Cate Blanchett, Hugo Weaving (yes, Agent Smith from `The Matrix' plays the benevolent Elf King- this film is every geek's dream), and Sean Astin. Above all, though, Ian Holm's screen time as Bilbo is worth the price of admission alone.

I'm not a die-hard `Rings' fanatic, so die-hards may think I'm a little too quick to applaud the `hollywood-izing' of their favorite classic. To be fair, then, `Fellowship' gets a `B+.'
