title: Minor flaws, but a good adaption nonetheless
review:
Well, this turned out to be a pleasant surprise. As a major Tolkien fan, I was rather apprehensive, especially knowing how Hollywood usually fouls up a good book's plot. Peter Jackson has done a very good job sticking to the main plot, and the visuals are stunning.

A few highlights:

  • The look of the film is closely modelled on the existing artwork surrounding Tolkien's work. When Gandalf enters Bag End, it looks just like the picture that is included in some editions of The Hobbit. In fact, Gandalf himself is obviously modelled on Alan Lee's Gandalf as depicted on the Millenium Edition of the books. The visuals suck you right into the story.


  • Arwen. Aside from 15 seconds of bad dialogue, Liv Tyler pulls of a very convincing Elven princess. The expansion of her role is understandable (We only get to see the full story of Aragorn and Arwen in the Appendix in the books) and a fine demonstration of how Peter Jackson chose his trade-offs in adapting the books.


  • Galadriel. A nice touch I thought was the obvious resemblance between Galadriel and Arwen (She is Arwen's grandmother after all). The temptation scene was stunning. Only niggle is that Galadriel's age is not emphasized as in the books. It would have lent a little more depth to her temptation I think.


Now for the niggles:

  • The dialogue is on occasion horrible. It happens in only a few spots, but it is jarring and it mars the suspension of disbelief. Gimli's words on the Sorceress of the Woods are a clear sample, but there's a few more.


  • Although Peter Jackson does a good job of condensing subplots into the main plot, occasionally he could have used a little more exposition. A lot of character history is left out. Especially Gimli and Legolas remain flat and lifeless. The reason for Aragorn's exile could have been made clearer too, as it is presented as a major plot point. The scenes between Aragorn and Boromir are obvious setups to 'The Return Of The King', so they could have done with some exposition at the expense of fluff elsewhere in the film.


  • Boromirs fall from grace is too obvious. He gets nearly no screentime, and in what little he gets he is obviously being set up. The actual temptation scene is wonderful though, but his redemption as he lays dying could have done with a little less dialogue.


  • Elijah Wood does a good job on the scant material he is given. His acting is fair, but the character of Frodo gets almost no room to develop.


  • If you go see it, take a back seat in the theater. The mass scenes are too crowded to properly follow on a wide screen if you're sitting too close.


Overall, there's nothing wrong with this movie that can't be fixed in the sequels. It is a good adaptation of the books, and a very good film in its own right. Worth seeing more than once.

title: Strangers from distant lands, you shall unite to see this brilliant film, or you shall fall.
review:
WARNING SPOILERS

This movie trilogy better be good for the amount of money being pumped into it. And to a certain extent you can see where the money has gone. As an avid fan of the book I can only say that it's a pretty damn good adaptation. The reason why this book has taken forever to reach Hollywood was pretty obvious; it was always too hard a project. With Peter Jackson (who I can see as a LOTR nerd) as the director he has delivered an admirable film.

The hapless Frodo is given a magical ring by his adopted father, and when Gandalf (a wizard) finds out that this is the one ring that the evil lord Sauron once owned, Frodo is charged by Gandalf to make his way to and Elven stronghold: Rivendel. On his way Frodo and his companions are chased by the servants of Sauron, the nine black riders of Mordor. When Frodo makes it to Rivendel the Elf Lord, Elrond, makes it clear that the ring must be destroyed at Mount Doom in Mordor. A fellowship is created,with Frodo as the ring bearer, to enter the dark lands of Mordor and destroy the ring. The final part of the movie is the obstacles they encounter from their enemies including Saruman, a wizard, who has succumbed to the evil of Sauron. For those who have not read any of Tolkein's books they will find that the story is not hard to grasp but the setting will be. The different races and different lands can become confusing but Jackson has done it as simply as he could.

Firstly, I'll compare the movie to the book. The movie follows the book very closely with only few admissions. The most obvious omission is the Tom Bombadil sequence, and I don't think I am the only one who thinks that this was an excellent move. Jackson also greatly shortened the Counsel of Elrond which was a must for in the book it is extremely detailed complex. In addition, the sequence in Lorien where the fellowship meets Galadriel was shortened, and I think this was to the detriment of the movie. A couple of scenes where needed elaborate the Galadriel character.

There were two major sequences where the movie added to the book, the first was done brilliantly. I am talking of the introduction where Galadriel socialises the audience to the history of the One Ring in middle earth. The scene where the humans are battling Sauron's army was breathtaking and is a good sign of things to come. The second was of course the extension of the Arwen character. I like many other LOTR nerds were skeptical, but I was delighted when I eventually saw it.

However, can the movie stand on its own two feet? It most certainly can. The story was exciting and beautifully told, the characters were fully introduced, and the movie was visually spectacular. Although I don't rate it as one of the greatest movies of all-time it is certainly a commendable achievement.

title: Fantastic...
review: I thought the movie was on the mark with the casting and portrayal of the characters... the story was done very well and was probably as close to the movie as was possible, although considerable parts are missing such as Tom Bombadil ... missing scenes are made up by details in the background that true Tolkien fans will notice. Scenery is perfect as is cinematography and special effects... Overall the movie is fantastic and leaves you dying for the next episode.

title: It's all been said...
review:
Wow, what an experience.

It's all been said already.. The cast is exceptional; the plot was already established as fantastic, the acting superb, the cinematography and effects are outstanding...

My only gripes with this movie are that Viggo Mortensen (Who I *do* believe did a great job) and in particular Sean Bean (yet same again, IMHO the right actor for the part) were maybe not fulfilling their roles as far as 'warrior' is concerned.

I also feel the battle scenes were a little too blurred and frantic.. However it's worth noting that in melee battle this is actually quite true to form as one doesn't get much of a glimpse as to the next event...

I feel the ending, although pre-determined in place and time, was a little *too* abrupt. Personally filling me with more annoyance (that it had finished so suddenly) than anticipation of next year's release.

Regardless of these words, the film is outstanding. Definitely The movie event of 2001 *and* I expect the majority of 2002.

Well done to the team that brought the first decent LotR movie to our eyes... Let's hope the next two are even more outstanding, beautiful, impressive and fantastical... Lets also hope that the audience doesn't get bored in the meantime.

Well done Peter Jackson.

title: Unbelievable
review: I took my husband, the fan of this sort of stuff, to this movie thinking I would be able to get a 3 hour nap.  Oh my gosh this is the BEST movie ever made and the best movie I have ever seen.  I can't wait till the others come out!!  I was warned that I should read the book and then go see the movie, they were wrong I think that you can follow the movie just fine without reading the book!!  I really enjoyed this movie and I think that any "non-fan" person would too!

review:

title: One ring to rule us all
review: About a month ago, I finished reading the first book of Tolkien and I was very disappointed. I thought they were too much descriptions and too much dialogues. I really wasn't sure if I would go to see the movie. Finally I went to see it and let me tell you that I would have been damned if I didn't saw it. I've never seen anything like it. I also appreciated the scene with Arwen even tough it wasn't in the book. Finally I recommend this movie to everyone you won't be deceived.     10 on 10

title: WOW!
review: WOW. That pretty much sums up my emotions after watching this movie. After having read the LOTR trilogy at least twenty times in my life, I have dreamt for this day to come. And I am hardly disappointed. The visual interpretation was fantastic, from Hobbiton to Bree to Rivendell to the Halls of Moria. Barad-Dur was amazing, as was Orthanc and Isengard. The detail spent on making everything look authentic and real was astounding. The costumes were great, and the music was fantastic. The casting of the parts seemed to be perfect as well. review: Wow!  This movie is full of surprises and thrills.  Maybe I loved this movie so much because it is so rare to have a fantasy movie be as good as this one.  I enjoyed every part of it even though some parts of the book were taken out or changed.  I would recommend this to anyone except those who hate sitting down for three hours. title: Great Movie
review: Having not yet read the book, I thought the movie was very lovely. You'll have to see the movie to see what took place within the plot....Take Care....Go to the MOVIES!!!:)

title: I am thrilled with efforts to bring these movies into home.
review:
Although I wish for more, it would probably take 9 - 3-hour movies to cover all the wonderful characters Tolkien has provided for us. As for the efforts of Jackson, cast and crew. Hats off. We are getting closer and without you we would not have a prayer. THANK YOU THANK YOU.

My only criticism would be too much focus on romance with Arwen and not enough on the terrible trouble of getting off Mt.Caradhras and the gifts given by Galadriel to the others of the fellowship.

I, as many others in my theatre, were in tears already--at just the idea of this wonderful production being brought to life for us--let alone the reality. Thank you.

title: True to the Spirit
review: Peter Jackson said that the movies would have to please the fans of the books first. As a serious Tolkien fan I must say that on the whole he has succeeded admirably. Yes... there are little things to nitpick (a wholly delectable occupation) but they do not affect the most important thing. This movie has all in all captured the spirit of the books. Whether Gimli wore or did not wear a Helmet prior to Edoras is a fun thing to pick at (he did not) but it affects the movie not at all. The feelings of terror inspired by the Ringwraiths are correct. The revulsion at the ugly Orcs is also. The beauty of the Shire, Rivendell and Lorien is also gloriously represented. Those are the best parts of the movie. The darker scenes (which also contain, naturally, most of the "action") suffer a little bit from the action movie genre stereotypes. That would be my only complaint of what is a ravishing screen version of Tolkien's masterpiece.

title: Beautiful, fascinating, but interminable
review:
There's a lot to like here, but ultimately this film should have been

an hour shorter. The plot is incredibly repetative: the heroes face

horrible danger, fight their way out, and then barely escape--repeat, repeat, repeat. There is almost no character

development, or for that matter, development of anything other than

thrills. But thrill after thrill eventually gets boring, and two hours in, I

couldn't wait for it to be over.

All is not a loss, however, as the magical environment and special

effects are dazzling and almost succeed at keeping the film going.

title: Old "Ring-head" says trust this movie!
review:
They did it! The first movie of the trilogy showed this old "Ring-head" some new truths about the original, mainly with inspired casting and marvelous performances. The "new truths" part isn't that difficult really, as any good commentary or critic shows a fresh side to this world. It's just such a relief to be able to trust a big movie (or three) with something so important; after all I'm a twice-a-year reader since 1973 with a daughter named Elbereth (now twenty-three) and Middle Earth home furnishings!

Naturally I hate having to gallop through scenes I usually love to contemplate, but I will never see Gandalf or Aragorn the same again. They even got Merry and Pippin right! (Gimli needs more good lines.) I react to the changes in plot almost as to the differences in the Gospels in the Bible; they don't so much contradict as enrich or broaden the story. I wasn't distracted by the special effects; they simply made some of J.R.R.'s descriptive passages (which I memorize) become spectacularly visual. I'm not sure how many more times I'll see this one waiting for number two, but it'll be a lot.

title: Visually stunning, but seriously flawed.
review: The best film version of this story so far, but hardly worthy of being called the best movie ever made. The deepest flaw in the film is pacing. While the first half moves at a nice clip, it slows to a crawl at midpoint. Almost nothing happens in the last 20 minutes, and then it abruptly ends, with the story left hanging in limbo. The film doesn't stand on it's own. It's entirely dependent on the next installment. All that aside, there are scenes I found irritating. The battle of the wizards was lame and repeditive, throwing each other to the ground. The scene with the giant troll is just a big blur, with the camera constantly thrashing back and forth. It seemed to be a deliberate attempt to ovoid focusing on the monster, which was a weak element. If you removed all the shots of the ring itself, you'd trim at least 30 minutes off the running time. Why repeat the same footage of the severed hand three times? This isn't advancing the story line. There seems to be a lot of padding, with no dialog. I firmly believe this should be heavily trimmed to 2 hours. Then you'd have a more entertaining film, that kids could sit through. Now, in your mind's eye, picture a slow camera push, on the ring in Frodo's hand. Now repeat that a dozen times or so....

title: The greatest film I've ever seen!!!!
review:
This movie is my #1 pick of the greatest movies of all time in my list. #2 is "South Park: Bigger, Longer,& Uncut," #3 is "The Matrix," #4 is "Gladiator," and #5 is "Scary Movie" and "Scary Movie 2." This movie has everything: great direction (Peter Jackson), wonderful cast (Elijah Wood, Liv Tyler, Viggo Mortensen, Cate Blanchett, Sean Young, Sir Ian McKellan, Christopher Lee, etc.), amazing special effects, a great screenplay (Fran Walsh, Phillippa Boyens, & Peter Jackson), wonderful music (cmposed by Howard Shore), and good fight scenes. Based on the book by J.R.R. Tolkein, Jackson did a fantastic job on keeping the movie the same level as the book. I couldn't think of anybody to do this than Peter Jackson. For anybody who hasn't seen "The Lord of the Rings" yet, go see it. I guarantee you're gonna love it.

****** (out of ****** stars) 100/100 A++++++

title: Spectacular adventure
review:
"The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring", the first movie in "The Lord of the Rings" trilogy, is a spectacular movie epic in every way. This film succeeds in all departments: acting, directing, writing, cinematography, editing, art direction, costume design, music score, sound, and special effects. You name it. The big name cast that takes part in this outstanding motion picture includes Elijah Wood, Sean Astin, Cate Blanchett, Liv Tyler, Ian McKellen, and Christopher Lee. They (along with others) play characters that were originated by J.R.R. Tolkien, the author of "The Lord of the Rings" books, and brought to life by director Peter Jackson (who shot this and the two "Lord of the Rings" sequels simultaneously in his native New Zealand). This, along with "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone", stand head and shoulders above all the other 2001 movies. But I don't want to say that "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" is the best movie of 2001 yet. Right now it is (with "Harry Potter" at #2), but there are still a few other 2001 releases that I want to see that I haven't seen yet (like "Black Hawk Down" and "Gosford Park"), so probably a month or two from now I will know for sure if this terrific fantasy/adventure will finish on top as my favorite movie of 2001. But what a fantastic movie this was.

title: This is a film, not a book!!!
review:
Perhaps I'm biased in my review of this film, in that the director is a New Zealander like me, and much of the film was filmed in my country - and we are a small country with not a lot going for us, so I'm hoping that this film will be successful. Therefore, I am getting a bit tired of reviews that constantly compare the film to the book and try to pick holes in the adaptation. I went to the movie with my wife and a friend, both of whom had not read the Lord of the Rings. They were fortunate enough to be able to enjoy the movie without being prejudiced by their vision of the story obtained through reading the text. They exited the theatre spellbound and very happy with the film. Sure, it probably has its down points, but for the three of us, it was an amazing experience. If only people would watch the film for what it is - a film - and rate it on that, instead of rating it on its adaptation performance.

For me, I enjoyed the wonderful interplay between the characters. I felt that the character of Aragorn was portrayed very well. At the beginning of the film he was rejecting his lineage, afraid of becoming like his doomed forefather. He then had to contend with Boromir's jealousy / refusal to accept him as king of Gondor. Then Boromir's opinion changed and he wanted Aragorn to become king, but Aragorn was still undecided - up until Boromir was about to die, when he chose to accept his inheritance. Whilst this all came from the mind of Tolkien, and was probably represented in the books, I never picked up on it when I read them. The books are very detailed, and quite long winded. So, for me, this film enabled me to pick up on things that I never would have noticed by reading the books.

As for adaptation, I decided before I went to the movie that I would watch it for what it was and forget the books - which I pretty much did, apart from picking up on things missed when I read the books. The acting was excellent, casting good (although, I would have chosen someone much more beautiful to portray Galadriel - not that Paltrow is all that ugly - perhaps this is my mind playing tricks on me, in that when I read the book I had a far more beautiful being in mind for Galadriel and this was gnawing away at my subconscious), the scenery is fantastic (very proud to be a New Zealander and feel very blessed to live in such a wonderful country), and well, the whole thing was just excellent. I think that in 400 years time, people will be talking about this movie like we talk about Shakespeare now.

Okay, perhaps that is an overstatement, still, you never know. But I do think theatres will be replaying this movie in 25 years time, celebrating its 25th anniversary, just like the Star Wars trilogy was. All of us watching it now will flock to see it, along with our kids (or grand kids, depending on your age).

title: The greatest epic ever?
review:
Within the first minutes we know we are in for something of greatness.

Having followed Peter Jackson's movies from the very first "Bad Taste", a very cheep but funny flick. I've always had an inkling that this man could do great things with cinema. But to move from the very good, but only moderately succesful "The Frighteners" and "Heavenly Creatures", to a 540 million dollar 3 film epic is incredible!

I firmly believe if this movie had been made in the US with American hollywood influences we would only have a shadow of what is becoming an incredibly dark, tense and frightening tale. Even with 3 very full hours of film time, many of the books details had to be lost. But a great surprise is Peter Jackson's team who have re-written the story for the screen. This I believe has succeeded in keeping the spirit of the original, with a few concessions for modern thought. Some, like Liv Tylers Elf adding incredible excitement, and moving the story forward past what may have been a slow book section. Also much of the anguish over the ring,s control of the characters is brought more to the fore, instead of the books long character studies.

Many may complain about the films fight scenes, but I see this as a style of representation. The shock of film cuts and the confusion created add to the tense atmosphere. Also the point of the film is the story, not un-necessary blood and gore which would have led to the film being given an adult rating. Remember most modern films us fist fighting and guns, which can show full violence without as much blood as swords hacking off limbs. Peter Jackson has aimed, like Steven Spielberg does, for a movie that all ages might see and enjoy.

This film and its sequels will, I predict, smash all box office records. It has easily ranked itself as one of the best movies I have ever seen. In time It may even be my number one. 10 out of 10 !!!!

title: The Longest Story Ever Told!!
review:
Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" was eagerly awaited by many. From the very first time I heard of it, I had no interest to EVER see this film. After I came across a very positive review by a critic I enjoy very much, I thought to myself, well, why not. I'll go and see this movie.

Now, to be honest, in the first 20-30 minutes of the film it has a nice fairly-tale quality to it. I liked the production designs and the costumes and the art direction all of that stuff! It was a film where you can tell took a lot of time and craft to finish. And, if you have any appreciation for films, you would have taken noticed to that. But, for me, the charm wears off! When you have a movie that is 47 hours long, no story can sustain that time frame. The story to this film is not "strong" enough to go on so long. As I sat in the theatre I kept asking, 'Why can't the movie end now?'.

Certain books make wonderful films. Alexandre Dumas' "The Three Musketeer's" is one of those kinds of books. James' "The Portrait of a Lady", and Jules Verne's "Around the World in 80 Days" & 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea". These books work in a visual medium. But for some reason, I don't think this book works in this medium. I've never read this book before, and I plan on keeping it that way, but, I'm sure if I did read it, it might be an exciting book. Full of suspense of action. And my mind would go to work on how everything must look. And might of taken me to a new world, as the best books do. But, this book, just doesn't work! I know many will disagree, saying it's full of life, and charm. But I sat in that theatre bored half way - no - completely OUT OF MY MIND! I couldn't take it anymore. I honestly don't mind a long movie. I've seen my share. "The Godfather", "Gone With The Wind", Bernardo Bertolucci's "1900" (which is actually longer than this film. That movie is 4 hours long.) and Theo Angelopoulos' "Ulysses' Gaze". And I enjoyed them all. Because they all had a story! A story in which we felt for the characters, we went along with them enjoying the experience. "Lord of the Rings" did not affect me in this way. The acting in the film is good. I liked Ian McKellan as Gandalf, I also liked Ian Holm as Bilbo Baggins, and I thought Elijah Wood did a nice job as well. There are some mildly good points to say about this film. But, the story goes on far too long. Many will say, so what! If that's your only complaint about a movie, well, that's not a good one. I got news for you, it's the best one! Cause if your bored watching a movie, clearly what your watching is not holding your attention. Your not interested in the characters, the action, or anything else for that matter. If they would of cut this movie down to at least two hours maybe my reaction would be so strongly against it. I will never understand the hype surrounding this movie, nor will I ever understand why it's the #1 pick on this database. It's actually over such films as "The Godfather", "Wild Strawberries", & "The Bicycle Thief"! Truly a major disappointment of a movie. * 1\2 out of ****

title: Despite significantly altering the book, The Lord of the Rings is an outstanding achievement, and will go down in history as one of cinema's milestones.
review:
This is a terrific achievement. The Lord of the Rings presented one of the greatest challenges for cinematography, yet this production scales the dizzy heights with breath-taking effects. It is, essentially, one big adventure movie. In fact it feels rather like being inside a computer game! But it is none the worse for that - and assuredly resides as the pinnacle of all adventure movies yet made. It is a superb achievement. But there are some problems, at least for fans of the book...

The film deviates from the book far more substantially than some critics seem to realise. As someone who knows the book inside-out there was scarce a frame where I did not recognise a deviation. Of these, the most significant of all is the denuding of Aragorn of his mystical power. Indeed, Aragorn becomes a rather weak man, unaware of his destiny, and trying to deny his true fate. In the film the broken sword remains at Rivendell; whereas in the book he carries it with him and shows it to the hobbits at Bree. In the film it is Legolas who speaks of a shadow growing on him down the Great River; in the book this is Aragorn's role. In the film Aragorn appears to deny his calling at Rivendell; in the book he shows the Council the sword and declares his identity. In the film it is Arwen who rides out and rescues Frodo; in the book Aragorn carries him 2 days out from Rivendell, and then the frankly ludicrous figure of Glorfindel brings him in. I could go on with many such examples. This is an intriguing alteration, and I think I see what Peter Jackson has done. Essentially, he has given mystical power to the elves and the elves alone. 'Men' are earthly, mortal, very much like men today. This is fine for attempting to bring a sense of realism to an essentially fantasy world, but it does rather miss the point that Aragorn is a descendant of Numenor, and thus a man with a combination of the mortal and the mystical. That is what is supposed to mark the great kings of old.

Other alterations are slightly less problematic. I like the neat touch of giving Frodo the key to opening the gates of Moria (in the book it is Gandalf). Why is this neat? Well because, as we all should know, hobbits are good at riddles (that's how Bilbo got to keep the ring)! Saruman's role is much enhanced - but has to be because the book describes events retrospectively. The whole birthday party scene is altered considerably. Pippin and Merry suddenly become petty thieves. The flight from the Shire has Gandalf present at the outset - completely different from the book. The hobbits arrive at the Brandywine much sooner in the film than the book, and they intended that route all along. Merry and Pippin do not meet them in Farmer Maggot's field. The Old Forest and Tom Bombadil have disappeared entirely (because they have little or nothing to do with the plot, even though the former of these is a glorious piece of writing - arguably the best part of the book). Thankfully Jackson made no attempt to translate Tolkien's awful songs to the screen.

What are we to make of these alterations?

Well... as someone who loves the book, I applaud Peter Jackson. The HUGE mistake with the Harry Potter movie by contrast was the attempt at an exact translation of the book to the screen. The result was wooden and clumsy - and I don't care how many people have been to see it. Books and films are different genres, and MUST be treated as such. What works in a novel does not necessarily work on screen. I take my hat off to the production team for realising this, unlike that extremely disappointing Potter film.

The Lord of the Rings is an outstanding achievement, and will go down in history as one of cinema's milestones.

title: Christopher Tolkien is right.
review:
I first read the trilogy in the late seventies. Suffered through the Bakshi debacle and the lame version of the Hobbit on tv. When I heard that 3 full length movies were being made, I was completely overjoyed. I waited with great anticipation for over 2 years for the first movie. I read all the reviews from Europe where the film was first shown, and thought that maybe someone finally got it right. Alas, after viewing the movie, I have to agree with Christopher Tolkien, this book cannot be made into a movie that stays faithful to the story. The frenetic pace of the movie was mindboggling. What made the first book so charming and enthralling, was the development of the characters at a leisurely pace, along with the mounting tension and danger that ensues as they get closer to Rivendell. In this movie as soon as the hobbits leave the Shire, the story moves like a runaway freight train. There is no time to understand and care for the plight of the hobbits.

What has upset a lot of true Tolkien fans, is the changes that Jackson made to the story. Most notably the Arwen character. But I must say, though this upset me too, it wasn't as bad as some of the other changes that were made. Where was the party tree? The tree is an important symbol in the Scouring of the Shire in the third book. Frodo and Sam do not meet Merry and Pippin at Farmer Maggots farm. At the Prancing Pony, Frodo accidentally slips on the ring as he falls from a table he is dancing on, not from catching the ring as he is pushed to the floor. Arwen at the ford. Arwen at Rivendell. Arwen mooning over Aragorn at Rivendell. Aragorn telling Frodo to leave the fellowship at the end. Frodo being visible in the boat as Sam jumps in the river. And finally the Lurtz character. All of these changes were unnecessary and detrimental to the telling of this story on film. It's a shame that Jackson felt it was necessary to make these changes, for the film suffers for it. I gave this film a 7 out 10. It's a good movie, not a great one.

title: one word, disapointing.
review:
`Lord of the rings, Fellowship of the Ring'

1 ½ *'s out of 4

Reviewed by Matt Doolittle

`Lord of the Rings' is likely the most speculated film of the year. Unfortunately if you are one of the few who haven't seen it yet, don't expect a lot. Like most of the other critics I was excited to see this film come out and like few of the other critics I was very disappointed. `Lord of the Rings' is a film about a hobbit named Froto who inherits a ring from an older hobbit. Little does Froto know, this is no ordinary ring. This ring is an extremely evil ring created by an evil emperor that is trying to take over the world. The emperor was killed but his spirit lives on in the ring and takes over who ever holds it. Froto and his posse, featuring the best of every creature in the land, go on a journey to destroy the ring in the volcano in which it was created. They are stalked by an evil wizard and his army of evil creatures that have come back to life.

The problem with this film is that it never sets any limits. A wizard can make lightning strike a mountain the group is walking on, but he can't strike the group? A bird can save a wizard when he is trapped on a tower, but he can't be saved when he falls into a pit of fire. This same wizard can block the whip of a huge fire monster at one point, but a second later it wraps around his leg and pulls him into a pit of fire. As this movie goes along it gets downright ridiculous.

The only reason I didn't give this film a zero is because of the fighting scenes and the wonderful sets. The scenery in this film is great and the makeup and costumes are outstanding. The fight scenes are the only things that kept this film moving along and in the middle when there are none, you find yourself having a conversation with the person next to you. The fairy scenes are pointless and are not worth watching.

The plot in this film is the controlling factor of everything. When a character is saved it is only because they are needed later in the film. A different character dies only to create an intense scene in this boring, predictable quest of a hobbit and a ring. Another reason this film is a flop is because when you make a book into a movie, you can't use ever piece of dialogue or every scene in the 500-page book. You have to cut it down into only the important things and this film neglected to do this. This film could have easily been cut to an hour and a half instead of almost 3 hours long. If you haven't seen this film yet and still want to, let me give you a little bit of advice. Watch the first half-hour take a nap for 2 hours and wake up just in time to see the final fight scene, trust me you won't miss anything important.

title: Masterpiece Far Larger Then Any Ring
review: One need not be a fan of the popular J.R.Tolkien book, nor even a fan of Dungeons and Dragons time period. This film is a masterpiece of epic proportions and very entertaining to watch. The special effects and landscape is unbelievable and the acting is solid all the way around, especially that of Ian McKellen who plays the Wizard. The only gripe I have with the film is it does leave you hanging at the end and you must wait another year to see how it continues and 2 years to see how it all plays out. The 3 films were finished before the first part was released and I feel they should have released them all within 2 weeks of each other to truly make it one of the most Epic film experiences ever created. This film now stands #1 of IMDb's top 250.

title: Excellent movie, but have an open mind.
review:
First of all, I have to say that this was an excellent movie. I have been waiting ever since I saw the first stills when they began principal photography and I was not disappointed. Peter Jackson makes the locations and the characters come to life. This is a movie that is definitely well worth the price of admission.

I want to post a small response to the people who are complaining that the movie "deviates from the book." I respect your opinion. However, of course the movie deviates from the book. If the book were to be filmed as written, each movie would be six hours long. I admit that there are some plot points that differ from the book for apparently no reason. However, you also have to realize that the filmmakers cannot appeal solely to the fans of the book. The average movie-goer (myself included,) has been fed a steady diet of action flicks that are rife with cliche's. All audiences must be catered to.

All I can say is, go see this movie! Sit back and enjoy it for what it is, which is a mostly faithful adaptation of one of the greatest, most respected literary treasures. Just because you enjoy the movie, doesn't mean you have to stop enjoying the book. If you are so upset that the movie differs from the book, read it again and let your imagination create all the places and events that are described, just like it did the first time you read it.

title: What else can be said about such a beautiful movie????
review:
With so many reviews telling you this is a great movie,

I can only repeat that.

I saw it 3 times and it grows on me. I can't wait for the sequels. I think Peter Jackson is great. Elijah Wood grows in his part as Frodo during the movie. Everyone turned in a great performance.

The only thing I don't like is that I am not in this movie. I would have loved being an actor or extra in such a production.

Go see it, you won't be disappointed. I promise.

title: Close but not perfect
review:
I knew from the beginning that LOTR really couldn't be put to film, but since it has been done, I am glad that Jackson and his crew have done it and not Spielburg and his hollywood cronies. Great costumes, make up, fight scenes and scenery, but the awesome element about the books is the epic feel of the tale and the length and scope of the story. It is amazing that Tolken created a whole new world. The problem with the movie is that there is too much to show and tell in too short a time period. But it is good and could have been a lot worse. I have a big problem with what they did with Bilbo. He was the best character in the books, but they ruined him in the film. The last scene where his eyes pop out and he scowls and grabs for the ring DOES NOT HAPPEN. They bastardized his character. The other problem is that o think they tried to put a moral in the theme. JRR states in his Prologue that this is simply a story and has no moral theme.

Anyway, i give it a 8/10

title: The Greatest Movie Ever Made
review:
This movie is utter perfection! Never did I think I would see a movie that was this PERFECT. This almost seems real - not simply a movie. It has changed me in so many ways.

The movie of a lifetime....

title: Brilliant
review:
While Jackson's Fellowship of the Ring doesn't always follow Tolkein's first book, it does not suffer because of it. The film is brilliant in story, pace, casting and sheer entertainment. The only fault I can find is that I will have to wait a full 12 months until the next instalment.

Definitely my film of 2001.

title: Good Movie.
review: Having never read a single word of Mr. Tolkien, I came to this film without any expectations. In reading the comments of our European friend though, it seems they got a better version of the movie. I thought the cinematography was superb. I didn't give a hoot where the rest of the fellowship came from or what their background was (except maybe for the archer)since I can read the book to fill in that info. What really surprised me was my wife liked it, and she never likes anything that is not grounded in reality. If you like adventure, awesome landscapes, and unrelenting excitement, this is your boat baby. Be forewarned: even though I knew that the book was a trilogy, I wasn't prepared for a totally inappropriate "to be continued" type ending. If you expect part one to conclude neatly, save your $8.50.

title: Again the saga of the fight between Good and Evil
review: The fight between Good end Evil has been the object on numerous stories and legends throughout the centuries. This movie is one more of them combining the story of the Ring of the Nibelung with Excalibur. I don't know exactly why authors have so much attraction for medieval tales to mix them with sci-fi stories and witchcraft atmospheres. Well this movie has got an almost perfect combination of those ingredients plus the usual computer made special effects some of them of high quality. As usual the purity of Good is personified by a young boy who has the almost impossible task of fighting the powerful forces of Evil. Summing it up, a well made movie is not the same thing as a good movie.

title: Fellowship squeezes into 3 hours...a tight fit
review:
Just a few years ago, an hour and a half was considered too long for a feature film. But now, three hours just isn't enough. Having watched Peter Jackson's "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring," I am amazed that he fit as much of the story into his film as he did.

While staying mostly true to the books (remember, it still has to play like a movie) he managed to tell the story of Frodo Baggins and his journey with a "Fellowship" of nine, who attempt to carry the "Ring of Doom" (something like a symbol of oppression and the "ultimate weapon" rolled into one) to the fires where it was created in order to destroy it, in a fast paced, roller-coaster-ride that exchanges Professor Tolkien's slow, laconic style for a seat-of-the-pants dead run.

Fans of the book can see the tiniest details of their beloved Middle Earth fly by at 80mph yet the uninitiated will enjoy the rip-roaring adventure.

To anyone who has read the epic trilogy, it will miss a few favourite details here and there: "This isn't MY Lord of the Rings.

That's not the way I imagined it..." My favourite chapter of the book was broken up with a gratuitous action scene that looked like something from "Raiders of the Lost Ark." Darn! But Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings gets enough of it right that the rest doesn't matter. After all, it is worth the price of admission to see the Mirrormere lake, or The Watcher, or Rivendell, Sauron or even the Balrog for that matter.

The downside? There are two: The first is that three hours is just not enough time to tell the story AND develop character. I've heard rhumor that Jackson shot every scene in the book. If that's true, I'd like to be the first to scream "DIRECTOR'S CUT (Please!)" The second downside? You've read it everywhere, but I still have to complain: I have to wait for another year for the next installment. Now THAT's a tragedy.

Peter Jackson's "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" ROCKS!...and if you can find it on an IMAX screen, see it there!

title: Fighting and threats lacked subtlety
review:
This was an amazing movie, and my hat is off to the director and screenwriter for accomplishing the nearly impossible.

Rather than repeat the well-deserved praise, I'd like to point out that movies and movie goers seem to need a hit-em-over-the-head approach.

I thought that you could have halved the numbers of warriors and orcs and bad guys in most of the fight scenes and had a better fight scene.

The kraken pulling Frodo completely off his feet and waving him around in the air -- too much.

If that Black Rider can get his nose within a foot or so of Frodo and the ring still not smell him or detect it, he needs a new job.

Some of the fighting should have been cut out to give five minutes to the development of the devotion that Gimli feels toward Galadriel in the book -- it would have added a great deal to Galadriel, Gimli, and elves and dwarves in general.

How about some golden lighting in Lothlorien and some sense of the joy of elf-life?

Still, I was enthralled through most of movie. What can you say about a Fellowship of the Ring that begins with a perfect Gandalf and a perfect Bilbo? Astonishing.

title: Star Wars, Schmar Wars
review: I love Star Wars.  I love every second of celluloid dedicated to the "Holy Trilogy," but the time has come for a new franchise to reign supreme.  Lord of the Rings is that franchise.  Fellowship is that good of a movie and knowing what happens in the next two books, I can only imagine how good the next two movies will be.  Even if you have never read the books, you can still understand the movie because they cut out everything that isn't important and they condensed a few things together to save time, but the important stuff is all there.  In fact, it might be best to see the movie and then try reading the books.  The movie will probably help you understand the book a little more and with more ease.  Basically, you have to see this movie, if for anything, Orlando Bloom as Legolas.  Sure Gandalf and Aragorn are bad ass characters and Elijah Wood plays Frodo with perfection, it's Legolas who steals the show and he steals it in the last 10 minutes of the film with one quick move.  When you see it, you will know what I mean.

title: What a Fine Christmas Present
review: This is by far the best film I have ever seen.  I am a Tolkien fan with no qualms about this adaptation of the book.  The visuals are stunning and the battles scenes are well done looks realistic not a bunch of dance moves like in Phantom Menace. The only problem I had was with Elrond.  I keep waiting for him to say "Frodo, It seems that you've been living two lives. One life, you're Frodo Baggins, program writer for a respectable software company. You have a social security number, pay your taxes, and you... help your landlady carry out her garbage. The other life is lived in computers, where you go by the hacker alias "Neo" and are guilty of virtually every computer crime we have a law for. One of these lives has a future, and one of them does not. Other than that I'm cool with it.
