title: a powerful movie (some minor spoilers and ONE BIG SPOILER)
review:
In this day and age, there are way too many movies that totally brush aside the emotional integrity for some blow-em-up scenes that have no real relevance to the actual plot. Example: The most confusing, talent-wasting, horrible piece of sludge that I've ever had the bad fortune to view in a theatre. I'm of course talking about the 1998 flop, THE AVENGERS, starring Uma Thurman and Ralph Fiennes. Thank God in Heaven that LOTR is not one of those movies. This, my friend, is a movie with HEART. When I first saw the trailer for LOTR in the theatre before Harry Potter, I was incredibly excited. I of course knew about the trilogy beforehand, but this was the first time I had seen it in the theatre, and not on my computer at home. I have never read the books, but I knew that it was going to be pretty emotional and special effects filled. I wasn't let down. This movie doesn't substitute emotion with special effects. It's a story on its own. And a lot of people are saying that it's all about the fx and they don't show a lot of the friendships between Frodo and Sam and Merry and Pippin. All I have to say to them is: Where are your eyes??!! You see it when Frodo wakes up in Rivendell and Sam runs to his side, nearly crying with happiness that he's all right. You see it when Frodo is reunited with Merry and Pippin. You see it when Merry and Pippin distract the Uruk-Hai away from Frodo so he can escape. And you see it at the ending, which I enjoyed very much, because it's a trilogy, and there shouldn't be a lot of closure until THE RETURN OF THE KING. The relationships that the actors formed are really noticeable, because the chemistry just explodes off the screen.

Okay, now on to the actors. I've always loved Elijah Wood (he's a hottie, I'm not going to lie), and I make no exception here. I thought he WAS Frodo Baggins of Bag-End. But the closeups of his hands holding the ring, honestly, made me wince. He's probably a serious nail-biter, and although it could've been worse (they could've been all ragged and nasty looking, they were actually quite nicely kept), they were way too short for my taste. But, that's just quibbling. He was amazing, and I thought he really took the role to heart. The best scenes were at the end when he was crying and looking into the camera, his blue eyes brimming with tears. I nearly started to cry. Okay, I'm getting off track. I thought that Sean Astin as Sam was brilliant. I loved him in his role as the best friend. But I have to say that my favorite characters (other than Frodo) were Dominic Monaghan and Billy Boyd as Meriadoc Brandybuck and Peregrin Took, or Merry and Pippin. They were so unbelievably comical. I laughed a lot when they took Gandalf's rocket and blew it up in the tent. However, they also showed great dramatic depth in the scenes following Gandalfs supposed death. When that happens, we see Merry consoling a sobbing Pippn in his arms. A lot of people said that you never see them unless they are acting up and being stupid. Well, just look at that scene!! Ian McKellen was fantastic as Gandalf. Just beautifully portrayed. And the CGI in this film blows away anything that Harry Potter had to offer. The cave troll in this one makes the Harry Potter mountain troll look like Scooby Doo. I especially, however, liked Orlando Bloom as Legolas Greenleaf. He is a very good actor, and I liked him very much. Viggo Mortensen was wonderful as Aragorn/Strider, and Liv Tyler was beautiful as Arwen Undomiel. I loved Cate Blanchett as Galadriel, the Elven Queen. She was breathtaking

I did not see anything wrong with this movie. I loved it so much. The only movie this year that made me laugh and cry both at the same time. The only thought I had after it ended was, "When is THE TWO TOWERS coming out again?"

title: only as disappointing as I expected it to be
review:
The movie is never as good as the book, as everyone knows. While there may be a few exceptions (I might include Silence of the Lambs), Jackson's Fellowship of the Rings is not one of them. Don't get me wrong--it's a good movie, very entertaining, and it is strikingly loyal to the book. Jackson certainly didn't ruin the Lord of the Rings, but I still felt disappointed after viewing the film. I don't really have a problem with subplots that Jackson dropped or even the content that he added. But I do love Tolkien's trilogy, and over the years and the re-readings, I've found a great deal of pleasure in the details of the books, so it's little surprise that my disappointment in the movie can be traced to many equally small matters in the film. At the risk of seeming hopelessly picky, let me list a few of the devilish details that take a little of the edge off my appreciation of the movie:

1. The casting is excellent except for Elrond. Sadly, I couldn't get the Matrix villain out of my head when watching Elrond speak, and that wasn't a good thing.

2. While I'm on casting, let me mention the two elvish women, Galadriel and Arwen. Unfortunately, these two women are supposed to be ideals of beauty, far beyond the limits of human beings, which, of course, creates casting difficulties. I can appreciate this. Even so, I feel like there might have been better choices than Liv Tyler for Arwen and Cate Blanchet for Galadriel. I like Cate Blanchet quite a lot, but her face is too hard and cold to play Galadriel whose beauty tends to be described (in the book) in terms of daylight and sun. And I don't understand why both Tyler and Blanchet are forced to deliver most of their lines in lispy, far-away, dreamy, annoying whispers.

3. As with Galadriel herself, Lorien is much too dark, gray, cold, and Gothic. It looks like stone rather than wood. In the book, even though we see Lorien in winter, gold is the color that stands out in my mind's eye. The Lorien sequences were too short in the movie, too.

4. If I could cut one scene from the movie, it would be the wretched fight scene between Gandalf and Saruman. It's just plain silly to see these two venerable, powerful old men squeaking across the marble floors. And the absurdity comes to a climax when Saruman forces Gandalf to break-dance circles on the floor. It's laughable when it should be supremely unfunny. Certainly the scene could have been staged with more grace and gravity.

5. I understand that extensive character development is difficult in a movie, especially when even the book doesn't always offer much character refinement (Merry and Pippin, for instance, seem largely interchangeable until well into The Two Towers). Still, some points would have been easy to add, such as Gimli's changed attitude about Galadriel, a transformation which is set up by Gimli's grumbling comments about her before they meet. This could also provide the gateway for portraying the beginnings of Gimli's friendship with Legolas, one of the more touching and redemptive strains in the Lord of the Rings.

To be fair, there are countless brilliant details that make this movie enchanting. One that stands out is Jackson's use of the work of notable Tolkien illustrators, like Alan Lee. In several instances, movie settings seemed to bring Lee's painted illustrations to life, such as the images of Bag End, Rivendell, Orthanc, and the great halls of Moria. The movie's settings are stunning, the fight sequences are exciting, and most of the casting (esp. Frodo, Sam, Gandalf, Legolas, and Gimli) is superb. The movie is well worth seeing, but I can't help but note its "flaws," even while realizing that what are flaws to me are strengths or irrelevancies to others. See the movie, but if you like it even a little bit, be sure to read the books as well.

title: I really do know what I think..... Honest!!!
review:
*Definite Spoilers* (although you've probably read the book so you know whats going to happen anyway) I had my ticket bought when they went on sale over two weeks ago and I've never looked forward to a film so much. Was all of the anticipation going to have been worth it. Well, i've never left a film and criticised it so much on the way home. Did I hate this film I hear you ask? No. Far from it. This film could very well be the best film ever made. I've sat through a few similar length cinema films (Titanic, The Green Mile) and I thought they seemed to pass quicker the LOTR did but I'm not saying this dragged. If the next two are anything like this then this could be the best trilogy ever made. Criticise was the wrong word, it was more comparing where the film differed from the book and how things were omitted or changed. These differences didn't detract from the film especially if you've not read the book yet anyway. The opening fight sequence was just awesome, much better than Gladiators opening battle sequence. The special effects all they way through were totally believable. New Zealand's unspoilt countryside was utterly breathtaking, this film could not have been made anywhere else. Tolkien's descriptive writing made Jackson's job easier when it came to landscapes. It's almost as if Tolkien had New Zealand in mind when he wrote it. I think the audience I watched it with mostly hadn't read the book because when Gandalf falls there was complete and total silence in the cinema, you could feel the sense of shock.

The ending wasn't as much of a cliffhanger as the book leaves it but I think it works equally as well this way. I was unhappy on leaving the cinema because my near 3 hour rollercaoster ride was over and apart from experiencing it again i have to wait a whole year for the next trip. In the meantime I suppose I'll just have to go and see this one again and again and again and again.......

title: Far away from the best film ever still superb!!!
review:
I was tired of all these commercials before I went and saw it.Every were it´s Lord of the rings posters and I can go on and talking about all of these hysterical commercials.

I love the books(I read them a couple of years ago)and the thing that makes this film special is that Peter Jackson have really found the right mood for this film.I have never doubted about that Jackson should have made this film bad.The acting is superb,great editing and good cinematography.It´s very hard to make a film of the books but they have really made this film to a beautiful adventure.

I can´t wait to see "Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers".I still can´t understand why this film is voted as number one in the top 250 films. I found it very hard to rate this film because I think that when you see the whole trilogy on DVD I am sure that it will be a masterpiece.In maybe 30 years this trilogy will be counted as a classic.But I will rate the first one 9/10.

title: No movie's perfect
review:
Everyone is just saying the movie just like the book, but I say they are very different. There are lot of things missing in spite of the length. They have had to quicken things to show everything essential (and to get time for the end scenario). Because of this the characters seem somewhat hollow and someone who hasn't read the book will not get familiar with them just by watching this movie.

Makers have invested on creating a beautiful world and it shows. Movie is like an art gallery. It just that I didn't go to movies just to watch art, but to experience a great story. Well, it was a great story but different than I expected. The book is more than just sword fights and escaping black riders. I hope the next episodes will lighten up the relationships between the characters.

title: Movie bored me silly
review:
I never read the Ring books. Therefore, I had no idea what this movie was all about or who the characters were.

This is the story: There's some kind of magical ring that looks like a wedding ring with weird writing on it. It holds some evil magical powers. Frodo, who is a little guy with curly hair and big ears, is supposed to take this ring somewhere. A group of guys gathers together to bring the ring with him. They walk along and then are attacked by a monster. They fight off the monster. Then they walk along. Then they are attacked by the monster. They fight off the monster. This repeats for three hours. After a while, I did not care which monster it was. Some of the monsters were rather clever, however.

What makes a good movie? I think story, plot, character, character interaction. These factors may have been obvious or available to those who read and loved the book. But for those of us just seeing this as a film, I think we had no idea. If you are not a die-hard fan, this movie is of little interest. It IS beautiful with wonderful scenery interwoven with sets, and colorful characters. I would say go to see it if you think you want to. It did not give me a moment of thoughtful reflection either during the movie or afterward. It did not inspire me or give me any particular emotions, such as sadness, happiness, curiosity, etc. It is a spectacle meant to make money. That is what it is doing. It is not a heartfelt work of art, though as you can see from other user comments, many disagree.

title: unbelievable...
review: I can't even begin to describe how fantastic this film is.  Jackson stays remarkably true to the book, but of course in the interest of brevity some scenes needed to be cut.  And no book-based film is going to please everyone.  However, I've read the book and am blown away by the way this movie brought the characters to life... and I know several people who haven't read the book and loved it as well.  Either way this was a daring venture, and I am overjoyed to see the movie doing as wonderfully as it is. Go see it!

title: Have you all been brainwashed or something....??
review: How on Earth can anyone say this is the best movie ever..? This has to be the most overrated film I have ever seen. Prior to seeing the movie, I checked it's rating on the IMDB scale (best movie site ever), and to my surprise it was rated in the top spot. I mean, that makes it better than Pulp Fiction right?. Wrong. Let me say first off that LotR is a good movie. The direction is flawless. Very pretty. I fell in love with New Zealand. My main gripe is that the story is boring. Stupid actually. Not enough to sustain my interest for the three hour running time. The Visual Effects are not spectacular. Pearl Harbor, in my opinion has the best visual effects in a feature film. I even enjoyed the flawed Pearl Harbor more so than LotR, even though Pearl was deeply flawed. But this all just my opinion, and I just cant stand people saying this is the best film ever, when The Usual Suspects is.

title: Perfect film adaptation of a perfect book
review: I thought is was impossible to bring Lord of the Rings to the screen, but Peter Jackson the cast and crew have produced a screen version that is equal to the book.  No film will ever be 'as per' the book, so all the critics of the film should stay to a single media with their anoraks on. A awesome film, outstanding acting and second to none, special effects - its a shame we have to wait for the two towers. 10/10

title: Cinematic perfection?
review: I want to say that The Fellowship of the Ring is the most perfect example of cinema to come along since the large-scale productions of the 50's and 60's. I want to say that everything in it works, from the acting, to the special effects, and all the things that fall in between.  I want to say these things, but I can't.  What I can say is that I have not seen a more affecting story or a more rousing adventure on screen since films like Raiders of the Lost Ark or the original Star Wars.  The film just works, in spite of the flaws, and gives me hope that maybe (I know I'm dreaming here) Hollywood will remember what made movies like the ones I mentioned before truly great, and give us more, and less of the soulless, heartless drek that fills the theaters now.

title: One movie to bring, rule and bind the audience in Tolkien's imagination
review:
It seems an eternity since I heard for first time about the film production of "The Lord of The Rings" (LOTR), the adaptation of J.R.R. Tolkien's literary masterpiece. And when I knew Peter Jackson was behind all the party, I was quite surprised: the creator of "Braindead" and "The Frighteners" conducting one of the most awaited trilogies in the cinema history? A bit strange, I must say...

Well, after 2 years of waiting, several teaser trailers, and lots of previous merchandising, the LOTR is now a reality. The first chapter, "The Fellowship of the Ring" (FOTR), has arrived like a blessing for all the film industry, in all possible meanings of blessing.

For anyone who has read the book, the first impression that you should get from the film is that Peter Jackson has created a pretty close adaptation of the novel. Everybody knows that the novel adaptations to the screen are often not as good as the original book. Just read The Lost World or Sphere and compare with the films. Then judge. :P

But in the FOTR, the adaptation is incredible. And also creating all the landscapes and the different locations of the novel: lots of people say that it's exactly how they had imagined it.

Thank god Peter Jackson has joined a cast crew of "not so known" actors! ^_^ Just imagine, for example, Sean Connery playing as Gandalf, or Brad Pitt as Strider... That doesn't mean that Sir Ian McKellen, Elijah Wood, Sean Bean, Viggo Mortensen, Hugo Weaving and the rest of the actors aren't good! Just the opposite! All characters are incredibly performed. Probably everyone should find in each character little differences from what he/she was expecting, but we can affirm that it was the way Tolkien would have wanted it.

Talking about the film: the landscapes, the crowded battles, the incredible special effects... Everything is joined in astonishing harmony to bring into life a totally new world of fantasy and adventure. Probably the weak point of the FOTR is the rythm of the action. And it's not a lack of tempo, is possibly an excessive speed of the story. It's like they have tried to condense all the book in a 3 hour movie, which is quite difficult.

Of course that there're some missing parts in the film (like Tom Bombadil), but I can imagine the producers saying "Hurry! Hurry! We're in the 2nd hour of the film and we're still in the middle of the novel! 400 pages ahead!!" :D

Anyway, the film is an incredible masterpiece that has reached Tolkien fans and people who have never heard about the novel. I recommend to read the book before watching the film, it'll help to understand what's all the fuss about.

I will steal the ending from another IMDB user comment: "Lucas and Spielberg, learn how to do cinema". WORTH LOOK!!! 10/10

title: A remarkable movie
review:
The Lord of The Rings, is made almost perfectly, and almost unimaginably true to the book(s). Small details are not a reason to badmouth the movie but in all it's perfect glory, some details are left out, to get a better feeling of the Fellowship, etc. The book describes Legolas and Gimli insulting each other to a degree that is hilarious, knowing about the Elven and dwarves disgust of each others races. But this insulting is left out in the movie, only mentioned by Elrond (the dwarves dug out evil because of their greed). Dwarves are greedy, and they dug so low that the Balroq came in place.

The movie is well made, and definitely worth a 9 on my scale. When the movie was over, I wished the 2 sequels would be shown right after, but waiting a year and 2 seems ridiculous.......

title: A film worthy of Tolkien's imagination
review:
As a fan of Lord of the Rings, I am pleasantly surprised at the very positive critical response to this movie. I think it is a compliment to Tolkien's material, and a credit to Mr. Jackson's direction. Even hardened critics begrudgingly enjoy at least some sets, some of the acting, and most of the CGI. I liked the graceful scenes, the eloquent language, the unfolding of the sets, and the wholly artistic approach in Mr. Jackson's directing. In the scene where the Fellowship quits the Mines of Moria, and the Ranger says that by nightfall "this place will be crawling with Orcs!" I felt that lesser films would have been subjected to laughter, but it is a testament to the actors and the director that the audience believed the Ranger's words, and feared the worst. I was not scared by Mr. Jackson's Black Riders, the overworked Orcs, or a few other monsters I seem to have seen in other horror films.

The only let down for me was the Alien/Hellraiser/Nightmare on Elm Street similarity of the LOTR monsters. The only exception being the Orc's pet Troll in the Mines of Moria, and Gollum, whose eyes were absolutely superb! The entire sequence of fighting the Troll in the mines is simply the best thing I have ever seen on a cinema screen! At times I heard the audience sobbing out loud, and cheering at the triumph of a hero, ...something I rarely hear in a movie and never both together ...until now! Add laughter, and you know people are having a great time! For the first time, I felt like I got more than $8 worth of entertainment from a film!

I was too busy working and going to school to see any "hype" about this film. So, I was surprised to hear of any. It surpassed my expectations, and wins a 10 from me. I know the fans of other movies may be disappointed that their's is not number one right now in i.m.d.b.. And, yes, my mother once told me that Marloon Brando, who said "STELLA!" really cool, and pretended to have a heart attack in one of the godfathers pictures, (and who was too good for another Oscar apparently) was the best actor ever, but I haven't seen much of Brando lately, so I have to make up my own mind, and Ian McKellan as Gandalf is the best acting I've seen in my lifetime! Oscar, where are you? The Lord of the Rings is a movie for the post baby boomer generations, and those without an imagination won't "get it." ...You see, there is this whole other world within Earth's past with different languages and different people than you've ever seen, all with their own civilizations...

title: The best story ever told on the big screen!
review: This movie had all the characteristics necessary to make history, from the best set design to the best cast.  I thought the mood of the movie was perfect in every scene, and there was a perfect balance of emotions.  I could truly feel the power of the ring in the eyes of each character who peered into it.  I had doubts that Peter Jackson could successfully capture the greatest story ever told in a modern-day movie, but he did it.  He converted Tolkien's masterpiece into the best story ever told on the big screen.  I thought the set design was the most outstanding part of the movie, from the forrests of Lothlorien to the small town of the Shire. And I must say bravo to Ian McKellen, who deserves the award for best actor of the year for his impecable work in the role of Gandalf the Grey.  The rest of the fellowship deserves all the credit in the world as well.  If you miss this movie, you'll be the laughing stock at the water cooler!

title: Perfectly done
review: Very few movies are near perfect in every aspect.  This is one of the rare few.  The characters, the actors, the acting, the special effects, the sound, the lighting, the locations... all outstanding.  Thank you for not ruining the Trilogy.

title: Pretty, insipid movie
review: Very, very pretty to look at but not much substance nor emotions. The ludicrous story is a series of badly set and edited fights in which literally hundreds of villains of all stripes are cut to pieces by a group of nine fellows, four of which are puny little things you wouldn't trust to defeat a hamster. Unless you are already a fanatic, there is nothing to appreciate but the artistic direction which is flawless.

title: Absolutely Incredible
review: This film is amazing...  Beautiful direction, acting, writing, cinematography - it's a stellar piece of film that I will be enjoying again very soon.  Rarely does a family film deliver with the goods that earmark Lord of the Rings - bone-crushing action and mind-blowing visual effects interlaced with genuine laughter and heart-wrenching drama.  Truly one of the greatest films ever made.

title: GREAT STORY! MUCH BETTER THAN I THOUGHT!
review:
First of all, let me say that I had never read the books before seeing this movie, and that did not detract from the greatness of the film. Anyone who criticizes this movie could not be farther from the truth. Some say that there is no character development?? What the hell is wrong with them?! You watch Frodo go from a Shire-hobbit to the bearer of the most powerful thing in the world.

I think the best part of this movie is the plot. What a genius Tolkien is! The story is the pinnacle of greatness. Anyone who got bored during this movie must have been dead during the film. The effects, although "fake" at times, are overall great. They do NOT take away from the essence of the movie. It is extremely well written, and well acted. The scenery will blow you away! I can't wait until the next one!!

My Ratings (out of 10):

Acting - 9 Writing - 10 Effects - 9 Plot - 10 Scenery - 10 Dialouge - 10

OVERALL - 10

I give this movie a 10/10, ****, four stars, whatever the best is! Although it may not be as good as the Godfather or The Shawshank Redemption, it well deserves to be in the top 10!

title: beg borrow or steal a ticket!
review:
Quite simply one of the best films,in any genre,that I've ever seen.

Excitement,adventure and really wild things,an utterly absorbing three hours in which your transportation to middle earth is accomplished without effort.Everything you see is real,everything you feel is real,with the characters becoming like new friends,drawing you in on their journey.The special effects are totally awesome,with not one "how did they do that?" moment.If the sequels are as good as this,The Lord of The Rings is going to be bigger than Star Wars!!

title: I actually got to LIVE the adventure!
review: It was SO worth the wait to see this fabulous film! Tears were streaming down my face as I finally met the old friends about whom I read so many times before. True to the book (with the occasional but unimportant concession to time), this movie will prove to be a true classic. Now I shall have to patiently bide my time until the next two- thirds of the trilogy come out.

title: Read this only if you can stand the truth
review: I was disappointed by the film. The production was shoddy. The effects were well below the state of the art. Many scenes were muddy and poorly composed. Often you could see the characters sliding around on the ground while running. The audio was often unintelligible. Towards the end of the film, it was apparent they ran out of effects budget - there wasn't a single effect for a long time, resorting instead to cheesy closeups of guys in orc masks. Many of the takes selected looked like they picked the wrong take, or never quite got the right shot. I especially didn't like how the characters who were supposed to be good guys would turn into demons whenever they got near the ring. The balrog was really poorly modelled and animated. The hobbits, who were supposed to be smaller than humans, were quite convincing in some scenes, but then in many others they looked to be about the same size as the humans.

title: I waited 32 years for this movie. It was worth the wait!
review: I waited 32 years for this movie. It was worth the wait!I first read the book in the 60's, and suffered through the animation movies. I and thankfully the director were ready for the version Tolkien would have made, if he had made movies instead of legends.

title: Love it in a different way then the books.
review: I have read the Lord of the Rings since I was in grammar school and I must say that I was nervous when I heard that it was going to be made into this huge movie trilogy.  I even contemplated not seeing it.  After much thought I decided to take the chance and see it.  I loved it,though in a totally different way from how I love the books.  The book in itself is a marvellous piece of literature, and the movie really brings it to life.  It is a visual spectacle and should not be missed by people who have read and loved the books and by people who have not yet experienced them.  The characters are beautifully drawn out and the settings are wonderful.  I re-read the book after I saw the movie and was amazed at how well it was followed even though many thing where cut or changed.  I put them into two different categories and see them as seperate from one another.  Both are amazing and unique in both of their mediums of story telling.

title: Brilliant!
review:
I get the impression that most of the people who did not like this movie also did not read the book. Having read the book dozens of times since the '70s greatly enhanced my enjoyment of the film. I can see how the uninitiated might not "get it"--one hapless viewer commented that he didn't think Galadriel's character was necessary. Tolkien fans will get the most out of this film because they can "read between the scenes" so to speak. However, Jackson did a fine job making the film comprehensible to those who haven't read the book, which is no small feat. Others have complained that the special effects were imperfect and not as good as those of The Matrix (yawn!). I was pleased that the effects were just good enough to be convincing--I went for the story, not to marvel at gratuitous digital technology. Others have complained that Jackson made some changes to the story. First of all, Tolkien thought of himself as a translator of a historical record which was LOTR. The published version of his account can be thought of as The Bible, written by divers hands long ago. For all we know it could be a flawed account or inaccurate. I consider Peter Jackson's version as a different but very similar account--imagine two different books on WWI--you would expect a few minor discrepancies. None of us know for a fact that Arwen didn't rescue Frodo from the ringwraiths. That's not how it happened in Tolkien's book, but it's more fun for me to think that either version is possible. That's how legends and myths are made, tales handed down through the ages, sometimes embellished, sometimes diminished, but in all of them are the grains of truth.

What I liked least about the movie: I have very few complaints. The worst moment is when Aragorn and Frodo are poised on a teetering rock in Moria and Aragorn says, "Lean forward!", eliciting a groan from the audience. They could have just leaped and gotten it over with. There were also a couple of "weed" jokes which don't exist in the book. The soundtrack got the mood right, in a generic way, but it could have been more "medieval" in flavor. Enya and Liz Frazer were clever choices, but why not go one step further and get Dead Can Dance to contribute?

What I liked best: Galadriel's transformation as she is tempted by the ring, the interior of Moria, how the elves were portrayed, and the generous length (three hours!), because I never wanted it to end.

title: No patience? Stay home then!!
review:
Although there are a zillion of reviews out there, I've been inspired enough by this film to not only register for this site, but write my own review as well. This is easily the best film I've watched when it comes to large-scale visual effects since titanic. Kudos to Jackson for having such a beautiful vision and re-creating it on the screen so that we could all share it. I've read the trilogy several times and was very impressed w/ his ability to bring the orcs, cavetrolls, and even the vaguely described (in the book) balrog and ringwraiths to life. What really makes this work is the cast. As everyone else has already praised Ian and Viggo for Gandalf and Aragorn, I'd like to direct a little of this praise towards Orlando Bloom for his first major picture role- Legolas. He slipped into the role with both elegance and direction (of course the pretty face didn't hurt. :P The only one in the cast that was slightly disappointing was Sean Astin as Sam. Somehow, he just doesn't fit the picture. Plus his accent seemed to vary a bit throughout the movie.

Lastly, I'd like to briefly respond to the following criticisms of the film. It's too long??? Already certain important scenes have been cut just to bring this movie to it's current length. That jackson was able to compress 500 pages into 3 hours is already impressive. Complaints were also filed about certain characters missing - such as Bombadil, Glorfindel, and that other wizard. With such a large main cast already, it is perfectly understandable to delete certain parts that do not play an integral part in the plot. Either way, ppl will complain about either the extended length (if more characters are added), or if they are missing, so i think jackson made a fitting choice. And sure, the movie doesn't follow the book's timeline, but do you REALLY want to see viggo mortensen dressed/made up to look like a 50 year old man??

So basically if you haven't seen the movie yet, give it a try. And keep in mind that 3 hours can fly by quickly if you keep your mind open and realize that this movie was made based on SOMEONE's (not YOUR) imagination, so there will be differences. If you are such a stickler for detail, stay home and reread the book.

title: This is tough, because it's not really a movie
review:
All of the comments that you've seen here will become immediately understandable once you understand a central truth about this film: it is not a movie.

LotR:TFotR is an artistic travelogue of a novel. Its purpose (as far as I can tell) was to put images to a story that we already know and love.

Viewed only as a movie in its own right, it's hard to imagine that it could be considered a great one. The plot isn't an encapsulation of a short story or novella that can be told in a couple of hours. It doesn't revolve around a few characters simple enough that they can be fully developed in a couple of hours. It can't, by itself, have a plot, fully developed characters, an ending, and all the other things that are the sine non qua of a great movie, because at best it's only 1/3 of a story.

It could only ever possibly (at best) be a travesty to turn this book into a "movie" in the traditional sense.

On the other hand, there's also no way that it could be a faithful adaptation of the book. Issues of length aside, all of the previously mentioned "flaws" would doom it to being incomprehensible and as non- "micro-emotional" as the original. You can't take a true epic, one where learning to care about the characters and their story takes a thousand printed pages, and adapt it to the screen.

At best (and, WOW, what a best this was), you can paint a picture of the first installment of this 3-volume novel (it was never a trilogy... it doesn't have the structure of one... none of the books stands alone).

Viewed in that light, LotR:TFotR was stunning and perfect. You don't have to see all the scenes in the book, nor could you. In fact, you don't want the same proportion of the "movie" devoted to various occurances as happened in the book. It's actually a plus that the "movie" paid close attention to things that were skipped over in the novel. If you just wanted a copy of the novel, read the novel.

Also, the movie did a better job of conveying the terror of the flight from the Shire than did the books... It's pretty hard to be terrified continuously for ~100 pages...

Ok, I'm as annoyed by some of the liberties taken with the plot as the next rabid Tolkien fan... I have, after all, just finished my 44th reading of the LotR. But as far as I can tell, they were all pretty much necessary.

Let's start with the fact that 27 years of history were compressed into a 30 minute chase scene. Or should we start there? Those years weren't dwelled on in the book either. They added to the story, but only in a very peripheral way (by providing enough time for various other events to happen in the backstory that wasn't exposited until the 2nd and 3rd volumes). In turn, though, that langorous pace detracted mightily from the terror of the Nazgul...

Moving on from there, there's the omission of the Tom Bombadil scene, but in the plot of the books, all this served (besides some comic relief) was to explain how a couple of hobbits acquired some cool weapons that were later important to the plot. Having the heir of a king from times past give them weapons serves this purpose just as well, and takes a lot less time. Besides, given all the controversy over Bombadil, all it would have accomplished to show this scene would have been to p**s off all the various people whose theories about him weren't supported by the film. :-)

Glorfindel is a throwaway character in the book too, BTW...

I could have done without the dwarf-tossing joke, though.

All in all, it did almost perfectly what it set out to do. As for those that say there wasn't enough beauty in the film... I have to wonder which "movie" those people were watching...

How does one compare this to other movies? You can't, which is why it's at the top of the heap for now... Probably to avoid that you'd have to have a new category, which would hold only this film.

title: Simply the best I've ever seen...
review: This movie is a dream come true. I am a lover of fantasy reading and I've read The Lord of The Rings some years ago. Finally a production that joins modern special effects to obtain a visual representation of what I could only imagine until now. The books were a breakthrough for the fantasy reading genre, and I hope this movie will be the same for fantasy cinema.

title: The most powerful movie-going experience of my life.
review:
I'll say, first off, that I've loved the Lord of the Rings (the book) ever since I first read it as a teenager (35 years ago), and that my reaction to Peter Jackson's film adaptation is in large part due to my love of the book.

However, I must give Mr. Jackson full credit for the incredible job that he has done in adapting a literary work that I had previously considered unfilmable. It's a vast story, with an entire world history and body of literature behind it, yet Mr. Jackson's film has brought the story to life in such a way that both Tolkien-veterans and novices alike are able to love and appreciate. This is a landmark film, as shown by the response of both movie reviewers and the viewing public alike. Go and see it. I should also add that it's very much much worth seeing more than once. I was very impressed the first time I saw it, but the second time I was just blown away by it.

title: Yes, it's condensed, but Wow!
review:
The enormous risk in this particular film is that so many liberties might be taken with events and dialog that it becomes yet another sword and sorcery hatchet job. Not so with "The Fellowship of the Ring."

Peter Jackson, the director (and part screenwriter) decided to give some background to the Ring right away to set the stage for those poor unfortunates in the audience who have not read the novel. It is simply splendid. A film can fill in details not given in a novel since action can be so hard--and take so long--to describe. I could quibble with the manner in which Isildur, Aragorn's ancestor, cut the ring from Sauron's hand; but, I must admit, that the sequence is thrilling and Sauron himself is wonderfully fearsome.

The sets are marvelous. The actors are spot on. Ian Holm, cast as Bilbo, was an inspired choice. Ian McKellen as Gandalf is equally as good. And Christopher Lee as Saruman is glorious. What a voice!

As far as the language used in the film I can report that I am well satisfied with the pronunciation of the little bits that were used. I got a small thrill from hearing the voice of Sauron repeating, "Ash nazg durbatuluk, ash nazg gimbatul," etc., at a few points. The voice was almost subliminal but I chimed right in out loud. I've known that verse since I was 16.

As I'm writing this I'm thinking of all the "liberties" taken by the film makers with the story...but I forgive them because they had an immense task: to make a "Reader's Digest" version of 'The Fellowship of the Ring' and make it visually compelling. They have done so in spades.

There are things about the film that remind me how well stories in a book can be rendered visually. The orcs crawling down the pillars in Moria; the Balrog (oh, my god!); the roof of Orthanc; the way Frodo sees the world when he wears the Ring; the flood of the river Bruinen; the Watcher in the water; Rivendell; Bilbo's hobbit hole; the opportunity Isildur had to destroy the Ring at the end of the Second Age; Gollum (!); the ruins of the tower of Amon Sul and the attack of the Nazgul; the pillars of the Argonath; Minas Tirith...to see these things after having read the novel a couple dozen times is really quite marvelous. It in no way spoils what I see in my mind's eye because the vision of Peter Jackson is quite as good if not better. Using the talents of Alan Lee and John Howe, two of the best-known Tolkien illustrators, was very smart.

Yes, there were times while watching the film that my mental images clashed with Jackson's approach. And, inevitably, there are things that get short shrift and things that are not explained well enough. I figure that most people will wonder how Bilbo got so old so quickly after leaving the Shire. In the novel it's clear that Frodo doesn't set out with the Ring for another 17 years after Bilbo departs; in the movie it seems like it can't be more than six months. I also imagine that people unfamiliar with the novel will wonder why Frodo and company stopped in Lothlorien at all and what was the purpose of looking in Galadriel's mirror.

Other things missing include the building of the friendship between Gimli and Legolas; Frodo's song at The Prancing Pony; Tom Bombadil; the Barrow wights; Farmer Maggot; the "conspiracy" of Sam, Merry, Pippin, and Fatty Bolger; the importance of Bill the pony to Sam; Glorfindel, the Elf; the lake of Kheled Zaram; dealing with the wound that Frodo got in the Chamber of Mazarbul; and the gifts that Galadriel gave to the other members of the Fellowship besides Frodo.

But, golly whollickers! There are plenty of things that make up for those missing events. The "birth" of a new type of orc in Orthanc; the surprisingly good performance of Viggo Mortenson as Aragorn (I'd only seen him in 'G. I. Jane'); superb characterizations by Sean Bean as Boromir and Orlando Bloom as Legolas--whoa! that guy can shoot a bow!; the wonderfully horrible settings of the Dark Tower, Mount Doom, and the ring of Isengard; the absolutely, flat-out, incredibly fabulous Moria...and especially the Balrog.

If you have any appreciation for the action/adventure genre you won't be disappointed. If you've read the trilogy then I believe that you will find that the movie sets a new high water mark for the rendering of novels into film. This movie is enough to make me want to buy a DVD player in preparation for the release of the DVD. And the music is good, too!

It wasn't the best movie I've ever seen (I still put 'Alien' and 'Silence of the Lambs' and a few others ahead) but it was wonderfully entertaining. Its greatest value for me, I think, is that, once again, I was treated to the spectacle of someone else's imagination made tangible and memorable. It stimulates my own way beyond what I thought possible and increases my undying appreciation for Tolkien's masterpiece.

See it!

title: Go with an open mind
review:
Just go with an open mind and enjoy.

Whether you like fiction or non-fiction, fantasy or not, are a hardcore Tolkien fan or not, just go with an open mind and enjoy this wonderful film.

Peter Jackson has produced a fantastic film despite 1000 ways he could have screwed it up. Don't think, just enjoy. This film is everything that people go to see films for, something I haven't felt in many years. It has restored my faith in Hollywood a little.

title: Wow!
review: I'd never read the books before but went into the movie with high expectations.  I can assure you they were met and blown away.  This movie was fantastic and really lives up the childhood fantasy many of us had of ever going on a quest of magic and heroes.  Elves, orces, dwarves, hobbits, dragons... wow.  Everything in this (what seemed to be short) film.  I'm going to go out and read the books now because I can't wait to next year to see what happens next.  Excellent film.  Go see it!

title: Great, just great!
review: I'd looked forward to this movie for months, even years, though i haven't read the books. I had high expectations, and I didn't get disappointed. The one thing that is so amazing with Peter Jacksons masterpiece, is the acting. Ian McKellen, Ian Holm, Sean Bean, Christopher Lee(but not as good as in The Wicker Man) and Viggo Mortensen are just superb, especially McKellen and Holm. Though i haven't read the book, they seem like the perfect choice for the characters. The rest of the cast are very good also, and thank god that New Line Cinema had faith in Peter Jackson, no other director could have done this movie better than him. The question now is, how can Jackson do the sequel as good as this one? It seems impossible, but Lucas did it with "The Empire Strikes Back". 10/10

title: Beautiful direction for a beautiful film
review: I never read the books of JRR Tolkien, but the story interest me for a long time. Since I know that Peter Jackson is going to adapt them in 3 movies, I am very impatient to see them. The result of this adaptation is better I thought. The first movie was beautiful. A great direction who should be a success around the world. The readers of the trilogy should be satisfy of this adaptation. I'm waiting the next chapter for the next year.

title: I voted a 10 only 'cause there was no 11 or 12 to choose from
review: The music, the scenery, the spoken elvish, the Balrog, the little things that someone who did not love the Trilogy would have forgotten, all combine to make this the only film in my life that I have ever seen three times in a week (and it'll be four times by New Years).  35 years ago when I read it for the trilogy for the first time, I absorbed it in 4 or 5 hour stretches of time and never forgot the beauty of the story.  I have read it 2 more times since then and am in the midst of a third -  reading LOTR to my daughters.  They did a beautiful job bringing this to the screen - and yes, I know they changed some things, but Jackson's vision is consistent and clearly he loves this epic.  I am sorry that Tom Bombadil is missing and I harbor the secret hope that when the DVD comes out he will be added back in as part of the directors cut. Now the bad news is that we have to wait a year for TTT!  What would you say to starting a campaign to get them to release it earlier!!!

title: simply amazing!!
review: The very first novel i ever read was Lord of the Rings, so when i heard last year that a movie was being made based on it, i was very excited and nervous. After seeing the movie, i was amazed and delighted. Bringing a novel to the movie screen is a very very hard task, and we've all seen the mess ups over the years. However, I feel that they did a remarkable job of bringing Middle Earth to light!! Now granted some things where changed, but understand that not everyone who sees this movie has read the books. (hopefully they will and find the amazing world of Tolkien for themselves!!). This movie was able to delight the Tolkien fans, yet was also great entertainment for those who had not read the books. I was spellbound for 3 hours!! The acting was brilliant. I thought that each actor brought the characters out perfectly. For 12 years I have kept middle earth in my imagination and it was an amazing treat to see it come to life. I love this movie!!

title: Solid movie, but you can't please everyone all the time.
review:
*** This comment contains minor spoilers ***

The production team faced a serious dilemmas working on their adaption of the Lord of the Rings Trilogy. They had to make the films accessible to the mainstream crowd to get a good return on the hundreds of millions of dollars invested in this project, and they wanted to "stay true to Tolkien's vision", as Peter Jackson put it in an interview with German television.

The did a pretty good job on both accounts.

Whereas several episodes of Tolkien's original story had to be rearranged to make the plot easier to understand for the masses, most important details have been left where they belong. True, Arwen UndÃ³miel (Liv Tyler) has a much smaller role in the books, but this being a mainstream movie, you have to include a female character as an identification point for female viewers and an eye catcher for the males. And lets not forget that times have changed since J.R.R. Tolkien's British university old boys club days. Though it would have been nicer to have Gandalf and especially Elrond call to the river Bruinen to sweep the Ringwraiths away, to get a notion of the vast power they possess. And do you truly believe that the average movie goer would have been interested in watching 15 more minutes of the council of Elrond, instead a few cool fight scenes? Which where in my opinion not that cool. True, there are many impressive shots, but overall I found them to have to many cuts, especially in the Moria fights. I hope this will improve in "The Two Towers".

The special effects and the production/visual design were outstanding in most scenes, as has to be expected, given the vast production budget.

The only two gripes I have with effects and production design are the look of the stone troll, which was much to smooth skinned, after all it is born from stone and fashioned after an ent, and the tempting of Galadriel, a little bit of red would have been much preferable to the blue tones used in the scene.

My only somewhat bad impression comes from the dialogue scripts. Although I see a certain validity in the argument that the dialogue had to be adapted to modern taste, we are dealing with epic fantasy here.

Sacrifice, death, grand battles, the destruction of almost everything good in the world. This is not a D&D (tm) movie. I firmly believe that pathos has its place in modern pop culture.

Overall I'd rate the film at 75 out of 100 possible points.

title: Best Story Ever
review: The thing that makes Lord of the Rings so great, is all the elements that came into play in the movie.  I didn't even read the book and I think it's the greatest movie I've seen to this day; visual effects, sound, music, art design, costume design, direction, acting and screenplay were all top notch. There's very little wrong with this movie, it should have been pushed to an R rating so there could be more done.  Lord of the Rings - 5/5

title: awe inspiring.. a wonderful tribute to the genius of Tolkien.
review:
When you wait years for a film you tend to watch the trailers *too* many times. You read the advanced reviews and your expectations grow. Then you get to the day before you see it, maybe even losing a bit of sleep the night before. You eventually make it to the theatre.. and you're disappointed. You've seen it all before. You wonder what all the fuss was about.

WELL NOT THIS FILM. I film myself struggling for words to describe the superb images in my mind as I look back over what truly is a masterpiece. First of all, the acting is masterful, McKellen revels in his role and everyone fits the bill just nicely. The effects are perfect.. Gandalf's fireworks and the flight from Moria most notably. The sound is the best i've heard in film for years... an enchanting score with stirring sound effects. The screenplay was completely up to the highest scrutiny.. all changes from the novel were absolutely in keeping with the ethos of the book and were never simply changes for the sake of changes.

So overall? 10/10. Bring on The Two Towers. Definitely see this one when it opens on Wednesday.

title: The Word Epic was Made for Movies Like This
review:
In a lot of ways, the term "epic" has been diluted in movies by today's standards. However, there are some films that do fit that term. The movie made from the first book of the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy deserves to be in that rarified air. Understand one thing first; I finished the book literally two days before I saw the movie, so I went into the movie wanting to dissect it from the standpoint of someone who has the information from the book. OK, let's get the negative out of the way, which deals primarily with the translation from book (from J.R.R. Tolkien) to film. The biggest problem I had with the translation is the passage of time. One of the flight sequences, in the book, takes a month or more. This same sequence in the movie takes two days. This does not detract from the movie, but it does cause a disparity for those who are fans of the book.

Other than that, the movie does not cease to amaze. The grand scale of the movie, the emotion of the characters, the joy and sorrow all make this a must see. Even if you are not a fan of fantasy, you will be enthralled by the movie for it's sheer emotion.

The "Lord of the Rings" was not written as a trilogy, though it had been originally released in three parts. It is to be one complete work. In the same way, you are left with a semi-conclusion in the movie. You will be satisfied after the three hours spent watching, but you will leave knowing Christmas 2002 can't come soon enough.

title: excellent!
review: high expectations were met and then some. really wonderful film. they really captured the beauty, excitement and comradery of the books. it's one of the best movies i've ever seen....if not the best. it gives classics like star wars (the original) a strong run for their money.

title: The Greatest Show on Earth
review:
What I appreciate most about "Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" is how, from the very beginning, it sits you down and just starts shamelessly pummeling you with the story of the rings and Middle Earth. There's this cool confidence evident in all of it, like the film is alive and believes in itself.

The opening montage, the prologue that explains the history of the ring, is as good an excuse to not walk into a movie late as there has ever been. What follows is, in terms of modern filmmaking, a revolution. Peter Jackson leaves nothing to chance. He doesn't believe in the saying, 'you can't please everyone.' His first installment of the trilogy makes sure a good time is had by all. It's the ultimate in film entertainment.

"Ring" has the inside track to not only get nominated for the Best Picture Oscar, but to win. Like "Gladiator" last year, "Ring" is the greatest overall achievement in filmmaking of the year. Its only legitimate acting nominee would be Ian McKellen, who deserves a Supporting Role nomination. If not, there is a precedent for films winning BP without any acting nominations. "The Last Emperor" did it in '87. Before that you have to go waaay back to the 50s for "Greatest Show on Earth," "Around the World in 80 Days," and "Gigi" to find others who accomplished this feat. It hasn't happened much, but it could happen again this year.

Grade for "Lord of the Rings: Fellowship of the Ring": A

title: best genre film in recent memory
review:
i loved this movie, but let's not get carried away, people.

some people are saying this is the best movie ever made. that's lunacy. ever see citizen kane or casablanca?

no, this movie is not in that category. it shouldn't even be suggested as being so.

however, it's hands-down the best genre film in recent memory (IMHO), easily blowing away the likes of the weak and jar-jar-laden phantom menace.

let's remember that it's the first movie of 3. that means that it's busy setting up characters, motivations and other plot hooks that will be exploited in the second and third films. accordingly, it's got to try to both be a decent and engrossing film experience in its own right and simultaneously seed the way for the coming plot developments.

i think it's almost impossible for the first movie in any series to be successful at doing these things.

8.5 out of 10 for me.

If you have not seen this movie...GO SEE IT!!!!!!!!

title: It's worth it.
review: Just go.  Stop reading all these reviews, let yourself be swept up in the magic of film once again! Even if you haven't read the books, (or perhaps you have children who will tell you the whole story!) it's simply stunning, and I look forward to the next two installments!!

title: A great movie
review: This is one of the best movies that I have ever seen. I've actually now seen it twice within a week (something that I have never done) and would see it a third time.  The movie is a super presentation of a wonderful story. See it twice, in a movie theater, because the first time is such an overwhelming sensory experience. The second time will let you look more carefully into the wonderful work that went into the characters and cinematography.

title: Something truly magic...
review:
This was a masterpiece of cinematic magic, the likes of which I hadn't expected to see in theaters. There were flaws, but there were flaws because Peter Jackson took the kind of risks this story deserved. This is the kind of movie that can be made when a talented director and a talented cast have a passion for their work. The acting overshadowed the special effects.

The only reason I am able to wait for the Two Towers is the feeling that I, as the audience, am part of something special. Thank you, New Line Cinema, for taking this risk.

title: Stunning epic fantasy
review:
Saw LotR last night. We had really bad seats, but I soon forgot about that - the film was really amazing. Fabulous sets and scenery, wonderful costumes and make-up. It was fun, playing name-that-actor with my father afterwards (lots of the actors have been in Masterpiece Theatre and Mystery!s before). All of the actors chosen were, I thought, absolutely perfect for the role they were cast in.

The screenwriters did an incredible job translating this long, and often ponderous novel to the screen, hinting at just enough of everything that you got the big picture and understood things such as the history of the Ring, and so forth, without having to make the movie ten times longer (and duller, for those audience members who were not fond of the fantasy motif of which I am a great fan).

The music was absolutely beautiful - it's not too often that, whilst watching a movie (especially for the first time and in a cinema), you actually notice the score. But I did, as did my father, and both of us agreed that the Lord of the Rings soundtrack is one CD we'll have to get.

We had a lot of trouble with audience members who talked LOUDLY and left their cell phones and pagers on, then had the audacity to say that it was 'stupid' at the end. But what most of them didn't realise is that Fellowship of the Rings is but the first of three. I think the PR people ought to do something about that situation - call it Lord of the Rings Part 1: The Fellowship of the Ring, or something like that. Maybe call it Fellowship more and Lord of the Rings less. It really does have a cliffhanger ending (naturally) that would make it seem like a terrible movie if you didn't know that there would be two more coming, as in the Star Wars style.

All in all, I think this is a really tremendous film, and I will definitely be buying it when it comes out on video. I recommend it to everyone, it's simply stunning.

title: All I could have hoped for; I forgive them for cutting Tom Bombadil.
review: It was all I could have hoped for. An outstanding achievement - bringing to life such a deeply-detailed fantasy. Excellently cast. It all works. I even forgive them for cutting Tom Bombadil.

title: Truly beautiful, second viewing cleanses all =)
review:
I went to my first screening of 'Fellowship of the Rings' with over 40 readings of 'Lord of the Rings' under my belt and having read probably 100 movie reviews. By the end of my first viewing of the movie I felt like I had just done 3 rounds with Ali. Too many thoughts and emotions were competing with Jackson's movie.

The second time I saw the movie, 2 days later, was absolutely marvelous the nerves were gone preconceptions jettisoned. I absolutely adored and relished my second viewing of the movie.

Something happened that I never thought possible! Elijah Wood's portrayal of Frodo improved on the book. My greatest fear was the spirit of Frodo and Sam's friendship would be lost, I need not have feared. The scene at the end between Frodo and Sam was magic only a movie could deliver. For that alone Elijah, Sean and Jackson are forever my heroes thank you! Frodo lives in Elijah and I rejoice.

Don't listen to the nay sayers Jackson your way is wonderful Bravo!

P.S. I will be watching Fellowship again tomorrow and cannot wait.

title: Awesome
review:
It's not the film of the book, but it's a fabulous film and I really, really enjoyed it.

Having read the book 12 times in 20 years, I obviously have my favourite characters and chapters. I was both very keen and a bit apprehensive to see how it'd all been interpreted, and I was delighted with the outcome.

I could have sat through an extra hour to see some scenes dealt with in more detail: the Inn at Bree; the battle on the hill with the ring wraiths; and particularly Lothlorian and Galadriel.

However, as entertaining as these chapters are in the book, they have been slimmed down to keep the main plot and characters moving along.

There are also some improvements: Merry and Pippin came over very well, they're not the upper-class twits of Tolkien's "Fellowship". The party was handled brilliantly: straight to the point, without getting bogged down in detail.

Arwen's character has been involved in the main plot which redresses Tolkein's male-character bias (in the Fellowship at least).

Moria and the balrog is the stand-out sequence for me, quite stunning. Bringing forward Saruman's involvement from the Two Towers to the Fellowship was also an inspired idea, and Christopher Lee was in great form, never better.

I've read some uncomplimentary things about the acting, but I thought all the main characters were superbly represented (especially Gandalf and Bilbo).

Would Tolkein have approved? No, I think he'd have HATED it, because so many of the key character-building scenes are missed out (mainly the woods, the barrow-wights, the Inn at Bree and how Bill the pony got his name, and Lothlorian).

The film is a lot more action-oriented than the book, and all the better (as a film, as opposed to a story) for it.

To have recreated the book in detail would have needed 6 to 8 hours, and achieving what was done in "only" three hours is a stroke of genius.

My one and only complaint: why do I have to wait a year to see the Two Towers....?

My hope: the DVD release has lots and lots of deleted scenes added into the main film (not on disk 2) to flesh out the storyline even further.

A well deserved, justified and not-at-all-hyped ten out of ten.

title: Stunning.
review:
It's been said before, and I'm going to say it again: This is an excellent film. True, it's not completely faithful to the books, and it misses out some quite important pieces of the book (especially some of the character's backgrounds)in favour of more dramatic action sequences.

The only other problems I had with it was that some of the CGI was a little too obviously CGI (a problem shared by Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone), and the battles were a little bit hard to follow (but then again it's just as easy to argue that the camerawork reflects the confusion of a good old fashioned melee), but in a film that kept me entertained for 3 hours, these are insignificant problems :).

Hopefully people not familiar with Lord of the Rings will see the film and be sufficiently impressed by it to read the books, and see the amazing world Tolkien created.

title: loved the movie even though I didn't read the book
review: This movie is unlike any other I have seen.  I bought into the storyline and couldn't wait to see what happened next to the fellowship.  It is good fun and you should see it for yourself.  I don't think it is the best of all time, but certainly best of the year.

title: Loved it and will see it again (and again)!!
review:
I loved this movie. The Hobbit and the Lord of the Rings trilogy are books that I have re-read often since I was a teenager (suffice to say that has been a long time). I have often pictured how a movie of the books would look. THE LORD OF THE RINGS (2001) has captured the essence of Tolkien's stories. Frodo, Bilbo, Gandalf, Legolas, Gimli et al, looked just like I imagined they would. My only criticism is that it is going to take too long for the second and third movies to be released.

My recommendation? Go see this movie!! I give it a double thumbs up.

title: The saga Tolkien was looking for
review:
A lot of the publicity around the launch (in the UK anyway) pointed to Tolkien's ideal of creating an 'English' saga. I must admit I'd not really got this from the book, but certainly did from the film.

Like the Norse sagas, there was great interaction between the 'powerful' and ordinary people. And like a lot of sagas, the not so powerful are key in the end.

Overall Tolkien's vision plus Jackson's interpretation achieves a masterpiece... one which I think will improve over time - I'd certainly get more from a second viewing.

title: Believe the hype - you'll enjoy it more
review:
There's been a lot of hyperbole surrounding this movie. And is it all true? That depends. What we have here is a very good movie (maybe a great movie) and one of those rare occasions when if you believe the hype, you're likely to enjoy it a whole lot more. It's a throwback to the good old days of Jaws and ET and Raiders, when a film could be great without trying to be deep and meaningful - when blockbusters were GOOD. It's an event.

The movie itself makes no attempt to hide this fact. FoTR KNOWS its an event movie. From the moment the titles fade and the cinema fills with foreboding choral music and strange, whispered elvish speech, this movie feels big. Taking a leaf out of Spielberg's book, Jackson doesn't keep the epic battle scenes for the climax, he introduces them only a couple of minutes in. And it's not all for show either, these scenes are vital in setting the tone: don't be fooled by all the cute little hobbits - this is serious end-of-the-world stuff. The sense of gravitas is carried beyond the prologue and into the first act of the movie proper by the two Sir Ians, Holm and McKellen. Holm's Bilbo Baggins is a sad old man who is slowly being eaten away by his addiction to the ring of power and does not yet know it. McKellen's Gandalf is at once powerful and playful, clearly deeply concerned for his old friend, yet pulling no punches when it comes down to business. Whenever the two share the screen you can be in no doubt that you are watching two of Britain's greatest living actors. As for Elijah Wood's Frodo, the term 'more than just a pretty face' has never seemed more apt: from the childlike, carefree halfling to the disturbed, weary adventurer, the transition is played flawlessly and it is heartbreaking.

This is of course an adventure movie and it's once the adventure begins that it really kicks off. Like the book, it's fairly linear plot-wise, structured as a string of set pieces as Frodo & co battle first the nightmarish ringwraiths, then orcs, squids, the demonic Balrog and the vicious Uruk-hai, who bear a striking resemblance to Mel Gibson's William Wallace. The lack of a single tangible bad guy is compensated for by infusing every scene with a sense of menace. The ring itself becomes the real baddie, whispering sweet nothings to tempt even the most pure hearted of Frodo's allies, while the Dark Lord Sauron appears as a giant flaming eyeball (it's scarier than it sounds - honest!), endlessly searching for Frodo and the ring.

What really lifts this film above the ranks of hollywood popcorn fare is the imagination and deep affection that has clearly gone into making it. There are countless blink-and-miss-it moments that any old rent-a-director simply wouldn't have bothered with. To mention but a few: when Bilbo drops the ring, it falls to the ground with a thud - not a clatter, nor a tinkle, but a thud; when we see the nine kings of men who are given the nine rings, we see them looking sinister and shrouded in blackness - a hint at what they are to become; when the ringwraith crouches over the hobbits, centipedes and worms squirm out of the earth to get away from it; and Gandalf's face when Frodo volunteers to destroy the ring is a picture of deep, deep sadness and great love - credit to Ian McKellen for that. There are too many of these little moments to mention but every one adds a dimension to the world that Peter Jackson has created.

Sadly, as this is only the first part of the story, it suffers from an abrupt ending and a lack of character development. It would have been nice to see more of the Fellowship. Legolas should have been allowed to do a little more that look distant and say things like 'I sense danger' whilst Gimli's heritage could have been fleshed out a tad. But these are luxuries that, even in a 3 hour film, there really isn't time for. The more important characters, Aragorn, Gandalf etc. are all captured perfectly. You really want to jump out of your seat and cheer when Aragorn saves Frodo on Weathertop, and Boromir redeems himself so valiantly in his attempts to defend the hobbits and his downright refusal to die that you really do care when he finally snuffs it.

The key to really enjoying this film is suspending disbelief, believing the hype and enjoying the ride. I could go on for hours but I see that I already have, so all I want to say in conclusion is that this may not be the best movie ever, but it was well worth three hours of my life and I'd give it another three tomorrow. I know which episode 2 I'll be most looking forward to next year and it aint nothing to do with Clones.

title: An average movie at best
review: This is not a great movie and in no way deserves to be ranked #1 of all time. Innumerable camera and lighting tricks, stilted dialogue, a complete lack of character development, and a persistent dark, gothic feel--including constant, over-the-top "mood" music--destroy its enjoyability. It looks like all of these people who ranked it a "10" are so in love with Tolkien's story that they are blinded to the movie's lack of quality. And yes, just in case anyone is wondering, I have read the Hobbit and the LoR trilogy--at the age of 12, in my mid-teens, and I am currently reading them to my 7 year old son.
