Of course, to repeat myself, no movie is as good as the book (to my way of thinking) but this movie had enough to make it interesting and little enough to make you want more.  NOTE TO ALL VIEWERS!: The movie WILL leave you hanging.  A lot of people i have seen were very confused about the way the movie ended but there are 2 sequels.  just thought i would warn you! well, Bon Voyage!  Enjoy the movie!

title: Best Movie Ever? No, it's not.
review:
This movie has received a lot of 10/10 ratings from IMDB viewers, pushing it to the #1 all time best movie. A rating of 10/10 implies a "perfect" movie. However, most writers on IMDB who gave a 10/10 also wrote that the movie has it's flaws. So which is it? 10/10 or flawed?

The movie has that "reduced color" appearance to give a near-black&white aged appearance, and it wasn't done well, so it looks grainy and bad. There's little color in the film. The film is overly loud in segments where the sound should be quiet. Don't see the film in a multiplex since these theaters tend to go cheap on the sound system. You'll get a headache. Most of the characters look like human actors with fake ears glued on. The hobbit's large feet are prosthetic and look fake. The various zombies in the movie all look like The Mummy. Frodo has the same expression on his face throughout the entire movie. Sort of a very worried look. These elements and others constantly reminded me I was watching a movie. Overall I enjoyed the movie, about the same level as I enjoyed "Willow".

Classics such as The Godfather and Shawshank have earned their high ratings over time, not by jumpy excited fans who just saw it. It is unfortunate that the IMDB rating system has been diluted by goofy Ring fans. Over time this movie will slip into obscurity along side Willow and The Dark Crystal in the fantasy tripe isle.

title: My God! It's knocked off 'The Godfather!'
review:
Never did I think a film could take The Godfather's reigning role as #1 on the imdb top 250 films, than today I find out one has! Imagine my shock!

I'm not sure if the movie deserves to, it is a wonderful film, but... The GODFATHER! That is like comparing Julia Roberts and Meryl Streep. Julia Roberts is an accomplished actress, one of today's best... but MERYL STREEP? She is like the goddess of screen. So what I am trying to get at is this: Though a great film, 'The Lord of The Rings' is NOT as classic and uplifting as the great and holy (movie-wise) 'The Godfather.' I'm just warning the people who created 'The Lord of The Rings' to watch their backs.... if you know what I mean. ;)

title: Wonderful but lacked finishing touches.
review: I thought the movie was wonderful...  I was disappointed in the larger shots that occurred outside and in between the different towns and kingdoms... The quality of the background was very grainy... It took a lot away from the wonderful imagery in other parts of the film.

title: While not quite the book, Excellent nonetheless.
review:
While there were some things with the movie that were changed from the book that I didn't really like, for the most part it was very well made, without any of the really dumb dialogue that appears in most new movies of this scope.

I'm not sure I liked how Saruman was so evil from the get go. In the books he is a character who is pitied because he was twisted to evil use and could not escape it because he didn't recognize it for what it was worth. However, I understand that movies can't be as subtle as books without losing their audience.

So while I'm not quite pleased with the way the movie portrayed Saruman the White, I doubt if it could have done much better considering the medium. Other than that the movie is beautiful and oozes of real places and real people, just don't expect it to be exactly the book. Enjoy the movie for what it is, which is excellent.

title: I Kick Arse for the Lord! (of the Rings)
review:
Wow.

I'm not going to mince words here. The Fellowship of the Ring is the best adaptation of a popular novel since The Godfather. Majestic, sweeping, awe-inspiring  and that's just the scenery. Over three short hours, the film races at breakneck speed through the trails and tribulations of the Fellowship. Exciting, exhilarating, tragic, funny, scary  it perfectly captures the essence of Tolkien's incredible tome.

Wonderfully directed by visual genius Peter Jackson, perfectly cast, acting worthy of the nods from the academy, jaw-dropping action sequences, a momentum that never lets up, the enduring beauty and terror of Middle Earth captured with perfection and an ending that leaves everyone salivating for more. This is the kind of film they invented the term epic' just to describe. At last  an over-hyped movie that lives up to its hype. Hats off to New Line Cinema, who have risked their entire studio on this project and who deserve to be thoroughly rewarded for coming up with the goods. This film will set the benchmark rest of the twenty-first century.

The idiotic gripes listed in the imdb's user reviews just beggar belief. The classic whinge of the film is not as good as the book' always leave me dumbfounded. People who resent the fact that their interpretation of a given novel does not exactly match the director's visualization are simply crazy  they are never going to. If you prefer books to film so much  don't bother seeing any literary adaptations. Ever. To film a motion picture of the book voted the best of the twentieth century is no small undertaking and Jackson has performed above and beyond the call of duty. As to the bits he missed out  good! They where boring anyway. Confused with all the characters? The ones with little guys are good and the ugly ones dressed in black are bad. The goodies are on a journey to destroy an evil ring, the baddies want the ring to enslave everyone  not too tricky eh? If you want to see a film that doesn't explain itself very well, have a peek at Lost Highway. Sit back and just enjoy the damn thing without feeling the need to nit-pick.

Without a doubt, one of the greatest films ever made.

Bring on The Two Towers.

title: Incredible
review: Well, the movie is about three hours, when it was finished I thought it had gone 85 minutes. It was absolutely stunning, from the beginning to the end, absolutely NOTHING to complain about, it felt like the actors really were the characters they played. Yes, this was really amazing.

title: So good I quenched my desire for the urinal.
review:
Shortly before walking into the theater to see this movie, my friend bought me a medium drink. And even though I'd emptied my bladder before said purchase and sipped sparingly from said drink, I found myself in desperate need of the restroom just as the hobbits reached Rivendell.

But I endured.

So absorbed in the story was I that I tapped my feet, squinched my legs, and performed all other manners of contortions to keep from wetting myself so that I could take in every second of cinematic bliss that unfolded on the screen before me.

So take heed -- drink nothing for several days before going to see this movie. Or take a bedpan with you.

title: hrng!
review:
This week I watched "Atlantis" and "Lord of the Rings". Atlantis, of course, was a ridiculous film, only made to show the world how trendy Disney can be and how astounding their CGI-Works... too bad.... I thought Lord Of The Rings was better. And after watching, yes, it IS better, naturallement. But both films have mistakes that make watching it very difficult or should I say... nerve-racking...?

I mean music: You can hardly find moments where there is no music during the movie.... there is music while there are fighting, walking, talking, I think even when they are just sitting or sleeping there is music. After 3 hours your ears are so exhausted... I was thankful for every second without, but you can be sure the next minute a new violin or trumpet sound will appear. Sure, it is just for emphasizing the action, but after an hour it starts me to upset. So many moments where it is just unnecessary.... So many scenes of beautiful and breathtaking landscapes and persons.... it is better to show them longer and without a destroying comment.... bluargh! As if the audience was so dumb that they couldn´t understand the pictures and dialogues by themselves.... too much music and effects are usually to conceal bad plot or bad acting... this film has good acting and an exciting story.... but there is really too much music, too much obvious computer effects and too many cuts, you just can´t calm down and enjoy. Many scenes like the village of the forest queen or the knight trying to get the ring from Frodo.... impressing but too fast. They should concentrate such fast cuts and music for the visually brilliant action scenes like the fight in the mine or the nine kings attacking the hobbits on that tower. That would have more effect... But... such films are like video-games... non-stop action. I get fed up!

It seems like the director just want to show us "Look how cool my movie and its SFX are! look what astounding sceneries we can make!" It´s too obvious! It´s vain! It´s boring like Star Wars Episode I.... Lord Of The Rings have deserved it better!

To everybody : Lord Of The Rings is great.... watch it! and hope that the next two episodes are much more atmospheric!!!!

title: a one???
review:
votes of one are best reserved for movies like "cave dwellers" or "plan 9 from outer space". Maybe people who voted as such were thinking of the Ralph Bakshi version with the outlines of the nazi soldiers with the painted red eyes. I loved it, I give it a 10. wholeheartedly.

It was not strictly slavish to the book, had wonderful vision, managed to keep moving (tolkien's writing tends to be dry, so this was a great feat), and had me on the edge of my seat in many sections. While having read the books at some point would certainly help the average viewer, I don't think it's entirely necessary.

title: Wow!
review: A visual masterpiece that brings Middle Earth to life. The characterizations are true to the book's flavor. Nobility makes a return! this story is a true lesson in what we are as humans, and perhaps what we have lost.

title: Genius + Vision = Perfection
review:
Tolkien was and is a genius. When you combine the work of his masterpiece, with the remarkable vision and dedication of Peter Jackson, you have such an awe-inspiring film that stands as probably the best film of all time.

I've never seen a film that captured the true essence of the word "epic" that was also full of rich emotional and moral depth that other movies like "Titanic" and "Gladiator" were sorely missing.

The special effects are top-notch and are not gratuitous unlike special effects seen in "visually-rich-but-poor-plot" films such as Star Wars. Every ounce of special effects carefully augments the story and brings out the full flavour of Tolkien's world.

The acting is marvellous to behold. One is totally convinced of the identity of the characters. Each actor has artfully transformed into their character such as to surpass the imagination of the readers of the trilogy and utterly convince you that they *are* the character!

Peter's creation is scary, exciting, dreamy, epic and rollicking good fun. What more can one ask?

title: Ok, but not great
review:
I've waited for a movie version of The Lord Of The Rings since I first read the book some thirteen years ago. I reread the first part of the book before I went to see the film. And now after seeing it here are my thoughts:

The feel of the book has been captured well. All the changes made to the story itself can be justified by the change of format. The People, landscapes and monsters of Middle Earth appear as I've always imagined them. The actors are mostly Ok, portraying their characters true to the book. My personal favorites were Ian McKellen and Ian Holm, who played Gandalf and Bilbo Baggins respectfully. Especially their scenes together early on in the film worked very well.

There are also problems with this film, which are caused by the sheer amount of information and pages in the book. It is too short even with it's length of three hours to carefully introduce and develop the characters and advance the story. After Frodo leaves the Shire events simply rush by at ridiculous speed until he reaches Rivendell. In the book this point divides the story in two, but in the film the first half of the book takes up something like only third of the length The Council of Elrond is one of the most disappointing scenes in the film. If it were done properly it would have been a good spot to introduce some of the characters to the story giving more information on their background. Now it feels like it's straight from some b-class fantasy film which this film is definately not. Artistically it would have probably been better to divide the book into six two-hour movies, but sadly it would likely have not been commercially feasible.

Even with all the downsides it's still one of the best fantasy films (non-animation) ever, and a good start to the trilogy. 8/10

title: A worthy addition to coverage of this story
review:
To separate myself from possible spoilers also commenting here,

I won't criticize the Bakshi and Rankin/Bass efforts of previous

years, but this first Jackson film is quite worthy of a look - even if

the viewer hasn't gone on to the novels - which everyone should.

Not only is more detail there regarding this story of good and evil,

but Tolkien, a contemporary of Winston Churchill and an Oxford

philology professor, wrote with a quality comparable to the

wartime Prime Minister. The reader gets an education in English

oratory in the most painless of circumstances: read the books!!

title: ***Spoilers***
review: This movie rocks. There are so many differences from the book and yet the overall story is not harmed in any way. Some differences (other than the big ones we knew of: Arwen, Bombadil etc): Intro narrated by Galadriel depicting the history of the ring. Gandalf sends Frodo and Sam on their own telling them he'll meet them at the Prancing Pony. Pippin and Merry join the band while running away from Farmer Maggot. No Crickhollow, no Fatty Bolger. No singing at the Prancing Pony, instead Frodo trips and accidently slips the ring on. Arwen brings on the flood at the Ford, not Elrond. No mention is made of Gandalf having added the horses effect. Gandalf sends a butterfly to fetch Gwaihir; No Radagast. The council of Elrond is very concise, most of it having been shown in the Intro. Gimli suggests going through Moria, not Gandalf. Saruman commands the storm on Caradras. A lot more is shown of the Watcher in the lake than is described in the book. Frodo figures out the 'Mellon' password, not Gandalf. Gandalf tells Frodo that Gollum has been following them for three days. No blindfolding at Lothlorien. No Sam at the mirror of Galadriel, instead Frodo sees both visions. Galadriel's ring is not used in the script, although you do see it on her finger at the departure of the Fellowship. Saruman creating his army of Uruk-Hai is given quite a bit of screen time. The breaking of the fellowship is different. Frodo tells Aragorn that he will go into Mordor alone; Aragorn agrees. These are just some of the differences I can remember; as you can see, they do not impact the story very much. Goose bump sequences: The hobbits are fleeing the Back Rider and run right into him. Bilbo's reaction to seeing the ring once more. Galadriel's test at the mirror. Awesome, really scary. Ultra cool sequences: Anything with the Nazgul, especially Weathertop. Arwen and Frodo's ride to the ford. The balrog. This movie is just spectacular. I loved it. Biggest regret: Not enough of Tolkien's poetry, especially the prophecy from Boromir's dream.

title: Best film I have seen!!, and I've seen some greats!
review: As a fan of fantasy films since my child hood I have eagerly awaited this film since I first heard it was being released, I remember being read the books when I was younger and being enthralled although I remember nothing from them. Fantasy films have sets and costumes that build magical worlds that the audience can be lost in but of all of them bar Star wars, none have been exceptional and all flawed in some way. I like the sword and sorcery slant more than anything else but have never had a film that nowadays I could look at critically and call excellent. My favourite film of all time is Masters of the Universe, no other film filled me with such excitement as that did, but it is majorlly floored, other favourites include Legend a film that visually was breathtaking but that was about all it was. Anyway this is the complete article. Visually this is the greatest film ever from the sets, effects down to the amazing and groundbreaking effects. Some of the flowing camera movements are vertigo inducingly brilliant, an example could be the opening battle scene as the camera sweeps through hordes of battling soldiers falling off cliffs or bludgeoning each other as the camera takes us through the battle fields. Peter Jackson's direction is dynamic and at times breathtakingly brilliant. The hairs on the back of my neck stood on end throughout this film, I was lost in middle earth for three hours thanks to Jackson's mastery, his imagination obviously running rampant in the designing of the characters, worlds etc based on nothing more than descriptive story telling and perhaps a few odd sketches. I am glad I decided not to bring in any popcorn or sparkling beverage as an unwelcome need to go pee-pee may have resulted in me wetting myself and the fellow viewers either side of me parting like the red sea from the subsequent whiff. Apart from the amazing visuals the films story is imaginative and engaging but what do you expect from a classic fictional epic like Tolkiens Lord of the Rings trilogy, and Jackson as far as I know has stayed faithful to the story but of course needing to cut down a few moments of the piece and of course these will go noticed by some to varying degrees of noticability because of course everyone has their own ideas of what parts of a book they have read is important compared to somebody else's opinion. What is great about Tolkiens world, and characters is they are universally compatible, you don't need to have read the books to fully enjoy this, its easy enough to pick up, good versus evil and we get an opening story telling about the rings creation as well as other things of importance. The actors are all well cast here, and all of them perform excellently. Elijah Wood is very good in the lead; he manages to hold the film together in such a big role where others may have lost it to the supporting cast. Ian Mckellan is also brilliant as the wizard Gandalf and others who impress are Sean Astin, Orlando Bloom, John Rhys Davies, and a very good Sean Bean in a key role and all the others in this film performed to a level bettering anything I have seen them in. Worthy of note are the two main females the gorgeous Cate Blanchett as the wise and at times scary elf queen, and the impossibly attractive Liv Tyler who must surely have silenced unfair criticism with this performance, she is exceptional in this. She is sexy, tough, gentle and she steals the screen whenever she is on it, simply said she looks hot! One person I have not yet mentioned is Viggo Mortensen who plays Aragon; he for me was narrowly the star of the film. Viggo makes an excellent action hero in this and his performance is outstanding, I genuinely believe he is worthy of Oscar consideration for this film. The only minor fault of the film I would say is the end, because being only a third of the story of course there is no conclusion so it ends all so suddenly. Like pulling a bottle of milk from a baby's mouth when he was only half done I felt mildly annoyed and desperate to see part two, and considering I have to wait a year, I became equally desperate to watch the film again. I do feel that a whole year is a lengthy time to wait and I can see it as nothing more than a marketing ploy to build demand and expectation for the sequel. Anyway Christmas time has once again become an exciting time for me thanks to the Lord of the rings trilogy. Also excellent about this film would have to be the ear poundingly good sound effects, they were astounding. This added to the feeling of the film and like for instance Gladiator this film is one you just have to see on the big screen. I give this a definite 10/10 and it is number one in my mind. What excites me the most is that the sequels are supposed to get better and better. Bring on number 2.

title: Wait For The Book To Come Out
review:
LOTR is not a bad movie. It is fantastic and exciting, colorful and scenic. The main characters are charming and well played by Elijah Wood and Ian Mckellan. The action scenes, though there are too many of them, are thrilling and heroic.

But the story is not all that intriguing. Said and done, this is nothing more than the tale of a perilous journey. The hero treks toward a somewhat contrived destination, encounters multiple bad guys and large monsters. And that's about it. This is merely Jason, Sinbad and Ulysses recycled through the 21st century special effects system. The actual plot is minimal and the story plays only on a superficial level. I suspect the book is more detailed and more stimulating. But that didn't help me as I sat in the theatre wishing for a third course to round out the meal.

Even the aforementioned action sequences could have been handled more efficiently. For the most part, they do work. But the visuals are cluttered so that it's not always easy to tell who's doing what to who. That's the very last thing a fight scene needs.

There is an appealing fairy tale flavor to this first installment of the popular trilogy. A sense of mystical, other worldliness that makes for pleasant entertainment in spite of the film's many shortcomings. But from a genre that knows no limitations, I expected more.

My own fantasies are much better.

title: I've been watching films for 3-and-a-half decades, it IS the best film I have ever seen.
review:
Contains 1 hinted-at spoiler (tells of a change from the book, but not WHAT is changed).

10 stars. I took the kids, they were in awe throughout. On the way home in the car, I got "Dad, why is..?", "Dad, why did..?", "Dad, who is..?" for the full 30 mins, normally a drive-home film re-assessment last 2-3 mins. They haven't read the books, they both want them as last minute Xmas presents. "Dad, can we go and see it again at the weekend and take our friends this time?".

My kids are 14/12, it is ok for 8 year olds, I reckon, just.

Me? I've hoped for 25 years that there would be a proper film version of LOTR. I read the books about once a year on average. I hoped the film would be good and true to the book (it wouldn't need to be 100% as the book for me, 99% would do), IMHO it is. I WAS worried it would deviate too much from the book. Having seen the film, I am pleased how little it deviates from the book *in the detail* (the obvious change at the Ford of Bruinen, for example, just seems odd), in spirit, it's just like watching the book brought to life.

Personally, I wish the film was longer and that more time could have been taken over all the elements of the film. I wish the Balrog could have been made more evil/menacing than it appeared. I wish I was the director, but I'm not, PJ is, and my only wish was that the film was made and it has been. My wish has been granted. How often does that happen?

Generally, fantasy films fall short on storyline, character build, emotion, etc. LOTR hits the spot on all these (but maybe I get the character build from the book). If in doubt, go see it, you will not be disappointed, I am so sure of this. I've been watching films for 3-and-a-half decades, it IS the best film I have ever seen.

title: Best Film Ever? - No; Merely, Very, Very Good!
review:
For many years it has been widely stated that The Lord Of The Rings was un-filmable. Tolkien sold the film rights to fund his Grandchildren's education, and until his death feared that the book would be turned into some awful cartoon (boy did he get that one right!)Now, nearly 30 years after the authors death, Peter Jackson has done the impossible, and created a masterpiece. Only once before ( La Vita e Bella - 1998) have I sat in a cinema with an audience that was completely spellbound. For 3 hours a couple of hundred people sat hanging on every image, we all lapped it up. Performances throughout are superb, especially Ian Mckellan and Christopher Lee (what a fight scene!) Elijah Wood as a Hobbit concerned me when reading through all the publicity, but he is very good, a small criticism would be that one did begin to tire of shots of his big blue eyes. The depth of the characters will only be judged this time in 2 years with 'The Return Of The King' TLOTR is not a trilogy, it is one book, To build character and pace a 10 hour film is necessary but impractical, hence three shorter ones. Special effects for once complement the actors, and do not steal the show, and Middle Earth is exactly how I imagined it to be, Moria was incredible.

I doubt this will remain at No. 1, but I have to say it is far superior to the over-rated Star Wars 4, 5, & 6.

The film of the year without doubt.

title: Awesome!
review: I've never read the books, but I must say that I was captivated by this world!  What a great movie!  I've never had a movie-going experience so rewarding.  I was completely wrapped up in Middle-Earth.  I can't wait for the sequels.  If this does not get recognition by the Academy, there is a major problem!

title: As close to the book as could be expected(Warning:Spoilers)
review: This was a fantastic film. The characters were perfectly casted. The scenery was stunning. Special effects were unparalleled. It was also perfectly adapted to the 21st century. What the movie lacked was character development. Having read the books I felt that the movie was moving at warp 9. I am used to having to read for hours for something to happen but the events in the movie were happening one right after the other. I felt that this series could have been made into six or seven movies starting with The Hobbit. Unless you read the books you wouldn't know what some of the references to the books meant. The Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers, and The Return of the King were each divided into 2 books. If they had made 6 movies there would have been enough time for character development. Six movies isn't all that ridiculous (Star Wars, Star Trek) especially since they were all filmed at the same time. I did like how Jackson toned down the Hobbits' overly sensitive nature that was portrayed in the books. I feel that along with Tom Bombadil wouldn't have been widely accepted by many viewers. Many kudos to the cast and crew of this movie.

title: Incredible
review:
I am a huge fan of everything Middle Earth. I must say Peter Jackson has done an incredible job bringing TLOTR to the big screen. People are complaining about character development, changes made to the story, what do you expect? It's a movie, not a novel! Anytime a book is adapted to a screenplay (especially one as descriptive and in-depth), you will have changes. The way a story is told visually is completely different then the way a story is told through words alone. The other thing that bothers me is everyone complaining about certain character traits, the beauty of reading a book is coming to your own conclusions about the characters. Certain people are far to narrow minded to think that their interpretation of Tolkien's words is the way it should be and Peter Jackson is wrong.... pathetic.

Peter Jackson I salute you! You've really done an excellent job. The fight scenes are fantastic, you feel as though you are there (sporadic camera movement and constantly trying to follow what is happening gives a feeling of realism, that style has not been used in many recent films). I love this movie and I highly recommend it to anyone.

One part about the story that did irritate me was the Council of Elrond scene, it was far to brief and should have included the stories of recent events from each of the races the caused the meeting to take place. This would have cleared a few things up, namely the reason why everyone eagerly joins the fellowship. My favorite part was the Mines of Moria battle that starts with the orcs and cave troll and concludes with the Balrog, amazing stuff! An almost Perfect 10!

title: Loved it, no spoilers
review: 10/10 For the following reasons:  Acting in which the actors made me believe. A score that didn't over power the movie but complemented it and gave emphasis when needed.  Eye candy FX.  Detail. Detail. Detail.  For taking on the challenge of adapting the first of three books to the big screen, and meeting my expectations.  A long movie to be sure, but it could have been longer for me.  It seemed a bit rushed at times.  I accept the missing parts of the books and understand that most would never see the 5 hour movie that would have been needed.  I would.  I simply never thought that the books would or could be made into movies, at least not this good. I can't believe they've finally done it.  The best 3 hours I've ever spent in a movie theater.

title: A production that lives up to the epic size of the story
review:
Ok, would all movie producers please leave the room. We do not need you any more: you just got blown out of the water!

Can someone say "Oscar city"? The only reason they might not beat Ben Hur and Titanic in number of Oscars won is because there are very few feminine roles, lead or supporting. Everything else a movie can win... well, as I said, all other producers, actors, musicians, sound effects specialists, visual effects specialists and so on might as well leave the room, they've already lost.

If you've read the book, you will NOT be disappointed, not one little teeny tiny smidgen.

If you have not read the book, you will NOT be disappointed, not one little teeny tiny smidgen.

If you hate adventure stories, and prefer action movies, you will (probably) NOT be disappointed...

If you prefer drama, you will NOT be disappointed.

The only people who may really not want to see this are people who want a pure love story a la Casablanca. Oh wait, you will probably love this, too!

It's simply too well made, and the story itself is simply fascinating enough to captivate pretty much anyone. Frankly, unless you simply can't afford the extra expense of a movie, go ahead and see it. Don't let the length of the movie frighten you, either. I've seen other long movies in the theatre ("Dune", for one, which I thought was quite good, but not nearly as good as this), and I've never found myself quite so enthralled before. In fact, never once did I think "Oh man, I wish this would end, I want a cigarette!" The audience was probably the best behaved I have EVER seen. Not a word, not a peep, not a cellphone, NOTHING. I'm pretty sure anyone who goes see this in the first few days will find similarly captive audiences.

If you can, go to a theater that has Dolby-Surround sound, it's definitely worth it.

Run there. Don't walk.

I will await the continuation of this story with great trepidation.

title: Excellent!
review:
This movie is, in my opinion, the best of the year. It's filled with excitement, adventure, and suspense. And is great in its quieter moments too. Peter Jackson and company have crafted a great piece of film-making that may end up as a classic. It is based on the wonderful and imaginative books by British author J.R.R. Tolkien, who incorporated much of his childhood and own experiences into these books.

The books follow the adventure of a young hobbit who acquires the One Ring of Power. The Ring was forged by the evil Sauron, the Dark Lord of Mordor to enslave the world, but thanks to the might and strength of men, he was overthrown. But at the crucial moment in which the mortal King Isildur of Gondor was given the opportunity to destroy the accursed Ring, its power corrupted him and he turned away. The Ring tends to do this to its bearer. It corrupts all that come across it and betrays them. Once thought lost, the Ring winds up in the hands of hobbit, Frodo Baggins who acquires it from his cousin Bilbo. But after warning from the wise wizard Gandalf, he must set forth on an adventure to rid the land of Middle-Earth from this evil Ring, and destroy it in the land of the Enemy before the evil forces of Sauron get their hands on it. And so the Fellowship of the Ring is banded to aid the Ring-Bearer on his quest.

This is a faithful adaptation which I found a joy to watch. And as some may say it was too long and boring, I thought it wasn't long enough. I could have stayed in the theater for about another hour if it meant watching all of the great scenes from the book that were omitted from the film. I hope they actually shot some of these scenes because they are more for character development, and they wind up on a future DVD release of the film. This is a great film. It depicts the classic struggle of good versus evil at its most inventive. It is a must-see for any film-lover and definitely will be a contender this awards season.

title: Even a Tolkien fanatic like myself was impressed.
review: Tom Bombadill would have no problem with being cut from the story.  He was a more than good natured chap.  While I was bummed he was cut, I was please with the project as a whole.  Remember this director sought to place on the silver screen what only one man could do in his prose.  Not only was this a bold attempt, but it also was a resounding success.  It would be impossible to appease such a distinguished appetite as that of a "Lord of the Rings" fan.  However, this movie brings a story to the screen that will tickle the fancy of even the most critical.  Way to go, and thank you Kiwi's for letting us borrow your beautiful countryside, so that "Middle Earth" may be brought to life.

title: Judging the film as a film and not as a book
review: Going through the other reviews, I have to say I am a bit disappointed. There are multiple reviews that begin to explain how the film was a bad adaptation of the book, the scenes that shouldn't be cut, the characters, blah blah... I read all 3 of the books of Lord Of The Rings, alongside Hobbit, I watched the film. Despite the fact I already knew the plot, I tried to just forget what I read and try to relive the story, behind director Jackson's eyes. Seeing The Fellowship of the Ring was a life-time experience for me. Surely the best film I've ever seen, perfect from every aspect. I was struck by just about everything in this masterpiece. Exceeding every expectation, the film is maybe the new Star Wars of our time (only Star Wars enjoyed the advantage that there wasn't a book to be compared to). The effects are absolutely ground-breaking. The scenes, the camera movement is setting new limits to film-making and both the casting and the acting is brilliant. No need to criticize, if you like to find bad things about this movie, you need to try really hard. All I know is that if the movie had the hype of Titanic or even Harry Potter (movies drawn in mediocrity), everyone would live for 3 hours (and 6 to come) in the fantastic world of Tolkin.

title: If a twenty year old boy can cry in this film, I think anyone can. Everyone, go see Fellowship of the Ring.
review: At a time in our history when evil is everywhere, and it seems hard to believe that love is overcoming, we have a story such as this to make us believe in heroes and in good overcoming evil.  The Lord of the Rings makes me believe that we have a chance. This is possibly the greatest film I have ever seen.  And that is saying a lot from a person who grew up loving the Star Wars and Godfather films.  I have been a Tolkien fan for years.  I have read the books and I visited New Zealand during the filming of FOTR.  I did not see and filming or anything, but I can now I say I have been to Middle Earth 3 times now.  It will always be the greatest story ever told in my opinion.  It teaches me a lot about life and what we must do to live that life. I must say that this film touched me just as the book did when I read it. I needed this film now more than ever when I am unsure about my life and the road I must take.  It gives me hope and faith that even if I must walk into Mordor, I will not be alone.  Thank you Peter Jackson above all, and everyone else involved with this film.  And of course, thank you Mr. Tolkien.  I hope that wherever you are, you can see this film and be happy that some of us are keeping that hope alive.

title: This ain't no "Potter Pic"
review:
As good as it gets. This met all expectations even with the big build up. I can't wait for next December. I saw a lot of little (<10) kids at my showing. The battle and visuals are pretty intense for little kids. This is not Harry Potter time.

The Cast is perfect. I even got used to "Rudy" as Sam. I thought this might have been a fatal flaw when I saw it on the cast sheet but it works out OK. Elijah is Frodo, as the others are also just right. And what else can be said about the lovely Liv. The best looking 3,000 year old elf ever. I heard that one of JRRT's sons did not want this film to be made and would not see it. A pity. It is marvelous.



Slicer-2

title: additional comments
review: Some people have asked in the comments how dare we put it up there with movies like "The Godfather" or other "beloved" classics. Do I think it's as good as "The Godfather"? Yes I do. It's better in my opinion simply because I am a huge fan of fantasy. The Godfather is a classic, but it also bored the *&^% out of me. I really don't care about criminals or their lifestyles and I really hate movies that sensationalize them. 17,000 people have loved this film enough to give it a 10. It's my guess that the vast majority of this 17,000 are avid movie lovers which is why they have sought out a website like IMDB in the first place. I base my first opinion on whether a movie is good or not...on whether I enjoyed it, learned something from it, or it evoked some emotional response. I can appreciate Citizen Kane for it's contribution to movie making and directing, but if given a choice of watching it or LOTR over and over again locked in a room for 24 hours...guess which one I'd choose.  "Our Vines Have Tender Young Grapes" "Ghostbusters" "The Ox-Bow Incident" "Night of the Hunter"  "How Green Was My Valley" "Empire Strikes Back" "Jane Eyre  (1944)" "On Borrowed Time" "Excalibur" "The Thing"  "Windwalker" "Babette's Feast" etc These are among my favorite movies and I think LOTR would fine them pleasant company. Don't assume that the votes given to this movie were uneducated ones just because you believe yourself some sort of aficionado of the cinema. I still believe that it's unfair of people to give this movie a 1 just because they're trying to change it's rank in the top 250. I'd much rather see a movie about the humble and unassuming overcoming great odds to defeat evil like LOTR in number 1, than a movie about selfish brutes killing one another and upholding archaic outdated notions of honor in "The Godfather".

title: One of the most powerful (emotionally) movies this year...or maybe ever
review:
Most action movies I have seen (And I've seen some doozies) will brush aside plot and emotion in favor of stupid blow-em-up scenes that have no relevance to the actual storyline. Case in point-one of the most confusing, unemotional, and HORRIBLE movies of all time, THE AVENGERS, starring Ralph Fiennes and Uma Thurman. But this is not a review about that. THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING is, thankfully, not one of those movies. I would say that it is not about the special effects or the battle scenes (which, by the way, are incredibly realistic). It is all about, in the end, friendship and sticking by the ones you care about. I walked into this movie not ever reading the novels, however I do have a lot of knowledge about the plot. I saw HARRY POTTER and thought it was really great. But that was a movie for kids. Skip the hamburgers, I wanted some steak!! I knew that this was going to be very different from HARRY POTTER because it was directed at an older audience. I was right, in a very very good way. This movie is totally about the friendship and comradery between the hobbits and the rest of the fellowship. You see it when Frodo wakes up in Rivendell and Sam is right there and Gandalf tells Frodo that Sam hasn't left his side for more than a minute or two. You see it when Frodo is reunited with Bilbo at the land of the Elves. And you see it at the very end of the movie, when Merry and Pippin distract the orcs and ::SPOILER ALERT!!:: get captured themselves so Frodo can escape to the other side of the river. Okay, on to the actors. I've been hearing a lot of mixed reviews of Elijah Wood and his portrayal of Frodo Baggins. I might give a biased review because I have a HUGE crush on Elijah. But I have to say that he did an AMAZING job in this movie. He really gave a stellar performance. I think he's one of the finest actors in his age group. Him and Hayden Christensen are both amazing in what they do. Here, Elijah really brought the innocence and goodness of Frodo to life. The friendship and love between him and Sam Gamgee (played with a heartbreaking tenderness by Sean Astin) is really drawn into the light. I think the best shots of the movie are when the camera is drawn into Frodo's innocent face, full of skeptiscism and worry. Everyone keeps on talking about the eyes. To me, Elijahs' eyes are a wonderful acting tool. They are so big and blue that you can almost see into his mind. Okay, I'm getting off track LOL. I'm going to talk about someone else now. I LOVED Ian McKellen as Gandalf the Grey. And some reviewer was wrong. They DO mention "the Grey" in the Prancing Pony. He really did become Gandalf in this movie. He brings out the kindness and intensity that his character should have. Billy Boyd was wonderful as the comical Pippin, and Dominic Monahagn was great as the sort of "straight man" Merry. But there are some points where you can see the vulnerability that Pippin and Merry both show. Right after the little accident in the Mines of Moria (when Gandalf...you know, has that fall), you see Merry crying and holding a sobbing Pippin. Someone said that you never see them serious in the whole movie. That's a pretty damn good example RIGHT THERE. Liv Tyler was an extremely good surprise. She was very good as the elven princess, I didn't think she had the acting ability. Cate Blanchett was pretty freakin scary as Galadriel, but still, she did an amazing job. Orlando Bloom as Legolas was a great performance. I loved it when he took one of his own arrows, stabbed an orc with it, and then proceeded to take out the arrow from the orc's eye and then shoot down another orc with THE SAME ARROW. I thought that was really great!

However, on to the revisions and cuts. The only time you see Glorfindel in the first book was when he takes Frodo to Rivendell after he's injured. Peter Jackson did a surprising choice when he made Arwen do it, but then again, she doesn't really have a good role in the first book, and this expands the romantic angle a little bit. I loved it at the beginning when Frodo pushes Sam into Rose's arms when he gets too shy to ask her for a dance. The rest of the journey is really a growth period for them, too. The ending when Sam almost drowns trying to reach Frodo's boat is nothing short of heartbreaking. I cried, I have to admit.

All in all, a fantastic movie. I've seen it twice, and the first thought I had when the footage of Sam and Frodo trudging to Mordor faded was, "When can I find the time to see this movie again?"

title: Slightly disappointing
review:
I think given my love of the story, and great respect for Peter Jackson, some amount of disappointment was to be expected. Perhaps I was expecting too much, and since there was so much plot and character development in the book, whatever movie Jackson produced was going to have a difficult time fleshing out all the elements.

That said, I did enjoy the movie. It's getting great reviews, but I wonder how folks who never read the book could follow everything. My biggest complaint is that it seemed to move so quickly through lots of details that would seem to be important when establishing the "epic" nature of the story. Of course, it may be that the plot carries itself, and that you don't necessarily need to know all the back history and whatnot to enjoy the film, but who knows.

In any case, I'm still a Peter Jackson fan and hope the next two installments can bring out more of his genius, as well as building on the rich detail of the story.

title: Wonderful like the book
review: This book was the visual interpretation of the book.  I felt so close to the characters, Gollum, Bilbo, Frodo, Boromir, etc...  Its not a usual occurrence that a director can visualize a book and Peter Jackson did this very well. The presence of evil was very real in the movie, from Bilbo's evil visage coming out to Gandalf being afraid of the ring, it just makes you realize how evil the ring is.  Very good directing and acting.  I can't wait for the next one.  Some thought the inclusion of Arwen's rescue of Bilbo was sacrilege.  It was merely filler.  That kind of thing has to be done in a movie.  Overall this is what excellence in a film should be.  I rank this movie with new greats like The Shawshank Redemption and Braveheart.

title: For once, length and excellence
review:
This is the first film I have seen reaching the 150 minute plus mark where I didn't want to leave the cinema.

In all aspects it kept me gripped and entertained from beginning to end was overly mesmerising in all facets. The extent of characters, brilliant landscapes, rich and substantial personalities make this without doubt one of the best movies I have ever seen.

In the past films with a serious and dramatic have, in my opinion, quite wrongly occupied the number one or top 5 spot in all time greatest films polls. For once, and quite rightly, a movie that entertains with positivity and pure film making claims the spot. Films that grab the number one spot containing gratuitous use of nonsensical violence and/or shocking value seem to be regarded as "great" films for no real film making qualified brilliance.

Thankfully, Lord of the Rings has grabbed this. My thumbs up for such a brilliant movie.

title: Dumbfounded by the critical mind
review:
I won't bore you with a blow by blow account of why I absolutely loved this film. I am here to express some feelings concerning critics of the film and the specific problems they have with it, if I don't get this off my chest I will explode.

Before I begin let me give you a little perspective on where I am coming from. I am not the type to judge someone's intelligence based on the films they like, nor do I feel that my taste is the preeminent gauge of all that is right. Even when someone tells me that their favorite film of all time is Top Gun, Or Rush Hour 2 was the best film of the summer I don't judge, I just pass it off as "hey,every one has an opinion, they are only films and obviously these kind of people don't take them too seriously and have more important things to do, I think"

Anyway, the things I am reading in negative reviews of Fellowship of the Ring just blow my mind. First off one of the constant complaints I hear is that the action scenes are poorly constructed and filmed. I would never have the arrogance to make a statement like this unless it is truly a bad film or overtly apparent that the guys who filmed the scene just suck I mean can these reviewers even come close to making a film like this, let alone film an action scene, even in its basic form. My only thought as to why people feel this way is that they sat too close to the screen, this would cause confusion and poor focus. How can I sit there and follow the fights perfectly and just be amazed at the beauty of them and the next guy can only complain about how bad they were handled? It must be an American thing, no offense, like the fact that the FOX network had to have glowing pucks for their NHL broadcasts because Americans couldn't follow the puck, maybe its the same thing. So that complaint doesn't wash with me.

The other complaint is the comparison being made to every detail of the book,they should of kept Tom Bombadil or give the members of the fellowship more of a back story. Jesus Christ! what more do you want, why not film every page of the book verbadem, and we can all sit in a theatre for 3 weeks. The fact that Legolas, Gimli, and Boromir see more heart and selflessness in this little hobbit then they do in themselves or each other and decide to follow him and protect him in his journey is enough to give you a good indication of who they are and why they go, I mean they see the threat.Tom Bombadil for obvious reasons could of and should of been cut.Lets get some solid criticisms please.I actually heard a guy behind me laugh at how unreal the film was, like that guy could shoot arrows so fast, holy s**t,can you believe that? What a moron.

The film is flawed, but man that adds to its beauty, like little imperfections on a beautiful girl, gives her character and Peter Jackson has transferred the essence of Lord of the Rings to the big screen and was able to maintain its character and even intilling it with his own love of the material. What about Star Wars? That film and its successors have way more flaws then Fellowship, i.e "This R2 unit needs a new power converter" very poor dialogue, but Star Wars is a great joy and most people regard it as such. Fellowship is a beautiful film and unfortunately some people have totally lost that little child like wonderment inside them and let the dark side of their critical mind poison them, negative old b****rds they are.

It amazes me that a person can sit back and decide to cut up a beautiful thing like this, why, jealousy, self hatred? Even Ebert isn't immune to falling victim to his critical mind, his review just didn't seem truthful, I strongly feel that for Ebert and many others this film will grow on them in time, and when all three are finally viewed they will be regarded as they greatest fantasy adventure films ever made

title: Brillant adaption of J.R.R. Tolkien's novels
review: I was really impressed with the movie. I'm amazed that many scenes were as I imagined while reading the books. I thought making this movie was an impossible undertaking, but I was wrong. I wished the ending had more closure (I'll be digging out my books to check how The Fellowship of the Rings ended) I would suggest that those who slam this film without having the benefit of reading the four books in this trilogy (The Hobbit as an introduction) are speaking from total ignorance. The film could be considered boring without the added prespective found from reading it's source. Better to hold you tongue and read the books: than make yourself a fool by boasting about having NOT read them. However, for those into the battle of good and evil, and the mythology of trolls, elves, and the like...the film is engaging enough without having read the basis. I would give this film  a 10 out of 10 - with one caveat...this isn't a kids film. Filling a young childs imagination with these spectacular scenes would induce many a nightmare.

title: Good, but could have been great
review:
I found myself frustrated with the film, because with just a few small changes it could have been great rather than merely fairly good. My objections are based on failures of editing and storytelling, not on lack of faithfulness to the book.

The acting was nearly uniformly very good. I was least satisfied with Hugo Weaving; when he talked about the decline of men, he came across to me as crabby and sour about it rather than with the noble sadness I get from Elrond in the book. Other character portrayal problems were more attributable to the script. E.g., Gimli was more skewed towards comic relief than in the book.

My chief objection was that a number of important characters are not given sufficient reasons for being there, or for doing some of the things they do. Merry and Pippin' relationship to Frodo should have been established first - then they'd have proper motivation for joining the trip. Similarly, we are given no reason why Gimli, Legolas, and Boromir are along for the ride except for Elrond's commitment to racial diversity.

If the movie's opening scenes had been moved to the Council of Elrond, with Gandalf and Elrond giving the narration, Gimli and Legolas at least could have interrupted briefly with their reasons for coming to Rivendell. It would have been just a matter of a few extra seconds to establish their motivations. (Gimli would only have mentioned the offer of dwarf rings just as the history of the dwarf rings was given; it would have been reasonable to save time by omitting mention of the loss of contact with Moria. Boromir would have required a minute or two.)

Saruman's screen time could have been used to give him the full complexity he possesses in the book. Time could have been made by omitting the dialog-free visual parts of the encounter with Gandalf and the industrialization of Isengard.

The only omission that seriously annoys me is the meeting between Gimli and Galadriel. Quite aside from its importance to later events in the trilogy, it would have given us a lot more reason to care about Gimli for the rest of the story - and by extension, about Legolas, as their friendship grows.

In a nutshell, I wanted more dialog and less action and scenery. One can only hope that at least a few of the problems will be fixed when the DVD comes out, and stuff left on the floor to get the movie down to three hours can be re-inserted.

title: Star Wars of this Generation
review:
The Fellowship of the Ring is by far the greatest film I have ever seen. I am a film student who is introduced to great films on a daily basis and this is the premier piece of movie making of all time.

I initially had reservations about this movie being made in the first place. I am an avid fan of the books and feared that nothing could live up to the writing of Tolkien. I am pleased to say that my fear has been quelled. The movie could not have been made any better.

Indeed The Fellowship is the Star Wars of this generation and it exceeds its predecessor in cinematic quality.

title: Very well done, but doesn't deserve the ratings on IMDb...
review: Beautifully filmed, acting superb, but overall a tedious experience for the novice viewer (those who haven't read the book series).  I like the Fantasy genre and appreciate the depth and scope of the story, but I found myself squirming in my seat after the first 2 hours and disappointed that it was only the first "installment" of the series (i.e. no big battle in Mordor at the end of the movie).  Trying to look at this from the perspective of a person that hasn't read the books (which I haven't), this film does not rate as highly as the other wonderful movies that are on the top of the IMDb Top 250 - those are just as superbly done and are entertaining to "veteran" and "novice" viewers alike.

title: The Best Ever!
review:
This movie is one the best movies ever produced not only in the fantasy genre but all. I am a fan of fantasy stories. I have watched many fantasy movies and read fantasy novels. I have read most of the dragonlance novel series and not to mention the lord of the rings novels.

When they announced that they wanted to make this movie, I just cant wait to see it ( next to Star Wars, another movie that I really like).

When the movie finally arrives, its not disappointing at all. All that are depicted in this movie are just like i imagined when reading the book. I think that this movie will not only appeal to fantasy fans, but others too. This movie has got it all. It has action, suspense, sorrow, adventure, humor, a little bit of romance, good looking actors and actresses, very beautiful scenery and costumes and more!

The special effects are cool too! This is the only movie that i think can compete with Star Wars in terms of special effects! Yes, its as good as Star Wars's special effects, and its not even from ILM or any ohter major effects studio such as Digital Domain! Its from New Zealands own effects studio.

The only complaint I have about this movie is its score. No, the score is very good in the movie, but its not memorable. For a big movie like this, i'd rather have a score that can be memorable and once we hear it, we can identify it with the movie, such as the Star Wars theme, Conan the Barbarian and the Indiana Jones theme.

I hope the next two movies will be as great as this or better. I think The Lord of The Rings can be the next Star Wars for the new generation!

title: Great movie, surprised by some of the poor reviews
review: I thought the movie was great, but I can't believe some of the bad reviews. I'm not going to go on and on about how good the movie, effects and other aspects of the movie are. I would rather add some comments about the negative reviews. 1. Movie length & character development - Many say it's too long. While we all know not everyone has read the book, this movie is billed as an epic adventure (epics are generally longer than just plain adventures). If you have read the book you would say to do the story justice you would need a 5 part, 2 hour each nite mini- series....... While Character development should be a seperate item, I think it falls with movie length. They had to cut certain things to get the movie down to three hours and some things couldn't be cut because they come into play in future movies. My opinion - this movie did the best it possibly could have in the SHORT amount of time it had. Something always will have to be cut for time restraints and someone will always think they cut the wrong thing, I think they did a great job. 2. Complaints about the powerful "old geezer" wizards. Have an open mind folks, these are not your typical spell casting old men. You don't even have to read the books to understand that this is a story, and they don't have to be the "typical" wizards you are used to. Gandalf was supposed to be a unimposing looking yet extremely powerful old wizard as was his conterpart in the tower (who is not Sauran, yet the name is similar). You should have picked up on that with the Bilbo encounter over the ring. Gandalf is one of the most powerful people in middle earth, and all appearances can be very deceiving. 3. Complaints about the story going here and there. (Continuity).....Very true to the book, and in fact some concessions where made for the movie. Whats wrong with traveling, fighting, traveling, fighting? I wonder how much time some of you think may have passed during this film. I don't recall them really making much mention of time during the movie, but perhaps they should have. Do you think it was weeks or months? The mountain pass alone was a few months. Maybe they didn't convey the time as best they could have but it still doesn't mean a movie can't do what this one did. You people are probably the ones that complained about Pulp Fiction going to and fro because you couldn't understand the story. Ahh, when I started this I was going to go more indepth, but I have more important things to do.

title: The Bore of the Rings
review: Gees....what a disapointment.  This movie was so dull and I mean DULL!! Way too long!! Not enough humour! Something was lacking.  The acting is great...particularly by Sir Ian McKellan and Sean Astin. Plus you do get some amazing photography of my country of New Zealand.  But does it really need to be a nauseating 3 hrs long?

title: Ballsy, Beautiful, Engaging, Exciting, Profound, Smart, Satisfying
review:
I am not someone who uses adjectives like those lightly. I'm very much a discerning film viewer,have spent my life working in and studying the arts and literature, and have little to no love for the average Hollywood mediocrity, be it the sad attempt at social profundity known as AMERICAN BEAUTY, the latest marketing masterplan like HARRY POTTER, or the annual exercises in macheesmo, like GLADIATOR and BRAVEHEART. That said, I love this movie, because it has everything the big blockbuster is supposed to have- action, romance, brilliant visuals- plus everything I've come to only expect in indie and foreign film- truly complex characters and plot lines, genuine respect for the brains of its audience, conviction in it's themes and story, and an overall emotional strength and consistency that leaves one haunted by the film for days. Of course I know that Tolkein's monumental novel shares much of the credit, but film is a completely different medium than literature and has many different objectives and problems that need to be overcome and so the movie is Jackson and company's baby- and they deserve it. It is one of the most successful literary adaptions I've seen since James Ivory's A ROOM WITH A VIEW, in the sense that it succeeds in becoming a brilliant movie in and of itself, as well as maintaining the spirit, story and themes of the original novel. Pulling off such a feat isn't easy- observe such failures as THE SCARLET LETTER, or DUNE for examples of how NOT to adapt a famous novel.

OF course the movie isn't flawless- Arwen's plea for Frodo to live (just after she's squelched the Nazgul- a totally viable change, I think, in light of the fact that Glorfindel does nothing else in the novel and Arwen, whose story is essential, desperately needed something to expand her into what a modern audience would consider an acceptable mate for Aragorn)is so schmaltzy and gooey that it stands out in an otherwise fascinateingly gloomy film flooded with complex emotions. Also, the almost complete lack of Gollum was a little disquieting, and will probably bite the filmmakers on the ass later on when Golem becomes so essential in part two and everyone in the audience who hasn't read the book goes, "What? He's been following them all along? Who is that slimy thing?" I mean, come on Jackson, all it would have take was two more well placed shots of Gollum trailing the Fellowship, just for continuity's sake.

But really, stuff like this is so nitpicky, and proof that this movie is so amazing- especially compared to similar films in the genre, like the new STAR WARS films. LORD OF THE RINGS succeeds where PHANTOM MENACE, for instance, ultimately fails: Middle Earth is so tangible, it's denizens so believable, that you really do believe in it and get caught up. Superbe attention to details- from close up shots of people's hands that were ACTUALLY DIRTY, to houses and gardens and skyscapes that were real and not computer created, to ornate belt buckles, bootheals and arrowheads- permeates the film, creating a rich, almost tangible world. The special affects are totally tasteful and mostly reserved for the Ringwraith's world, which is appropriately spooky and alien. True, the Troll seemed just a touch too CGI, compared to everything els, but he looked a hell of a lot better than the centaur in HARRY POTTER, which didn't even look like the animators finished before the film went to print.

Performances also make this movie amazing- because normally, directors and producers of special affects ridden adventure epics don't feel that the actors need to be good so much as pretty and famous- but these actors are all amazing, and if they were famous before this film, they were generally people famous for being generally amazing- Ian McKellan (a fantastic choice as Gandalf), Ian Holm (genuinely touching and riddled with pathos), Cate Blanchette (celestially beautiful and a wonderful combination of infinite power and infinite sadness), Christopher Lee (spectacularly evil). Viggo Mortensen (so good in PORTRAIT OF A LADY) finally gets a chance to shine, and Sean Bean gives his best performance to date- as does Liv Tyler, my only real casting fear before seeing the film who does a surprisingly good job. Elija Wood and Sean Astin both come of age in this movie and considering what the future holds for Frodo and Sam, I can't wait to see how they actors will grow with the characters. Orlando Bloom and Jean Rhys Davies provide wonderful supporting performances, and also make me look forward to the future which brings, amongst many other things, masisve expansion of their characters.

What works the best about LORD OF THE RINGS, however, is not the effects and design, or the actors, but the sheer scope of the film, it's overwhelming sense of trying to fight for the good in the face of exponentially increasing evil and terror, and it's fierce rejection of the sugary, feel good HARRY POTTER syndrome. True, some people might be disastisfied with the ending, but the whole point is that this is hardly the end (and if the ending of the film of TWO TOWERS is like the book, people are gonna be REALLY disappointed come December 2002), and if the same people find the movie too depressing, my only reponse is- too bad. A) it's going to get more depressing before the happy ending (and hey, isn't life often like that?) and B) if you can't find the beauty of heroes remaining heroic even in spite of growing doom and gloom, then it must be generally hard for you to find beauty at all. And since LORD OF THE RINGS, both the book and the movie, is mostly about the incredible endurance of that which is good being able to survive that which is evil, it's no small wonder this film will be lost on an audience grown accustomed to easy endings, easy solutions, and easy emotions.

And hey, the movie made me want to write a fantasy novel, propose marriage to someone incredible, and kill some orcs. It's been a while since any movie has made me want to do that.

title: A retort and a review at the same time.
review: I typically enjoy reading the critiques on the IMDB. usually being surprised by the professionalism of the writing and examination of the film in question.  Being a filmmaker and harsh critic myself, I can appreciate good criticism. but after reading some of the trite comments made about LOTR, I feel my only recourse is to actually retort to the statements made by fellow reviewers. Disliking a film for any number of reasons is every person's right, especially given the subjective nature of film.  The ability to articulate your angst is equally important.  I am a harsh critic of films myself, despising most of the `disposal cinema' made by Hollywood.  I have no problem telling someone why I dislike a film, director, actor, etc. once I have examined the work thoroughly and looked at what lead the film to its present state.  Too say a film is bad is one thing but state `that it sucked' is just ignorant. and then to follow up by saying, `The movie was repetitive and unoriginal. It felt like a second Harry Potter', now that is just mind blowing.  Don't you people understand that J.R.Tolkien's books ARE THE ORIGINALS?  Written in 1954, these are the forerunners of all fantasy. If you asked a fiction writer of the works that most inspired them, you would find the name Tolkien as a common occurrence.  I could list off movies and books that have drawn directly from the trilogy, but that would take years to complete. LOTR was a technical masterpiece.   Its flawless set design and musical score complimented the fantasy genre.  Creating a fantasy film of this magnitude has never been attempted before. and yes, that includes Harry Potter.  Don't get me wrong, Harry Potter was excellent in its own merit, but it still takes place for the most part, in a school filled with human children and wizards.  The few actual fantasy creatures in the movie were computer generated and looked like video game rejects.  To compare the two in the category of fantasy is plain silly.  One takes place in a localized area (Hogwart's) while the other spans across an entire world (Middle Earth). Too look at this movie and complain that there were giant birds, magic, and old men of immense power, makes very little sense.  You are dealing with fantasy.  A genre that takes unexplainable acts, and attempts to give them a base-entertaining explanation.  Why is it so hard to suspend your disbelief when two old men are using magic to battle each other, yet easily do so when a three foot tall, green-midget-alien lifts a spaceship with his mind? That answer is simple. YOU DON'T LIKE FANTASY.  If you don't like fantasy that's fine, but why did you spend $10 to see a 3hr movie?  Because like most people, Hollywood said `See this movie' and like cattle, you followed the herder into slaughterhouse, regardless of your own interests.  Only after the fact do you realize that wasted your own time on a genre that you weren't very interested in to begin with. Yes, the movie was three hours long and yes; it's part of a trilogy. These are all things that you knew before you saw it.  A story this large couldn't be told in a 90min movie.  They tried that in the 70s with the animated versions and they were atrocious.  The current LOTR was 3 hours long and they still had to cut out parts of the book.  As a fan of the books, I can say that I was not disappointed with the movie adaptation.  Sure some things were sacrificed while others thing were changed or added, but that is part of making a viable movie.  And. yes, it leaves you with a cliffhanger. The story is unresolved, it's supposed to be.  There are two more parts to the movie, but it's not like it ended amidst a battle sequence.  The story paused at a crossroad.  A new dynamic had been created and the quest had been altered by present circumstances.  There couldn't be a better time to set up a cliffhanger. Overall, this movie was fantastic.  The first true fantasy film.  It's not the greatest movie of all time, but I would recommend it to all people who love fantasy or have the slightest interest in it.  It is a movie of true imagination that will go down in history with its written counterparts.

title: "...anyone who has read the book would know..."
review:
There will be two types of people who go to see The Lord of The Rings. Those who have read the books (and who might also have studied Tolkien's other works), and those who are new to Middle Earth.

The Lord of The Rings is considered by many to be the greatest work of imaginative fiction last century, and the reviewer if of this opinion. A review of the book is best handled elsewhere.

It would be easy to start any review of LOTR with "...anyone who has read the book would know...no movie could ever do the book justice". But this would simply amount to trite literary snobbery. Of course, there will be many millions who see the movie with no previous knowledge of Middle Earth.

I am a four-time reader of LOTR, back in my teen years, as well some years consumed by Tolkien lore thereafter. Reading Tolkien books is (and always will be) a rite of passage for many escapist boys of pubescent age, and I was one of them.

The movie clearly has much to offer the viewer. In this age of ever-competing attractions, in that Las Vegas land of brightly flashing lights competing for your attention and dollar, entertainment has to be delivered in short (even for three hours, LOTR is short compared against the written work), intense bursts...

LOTR did not fail to please me, and Peter Jackson is to be commended on an astounding technical masterpiece, and cinematic history is obliged to chalk it up as a triumph, and no doubt as the financial success it must surely turn out to be.

Sets, props, makeup and acting are uniformly excellent.

LOTR is not perfect, no motion picture ever will be. Much is left out from the original novel; some camera angle do not work...and look for that huge zit below Frodo's lip in one scene, which has miraculously disappeared in the next!

Another fault (though a limitation of the medium, rather than any fault of the movie maker), is that the vast distances that the Fellowship have to travel are not really conveyed to the viewer...for example, when Gandalf rides of to see Saruman, it seems like he's only nipped around the corner, and not the many weary leagues the journey actually took. when Arwen

But movie-making is a flawed process, and Jackson has done an enormously satisfying job, given the limitations of the format.

I do believe that one day a "time-line" edition of LOTR will be produced, when computers of the day will be able to cope with the insane amount of data that would be required to simulate every blade of grass and every character's action in Middle Earth, from Shire to Mount Doom. Only then, will the full grandeur of LOTR be comprehended...or, you could just read the book ;)

title: A Tour De Force in movies (from someone who has never read the books!)
review:
Well, what can I say? I had heard so many mixed reviews from so many quarters before seeing this movie, that I was a little nervous. I mean, was I going to waste my hard earned cash, and "my precious" christmas vacation time spending close to three hours in a movie theatre? Well, the answer was no, it was certainly not a waste of money!

This is a review from someone who has never read any of the books - has actually attempted to, several times, but found them far too unappealing and much too much like hard work, yet I still was fascinated enough to want to see this movie.

I couldn't say if it is a faithful adaptation of the book - having seen the first Harry Potter movie (and knowing what was left out of that), I would say that it is unlikely that the director could fit everything in. But looking at "fellowship" as simply a movie, it is one of the rare classics that will be watched over and over again, and no doubt, we will all find additional parts that we missed the first time too.

Elijah Wood is exceptionally well cast as Frodo, as are the rest of the cast members - especially Viggo Mortensen, who puts just the right amount of regal bearing into his moves and actions to make you yearn for Part III to arrive, so we can see the Return of the King.

The scenery (very irrelevant to the plot and movie critique I know)was amazing, making me now want to visit New Zealand, and altogether I thought this was well worth a full price ticket.

My only "con", if you like, is the number of people who took children under the age of 5 into this film and my comment to all of you who are thinking of doing this in the future is PLEASE DON'T. For one thing, these children found the fight scenes and monsters very scary, for another they got bored, as they did not have the intellectual skills to follow the plot. And lastly on this point, if you can afford a frickin' movie ticket, then surely you can afford a baby sitter so that the rest of us poor theatre goers don't have to put up with your kids being in a pain in the.....THIS MOVIE IS NOT FOR YOUNG CHILDREN!

Go and see this movie once, just to say you went, a second time, to get all the plot points, and a third time just for the hell of it.

Roll on next year and Book II of the Lord of the Rings trilogy - an outstanding movie to end the year with!

title: This is the best movie I have ever seen.
review: Aside from being more or less true to the book (roughly 5 chapters all told are removed and some characters have slightly changed roles) this movie depicts Tolkiens Middle Earth in what must simply be what he intended.

title: Movies are supposed to be this good.
review:
Movies are supposed to demand repeat viewings and get better instead of worse with each new foray into their depths. The Fellowship of the Ring was twice as good the second time I saw it.

I have read the novels many times and had tremendous expectations. This movie faced a deck stacked with hype, history, and hopes so grand that I could almost never dream of being satisfied. My first viewing suffered because of this. Of course, I loved it, and was spell bound. It was too much to bear, three hours of non-stop exhiliration and wonder, tempered by constant comparisons to past interpretation, as well as the great novel itself. To make matters worse, I had aching pains by the Mines of Moria sequence do to my lack of foresight with regard to basic bodily functions, and had to run out to satisfy this problem. I missed the introduction to Lothlorien. The movie was incredible, but still, did not feel right. I thought the ending was a little heavy handed, the Enya, too much, but with my second viewing, all of that changed.

It takes that second viewing to purge the hype. Aragorn became Aragorn, because I wasn't busy judging performances. Instead of wondering how Jackson would pull it off, or whether it was what I expected or not, I allowed it to tell its tale, and allowed the characters to be who they were. This movie is different from the book, it faces necessities due to the medium, and succeeds brilliantly because it captures the books greatest quality, sincereity. A novel or movie in this setting with these characters and ambitions, must not be cynical, snide, or cocky, and thus this movie is not like any movie which has come out in a long time.

What this movie has is passion. It trusts its story and characters to illuminate themselves, and though the filmaking is of the highest order, it doesn't overstep its bounds; Jackson has amazing trust in the material he is working with, and this is the only way Tolkien can be filmed, because the tale itself is enough. Cynics will claim the movie is too simple, the characters blah, blah, blah, or they won't allow themselves to beleive in this world and what occurs in it, questioning everything. If you want to enjoy this movie, then check your cynicism at the door. Beleive and trust; you will be enthralled, and waiting eagerly for the next installment. Watching this movie is simple, enjoy it for what it is, and at the end of Fellowship, (possible spoiler ahead) beleive that Aragorn has chosen with difficulty the direction of his birthright, that Legolas and Gimli are ready to face death to save Merry and Pippin, that Sam would rather drown than abandon his master.

Is the movie flawed? Of course it is. No one can ask for perfection. Jackson can't film the novels word for word. Some characters could use more development and screen time, but ultimately all of the characters make noble and exhilirating choices, some that cause suffering, and are ill-fated or misguided, and that is where the magic of Fellowship lies, in the novel and in the multiplex. These choices will be tested in the upcoming installments, leading to even greater tests and choices, and that is how the best stories are told. If you haven't read the books, beleive me when I say that the novels and movies will only get better. (Each and every time that you return to them)

title: Incredible!
review: It's the best fantasy movie never made.. incredible. It's so real... and Peter Jackson has translate the books into the Film language very good...
