title: review from a non-fanatic
review: According to the voting, this is apparently the top movie of all time.  I have to strongly disagree with that.  To say that this movie is superior to films like the Godfather is an outrage.  It is in fact entertaining, but if you're not into fantasy books the story is a little "weird" at times. Don't get me wrong, the visuals are gorgeous, and the action is good.  It just left me with a so-so taste in my mouth.  Good, but nothing special.

title: slow first hour, but the rest rocks
review: Lord of the rings really surprised me. I have never read the books but after seeing this movie, I am already in the process of reading the first book. The movie did have slow parts, such as the first hour, but the rest of the movie made up for it. I have never seen a movie like this one, and I certainly hope the second one is as good. The mine scenes left me breathless, and the scenery blew me away. If you are wondering what to see, and you haven't seen this beautiful film yet, go see it!!!

title: First Impressions - Final Verdict
review:
I have just returned from seeing a midnight showing of the Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, one of the first showings. My first impression of the film is that it is a work of art. It is stunning to the eye, and true the books. There have been minor alterations to the story to make it fit better into a film format, but the essence, and details that are important to the plot of the books has been captured with great detail. For a three hour long feature I was surprised to find that it did not feel so long. The film holds a good tempo, and keeps you interested. For those of you who have never read the books, the story has been explained, but not in a way that would lessen the experience for those who have read the books.

For those of you, who have never read the books, please remember that this film is three hours long, and for good reason. It is an adaptation of a story that helped to create a genre, and fantasy books today have evolved into a writing style that is somewhat faster in pace. This film, like the book that it represents, can take some patients to enjoy it.

My final verdict is that this film, and the following films will be winning many awards in the coming months, and they will become centerpieces to fantasy fans DVD libraries in years to come. I intend to see this film at the very least two more times, due to the wealth of details, for I feel that I did not see everything in the first sitting.

One Ring to rule them all, One Ring to find them, One Ring to bring them all and in the darkness bind them.

  • J.R.R Tolkien (The father of contemporary fantasy)

title: glad it wasnt dumbed down
review:
SPOILER alert

Let me say that i am extremely pleased how this movie turned out. i was very much concerned that it would end up being aimed primarily at those who had never read the book. As it stands though i am happy that the film didnt try to sit there and explain everything to the unwashed masses. Quite frankly if you havent read the book then this movie is no more important to you than another Star Wars or Rush Hour and i honestly dont care what you thought of it.

For those who have read the book the movie was perfect. bearing in mind that i do not perceive this movie as being intended as a seperate entity from the books but rather as a supplement.

If youve read the books your primary concern will be to finally be able to see the fantastic and dramatic moments and characters you have long imagined. if you have read the books you do NOT need to have things explained to you that you are already well aware of or listen to actors recite reams of character building dialouge.

The pacing and lack of character building and background information are the majorflaws in this film when viewed from a traditional viewpoint. But if you have already read the books then these things are not an issue. thus this is perhaps the best adaptation of LotR that we could have hoped for.

The one change that i found a little off putting was the fact that Aragorn knew before hand that Frodo was leaving and neither attempted to stop him or join him.

PS at the end when the credits came up i had forgotten that it was only the first movie of three and was disapointed beying beleief when i realised that i would have to wait a year for the next installment.

title: Fine movie, just a little rushed
review:
With all the hype that Lord of the Rings has been getting, my hopes were way up before seeing this movie. As an old Fantasy/ Middle Earth fangeek, I figured if the other fans are loving it, they can't all be wrong.

Well, I did like the movie, but it wasn't the epiphany I was expecting. It's an entertaining take on Middle Earth, and what is in the movie is done well. It's what's missing that I was dissatisfied with. The movie feels rushed. It's a huge book to adapt, but I feel that the story told in the movie doesn't really hang together and isn't plausible without understanding the book. It's a good try, but I would say that movies like Star Wars or the Matrix, which create their own mythology, or movies like Blade Runner which doscards much from the text it's derived from, have the advantadge over movies like The Fellowship. The sheer amount of detail and plotting that went into the book are difficult to convey onscreen. Not having that detail and plotting detracts from the movie, even without comparing it to the book.

title: Speechless
review: This movie is great and the greatest in its kind. I got nothing to comment other then i didnt really like the sentimental bits between the hobbits with the rest of the fellowship :). Other then that the movie is excellent

review: The movie was excellent; just too great to put into words.  It did the book justice just as The Two Towers and Return of the King will do.  Do not miss this movie! Perfect dream-cast! This movie will rival all others the end of this year and on into 2002!

title: Huh, what did I miss?
review:
It is now 4 days after I watched LOTR and I still can't shake off the feeling of being cheated by the producers. For one I have not had the luxury of reading the multiple volumes of the novel before watching the movie. So, I do not have a headstart in trying to understand what the movie was about. None the less I think the producers should have been a bit more professional and create a movie the suits the majority of movie goers whom I think have not read any LOTR novel before. In this matter the producers looked like they were trying to show they were hardcore LOTR fans. I myself have not read about Harry Potter too but I have no problem trying to follow the movie from start to end. LOTR may have a start, if you call the 5-6 minutes of story telling by a background voice ala Toy Story a start, it is even more difficult to explain what happen to the ending for the movie.

It was a well done trailer but I was expecting more than just a good trailer. Honestly I am not looking forward to the sequel because I felt cheated. Normally movie goers would be propelled to watch sequel if the earlier version was good. Literally speaking the movie is 'forcing' you to watch the sequel, not encouraging.

title: Excellent beginning to what should be excellent trilogy
review:
This movie is not the best movie ever made. However it is a magnificent achievement. The cast is much better than I hoped and the portrayals were amazing. I was not totally pleased with Arwen although this was not the actress's fault, she played it perfectly. There just seemed to be something jarring about it (perhaps I've been steeped in the book too much). The beginning (for fans of the book) is much different than the book although it remains true to the spirit of Tolkien and so I found it to be fine.

The only real problem I had with the entire movie was with Aragorn (Strider). It was not a problem with the acting. I didn't believe anyone could portray him so well. It was with the script. In the book Strider is a towering figure, exuding mystery, wildness and danger. No problem so far. However as leader of the company he is plagued with self-doubt. This makes him more human. He is the one who recommends the Mines of Moria (not Gimli) and when all goes not perfectly (be patient I'm trying to avoid a spoiler) he blames himself. Every small problem they have is a result of his decisions and he blames himself for them. A flaw in an otherwise perfect character. This is missing from the movie. Does it detract overall? Not really, it just might be better if it was in the movie to add depth to the character.

Personally, I would have preferred an extended version of Lothlorien. The gifting of the cloaks, the brooches and the box of earth (to Sam) are missing and (depending on how the movie is portrayed) could be very important. The softening of Gimli to the elves begins in Lorien with his devotion to the Lady Galadriel. This also marks the beginning of the thaw of relationship between Legolas and Gimli.

However these are all very small points and personal preferences. If the rest of the trilogy continues in the same vein, it will be one of the most amazing pieces of cinematic work I have ever seen. In a much earlier comment, someone said that the worst part was having to wait a year for the next movie. I agree.

title: I never thought sheer scale could make a film!
review:
Firstly let me say that this film is a true masterpiece. Yes, it is not perfect, but nothing ever is, but the small niggles, are just that, SMALL!

I read the books when I was eight years old, and thought them great, and I saw the cartoon version (a personal favourite when I was small), but I did not think I could be as impressed as I was but this wonderful piece of film-making.

Let's look at what is wrong with the film. Some of the CGI is a bit ropey, but only in incidental scenes, where the aformentioned CGI is not in the main shot, or you only catch a fleeting glimpse. The orcs where a bit too "muscle men with face paint" for my tastes. This was one thing I preferred in the cartoon; the orcs where more varied, some fat ones, some thin, some drinking, some bickering. Also the orc's voices sounded a bit too synthisyser-esque. Arwen rescuing Frodo, not in the book, and (I may be wrong about in the book, but in the cartoon) when Frodo rides to the ford on his own, it shows what a strong character he is, fighting for all he is worth against the power of the Ring Wraiths.

Now to what makes the film.

This movie is filmed as if it was real. I will try to explain what I mean by this. How many times in a hollywood film have you seen beautifully clean hair and skin? In this film there is dirt under the character's fingernails, grease in the hair, they look tired and cold and harassed. You empathise so much more with them, with the quest.

The other main point that makes this film is the sheer scale of it. The landscape of New Zealand is the set, and so it does look huge and beautiful. The characters are put into scale with the environment, and it really does work. You believe that it is a world, not a set.

Onto the story. I have read some of the negative reviews on this site, and it seems that the people just did not get the point of alot of the plot. The whole idea of the ring is that it is controling. It has an influence on the characters and plot. You could almost describe it as another member of the cast. This is why the film ends like it does, because the ring is trying to stop the fellowship.

Some of the added pieces of CGI, with Galadriel and Bilbo changing in the precence of the ring, really add to the feeling of power from the ring. THe Balroc is, quite frankly, stunning, and the battle sequences, and fights are brilliant. They even manage to make the use of a bow and arrow at close quarters look fessible. And I also have to say that you need to sit somewhere in the theatre that allows the screen to fill your vision, as some of the sweeping shots can out-do any ride at Disneyland!

The acting is excellent, with Sam and Frodo actually coming over as likable characters. One review I read said the Frodo is too whingeing, but, with Peter Jackson being as faithful as he can be to the books, the fact that you don't want to throttle Frodo and Sam after 20 seconds is remarkable. Gandalph is played beautifully, so that you can see the underlying power of the character. Sean Bean really does prove that he can act, and Orlando Bloom will be a very big star before long. The rest of the Fellowship just add to the experience. They ALL look like Tolkien drew them, and act as he wrote them; they are their characters.

Even the dodgy throw-away lines, added for comedic effect, don't detract from the film but embelish it.

To sum up, yes this film has faults, but the minute you let such little points take away from such a wonderfully engrousing experience you are selling yourself short. This film is here to be enjoyed, and savoured.

Without doubt 10/10.

title: Know your Tolkien before you read this review.
review:
Let me begin by stating that I am something of a Tolkien devotee. Now, there is no such thing as flawless movie, but Peter Jackson's vision held me and a large (and very critical) group of friends in awe for the entire length of the film. Where to begin...

I was frankly worried a few years ago when I heard this project was underway. I didn't believe it could be done faithfully. How would one do Hobbits convincingly? How would the Eye appear? How does one portray the majesty of the elves, even in their decline? Jackson does all of this in a thoughtful way. While I do not always agree with his choices, they are his and I respect him for his vision in taking on a seemingly impossible project.

Truth be told, it is not 100% faithful to the original story, but as another reviewer here indicated, the "flaws", which I refer to as license, are understandable and even necessary to make the film shorter, and it is not short by any stretch of the imagination.

I will avoid tackling the minutae of changes - they do not detract from the story - but there is one change that has caused a great deal of comment in some circles, and that is the role of Arwen. Obviously her role is greatly expanded. I see this as positive and filling several needs. First, she reduces the overall character count. Glorfindel (the original rescuer) is not key to the story. Second, the females amongst the elves are not all wispy, fragile beauty. Arwen is the daughter of the Firstborn, and has all the gifts and might of that people. The other explanations for her role; stronger female characters, sex appeal, etc., seem like contrivances of our world.

All of that said, I wholeheartedly endorse this movie. I have seen it twice as of the time I write this review, and will see it several more times in the theatre I am sure. Jackson has imagined and created a stunningly real Middle-earth that has reshaped and improved my own vision.

title: The impossible dream.
review:
First comment: If this was a straightforward, easy story to convert to celluloid, the Hollywood dreck machine would have churned out 7 versions by now, and not one would have achieved what Fellowship Of The Rings has done; it has SUCCESSFULLY transferred the ultimate fictional story of our time into an enjoyable, watchable, engaging movie. Lord Of The Rings is infinitely more complex, textured and character rich than The Wizard Of Oz, and there's no cheesy song and dance routines to patch up what amounts to 10 minutes of script. It was never going to be perfect. It was never going to satisfy the hard core Tolkienists, nor win over the Schwarzenegger set (thank God). And of course, the chronic complainers, antagonistic afficionados, cool-cruel critics and pessimistic punters will have gorged themselves on enough pre-release hype and promotion to be able to take all the cheap shots they want at some of the movie's imperfections. "After all the expectations...blah blah blah..".

Those who think of "Star Wars" as a measuring stick stay away. Those who think for themselves, go and see a magnificent story brought to life as well as anyone could have done. Perhaps the body count boys and cheap thrill conjurors in California could take note. To make a GOOD film, first take a GOOD story.....

review:
I have read LOTR, so I sort of had high expectations for this movie. Let me tell you, after seeing this movie I realised that my expectations were low! It is definatly one of the best movies I have ever seen.

A lot of people are comparing this movie to the book......Why? Everyone knows that a film adaptation of a book is never better than the book itself, especially a world famous book like LOTR. Others say that it sucks because it doesnt have Tom Bombadil, again this doesnt have anything to do with the movies story line. If Peter Jackson put in everything we would have a 5 hour movie!

I have read the Star Wars Episode 1 novel, and so have many other people. I dont hear them complaining about there beloved SW. People are not used to a lot of old style Fantasy, Thats why they compare LOTR to D&D? just because they both have Dwarves? Stupid if you ask me...

To sum up, this movie is legendary when you look at it as just a movie. If you compare it to the book it will seem a little too fast and rushed.

9 out of 10

title: A good adaptation of the book
review:
For the first time I feel the need to actually bother putting some comments on a message board. As I have been reading the other comments about The Lord of The Rings first film, I have become slightly incredulous about the variety of comments put to this film.

I went into the film, having read the three books making up the LOTR, the Hobbit, and I had started on the Simarillion(though I had to give up as I was about 14 at the time and found it very hard going). I therefore went with many preconceptions about the film, and yet a sense of expectation. I was not overly disappointed. For starters the casting was impeccable. The hobbits were fairly well cast, though I have a few doubts about the development of the characters and Frodo's character seemed to have started the doubts about himself that only appear in the closing chapters of the last book. Gandalf was as he should be, old, grey, withered, but yet able to produce the power that is inherent in him. If you read the books you will find that is how he is supposed to be. A little disappointed with Saruman, not for the way he was portrayed, which was fine, but with the way the storyline had been adapted around him. Aragorn was as he should be, and the development of Arwen's role gave a better view for those who had not read the books about their love affair, if it was not perhaps a little hamfisted in the way it was done. The Council of Elrond, and in fact Elrond himself was perhaps the worst part of the film. This was mainly due to the speed in which it had to be done and the unfortunate quick inclusion of the other characters. Obviously there could not have been, as in the book, the full detailed accounts of each character's story and their reasons for being at the Council, purely due to the time limits. The re-forging of Narstil, again unfortunately skipped, left me wondering how the story was going to evolve. I noticed a few complaints about the fight scenes in some of the comments. Admittedly, for the "Matrix Generation" of slow-stop camera trickery, these would have seemed poor, unrehearsed and confusing. Welcome to the world of melee fighting.

The breaking of the Fellowship, I admit, would have been done better in the way that Tolkien did it, and I thought that would have been easier to do on the screen and more credible. Obviously from the comments about how people were disappointed at the ending, the Tolkien ending would have resulted in yet more complaints about the film.

Finally, to sum up and before I get off my soap-box, a few closing comments. I found the film to be an excellent rendition of a huge and difficult novel to transfer to the big screen. I was a little disappointed by small niggling details, but on the whole cannot wait till next Christmas for the "Two Towers". I do think it is an outstanding film, possibly better than the Star Wars trilogy, but only perhaps because of the technological advances since the Star Wars trilogy came out, and because of the story behind it which is more of an epic than Star Wars. Star Wars was a film pure and simple, LOTR is a film based on a highly successful novel.

However there are some who don't seem to know what they are talking about. It is chapter one in a TRILOGY, not film one in a series of related, yet not directly following on from one other films. You cannot end the story at the end of chapter one as it would not be a novel, rather a collection of short stories.

Finally, and I mean it this time, if you are still having problems with "understanding" the story: Go and Read the book.

title: The Whole is less than the Sum of the Parts
review:
The Fellowship of the Ring delivers on nearly every level: Superb acting (Ian McKellen and Ian Holm shine), CGI as you have never seen it before (without indulging in its own splendour), superb score (even if 'only' supportive of the action in the film) and great visuals. The different shrinking methods work superbly together.

What it lacks is the soul and spirit of the book. I know, that this opinion is not that of the majority right now, but I still believe that the sense of awe - that there is so much more in the world of Middle-earth than you read - is lost in the movie. Probably that's not the fault of its makers but rather of the nature of the story. I think that hardly anybody could have made a better film out of this material than Peter Jackson and New Line. Still I did not enjoy it nearly as much as the book.

You may have already guessed, that this is a review by a purist. I don't mind changes to the book, when they are necessary to transfer the story to the screen, but generally the film shines the most whenever it keeps closest to the words of Tolkien.

The things I liked least of the plot(*spoilers ahead*):

  • The sense of the passing of time is totally lost.


  • The typical Hollywood-problem: The bad guys - although equipped with great powers - seem just to be there to be beaten eventually. Tolkien makes you feel the mortal danger in every confrontation. In the movie Aragorn beats up five ringwraiths - I absolutely hated the way the last one instantly caught fire with just one throw of a torch -, Arwen sweeps the Nazgul away with just some ad hoc-sorcery, later Aragorn takes on the Uruk-hai all alone and prevails. However the Balrog works, but unfortunately its significance is lessened by the cave-troll which is given much more screen-time.


  • The changes in Bilbo and Galadriel when tempted by the ring.


  • Everything between Hobbiton and Rivendell.


  • Saruman. It was such a nice twist in the book, when you learn of the nature of his treachery only after he is cast down. In the movie he appears as Sauron's minion from the beginning onward. The wizards' duel also seemed rather ridiculous.


  • The comic relief. No big movie seems to be able to avoid it nowadays.


The things I really liked of the plot:

  • Character development. Even though there are a lot of main characters, each one of them is given his due.


  • The introduction. No information-overkill, but everything important is conveyed expertly.


  • Moria. As soon as that skeleton drops down the well, you are in for one of the greatest action sequences ever.


  • The ring. The idea of giving the ring its own personality and voice really works. Also the change in Frodos perception whenever he wears the ring is great. The Ring/Bilbo/Gandalf- and the Ring/Frodo/Boromir-scenes are also convincing.


  • The inclusion of Boromir's death in the first movie.


What non-readers of the book might find disturbing:

  • Too many names. It might probably have been better to use only one name for every person/location (ie there are three different names used for 'Moria' in the movie).


  • You never learn, why Sam calls Frodo 'Master'.


  • Sometimes the pacing is too slow as the movie approaches and passes two hours. Especially Lothlorien might be a problem. Of course Galadriels otherwordlyness is emphasized by her way of speaking, but it is more effective than any lullaby (I watched the German version, maybe in the OV it is different). On the other hand perhaps I shouldn't have watched the whole thing at 0:01 am (earliest possibility for 'ordinary' people in Vienna on the 19th).


  • Geography. Lots of references, where they might be or are actually going, but you don't get the big picture.


  • The ending. Such a cliff-hanger. Not everybody will be happy about it, even though there probably was no other way.


This movie is still the second-best I have seen this year (after 'Memento'), perhaps I just expected more since the books had been my favourite since childhood. I will watch it again, probably then I will see it more as a standalone movie and not a book-adaptation. For now I give it a 8/10.

title: The perfect adaptation of the novel
review:
The expectations were really high after seeing all these trailers and other stuff, but they were exceeded by far. Peter Jackson did a great job by bringing the landscapes and the characters to the screen in such a perfect way. This IS really Middle Earth.

There are some scenes I did not like, e.g. Frodo's encounter with Galadriel, or the octopus-like beast at the entrance to Moria. But they are negligible compared with the scenes that I did like: Ian McKellen and Sean Bean may be the best actors you could find for their roles. The greatest surprise was Elijah Wood, since I did not expect, that he would make such a good Frodo. Seeing the mines of Moria, the Shire, or the river Anduin, it may happen that you forget to close your mouth due to your astonishment. After seeing this movie my only wish was to see it again from the beginning, and I surely will.

This is the perfect adaptation of the novel, and three unforgettable hours. I gave it 10/10.

title: Rave Review
review: I was lucky enough to view this film at the Australian first screening, before the American release date, and all the high expectations, hopes and anticipation for the film, was not only met, but totally exceeded everything I could possibly have hoped for.  Every single performance from the incredibly emotive Sir Ian McKellen down to the very briefest cameo appearance from Peter Jackson and his children.  Not only a redemption of the fantasy genre not only in film, but in literature (particularly after the insanely dismal failure of D&D), but an absolute triumph of film making, aesthetically sublime and emotionally turbulent, exquisitely made and painstakingly cared for by its unparalleled cast and crew.  Peter Jackson has crafted an amazing film, with the visual effects not once out of place, but seamlessly integrated throughout the entire piece.  This whole film was a wonderment to behold.  Congratulations to Peter Jackson and the whole cast and crew of the Lord of the Rings trilogy - you have created cinema history.

title: The most incredible movie ever!
review: I am an avid fan of Tolkien and have read many of his books concerning Middle Earth.  I was so glad that someone finally gathered up the courage to undertake the task of creating his world.  The movie brings to life all the images readers enjoy from the stories with amazing special effects.  But the story is more than a special effects extravaganza, it's a story of hope, courage, and bravery that touches us all.  I recommend seeing this movie more than once, as I have, to gather as much of it as you can until The Two Towers debuts next year.  I personally cannot believe we have to wait another year to see the next release, but it'll be well worth the wait!

title: Very enjoyable
review: I've only so far read 1/2 of "The Hobbit", but the film seems to have done a wonderful job of bringing to life the nuances of this universe.  Great casting.  Great production values and truly fantastic effects.  As already commented, the directing of the action sequences seems a bit off at times. A bit flawed like the action sequences in "Gladiator".  Nevertheless a very enjoyable movie, and I can't wait to see the next one in this trilogy.

title: Close to Perfect
review:
All of those people who have written how bad this movie is must be out of their minds!

Well, actually, there are not that many in reality, it is just that they are more likely to write comments than the rest of us. This movie is sooo close to perfect, the computer animation is extraordinary, far beyond anything I have ever seen before and the wide landscape pictures simply took my breath away. The acting is brilliant, the pacing is wonderful, making sure the movie doesn't drag on like the book while slight changes make it all the move believable and suited to a movie. The acting is beyong reproach, I simply cannot think of any flaw.

I cannot believe I will have to wait a year for the next installment! Take my advice, ignore the ungrateful crazies who have written that this movie is terrible, go see it for yourself, today if possible, and experience this extraordinary movie for yourself. You won't notice a moment of the 3 hours passing and you're sure to come out of the theatre a devout fan of Tolkien and Peter Jackson.

title: A front runner for Best Film of 2001
review:
It had been a long time (2 weeks) since I'd last been to the local cinema down in the multiplex. My previous outing had left me scarred: Harry Potter and The Philosophers Stone was its name and it had thrown my expectations and desires to the wind. After that everything changed: Cameron Crowe films seemed pointless, teen buddy comedies like American Pie 2 were abysmal and even a DeNiro-Brando-Norton collaboration appeared to be fruitless.

It was at this point that I decided once again put my faith in film and allow myself to be swept up in hype. This time it was a New Zealand produced film by the name of "Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of The Ring" and it looked to be the next "big thing". Toys, books, dolls, cups, cards and posters came, each cheesy piece of merchandise grabbing me and seizing my wants and needs inch by inch.

By the evening of Christmas I was at the foot of my bed praying, not for the wonderful presents and other assorted gifts I had accumulated, but that this film, just this one, would fish me out of the deep and never-ending pit of dissatisfaction that had been set by it's cinematic brothers and sisters. And so on the 27th of December at about eight thirty in the morning there I stood in a queue down at the local Greater Union cinema, that odd feeling and the words "LORD OF THE RINGS" echoing throughout my mind and pulsating through my veins like quicksilver.

At about ten thirty the doors open and I sat in the cinema on the middle right, my preferred seating venue. After a few almost insignificant trailers (save Episode II) the movie started. Suddenly the on-screen title sprung up "The Lord of The Rings". It had begun.

What followed was one of the most incredible cinematic experiences that I had ever had the grace of attending (keeping in mind I'm sixteen) and an event that will surely change the face of Fantasy film forever. Firstly, the Special Effects and other graphic aids created by the WETA team are superbly spectacular. Included in the greatness of the film is of course the set decoration and art direction which in my opinion, not only matches, but overtakes the efforts in Star Wars Episode I: The Phantom Menace. The detail and depth of Hobbiton is a primary example of the level of authenticity.

Secondly, the performances contributed by all involved are first grade. You can tell there were no second preferences here (save Viggo Mortinsen who was not originally slated to play the role of Strider, but who does turn in a finely restrained and forcefully stable performance). Particular attention however must be paid to Ian McKellan for his deliciously perfect portrayal of the aging wizard Gandalf, Elijah Wood for his lively but surprisingly calculated and subdued Frodo (he avoids over-acting) and Cate Blanchett for her riveting and enchanting characterization of one of the oldest characters in Tolkien's saga's, the Elf Queen Galadriel.

The strength and overall intelligence of the screenplay (written by the director Peter Jackson and several other collaborators) truly captures the brilliance and distinct feel established in Tolkien's prized books. Although a few scenes and intricacies throughout the book have been altered or even deleted, the screen envisionment can proudly hold a flame to the legendary tale. Note: Tolkien aficionados may criticize the film due to its lack of areas included in the tale and do have a basis for complaint, but are reminded: if you are going to mame the film for it's literary shortcomings please do not complain of its length, which leads me to my next point.

Although the film is arduous (at over three hours) it does, somehow, maintain interest throughout the lagging scenes and keeps the viewer ever interested. And for those out there who are thinking of boycotting the film because your favorite critic or critics have said it was too long, keep in mind films such as Pulp Fiction, Titanic and Saving Private Ryan were also accused of being too lengthy.

Finally, the direction by Peter Jackson (of Heavenly Creatures fame) is an example of ideal modern epic film making and how to execute it properly. The brilliant narrative and overall excellence of the film deserves to win Jackson his first Oscar (though it should be his second).

Although The Lord of The Rings: The Fellowship of The Ring does have its shortcomings, notably a few under developed characters and a penchant for a sappy love story in between, it is definitely the strongest, wisest and best film of the Year of 2001. This is, undoubtedly, the cinematic event of the year. I only hope the Academy realises this and does the right thing before its too late (I call to mind STAR WARS).

Overall: 9 1/2 out of 10

title: Boring Story
review:
I've never read the books, but I love fantasy films (Conan,Dark Crystal,Excalibur). I have to say this movie failed in it's plot and characters. There was no clear cut moral choice our characters face. It was basically as this: the bad guys are bad because they are ugly and slimy. So there is no real threat. I didn't care who won or lost in the story. Some brief rambling about the world falling into darkness isn't good enough to create tension. And to top it off, the villains were uncreative in appearance. Black skin with fangs and color contact-lenses? Jeez!

Another big problem with the story is that there were no rules to it. Giant birds and fire breathing demons just pop in and out with no rhyme or reason. Trained Orc warriors are easily slaughtered by the dozen. A boy is sent on a mission to save the world with no combat experience, because it is "meant to be." And there is neither an explanation as to the rules of magic. What is it this ring can and can't do? The Death Star can blow up planets. But what can the ring do?? And far, far too many characters made a muddle of things. A frustrating film to watch with no payoff at the end.

title: Jackson's adaptation is true to Tolkien
review:
All things considered, The Fellowship of the Ring is the best adaptation of a novel I have ever seen. Director Peter Jackson and crew deserve accolades (i.e. Oscar nominations) for creating an uncanny, cinematic clone of J.R.R. Tolkien's source material.

Occasionally, a movie surpasses the author's original work. The Godfather and Jaws are examples. Never mind that Mario Puzo and Peter Benchley penned fine best sellers; it took auteur directors like Francis Ford Coppola and Stephen Spielberg to turn entertaining summer reading into film greatness.

Other books transformed into movies are more like a tie. Ira Levin wrote a damn original story called Rosemary's Baby. Yet, brilliant director Roman Polanski and vulnerable actress Mia Farrow make it tough for me to decide which is better. Likewise, Stephen King's The Shining was given excellent silver screen treatment by the late Stanley Kubrick.

And, let's not forget Harry Potter. I haven't read the Potter novel, but I gave a maximum rating for the film. The Potter movie is ideal for kids and fun for adults, but lacks the emotional complexity of Jackson's masterpiece.

Peter Jackson's The Fellowship of the Ring surpasses all of these adaptations because it is the most "unfilmable" film of its kind. Like an Olympic diver's routine, the movie must be judged on a difficulty rating.

Jackson's film could not have been made ten years ago. The CGI effects that make Gandalf (Ian McKellen) appear four feet taller than Frodo (Elijah Wood) simply didn't exist. But, effects are not what makes The Fellowship of the Ring one of the best pictures of all time. Instead, it is Jackson's overall recreation of Tolkien's original vision that is extraordinary.

First of all, Jackson captures the tone of Tolkien. The characters range from ultra-pure to outright betrayers and every layer in-between.

The look of the film mirrors the tone. We have the brightness and open green fields of The Shire juxtaposed by the stifling, claustrophobic Mines of Moria This is one of those occasions where art directors and cinematographers and costume designers, etc. deserve full credit for their work. Yet, like the man who receives an Oscar, I don't have time here to praise everyone: thirteen producers (is that a record?), Cinematographer Andrew Lesnie, five Art Directors, four set directors, two costume designers, eight members of the makeup department, five casting directors, original music by Howard Shore and songs by Enya (no less).

Still, Jackson's vision is limited by the ability of his actors. No fear. I can't say enough about "The Fellowship." Ian McKellen is Oscar caliber as Gandalf. My favorite character from the novels is portrayed by a British Shakespearean actor capable of registering sternness and compassion in equal doses. McKellen's old, craggy face is as comforting as a soft pair of slippers, but never think him senile.. As Frodo the "ring-bearer," Elijah Wood is as equally well cast as McKellen. Likewise, Legolas (Orlando Bloom) and Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen) seem to leap off Tolkien's page onto celluloid.

My final argument for The Fellowship as one of the all-time greats resides in the film's action sequences. The battle scenes are "terrific" (in the true sense of the word). I remember vividly a brief moment worthy of anything Spielberg ever filmed: Legolas lets three arrows fly in the space of three seconds. It's just one example of technically marvelous filmmaking where the sound effects and the acting and the editing make it all seem believable. There are many such action scenes in The Fellowship of the Ring.

To try and describe these scenes in writing is superfluous in the wake of J.R.R Tolkien and his capable admirer: Peter Jackson.
