title: The film is remarkable in its faithfulness to both the book and marketability.
review:
The film is remarkable in its faithfulness to both the original material and to the needs of today's film market. Obviously, inclusion of every detail, side jaunt, campfire tale, poem, and such could have produced a six-hour (or longer) film. Equally obviously, that would not have been marketable. Jackson has compromised by leaving out a few entire characters and situations. However, many subtle details are left in without overt comment, and nearly everything said and shown is largely in agreement with the text.

Of course, the film ends (as does the first book) at an uncomfortable moment. The Fellowship has been forged and broken, and the Ring has made significant progress in its journey. But the real story is only 1/3 told, and two more films are scheduled to follow at one-year intervals. In fact, there is probably no way to remain true to the text and end the film any other way.

Fair warning: spoilers abound in the balance of this review.

Critics have made much noise about the enlargement of the role of Arwen. Indeed, she is more visible in this film than in the original text. However, nothing was done with her character that is not supportable by published (and unpublished) material outside the original text.

In fact, it may be best to think of the original text and this film as parallel retellings of the same historical events. The text was by a contemporaneous author (possibly Bilbo), his worldview didn't allow his queen to be seen to have an overly active role, and so he downplayed her involvement in the story. The film, on the other hand, is by an historian with access to the work of Bilbo in addition to other historical sources, and so takes a more modern view of the role a future queen might play in support of her beloved, unacknowledged king.

This same explanation supports the omission of Tom Bombadil, and the other events that are glossed past without deep explanation. The film is attempting to be popular fiction about these events, and so spends greater effort on the main story line at the expense of the deep historical background. Of course, the interested reader can turn to the text to learn more.

The only place this lack of depth really hurts the exposition of the film is in the backgrounds of some of the members of the Fellowship. The back stories of Legolas, Gimli, and to some extent Boromir are cut short enough that their presence is somewhat mysterious to a viewer unfamiliar with the story. This then weakens the impact of the discovery of Balin's tomb in Moria.

Some of the film reorders the telling of the story for better cinematic effect. The fact is that the reader is often a more patient animal than the film audience. On film, it is possible to intercut multiple story lines, allowing for pacing of the action on multiple fronts and the result is often better cinema than if the stories were simply told separately. The opposite is often true on paper. This film takes advantage of this to fill in Gandalf's problems with Saruman while the Hobbits are making their way to Rivendell. It works. I expect to see more of this in the next two movies since the books spend significant spans of text (half a book at a time) on each of three points of view before things come together for a dÃ©nouement.

Turning away from the content, lets look at the form of the production.

First, the combination of skillful location choices, amazing sets, and phenomenal effects produced almost impossibly believable images of Middle Earth. Without intimate knowledge of the production and the New Zealand locations, it is difficult to distinguish the boundaries between disciplines.

Second, the casting has largely produced actors that fit my own images of the characters. Elija Wood as Frodo and Ian McKellen as Gandalf seem, in particular, to have been born to play these roles. The others fit nearly as well. The sole exception is the casting of Hugo Weaving as Elrond, where my own imagination would have him be taller and broader, in short more obviously half-elven.

Often neglected in critical reviews is the casting of Ian Holm as Bilbo. The film touches on Bilbo's finding of the Ring during the events of The Hobbit, but really focuses (as did the book) on the last part of his life. Holm plays Bilbo at several ages, and manages to give a great deal of depth to the old Hobbit, even though his part in this tale is very much on the periphery of the action. An extremely strong scene that is extrapolated from the text comes during Bilbo's 111th birthday party. A visibly animated Bilbo is caught telling the tale (from The Hobbit) of his nearly being eaten by Trolls to a rapt audience of local hobbit children. The cluster of wide-eyed, curly-haired hobbit children waiting on every word and squealing at the right moments is both touching and intensely funny.

A nice touch is the later use of the Troll's lair as the location for one of the scenes with Strider during the flight from the Shire to Rivendell. A similar scene occurs in the book, but in the film the audience is left to notice on their own the large, stone Trolls visible behind the action.

Third, the editing produced a film that ran over three hours and left the audience wanting more. Strong action is relieved by quiet moments. There is room for touching moments, fabulous vistas, fast-paced fighting, and clear exposition of Frodo's fear of discovery when forced to use the Ring.

Finally, I was really impressed by this film. It really does live up to its hype, and manages to pay homage to a significant work of literature without loosing the charm of the original novel, or mangling the story beyond recognition. It is accessible to both the student of Tolkien and the neophyte alike, and apparently enjoyable to both.

title: Recommendable
review:
I went to the movie fearing the worst, because I have read the book numerous times. I loved it from the start and then started to fear that those who had accompanied me to the movie and had not read the book might not like it. This wasn't the case.

So I can recommend it to those who have read the book and those who haven't. But beware, you will have to wait one year to see the second part.

title: Incredible...
review: My two cents: Awesome! I'll try to let that be my summary contribution to the growing list of well-deserved one-word accolades for this film. Everything has been pored over in minute detail so it's not necessary to reiterate. I won't relay the story or plot because there are so many well-written recaps already (and you need to read the books anyway). I'll just say that I have been a Tolkien fan for 20 years...and this visual interpretation was worth the wait...that should say it all. The acting was above par, the SFX nearly seamless (arguably the best ever), the music moving and appropriate and the editing (considering the mammoth source work) was superior and far better than I anticipated. The (relatively) minor changes and omissions bothered me little. The one and only thing I truly missed was the conflict and blossoming bond between Gimli and Legolas. Alas, it is small worry in comparison to the spellbinding overall effect. The film maintained it's wonder even under the scrutiny of a second (and much more analytical) viewing. Suffice it to say that my wife and brother, both of whom have never read the books, nor cared to, were fascinated and kept me up until nearly 1 AM for Tolkien Q&A. Both now desire to read the books and have begun the fantastic journey of exploring Middle-Earth.  10/10 for the most accomplished adaptation in movie history, in my opinion. Thank you Peter Jackson and ALL the hard workers (extras, wranglers, techs, carpenters, farmers, etc.) who labored long to bring to inspiring fruition the dreams of little boys the world over. Count me one.

title: Super quality, but there should be a 'long version'.
review:
The first two hours of the movie: (score: 8 1/2)

During the first part (until the mines of Moria) I watched it mostly detached from what was happening on the cinema screen. It was great stuff, but I found myself mainly comparing it to the book I read (a long time ago).

I very much liked the quality of detail of stuff that made it in the film. I didn't like the speedy travel from the Shire towards Rivendell, a slightly too superficial introduction of some people and their weapons at Rivendell, and the speed of travel through the snowy mountains. All in all, during this first part things were just a bit too hasty for me. I felt I was looking at no more than a very good attempt of puting the Lord of the Rings to film.

The last hour of the movie: (score: 10)

In Moria this changed however. The entry to the mines was done like it should, the Cave Troll was done superbly as was the sequence at the final bridge. What followed were some of the best movie sequences I have ever witnessed: The loss of Gandalf, the conversation with Galadriel, the 2 huge statues, the betrayal of Boromir and his ultimate sacrifice. All these were done with such stunning power that I have very little to compare it with. Better than Schindler's List, which is the best I have seen from Steven Spielberg, and uptil now my favorite movie and director.

Conclusion:

In my opinion this movie sets new standards for high quality visuals, drama and music (during the most dramatic moments).

Should a 'long version' of this movie be made, paying special attention to my complaints of the first part, I would give this movie a perfect 10. Some parts at the end were done so amazingly well that I will still give this movie a 9 1/2. Thanx Peter Jackson!!

title: #1? C'mon people... (7/10)
review:
10 out of 10? So, in other words, FotR is on par with or better then classics like 'The Godfather', 'One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest', '12 Angry Men' or even "instant classics" like 'American Beauty', 'The Shawshank Redemption' and 'The Usual Suspects'? To quote a line from another classic (Austin Powers): righhhhhhhht. The rating you give is supposed to be a measure of the quality of the movie not if the movie was true to the novel or how it measured up to other fantasy movies (I would argue 'Excalibur' is the superior fantasy film). Of course all this is falling on deaf ears because the hype machine has a firm hold on FotR just like another film released in December (I think) a few years back about a sinking ship.

FotR is beautiful to look at and to hear, has an interesting central plot and has intriguing, if somewhat underdeveloped, characters. The CG employed in the film is very fluid and not overdone. All in all, one of the most enjoyable films of the year and one of the best fantasy films I've seen (not that it has a lot of competition).

After our favorite hairy-toed hero leaves The Shire, FotR basically follows the same pattern: walk and talk, meet some new characters, Frodo slips on the ring and gets scared by the big eye, fight some baddies where the heroes are 3 touchdown underdogs, bemoan the fact that fate has placed this terrible burden on poor little Frodo, and then make another fateful decision that begins the cycle all over again. Throw in the repetitive dialogue and scenes to describe the history and power of the One Ring just in case we forgot from 10 minutes prior...well you get the idea: FotR main problem is it's repetitiveness. It's a shame that Mr. Jackson et al decided to repeat the same themes over and over again instead of using the screen time to develop the characters more fully because I found myself wanting more.

The overall feel of FotR, as others have pointed out, is more like a commercial free marathon of the first season of a superb fantasy television series then a film. Maybe if it was a television series I could forgive Ring's redundancy but since it's not, I really can't. I do not hesitate to recommend this film to fans of fantasy and fairy tales but don't expect to see a '10'. Instead, prepare to be transported to a fantastic world of wizards, elves, and orcs that will take your breath away by gasp of excitement and wonderment and, occasionally, by yawn of boredom.

title: the Greatest Story Ever Told...
review: The first part of "Lord of the Rings" blew me away, and it is by far the best fantasy adaptation ever to grace celluloid. In fact, it is so good that it is in a class all of its own. There have been so many attempts in this genre, and so many that have failed. "the Fellowship of the Ring" raises the bar of fantasy/science fiction so high that things will never be the same again. Forget Star Wars, I can't wait to see the next installment of the greatest fantasy epic ever.

title: Go see it ! run !
review:
I have seen the movie last night (December 17) at the avant-premiere here in Montreal and it already figures atop my list of favorite movies of the year, the decade and maybe even the century.

The greatest strength of this marvelous piece of art is its way to make you believe in a world where orcs and trolls fight elves and dwarves and where hobbits cross the path of humans without arousing any suspicion. I mean, as I got out of the theater, I was starting to plan my next sumer vacation in Lothlorien. I just believed in the freakin' place.

Peter Jackson surpassed himself on that one. Don't you miss it in theaters while you can. I just can't wait for the next chapter in 2002.

title: Absolutely Breathtaking!
review: Wow. I am still stunned at the beauty of this film. I have seen it four times and still want to see it again and again. I cannot think of one negative comment I could make. Well worth the price of a ticket and 3 hours. I would recommend this to everyone, from age 5 to age 95.

title: Possibly the best movie I have ever seen
review:
I estimate I have seen maybe two hundred movies in my life, the vast majority of which have made no impression whatsoever in my memory. This isn't to say I didn't enjoy seeing many of those movies; it's just that most films are insubstantial enough not to linger in my mind for long.

Only a half-dozen movies really stand out for me, and among these the Fellowship of the Ring makes a case for being the best (and I'm not a particular fan of the sword-and-sorcery fantasy genre). In my personal pantheon, the only movie that I could justify as being better overall than FotR is The Godfather (part I). While obviously very different films, both share several common threads. Both are reasonably faithful film adaptations of extremely popular novels. Both films' directors gambled on, and succeeded in, setting a richly detailed, wide-ranging, epic scale to their respective works. And in both films the protagonist (I can't call Michael Corleone a hero, but he certainly is the protagonist in the Godfather) tries very hard to shun the role fate and circumstance thrust upon him.

Okay, so what's so good about FotR? Well, like great wine it's got plenty of upfront appeal, but also tremendous depth of nuance and subtlety. The upfront appeal comes in what I would call the outer threat to our heroes. The enemies are foul and ugly, our heroes strong, and the battle scenes exhilirating, scary, and exciting. Here the storytelling is vastly superior to modern action-adventure staples, especially because we see that our heroes' victories are not without sacrifice. The nuance and subtlety come in what I would call the inner threat. Our heroes must not only battle the wraiths and orcs bent on killing them, but also the seduction of the Ring as it insinuates itself into their own weaknesses: lust for power, greed, and corruption. The movie makes the viewer wonder: who will resist and who will falter and betray? (If you've read the books you'll know, but that's besides the point). Oh, and I very much like the fact that the principal hero is a little guy who spends much of the movie looking like he's going to be sick from fear and trying to get other more powerful beings to relieve him of his burden. Ian McKellen's Gandalf is outstanding, as expected from him, but what takes this movie over the top is the superbly expressive face of Elijah Wood as Frodo.

What's bad about FotR? Well, I think it's too long. I won't argue with any of Peter Jackson's departures from the novel; I think they mostly work and make sense in telling the story as a movie rather than a book. However, after two viewings of this nearly three hour long film, I thought there were several scenes that could either be shortened significantly or eliminated altogether, resulting in a better film. There really are too many shots of Frodo opening his hand to reveal the Ring. Sometimes I think they made only two actual shots of this (one with clean hands, one with dirty) and just repeat them over and over again at intervals throughout the movie. The whole business with the crumbling staircase in Moria is a waste. It's really just a cheap-thrills roller-coaster ride which has no consequence to the story, but it takes up a lot of screen time. The Lady Galadriel speaks way too slowly (but boy, does she lay a real bummer on poor Frodo!). And the lovingly rendered shots of Sam underwater last so long that I wished he would just get it over with and drown. Really, I think this movie could have been better brought in at around two-and-a-half hours. So FotR is not a flawless move. It's just a really excellent one.

title: Excellent movie, in fact best movie of the year!
review:
The movie follows the book almost perfectly and in areas where it doesn't it still works. In my humble opinion this is the best movie of the year! For those 429 people who gave this movie a ranking of 1, whay did yo do that? Probably to sabotage the ranking as no one in their right mind would give this masterpiece a one. Even if you didn't like this movie because of the subject matter you still couldn't give the movie a ranking lower than 7(good) or 8(excellent) because of the skill that went into making it. Be objective when you vote. Even I didn't like the movie's subject matter, I always give points for good movie making. SEVEN was a movie that in my opinion was amazingly put together, but I didn't care for the subject matter and it was hard to get through it because it was was disturbing, but I give it an 8 or 9 because I recognize the skill. Anyway, go see this movie, over and over again. I've seen it three times now and find more details I've missed each time.

Only thing about this movie is that they had to market the heck out of it: can you say "Lord of The Onion Rings" anybody? -Daniel Pryor

title: Pure Drudgery
review:
I endured this three and one-quarter hour sentence a few days ago and, toward the last one third of it, was literally counting the minutes until emancipation. Lots of sword fights and good-wizard-versus-bad wizard drama conspire to make this movie exactly what I was dreading. Extremely sophomoric moralizing and some borderline ridiculous hiding scenes where the much coveted ring is apparently trying to get rescued by the bad guys. Cheesey costumes as well. I think you would have to be either a teenaged boy or a hard core fan of fantasy novels to get into this movie. My husband (j. allott) loved it.

  • S. Watts

title: Watch with your heart, not head
review:
Positive and negative comparisons to the Star Wars movies (Trilogy and Phantom Menace) are inevitable for this production, but amidst the criticisms, I'm reminded of a few things:

Firstly, (of Phantom Menace) someone else said that, yes, you can get caught up in how annoying JarJar Binks is, or how silly all of the child parts are. But he reminded us that George (Lucas) had Phantom in mind as a movie that was *supposed* to appeal to children too, not just for adults...! "If you look at Phantom through the wondrous eyes of a child, it's not so bad", to paraphrase.

By contrast, Fellowship is not *nearly* as blatant a children's movie as Phantom was meant to be, as far as targeting the pre-teen or even young adult demo; thankfully, this production saves the kid fare for action-figure and Burger King marketing. I also get the feeling that any reasonable translation of the Lord of the Rings is meant to be fairly serious, given that Tolkien's inspiration for writing it was borne out of the tragedies of World War 2.

Secondly, ask yourself what kind of feeling you came away with when you saw it. Me? As a life-long fan of the story, I was very inspired by the tremendous attention to detail, and the heart with which the cast and crew poured 2 years (or so) of their lives into the Lord Trilogy - as evidenced in The Fellowship. It literally made me feel transported into their world, and although I know the story, I came away feeling like the $10 I spent was actually worth it in a LONG time. If you hate fantasy movies or 3-hour productions, I might recommend you to stay away. It won't convince anyone to convert who has a serious problem with this type of fare. But otherwise, PLEASE see this most lovingly made movie. Your main regret might be waiting for the other 2 thirds!

title: I was bludgeoned
review:
Peter Jackson's FOTR is a movie designed to quite literally beat a movie audience into submission. For three hours you are bombarded with enough imagery, action, characters, and plot to give the average hobbit an aneurysm. It's been a week since I saw the movie and I'm still grappling with the experience.

The fight scenes - and there are a lot of fight scenes - make your mind and eye whirl. Its like a super fast merry-go-round. You know that there are a lot of things happening, but its happening so fast that your brain can't keep up. Regardless, the experience as a whole is much too marvelous to ever turn your back on.

The characters are so real they seem strangely out of place in the genre of fantasy. Gandalf is the grandfather I never had but always wanted. Smart, edgey and wise. Ian Holms conjures a wonderfully flawed 3-D Bilbo Baggins that is likable, laughable but at times frightening. The elves also deserve special mention. They are both charming and calming. Perhaps it's the ears.

The sets and the scenes are pure magic. As a New Zealander I am very familiar with the landscape of my home country, but Peter Jackson somehow shot an eerier New Zealand then the one I know. Every place shown is strangely familiar, but completely different in mood and feel.

The one flaw that irritated me throughout the movie is that the CGI - in parts - looks like it belongs in Toy Story. For the most part however, Middle-Earth swallowed me whole and left me happy to have been overwhelmed by the experience.

title: Jolly good! Can I have another one now, Mr. Jackson?
review: This was a very well-done adaptation of the first part of Tolkien's magnum opus. As a movie, it is a feast. Movies as good as this one are few and far between. There were deviations from the book, but they were, IMHO, more of the "pebble in one's boot" variety than the "slap across one's face" variety and, for the most part, it is easy to see why each of the changes were made. It is difficult to imagine how Jackson could have done a better job of balancing the need to remain faithful to the spirit of LOTR and yet create a movie that would be compelling and exciting even for the uninitiated.

title: My new favorite movie!
review:
I saw this movie with my husband, also a huge JRR Tolkien fan, and we both positively loved it. The music simply transports you away into Middle-Earth, and the theme is beautiful and will surely remind people of the movie, just as the Star Wars theme takes you back to a galaxy far, far away and the Gone With the Wind theme evokes memories of the Old South. Then there's the acting. Elijah Wood IS Frodo Baggins. There is no other way to put it. The expressions on his face let you feel his joy, his grief, and his fear. Orlando Bloom, Ian McKellan, and Viggo Mortenson do magnificently as well. The effects are also amazing. Who would have guessed that Gollum was entirely computer generated? The balrog and the Watcher in the Water are also very scary, and the Eye of Sauron is just plain terrifying.

2 things that I think could have been better: the developing friendship of Legolas and Gimli is not portrayed at all in the movie; maybe it will be more so in The Two Towers. Also, if you haven't read the books, you will miss a lot of details throughout. You will still understand the story, but you miss a lot of fun stuff.

All in all, a fantastic movie. My new favorite!

title: Almost total failure
review: It's a shame but The Lord of the Rings is a movie without any rhythm. Jackson drowned himself into the heavy machinery of the special effects and failed to give a soul to his film. He gives us another actioner full of "levels" like in the video games and the characters are just stereotypes with no real depth (poor Elijah Wood). Adapting The Lord of the Rings was a very big risk and Jackson can be proud of taking it. It's just what's left to him.

title: Brilliant and intelligent
review:
For those of you like myself who are fans of the books of the same name,you will not be disappointed by this movie. Unlike the animated versions that have previously been made where much of the story was condensed either for budgetary constraints or time limits, the Fellowship of the Ring while it does take a few shortcuts, there are very few. It is very exciting getting to see places that up until now have been purely figments of my imagination portrayed by someones elses imagination on the silver screen. I felt myself holding my breath waiting to see the various locations of middle earth and how others have dreamed of them. The movie does a breathtaking job in transporting the viewer to this other world and does so with magic good enough to be from the hand of Gandalf himself. Yes, there are places where for dramatic reasons or to prevent a lengthy historical context that certain events from the book were either shortened, modified or changed. These changes however do not change the storyline itself and makes for a very entertaining movie. I do feel however that if you are one of the uninitiated, it would serve you to either read the book before going, or immediately after the film pick up a copy and read it as it will provide more breadth to the story than what an almost three hour film can portray. In addition, there are several scenes in the book that while not central to the main story, add more to the lore of middle earth and help to explain some of the history leading up to the time of the story. The characterizations in the film were very well done and the choices of the actors to play the hobbits were perfect. While I was somewhat anxious to have Elijah Wood as Frodo and Sean Astin as Samwise, after seeing how well they were portrayed on film left me no doubt that these actors did a very admirable job bringing the characters to life. The majority of the cast has some English accent which was my main concern. Both the principle American actors portrayed a passable English type accent themselves which helped prevent them standing out on their own. How the filmmakers made several average height men such as Wood and Astin, and probably more so John Rhys Davies as Gimli appear much smaller than their Elvish or human companions is spellbinding. Special effects in this movie while at first don't really seem to be that obvious eventually take on a more obvious tone as the fellowship moves further into the adventure. As one would expect from a magical world, many things which we take for granted from reading the books are very difficult to accurately portray in a live action presentation. The filmmakers not only did a good job, they surpassed by far my expectations and truly made the experience an enjoyable and fulfilling one. As with any film where there will be sequels coming out, the ending left me longing for December 2002 to follow our adventurers further on their quest.

I will caution parents who are thinking of taking their children to see this movie that it is not a movie made or intended for children. Much Parental Guidance and forethought should be taken before taking children under 12 to this film. Aside from a film which lasts almost three hours in length where much of the dialogue while important to the story is not well suited to entertain small children. In addition, several of the creatures created for the film will probably terrify younger audiences. If you want to take your children to see this film, I might caution you to view it without them first and then decide to take them on your own judgement. Hey, if you do see it first without them, you can see it again right? I plan on seeing it more than once anyway. All in all, this is a well developed motion picture where a great deal of thought went into it's development and execution. I am thankful to the filmmakers for having the courage to tackle such a well known, well loved story with an audience that has a very well organized preconceived notion of how they view the world of Tolkien. The filmmakers did the book justice and that is the bottom line unlike Bakshi's version of 1978 which was a disappointment at best and unfinished as it's final release turned out to be.

title: A Noble Effort
review:
I think the problem with those of us who are Tolkien fans is to avoid following into two different traps that prevent us from giving this film an unbiased and fair review. The first trap is that of holding the director to task for our own little pet bits of material being excluded or just not quite done quite the way we had envisioned. I am very disappointed that Tom Bombadil was excluded from the film. Merry and Pippin are portrayed in a way quite different from what I had envisioned. The Lothlorien section should have been longer, I particularly lament some of the excellent Gimili material that is absent as a result. I thought the Galadriel's Mirror scene would have been stronger without the special effects. The problem is that this isn't my vision of Middle Earth.. it's Peter Jackson's. We can't expect him to have directed a film that includes all of our personal favorite bits. We can demand that he create a film that treats Tolkien's material with dignity and makes his world come to life. I'll reserve judgement till later in the review.

The second trap is that of being so excited at seeing Tolkien's world come to life on the screen that we forgive too much. I've seen a lot of reviews calling this film perfect, or the best film ever, or both. I'm not saying that conclusion is impossible to reach I am saying that it is likely to come from being to eager to like the film.

Here's how I see the film. There are some excellent performances. Viggo Mortensen really captures Aragorn. Sean Bean was Boromir. Ian McKellan does a good job showing Gandalf's kindness, and his wrath. Elijah Wood is nothing short of brillant as Frodo. Orlando Bloom's Legolas is convincing indeeed. Liv Tyler does a verry good job with Arwen in what little time she is on the screen (I must say that though not textual this part of the film really worked for me), ditto Kate Blanchette's Galadriel. Merry and Pippin are played as comic relif, there is no character development here. The actors don't do a bad job, they simply are crippled by the script. The screen writer and director don't seem to have a grasp on these characters. That being said I did laugh and their antics, and it does serve to add some lightness to the film that would otherwise be absent. I also argue that part of this is do to a weakness in Tolkien. Tolkien didn't write character driven fiction. He wrote epic. John Rhys Davies is a total dissappointment as Gimli. He turned Gimli into a caricature. His performance is by far the worst in the film and it is fortunate his role isn't that large. So on the whole we have several outstanding performances, a couple of so-so ones, and a absolutely terrible Gimli.

The special effects were too much. Sauron looked like a Cartoon character. The cave troll battle was stupid and not in the text. Frodo receives his wound from "a huge orc" of "nearly man size" not a massive deformed Troll. This is is a major weakness in the film. The evil in this film is too comic book like. I thought the Balrog worked, but most of the other visual effects were simply overkill. Evil in this film is based on a Spawn like vision of Hell and it lacks the subtlty to be truly frightening. The Ringwraiths are an exception here. The are done perfectly. Some of the effects seem to have been done with a, because we can do it mindset (the non textual and insipid Troll battle, the and the visual chicanery in the Galadriel scene were particularly troublesome to me). The digital world creation worked for me.

On the whole this film is, for me at least, an odd mixture of really strong elements, and some really bad ones. There is little mediocrity here. Everything is either a marvelous success or a spectcular failure. I think this is why the reviews have tended to extremes. I think in the end Jackson succeeds in breathing life into Tolkien's world. At times he succeeds at making the story come to life as well, the Boromir scene at the end of the film was remarkably well done. I don't think this is the best movie of all time. It's a good film with flaws. It is however the best fantasy film of all time. That's good enough for me to give it a 10, inspite of it's flaws.

title: One of the Best Ever...
review:
I have yet to read the trilogy by Tolkien, so I cannot compare the movie to the books. (But this movie has really compelled me to.)

I am a movie freak, I'm not going to deny it. I see a lot of really good movies, but I do have to say that this is one the best movies I've ever seen!!!I went into the theater with high expectations and came out feeling awe-struck.

The casting was great because I cannot imagine anyone else better for the roles than the people who played them. Sir Ian McKellan was great and Elijah Wood was eerily perfect for the role of Frodo, as were Christopher Lee, Ian Holm, Sean Astin, and Sean Bean. The strength and power of all the characters was not at all surprising.

Though they didn't really give back stories to majority of the Fellowship , they still kicked ass. Legolas especially. The affair between Aragorn and Arwen seemed a little out of place, but still somehow fit into the movie. The scene with the troll was great and the visual effects in the movie were absolutely fantastic.It had a strong story that did not falter, with its romance, action, adventure, comedic relief, and drama. Everything in the movie meshed together perfectly! What I write right now isn't even half of what I'm raving about this movie, it deserves much more.

I don't know how I'm going to wait twelve LONG months for the next installment of this motion picture masterpiece. I will be anxiously be waiting for next Christmas, not for the holiday, but for The Two Towers.

title: One of the Greatest Moments of My Life
review:
I shall never forget Christmas Day 2001 when I first saw Lord of the Rings. A beautiful beautiful movie that gives me a great feeling deep inside just to be alive. It makes me content and happy; it makes me smile and I absolutely can't wait to see it again. Long live Hobbits!

Thank you Mr. Jackson -- I hope I have the honor of meeting you one day. And especially thanks to Mr. Tolkien, for the endless dreams and inspiration.

2002 is going to be a VERY long year indeed. ;)

-J

title: The best movie ever created...YES!
review:
This is the best movie I have ever seen. I would argue that it is the best movie ever created.

It will only (possibly) be beaten by LOTR:Two Towers (#2) or LOTR:The King Returns (#3). We shall see...

title: Inspired and Beautiful
review: Peter Jackson rises to inspired heights with his first entry to Lord Of The Rings. It's a masterful work that evokes the same kind of feelings you had the first time you saw Star Wars or Raiders of The Lost Ark. A fantasy that takes on a life of it's own. Jackson crafts a strong theme of self sacrifice throughout, binding the Fellowship together with a simple emotional glue, often missing in fantasy films made after the Lucas/Speilberg golden years. The theme works so well infact, that it plays out amongst the characters like a conversation between old friends. A conversation you will be sorry to see finish. Powerful and full bodied film-making keep the occasional lack of back story and plot holes from diminishing what is without doubt the most important film of the last twenty years.

title: Very very good
review: You can never keep everyone happy, and it would have been impossible to make a movie line for line exactly the same as the book. Peter Jackson does however make an unbelievably good movie of the books, and I cannot see how it could possibly have been done any better. Easily one of the best movies I have seen in a long time, and it makes the other fantasy movie of the season look pale and clunky. I am very very happy with the movie, and it makes me want to go back and read the books again. I can't wait for the next two!

title: Visually wonderful and riveting
review: Although its ranking will certainly decline on the IMDB list as time wears on, this is undoubtedly the best fantasy movie ever filmed.  Unlike movies like "Star Wars", which was part of a series yet self-contained with a definitive conclusion, this motion picture ends in the middle of the story and leaves viewers (especially those who have never read the books) unsatisfied.  That being said, "The Fellowship of the Ring" contains some of the finest scenery ever put to film and great acting to boot.  After the prolouge, it begins slowly and methodically in the Shire and builds to the fantastic battle and escape from the Mines of Moria.  What is really unique for a movie of this type is the true emotions that spill from the screen. You feel the inner turmoil of the characters as they try to decide how to handle the One Ring and battle the urge to use it for their own means. You simple can't find that type of emotion or acting in any other fantasy film to date.

title: Purists beware....
review:
I loved the movie, absolutely brilliant.

But as a 10 times reader of the books, I really missed some of my favorite bits.

I can understand how some may feel they hated this movie ... one of my favorite bits of the book is the gifts to the fellowship, without it I felt robbed as the 9 took to rafts.

So for frequent readers, please leave the book at home before you see this movie.

My score was 9/10 (19/10 for what was there, -10/10 for what wasn't).

title: Great movie
review:
I have been waiting years for this movie to hit the screens, and the last week or two has seemed like years, especially since the movie was released as it was only released in Australia today. But naturally I took my family to the very first screening in my hometown of Geelong.

Of my family I am the only one that has read the books, I actually own three copies of the books.

I had spent a large part of the last two weeks reading the user comments on this site. From this I was aware of some of the negatives and all of the positives. Because of this I made sure that I stressed two key points to my family, one is that the book had to be condensed to fit into a three hour movie and that this movie is unlike anything else from hollywood in that it truly is the first part of a trilogy. Not a complete story within itself as some people seemed to expect or want.

After now having seen the movie I realise that I truly had no idea just how hard it must have been for Jackson to have fitted this into a three hour movie. In my opinion for him to have included the full book and give enough time to develop the characters fully he would have needed 10 hours or more. One thing I note from other comments here is that very few people have commented on the fact that a number of the characters don't really get developed until the second book.

My own personal gripes with the movie, Galadriel was far from convincing in her part and was poorly displayed. The part where Frodo offers her the ring was rather pathetic and was not at all clear, my family asked afterwards about what was this "test" that she claimed to have passed. Secondly, there was no mention of why the black riders weren't chasing after the ring in the second half of the movie, after being swept away by the flood at the ford they totally disappeared from the story without a mention. The casting was excellent, with the exception of Galadriel and Elrond. Also, there was no real explanation of the council, everyone just showed up and it started. No background or introductions, who were these people? why were they there?

Being a Tolkein fan made it difficult for me to view this movie as being just a fantasy movie, I constantly found myself thinking "the book had it set out this way" or "hang on, they skipped about 18 years in the blink of an eye". I know the story very well as I first read the book around 16 years ago and I've read it 20 odd times since then, I lost count after the 13th reading. I've also read Unfinished Tales and The Silmarillion.

Given that I have yet to view the movie without seeing just "the movie" I have yet to give it a rating, I doubt I would give it a 10 there are just a few too many minor flaws which I feel detract from the professionalism of this movie, like the hobbits changing in size or appearance from one shot to the next. In some scenes it was very clear that what was meant to be hobbits were actually child sized doubles, ie when Aragorn is holding two of them in his arms.

My family all thought it deserved 10 out of 10.

title: Best fantasy movie ever
review:
This is the best fantasy movie ever, no doubt. Is it the best movie ever? I do not put such labels on single movies since they all strive to achieve different goals and show different things. Everyone complains about this being a lightweight compared to such great movies as The Godfather and The Shawshank Redemption. Is it really? I think not. The Godfather wants to portray a mafia family and its history, The Shawshank Redemption an innocent man and how he cunningly tricks the evil prison warden. Both movies are made to look like they might actually have happened.

The Lord of the Rings has no such pretentions. It is a fantasy movie with goblins, ghosts and brilliant heroes that defeat evil time and again (and hopefulle get the chicks too). I wouldn't compare it to the two mentioned above at all since they are so different. I guess I'm trying to say that one should not label movies as "best movie ever", but as "best drama", "best action" and so on.

And BTW, I really think LotR is a really great movie! Yes there are flaws, mostly visual, but it IS breathtakingly beatiful, it IS truly epic, and the actors actually ARE fantastic! I gave it 10/10, but that is because I thought it would never come close to my expectations after having read the book. Maybe the right thing to do would be giving it 8/10, but... nah! Peter Jackson rules!

title: Waaahhhh
review:
Bah, get over it fanboys/girls. Even though you've read the Ring series and/or the Hobbit 2 dozen times and dress up as Gandalf or elves or whatever, just quit the nitpicking and enjoy the movie for what it is: a cinematic masterpiece that tries to do justice to the books. So please, stop stating the obvious that this-part-was-cut-out-and-this-was-changed, we are all well aware that Tolkien's series could never be made into a full, every second with the hobbit feature we'd like it to be. Tolkien himself would be proud of what Mr. Jackson and Co. have done and would realize that books of that scope would never be able to be realistically and financially made. Besides, I think Dune fans (of which I am as well) should be the ones to nitpick more; they've had it done twice and both were pretty bad movies, but thats a different thread.

A Tru Tolkien fan

title: Thank you Peter Jackson et al!!!
review:
I'm not a movie critic. I've never written anything like this before. But let me just say this: This movie is perfect in every way. My friends and myself have made a pact to see this film nine times before it leaves the big screen. Call us crazy, but we've been waiting for a movie like this for so long. And yes, I've read the book. My friends are human Tolkien dictionaries. We couldn't have asked for a better adaptation. Thank you Peter Jackson et al for making a perfect film!

Googolplex out of 10

title: EPIC!
review:
Quite frankly - this is the most beautiful piece of cinema I've ever seen. At first I was worried that the 3 hour running time would kill the film - I was WRONG!

I could quite easily have sat there for 10 hours (naturally with a hefty supplies of Nachos of course).

First class action, special effects to die for and a level of acting two steps above anything seen in your run of the mill blockbuster.

I agree with other comments made on the abrupt ending - but that is just nit-picking.

All in all - I give it 9.9 (rounded up to 10!)

title: Pure magic
review: As faithful to the book as a movie can hope to be. Peter Jackson shows he is truly a master of the silver screen, captivating the audience with this wonderful tapestry of light sound and feeling woven on the medium of cellulose. Magic

title: wish it had been longer
review:
This surely is one of the best movies ever made..... its three hours long.... n there is not a single moment during which my mind wandered away from the screen.....MiddleEarth has been presented almost as I had imagined....scenery is wonderful....the characters seem rite out of the book.

Every character is well played....and faithfully translated....Elrond has that wide forehead....aragon the raggedness....though i felt Gandalf could have been improved....he seems too weak and non-humurous in the movie.

Saruman's role has been changed....but i felt that was a plus point to the movie....it actually makes the happening more interesting....

I only found one weak scene....Galadriel with Frodo was a absolute laugh. But all in all its an almost perfect movie of my favourite book...and i can hardly wait for the sequel.

title: Breathtaking!
review: Because of my love for the book, I was afraid i would be very disappointed. But i loved the movie. The characters, music, battles, everything was great! The makers of the movie did a job Tolkien himself would be very pleased with. When I gave it a ten it occured to me that the score-system should have been adjusted!!!!!

title: The Movie Wizard: Peter Jackson
review:
This movie is a masterpiece which everyone, who is into adventure and great battles, should see. The story is of course written by the great Tolkien who sadly left us in 1973. He took 15 years to complete his 3 books about Sauron, Frodo and the great ring. Making 3 movies about these books is of course a great adventure in itself. Peter Jackson's masterpiece completes the books and gives a movie experience seldom felt today. Peter Jackson is now the wizard that George Lucas and Steven Spielberg already is. There are people out there, including me, that thinks that Peter should direct Episode 3 StarWars in 2005 as he is the new movie wizard. This is the new beginning for Peter Jackson as a great movie maker and it will be very intresting to see how Peter will handle the 2 big movies following Fellowship of the ring. Good luck Peter och God Bless Great movie directors and actors.

Sincerely /A

title: Breath-taking!
review: What an amazing film! I went with my husband who works "in the industry" and even he was impressed. There were a couple of areas where the dialogue was hard to understand, but nothing that effected my understanding of the story. There were a couple of scenes that I couldn't watch due to the violence of the scenes, but I made it. Be careful of taking younger children. The effects were stunning and flawless. I can't wait for next year to see what happens next. I might actually have to pick up the books.

title: Every fan's dream
review: As a long-time Tolkien fan, I have anxiously awaited this movie's debut. I've been following it's progress online for the last year and was very pleased with all of the pre-production details.  Now that I've actually seen the movie (twice so far and hopefully several more times before it leaves the theaters) I'm happy to say that it was everything that I'd always hoped for!!!  The casting, character development, set design, costumes, well...everything surpassed even my greatest expectations.  I have to admit, that I was a little apprehensive about the casting of Liv Tyler as Arwen and what seemed (from the trailer anyway) to be a much expanded role from that of her character in the books.   For some reason (call me jaded) I had imagined the worst, that in order to cash in on her celebrity, she'd end up in scenes she had no business in, perhaps she'd single-handedly fight the balrog as she rebuilt the bridge at Khazad-Dum brick by brick, then carry the fellowship across on her back...but happily, that wasn't the case, she didn't have nearly as much screen time as I'd feared and what time she did have, well, it worked.  It seemed as though they took some of the images right out of my head (and my heart) and I wasn't alone in this sentiment, several people I know who have seen it have said the same thing.  The love that the filmmakers have for these books is obvious.  They remained as true to the story as they possibly could and have created a world as rich and beautiful, and at times as dark and frightening as any that I have ever seen on the screen.  For me, it's going to be a very long year as I wait (somewhat impatiently) for the sequel.  In the mean time, I'll see it again and again and encourage everyone I know, whether or not they're fans of the books, to see this movie.  I think J.R.R. Tolkien would be proud.

title: Breathtaking film
review:
Even though, as a big Tolkien fan, part of me was saying "that's not the same as the book" and "that's not how I pictured it", the rest of me was going "Ooooh". When I walked out of the theater after my second viewing, I was torn between, "How long should I wait before I go again" and "A whole year before the next one!!".

Now for details. Sean Bean was a showstopper, in a role that could easily have been one dimensional. McKellan, as Gandalf, was, in turns, gruff, menacing, and playful. The hobbits, and Gimli the drarf, looked great, whatever effects or camerawork gave them their smaller stature blended seamlessly with the rest of the cast. My only problem was when Gimli ran, he looked a bit like a child.

Merry and Pippin were not developed to any great degree, but that should come in the next film and the actors did a good job. My only complaint was

Viggo Mortenson(sp?) as Aragorn. He seemed a bit wooden. Part of this was because Bean's character was more active, but some of the blame must fall on the actor.

Great film overall. While there were a couple of scenes I would have liekd to have left in, including every fan's favorites would have bloated the film and made it unwatchable and unmarketable.

title: good in the beginning, boring in the end
review:
Spoilerwarning

Hyped by the high score on imdb I went to see the movie with great hopes, but came out disappointed. I have to admit that it came true the first 90 minutes. After that it became an ordinary movie with fights, runaways, fights, runaways, etc. Even the graphics couldn´t make me really enthousiastic. Rocks with the height of a big house falling down cause more dust than was seen in the scene when Gandalf died. I think. But my biggest complaint is that I just didn´t like the story. For me it was a boring film and I will not go and see the other two parts nor read the book.

title: Top of my list for 2001
review: Arguably there have been a bunch of good and bad movies this year. Opinions abound on the selection and diversity but the bottom line for me is that there has not been a single film that has blown me away. There have been plenty that I enjoyed and thought were very well done and many others on the opposite spectrum. But finally for the year 2001 (as it draws to a close), I can finally say that I have found a movie that has taken my breath away. I am die-hard fan of the novels, having read Tolkein's works and though many other die-hard fans have noted/criticised the absence of Tom Bombadill, the extra scenes of Lady Arwen and the lack of character development for Boromir, Gimli and Legolas... I say to them, "You try and bring a legendary tale that has captured many imaginations to the big screen and try to fit it all in under 3 hours." For while my heart, too, ached that I wished to have seen Tom dancing over the hills, seen more of Gimli recite the history of the dwarfs as they went into the mines, and watched more development between Frodo and his fellow stalwarts, Sam, Pippen and Merry, I would have probably ended up with a 10 hour movie in order to tell the whole tale in its entirety. In fact being a die hard fan I probably would have sat through 10 hours if that's how long the movie took but most others probably would have fallen asleep at the pace. For three hours, it's pure magic and that's what fantasy story telling is all about. It's the first movie where afterwards I came out talking about it for hours on end (even talked about it longer than after seeing Memento). It's utter cruelty that we have to wait until the end of next year before "The Two Towers" graces our screens. It's about time that the "fantasy" genre has come forth in proper force. Whilst sci-fi, drama, comedy, war, action and horror and all the other genres have been given their fill, "fantasy" has never been done to the potential that our imaginations conjure. Finally this movie does just that... and that's the bottom line.

title: wonderful
review: The Lord of the Rings was probably one of the best movies I have ever seen. The actors were fantastic.  They were very believable and made it seem as if you were right there.  You could tell what they were thinking and feeling. Also, the scenery was amazing. And the music brought you right into the movie. On a scale of one to ten I would give it an eleven. Definitely worthy of all the praise it is getting.  They hardly left out anything from the book.  At first, when I heard it was three hours I thought it would be boring and mostly romance (which is, in my opinion, one of the most boring type of movie) but it wasn't.  It had you captivated the whole way through. I couldn't take my eyes off the screen for one second.  To sum it all up: fantastic, thrilling, and fun.

title: BEST MOVIE OF THE YEAR
review: This is one of the best movie of the year i believe.The special effects are well.The storyline is good and it is just almost like the book it doesn't try to change anything around.The characters who played each part deserve alot of credit for their good work.If your thinking about seeing this movie or Ali i suggest you see Lord Of The Rings.It provides you with action and fantasy.I give this 10 stars it is well deserved.

title: I have seen the future of filmmaking...His name is Peter Jackson
review:
It is extremely difficult for me to describe the love and passion I have for this movie. I have never been in such awe in a movie theatre in all my life. It is just perfect. I have always had great respect and admiration for Tolkien, but was never exactly a true fan. In the future his name will be heard with the likes of Steven Spielberg, Alfred Hitchcock, David Lean, Frances Ford Coppala and many others. Think I'm crazy? Watch and see... So Peter Jackson...I salute you. Also a big congratulations to the entire cast and crew.

One word to descibe this movie:FLAWLESS

review: This movie is one of the best works I have ever seen. There ARE NO WORDS to describe this movie. I really hope that the Academy pays due respect to this film. I give it a 10.

title: One of the best films ever!!
review:
I had the opportunity to go to the North American premiere of the most anticipated film of all time. The excitement was palpable sitting in the darkened theater, a week before general release, with Peter Jackson, Elijah Wood, and other cast members in the audience. To sum it up: "Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" is a triumph of cinema and art which does justice to Tolkien's work.

I came to the movie with an open mind - I hadn't read the books in over a year, and had intentionally avoided most major movie "spoilers." That being said, I felt that the movie captured the spirit of the story without hanging on every word from the text. "Harry Potter" was an enjoyable experience, but it required (and assumed) prior familiarity to fully understand and appreciate it. Peter Jackson's LotR, on the other hand, is more than just an excellent copy of literature: it stands by itself as a wholly separate work.

Omissions of beloved scenes are hardly noticed with the quick pace of the story. The transition from the Shire to Bree is smooth. Certainly Tom Bombadil would have been a joy to see onscreen, but the episode would have tacked on another half hour to an already very long movie and perhaps tested the patience of nonfans. Yet even at three hours, the time breezes past.

Middle-earth has truly been brought to life. New Zealand's natural beauty provides ideal landscapes. The idyllic Shire is shown just as we had all imagined. The grotesque orcs and Balrog are terrifying. The evil atmosphere of Moria, Isengard, and Mordor is chilling, leaving the viewer anxious for a more extended glimpse into the Land of Shadow.

Another admirable aspect of the film is that even with epic battles and CG monsters, appropriate time is allotted to develop the major characters, the story's heart and soul. Frodo's friendship with Sam is given due prominence, and Ian McKellen's Gandalf is superb. A small gripe of mine is that the minor characters were not given the individuality that they deserved: by the end, I was still unsure over which Hobbit was Merry and which was Pippin; and Legolas and Gimli were peripheral figures. However, given that their friendship is more a focus in The Two Towers, this is not a big problem.

The film is destined to become a classic (and gross hundreds of millions of dollars in the process!). After such a long wait, the success is a satisfying relief. I will undoubtedly return to see it again many times, and I've already started counting the days until December 2002!

title: Exquisite production, with NO room for complaints
review:
Once in a great while, a movie will exceed expectations.

The Fellowship of the ring is certainly to be included in this category.

There were so many methods available for ruining this film, or at least leaving something to be desired. To my surprise, all of them were avoided and the result is a movie that can be measured as "great" in several ways, not the least of which is that the translation from the great trilogy to the silver screen was nearly flawless in it's capture of the care and empathy generated for the characters of the story. Compelling to say the least. The key to this film's success and the main question to be answered was whether or not we would "care" if Frodo succeeds. The story was there for the taking and a grand adventure it is. But as the first rendition of Dune showed us, a great story and grand adventure means nothing if you could care less about the characters involved.

This movie does it right in every aspect from special effects to photography to pacing.

The expectations for the next two will be that they too are as well done (and since all three were filmed in one stretch by the same people, this is a shoe-in).

title: Wonderful
review: Fantastic. I really, REALLY enjoyed this film. Having been so disappointed so many times at the cinema I braced myself for yet another let down........I needn't have bothered. The film was quite simply flawless in my opinion. Others have already summed up the experience far more eloquently than I could, so I'll skip that and just point out just one of many things that made the film meet and in some cases surpass the book. The relationship between the members of the fellowship. Such an obvious bonding. The trust, reliance and companionship is evident and develops so effortlessly.........in particular I loved the scene in which Boromir was training Pippin and Merry, whilst Aragorn threw in useful tips. So simple but it added so much. A wonderful film that lived up to my expectations (which were immense). I can't wait for the next one!

title: Nowhere near the equal of the book
review: While this film was quite remarkable visually, I found it lacking in plot and especially characterization. While the plot had to be simplified from the book's to fit it within a single movie, the plot changes introduced made little sense. The characters were much more confrontational than in the book, thus losing the courtly nature of the heroes. This was one of the things that notably distinguished them from the villains, and was indicative of Tolkien's worldview. He hated the rush and inhumanity of modern life. The whimsy of the book was also lost.

title: Well worth it even for non-Tolkien fans
review: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring is taken from the series written by J.R.R. Tolkien. Never has there been a film that so magnificently portrays the story of the hobbit heroes as this effort directed by Peter Jackson. The cinematography is breathtaking, and the intensity of the film will leave the viewer stunned. Every detail in the book is seen to, down to the color of Bilbo Baggins' door. Despite being almost three hours long, the film moves along quickly, but not to fast as to leave the watcher confused. As far as I am concerned, the only real problem is the year long wait for part 2.

title: Not quite faithful to the book, but good nonetheless
review:
The Fellowship of the Ring was marvelous, largely due to an intriguing story, along with wonderful character development. I'm referring to the novel. Although the movie was very good, it was woefully lacking in character development. There were scenes and characters omitted, which was clearly necessary in converting a 500-page book into a movie. This is perfectly understandable. However, I think there were a few major shortcomings.

First, and foremost, only two of the nine characters in the fellowship were adequately developed (Frodo and Gandalf). Gimli, Legolas, and Boromir, the representatives of the three major races, are barely even introduced; we are not even told where Gimli and Legolas are from. Merry and Pippin are mostly there for comic relief, and their friendship with Frodo is not explained at all. As for Sam, he has far too few lines for a character of his importance, and his relationship with Frodo is explained barely more than that of the other hobbits. Lastly, we have Aragorn/Strider. His character is pretty well developed, but I took exception to one omitted scene regarding Strider which I deemed fairly important in the book. The famous lines "All that glitters is not gold..." were OMITTED from the movie. In the novel, he recites this poem to the hobbits in Bree; the lines describe Aragorn and foreshadow events to come. I think removing this from the film eliminated Aragorn's aura of mysterious power and majesty.

My final quarrel with the film has to do with Saruman. Saruman is not even in the first book, except for a brief story concerning his betrayal and holding Gandalf as a prisoner in Orthanc. However, in the movie, he is made into a major character, and introduced from the beginning as a servant of Sauron. He uses the Palantir (not even mentioned until the 2nd book) to submit his power to Sauron. Saruman's mind and motives are sources of intrigue not just in the first book, but especially in the second and third. I don't see how this can possibly be recovered for the second and third films. His character in the movie is sterile and uninteresting.

Having aired these complaints, I must admit that I still found the film to be very good. The acting is incredible (Ian McKellen is wonderful as Gandalf). The scenery is extremely well done, particularly Rivendell and the mines of Moria. And for the most part, fortunately, the story is kept intact. Tolkien fans may be disappointed that Bombadil does not appear in the movie, but his is one of the side stories in the novel that does not really contribute to the main theme. Some parts of the book must be removed, otherwise the film would last twice as long. Bombadil is therefore not present, nor is Glorfindel, Bill Ferny, Ted Sandyman, Fatty Bolger, or Farmer Maggot, except for vague references. And I won't even comment on Arwen's augmented role, catering to modern audiences with notions of gender balance. However, I understand that these changes are necessary, and I do not think that they detract from the quality of the film. It's a fun movie from start to finish, but fans of the novel must be forewarned of a somewhat skewed translation.

Three stars from a Lord of the Rings fan.

title: This movie is true to the book
review: After seeing the movie I have to say it was so true to the book. I read all three books when I was a child and I was quite impressed with how they were depicted in the movie. The actors chosen totally fit the parts they played.

title: Tolkien Fans Should Be Proud Of This Movie
review: After reading the books several times and then having the chance to see the movie I am so happy of all the effort that was put into the movie. Most movie adaptations are so far from the book you wonder if they even read the book but Peter Jackson and everyone else that worked on it did a superb job. I am most certainly going back to see it again and I have been recommending it to anyone that asks my opinion. This movie had a lot to live up to from most fans expectations and I for one was not disappointed. I can't wait to see the next two films and I was glad to hear they are making them all at once...that way they don't have to worry about getting the same actors and the same effort will be put into them all. I'll be there opening day!

title: The best movie!!!!!
review: You've got to see this movie. I felt like I got my money's worth. Never boring or slow, moved along perfectly. Beautiful, engaging, suspenseful! I can't stop thinking about this movie, it is with me still.

title: Best fantasy flick ever
review:
We all know the movie wasn't (couldn't be) entirely faithful to the book...folks who continue to gripe about this really bore me. It's simply what happens during an adaptation, to varying degrees, of course. The real issue is whether in sacrificing certain elements of the story, the character of the tale, the inspiration, the foundation still come across clearly. The answer for Fellowship of the Ring is a resounding YES. This movie is astonishing in its breadth and scope. It tells the story in the best way it can, given that no one (except me, probably) would sit through a 6-hour version.

The action was riveting, the acting superb, the fx credible and spectacularly well-conceived (though rubbery at times, the fx never sank to the cartoonish Harry Potter levels.) And on top of it all, there is actually a worthy stab made at character development, which most fx-heavy movies tend to struggle with.

If you are a fan of fantasy (as Roeper clearly is not), go see this movie...it is everything you ever dreamed a fantasy movie could be.

title: Fermat's Last Theorem
review:
Having read jrrt in my early childhood, i had (and still do) considered them personal "property". I was, therefore, present world-premiere day ready to criticize the attempt to make this story popular domain.

I was, simply, flabbergasted. Jackson approached the book with the view of a true disciple. He focused on the characters and not the effects. He introduces Tyler's character in the first "book", because she will play a pivotal point throughout the saga. He removed fight sequences, that would probably be more pleasant to audiances (e.g. hobbits fight with the vampires in the cemetery), and even alters plot (Frodo's escape from the Dark Knight was not assisted by the "rafting" hobbits), i.o.t. provide insight into the relationships of the fellowship. This is the core of jrrt's saga: united we stand, divided we fall. I left feeling like how Andrew Wiles would have felt after solving Fermat's Last Theorem, like been 15 yrs old again. Thank you Mr. Jackson for making my favorite book into an equally favorite movie.

title: Not everything it could have been (7/10)
review:
Yes, I saw it on opening day and yes I liked it. Nearly everyone who saw this movie on opening day is a fan and has probably read the book. And that is one of the major troubles. To friends of mine who were also in the cinema haven't read the books. And they had a hard time following the story. Some things are just left unexplained. Even some of the cast confused those who hadn't read the book. The moment Boromir gets introduced some thought there were two Aragorns. They just look a bit similar. Names in movies are always hard. Sometimes you don't understand them, sometimes they are simply left out. And this starts to confuse people who haven't seen those names (and the places) in writing. You have: Bree, Rivendell, Nazgul, Gandalf, Saruman, Boromir, Strider, Aragorn (just another name for Strider), Gimli, Gloin, Balin, Gladriel, Arwen, Legolas, Pippin, Samwise Gamgee, Mary, Frodo, Bilbo, Elron, Isildur, etc.

Starting to get confused? Well that's what happens. Tolkien did a great job in the book with the map. Why not show it on screen (like they did in the Indiana Jones movies). That way you get totally lost. You have a lot of people, a lot of places, and you cannot grasp all of that. So in essence: you have to read the book to understand the movie.

The other thing that wasn't right was all the kitsch of the movie. e.g. Someone takes a lot of hits till he finally goes down (mortally wounded) and then takes more than 10 minutes on screen to die. Things like that are better left for romantic comedies.

But the movie also has a lot of good things. It's wonderfully made, the cast is nearly perfect, the action and the effects are good, and if you know the story you will enjoy it.

Read the book, than go see this movie. I gave it 7 out of 10

title: A master piece...
review:
This is a movie that you must see. Every man, women, child, young or old should have a chance, a once in a life time chance to watch this movie. It's a master piece that is not very often to be seen in movies these days.

Not a minute nor a second is really bad in Lord of the rings. For he people that has read the books will not be let down. And for people that hasn't read the books it will be an adventure movie with a lot to give to it's audience.

If you have not seen it, or if you're not planning to see it, my suggestion is that you go see it anyway. This is well worth the price for a ticket... I would even pay twice as much.

title: This Ring Brings them All!
review:
This film is an excellent interpretation of the Tolkien novel. Forget all the endless comparisons you will find in these pathetic `fan' reviews. These people insist on dissecting the script and offering what amounts to a whining & puling, endlessly complaining, chapter by chapter comparison. Then they say "The film is a masterpiece from start to finish." What?!

Let's ignore such long-winded, self-important, amateur opinions and focus on the reality of this excellent movie. It's all about storytelling - and "Fellowship" is a story told well. I'd recommend not reading the book (or reading it again if you're a freak like me) before seeing the film, because you'll just be cheating yourself. I think reading/re-reading in proximity is a cardinal rule for experiencing any adaptation. The movie is NEVER going to be what the book is, and vice versa. For better or worse, it's always going to be a retelling of the story, not a visual or written carbon copy. The novel was great, the movie is great; hope your New Year is great as well. Don't forget, if you see this film before January 1st, it's a tax write-off for 2001.

See it, love it, and see it again.

I was just kidding about the tax write-off thing.

Cordially, Mr. Bradbury~
