title: WANTED TO LIKE IT SO MUCH...
review:
I have read The Silmarillion (guess you can't underline on this thing...), The Hobbit, and The Lord of Rings "trilogy." Loved them. Don't know if I would anoint Tolkien as the greatest-fantasy-writer-of-all-time. Firstly, I lack any such official authority. Secondly, I have not read all fantasies ever written. Lastly, there're an awful lot of good fantasies out there. Nonetheless, the hobbit books are pretty amazing stuff.

I have somewhat loosely followed the production and the marketing of the New Line picture. Like many, I started out skeptical, especially after having learned that Elijah Wood was cast as Frodo. Elijah Wood's distinguished acting career, heretofore in my recollection, had been encapsulated into his one (and pretty much only) predominant facial expression, which can probably best be described with Joey-Tribiani's-(as-acting-coach)-pull-thigh-hairs-out-with-fingers-through- hole-in-pocket-to-convey-astonishment/surprise-with-painful-concentration technique.

But, somewhat irrelevant quibble aside, as critical reviews came rolling in overwhelmingly positive, and, more importantly, after having witnessed the unprecendentedly positive viewer-reviews posted on IMDB, I became swayed enough to be fully prepared to award the "my favorite movie of all time" honor to the Jackson film. While cautioning myself against being overly expectant, I, nonetheless, was fully prepared to be intoxicated by the movie's atmosphere, the acting, the heroism, the drama, the romance (in The Fellowship?!), the action, the everything, as many others seemed only too delighted to claim. Without any flippancy, I really, really wanted to like this movie. Because, to do so would have necessitated my having found fulfillment in its world, similarly to how I had found fulfillment in the world created in my head from having read the novels. I would have loved to have had an experience which would have resulted in my incessant gushing of praise for the film in this review.

I wanted to be yet another fan who respectfully protested the "brevity" of the running time, because my enrapture in the film would have caused a desire for it to never end. I wanted to be yet another fan who impatiently cursed in exasperation the studio marketing department's decision to put an entire forlorn, desperate year between the installments. I wanted to be so impressed with the brilliance of Jackson that, immediately following the movie, I wanted to run out, and finally rent "Heavenly Creatures," which previously had yet to successfully survive the "now, which one should I watch?" sweepstakes at the local Blockbuster.

It seems, now, that, having watched "The Fellowship," "Heavenly Creatures" will fare no better against its next video opponent. I should point out, before beginning my lament, that, immediately following the movie, I made the effort to ask a few moviegoers about their experiences. Most seemed to have really liked it. A kid, perhaps about 8 or 9, said he'd thought that it was really good. Another kid, about 50 to 55, said the same, and then gave it a 9 out of 10. That's pretty good praise, I would have to say.

As for me, I was so very disappointed that I had found the film so very disappointing. And it had very little, if anything, to do with any deviations between the movie and the books. It, for me, was just so uninvolving that, many times during the movie, I popped out of myself, and, levitating above my sitted self, stared intermittently between the screen and my sitted self, and wondered if it could be possible that I was watching some other version, some other cut, that none of the other IMDB reviewers had seen. How could their experiences, so involved, so riveted, so enraptured, so moved, so amazed, be so different from mine?

So many people have had so blissfully stated that how they had pictured, in their minds, the Shire, Rivendell, Lothlorien, Moria, Mordor, etc., were so faithfully recreated in stunning visual spectacle before their very eyes in the movie. For me, the worlds created with Tolkien's words and my mind were so much richer AND FANTASTICAL, that the screen paled immeasurably in comparison. Everything was too REAL. The CGI worlds, primarily Lothlorien, Moria, and Mordor, were significantly more "mystical" than the others, where considerably more "real" nature was "used." Yet, even among these CGI worlds, only Mordor, it seemed to me, was somewhat on the mark. Even then, it needed to be far more vast, far less "crowded" and "busy," and far more foreboding. The Shire, Rivendell, etc., where more natural surroundings were incorporated, were, simply put, too plain. Too real. There was no magic. No mysticism.

Many people have made attempts to compare the CGI between WETA and ILM. Both, to the extent allowed by current technology, have done good jobs. There's no doubt, however, when CGI is employed. For those wanting probably about the most inspired use of computer animation yet, with no pretense of "standing in" for real life, rent a DVD of "Final Fantasy." Not a great story, but quite a work of art.

Acting. Again, my experience, especially with regard to Elijah Wood as Frodo (and, really, pretty much all the hobbits in the movie) was completely diametrical to those of seemingly most. Sadly, Wood's singular expression is just as preeminent here as in his other work. This "singular expression" is just as intrinsically exclusive to, and definitive of, Wood as an actor, as each "singular expression" is for other actors such as Clint Eastwood, Kevin Costner, and Keannu Reeves. Not to suggest that they can't be effective as actors necessarily, but rather that whatever character they may be that they are chosen to play have to be structured/tailored around their, again, singular expressions/limited flexibilities for there to exist any chance at efficacy. Here, Wood, or another actor perhaps, certainly could have done more with the role of Frodo.

Perhaps due to time constraints, none of the characters were terribly deeply drawn. Ian Holm, as Bilbo, probably did as much as he could with his role, although, none of the hobbits, including Bilbo, looked like the hobbits in my head. The CGI altering of his face in Rivendell had an effect on the audience, but, I could've done without it. Gandalf, Ian McKellen (sp.?), as with Holm, did well with what he had, but, again, far short of my expectations/imagination. For me, there was a fundamental problem with casting, again totally contrary to popular sentiment. Although I tend to want to think that far better choices could have been made casting-wise, it may also be a possibility that, ultimately, using human actors may never quite achieve what I would need from the characters. Don't know. The elves are drawn to a sickening level of stereotype. The ethereal aura about them, the soft voices, the expressionless faces, etc. Again, didn't work for me. And I'm a fan of Cate Blanchett and Liv Tyler. You wanna see Liv Tyler in a good role? Watch "One Night at McCool's." Cate Blanchett? Just about anything else.

Casting for Aragorn -- disappointing. I'm sure Mortensen is a good guy, and all, but, Viggo was as inappropriately cast for Aragorn as the rockstar guy was in "Almost Famous." But, then, "Almost Famous" was probably one of the worst cast movies of all time... Bean, Boromir, did a fairly good job, although, as with, really, all the characters, I have far more affection for Boromir in the book.

Gimli? Just a totally unrecognizable Rys-Davies in dwarf mode, with a temper, and not much else. Drawn very shallowly. Again, none of the characters are drawn sufficiently deeply.

If you're looking for deeply affected scenes, such as the "You will not be Caesar" scene between Joaquin Phoenix and Richard Harris in "Gladiator," or the flying plastic bag scene in "American Beauty," among other similarly beautiful scenes in both movies, "The Fellowship" is not it.

The battle scenes. The action. The suspense. The first battle scene, in Mordor, during the narration of the history of the Ring, which is largely augmented with CGI, was probably the best. Nonetheless, nothing in comparison with the opening battle scene in "Gladiator," for example, or, in more modern warfare, with the opening scene in "Saving Private Ryan." Each subsequent fight scenes are over-cut, lending a decided feeling of masking the lack of skilled fighting. None of the actors seemed to have gotten the lessons and practice necessary to portray expert swordsmanship, unlike the gladiators in "Gladiator," or the Wu-dan priest in "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon." I wasn't as impressed with "Crouching" as most seemed to have been; yet, I thought the actor's fight scenes were the most beautiful of such scenes I had ever seen. And, although he had practiced extensively for 6 months in preparation for the film, he previously had never been involved in the martial arts. Far more beautiful than the fighting of the women protagonists in "Crouching," and they were actual martial arts experts. I digress.

The suspense. For me, there was precious little. The Uruk-hai, who the movie portrayed as being far more elite than mere Orcs, were no tougher to fight than Orcs. Neither were the Nazguls. The unsophisticated fight scenes eminently betrayed actors under make-up and costume instead of hardened and skilled soldiers proficiently carrying out their orders to kill. So many people, including Ebert, have commented on how frightening the Ring-wraiths were in the movie. Again, I deviate. They weren't frightening, and their chases weren't suspenseful. Wow, I'm really tearing into this movie, arent' I?...

The score. Marked the scenes. Distinctive? No. Distinctive scores? John Williams (although, if you're familiar with his influences, you'll realize that he's not the most original composer in the world, either...) with his "Star Wars"-related scores, his "Superman" scores. Hans Zimmer with the score for the "Gladiator." Bill Conti with "Rocky," etc. Definitely not this score.

Watching "The Fellowship," especially considering it in the context of my having read so many positive feedback with respect to it, was such a starkly shallow experience for me, I am left wondering if I was simply in a totally unreceptive mood. I really don't think so. I was truly looking forward to the film, and a wonderfully positive experience. Did I expect too much? Was I too lax in caution? I don't think so. I had high expectation, granted, yet, by now, I am also aware that some forced caution is generally warranted. In this case, however, because my appreciation of the movie was so lukewarm, I doubt that, even had my expectations been unrealistically high, there would've been much difference in my eventual opinion with respect to the movie. It, just about on all levels, did not work for me. And, having read the extremely sparse negative reviews about the movie, and having felt anger and pity for these "unimaginative" souls who presumably couldn't appreciate creativity and fantasy and all the other qualities that most others had touted about this film as having, I didn't think that I would be, or wanted to be, one of the ones writing the negative reviews. Unfortunately, I can't write a fawning one. And, because I feel like I had far more invested in this film than most certainly most others, I felt like I had to write a review. I would have preferred that it be laden with praise, but my disappointment will not allow it. Based on my recent experiences with Jackson's "The Fellowship" and "The Sorcerer's Stone," (I have read all 4 Potters, and love Rowling's work), I reluctantly have come to the conclusion that, unless crafted by a truly remarkable and heretofore nonexistent collaboration, with much love and extraordinary competence, the results of the transference of a great work of fantasy from novel to film will most likely fail to rival the worlds that a reader would have created in his/her mind. To date, it seems that no science fiction/fantasy filmmakers have as successfully created wholly new and fantastical worlds as Lucas has done with his "Star Wars" movies. And even these are far from perfect.

title: A masterful representation of J.R.R. Tolkien's literary classic.
review:
Let me first say that I loved the movie. Peter Jackson did a wonderful job in bringing this epic story, loved by millions, from print to big screen. Yes, there was some differences from the novel to the screen, but there had to be some omissions. No studio would have backed this movie with longer than a 3 hour run time and only the die-hard fans would have sat through it. Even at its 2 hour and 58 minutes, it feels a little long. I can't imagine what I would have cut out of this to make it any shorter. I also wouldn't have dared to add anything else. The $75 million dollar five day weekend opening was outstanding. I'm shocked it could pull that amount with the fewer times it could be shown due to its length. I've seen the movie twice now. I saw it on opening day in a packed theater and everyone loved it. I finished my second viewing earlier this evening and tried to catch some of the more subtle things intended for those who had read the books. For example, the cloaks that all of the fellowship are wearing when they leave Lothlorien.

What I liked ... All of the cast (yes, even Liv Tyler) was perfect. I can't imagine one person I would have changed. I have to admit that Hugo Weaving as Elrond still reminded me of Agent Smith from the Matrix. Gandalf was wonderful. I'd use his real name, but I think that is his real name now. Frodo and Aragorn were nicely played. The actor playing Legolas was given some of the greatest action moments.

What I disliked ... I'm hard pressed to find much. I would have liked the characters of Boromir and Gimli more developed. For instance, I think Gimli's transformation before and after visiting Lothlorien would have been great to see on screen. Jackson tried to explain Boromir's whole character in his last scene and it just isn't enough. The only other thing I might have done differently is the ending. I can tell you that there was a collective 'aaarrggghhh' from the whole theater both times I saw this movie. It really feels like you left the theater seeing one third of a movie, which is ok if you've read the books and understand that this was a natural stopping point. But if you are someone new to the Rings trilogy, it feels like they pulled the rug out from under you. Perhaps this was what Peter Jackson was going for... "always leave them wanting more." :) My favorite movie moment ... When Gandalf arrives in the Shire the first time. It is just magic! No pun intended. His playfulness with the children is priceless. I gave this movie a 10. Even though it is only a partial telling of a much larger story, it truly is near perfect. It's only shortcomings are brought about by time constraints. Thank you Peter Jackson!

title: Excellent; far better than I'd dared to hope for!
review:
Best movie I've seen in years. Great job of catching the narrative and the characters and really making middle earth a living breathing place. All the actors are wonderful and Vigo is especially good. And Liv Tyler makes me believe Arwen and her romance with Aragorn. Great work by everyone really.

The money obviously all made it onto the screen. Great sets, backgrounds, costumes and props (check out the great variety in the swords used.) This film scores a 10 in every category.

title: Great Movie, I love the books and was not dissapointed one bit.
review:
Let me first say I am a devotee of the Lord of the Rings books, not Tolkein or his other works as a whole. I do not think Tokein is a great author and his books are really boring and sadly, badly written for the most part. But I feel he is the best story teller of the modern era, one that could of used a ghost writer badly though.

Needless to say I have been wetting myself with anticipation for over a year with this movie, a hunger heightened by the sheer poopy-ness of the movies to come out this year for the most part. And I have been overwhelming pleased with the end result.

I feel almost every decision Jackson and Co. made worked wonderfully, most of all the inclusion of Boromir's "departure" at the end of the film. This not only made the conclusion more logical than the book, but also really non-readers want to see more...not to mention provided a splendid action scene to cap the film with. The extension of Arwen and the love story was OK, and I thought the inclusion of a visible Saruman and Lurtz the head Uruk-Hai were good moves, even though the latter was just blade fodder in an entertaining way. I also thought the prolouge at the begining was great. And I did not give a rats behind before seeing the movie or since that Tom Bombadil was not in the film.

Nitpicks of things I did not like were not to numorus. One was the lack of them showing Galadriel's gifts to the fellowship. And the secene where she became the "Abyss" like neon thingy freaked me out and was not as I recalled from the book. On that point the elves as a whole just kind of annoyed me, cept for Legolas who was da man. Also the rather disjointed time frame bothered me, for example it appears Saruman builds in army in a week or so. The soundtrack was too bombastique for me at points, espicially as my friend pointed out in the mines of Moria when the fanfare was deafening us but we knew we were looking at CGI images.

As for the film the direction and effects were awesome, from the shrinking to the Balrog. All the actors were good considering that this would be considered fluff material to most, I feel Sir Ian stole the award for best of the bunch and would not mind seeing an Oscar nommination for him. Make up and art in general were flawless, one of the best visual movies ever I have seen. I even enjoyed the considerable (as compared to the next two storys) sparse battle scenes, each were exciting to me and inventive. Legolas had my favorite "moves", like the immortal arrow to the throat poke and then used again as a missile. I appluade the entire crew taking a serious tone to the film most of all.

One of my all time favorite movies allready and a very good one...not in the "Schindlers List" or "Goodfellas" category of films but an outstanding one non the less. But I will be annoyed if it somehow wins a Best Picture Oscar, I enjoy my ability to seperate films I enjoy and are good as opposed to fine pieces of cinema and acting, Mr. Crowe I'm talking about you!!!

All that aside a great beggining to an outstanding triology.

title: Excellent
review: It was a pleasure to watch this film. It was enjoyable to see the world Tolkein created, re-created by Jackson. he did a fine job. while some parts needed to be cut in order to flow as a movie, it doesn't feel like you are missing much. the Balrog rocked, as did the entire Mines of Moria scene. the cinematography excelled in such scenes as showing Aragorn looking at the broken sword in Rivendell, showing his nobility hidden in exile. I only wished they had a small preview of what is to come in the Two Towers. that was my only qualm with the film. it satisfied the film fan in me.

title: One of the Best Movies I've Ever Seen

title: ho hum
review: Like a lot of fans of the "Lord of the Rings" i've been waiting on tenter hooks ever since the botched up animated version of the seventies to see a completed version,what we get here is the first installment just like the cartoon but less, we now have to wait a year until the next three hour episode and then another to the final three hour episode,this is where i have a problem in my opinion 75% of what is dramatically interesting in the book has already occurred how are they fill two more episodes? This is a decent film not "The Greatest" or even great the cast is made up of a good quality cast without any being particularly outstanding "none of the nine" bring a resume that would suggest they are amongst (perhaps Ian McKellen aside) the most sought after actors in film indeed most have found their fame in Television. Visually the film is stupendous but no one looks at a postcard for three hours,there is no real tension or character development,no real introduction of the members of the Fellowship who join later,here by the way the decision makers have blundered by casting Viggo Mortensen and Sean Bean as virtual twins playing the same role when in the book Tolkien has contrasting Characters in these roles. Perhaps this Ensemble will grow in later episodes and my comments will seem unfair,maybe one day after the third episode is finished a film buff will sit down an endure the whole nine hours or whatever in one sitting and will proclaim that it is "The Greatest" again but as of now after episode 0ne just like the cartoon i'm left hoping but still unsatisfied. 6/10 so far.

title: Even better than I had hoped
review:
Rather than just filming the book, Peter jackson seems (though it is not

possible) to be telling the same story in his own way. This is an incredible film; even its weaknesses (one of which, unfortunately, is Lothlorien and Galadriel - the scenes simply don't work) are quickly forgiven in the sweep of the story.

I've got to wait a full year for the next one? That hurts.

title: If I wanted to read the books, I would
review: I have my B.A. in English lit from UNC-Chapel Hill, and I have never read these books.  I tried, but I was a little too old for them by then. Frankly, I thought this was a great movie.  I think lots of movies are great, though. I don't think any movie I've seen is the BEST movie ever.  That's a little fanatical. Also, isn't it silly to sit and say it wasn't exactly like the book. Well, DUH!  Why would I want to see a movie that did the exact same things as the book?  I'd just read the book.  So many people fail to understand the difference between writing a novel and writing a screenplay...and, trust me, translating someone else's work from a novel to a screenplay is a daunting task. I commend the writers and the director for their work (and all of the other folks, too).  Prior to seeing the film I had no desire to read the books, but now I have a huge urge to read them all. I'd say that the people in charge accomplished their goal.  Wouldn't you?

title: One of the finest examples of a movie made from a book--ever!
review: The first installment of the Rings trilogy is such an exciting success that it is hard to contain oneself (coming from an old Tolkien fan).  I was also pleased to see similar response from critics that had not read the books. There are so many facets of this film to comment upon, that it is hard to pick just one--but that one should be that this is, quite simply, one of the best jobs of Adaptation ever pulled off.  The filmmakers have filled in Tolkien's backstory and all the stuff that happens off-stage in the book The Fellowship of the Ring so well that they have actually improved upon the book by making a seemingly unfilmable work cinematic.  This season we have seen the rote scene-by- scene adaptation worked on Harry Potter, which turned a light, charming book into a long, slow 2-1/2 hour stint in the theater.  By contrast, The Fellowship of the Ring has been transformed in its adaptation into something truly worthy of the big screen.  We truly haven't seen such a wondrous transformation worked on anything since the days of The Wizard of Oz and Gone With the Wind, two other works that have managed over a period of many years to maintain separate, viable existences in both book and movie form.

title: A Film Made For Fans (I Think)
review: Allow me to preface this by saying I have never read the LOTR books.  I am just a plain old moviegoer with no advance knowledge of the story.  That type of moviegoer, however, is who a filmmaker must reach for a film to be commercially successful. That said, I found LOTR (part 1, apparently) a visually attractive (I won't say stunning) yet wholly maddening experience. This film does have some positive aspects: several of the characters are well-drawn and compelling, the production design (when actual SETS are used) is well-done, and parts of the story are interesting. Unfortunately, this film seems to have been made for fans of the books. The entire story of Bilbo (apparently told in The Hobbit) is glossed over, so his importance later in the film is not really that compelling.  Many of the characters have little or no backstory, and although a complete personal history comes off as bad exposition, some kind of story helps to explain their motivations, specifically for the characters of Gimli, Legolas, and Boromir, but there are other examples as well. And then, there's the ending.  In an ideal world, filmmakers would have many opportunities like this: to tell a sweeping story over several films and have a profitable, loyal audience back for every entry.  This, however, is not an ideal world.  Moviegoes will tolerate some unanswered questions, for example, Wolverine's backstory in X-Men, but audiences expect a complete screen experience.  Even in the case of a series, each film should be its own complete package.  Star Wars is a the first in a series, but it does stand on its own.   LOTR, however, is an example of arrogant presumption. The assumption is that Episode, excuse me, Part 1, will be so good and so profitable, that it will justify a sequel worth producing before Part 1 is ever seen.  I felt cheated and insulted by this presumption.  So much so (and I'm sure my seven dollars doesn't matter a whit to New Line) that I may just blow off seeing parts 2 and 3.  It's not that I don't care about the story, I don't care for how they chose to package it.

title: BRILLIANT!!!
review:
After waiting over two years for this film, you will propably understand my hopes were extremely high. Most of the times, (just think of The Phantom Menace) such a film does not live up to the expectations.

Well, Fellowship of the Ring DID live up to my (and I think most people's) expectations. It thankfully has become a truly magnificent piece of entertainment, a masterpiece that will influence any film to be made in the future. It is the Star Wars of our time. But Fellowship is a much better film then Star Wars, where Star Wars is a thrill ride featuring some interesting - and charismatic - characters, Fellowship is a film with a beating heart and a living soul. Just think of the scene where Sam proves he would rather drown then to let Frodo leave on his own, brilliant!! But the film is also visually one of the greatest - if not greatest - achievement in movie history. Peter Jackson IS the visionair I always thought him to be and I think he will be one of the most important directors of the coming decennia. The prologue shakes you up and throws you right into Middle-Earth, and the Mines of Moria represent one of the greatest action-set-pieces of all time. Thank God Mr. Jackson knew what to do with the time (and money) that had been given him.

title: Overlong, but for the most part excellent.
review:
Having now watched the film, all of my friends who haven't are asking me the inevitable question, 'How does it compare with 'Harry Potter & The Philosopher's Stone'?

My answer has to be 'It's six and two threes'. Whereas HP appeared slightly rushed (but nevertheless entertaining) and could have quite happily sustained an extra thirty minutes' running time, I found 'The Fellowship Of The Ring' to be equally captivating up until the climax of the splendid 'Mines of Moria' sequence, after which a sense of 'just get on with it' set in.

POSSIBLE SPOILER!! I found the latter segment incredibly gripping. On the screen, Frodo's intense reaction to events reached me on a far greater emotional level than similar situations in 'Star Wars' (Episodes I & IV) ever did.

However, from a cinematic point of view, I felt that the aftermath of this would be the ideal place for the ending. The feeling of 'something lost but everything to play for' that was so much of what made 'The Empire Strikes Back' work so well would have been just as apposite here.

I only read the book earlier this year, in preparation, and obviously I intend to read 'The Two Towers'. Unfortunately, it seems that Peter Jackson has already spoiled the first chapter for me by including major events from it at the end of the first film.

He didn't need to do this, as they would have made a great opening to the second instalment. I saw 'Fellowship' in a packed cinema, and after two and a half hours, I could sense some restlessness around me. I don't know exactly what they were thinking, but I know I was saying to myself 'Great film, guys. You've earned your money, but any chance of letting me go home now?'

Of course, up until that point I was completely enthralled.

title: Taps into the source of mythic success
review: The success of myth is that it taps a deep yearning for getting beyond the status quo and accessing that which is transcendent. While I've read debates about the script and the action, I think as an independent work of art the film succeeds in this mythic sense. It has real compassion for all the characters, and a sense of their universal humanity that might have easily been missed.

title: To all those that complain
review:
I have been reading a great deal of the comments in various places around the internet, and have found that most of the criticism comes down to these factors:

1) length: too long or too short 2) filmography: not enough CGI or too much CGI 3) Intro: too much intro to Hobbits, not enough intro to Hobbits 4) Characters: Not enough background, too much background. 5) Action: too much action, action not clear enough.

I disagree with these criticisms, but held them in my mind while watching the various movies (see below).

To make sure that I was being objective, I saw LOTR again and then immediately saw The Godfather, Shawshank, Star Wars, And Usual suspects (movies that I like from the top 15). I tried to gauge my reaction to these films, as well as study their film style, the characters, the scope, etc.

I also took into consideration all of the other top 15 films that I have seen (but not as recently).

While some here are saying, "please don't make this the #1 movie," the problem is that what we judge to be the #1 is really very subjective. It what STRIKES you. Yes, there are certain things a movie must do to be great, but once you get in that "top 15" or so, they all make the right decisions. It then becomes a matter of what you relate to as being what you think is, "the best."

Trying to be as objective as possible, I found the cinematography, sets, acting, costumes, effects, story, plot, pacing, tone, mood, music, and everything else to be at par or more than any of the "great" movies (above). Yes, there were flaws, but every one of those movies had flaws. If you don't think The Godfather could be torn apart even more mercilessly than LOTR, then you haven't really watched The Godfather in a while.

Yes, you can nitpick this or any movie to death, but the reality is that this movie is both a) excellent and b) popular. To most in the snobbish movie community, popularity is a sin. Again, the reality is that LOTR (like Empire Strikes Back, or Citizen Kane, or The Godfather) excels at what it sets out to do. The fact that it has such a high rating is simply because good storytelling wrapped in a "hero's journey" makes sense to people right now, so in its own way, LOTR *IS* better than The Godfather.

title: One of the best films ever made.
review:
This movie is as good an adaptation of a book into a movie as the 6 hour Dune adaptation by John Harrison was.

Spoilers ahead.

I will preface this review with the observation that some will not like this film. The fight scenes are not pretty little bloodless artfests, like the matrix or crouching tiger, they are realistic and brutal. Characters die, even main characters. And they die in ways that are not pleasant, nor particulary heroic. Dead bodies are stacked like cordwood. Children under the age of about 12 probably shouldn't see this movie because of the brutality and plain evilness.

As a fan of the entire middle earth saga since 1978, I have to say that not only did I like the movie, but I think the movie is better than the books in many ways. Tom Bombadil's inclusion in the books always mystified me. If not for Tom the hobbits would have died twice, right on the borders of their own land. It makes more sense to me that they can walk down a road one county over and make it to the next town under their own power.

Tom's exclusion from the movie really removed a lot of puzzlement that people would have had from trying to understand why they didn't just give the ring to Tom and have him take it to the mountain of Doom and destroy it. After all, the ring had no power over Tom. I understand why, don't explain it to me. Try explaining it to someone who never read the book and do so in under an hour. To me Tom was just a Dues Ex Machina to rescue the hobbits a couple of times but with very arbitrary restrictions on his power.

I kind of missed the revealation of Sam being a spy for Merry and Pippin and their scheme of going with Frodo come hell or high water. In the book they were lifelong friends of Frodo and would have done anything. In the movie, Merry and Pippin just happen along and get sucked into the journey. I like the book version better. But hey, the movie can only be so long.

The meeting between Aragon and Frodo at the conclusion of the Fellowship was better than the book for many reasons. In the book Frodo leaves and Aragon just kind of figures it out. It doesn't make any sense. If you were a man of Aragons honor and integrity, would you let a little hobbit go on and get to Moria all alone? Neither would I. The conversation allowed them to honorably terminate the fellowship.

The picture was lushly shot, the landscapes and the details of Hobbiton, Bagsend, Bree, Rivendell, Moria, Mordor and Lothlorien are spectacular and the attention to detail are perfect. Casting was perfect, acting was awesome, and the monsters all were horrific and believable. The balrog was evil personified and was better than I had ever imagined.

The special effects were done in such a way as to almost be invisible, only being used to further the story and heighten the suspension of disbelief. I hope that all film makers in the future pay attention to this seemless integration of special effects and live action.

Everything combined to make this movie very real to me. Although there was one moment 2 hours into the movie where I realized that there was at least an hour left. 3 hours is a long time to sit still.

title: More talk-talk, less clang-clang
review: Fighting odds as large as Sauron himself, Peter Jackson has weaved a masterful film on a wide canvas. And yet, as others have pointed out, once the titled Fellowship finally forms, we don't get quite enough of the party traveling together, and we don't get enough time with Gimli, Boromir and Legolas. Instead, the progression of battles does tend to grow a little long (even for this adventure lover's taste), especially since all the clanging robs us of character-based screen time. As well, the nightmarish evil of the Nazgul was fabulously done, but we really didn't need that puffed-up computerized cave troll. As Jackson is still compiling parts II and III, let's have a hair more of the natural beauty and even some of the poetry and fellowship of the books. Keep the fights as well, but just keep 'em shorter.

title: It's not the book; it's the movie; and it's excellent
review: This is a long, fast-paced movie, a good faith effort to tell as much of the story as practical in an action movie made by people who apparently read and respect the book.  I've read the trilogy many times and am completely satisfied.  Some places were visualized as well as I hoped.  It seemed that every omission and change to the story was made in order to make a good movie for wider audience than those who read it.

title: Simply Stunning
review:
WOW!! What else is there to say? FOTR was pure magic from start to finish that had my breathing deep and my heart pounding. After reading all the hype ever since last year I went into the theatre wondering whether or not it would live up to my expectations. Ever since LOTR was written, it has been the consensus of many that it could not be filmed. Well, Peter Jackson has delivered something that so rightly deserves its title of "Masterpiece"; a film that will no doubt be the milestone of films of its genre, not unlike fantasy books have been compared to the original work.

What I find most incredible is just how every location in the film matched almost exactly the pictures I had in my head when I read it. Hobbiton, Rivendell, Lothlorien, Isengard and especially Mordor, were just as I had imagined them. I don't think that there has been a film that has matched my imagination as much. The grandeur of the landscapes, using CGI and the New Zealand vistas were moulded into something so far removed from our everyday experiences whilst at the same time being wonderfully familiar.

The casting was second to none, with full marks going to Ian McKellen as Gandalf (again, exactly as I'd imagined!). He so eloquently captured his character's nature, espcially in the scenes involving him and the Ring. And his performance in the Mines of Moria had me almost in tears.

If I had to venture one minor criticism, the character development was lacking slightly. Whilst Elijah Woods did a great job of playing Frodo, I felt that his plight, his fear of the unknown and his temptation by the Ring (written about so well in the books) wasn't concentrated on as much as it could be. It was only during his meeting with Galadriel (Blanchett) that we began to see something of his burden. I hope that as soon as Frodo gets closer to Mordor, we begin to see something deeper to his character.

Sean Bean (a fine actor) did sterling work and his confrontation with Frodo, subsequent battle scenes with the Orcs and final dialogue with Aragorn were extremely profound.

The effects were mind-blowing and the vastness of the Tolkien universe was truly captured using wide camera angles and vertigo-inducing, birds eye-view camera flight. The Moria scenes were just as fantastic as previous reviewers raved about; the fight scenes with the cave troll and the Balrog were truly awesome. One of the moments I remember so well from the book was Gandalf's confrontation with the Balrog and the tension of Tolkien's words were translated superbly in film. The fight between Gandalf and Saruman was also excellent.

I honestly cannot find any major faults with this movie. Although three hours is short for such an epic work of literature, Jackson captured exactly the flavour of LOTR and he rightly deserves his title of gifted moviemaker (I haven't caught anything else he's done). And I can breathe a huge sigh of relief that his massive gamble paid off. Here is a film that will stand the test of time and represent the pinnacle of movie making greatness, an important piece of work that cannot, and should not be ignored.

10 out of 10.

And Harry Potter? Let's not even go there!

title: Good not great
review:
I think some praise is deserved for this movie but I can't see calling in the greatest movie ever. I won't go into what it does well because some many others have already. What I will do is tell you what I didn't like.

I thought the movie did not do a good job conveying the difference between Hobbits, Man, Dwarves, and Elves. Maybe this is impossible to do in a 3 hour movie but I came away with the sense that the Hobbits were scripted and acted as if they were just young farm boys. The film did not do a good job explaining just how out of the ordinary the adventures of Frodo and Bilbo were when considering they were Hobbits. In addition it relied only back lighting, costume, and voice to differentiate between elf, man, and dwarf.

Where are the songs? The book relied heavily on song that is completely left out. I admit it would have been very hard to capture the magic of the songs without coming of silly but surely the `greatest movie of all time' could have done it. People rave about the music but ignore this simple fact. In addition I didn't consider the score to rival Glory or other movies with great scores. It wasn't bad but I didn't come away remembering any particular tune like in Star Wars or Indiana Jones.

In addition the movie did a poor job of conveying the fact that this was actually a long journey and not a weekend hike.

Lastly, the movie has no end. Granted this is because it is part of a series but most great stories at least come to some kind of conclusion while the epic continues. Think of the first Start Wars movie. In that movie there was a story that continue on but at least the audience was left with the satisfaction of some kind of accomplishment with the destruction of the death star. In this movie we are left with nothing of the sort. The excitement in building up to an epic battle and the ultimate result of such battle while not new is a powerful thing that makes or breaks many great movies. In this we are left with a skirmish in the woods. It was OK but not great. Granted this is a limitation of working with the book but one must consider that this limitation does take away from the movie and for that reason alone I could never consider this the greatest movie of all time.

In the end the movie suffers from what most adaptations suffer from. Less character development/definition (Hobbits aren't just farmboys with furry feet) and any limitations that existed in the original work.

title: Good but not great
review:

title: The BEST Fantasy film ever made
review:
Much of what I wanted to say has already been said by the commentators here or by film critics, but I had to put in my two cents on this wonderful cinematic masterpiece. It is so rare for a film-from-a-popular-book to be this good, this rich, this masterful, but it is. I am an avid reader of both the Harry Potter series and LOTR, and although they are vastly different many comparisons have been made due to the proximity of the release of their movie versions. And as much as I love Harry Potter (the books), I must say that LOTR the film far, far surpasses the quality and depth of the HP the film. I credit it mostly to the superb director P. Jackson, who has that esteemed ability to inspire fear (e.g. that little hide-and-seek the monster plays with Frodo around a pillar in Moria that had me at the edge of my seat, and that terrifying moment when Bilbo's face is transformed into that of a monster--Gollum's--at the sight of his old ring, man, that's some great stuff that Columbus will never be able to do with a million Home Alone's on his sleeve), and yet also inject humor and big, warm-hearted humanity into his characters and settings.

So, if you have not seen the film, and even if you've never been a fan of LOTR the book, please do yourself a favor and watch this film!

title: and the story has barely even started.....
review:
I had extremely high expectations going into 'The Fellowship of the Ring'. It is absolutely the greatest book I have read, and one of the greatest stories ever told. So to expect something short of it being one of the greatest movies ever made would be foolish. I wanted a film that would blow my mind, and I honestly thought they couldn't do it, and I thought they would disappoint me. When I left the theatre, however, the movie still had a strong hold on me and it is the best thing I have ever seen put on film. I thought my expectations were as high as they could be, and this film easily surpassed them all and took me along for the ride.

First of all, I have to say that Peter Jackson is absolutely brilliant. The direction in this film is astounding. He took what was probably the most difficult book to translate onto the screen and he excelled in a way that I didn't think was possible. The performances he got out of his actors was amazing. Even more amazing were some of the shots in the movie. The cinematography was absolutely amazing. Those of you who thought 'Crouching Tiger' was beautiful, well it doesn't even compare to the awe inspiring scope of this film. The whole sequence in Moria is breathtaking. I don't remember blinking when I was watching it. It is so astounding to watch it that you wonder how it is even possible that they did it. I've never seen anything as amazing as the Moria sequence and I doubt I ever will again.

The acting in the film is also fantastic. I was watching it and I did something I rarely do, I forgot that they were actors. Ian McKellan IS Gandalf. I never saw anything but a powerful wizard. He was so amazing and was how I saw him in my imagination. Elijah Wood IS Frodo. I assume you get the picture. I do have to comment on Viggo Mortensen as Strider and say that he is the absolute perfect choice. I always see Strider(Aragorn)as the ultimate hero, and Viggo captures my expectations in that character and made me believe in him. No one is out of place in this film at all, and Ian Holm is especially great as Bilbo is what portions of the film he is in. The casting director did the perfect job and I couldn't have, in any way, done it better myself.

Lets not forget to talk about the incredible sets and special effects. The Moria set is just astounding. I can't describe it to you, but when you see it, you'll get the picture. Lothlorien was beautiful. Different than what I pictured, but effective all the same. The Shire was perfect. You can tell that they paid careful attention to detail and finely crafted everything. The evil characters in the film were also great. The Nazgul were terrifying. There is really no other way to describe them. What amazed me the most was the Balrog. I had some ideas of how it could have been, but the image they gave me of it was great. I could also tell you how great Mordor looked, and how great the eye looked, and how great the two tower looked, but I won't. You just have to see it all for yourself.

At the end of watching 'The Fellowship of the Ring' a couple of thoughts occurred to me. First of all, it occurred to me that I HAVE to see this film again, and soon. And secondly, it occurred to me that nothing has even happened in the story yet. LOTR is of such a huge scope, and they have just touched upon it. This film absolutely blew my mind, and I am positive that the best it yet to come. That said, I have never in my life seen a film that was as good as this, and as a fan of the books, it was really powerful for me. It was not a film you sit in the theatre and watch, is it something you experience. The film sucked me in and it still has a strong hold over me. It is a very powerful film, one that everybody should see. Greatest story ever, greatest film ever(only until the sequals of course!!!!). Thank you so much Mr.Jackson and everyone else associated with it. And of course, thank you J.R.R. Tolkien. An astounding 10 out of 10, it doesn't get any better than this.

title: A Timeless classic

When Star Wars and Harry Potter are long forgotten, Peter Jackson's take on perhaps the greatest fantasy tale in history will stay with us forever.

title: Great movie, but understandably imperfect.
review:
Here we go:

For starters, I had not finished reading the Rings series before seeing the movie. In fact, I was in the middle of the Fellowship when I saw the movie this weekend. Therefore, I can say I hold very little bias towards this movie since I grew up on the Hobbit, Redwall, and Dune rather than the Rings series in general.

For the most part, I was quite impressed with this cinematic giant of a film. It had the best cinematography in a movie that I've seen since "A Thin Red Line" and "Braveheart", and I'll go even as far as to say that it has vastly outdone the others in that respect. New Zealand was the perfect setting for this film. The sweeping landscape shots are excellent, as well as the scenes from Isingod and the dwarven mines. Besides the cinematography, kudos go out to many of the fine actors and actresses who poured their hearts into this film. Ian McKellon as Gandalf give probably the best performance in the film, followed by Christopher Lee as Saruman or Elijah Wood as Frodo. Liv Tyler and Cate Blanchett aren't bad for their limited amount of screen time. Overall, mostly everyone was well cast and the screenplay was nicely written. My favorite scene would have to be the wicked wizard duel between Saruman and Gandalf. This movie ties with Memento as the best film that I've scene all year.

Now for the downside:

For avid Tolkien readers, many will be dismayed with the script's departure at times from the text. Some major omissions have occured in the form of the complete absence of Tom Bombadil and other changes which give some characters more important roles than the text had permitted. Also, the ending is kind of disappointing, but movie viewers should remember that unlike films such as Back to the Future and Indiana Jones, this is one book broken up into three major parts. The book continues after the end of a part, not starting anew with some brand new adventure so the static ending is kind of understandable. Other qualms arise due to the fact that some characters are severly underdeveloped, especially legolas, the Dwarf, and the other hobbits following Frodo. You don't get to learn a whole lot about them and in a three hour movie, you'd figure you would be able to(which brings me to my next point.) This movie is a three-hour epic in every sense, which means you must bring your attention span to the theatres and make sure the theatre you go to has good surround sound and comfortable seats.(Trust me, I saw this movie in a crappy and uncomfortable theatre, which made the viewing quite unpleasant.)

Finally my only other complaint is this:

MOMS AND DADS, PLEASE DO NOT BRING YOUR UNDER 12-YEAR OLD CHILDREN TO SEE THIS FILM UNLESS THEY ARE QUITE MATURE. THEY DO NOT HAVE THE ATTENTION SPAN AND THEY COULD BE QUITE FRIGHTENED BY SOME OF THE MONSTERS IN THIS MOVIE. THIS IS NOT WALT DISNEY NOR IS THIS A CHILDREN'S MOVIE. IT'S PG-13 FOR A REASON, AND NOTHING MAKES OTHER MOVIE GOERS MORE UPSET THAN CRYING OR INQUISITIVE CHILDREN WHO TALK THROUGHOUT A THREE-HOUR MASTERPIECE!!!(as you can see, I ran into a few of these cases during my viewing and I was not too happy.)

-In summation, The Fellowship of The Rings is a great movie with some understandable flaws. Many will enjoy it, Many will love it, and Many will hate it. It's changes from the book are understandable and are the interpretation of those who produced and directed it, and no book save maybe The Shawshank Redemption can be translated nearly word for word into a movie. Overall, I felt that Peter Jackson did an excellent job with this movie and I cannot wait for it to come out on DVD so I can enjoy it that much more from the comforts of my own home. 8.9/10

title: brilliantly brought to life, but . . .
review:
I must say that this work of cinema is nothing short of brilliance, but I also must say I am somewhat . . . disappointed. Though the movie does beautifully bring to life the characters, places and story of Tolkien, I cannot say that I am 100% satisfied with it. I feel, as a whole, the film is much, much darker than the books themselves. Honestly, what film has ever been made that is better than the book? It's simply not possible -- the image in ours minds will never transpose to the screen, I don't care how far technology has brought us. I feel director Jackson's vision of the books is not completely what Tolkien envisioned. The first novel, however perilous, was not as dark as the film came to be. There is a very gradual build in the books, and truly all three should be read as one novel. I feel the film jumps too quickly into the thrills and fights and narrow escapes. About one third of the first book of the trilogy is, (to some), painfully descriptive and slow to action, but I feel that was Tolkien's intention to make all the coming action all the more exciting when the reader gets there. Jackson jumps too quickly into it, I feel.

On the other hand, I DO agree with some of Jackson's choices. I completely agree with his choice to make Arwen (Liv Tyler) a larger player in the activities -- in the books she mostly remains in the background. Also, touching on Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen) and Arwen's love story was also a good choice. But, most of all, I DON'T agree with Jackson's vision of Lothlorien. In the film, it was a dark place, however good it is supposed to be, and Galadriel seems too distant and even malicious in the film. In the book, Lorien was much brighter and happier, and Galadriel was wiser and more of a character. Though Cate Blanchett plays her beautifully, I feel her character is too, for lack of a better word, creepy. The same goes for Rivendell -- there is not enough happiness in either place. As an audience member in the movie theater, I don't feel like there are many things in Middle Earth worth saving! All in all, I feel the movie is darker than what Tolkien saw.

In closing, I would say I am content, as it is a beautiful piece of cinema, but not satisfied with the film, with my knowledge of the books.

title: Awesome
review:
I dare anyone to walk out of this movie disappointed.

True, there are differences to the book; but these were necessary to transform LOTR into cinema. I have not seen Peter Jackson's previous work, and I did read the book 15 years ago. My comments are not director or `book fan' biased.

There are movies that leave a lasting impression on ones psyche (`Shawshank Redemption', `Godfather', `American Beauty'). There are also movies that break new ground and leave a lasting impression on the industry as a whole (whether it's technology, like the Wachowski brothers, reinventing the twist themed ending genre, like Bryan Singer / Christopher McQuarrie or M Night Shyamalan, or devising new filming techniques like Christopher Nolan).

Peter Jackson's work here is both mesmerizing and ground breaking. From the methods used (the whole trilogy was filmed in one year in New Zealand, the WETA effects, the amalgamation of Enya and Howard Shore's score, the roller-coaster camera work like zooming the viewer into the inside of middle earth from Saruman's tower) to the emotions captured on 35 mm (through the changes in the color of the lens, the `slow motion for non action'; the battles are real time, but the consequences are absorbed in slow motion, and capturing the delivery of Tolkien's writing `you do what you can with the time that you are given'), the LOTR deserves its ranking on the IMDB charts.

The LOTR proves that cinema, at it's greatest form, is a synthesis of the finest visual and audible arts: admiring a Caravaggio whilst listening to Mozart's 29th symphony, or admiring a Magritte whilst listening to Coldplay's `Trouble'- take your pick.

As I've said, I dare anyone to walk out of this movie disappointed.

10 of 10.

title: Surprise, surprise
review:
Just came back from a second viewing of this great film, and was yet again totally taken in by it. Just like the first time I was surprised by how they had captured Middle-earth on-screen, how the actors played their part with their heart on their sleeve, how utterly and totally convincing it all was.

Although there are already quite a few raving reviews from official film critics, plus a probable 100.000+ fan reviews to be found on the net, I would still like to add my two cents, if only to let Peter Jackson and all of his troupe know that I think they did an admirable job in bringing Tolkiens´world and characters to life.

I am not going into detail - lots of other people have done that, but I will make mention of some things that I liked, and that I haven´t read too much about yet. Minor spoilers ahead for people that have not seen the movie.

If there is one thing I have read nothing or nearly nothing about, it is Gollums eyes. Although Gollum does not play a big role in this first movie, he can be seen two or three times, and one of those times you see his eyes... Incredible eyes, very human, although much bigger and somehow filled with a sadness of long ages, and with a certain malice. Enough to whet your appetite for parts two and three, where Gollum gets to play one of the leading roles. And this guy is completely CGI, too! I read in a review about an ´alarming Jar Jar Binks likeness´... The brainless turd who wrote that review probably never read the books. Much unlike the intelligence-of-the-average-movie-goer-insulting Jar Jar Binks, Gollum was already a character in the books, who was not thrown in to get some toys sold! Nor do I expect him to speak in a ´funny´ semi-Jamaican accent.

Second thing I noticed, is the raw emotion that is up there. Characters are allowed to cry, to feel about other characters, to hug, to scream of pain or loss... It is a very emotional film. Anyone stating that we have cardboard characters here, not only completely missed out on the emotion that is on display, they also missed out on a more important pont: this film is not part one, basically it is the first three hours of a nine-hour film. Only when the three films can be seen as one (in a LONG run) we can judge the character development. As the next film will have several small groups to follow on their journeys through Middle-earth, I am sure we will see their characters develop. For the moment, we have to hold back on that particular feature.

Well, that is what I had to say about it.

I bow deep and low to you, Mr. Jackson, for pulling it off. For actually committing six years of your life (or is it even more) to this project and coming up with a first installment that is nothing short of brilliant. For giving us all the pleasure to see a well-known story come to life in a different, yet faithful way. Of course, should you ever come across these humble lines, the gratitude goes out to everyone involved, from the director to the best boys´ gaffer. Perhaps the biggest compliment is that my wife, who before yesterday had only heard of the books because I read them, now wants to read the books, wants to see the film a second time in the theater (would be the third time for me - no matter!) and can hardly wait for The Two Towers. But neither can I.
