This film deserves every single "10" that we have given it.

title: Heresy here! In some ways, the film exceeds the book
review:
Why does Tolkien's work persuade and endure? His genius lay not in his prose style, characterizations, or narrative structure, all of which are actually rather bland, but in the power of Naming. No motley assemblage of syllables, these, such as most fantasy works rely upon. This philologist-as-author could, with the surety of a wizard at work, clothe ideas with sounds that ring true. It is the names that give his works their resonance.

Just as sculpture demands a different approach from painting, likewise a movie cannot rest on the same strengths as a book. Exposition annoys; recitation wearies. The expressions and acts of characters are what films can best frame. When fine actors fill each role, the nuances of development need not be spelled out in plain-text.

Although I tried to keep anticipation in check, there was reason to believe that the director of a movie so raw and dark as 'Heavenly Creatures' would not sell this story short, or compromise its bittersweet flavor with cinematic syrup. It was a thrill to finally discover that Peter Jackson's rendition of the Rings saga was right-minded in every respect. The story demands that the characters move from point A to point B: this journey forms the movie's underlying and unavoidable structure. It is a travelogue. Along the way the most essential encounters have been retained, and the plot elements layered in an orderly and comprehensible way. I, for one, felt the departures and rearrangements from the book were salutary, and conveyed a readier understanding of some story elements (like Strider's reason for being a ranger) than a casual reading of the text had done.

The excellent performances of the actors did more than merely illustrate their written models. The contrasts inherent in Gandalf's nature; the conflicts implicit within Boromir's; the unlikely courage of the hobbits: these were realized through the actors' skill augmented by the camera's close attention. As a special treat, the non-humans displayed convincing racial differences that did not descend into caricature.

Those who criticize the fight scenes for not resembling the balletic choreography of 'The Matrix' or 'Star Wars: TPM' are simply making a category error. Broadly speaking, there are two schools in the presentation of combat. One approach smoothes and euphemizes it, creates something timeless and beautiful to look upon from a comfortable theatrical distance. The other offers a more participatory mode, communicating the ephemerality and tangled impressions of lived experience. The low-fantasy combat in FOTR was refreshing; it grounded the otherwise high-fantasy setting with an essential dose of immediacy. I was reminded of Branagh's 'Henry V', the pleasure of a battle that carried conviction and the possibility of pain.

It was the little things, at last, that carried the film. Most prized of all by this viewer were the details that made the One Ring emerge as a full-fledged character, motivated and manipulating, where in the book it had seemed little more than an abstract symbol of power.

title: Proper proper fantasy
review: Never since being 7 years of age (when I first saw Star Wars) have I ever felt so immersed in a film to the point that when it ended I actually felt depressed leaving the Cinema and then having to face the real world. This is truly a magnificent film. Its also so refreshing to see a film company have the balls to do what they want to do in the way they want to do it and not pander to the stupid ways of Hollywood and also to see the use of relatively unknown actors in main roles. Sure this is not 100% accurate to the books but come on! This is a film representation and a damn fine one at that. There are parts of any story that lend themselves to a book and parts to film. Its always the way with some people, they moan when something (like a film of a book) has not been made and then when it has they moan about the way in which its been done. I think Jackson and all involved have done a superb job and I can't wait to see it again and again and again. (Bring on The Two Towers!!)

title: Best movie ever
review: I just seen this movie and I loved it. It was just like reading the books again, maybe even better because i found the books a little too long and filled with to many pointless details, all of this was gone in the movie. Great actors, awesome fighting scenes and beautiful landscapes and of course one of the best adventure stories ever told.

title: Could there be a better adaptation?
review:
This was a really good movie. Anyone who says so is just trying to sound cool by not liking what everyone else does, or just does not like this genre of movies. The good qualities of this movie are rather obvious. Good to great acting, amazing special effects, breathtaking scenery yada yada yada. So ill get into what I didn't like about it... its more interesting:

I think there were several problems with the movies but I am not sure how they could all be avoided. many of the problems lie within the book itself. For example:

-Cliche good vs. evil battle. Much of this problem lies in the book. Perhaps it was acceptable back then, but modern humans have thankfully moved beyond such simplistic views of good and evil. Could this be helped? Probably... More could be focused on the problems of the good guys, and the bad guys need not look so evil (Saromon in the book does very little and is not nearly this Dark Vader to the Dark Lord (emperor) he appears in the movie.

-Cheesy parts. This movie did a very good job of keeping out corny, cheesy lines. Except perhaps "Lets go kill some orcs" at the end or what not. BUt there were some parts that could have been changed. 1. Council at Eldron. In the book this is a very important scene, hardly the PTA meeting the movie makes it out to be. 2. Ring brings Sauron back??? No. IN the book he has always been there, he just learns the ring is still in existence when it is used. This is a much better plot device. 3. Random meeting with Merry and Pippin make them join??? No. In the book they are long time friends of Frodo, it makes more sense.

-Lack of character development. WE only really get a look at Frodo and perhaps Gandalf and Aragon. The other characters are pretty flat, especially merry and pippin.

But there will always be problems. Overall this did a good job sticking to the book. It cut out the s*** that didn't matter (Tom Bombidil) and left in most of the important stuff.

so go see it, it is epic. ANd its 4 in the morning here... I go to sleep.

title: Absorbing, Fantastic Adaptation of the Book
review:
I went to see FOTR with the expectations that it must have been hard to translate Tolkien's masterpiece into a major cinematic experience. So what Peter Jackson did was incredible. His adaptation of Tolkien was crisp, he focused on the key points of the story, which in essence was Frodo's journey to Mordor to destroy the ring without losing too much in dispensing of some situations and characters. Totally following the book would have rendered a 3-hour movie impossible and would have been saddled with parts that would not have appealed to those who have not read the books.

The three hours passed pretty fast - without any reservations, the first cinematic adaptation of Tolkien's masterpiece was totally absorbing, making it the best fantasy epic of all time.

title: Oscar says, "Bring me Peter Jackson"
review:
This film is perfection and it should be mandatory viewing for all student film directors. Jackson has taken the near impossible task of creating a real world out of the pages of Tolkien and performed a miracle. Do not miss this cinematic confection.

The hardest part after watching this film is the twelve month wait for "Two Towers".

title: This is one of the best movies I have ever experienced
review: This movie was simply amazing.  It is one of the best fantasy films ever made. The three hours were well spent but I still felt that I wanted more. I can hardly wait for December 2002 to see the next book The Two Towers on the big screen.

title: I thought I hated every new movie, but I love this one!
review: Wow... see this while it's still in the theater. I hated, HATED Harry Potter, the Star Wars prequel, Titanic, and all these other super-hyped movies. Honestly, though, this is different. This is smart and a lot of fun to watch.

title: Personally, my best film ever.....
review: I went to the movie knowing I was going to like it. What I saw was the most incredible picture I ever saw, with a story that's as hard as a rock. Personnally, I still don't know what "The Force" exactly in Star Wars is, but seeing LOTR maked me realize that Peter Jackson should have directed Star Wars. Peter did an excellent job convincing the audience of the story, the orc's, the magic and the fantasy. He really showed to the crowd what "The Ring's" power really is. That's force for you Lucas. I rated LOTR a deserved 10. INCREDIBLE.

title: WOW---SEE THIS MOVIE
review:
Quite simply, the best sci-fi/fantasy movie I have ever seen. Blows Phantom Menace out of the water. This movie will be to this generation what Star Wars was to mine. You don't have to have read the books but it will help because they squeeze alot of info into 3 hours. Oh, and don't listen to those bad reviews from the 'Tolkein purists' that hated it because the movie strayed away from the original text here and there. If the movie followed the book exactly, it would have been 5 hours long instead of three.

***SEE THIS MOVIE, YOU WON'T BE DISAPPOINTED***

title: Best Picture of 2001
review: This is the MUST SEE picture of the year! Very well done! The characters are well developed and you care about what happens to these people (who are from a mythical world) but are very humanitarian towards one another. Even though they have there differences the fellowship of nine come together to fight a common enemy of EVIL who wants to destroy there land from within by corrupting men with a ring that promises power but brings destruction. Sound familiar? The acting is excellent, the cinemaphotography and soundtrack are outstanding. LOTR's is my pic for Oscar's BEST PICTURE of 2001! Don't miss it!

title: A near miss
review:
The main thing that is missing from the film is a sense of time passing. The relationships between the characters could have been established better with a only a line or two of dialog, or a facial expression here and there if only the viewer didn't get the feeling that these people had only known each other a few days.

Although I have read the Trilogy more than once over the last 20 years, I tried to imagine it from the perspective of someone who has not. It must have seemed to those unfamiliar with the story that it all takes place in the span of a couple of weeks or so, when actually from beginning to end the first book covers approximately one year. Simply displaying the date at the bottom of the screen from time to time would have helped flesh out the characters and their relationships I think.

Most of the departures from the book were unexpected. I had heard that Tom Bombadil was going to be excluded, but I figured they would work in the Barrow-Wight if only to add an action scene. Going in I fully expected the ending to be changed since its not very Hollywoodish, but by the end of the film I could tell it wasn't going to be.

I gave it an 8, which is probably more than it deserves, partly for the outstanding cinematography and partly because I'm such a huge fan of the Trilogy that I was able to fill in the gaps.

title: Just a few words of praise
review:
I am not going to write much here as it has all probably been said before. I am a huge, no, a HUGE fan of J.R.R. Tolkiens great work and as a fan of the books I was shocked by the changes the Peter Jackson has made to the them when bringing it to film. But I have to say that while there are a few scenes where I personally dont understand why he changed them, this does not detract from what has become one of the greatest cinema moments of my life.

If you go into this film as a fan of the books alone then you will be disappointed (as one of my friends where) but if you go in as a fan of the books and a fan of film then you will be a happy man/woman.

This is what cinema has been missing for a along time, truly great visual and emotional experience.

title: GLAD I Didn't Read the Books
review:
This movie is HEAD and SHOULDERS above anything Lucas & Speilburg have ever done. It makes their work look sloppy and rushed. It may be because Tolkein wrote the story and Peter Jackson's job was merely to remain respectful and loyal to the beauty of the book which he did remarkably so - I can say that with confidence because though I have never read the books, my husband, who accompanied me (no, carried me) to the movie, has read them all and has long held them as the finest pieces of fantasy literature ever written.

Tolkein fan or not - you'll be impressed with the flawless craftsmanship of the film, impressed that so much CARE went into it - and the strong lessons in character will never leave you. You'll leave the theatre moved, changed and proud - knowing your money was well spent.

For me - it's everything a good movie should be: a carefully crafted film of a story worth telling.

I think it's worth mentioning that Tolkein was a Reverend who spent time with and had much respect for the work of C. S. Lewis (Chronicles of Narnia). Blessings to all.

title: Absolute Perfection 10/10
review:
There are many (and I do mean MANY) wonderful reviews of Lord of the Rings: Fellowship of the Ring, so I will not stir over what has already been said... the film is one of the best, albeit maybe THE best, to grace the screen since this humble reviewer can remember.

As a society it is very important to recognize great pieces of work when they come around. Too often we play host to the mindless drivel that froths from the rusty machine that is Hollywood. Peter Jackson and company have shown us, without impunity, that true greatness can be achieved. We no longer have to settle for what is fed to us.

I look back over the years of films I have loved, or in many cases just wanted to love. They all pale now, brought down to stylish icons of modern cinema as opposed to great works of film. The myths that we have clung to for years tell us that films can only be so good. Those myths are gone. Gone and for many of us, they will never return and we are left staring at hollywood with contempt for the garbage that we must settle for.

I will settle no more. Because Peter Jackson has done the impossible and given us a window into another world. It never once feels as though this was something filmed or acted or scripted. It never feels as though this didn't actually happen somewhere in some far forgotten time.

Casting: Perfect Acting: Perfect Directing: Perfect Scripting: Perfect

Peter Jackson... I salute you. 10 out of 10

title: The best ever !
review:
What to say about this film? It is fantastic, brilliant.

How do I know that? Just imagine that you would have made this film, could you have made such a masterpiece? I don't think so! That is what makes this film so brilliant. Everything is perfect : from the direction of Peter Jackson, to the acting of SIR Ian McAllen, to the soundtrack from Howard Shore. Have you ever seen any set-decoration like this, it is really unbelievable. Have you ever experienced such an epic, with so much space for emotions? (except from old classics like Ben-Hur, Spartacus,...) The words of Gandalf : "Run, you fools" are already legendary, and the scene is much more shocking then DiCaprio's dead in Titanic. The photography is brilliant, and for those who say the actions sequences are bad, I have one question : Why would have Jackson shot them like this? I am convinced that Jackson can shoot the sequences you prefer, but for some reason, he doesn't do it like that. Try to find the answer!

The book is more then a masterpiece, but this is a film, so it is impossible to compare it with a book. For the film there is only one conclusion: It is a (more then) a masterpiece from start to ending! Some ask if the next 2 parts will be as good as this one, well, I can assure you that they will be as good ! (No, not better, because I think that is impossible. But maybe I am wrong, because what it still impossible after you have seen this film?)

This film is "The Bible" for all those who love film, and I will see it over and over! Peter Jackson, Sir Ian McAllen and all the brilliant people who worked on this film, thank you very much, for giving me the best 3 hours I have ever experienced!

title: it just grows and grows
review:
When I walked out of the cinema I was not sure what to think about the movie. I kept asking myself "What did I just see? What did I just see? Did I see LOTR?" and not until a few hours later is hit me "I HAVE SEEN LOTR".

This is a fantasy movie, but unlike other fantasy movies it doesn't feel like fantasy; it feels real, so very real. It feels like the movie was actually filmed in middle earth and not New Zeeland.

After the christmas holidays are over im going back to the cinema because I just need to see it again, I need to see it and memorize every little detail in preparation for the next installment december 2002.

I'm getting the DVD, I'm getting all three of them even if I don't have a DVD. This movie is worth the cost of a DVD player alone.

It's just.. OMFG

title: MERP-ers beware! (SPOILERS!!!)
review:
If you play MERP you will probably not be able to give this 10/10. You will probably regret some of the changes made just a little too much for that, and wish the makers had been braver and made it longer, maybe even four hours. It's so fast-paced as it is, everything whooshes past except the battles, and a little more time allowed on-screen to Gimli, Legolas, merry and Pippin would have been nice. Still, they'll have to get more in the next one! Also some of the accents will bug you at times, (Aragorn and Boromir). What I liked least was the fight between Gandalf and Saruman - it's not how magic is in Middle Earth, more like two unarmed Jedis using Force-fists.

All this said I did give it 9/10 - really great, but not perfect as we thought it might be. Hey, not even Bladerunner was perfect! See it!

title: Liv Tyler didn't ruin it!
review: This movie was phenomenal.  Upon going to see it, I was somewhat skeptical about how hollywood would wind up finally treating the LOTR.  Having been a huge fan of these stories for years, I subsequently had very high expectations and was not disappointed.  Upon seeing the trailers I was distressed at the casting of the very questionably talented Liv Tyler, but even she managed to avoid coming off as a moron and I found I could forget the awful cracker scene in armageddon (temporarily, anyway).  The rest of the cast was flawless. Elijah Wood could not be cast better, as an unlikely hero who really would rather be somewhere else but accepted his responsibility.  He had real screen chemistry with both Ian McKellan (they seemed to be old friends!) and the excellent Sean Astin as Sam Gamgee.  I remember seeing the Goonies long ago and am so happy to see Sean getting a good role and knocking it out as well as he did!  The scenery is simply breathtaking. Wow!! doesn't even begin to describe it.  The color, the sets, the detail, the fantastic fact that they don't rely on crappy CGI to do everything, but instead use real people in ORC suits for the bad guys and fantastic settings for what is a really fleshed out middle earth.  Most of the movie was almost exactly as I had imagined it reading the books. WOW wow wow.  I wondered how any movie came out and catapulted to the top of the IMDB list, but this movie really is like nothing you've ever seen before. A++++  10/10.

title: Read the books first!!! EXCELLENT MOVIE!
review: Saw the movie 3 days after the release here in sweden. I have read the book. Of course a movie never is as good as a book, but the movie follows the book very well and is a movie that must not be unseen! Its damn good, go and see it! :)

title: As good as it could be in 3 hours
review:
I thought this version was about as good as it could be given the constraints of filmmaking. I found several flaws but none of them really impinged on my enjoyment of the film. On the positive side I was glad that the film was directed towards those who have read the books. If you haven't, do so after having seen the movie and then see it again. Personally I get tired of having screen time wasted with old cinematic devices such as obligatory introductory passages... "Hi! I'm Old Soandso and I come from Wherever and this is why I am here". It sits in the same boat with Big Word Defining, but that's another story. Half the audience was naming the characters out loud as they appeared anyway... there was alot of ground to cover and it was nice to get on with it. Another high point was that even tho the story deviated from the book in small ways if you haven't read it in a few years, you won't know the difference. The important scenes are there. The best part of the movie, IMHO, was the way it looked. There was a pervasive feeling of Olde England that was just right. Another plus was the absence of annoying cutsey characters.... no Bobo's (Clash of the Titans). I couldn't believe I was actually worried about Sam drowning... good job!

On the other hand, I didn't care for the all-encompassing silver tone. I think that color could have been used to better effect. It was perfect in some scenes but was monotonous to have it used uniformly in nearly every scene. I also thought they used too many tight shots. The long shots were sufficient but the middle range was noticably absent. I think of long as being the Big Picture, close being the mind of the character and mid being You Are there... where you as an outsider would be standing in the action. The mid shots just weren't there, or didn't appear to be. Another short-coming was that the magic was pretty boring. I realize this can be overdone, but the magic could have benefitted from some nice special effects. I did think that the white horses in the raging river scene were excellent, so there is not much danger that other magic couldn't have been handled just as nicely. The firey writing on the Ring was just right, too. As in almost all films like this the feeling of compression was noticable. No idea how that can be avoided. There's just so much to cram in. Other peeve: too much shedding of tears. Maybe a few screen-moments could have been recovered here?

title: Forgive my shock...
review: ...but I stepped out of the theater, and out of Middle-Earth, only a few hours ago. Seeing "Fellowship" wasn't like just "seeing a movie". In fact, it was more like a trip inside my own mind as I read the Tolkien masterpiece. Peter Jackson has created a film experience that is as invigorating as reading the "Fellowship" for the first time. I did not think it possible. The various plot changes were not sacrilegious in this purists mind and mostly they made cinematic sense. Highly recommended.

title: Hyperbole
review:
Who are these strange people? What do they want? What is this Ring?

These are the questions I kept asking myself as the action in "The Fellowship of the Ring" kept hurtling forward at light speed. I read the books (in the late '70s) as a freshman in high school. And still, I had no idea what was motivating all these unusual people onscreen, except that we kept being told how evil the ring is.

I couldn't understand half of what the characters were saying, especially Ian McKellan. I didn't know half of the characters names, or why they chose to join this fellowship. There were scenes filmed in a style more suited to video games than Tolkien. All those swoopy camera moves made me ill.

Ian Mckellan could have been a fine Gandalf, if he didn't mumble half of his lines. Elijah Wood looked too girly. Boromir and Aragorn looked too much alike. ALL of the relationships were missing. The plot was the equivalent of Judy and Mickey saying, "Hey, I have an idea! Let's put on a quest!"

One of the most overrated movies of the year. It will not stand the test of time. The only way to account for the hyperbolic reviews on this page is to imagine that the Tolkien fans are out in force. Forget the movie--READ THE BOOKS.

title: Not great, but good.
review: The biggest problem I had with the movie was the period from Bilbo's departure until they arrive in Rivendel.  The timing of events is just plain bad. I mean, how can Gandolf expect to meet them in Bree, when they are both leaving at the same time and he is going halfway to Mordor first?

title: Too long...
review: For a film that starts out so strongly, it ends up being a rather tedious collection of amazing sets and unclear motivations.  As a 90 minute film, it's very fine.  As a three-hour one, a snoozer. Please keep in mind--some things are too complex to be filmed.

title: Without Parallel
review:
This film is simply without equal in the fantasy film genre, and stacks up as one of the best films I have ever seen. It is a classical Jungian archetypical good vs. evil struggles (for other films that hit on that motif, see also The Natural and the Star Wars films).

I read the books years and years ago, and this film had the same ability to suspend my normal cynicism and transport me to a mythical land.

Bravo, Peter Jackson and the rest of the cast. This will be a classic for years to come.

title: Fans of the book won't be disappointed
review:
I must have read the book at least 8 times and was therefore looking forward to the film enormously. I have to say I was not disappointed by this thrilling film and I cannot imagine anyone but the most obsessive fan feeling the same. OK, so they dropped Tom Bombadil, but his whimsy is fairly grating in the book and on film I feel he would distract from the pace. They have also compressed some events and altered others but a film, even a 3 hour one, must compress a pretty substantial book.

The casting in my view is flawless, Sean Bean IS Boromir and Orlando Bloom has got the coolness and remoteness of Legolas just right. Gimili is perhaps under written but even in the book he is slightly peripheral while the Hobbits are perfect. Frodo, who looks a bit weird in the posters, comes across much better on film and they have kept Sam's,"Mr Frodo, Sir", dialogue in which is nice in this egaliterian age. It will be fasinating to see their relationship develop and alter in the later films. Merry and Pippin come across better in the film than in the book where they always seemed indistinguishable and they provide some good comic moments without appearing trivial.

The set pieces are superb and I must say I disagree with negative comments about the fight scenes. I found them visceral and exciting, the blows seemed to have real impact and I felt that they were much better than Gladiator, which seemed to resort to slow-mo and therefore lost the sense of speed and violence.

Non-readers (in our party there were several), also enjoyed the film and despite the inevitable anticlimax of the final scenes found Boromir's battle with the Orc's shocking and moving.

Definitely the film of the year, better than Star Wars? only time will tell.

title: Forget the bad critics, this is how it is
review: Picture yourself being beamed back in time to 1954. Ok you got that? Read the "Lord of the rings" knowing that it is a complete new genre  the good man has created, along with a epic story-line unmatched by any other book except maybe the bible or other religious content.Right,now live your time all the way through to the year 2001 and then tell me that the movie being made by Peter Jackson is a "been there done that" movie, and that it looks like Harry Potter. Now, am I the only one who thinks this is really a bit of a strange thing to say? Isn't it so that all the movies/series/books of the same kind are actually all inspired by this man's work of art? Yes they are indeed. So how could anyone blame Peter Jackson for making a been there done that movie about a book that was created in 1954? He simply made the movie as is, because at it's time it was revolutionary. So if you possess only the slightest bit of intelligence you watch this movie as if it is the first of the sort you have ever seen, keeping the book and it's old age in mind. Jackson had to leave out certain parts of the film or it simply would have gotten to long. For sure I didn't want the movie to ever end because it captures the books atmosphere just about perfectly. People are never going to be satisfied about the casting being made, but if you take the scale of the trilogy in mind, and it's immense budget, you can forgive the moviecompany for casting some of the more familiar faces, because the risk would have been to great to take unknown talent for the more important characters of the film. This movie and ,my guess is, the next two episodes deserve to be firmly in the nr.1 spot of all time.

title: Unoriginal?
review: I don't know, maybe it's just my imagination. But did anyone else notice that the Hobbit's Shire resembled Teletubby land? Or how about Christoper Lee's character, surely one of the arch villains out of The Power Ranger (no really). Not only did he have the right look and manic laugh, but he too made dodgy looking big monster thingies to send after the heros.

title: Fell Prey to the Hype Yet Again
review:
Once again, I hear nothing but great and wonderful things about a movie, and once again it's an undeniable disappointment. Such is the case with Lord of the Rings: "It's the second coming of Star Wars!!!" gushed the critics. "We couldn't believe the finished film when we saw it!" the actors salivated...well, there's no denying that this film has a leaden pace, with more than a few goofy moments and some badly shot(and sparse)action sequences.

Maybe it's just that I was so young when I saw films like Star wars and Raiders of the Lost Ark, ET, etc that they were so indelibly etched into my mind that I subconsciously hold them in higher regard than any movie has a right to held. Maybe I should go into every film and not expect anything...then it has to be somewhat good. What I have to do is stop believing every critic who is likely in the pocket of the studio, and every starry-eyed actor who thinks that because they're on screen, the film is wonderful.

Anyway, that said, LITR is not horrible. It's got excellent effects and visuals, very good acting and some clever scenes - it just doesn't inspire awe, like so many movies of my youth did (and still do). I can only assume the 9.5 rating came from fans of the books who know all the backstory and can fill in the gaps automatically.

I still want to see the sequels, but only to see if they improve upon this one.

7 out of 10.

title: An awesome and terrible experience
review:
As a teacher, I know that one of my responsibilities is to ensure that children's sense of `Awe and Wonder' is allowed to flourish. The modern child seems so cynical and sophisticated that he can be very difficult to impress. When I was eight years old, a student teacher had tried to read The Hobbit to my class. I hated it. But seeing the BBC's 1968 radio adaptation of the story in Waterstone's when looking for something to listen to on my journey to work, (one which lasts an hour and a half, There and Back Again) I felt sure that I could overcome my prejudice. I did. I loved it. I was hooked. I wanted more. I bought the BBC's radio Lord of the Rings (1980) and was now a confirmed Tolkienite. Fascinated by the mythology, I visited the "official" Tolkien website and discovered that a film was being made. However, having seen Peter Jackson's hand held close-up-to-the-nostril style in "Braindead" and "The Frighteners", I was somewhat fearful of what he might do to the Frodo, Gollum and Aragorn imagined in my head. When I downloaded the first trailer, my fears were allayed more than somewhat. The hairs prickled on the back of my neck. Alas, I knew that I was going to have to wait another eighteen months to see a film about a book that I hadn't read; that if I read it I might be turned by the Power of The One Book into a Tolkien geek (too late already) and then be disappointed by the changes I knew Jackson would have to make.

I gave in of course, completing the trilogy last summer and rereading the Fellowship of the Ring this summer. Despite my enjoyment, Tolkien's writing leaves much to be desired and I became hopeful that a director who captured the spirit of the book rather than every dry detail would be doing us all a service.

When last night, the hour finally arrived, I was not disappointed. No, it was not like the BBC's version which I have now listened to countless times. No, the book has not been translated directly to the screen without any changes. Jackson has taken a number of liberties with the book, but has in the process, produced a film that in many ways is superior in vision to that achieved by Tolkien himself.

There is a theory that artists are not originators of their work, merely imperfect vessels for the expressions of universal truths. Whatever Tolkien may have intended by his book, there is a story, not necessarily his, to be imagined and reimagined by the readers, some of whom will baulk at seeing their version significantly altered. Perhaps the most obvious element missing in this film is the story and song, the literature and lore of Middle-Earth. But what is not only preserved, but magnified and rightly so, is the sense of a universe where the powers of good and evil, of nature and the landscape, are vastly greater than man can understand. Jackson's triumph is to have sewn this thread of truth into every frame, and, according to my wife, by no means a fan, `made it all look so real'. The essence of the book for me is epitomised by Gollum, a pathetic character so twisted by the lust for power that he has no control over his own destiny. We have yet to see his role fully revealed, but it is clear that Frodo, Aragorn and even Sam too are controlled by their fates. What Jackson has achieved is a realisation of the scale of the hidden forces which direct man in love, in battle, throughout life. It is the sweep and power of the opening battle which sets the tone for the whole movie, not just the narrative detail. The detail is almost irrelevant. It matters not that we do not see properly the individual thrust and parry of a fight, because this film is not about the mechanics of war. It is about the forces which drive man to wage war and which are beyond his understanding  the same force which drives man to fall in love, to lust for power, to procreate.

It is a marvellous achievement. This film scores over almost every other that tries to grapple with the same themes. Star Wars, often quoted by those of short memory as the top movie of all time, does not come close in projecting the real, hidden powers of the universe. For all its talk of `The Force', it fails to convey half the passion and fear to be found in Fellowship. Star Wars is of course a different film  clever, knowing, a technical marvel, paying due allegiance to many other films and books, most notably Lord of the Rings. But Fellowship is not about special effects, or baddies and goodies in the simplistic sense, or buddy-buddies, or soap-opera moments (`I am your father Luke!'). If it lacks intimacy it is because it tries to get beyond the individuals that make up the story and instead visualise the unknowable meanings of life. A risky strategy, but one which works.

Jackson delivers a hugely spiritual film; not the kind of spiritual experience that dopeheads declared Kubrick's 2001 to be, but with the same sense of awe which I must arouse in my schoolchildren; the same sense of the `terrible' (reach for your dictionaries folks) which filmmakers generally shy away from. `Awe and wonder' is a rather embarrassing and much underrated theme for filmakers in a post-modern world, which heaps endless praise on self-referential Tarantino movies. The grand and meaningful can seem so absurd that such films can only be made full of wise-cracks to make them accessible to the closed-minded. This epic is therefore only for the open-minded, the innocent, even the naïve, who are willing to allow `awe and wonder' to take over their lives for three hours. Like a six-year-old child, I can't wait for next Christmas.

title: Unfamiliar Fan Enjoys
review:
For all those of you who have never read any of the books in The Lord of the Rings trilogy, what I have to say might be of particular interested to you. I've never read any of The Lord of the Rings books. My dad read to me when I was three years old the first ten pages of The Hobbit, so I knew what one of those was, but other than that and the trailer, I had no knowledge of any of the characters of the plot of the film. Truthfully, I think this is the best way to go into the film for maximum enjoyment. My eyes were glued to the screen and I was on the edge of my seat the entire time. I had no clue what was to happen next, and with each scene I was more surprised by what events unfolded than the previous. Overall, I loved the movie. It quickly became one of my favorite movies of all time, being amongst others such as Star Wars, The Matrix and the independent flick, Memento. I did have some problems with the film though, some mentioned by huge fans of the series, others hardly at all.

First being were with the characters. I thought that Frodo, Gandalf, Aragorn and Sam were well developed. They were well acted, and I actually came to care for the characters, a rarity for me in movie watching; however, the two characters who had the potential for being the coolest in the film, Legolas and Gamli, were barely developed at all. It seemed like they were just dropped right in the middle of the story for the mere purpose of aids in battle. Legolas got a good amount of screentime during the fight sequences due to his jaw-dropping archery skills, but Gamli was hardly present. You could tell that there was some tension between the two when they were first introduced, but it was never explained nor further pursued in the film. Apparently in the book there is a great deal of history between the two and as a result, there is tons of comical bickering between the two.

Second was the plot. While the storytelling was excellent, there were some things that troubled me. Throughout the film, there were many mentions to events that occurred in prequel novel, The Hobbit, and in scenes from the book that were cut from the script. I thought this was rather confusing at points, although it wasn't exactly necessary to the comprehension of the film. Also as I watched the movie, it seemed that to tell the entire story, there needed to be more. It was obvious that three was something missing, and many scenes seemed rushed.

My last complaint about the movie would be the special effects. While many people claim that they were spectacular, I was not impressed in the least bit. The scenes in which blue screen was used, I thought it was quite obvious as the characters were all in differnet lighting, making the thing scene seem awkward. Also, other than the cave troll which looked great, all the other computer animated monsters seemed pretty fake compared to what we've seen in recent cinema. They were either hardly detailed, or simply looked too cartoony compared to the rest of the scene. Really I think the only scenes that had impressive special effects were those in which Frodo wore the ring and when the camera made sweeps of the landscape, especially those which recreated fantasy elements from the book such as Sarumon's tower and the sort. In my mind, I think ILM (responsible Star Wars and basically every other film in Hollywood) could've done a much better job, especially with the integration of characters into scenes and the creation of believable monsters.

Actually, thats about all the complaints I have about the film. Overall, I think The Fellowship of the Ring was an excellent movie. I loved just about every minute, and despite the fact that they were forced to remove a lot of the elements from the story, I think the director did an amazing job with what he had and he was able to do in order to maintain the audience's attention span. I definitely recommend this movie to anyone, even those of you who are not normally fantasy or science fiction fans. The storytelling is fantastic, and for those few characters that were actually developed, they were spectacular.

title: An incredible movie for those who have read the books and those who haven't.
review: I read the books twice, twenty+ years now.  While I remember the core story, some of the subplots have become forgotten to me.  I made a conscious decision to not re-read The Fellowship prior to seeing the movie. Movies rarely, if ever, live up to the books upon which they're based.  This movie does.  The story all came back to me as if reading it for the first time. What makes this movie unique is that I've seen it before...in my head when I read it.  The movie captures exactly the images I had while reading the book.  Not only that, but also the "feel" of the books.  Also the feel of being kids and running through the forest as Frodo, Sam, Aragorn  and Legolas, being chased by Orcs.  This movie exceeds on every level.  This is the best movie I have seen in a long time (and there have been some good movies).

title: In the Pantheon of movies, probably Zeus
review:
Movie was a masterpiece. The superb acting, casting, directing, special effects, music, and so on were all subjugated to the story... as it should be with any movie and rarely is. We will eventually see what history ends up saying about the movie, but at the moment of its birth it seems to belong to the pantheon of greatest movies. The art, science and craft of filmmaking mix to near perfection in this first installment of LOTR. Subjectively, it was the shortest movie I remember seeing despite the 3 hours.

Having said all that, let me proffer some criticism so at least you can't accuse me of an adoration blind to any possible shortcomings. I have to stretch to find any aspect that was not at the overall level of this visual symphony. Perhaps the Balrog's look could have been improved upon... it seemed overly large and a might artificial in contrast, say, to the physical presence of the dark lord Sauron. I must hasten to add that the anticipation of the fiend was sublime, especially the effect of dread on the lesser evil creatures.

title: Not entirely true to the book, and that is a good thing.
review: I read "the fellowship of the ring" earlier this year and I must say that the movie made the story much more enjoyable.  The pace that the movie had was far superior to that of the book.  Wonderful Story.  Can hardly wait for the next ones.

title: New age for Fantasy films
review:
This film delivers to Fantasy movies what Star Wars did for Sci-Fi. It will be the standard for all Fantasy movies to come. It exceeded my expectations, which were sky high.

LOTR movie depicts, on film, why I continue to play RPG's and does justice to a genre of film that should have been done long ago.

Excellent. Highly recommended! 5 stars! *****

title: Unbelievable adaption of The greatest fantasy story ever.
review:
Wow, I am amazed at what I have just seen. I loved this movie. I can not believe how moving it was. The acting was incredible. I think that Roger Ebert should not be allowed to comment on movies after the what he said about this. I doubt that Roger even saw the same movie. His comments about how the movie portrayed the hobbits as a burden to everybody and that they do not help in the quest at all. Frodo was the only reason that everybody is on the quest. He is the only one that carries the burden of the ring. If that is not doing something then I don't know what is. Roger read the books again, the hobbits werent there for there fighting skills.... they were there because of how innocent they are as a people....that is why Frodo is carrying the ring. He is not as easily corrupted to the evil as are the others. Without him there would be no fellowship.

This is the best movie I have seen in my life, and I am not afraid to admit that. Easily the best fantasy movie done. I love that it has the IMDB's #1 ranking.

title: whoa
review: when i left the movie house.... i dont know what to say...i was lost for words because of the beauty of the film... the effects were brilliant! boromir is really talented. i also like orlando bloom (legolas is my fave character) and i thought that he had played the role quite well. the thing with arwen is also good (although they sort of changed it.) elijah is a great actor and also ian mckellen. sam, merry and pippen were also great for their roles.... aragorn was brilliant... and john rhys davies is great for gimli. title: Seat belt required
review: In my short life, I have not remembered a time where I literally sat on the edge of my seat for a movie lasting 3 hours while disregarding the consequences of drinking a 40 oz. Coke.  The Fellowship of the Ring has it all.  Most of the big budget action movies have been one dimensional, with only the special effects carrying the picture.  This movie not only had mind blowing visuals and sound, but a solid, believable plot (despite the fantasy genre) and an amazing all around acting performance by the ensemble cast. I accredit the acting to Jackson's decision to use mostly experienced stage and British actors (i.e. Ian McKlellan and Ian Holm) instead of main-stream, unskilled American actors to make Tolkien's characters come alive. The movie differs from the book in several minor ways, but nothing will disappoint any fan.  One advantage of this adaptation is most of the explanatory parts are eliminated, resulting in a film that is a series of action sequences, preventing audience relaxation.  I did not even breathe through the mines of Moria section. The drawbacks of this film are that it does has a long running time and the main character will oft be misinterpreted.  Frodo will come across as wimpy and annoying to many non-Tolkien fans.  This happens because Frodo's true character is not developed until later in the trilogy.  If one watches the whole trilogy, they will notice a transformation from weak to strong and will then relate to Frodo's anyman personality.  Other than that, I will warn you that there a few jumps and frightening scenes that will not suit well for the young, elderly or weak at heart. If you were disappointed with the Phantom Menace, the Jurassic Park sequels, and all the other garbage that the movie machine has pumped out for the past 5 summers, this movie will return hope and bring you back to the better days of movie making.

title: Changes from book *not* by and large necessary
review:
A warning: I'll start out by venting my problems with the movie, and then move on to the positives. Overall I liked the movie very much, and admire Peter Jackson for attempting such a huge and risky endeavor.

Those who have never read the books say "die-hard fans may complain about some minor details that have been changed as a matter of necessity given the innate differences in the media." I must say that is a gross understatement. There were many major changes, some justifiable, some not.

Starting the movie with a battle scene defeats the whole point of stating in the Shire to make the evil to come a greater and more horrible contrast---but I can understand this change. Movie audiences don't want to wait an hour for action. Lothlorien, however, supposed to be one of the most beautiful and sacred places in Middle Earth, is made sinister and threatening in the movie. The blue color scheme (it's not called the Golden Wood for nothing, folks) that Lothlorien shares with two other parts of the movie---the shadow world of the Nazgûl and Moria, the two most evil places in Fellowship---brings it home that Lothlorien is cold and bad. This change has nothing to do with attention spans or time constraints---it is simply a directing mistake.

Speaking of time constraints, the removal of such a huge chunk of the early book (Buckland, Crickhollow, the Old Forest, Bombadil, and the Barrow-downs) is defended by saying "the movie was almost too long already!" If nothing had been added which had not been found in the book, this would have been understandable, but so much time was wasted on material that came from---I don't know where, but certainly not from Tolkien. Arwen? Arwen had to be pumped up to satisfy the female viewers? I know I'm not as intelligent as the combined force of screenwriters for this movie, so why did no one else realize that Galadriel was the solution to this problem? Galadriel was the strong female of Fellowship, and she could have been played up, rather than made sinister, contrary to all of Tolkien's designs.

If you haven't yet seen the movie, my advice to you is to try to forget the books and enjoy. If you try to watch and relate events in the movie to what you've read, you'll only get confused, since things have been switched around without mercy. A great mystery of the first half of the book---what happened to Gandalf?---is no longer a mystery, with Saruman's treachery revealed near the beginning (my personal regret is the elimination of Saruman's Robe of Many Colors, but that's a tiny detail, my mention of which probably marks me fatally as a Tolkien obsessee.) Another needless change was having Strider's sword in Bree not broken! A good deal of symbolism swept out the door---yet why was the sword shown so pointedly (pun intended) broken in the opening scene?

With my complaints safely behind me (except for the casting of sinister Agent Smith as Elrond, a chief good guy), I can now feel free to say that overall it was superb. The effects were great, especially the Balrog, the shadow world, the flooding Ford of Bruinen, and the Eye. I loved Gandalf, and Boromir's depth was wonderful. I was excited to see it once and will see it again. My positive review is much shorter than my negative, but that's only because most reviews have been positive, and I thought a little of the other voice was necessary.

title: The greatest movie of all time!
review:
I have been a Tolkien fan since I was 3. My father taught me how to read off of the books, and I have read them numerous times. When I heard they were doing the live action adaptation of the Lord of the Rings, I was skeptical (look what happened to Battlefield Earth).

I am pleased with what Peter Jackson has done with this first film in the trilogy. He managed to bring the book to life in a way I thought would have been impossible. I can honestly think of no bad things to say about this film. I can't wait for The Two Towers and the Return of the King. Bravo Jackson!

--The characters are believable, and the photography matches their descriptions to the book

--The book was mostly uncut from the book.

--the CGI's and the sets were spectacular

--the battle scenes were excellent

If you like fantasy you will love this film, I have never seen an adaptation that I enjoyed as much (even The Green Mile!) Rarely have I seen a movie that inspired my friends to read the books, but a few of my friends have already begun the trilogy because they loved the film!

If you have the time, see this movie, you won't be sorry!

title: This movie rocks. . .
review:
I saw this movie at an advance screening and all I can say is: fantastic. Peter Jackson and company have done a great job. As a fan of the books, this film did not disappoint in the slightest. In fact, the film gets better as it goes on.

Waste no time - see this movie as soon as possible.

title: Good, but a touch overrated
review:
The Lord of Rings certainly makes due of amazing panorama's, supurb acting and interaction, however I find it necessary to give a more critical review than to go estatic over a movie that moved me far less than Titanic did.

The Lord of the Rings works the hardest on the characters. Jackson does a wonderful job of character profiling, placing you into the shoes of the heros. However I found some of the characters to lack integrity. Many of the them seemed rather stiff, unsure, yet they poured their heart with elegance and finesse during the times when words were not spoken.

As a whole, it seems to have best picture material, but when you pick apart the pieces, you'll notice that we are left with is the same problem Jackson has had in all of his movies: his inability, or perhaps I should say, unwillingness to go the extra step.

The Mines of Moria sequence was probably the best I've seen from Jackson. Well constructed, well played out, some of the best acting, great sequences and a wonderful and moving ending that left me breathless and wondering if we switched to a secondary director. But nope, it was Jackson proving once and for all that he *can* take the extra step and move above the norm.

Jackson is a visionary but I found him selling out mostly in this movie. Going to normal shots when Jackson is better suited for a more abstract scene, abnormal yet balanced with a sensitivity to render an original, obtuse and exquisit scene. I saw Jackson only perform this duty once during LOTR; Mines of Moria. The rest of the movie had endless opportunities, where Jackson failed to go the extra mile into uncharted terrority.

I expect a lot from Jackson. I know his potential even if he does not. I feel we have yet to see his true talent, eventhough LOTR shows his capabilities.

I hope that Jackson allows his soul to emerge in the next installment. That he let go of the fear of maintaining some sort of normality and begin charting a new realm of movie making. Jackson needs to understand that his talent is being wasted every time he fails to jump the chasm Aragorn and Frodo had to jump.

Close your eyes, Jackson. Close your eyes, jump ... and fly!

I gave the movie an 8 out of 10.

title: This Movie Puts Other Movies To Shame
review: This movie will ruin other movies for you.  It doesn't take long for you to be convinced of another world (or is it an earlier version of our world?) and find yourself transported there.  There are incredible settings, fantastic special effects,  excellent and nuanced performances, frightening depictions of evil, epic battle scenes, all shot through with a gritty realism. And there is a depth and complexity to the characters and the story's moral underpinnings which are greater than usual for a "blockbuster".  But most of all there is a sense of joy in creation that permeates the film, the kind of artistic integrity that accompanies a labor of love.  No cutting corners or gratuitous sex scenes here.   This movie sets the mark very, very, high for future film-makers who don't want their efforts to look lazy and creatively vacuous in comparison to this triumph of a movie.

title: What cinema was invented for.
review: There are two types of people who will go to see this film, those who have read the books and those who haven't. I represent the latter half. So if you are in the same position as myself, why should you bother watching a film about Orc's, Dwarf's and Hobbit's. Well to start with this film is visually outstanding. CGI has progressed a lot in the last 5 years, but this film doesn't lavishly flaunt computer graphics in your face, in fact it will have you sitting there thinking 'How did they do that?'. The scenery will leave you breathless, from the snowy mountains to the boat ride down the river past the statues of the kings. But it's the attention to detail put into the sets. The Shires look like a million dollar version of the Teletubbies (which is a good thing believe it or not), and the camera work flying through the land of Mordoc is particularly impressive. Yes it has it's downfalls. The prologue is very good and gives you a really good history of the story to come, but the next half hour introducing Gandalf and the Hobbits drags for much longer than it should do, but the firework display is very impressive and leaves you hoping that one day you could buy fireworks like that. As a non Tolkien I felt that a lot of the characters had no back story, which left you wondering why they were there in the first place. This is most prominent in the council meeting where you are greeted with three new characters who you don't know a lot about. And also there is the point that the film has no ending, but this can be forgiven because there are another two episodes to come. Hearing what fans of the book have said about it adding parts to the story, like Arwen (Liv Tyler) getting more story than she should have, really don't ruin the story, in fact I think they improve it. But I didn't care, she looks absolutely beautiful in this film, and gives one of her best performances of her career. In fact all of the actors perform their socks off, particularly Viggo Mortensen as Aragorn who would be my bet for Best Supporting Actor at the Oscars. But my hat goes off to the whole of the fellowship, they convince you that they are really there and not just talking to a tennis ball against a blue screen. But the ultimate accolade should be given to Peter Jackson, Spielberg, Lucas, Scott and Cameron should be quaking in their directors chairs because this guy has just raised the stakes in Hollywood. In fact I think i'm gonna watch Bad Taste again on video to see where this genius came from. If he doesn't win an Oscar then it's daylight robbery.

title: The Beginnings of a Masterpiece
review:
*THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS*

I've seen this movie every day since it opened on Wednesday (okay, so I'm one of those nutty Tolkien fans), and I have to say, it gets better and I pick up more and more that I love about it with every viewing. I would have thought I would notice flaws, but no ... Also, I didn't feel the three hours at all. Perhaps it's because I love the material so well, or perhaps it's simply movie magic. Whatever the reason, I could have sat through the next two installments with eagerness and joy.

Of course, any movie, however well made, has flaws, and with this one, I noticed two major problems. At least, I consider them problems.

Arwen's role is one, and the love scene I could handle, but the flight from the Nazgul upset me because it was, in the book, a moment of strength and defiance for Frodo who shows the reader that he is indeed the one who is both strong enough and pure enough to take the ring to Mordor. In the movie, this moment was sacrificed to make Arwen's character bigger and more of the warrior princess mold that so many fantasy stories have. Her line ("If you want him, come and claim him.") at the river had me almost laughing, if I hadn't been so disgusted with it. The chase sequence was very well done and it gives me goosebumps, but it should have been Frodo's moment, not Arwen's. Ah, well ...

The other major problem I had (and why is it that both of them involve the women, I wonder?) is Galadriel's scene, when she is tempted by the ring and "passes the test". Well, the special effects team didn't, in that scene, and she seemed too much like a harpy. Cate Blanchett is a terrific actress, but she was too cold and remote as Galadriel, not the mysterious yet compassionate Galadriel I remember from the books. It's probably my least favorite scene in the whole movie, and if I have to leave for a restroom break, that's when I take it.

(On a side note: another special effect I found out of place was Bilbo's transformation in Rivendell. It wasn't needed and it didn't offer anything to the audience but a cheap shock or laugh, whichever way someone took it.)

And while not a flaw or a problem, I almost fell out of my seat in shock when Aragorn stepped up behind Frodo towards the end, after he had left Boromir. The scene played out very well, but it was startling, to say the least. Things like that make me wonder what other changes are in store for the future installments, what major events will be altered one way or another.

And also, while not a real problem to me, the pacing might be off for the uninitiated. In the books you got a real sense of the passage of time (as in the time between Bilbo's birthday and when Frodo finally leaves the Shire), and in the movie, while the feeling of urgency and fright is undeniable, you get no sense that this is taking place over quite a long period of time. As others have said before, it makes it seems as if the tale takes place over a few weeks. But perhaps the latter two installments will even it all out.

All that aside, the movie is incredible and far beyond anything I had thought possible. I was swept away from this real world and into Tolkien's world as smoothly and completely as when I read the books. The cinematography alone was worth the price of admission, and then you have the jaw-dropping special effects, the dream cast, and the inspired direction from a man who obviously loves this material.

What can I saw about the acting? Every time a character appeared, and this has been said before but I'll say it again, it was exactly as I had imagined them. Perhaps the hobbits are too "human" to be what many imagined them, but for me, they fit in perfectly with the rest of Tolkien's world. I never once got the impression of someone acting (well, okay, a few times with Liv Tyler), especially the nine who made up the title fellowship. Gandalf, Frodo, Aragorn, Sam, and all of them, perfectly cast and wonderfully realized. Perhaps a slight feeling of disappointment at how Merry and Pippin served as comic relief and not much else, but their roles increase in the latter two books and I'm hoping the same will hold true to the movies.

Sean Astin, I thought, was a wonderful Sam, but until the end (and just a few moments in Rivendell) his relationship with Frodo was never truly examined. This is not to criticize Astin, but I hope that with all the moving scenes between the two in The Two Towers and in The Return of The King, Peter Jackson and co. will not sacrifice this friendship to portray, for example, a more prominent romance between Aragorn and Arwen. In my opinion, this friendship between Frodo and Sam is the very heart of the tale and what it all boils down to, and I would hate to see it reduced to a side note.

And I must give special mention to three who held my attention the entire way through: Ian McKellen (Academy-Award worthy), Elijah Wood (a more perfectly cast character I've never seen), and Viggo Mortensen (incredibly charismatic). Anything I try to say as praise will seem redundant, so all I will say is that they make me ache all the more for 2002 and 2003, given what happens to them and the trials they will face and the triumphs that await them. Wood and Mortensen, especially, I long to see tackle the challenges ahead.

Aside from the acting, what took my breath away was the gorgeous scenery, absolutely enthralling and so much as I had imagined Middle Earth to be that it's a marvel hobbits and wizards don't inhabit New Zealand. And as for the special effects, they were by and large awe-inspiring and very well done. How they shrunk normal sized actors to seem like hobbits is utterly amazing. One scene that gets me each time is seeing Frodo and Gandalf sitting in the wagon in the Shire. It is so convincing that I forget that Elijah Wood is my height.

And as for the more "special" special effects: the Balrog, the bridge sequence, heck ... the entire Mines sequence, the opening battle scene, the sublime images of the Argonath and Rivendell and the white horses at the Ford. Masterful, and yet, never overdone. (Just the two I mentioned earlier.) The time spent in Moria is beyond my ability to properly describe. Let me just say that I was, for the first time in a very long while, afraid for the lives of the characters involved, even though I've read the books and knew the outcome. It is, in a word, spellbinding.

But enough gushing.

Well, one more thing. The ending (and they do go into the first chapter of the second book) is beautiful. It doesn't end with fireworks or an epic battle won or anything like that. It ends with Frodo and Sam quietly climbing down a mountain side after exchanging a handful of simple and heartfelt words. The scene feels so natural, so right, that it leaves me misty-eyed and hopeful and all of those other emotions I felt when I first read the books.

And that's about as big a compliment as I can give to the cast and crew of this masterpiece. The story seems so new and fresh to me, from the innocence of the Shire to the terror of the Mines and the burden of Frodo's quest ... it all feels as if I'm discovering it for the first time. And what a feeling that is!

title: One of a Kind
review: I have seen so many great movies, but never one quite like The Lord of the Rings, it is a movie above all, it will be a huge hit and a wonderful classic. The movie is so amazing, so unreal only few can come close to its greatness. I usually like drama or action movies, but this fantasy has it all. It is the most fulfilling three hours you'll ever see on the big screen, and undoubtedly the best movie of the year and one of the greatest of all time. I have not read any of the books but I sure will, this movie is so good, so thrilling you will not get bored for even a second. It is a masterpiece that has it all, action, suspense, drama, love and courage. Perhaps the most thrilling thing about this movie, is that you can feel that you are in it and the special effects are simply splendid. I can't wait to see the other two. 10/10, and I am not exaggerating.

title: Masterful cinematic storytelling
review:
Many images passed through my mind when I read the Lord of the Rings. The words seemed to take a form with each scene and that story played out in my mind as a series of dazzling and unforgettable images and, although other novels I have read were made into films, none have captured those images that lingered in mind as precisely as Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings.

Each scene was almost perfectly portrayed as I would have crafted them should my thoughts somehow have taken form on the silver screen. It was in short the most enjoyable cinematic event I have had the privilege of witnessing. In fact, from the warm sunlit fields and hills of the Shire to sliver of a bridge in the darkened mines of Moria, I could not have had an artist draw such a vivid retelling of this classic story.

Jackson's magic did not end with the props, sets and scenery. It appears he managed to pass on an infectious and accurate understanding of Tolkien's novel to the cast and crew of the movie. Each actor demonstrates an uncanny understanding of Tolkien's vision of the particular character they were portraying. The meticulous crafting of the fellowship results in characters you care about who drive the story to it's exciting conclusion.

I will eagerly await the Two Towers and the Return of the King. Because the sequels were filmed simultaneously with the present film, I cannot imagine the film maker nor his characters lost any of their fervor in their pursuit to masterfully create the complete tale.

Bravo Mr. Jackson.

title: Excellent movie, but read the books also
review:
I have noticed a few comments of disappointed people. Take the time to read the books and then see the movie again, then comment and see how you feel. This movie was not entirely true to the book, but then again what movie is. To me this movie is the greatest of all time, but thats my opinion.

I understand the movie had to be cut shorter than the books, but I know I am not the only fan who would not mind a fifteen hour sit to see it unabridged, but still Peter Jackson did a spectacular job and I take my hat off to him. Two thumbs up, Bravo!

title: Amazing, simply amazing...
review: In short, this movie was simply amazing.  I still to this day have not read the book, which may be part of why this movie impressed me the way it did. The story is the classic "naive youth becomes hero" and Elijah Wood gives a convincing performance throughout...in fact, all of the acting - though not spectacular - was convincing.  The scenery and camera work were breathtaking, with obvious and appropriate contrasts between the various locations of "Middle Earth".  Special effects added almost the perfect touch, and though I wouldn't consider this movie in the category of "eye candy", the effects were on par with any to date.  The part of the film that really made it a personal experience however, was the soundtrack. Congratulations to Howard Shore and all of the artists working with him for creating what I would call the "perfect fantasy soundtrack".  Everything from the instrumentation to the harmony within was a phenomenal supplement to what was already visually amazing.  Go see this movie!  Delay no longer...you will not be disappointed.

title: Majestic. Unlike anything.
review: Majesty is something rare to experience. You don't find it in everyday life anymore. I don't think I've ever seen it on the screen before. The end of the first Star Wars, episode IV, had a bit of it at the end. This has it through and through. It creeps up on you at first. The thrall enfolds you more during the passages of Rivendell. As the Company makes it's way south, it begins to overawe. As the boats pass the standing Kings, you are captured. And this is just the beginning!

title: An amazing film...
review: This film is more of an experience than merely watching a movie.  While not perfect, it outshines anything that has come out of hollywood in a long, long time, probably since "Titanic."  You can tell it was a labor of love, again like "Titanic."  Ian McKellan as Gandalf was superb, as was Viggo Mortenson as Aragorn and Elijah Wood as Frodo.  My only critique is that there seemed to be some things missing due to time constraints.  I assume Merry & Pippin were good friends of Frodo, since they were willing to accompany him on his quest, even though this was not clearly established. And it seemed like there was almost too much grotesquerie for my taste. But, overall, an incredible film that is an instant classic.  I'm going to try hard not to read "The Two Towers" before next Christmas.  Try, I say. And I will definitely be seeing LOTR:FOTR again!

title: A Beautiful Film that stays true to it genre.
review:
The Lord of the Rings, Fellowship of the Rings is a masterful film of fantasy and action. Having never read the Tolkien books, and coming into this movie with only slight knowledge of Dungeons and Dragons type creatures I was easily able to slip into this world and fully absorb the storyline. The special effects were seamless, the acting terrific, and it overall left me wanting more. (I think I'll go rent the Hobbit on DVD to catch up on the adventures of Bilbo Baggins. Then see the movie again next week.) I can't wait for the next LOTR film to come out.

The main reason why I loved this film, aside from the stunning visuals, is because it stays true to its genre. There are no black comedians doing slapstick antics. There are no characters acting in time to the tune of "We will Rock you" or other such inappropriate music. There are no "wooden" child actors in the film. There are no token minority characters in the film either, (Arwen is NOT played by Lucy Liu, instead by the beautiful and stunningly Elvish looking, Liv Tyler). This is a fantasy/action film through and through and it keeps its focus on the story on hand without the need of self deprecating humor. I only wish more fantasy films would take themselves seriously.

title: A dark vision of the book, but it works well...
review:
Firstly, this is undisputably one of the best films ever made. It is a modern-day adaption of Lord of the Rings, an intense three hour journey into a vision of the reality of Middle-Earth. As a film in it's own right, there is little to find fault with. The casting is excellent, the acting is flawless (Ian McKellen is perfection itself as Gandalf). The settings are amazing, in that you barely realise that it is a fantastical place -- everything seems very real. Shots are set up perfectly, with excellent positioning of characters within the frame. In several places, if I may be so bold as to say so, Jackson actually IMPROVES on Tolkien's masterpiece, and adds depth by drawing from The Silmarillion and other related works.

However, no three-hour version of Fellowship of the Ring could possibly capture all of the book and make everyone happy -- it would have to be a dozen hours to capture everything presented in the book. I think that perhaps Peter Jackson (a horror film director) focused a bit too much on the dark side of the story. After the ringwraiths appear, he literally takes the colour out of the film, making it almost black-and-white, and the hues -- and joy -- never returns. Bree is dark, and there is no fun in The Prancing Pony. Rivendell and Lothlorien become mysterious and menacing places. Also, almost all of the areas where Jackson added to the work were to make the movie even darker: Saruman's evil role is increased, the orcs/Uruk-Hai feature prominently, and there's a nasty cave troll added as well. This isn't to say that the movie fails -- but it is a far darker, and much more intense, vision of the Lord of the Rings than I personally might have preferred. It's definitely not a film for children -- mid-teens and upward only. All-in-all, I found that Jackson's version of Fellowship of the Ring is perfectly executed according to his slightly more "current", darker vision of it. I'm sure that very few people will find fault in that... one could argue that he makes it even more... "real"... with the more prominent and tangible evil. (And there's definitely no room for Tom Bombadil in Jackson's vision of FOTR, that's for sure!)

Some small technical issues that I hesitate to mention but shall nonetheless:

The music was excellent, but it really plays a subtle supporting role and lacks a certain... punch or originality (though some would say that is exactly as it should be, and I wouldn't dispute that.) The special effects were a bit unbalanced -- some elements, such as the cave troll and the incredible balrog were perfectly executed, while others were noticeably flawed and unreal looking. (However, the size-difference of the hobbits is handled well, with very few moments where you notice any problems with perspective.) There are scenes shown in the trailers which are not present in the final film (can you say "special edition DVD version"...?), and there are threads that sort of dangle with the edits. For example: Gimli makes grandiose statements about people falling under the spell of the "elf-witch" of Lothlorien... and someone who knows the book realizes this is a set-up for the moment when he himself "falls under her spell" and asks for a strand of her hair -- but this never happens; and the scene of them receiving brooches (a scene shown in the trailers) is missing... and yet, strangely, Jackson seems to go out of his way to show their brooches later in the film without explanation.

But, these are all nitpicks of an arm-chair critic -- this is an excellent film. I was spell-bound for three hours, on the edge of my seat even though I have read The Lord of the Rings several times. The three hours passed so quickly; I could have easily sat and watched the entirety of the trilogy, glued to the screen. It's going to be a long year, waiting for the next film -- and I'm going to pick up the books again as soon as I get home...!

One final nitpick: Is it just me, or was Arwen presented as a more powerful wizard than Gandalf? What's up with that? She commands the water to rise against the Nazgul, while Gandalf gets whipped (pun intended) in both his "magical" battles. (In the books, Gandalf takes credit for the water rising at the ford; in the movie, it is clearly Arwen who calls the water forth with magical words.)

title: Awesome, yet overdone
