title: Very different from other fantasy movies
review:
I am an avid fan of the fantasy genre. Like many such persons, I have read the Lord of the Rings before. That said, it has been some time since I have read it, and I did not go out of my way to read the books again before the movie came out. Why should be obvious: take a look at some of the more critical comments that have been written regarding this Film. They dwell on the finer points of the approach the adaptation takes, and fail to evaluate it as a movie. I would wager that even those vocal critics who don't hold the unrealistic notion that every little bit of the novel should be duplicated would differ on which points should be duplicated.

(WARNING: THE FOLLOWING COMMENTS CONTAIN MINOR SPOILERS)

The movie begins with a glance at the history behind this story... the conflict with the dark lord Sauron. This was quite visually impressive, showing armies clashing on a dark landscape. You "get the point" of why the one ring the focus of the story when you see Sauron batting troops aside like they were flies.

The sets and terrain mock-ups on this movie were breathtaking. Many people have spoken of the elven cities and the dwarven mines, which I agree are awesome. I also found the fortress in Mordor rather inspiring.

Other effects in the movie--and their handling for emotional impact-- are also noteworthy. For example, the flame-demon "balrog" was pretty impressive. When he was falling, I saw the tendril of the whip dancing around. Everyone who was familiar with the book knew what happens next... and I was entranced waiting for it... waiting... I thinking that they paced that scene with those who have read the book in mind.

The cave troll that the fellowship encounters is also a visual treat, used well in a very tense fight scene.

I'm not sure if I like the way they did the ringwraiths or not. The ringwraiths let out an intense shriek every time that they came on screen. The shrieking was eerie. It was also irritating.

They way that they did Arwen (the elven woman who rescues Frodo from the ringwraiths) is actually quite a departure from the book... but I actually like the way that they did it. The way that she dispenses with the ringwraiths is visually stunning and is a nice portrayal of the power of elves in Middle-Earth.

One of the biggest effects accomplishments of the books is the portrayal of the different races. Of these, the hobbits and dwarves are the best done. By means of forced perspective and editing, they make full sized actors appear as these diminutive races.

On the other hand, I did not like the orcs. They just look like TV sci-fi show makeup jobs, like magog from the Andromeda TV-series. In contrast to how much attention they paid to making everything seem so real, it just stuck out like a sore thumb to me.

The other thing that I didn't like was the elves. Legolas and Elrond seemed like... well, men with pointy ears. But Galadriel seemed so ethereal. It struck me as a bit of a discontinuity. I think they should have tried to make them all a little more eccentric. I'm not sure how, but there you go. In the same note, I did not like the Galadriel/Frodo scene. It seemed so... curt. "Yes, yes, I am tempted!!! I would be a QUEEEEN! But no, I couldn't do that! Hey, I passed the test! It's off to the lands beyond for me..."

That said, I found the film emotionally intense and... just so real. It was sort of strange how *real* this felt. I was expecting some over-the-top gratuitous fantasy schlock, but it wasn't there. They only used what they needed to to get the feel across, and it paid off. I felt very immersed in the film.

The acting was good to excellent. The actors that I associate strongly with other roles (e.g., Sean Astin, who I will always see as the loser from Encino Man) acted well enough that they managed to escape that type-casting in my mind. Others, like Ian McKellen as Gandalf, fit their roles so well that it was never a concern.

Although I have stated a few nitpicks, overall the craftsmanship of this film is immense. I think Jackson chose the right details to exclude and nowhere did I see the same sort of excessive creative license that has marred so many other F/SF adaptations (Starship Troopers comes immediately to mind.) Visually stunning, entirely immersive, Fellowship of the Ring should hopefully set a new standard in the realm of fantasy movies, a genre that has been ill-treated by movie-makers in the past.

title: Not a classic like EXCALIBUR, but close. II & III should be even better.
review:
I am truly upset that I have to wait one entire year for The Two Towers! It's going to be agonizing. Fellowship Of The Ring is a great book, but the least of the trilogy and fraught with pitfalls for film adaptations. The story is comprised of one long journey, with lots of battles, so translating that to film was a daunting task, but Peter Jackson handled it with incredible skill. The opening prologue, while too reliant on CGI (how I miss the days of EL-Cid sized armies), is a real heart stopper and sets you on a path to complete absorbsion into the film. It makes the prologue from The Mummy Returns look like complete crap (which it sort of is). :-)

The 3 hour running time is very nearly needed, with maybe just a few short scenes that could have been trimmed. Thankfully, all of the (what I call) filler in the first third of the book is excised and the story takes off as a result. Characters are built up and made believable and the Fellowship is made up of people you do truly care about. Performances are outstanding all around, with the biggest nod going to the outstanding Christopher Lee, who proves the man is the master ov evil. He IS Saruman!

The last hour of the film is outstanding cinema, with an incredible battle beneath the mines of Moria and then a big showdown/sword battle with the killer Orcs. The performances of both Sean Bean and Viggo Mortenson are particularly strong here.

It looks as though The Lord of the Rings is off to a great start and since the books only IMPROVE, I have no doubt that film adaptations of THE TWO TOWERS and especially RETURN OF THE KING will do the same and join films like EXCALIBUR and BRAVEHEART on the list of all time great epic films. Fellowship is not quite in that league, but it is close and I do believe Peter Jackson has shown sufficient skill and passion to translate parts two and three with the justice they deserve and that can only mean they will be classics for all time (I hope). Those of you who have been craving a true fantasy film, one without the annoying children's cliches (like in Willow) are going to be thrilled.

title: Do Not Let Die-Hard Fans Mislead you!
review:
Although well made, LORD OF THE RINGS: FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING is by no means the greatest film of time. After seeing it twice, I find it to be an enjoyable, though uneven, movie-going experience.

First, the effects. They are well done, but the quality varies from scene to scene. The opening battle sequence suffers from a reliance on swooping cameras and blurry, dull visuals. The entire film seems awash in darkness, visually speaking. Peter Jackson uses Dark, moody lighting to enhance the CGI, and quite frankly, he over does it.

The battle sequences are adequetly coreographed but poorly filmed. There is nothing especially ground-breaking or impressive in the swordfights here. After seeing Braveheart in 1995 and Gladiator just last year, The sworplay in FELLOWSHIP seems standard by this point.

The Characters, save Gandalf, are uninvolving. Frodo comes of as one- note and spineless. As a protagnist he generates very little sympathy and left me feeling indifferent towards him.

The corrupting power of the ring is very much over-stated. Every few minutes we are subjected to an overdone scene where a character is tempted by it. A few scenes of this nature would do just fine in establishing the rings allure, but the overkill ruins the effect.

This is by no means the Greatest film of all time or even the best Fantasy/Adventure film ever made (That title still belongs to THE EMPIRE STRIKES BACK, sorry LOTR fans). expect that #1 ranking to go down about twnety or thirty places over the coming weeks, as more people see the film. It is passionate and well-made, but it lacks energy and a sense of wonder. In the end, it's a rather dull labor of love.

This will do well at the box office, but not as well as expected. Tolkien fanatics are expecting TITANIC size grosses, but that is wishful thinking in my opinion. The opening weekend will be surprisingly huge, of that there is no doubt. But I think word of mouth will be quite different among average movie goers than it will be among RINGS fans. This thing is so tailer made for fans I think that the ordinary layman will be somewhat underwhelmed. I predict a gross of about $250 million at the most.

title: The best movie of the year bar none, and a testament to the creativity and vision of humanity.
review: The best cinematic experience I've had in a long while. I don't want to spoil it for you, but suffice it to say that you NEED to see this movie. It runs the gamut of emotions - from amusement to terror to awe to grief to pride. And every one of those emotions is genuine, not manufactured and spoon-fed a la Pearl Harbor. It has so many memorable moments that rank right up there with the ones we all love - Vader's revelation to Luke, for example. Everything about this film drips passion and effort. PJ embodies what a great director should be - creative, visionary, and most important of all, he has a love for what he's doing and pours his life into it. The cast, as well, is superb. You find yourself attached to them, and when any of them gets hurt, you wince and cover your eyes. McKellen, in particular, is Oscar-bound without a doubt. The special effects also deserve mention - make no mistake, people, these are the most imaginative and well-done effects you've ever seen in a movie. Not only are they perfectly rendered and real-looking - you really can't tell when something is CGI, unlike Jar-Jar - but they have the desired effect every time. In short, When you combine one of the greatest stories ever told, a genius of a director, a terrific cast, a superb SFX company, and $260 million, you can't really go wrong. PJ, New Line, and everyone involved in making the movie deserve the highest praise.

title: I expected something special - I got perfection...
review: ...or as close to perfection as I could ask for. What can I say that others haven't already? How can I add comments that justify what this movie means to me and obviously so many others. When I sat and watched Bad Taste back in 1990 if someone had told me that in little over 10 years the director of that cheesy schlock horror classic would eventually produce this, well it would have been choking on popcorn time! It is simply the most affecting film I've seen in all my adult life.

title: I expected it to be great, and it was better
review:
***SPOILERS*** ***SPOILERS*** Well, what can I say, other than I've pretty much been waiting all my life for this movie. I fell in love with Middle Earth when I was but a toddler seeing the Hobbit cartoon for the first time and have been a fantasy geek ever since. As soon as I heard they were making this movie, I was a little wary. It's a huge story, and I never thought the big screen could do it justice, but as soon as I heard it was going to be 3 hours each, and found out they were making them all at the same time, I knew it was going to be great.

Not only was it great, it was fantastic (literally). Everything I had hoped for and more. Yes there were changes, but they were all acceptable and many made the story flow better. Yes there were omissions, but it was made up for by the many great things added in this movie. What can I say, Jackson, the cast, the crew, everyone did a great job in this movie, and the 3 hours flew so fast I felt the need to reread the two towers all over again just to get to the next part of the story.

For those who are skeptical of any changes made, here they are:

spoiler alert

Firstly, To Bombadil was left out. I think Jackson felt the need to speed up the early part of the journey and get to Bree quicker, so this as well as Frodo and company's encounter with the elves in the woods near the Shire was left out. Unfortunately this also means that the conflict with the Whites on the Barrow downs was also cut out since there was no Tom Bombadil to save them. Although I kind of missed these scenes, there removal was understandable. The book starts out quite slowly and doesn't really start grabbing you until Strider is introduced at the Prancing Pony, and it probably would have been a little too sluggish in a movie. Hopefully we'll see these scenes on the DVD (if they even made it to the cutting room floor).

Bill the pony actually is in this movie, although he is only meantioned when Sam says goodbye to him. Glorfindel, however, is not in this movie. His scenes are replaced by Arwen. At first I wasn't too sure if I liked this or not, but realised, it is probably a good change for the movies since it better develops her character. In the books, she really didn't have a major role until the last book. With this scene, we get to know her a little more rather than just a passing introduction in Rivendel.

Minor omissions aside, everything else was pretty much intact. He really did a good job staying true to the book. I can't wait for the next movie. I guess we got Episode II this summer to fill the void.

title: A stunning epic
review:
It's been a good year for fantasy movies. First came the spirited satire of "Shrek," then the sweet charm of "Monsters, Inc." and the sheer wonder of "Harry Potter." Now we have the piece de resistance: "Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring," the first installment of Peter Jackson's film adaptation of JRR Tolkein's landmark trilogy.

For those unfamiliar or needing a refresher in Tolkein's basics, a lengthy but useful prologue establishes the story: in the ancient past of Middle-Earth, several rings of power were forged for the various races of the relm. A single master ring was also created by the evil Sauron for the purpose of dominating the other rings--and thus, the world. But in a massive battle Sauron loses the ring, which then passes through several hands until it comes into the posession of a hobbit (diminutive creature with large ears and hairy feet) by the name of Frodo Baggins. It lies with Frodo--aided by a company of stalwart men, hobbits, elves and dwarves--to destroy the One Ring by casting it into the fires of the volcano that forged it, thereby ridding Middle-Earth of Sauron forever.

Tolkein took great care in describing the lands and sights of Middle-Earth; therefore, it seems appropriate that the settings be the most memorable aspect of this film. From the cozy, green fields of Hobbiton to the stark waste around Isengard, from the etherial perfection of the Elven havens of Rivendell and Lothlorien to the faded splendor of the ruins of the Dwarf-hall Moria, the screen comes to vivid life, creating images that are not so much viewed as savored. The lush scenery of New Zealand provides all the right touches, and the result is one of the richest fantasy worlds ever brought to film.

The cast is uniformly excellent, with the strongest performances belonging to Elijah Wood and Ian McKellen. Wood is an excellent Frodo, an ordinary soul caught up in extraordinary circumstances. McKellen brings the right balance of strength and tenderness to the role of the wizard Gandalf. Viggo Mortensen gives quiet strength to the human Aragorn, a wanderer with some pretty big secrets in his past. Liv Tyler brings a touch of girl power in the expanded role of Arwen.

Although the film never bores despite the three-hour running time, the battle scenes take on a feeling of sameness as the film progresses. The best moments are in quieter hours, such as when the Fellowship mourns a companion fallen. And certain moments will no doubt differ from the visions of those familiar with the book: my personal quibble was with the characterization of the Lady Galadriel, played by Cate Blanchett with great grace but near-sinister coldness.

But these are minor complaints, and did little to detract from my enjoyment of the film. The groundwork lain here is promising; if Jackson follows through with that promise, this could be a "Lord of the Rings" for the ages.

title: Personal feelings about this film
review:
I thought this film was especially interesting. A friend of mine loaned me "The Hobbit" before the movie came out, so that I could read it and understand what was going on. The book moved rather slowly for me and after a week I stopped reading it. I went to see the movie with the friend who loaned me the book...

review:
When i first went, an saw this movie (which i have been expecting for nearly 2 years) i thought "it was okay, slow start, but okay".

title: Exceeded my expectations
review:
As a teenager, I read the "Lord of the Rings" at least three times, so I guess I fall into that category of Lord of the Rings fanatics. I am however not alone, as, for my demographic profile(growing up in the 70's in the US), it had for many the impact that "Harry Potter" (unfortunately hopelessly commercialized and put into a film version, so many will not bother to read the books, which are charming) appears to be having on the current one. I was concerned that the movie might, as previous attempts at film versions, be a huge disappointment. I was pleasantly surprised--although the "Fellowship of the Ring" necessarily edited out portions of the book and as a result also altered some details, it captured the spirit of Tolken's world so well, I was transported back to the wonder I first experienced as a young reader. The casting was inspired, the acting wonderful, and the movies visuals and pacing right on target. Although the entire cast was great, I want specifically to praise here the powerful performance of Sean Bean in his portrayal of Boromir (as the character will not appear in the next two films). I hope that this role will lead to future parts in film.

My one criticism is aimed at Hollywood's marketers. I was forced to sit through fifteen minutes of tedious trailers clearly targeted at a teenage male audience, which of course indicates their anticipated audience for the film itself. (I finally understood what torture it must be for a man to sit through the trailers that precede the typical, sugary romantic comedy--e.g. "Kate and Leopold"-- but I wont comment on that one here.) It indicates a complete failure in researching the actual readers of the book and in understanding both the female (and possibly--hopefully--much of the male) audience and the nature of the "Lord of the Rings" itself. Far from a simple action story, it is a world so completely imagined, it far transcends the more typical fantasy/action flicks (as well as books)that have followed it and appropriated much of its imagery, without however, its breadth of vision. Did they even read it? Thankfully, the director and cast clearly did.

title: See this film...NOW!!!
review:
I've been a Peter Jackson fan for some time now...from the moment I saw "Bad Taste", I was hooked. Then came "Dead Alive", "Meet the Feebles", "The Frighteners", and so on. So basically I've been slavering to see "TLOTR" ever since word of its production.

I was not let down.

See this film...NOW!!! It is amazing, entrancing, and any other positive "-ing"s one can dream up. Sure, Tolkien fans may be a bit upset over the reworking, but if there were none, we'd have a 5-hour movie instead of a 2 1/2-hour movie, wouldn't we? I gladly traded some overlapping stories and reworking for the opportunity to see some of the most fantastic cinematography, CGI and prosthetic work (let us not forget Jackson's background in "traditional" SFX), acting, and attention to detail onscreen in some time. The fight/battle scenes in particular were most memorable. Jarring and disorientating as the camera work may be, it makes one feel...jarred and disoriented. As I know *I* would feel during a fight or battle. I could feel myself tense up during these scenes; in my book, Jackson did his job. The casting was dead on, except for Sean Bean as Boromir and Liv Tyler as Arwen. I felt Bean's talent was wasted on such a transparent character, and quite frankly I could have done without Tyler's sneeze-and-you-miss-her Arwen. There were enough delightful performances to carry me through the movie, especially Orlando Bloom as Legolas. Although technically a secondary character, Bloom's Legolas stands out with some *phenomenal* archery and fighting skills. And Ian McKellen as Gandalf...well, I really couldn't see anyone else in the role. He *is* Gandalf. (And of course Jackson pulls his usual "Hitchcock" in this film...=) ) When I saw "TLOTR", there were quite a few parents who had brought their young (I'm talking around 6- to 8-years-old) kids. Mom, Dad...unless you want squirming offspring after the film hits the 2-hour mark, or toddlers with interesting nightmares for the next few days, don't take your young kids to see this. The Dark Riders ALONE are enough to freak out even the stoutest little heart... All in all, I give Peter Jackson kudos on what has obviously been a (triple) labor of love. It shows. I'm eagerly awaiting the next two!

It is a must see.  the acting is wonderful and the effects are so cool.  it swayed from the book a little bit but it was still very accurate and wonderful. title: Faithful, Beautiful, Magical Adaptation
review:
Peter Jackson is perhaps the best kept secret to film making. After

Lord of the Rings, his secret status is in serious jeopardy. His

adaptation of The Fellowship of the Ring is the most faithful,

remarkably beautiful film to come out of Hollywood in a long time.

This coming from a New Zealander best known for a lawn mower

graphically splattering hundreds of zombies across the silver (and

crimson screen). Who would have thought it? Well, those of us

who have been enamoured of Jackson's peculiar genius for the

last few years knew he was the man for the job. Now all

speculation can cease.

In the three hours that Fellowship of the Ring unfolds before our

eyes, we are greeted to a rich and thoroughly detailed fantasy

setting, one which is as real as it is fantastical. The Shire is

everything that it should be, Rivendell is unpredictable yet

stunning, and Lothlorien is nothing short of magical.

If sacrifices were made, it was in the fleshing out of the

"secondary" members of the Fellowship, such as Gimli, Mary,

Pippin, and Boromir. Nevertheless, Tolken's work is such a

detailed creation it was inevitable that some characterization

would be lost in a cinematic retelling. Jackson does the best he

can within the confines of a limited time frame presented to him in

the film format. Hopes run high for an extended DVD which further

develops the important supporting cast.

Despite this one small quibble, The Fellowship of the Ring cast a

cinematic spell unlike any I have been subject to in a very long

time. For 180 minutes, I sat quivering in my seat, unable to look

away even for a split second.

No spoilers and please, avoid reading any reviews that include

any before you see the film. There are some spells that are best

experienced without the benefit of a crystal ball.

title: A very enjoyable movie experience; I'm ready to see it again.
review: Like many people my age (40ish), I read the Trilogy 30-odd years ago, so I am both unable and unwilling to compare the movie to the book/s,nor to compare the Middle Earth in my head to director Peter Jackson's.  I was not blown away, but I certainly was satisfied with the movie, extremely satisfied.  I left the theater knowing I would see LOTR again, and soon.

title: 365 days is too long :(
review:
Its so awful having to wait one year to see the next one :( There is no need for the oscars this year, all the statues will go to Lotr!

It was a really good movie!

title: Incredible
review: This was the most incredible movie I've ever seen.  Yes I read the books YEARS ago, which helped fill in a few gaps, but it was sooo good.  Do yourself a favor, see this in the theaters.  I'll be the first to own it on DVD, but this is something that you ABSOLUTELY MUST SEE on the big screen. I'm going, again, tonight.

title: Quite the Epic
review: This way a truly amazing movie. It stayed respectably and reasonably close to the book, and the directing and acting were both excellent. Elijah Wood, who I do not normally like, and Viggo Mortenson were especially good actors and really portrayed the emotions and thoughts of their characters. Cate Blanchett was a lovely Galadriel, though the scene where she was tested by the ring was the only slightly over-the-top ordeal. The special effects were very well done and not overwhelming, specifically Gollum. They did a good job of making the Hobbits and Dwavres smaller, and Boromir was portrayed very well by Sean Bean as a patriotic but weak-willed man; he did not seem foolish or evil. Of the "secondary" characters in the Fellowship (Legolas, Gimli, Boromir, Merry, Pippin), Boromir was the best, and Gimli was not as well written as the others. Legolas was well played as a feminine but strong and occasionally vicious elf. All in all, a wonderful movie that I will definitely buy.

title: Very Good, Unless a fanatic
review:
This was the best adaptation of a book that I have ever seen. Not to mention the whole thing looks fantastic!!!

I know things are missing, but surprisngly few considering the ground covered in 3 hours.

A not to be missed movie.

title: The Best Movie out of Hollywood in a LONG Time
review:
Given my disappointment of "Star Wars: Episode One," and my knowledge that there is no possible way to encompass all the depth and subtlety of Tolkein in ANY movie no matter how long, I was absolutely delighted with the first segment of "Lord of the Rings."

It is definitely the best movie to come out in a very long time and is long overdue. Despite some obvious parts of the book being left out, and other parts being abbreviated, I don't think even the most cynical of fans could expect more from any motion picture treatise.

For all the limitations of the motion picture vs. the literary form, "The Lord of the Rings," in my humble opinion, did not disappoint.

The only part I found laughable was the "Jedi" battle between Sauraman and Gandalf that never took place in the book. Again, motion pictures are limited, and I am sure the writers thought a battle royal would entertain more than a battle of words.

All I can say more about this movie is see it! If I say more, I give away too much.

I wonder if those who are panning the movie have even read the books. I have and I loved this movie. It was so good, that it more than made up for its faults.

Word to the wise, it is not (again in my opinion) a movie for small children. The Lord of the Rings were violent books, and make for a very violent film. Lets put it this way--if you would not take your child to see "Braveheart," don't even think of taking them to this film.

title: Shortcomings aside, one of the best movies in a long time.
review:
I'll keep it brief.

It's nice to see a movie with a story to tell.. and tell it well, it does. From the great cast (I was weary of Elijah Wood as Frodo when I first heard, but I'm very happy with him) to the great sets and the special effects, it's truly a great movie. The shortest 3 hours for me in a long time.

title: In a word- Incredibly excellent (two words had to do it)
review:
First of all, thanks to Peter Jackson, the crew, the cast and everyone who made this film possible (sounds like an Oscar-speech aye?).

LOTR The Fellowship of the Ring is the greatest movie I've ever seen. It's like seeing the book on the big screen. Magnificent! Having said this, I think that it has a very good balance between following the book, and it's own unique script. Ex: We get a better impression of Sarumans betrayal, and a more passionate view of Aragorn and Arwen's love. Superb!

Of course some of the elements in the book is cut out, but that's inevitable when transferring a book of 400 pages into a three hour film. Peter Jackson does the job great

SPOILER ALERT!!! One of the great things in the movie is the prologue. The basic things in "The Hobbit" is repeated splendidly; The Dark Lord, Sauron is portrayed as pure evil; and everything is excellent told with memorable quotes as: "History became legend, Legend became myth, and something that should not have been forgotten where lost..."

I saw the movie Friday night (21st December), and was so thrilled that I had to see it again Saturday night...

So what are you waiting for? Go see it (again)...

title: Computer game on a screen
review: No No No - Some nice National Geographic type scenes which were the highlights for me (like going back to Wales or the Grand Canyon) but I felt like was watching Saturday morning cartoons for three hours. Belzimorph, Cultar, Jeemommabeb, Gyrthumm - make 'em up as you will, it's just a pile of swill with not much merit to it in my opinion. Boring! The elves in the very green grass reminded me of 'The Wizard of Oz' on a set that reminds me of my childhood train set layout. I've seen the 'fiery monster' in another, older movie. Add 'Night of the Living Dead' and a touch of one of those Quake/Dungeon whatever they are video games and a blue-eyed kid with a magic sword and an indestructible ring - gimme a break! Nearly fell asleep but the noises kept waking me up.

title: A great, beautiful and emotionally captivating movie...
review: From the way the movie followed the book almost precisely to the landscapes this movie is one of the best, if not THE best movies I've ever seen. The way characters are portrayed are exactly as I, a LOTR fan, imagined them, from the Ringwraiths to Lady Galadriel of Lothlorien! I truly recommend it to everyone...

title: while not entirely accurate, an excellent job of turning a book into a movie
review: what can i say but incredible? beautifully done, absolutely wonderful to see a piece of work prepared so well. while not entirely true to the text of the novel, it was true to the spirit of the novel. the book was basically transformed into a screenplay - what had to be discarded was, and what was kept was great. it was a little disappointing to see some things left out, and a few things were just glazed over (the weak point of the film), but it was fantastic nonetheless. DEFINITELY worth it.

title: How many people got paid off and a warning
review:
Amazing that Time-Warner has this much control over the media (oh wait--they are the media)! I wonder how many people got paid off to say they loved this movie. JRR is rolling in his grave!

I also want to warn parents that this movie should have carried an R rating instead of PG13 (how did this one slip by$$$?) for intense, graphic violence (i.e. graphic decapitation).

title: GREAT!!!!!!
review: This film is one of the best, if not THE BEST adaptation of The Lord Of The Rings I've ever seen, I can't wait for part two & part three!  This is a DEFINATE purchase when it comes out on DVD!  Puts that silly Harry Potter movie to shame!

title: A voice of dissent
review: Its very good, but not THAT good! I haven't read the book and on the strength of the film nor am I compelled to do so. I also did not turn up at the cinema with pointy ears and a table-cloth cloak. Don't get me wrong, it was a quick 3 hours and I thououghly enjoyed it. However, there are holes I can pick out (although I'm unable to do so without spoilers). I think Pete Jackson has done a very good job although personally I preferred his earlier work (Bad Taste, Braindead). Finally I would say that it is not as enduring as Star Wars, although it does defecate on The Phantom Menace from way on high.

title: Gut-wrenchingly, Mind-blowingly awesome...
review:
By the gods what a film! More to the point, what an adaptation. I write this 5 days after release and I've already seen it 3 times..... I can't remember ever seeing a film 3 times at the cinema, EVER.

Being a massive fan of the books I was terrified that too much artistic license was being taken with the story - namely the trailer depicting Arwen protecting Frodo over the river - and that the vast amounts of information and fantastic locations would get lost in the rush to cram it all into a 3 hour (just under in fact) running time.

Boy was I wrong, in a breathless rush clear across half of a fantastically realised Middle Earth we follow a host of wonderful characters through some truely incredible set-pieces.

Sure, there are some omissions or changes, the running time necessitates it. But none of the changes affect the film in a bad way or take away from the wonderful story. The Shire build-up is rushed through with farmer Maggot being basically omitted and Bree's experiences being shortened but the story gains urgency for it. There are other changes but for the most part, they are for the better. The endless days of travelling which sometimes caused the book to drag have been swept aside for fantastic shots of the New Zealand country as the nine companions toil towards their target.

And I defy you not to be totally taken in by the simply sensational fight scenes, the brilliantly created Gollum (I hope he holds up as well when we have to see more of him), and the utterly magnificently rendered Moria sequence and sets.

There are points which could maybe have been handle differently. Most notably, Saruman's betrayel, I feel, should have remained for his own ends rather than having him join Sauron so openly.

Minor quibbles aside, what an awe-inspiring take on the fantastic realm of middle earth and I'm just completely gutted that I'll have to wait a year to catch the second part.... I'll just have to content myself with seeing the Fellowship of the Ring some more!

title: Not the greatest ever...
review:
OK, I don't mean to be a party-pooper or p**s on anyone's bonfire or anything like that but I have to say that my honest opinion of this film is that...well...IT SUCKED!!! O.K. I understand I have not read the books, and maybe I should have done, but I did the same with Harry Potter and thought that it was way superior. The problem with the Fellowship of the Ring was that there was too much storytelling, which, after two hours, got a little bit tedious. The action scenes were the best part of the movie. The fighting was done brilliantly and the scenes from Frodo's point of view when he wore the ring were pretty special, but the rest of the movie was not as good as it could have been. I know there are another two episodes to come, but on the viewing of this one, I will not be going to see them. Hype surrounding a film is a pretty dangerous thing nowadays. Movies like The Phantom Menace and Titanic were hyped up beyond belief. Occasionally a movie does live up to it's hype (Phantom Menace) but more often than not, it doesn't and here is a film that falls into the latter catergory. It's alright for movie-goers who liked the film to say "But you have to see the other two parts to "Get-it"", but the first part should be good enough to make you want to watch the next ones. Star Wars Episode One did this and I will definatly be seeing episode two in May!!! Before everyone starts to jump on my back regarding my opinion, I want you all to realise that it is only opinion and the fact that I did not like the movie does not mean that those people who have not seen it will not like it either. I just felt I had to get my point across about the film that has probably failed to live up to the hype more than any other film ever.

Credit to the actors however for putting in a fine performance, especially Sean Bean's moments...I won't say too much...but he battled on...

title: Does it get any better than this?
review:
I had high expectations on Lord of the Rings. After reading the books, playing several different role-playing games such as Dungeons and Dragons, for not mentioning the great Baldur's Gate computer games, this movie, I felt, had a lot to live up to.

To my surprise, it did. It even went further than that. With such a grand epic tale, its visually stunning and breathtaking cinematography, its pulsating battlescenes and emotional packaging makes the Lord of the Rings a movie extraordinaire. It has good and evil, demons and magic, bravery, villains and heroes, love and hate. It has everything one could ask for in a tale of this sort. I would dare to say the Lord of the Rings is a strong, if not THE candidate of the most interesting tale ever depicted on the silver screen!

title: Throw out the book comparisons - A great film
review: Novels adapted on the big screen are victim of criticism by the book geeks (no offense) which is what is happening with The Lord of the Rings.  Once the viewer realizes that The Fellowship of the Ring couldn't be cut out and pasted onto the big screen due to time restrictions and simply to make it more interesting for those who didn't read the novel, it is much easier to see what a fresh and wonderful film this is.  Elijah Wood and Ian McKellen bring to life Frodo and Gandalf, respectively, in great fashion.  Yes, some characters and events are not included in the movie but if you want to complain about what you conceive as an important event left out, then go read the book.

title: The best movie of the year.
review:
The First Lord of the Rings movie of Tolkien´s epic fantasy adventure trilogy met all my expectations great characters good as well as great evil, great valiant battles, sorcery, friendship, bravery and honor. This may be because I haven´t read the books yet, but saw the animated Lord of the rings, which was good but incomplete since the finance wasn´t there for a sequel. So it is a blessing that Peter Jackson has made these movies. Story: Forged by Sauron a small ring containing great evil passing from one hand to another until it lands in the hands of friendly hobbit Frodo, who with the help of wizard Gandalf and a band of other races taking the ring to the great Mount Doom to destroy it. The Fellowship of the Ring (the first part of the trilogy) is made with great landscapes and attention to detail also featuring some of the best CGI and other SFX available, the monsters and creatures look very much real, not only that, he also managed to convey the different sizes of the characters by using film tricks, notice in the first scenes of the hobbit village, how the sizes of Elijah Wood (who plays Frodo) and Ian McKellen (who plays Gandalf) who are both regular sized people differentiate so radically. The movie in some places really gets you emotionally intense and gripping. But there are clearly some flaws here and the in the character developments, not spending too much time getting to know more about them, this is clearly an excuse to making way to the story which in itself bares no flaws. The movie despite this is cast flawlessly with great acting, it has an international cast. From the UK: Ian McKellen, Ian Holm, Sean Bean, John Rhys-Davies, Billy Boyd and Christopher Lee, US: Elijah Wood, Sean Astin, Viggo Mortensen and Liv Tyler, Australia: Cate Blanchette and Hugo Weaving. I highly recommend you all to see it. And roll on The Two Towers film next christmas and The Return of the King the christmas after.

PS. I have now begun to read The Hobbit, which is a prelude to LOTR books and gives you the back story of Bilbo Baggins on his adventures, then I will continue with the LOTR book trilogy accordingly.

THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING 4.5/5

title: I guess it was, well...
review:
Well, let me start out by mentioning that I've only read the first 100 pages of the Fellowship of the Ring, so I'm not really in a position to compare the film to the book. Despite this, I'd like to make some comparisons. Which could be a very stupid decision on my part, but what the hell. Just take what I say with a big chunk of salt.

In comparing the film to the book, I'm not concerned about technical details--I don't get hung up over the fact that the plots of the two movies may be slightly different. I'm more interested in the feeling and mood. In this vein, I would easily call the movie "action-packed", but I would not say the same of the book. One of the things I really admired about the small part I read of the book was, well, the "patience" of it all. Maybe that's not the right word for it, but one of the things that set LOTR apart from other fantasy novels for me was the way Tolkien used the English language, and the way he paced the story. Everything I read had a very balanced, restrained mood to it--even parts that had a lot of action. For instance, the dark riders in the book evoked in me not a sense of horror or outright thrill (as they did in the film), but more of a malicious kind of mysteriousness. And that mysteriousness was subtle, or at least restrained: the less Tolkien used language to concretely describe the actions and appearances of the riders, the more scary they seemed in my mind. For me, at least. And although I only read 100 pages of it, LOTR didn't really seem like the kind of work that would focus on battles and fighting mayhem quite as much as the film--in fact, as I recall, those hundred pages I read didn't mention a single one.

Well, anyways, that's just a few examples. In the end, all I can really say is that the film was very visceral and intense, and what I read of the book was not. The special effects were wonderful, but many times the film was just visually over-stimulating, flooding me with so much eye candy that my eyes just went sort of "numb" to it all and I got bored. And sometimes I felt as though substituting some special effects with more traditional techniques--such as cutting, changes in cinematography or more abstract visual presentation (e.g. showing the shadows of the dark riders instead of what they actually looked like), or simply the removal of the effects--could have made parts of the movie more immersive. A few of the characters were paper-thin, such as the dwarf Gimli, and a few were just underdeveloped or a little confusing because they didn't have very much screen time, like Galadriel.

All this isn't to say that the movie didn't have its memorable moments; in fact, it had many. Although some of the action scenes in the movie got very tedious and routine, some of it was also incredibly cool. Although nothing in the movie was really tear-jerking for me, I did share the joys and laments of some of the more well developed characters. All of the performances were great. And knowing what I don't like about the movie now, I imagine I'll focus more on the positive aspects of the film when I see it next, and I'll probably enjoy it a lot more. For the time being, though, I do wish the film shared some of the "patient" style of storytelling that the book had--it would have been very interesting to see, say, Wim Wenders or Jim Jarmusch direct this--but at least the final product was far better than most other fantasy films I've seen.

title: Superb adaptation!
review:
Incredible! Peter Jackson has managed to create a stunning, exciting, fast-paced movie out of - let's be honest here - a rather ponderous book.

I wouldn't be at all surprised if Lucas, Spielberg and Cameron were getting a little worried...

title: Two out of three ain't bad
review:
Jackson captured the power and the glory of the Fellowship. Incredible work at the entrance to Rivendell, in the Mines of Moria, Isengard, and Mordor itself capture Tolkien's heavier themes. But too much of the "fun" is missing. Don't take it wrong, two out of three ought to be enough for a huge box office, Oscars galore and fantastic acclaim. This movie stands above the rest.

The fireworks at the Long Expected Party are some of the best fun in the movie. More of this would make this movie a cosmic success.

At the Prancing Pony, Frodo fails to recite his rendition of the Cow Jumps over the Moon before disappearing under the influence of the ring. The movie turns the Pony into a version of the Star Wars bar where Luke meets Han. The movie loses its chance to portray the innocence and joy that Tolkien sees in a species driven from paradise.

More of the same during the flight to the ford. Trolls can be spotted in the rock formations, if you are looking. Sam fails to notice and the audience misses his engaging rendition of "Troll sat Alone."

A few other lighthearted scenes leaven the show but without editorial emphasis. As Legolas walks lightly the others trudge through the snows of Caradhras. At the mouth of Moria, Frodo solves the riddle of the Friend. There are no songs, no epic poetry, no light to complement the courage of the fellowship.

Tolkien may be pleased but I feel the story is incomplete.

title: Now Other Film Has Achieved The Greatness Lord Of The Rings Has!
review:
Sitting in the cinema as the trailers finished and the lights dimmed, I expected to be shaking, I expected waves of excitement to be spreading all over the audience. What was there? Nothing. But as the credits came on, and the legend of the One Ring was explained, all hell broke loose as the audience could not be contained.

"Fellowship" had been hyped up for months and I could only see two ways in which it could go - 1: It would live up to the hype! 2: It would fail miserably! Being the movie that it is, it chose a third path - it surpassed all expectations and is he greatest film of all time. If you, like myself, think watching Darth Vader and Ben Kenobi battling to the death was exhilarating, and if you thought watching the Death Star explode was amazing, you, are in for an unimaginable time watching Fellowship. If watching a classic battle between good and evil doesn't interest you, or state of the art CGI's, or superb acting on all fronts, or some of the best makeup I have ever seen, or the magnificent battle scenes then there is something seriously wrong with you - if your on medication, come off it, and if your not I recommend some!

The fact remains that Fellowship is by far the greatest movie of all time. Star Was will always hold a special place in my heart as one of the greatest movies of all time, but Lord Of The Rings is light years ahead. For those familiar with the story then everything you have imagined will come to pass, but for those who are not, you'll wish you were!

Lord Of The Rings: Fellowship Of The Ring is a masterpiece in story telling and perhaps the greatest movie of this millennium! There is something for everyone and people of all ages will sit in awe at this magnificent work of art! JRR Tolkien would be proud!

title: I have been waiting 40 years to see the best movie that has EVER been or EVER will be made...
review:
I have not nor will I read other user comments...I do NOT want to be angered by their inanities. I have seen this movie twice in as many days and have decided unequivocally that this is, by ALL interpretations of cinematic techniques and creative abilities, the BEST interpretation of the HOLY writ by J.R.R. Tolkien that has ever or will ever be attempted by any human on earth. Bakshi's junque was just that junque and will always be regarded as such. The Rankin/Bass attempt was the most laughable piece or trivia I have EVER had the misfortune to experience.

Others may disagree with what I have just said..if so, so be it...I pity their ignorance. No matter what anyone else says, this series of films will live long in the annals of filmdom as the BEST rendition of the Holy writ of J.R.R. Tolkien that will EVER exist.

title: A landmark of film-making, that will be revered a century from now.
review:
Considering myself a diehard Tolkien-ite, I must say I'm simply astounded by the translation. Yes, things have changed from the original narrative, but this is a different medium and change is subsequently necessary. A friend remarked after viewing the film, "They couldn't have made it better, only longer." Well put.

Anyone, who finds fault with the discrepancies of plot, is missing the point of what has actually been achieved. Stop being so cynical and open you eyes to all the wonder and magic that IS on the screen. I, along with millions of others, have been waiting decades for this moment. Sometimes your dreams can come true.

Now if only Mr. Jackson will make the DVD an hour or two longer....

As fine a motion picture as I've ever had the pleasure to view.

title: Believe in the One Ring
review: What can be said about a story upon viewing only the first third of it? Certainly one can grasp the feel of the story, the characters, the locations, and the overall feel. Upon viewing the FoTR the first time I must admit that I was overwhelmed.  There was so much to review after the credits had rolled, so much that was laid before us that it was hard to gather an impression of the film upon the first viewing. And I also made the mistake of taking the film and comparing it to the book, which I know and love. I kept pointing out to myself things that the production had missed, things that I loved but were not in the movie, or worse yet, were changed in the movie. I had to go see it again, and again, and still again to really gather an opinion. I have done this, and this is my conclusion: Peter Jackson has managed to capture the heart and soul of the LoTR and bottle it into a neat little package for the viewers. The movie does not go word for word from the book, that would be impractical and impossible, but he takes the elements from the book and puts them on the screen to be felt. To be felt. A rare experience in the cinema today. After stewing the LoTR:FOTR in my head for a few days, I can happily attest that it survives on it's own merits as one of the greatest works of fantasy (Scifi is included in that) to come out in twenty years. The scenes I think of when talking about the film will be with me the rest of my life: the entire Mines of Moria sequence, Hobbiton, Weathertop, every scene with Boromir and/or Aragorn, Gimli and Legolas fighting, the statues of the Kings, the Uruk-Hai captain's fate and the ending. All done to perfection. If this is a glimpse of what is to come, then next two installments can't come soon enough....I haven't said that about a movie ever. While the movie isn't a word for word transition from Tolkien's works, it is still the LoTR and Peter Jackson has done the best the can be done within the confines of the film medium.  He has done it justice.

title: even sean beans good (possible spoilers)
review:
Before i get into the film itself i would first like to say that im a massive fan of the books and consider them to be the finest work of fiction ever published. When i first heard they were making a Lord of the rings trilogy i was ecstatic. As more and more information came out i was less than optomistic - sean bean, stu townsend now viggo mortensen, liv tyler, book changes. Then the trailers hit screens and my appetite was well and truly taken.

I saw the film a couple of days ago and was blown away. This is the true definition of epic indeed. Nobody should go and watch this looking for a tolien film, this is without a doubt pete jacksons vision and interpretation of a classic authors vision. The greatest things about the film is the stunning cinematography, Hobbiton looks amazing, the mines of moria and the acting of all concerned especially ian mckellan, wood, lee, mortensen, tyler and sean bean gives his best performance ever. Utterly brilliant. the film is a must see for any fan of film, absolutely amazing and a strong oscar contender in several categories. Not sure whether i would choose between this or the underrated AI for best picture. The only gripe i have with the film is the non inclusion of my favourite character tom bombadil but it is obvious that such a powerful character included for such a short time might make the less clued in viewer not understand, plus the running time would have been too long, it's just right as it is and it doesnt seem like three hours at all. See it and be amazed

title: Very Good, but not Amazing
review:
Discredit me if you'd like, since I haven't read the book. Thus, this little review will not touch on it's faithfulness to the novel itself.

So, I saw the movie on opening night in my home town of Dallas. I must say that I am embittered against the movie makers for revealing so much of the movie in trailers. There were, what, 12 trailers of the movie that were aired on T.V. and in theaters in the months that led up to the movie's release? I mean, after seeing the movie (which felt like a VERY quick 3 hours, by the way), I felt like I'd just seen a long trailer. That, however, my only criticism, lies with the movie publicity people. Idiots.

The movie, however, was quite good. But I'm sure it was more special for those who have not been poisoned by all sci-fi crap hollywood's put out in the last generation or two. For me, a fantasy-challenged movie viewer, "rings" was epic in appearance, but formulaic in essence. Not to detract due credit from J.R.R. Tolkien who has crafted probably the most detailed and beautiful fantasies of all time, however. It's just that who, these days, hasn't seen a movie about a bad guy who's lost his something valuable to him, and the underdog good guys trying to destroy the thing he wants before he can get to it? Of course, one could probably over simplify anything if one wanted to. Even the untouchable Lord of the Rings. Oh well. Good movie, though. DEFINITELY not deserving of the #1 movie of all time nod, though. I think a mass of Tolkien groupies must have hit IMDB the evening of the 19th and have messed up the system.

title: Purposeful, and overtrimmed.
review:
This movie is fabulous. Far and away the greatest fantasy film ever made... but... you have to be able to think to understand it fully (ie. If when an action adventure has actual acting you get bored, don't go see this) and it is not complete in at least two ways.

1) Its original running length (Dir. cut) was 3.5h, much too long for contemporary cinema. You could sense the missing parts when things did not quite "fit." It must have been hard to slice and dice. I cannot wait for the DVD. That will be the real movie.

2) It is really the first 1/3 of a 9 hour movie. It left us at the edge of a knife.

Good cinema leaves us entertained. Great cinema gets better with every viewing. I have seen this movie 3 times and every time it gets better. I cannot ask for more.

`Let us hunt some orc.'

-Hermit

title: BEAUTIFUL Adaption Of A Wonderful Story.
review:
I've grown up a fan of both "The Hobbit" and the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy. As a child, my father used to read these stories to me before I went to bed. And now... I've seen that world come to life.

Before I get into the bulk of my review, I'd like to remind and point out a few things to the casual viewer or those who have never touched a Tolkien book: "Fellowship" is the first of a three part series. Unlike the Bashki animated film, which covers the majority of the first two books, this only covers Book One, and it is left very open ended and unresolved for a reason. Secondly, yes, this is a very grim fantasy film. These characters are fighting for the fate of their world, and sacrifices will be made throughout the course of the story. Both of these points are directly how the book addressed them. The story has only begun in this film. There are plenty of character developments and plot resolutions to be had. Be patient. Also of note: Is this a film for kids? No. Don't take your five year old to this expecting this film to be another "Harry Potter". But again, this is how the books were. Lastly, in regards to an earlier comment, the characters of Merry and Pippin are nothing like Jar Jar Binks.

With all of that off my chest, I shall touch upon the film itself: Wow. It truly is everything I wanted from this book-turned-film. The landscapes of Middle-Earth (especially the Shire) are breathtaking. Wonderful set design. The character portrayals are accurate to the characters from the book and are given a sense of dignity and comradeship that they would have needed. I was very pleased by the casting. The musical score is excellent. Warm and cheerful, intense and brooding, sad, and uplifting all as needed. The battles are ferocious, with a Braveheart-esque quality to them, and yes, they're a bit gory (what, did you really expect sword battles to be clean?), and the scary parts (especially the Riders) made even myself uncomfortable.

I've never seen a book-tuned-movie touched upon with such loving care (although this year's "Harry Potter" did a notable job). Peter Jackson did a fine job creating Middle-Earth and its locations in their full splendor. True, there were some plot and character omissions and changes, but again, you can only squeeze so much into a 3-Plus hour story. However, I can say that very little was left out or altered, and they kept more than they took away. I have little reason to believe that the next two films will be anything less than as spectacular.

As with "Harry Potter", I could see why people would have a sense of confusion about this story if they have never read the books. But hopefully, it will motivate them to read the stories for a better understanding, instead of scratching their heads or blindly criticizing the film. This truly is a remarkable film from a technical and storytelling standpoint, regardless of whether you like this genre or not.

I feel safe in saying that Tolkien fans have very little to worry about, and hopefully the average movie-goer will find a great deal of enjoyment out of this film, but they need to keep in mind before seeing this film that this is only the first part. The sequels are there out of necessity for the story. As for myself, I was taken back to that time when Dad read those stories to me just before I went to bed. I loved that story now just as much as I did then, only this time, my mind's eye was projected at the local cineplex. Truly recommended.

title: Worth the 14-year wait.
review: Having read "The Hobbit" over 15 times, the first when I was 7, and the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy over one-and-a-half, lining up to see this movie was both nerve-wracking and euphoric. But without giving away any details, I was unable to move from my seat the whole 3 hours, almost cried once, did cry twice, and could not force myself to leave the theater until the credits were finished rolling. For a Tolkien fan like myself, this was ungodly surreal; for an Elijah Wood fan, this was heart-wrenching; for a fantasy genre fan, this was heaven. Go see it, even if you've never read the books; if the movie itself is worth the 14-year wait, think how amazing the books and their creator are.  Rock on, Peter Jackson.  Rock on.

The climax with Balrog marks a climatic ending, but the movie continues for another 40 minutes. Other than that, I have no complaints. Who cares if they cut out the scene with Tom Bombadil? Not me. Any person who owns a horse named Fatty Lumpkin deserves to be left out of the movie. Yes, I have read the book, and I read it thoroughly. I am very well aware of the Christian allegory written in the story, and I feel pretty certain I understand it much better than most of you do, being a Christian and all. The opening of the movie is symbolic of Satan's war against heaven, the elves are angels and the orcs are demons. Gandalf is the representation of Jesus, and Saruman is Lucifer, the angel that became Satan through betrayal. I saw the movie with three of my friends, two of them never read the book. All four of us left agreeing that it is the best movie we have seen in a long time if not ever. Some people may complain about lackluster special effects in some areas. I did notice them too. However, I thought the Mummy Returns had the worst special effects I've seen in a while, but when I bought the DVD, the effects looked much better than I remember. (However, nothing could fix the hideous Scorpion King). Once it is out on video (New Line cinema promised it by August) I'm sure the effects will look much better. I can't wait until next year, the Two Towers is probably going to be even better.

title: One book to rule them all
review:
So, how long did it take for me to understand that I am irrevocably in love with the film? Let me see... two seconds.

OK, I read the book for the first time when I was nine, which was twenty years before I saw the first part of this trilogy. It had a tremendous impact on me: for nearly fifteen years I thought it must be the greatest book ever written. That kind of thinking has to leave its marks, even after another book (and yet another after that) claimed the title.

Still, after the lights went out and the text "Lord of the Rings" was projected on the screen, I could not stop trembling. I know it is a silly thing for a grown up man to be so moved by a simple text on a wall. That was, however, the moment when I understood that no matter what, I was going to love the movie.

It is one of the reasons why I gave this movie a 10. Other reasons have already been listed here, but for me personally, the most significant single factor is the love for the book. It must be one of the greatest adventure stories ever told, and I will (hopefully) never grow too old to read it once again and enjoy it as much as I did the first time.

This movie does justice to the book; it could not have been done better.

title: Classic material, will it be a classic movie?
review:
If you are unfamiliar with Tolkien's work, then let me say that "The Lord of the Rings" is no "fairy tale" any more than is Homer's "Iliad". Tolkien's trilogy is a classic in the true literary sense; it is "Iliad" and "Odyssey" in one tale, but running concurrently.

"Classic" is a phrase that gets tacked on to too many movies these days. Whether "Fellowship of the Ring" or Peter Jackson's entire trilogy of movies truly achieves that designation is something only time will tell.

If I say, "Rosebud", or "I'll get you my pretty!" or "Frankly, Scarlet" you know exactly what movies I'm talking about, and the scene will come to mind. That, I think, is a true test of a classic movie in the post-silent era.

If, in 30 years, I can say "YOU SHALL NOT PASS!" and the image of Sir Ian McKellan as the wizard Gandalf at the bridge of Khazad Dum comes to mind, then this movie will have achieved classic status. If not that scene, then Peter Jackson has two more tries at gaining film immortality with the next two movies in the Tolkien trilogy.

Great movies are not made great by special effects, but by the performances of their actors. And acting in this movie is superb. This movie is not all "swords and sorcery" and comparing it to something like "Conan the Barbarian" would be a travesty. This movie has more similarity with "Braveheart" than with "Conan".

In my opinion, "Fellowship" is a better movie than "Braveheart". It is deeper in its scope but more basic in its concept. This is myth come to life - a story about how man came to rule the world and how sorcery and magic passed into a history that is now long lost. Like any myth, evil and good are clearly defined, and the story itself serves as allegory for the universal quest.

Unlike the myths of old, the true hero of this story is not a mighty warrior, but an everyman who has a seemingly insurmountable task thrust upon him. Frodo Baggins is no Odysseus. He is not larger than life. Unlike Odysseus, Frodo's "bow" could be easily bent, but how many of us could bear his ring-burden and not become corrupted by it? That is what makes the story of "Lord of the Rings" a classic in the truest sense of the word. This is a story about confronting the weakness in us all to choose an easier path ignoring responsibility to the future for the comfort of the present.

Movies are based upon the suspension of disbelief. Anytime a filmmaker attempts to portray a myth he has a doubly daunting task, for this is fiction within a fictional context; a story twice removed from the truth.

My main concern about "Lord of the Rings" was not how well its actors portrayed their roles or how good the costumes or special effects would be. I knew they would be good. I was concerned with whether Peter Jackson "got it" - the story behind the story, and did not just gloss over the tale with fight scenes and special effects with a smattering of good performances by some excellent talent. This is why George Lucas failed in "Star Wars: The Phantom Menace." Lucas forgot what his own series of movies was about and,

instead, gave us, in "Menace", a story we did not care about. He did not suspend our disbelief.

Peter Jackson's rendition of this classic story finally does justice to Tolkien's tale where others have failed. This is an intelligent portrayal of Tolkien's world and Jackson puts you smack dab in that world for 178 minutes and does not let you leave until he is done with you. Two days after seeing "Fellowship of the Ring" I don't feel like he is done with me yet. I am still "suspended" and probably have no chance of coming down until "Return of the King" is released in December 2003.

title: Wow
review: I didn't read the books because I dislike fantasy.  Yesterday I took my family (our ages are 46, 20, 9, and 7) and we all loved the movie.  The art direction was particularly amazing.  Any movie which can hold the interests of two little boys for almost three hours has a lot going for it.

title: O.K. but could have been so much better.
review:
I was disappointed with the film. Specifically, with the SCREENPLAY. There were just so many changes from the novels. And so many of them seemed not to serve any justifiable purpose; i.e. lack of time etc. One small irritating example is the gate of Moria scene. We all know how it goes. Gandalf Can't see the forest for all the trees' if you get my meaning, then realizes his mistake. Why change it? How is this way better? It would have taken the same amount of screen time to tell the story exactly as it was written. How was the scene improved by changing it?

Now, I'm not some anal-retentive Tolkien freak who is offended by even the smallest change. It's really quite amazing that the movies got made at all, what with the typical Hollywood politics and bureaucracy. It's just that there are certain lines and situations in the story that are pivotal and necessary to tell it correctly. Just as there are certain lines in Hamlet and Julius Caesar that are mandatory, so it is with The Lord of the Rings. So many times throughout the movie, I was ready for a particular line and it never comes. And don't even get me started on the whole Arwen situation. Her scenes with Frodo and Aragorn had a distinctly tacked-on feel, as if some focus group said `Hey, how about some stuff to keep the ladies interested?' I guess when there is this much money at stake people can't help but try and improve their chances of producing a blockbuster; to try and drag the story as close to the middle of the movie going audience as possible to insure the broadest appeal.

And that's really a shame in this movie because in my opinion EVERYTHING ELSE WAS DONE RIGHT. The sets were incredible, the actors were very good, and the costumes and special effects were simply marvelous to behold! The visual impact of Moria and the orcs surpassed all my highest expectations! The portrayal of Sauron before his loss of the Ring was absolutely fantastic! The Balrog was magnificently terrible! The armor and weapons... everyone involved did such a great job. Someone should get an Oscar. Really.

All in all, I was surprised at how let down I felt on the way to the car. Too many changes and added crap made for a movie that was at times quite boring to me. I've read other reviews that said that the movie was too hack-and-slash, but I honestly found myself wanting more of that. I suppose it was because when there was some action happening I felt like things were finally moving along at a decent clip.

To sum up Was it good? Yes and no. I suppose with time and more viewings I might grow to enjoy it more than I do now. Will I buy it? Probably so. I own all the other versions of Tolkien's work on film. Will I go to the next two movies? Of course. I have to. I hope that the next movie is written better, though.

If you have bothered to read this far, Thanks and I really appreciate your taking the time.

John Chavous
