title: Ramblings
review:
I had anxiously awaited this movie, had been for a year, read the first 2 books so I'd have a background on it, would have read the rest but the 3rd book disappeared from my room. I sat in the theater in the midst of the crowd, surprised at how many empty seats there were, and sat through the torturous previews, wishing that for once they could be skipped.

Finally it started. I was gripped from the very beginning. Now I have a pretty good imagination, but somehow everything looked better in the movie than I had imagined. Like many fans, I was a bit depressed over the omission of Tom Bombadil. I also didn't remember Arwen in the book, but I guess they had to get Liv Tyler in there somehow or she would have thrown a fit. I think the movie was wonderfully done out, and there were a few things I picked up that I'm not sure many people did. The main thing was whenever the fellowship was running, most ran like normal people, but Legolas, having the natural grace (and beauty) of an elf was noticeably more graceful than the others. Especially in the parts where they were on the mountain in the snow, he was walking on top of the snow while the others trudged through it. Little things like that made up for the minor flaws.

Even if you haven't read the books or seen the cartoons (which actually bore me, I have yet to stay awake through them) you won't be lost, unless you don't see this movie. Before it comes out on video I'm sure I'll have seen it in the theater at least 3 times, only wishing I had the money to see it more. Definitely deserves it's spot as the #1 movie on the IMDB charts!

title: Amazing
review:
What a treat it must have been to watch this movie and have no idea what the story line entails. I found myself excited, amazed, and thrilled as I followed the story line, even though I knew everything that was about to happen. My wife who has never read LOR, or any fantasy book for that matter was asking me all sorts of questions about what was going to happen in the next two films. The scenery was stunning and I found myself thinking to myself, that is exactly how I pictured it in my head when I originally read the books. The portrayal by the main characters was right on target. Ian McKellen as Gandalf the Grey was far and above any expectations I had for his character. I don't think I am going out on a limb when I say he should be a shoo in for best supporting actor. Elijha Wood plays Frodo to a tee as the meek, unassuming, plain hero.

The real winners here are the hoards of young children I saw at opening night. I hope they are inspired and go on to follow and support the genre of fantasy for generations to come.

title: when the film was over, i was not disappointed
review:
I have read the books. This is important. It is all fine and good for somebody who has read the books, is a fan, and has been waiting for most of his life to see these films, to say that it was a fantastic movie. It is quite another thing for someone who has not read the books, has never known the story, and didn't have any expectations, to say that this is a fantastic movie. It is a fantastic movie. I have been a fan for over 12 years and have read the trilogy, and many books relating to the trilogy, and many essay's written on the trilogy, time and again. When I first heard that a film trilogy was being made, about three years ago, I was ecstatic. My excitement never died, but as opening night drew closer I found myself more worried about how faithful an adaptation the films would be. Were all the fantastic reviews I had read true? Were all the horrible reviews I had read true?

As a fan of the source material there were two ways I could have viewed the film, as a fan or as a purist. As I am not a purist when it comes to film adaptations from books, I chose not to hold the fact that Peter Jackson did not make a nine-hour Fellowship film against him. With the three hours he had to work with he made a film that included as much out of Fellowship as he could have. There were changes in the film, from beginning to end. I saw all through the film things that did not match the book, things that were not right, even some things that struck me as completely unnecessary changes. I thought that it moved very quickly from point to point. I thought that the action sequences seemed to come one after another with very little time for much anything else. All these things I thought as I watched this film. And when it was over, I was amazed. I knew just what I needed to know about all the characters, and I felt about them all just how I needed to feel. I knew exactly where in the story we were at, and had no problem understanding what was going on. Amid the stunning landscapes, and CGI created caverns, and action shots followed by action shots, Peter Jackson had managed to magnificently tell the story of the Fellowship of the Ring. He had managed to tell the story so well, that despite all the changes and all the omissions and all the action, I had nothing bad to say about this film.

The trick, though, is having people who are unfamiliar with the story feel the same way. When people who have not read the books walk away from this film, do they know where the story is? Do they understand what all has happened? Are they as impressed with the story as they may have been if they had read the books before the films had been announced? Overall it seems that they have. Several of my companions to the show had not read the books and knew only what they had managed to retain from the cluster of information I have managed to confuse them with. These companions walked away fans of the story, every bit as impressed with the film as I was.

And that is all I have to say about the Fellowship of the Ring.

title: As good as it could have been
review:
I think perhaps that some people have been a little harsh when they have come to criticise this film. As a person that has read and enjoyed the books and also been a fan of Peter Jacksons work in the past I couldn't have been happier when I discovered he was directing it.

I think nearly everyone agrees that things had to be changed to cater for the audience that hadn't read the books and for this reason it was necessary to keep to the main central storyline. It is near impossible to take the book in all at one go let alone try and make the movie the same. This aside however the movie still stays fairly faithful to the book with most events simply being trimmed down as apposed to omitted completely. The journey to Bree or the introduction of Aragorn for example. It takes many, many pages before the character of Aragorn is clearly defined in the book and as one of the most interesting and entertaining characters you couldn't use hours of screen time telling his ranger stories for example. Replacing Glorfindel (the elf who rescues Frodo from the Wraiths) with Arwen was a clever way of adding a more prominent female role (for which the origonal book was critisised in lacking)to the story.

In terms of the other main characters people must not forget that there are two whole books and two whole movies still left. The chapter in the book where we are introduced to Gimli, Legolas and Boromir (The Council of Elrond)is fairly boring in terms of the rest of the book and slows down the pace a great deal something perhaps fatal if done badly in the movie. Personally I feel Boromir was presented very well in the movie we know that inside he is a noble man who will fight for the good cause but his worry and fear for his own people leads to him being corrupted by the rings power yet he redeems himself and dies a hero just as in the book. His people and homeland we learn about in book 3. As for Gimli and Legolas their role in the fellowship is perhaps a little under developed but it is in book two as their inter racial friendship forms that they become the characters we love. People must also not forget that the film already clocks in at 3 hours which is long and any longer would perhaps be suicidal. It will be interesting to see if there are any deleted scenes on the dvd that were cut due to running time that perhaps help these causes.

I think to say the fight scenes are bad is wrong. This movie isn't the Matrix or Crouching Tiger and its fight scenecs are both energetic and enthrawling. Some of the camera shots are almost nauseating they make the action seem so real. Jackson stated he wanted the audience to feel like they were in middle earth. Long shots may let you soak up the action but they also make you an outsider just watching, not being a part of it. Granted that is what you technically are but what makes Lord of the Rings so good and different is that the book is written in such a way that you dont think you are reading about a fantasy you believe its real and Jackson wanted to bring this into the movie and in my opinion succeeded with A+ honours.

title: The Good, The Bad
review:
Admittedly, I expect nothing of a movie these days. THEY ALL SUCK. So, I expected Fellowship to suck as well. But it didn't suck. It had many redeeming qualities. Still, all the main actors are white. That is really stupid. I mean, J.R.R. Tolkien lived in South Africa in the 1930's and 40's, so it's no wonder his story wld be so ethnocentric. But come on. The only black character is an ork!!! What kind of msg. does that send?

But, as for the complaint that LotR doesn't have enuf character development and is too much like a big $$ action flik, well, so what? Who goes to the movies for character development anymore? Give me a break. If you want close personal relationships, go to a bar or something. I dunno, get out and spend some time w/yr friends. But don't complain because LotR didn't waste too much time on dialogue.

I think the fact that it lacked character development is one of the BEST things about LotR. We got plenty of character development for Frodo and Gandalph, in any case, and they're all that really matters. People are whining b/c LotR plays the Hollywood game a bit too much, but what do you expect? LotR is better than Star Wars. Star Wars is a crappy B-movie with bad special effects and worse acting. Its only redeeming quality were the awesome sound effects (the tie-fighter noise, Chewbaca's rawr, Vader's hoo-pah), the blue trailing light on the Falcon's engine, and Chewbaca (again, not really the wookie himself, but just the noises he made). Acting wise, Harrison Ford was the only redeeming feature. LotR is better than the Godfather. You want a movie with wooden characters? There's one. Any character development? Nope. Just stereotype mafia guys running around. I would say LotR is just slightly better than Empire Strikes Back combined with Aliens and a good D&D adventure. You can't knock D&D for just being an excuse to play hack & slash, and you can't knock history for being a segue to war. You can't knock LotR for being too much like history, or too much like an action movie. This ain't about the characters, it's about their QUEST, and it's a gory, battle-ridden quest (just wait until the next two movies! half of the rest of the entire story is one gigantic battle scene!).

I give LotR a 9.5/10, and the missing .5 is only because we didn't get to see a bona fide love scene between Arwen and Strider (I wanted to see some skin, oh well). If you want character development, read the book. If you want a movie, go to the movie. Film isn't about art, it's about eye candy and making money--always has been, since the nickelodians. If you had any other conception, you must be French or an idiot, or maybe a chick who wants to see a chick-flick!! This ain't no stupid French chick-flick mon ami, this is Lord of the Rings!!! And it Rules!!!

=LILITH

title: I hope I live to see the next episodes
review: This is nothing short of the best film I have ever seen. It was very emotional to finally see the book of the century come to life on the big screen as the movie of the century. The scale of the book has been perfectly transferred to the big screen, not leaving out a single detail. The imagery is everything you had imagined when reading the book and then some. Where the book at certain moments seemed to be very slow and meticulous, the film goes on like a rollercoaster ride, leaving you feeling one rush after another. The fellowship never disappoints, lives up to it's hype and outdoes it with ease. The pace at which the movie comes along makes you want to come back for more, in fact I was telling my friend that I actually didn't want this movie to ever stop. It is to me the first correct representation of a fantasy movie, the first time an effort has been made to give the genre a serious approach, and it has payed off. review:

And in my opinion the reason why this film is so good than it is, is that Peter Jackson wrote his own story based on the book. review: This movie is to say the least, INCREDIBLE! I only have two complaints; The beginning is a little rocky for those who have read the book, there is a lot of things that are cut. title: What a movie!
review:
What I found very interesting, is that the images and the characters have stuck with me for 2 days since I saw it. I now find myself wondering what day I can 'sneak' off to see it again with Xmas so close. My wife didn't care for it, as a matter of fact she loathed the book.

Sure there were deviations from the books, and liberties taken here or there. The essence of what Tolkien was trying to say was, which is most important.

Visually it was stunning, I cannot recall anything like it in other films. The huge scope and sprawling world was right there on screen, for me to immerse myself. Whilst the FX were great, there were some moments of obvious CG which looked 'out of place' in this magnificent production. Always things you can do better next time.

NB: To the nitpickers mentioning that the action scenes felt rushed and blurred, I thought it emphasised the chaotic and manic nature of hand-to-hand battles. When was the last time you fought someone and stood absolutely still?

Finally, the film will not be everyones cup of tea, but it was mine just the way I like it. But what a ride.

See it and make your own mind up.

Many happy returns.

title: Peter Jackson Finally Has Something to Chew On
review:
The acting in _The Lord of the Rings_ is very good. The weak actors are strong, and the strong actors are wonderful. The writing is very good. The adaptation does enough of a job translating Professor Tolkien's work across media as to create a beautiful screenplay that feels very much like the original, which is more important than reflecting it (just ask Robert Fitzgerald). The scene design is very good. The sets and backgrounds are stunning; I have to think back to the original _Neverending Story_ to find a fantasy adventure film with as fresh and as beautiful fantasy settings. The sound design is very good. The sound editing is very good. The costuming is very good. The animation is very good, and its integration into the live action is very good. There are many parts of the craft of filmmaking, and this film does all of them well. However, all of these elements together would have only resulted in a very good film. _The Fellowship of the Ring_ is not a very good film. _The Fellowship of the Ring_ is a great film, or, rather, it is the beginning of what will be, upon its completion, a truly great film. The difference is in the direction. Here, the difference is Peter Jackson's vision and art as a director, and it is Jackson, above all, who deserves credit for putting together a wonderful piece of art.

The difference between a film with many, disparate and diverse virtues and a film which brings them all together with truly artful vision is profound. _Titanic_ is a film with many of the same virtues as _The Fellowship of the Ring_: sound, set, costumes, acting (okay, maybe not), writing (okay, okay, okay, definitely not), the film employed many of the best in the business, but the end product was a film that won a host of Oscars and ended up on the bottom of the Weekly Rental shelf at Blockbuster. The reason why _The Lord of the Rings_ will remain in the hearts and minds of those who have seen it for far longer is because of its coherence as a piece of art and the well-articulated and complex voice of the director, communicated with purpose and skill through all the media that film provides.

Sir Ian McCellan said, after completing the mammoth shooting schedule of this film that, as an actor, particularly as a film actor, he is not an artist. An actor acts; it is the director who must imbue the film with a vision. Peter Jackson's vision is a strong, distinct one that cannot help but burst forth on the screen. See _Dead Alive_ (_Braindead_) if you don't believe me, but only if you know you do not require sleep or sanity for a good 36 hours. It is a rampant beast of a film, assaulting the intellect, the psyche, and the eye with equal and determined vigor; it manages to conceal the obvious in terrible suspense and to juxtapose images of unparalleled depravity with those of terrible and hilarious simplicity. It manages to render the watcher powerless in determining the fate of the characters. Predictability and cliche simply cease to exist, because the force of his voice is enough to command the audience. _Dead Alive_ was a cheap horror flick. Here, Jackson wields the same tool in the translation of a powerful piece of intellectual and imaginative work, and the results are of such richness and power that I would definitely need to see the film two or three more times in order to appraise them fully.

Of course, to some, the three hours necessary to watch the film will be too much. The continually serious tone of the film will be discouraging. The unwillingness to gratify the audience with continual buildups in a string of one-lined, music-swelling climaxes (a la _Independence Day_ and the like) will be discouraging to some. Yes, there is complexity in the rising action, and I am overjoyed to say that the number of characters pumping their fists and shouting "Yes!" is truly inordinately small for a three hour adventure movie. Some people like that sort of thing. Heck, I like it from time to time. A bunch of years back, when I watched _3 Ninjas_ on a babysitting job, I enjoyed it. What casual watchers will confront is the fact that this is not an epic action movie. It's not even really an action movie, and if one goes into the film expecting an action movie, one is likely to not have that expectation met in full. Some people may find this frustrating. I do not deny that. However, I do believe that the beauty of this film is strong enough to overcome that frustration in all but the most dedicated and prejudiced of cases.

The action scenes in this are extremely well-crafted. Usually, in films of this scale, action scenes rampage across the scene, glutted with gory images and landed blows. Usually, armed conflict on film becomes a singular beast, where the individual characters are swallowed in the fury of the moment. This is true even in most high quality war films. This is not true in _The Lord of the Rings_. The violence in _The Lord of the Rings_ is in service to the drama, and that is a truly remarkable feat of directing. It is effortlessly clear who is being killed by whom at all times, and the violence is often placed against some far more important scene in such a way as to imbue the latter with a beautiful urgency. And, of course, Peter Jackson does violence as well as anyone in filmmaking, so, even though the PG-13 rating, with its prohibition of spurting blood, prevents Jackson from showing everything he learned in _Dead Alive_, the battles are brutal, deliberate, and largely devoid of romance (with a few brilliant exceptions). For some, this will disappoint. For those wrapped up in Jackson's vision, it all becomes part of the world and the journey Jackson is trying to bring to the audience.

If I must ennumerate the flaws of this film, the first is that, although the film does a good job of masking how abominable an actor Liv Tyler is, Liv Tyler is still an abominable actor, and her scenes are somewhat wasted, if not actively detracting from the film. The second is that the combination of CGI and bluescreen to create photorealistic composite images is overestimated, like it is in every single film in which it appears, and sometimes the characters exhibit a little fringe or the CGI characters move unrealistically. Of course, the overestimation is not of very great magnitude, and the special effects, as a whole, are excellent, but the audience will generally be more impressed by the camerawork than they will be with the CGI. Thirdly, there are two or three individual occasions where the film breaks its own character (I'm talking about any and all occurances of the notion of "dwarf tossing" as well as the single attempt at a Jerry Bruckheimer-style one-liner), but, of course, they only last for a second or two, so they hardly consist of a problem. The purist in me wishes the movie did not take such breaths, but, in Jackson's defense, the film is dreadfully serious, and that most of the audience probably needed a respite when these lines came along, which were generally at the grimmest moments in the film. And, of course, there are a few very minor continuity errors which will probably be corrected whenever the film is rereleased, if not for the DVD, but these are difficult to spot and generally do not affect the film.

All this notwithstanding, I saw this movie in a packed theater of two to three hundreds people. I sat right beside the door, and only four people left to go to the bathroom during the entire three hours, despite the occasional sound of running water. This film will capture your attention, and it won't let it go until it is done. This film will teach you something, take something from you, show you something you never knew you had, and all the other good stuff that anything that actually succeeds in being art can and will do. This film will make you say to yourself as you leave, "Why can't all the movies I see be good?" This film will make you see the hype for the empty gas it actually is. This film will make you realize just how little Harry Potter did to challenge you, and how depressed that made you. This film will probably make you want to read the books.

However, most importantly, this film will not make you regret spending $9 on it (or less, if you're lucky), which almost every other movie you will ever see will not be worth. Heck, for quality like this, you can even afford to spring for some popcorn! Seriously, see this movie in the theater. It really is that good.

And, if you need another reason, the Spider-Man trailer is awesome! It was the first time I've ever seen a film audience greet the end of trailer with a round of amazed applause.

title: Exactly what I've been saying all these years!!!
review:
For the last ten years I've been saying that Peter Jackson would do wonderful things if put behind the wheel of a 'blockbuster' movie.

To my mind, even his early exploiters demonstrated that he's one of the most imaginative and innovative film makers out there. He makes truly unique movies, has a great talent for putting money on the screen, and Heavenly Creatures went further to show Mr Jackson to be a very intelligent dramatist.

I haven't read Lord of the Rings. To be honest, I don't have much interest in Tolkein.

But this film was exactly what I've been waiting for this last decade. A Peter Jackson 'blockbuster'. What would happen? Would the money men take control of the project and leave it neutered? Would he get lost under this huge budget and not know what to do with it? Or would we end up with the diamond I'd hoped for?

I came out of the cinema gobsmacked.

Every tiny detail of Lord Of The Rings screams "THIS IS A PETER JACKSON MOVIE"

The visuals were stunning. The drama was good but not so thickly spread as to interfere with the overall pacing. We know all we need to know about the characters - enough to make us care - but Jackson never lets the movie slip into sentimentality, and for that we can all be thankful!

I had high expectations for Jackson's domination of mainstream cinema (something I really never believed would happen) and the result has far exceeded my expectations.

Great stuff!

title: Some things are better appreciated a second time round...
review:
December 19th @ 3:20am: hmm...is just me or was that just a trifle...dull?

December 20th @ 9:15pm: hmm...whatever was wrong with me? I like this film. Alot.

December 22nd @ 10:00pm: jeez...a third time and I still get water-eyed as Howard Shore's mournful music segues us from Boromir's death to a tearful Frodo, at river's edge, contemplating the immensity of his burden.

Depending, I suppose, on what sort of mood your in... Jackson's LOTR is a cup either half full or half empty. And, truly, though I've come to admire it greatly, the film does offer up some scandalously crude editing choices (particularly the river ride/orc montage, among others) and not a few questionable directorial ones as well (shooting ALL the battle sequences tight...even Isildur's death). But I will pardon Jackson et al because they are not representative of the whole, even if they do stick out like sore thumbs. Of course, I'm still under the assumption that a good many sequences were trimmed to the maximum to get the pic under 3hrs...which would explain the choppiness. Hopefully the DVD will remedy this. But, in reality, isn't that a dreadful thing to have to say. Still, there's no room in the marketplace for a 4 hour movie so its reincarnation on DVD will have to suffice.

Needless to say, the performances are uniformly excellent with Ian McKellen's Gandalf a sterling accomplishment and, should it seem odd to mention, an intoxicatingly radiant and unexpectedly accomplished Liv Tyler as the Elven princess, Arwen. Elijah Wood brings to Frodo the wide eyed wonder and weary of one caught up in a maelstrom. Almost angelic - he's beautiful when he cries. Vigo Mortenson as Aragorn brings a welcome return of chivalry back to the big screen; Cate Blanchett, as Galadriel, both ethereal and intimidating as one who knows her preeminance is soon to pass; Sean Bean, conflicted and ennobling, gives Boromir a level of pathos unmatched in the book; a surprising turn from Sean Astin, who would have guessed, as the redoubtable Sam Gamgee. And, finally, Ian Holm who, like McKellen imbues Bilbo with a degree of humanity rarely seen in the fantasy genre. Oh, and the Ring was very good too...

Technical credits are above par: the cinematography is ravishing. Howard Shore's score is sublime - a refreshing change of pace from the usual ersatz John Williams fluff, or John Williams for that matter. The CGI varies: from perfect to merely adequate but, hey, pixels aren't everything. But the art direction, set design and costuming are consistently stunning.

December 23rd @ 3:37am: Hmmm...I feel screening number 4 coming on!

title: Only somewhat disappointing
review:
I was expecting a movie worth an 8. I got a move barely worth a 7, so far. I believe many of the problems I had with the film will be fixed in the DVD. For instance, "Where did all of the events between the Shire and Bree go?!" The DVD will most likely contain those scenes and many other which were cut from the theater version.

Of what I did see, many of my favorite parts of the story were missing, such as the part mentioned above and the "Blindfolds" in Lothlorien. The biggest problem I had, though, was not a story problem. It was the poor cinematography. If I am going to pay over $8 to sit in an uncomfortable chair for 3 hours, I want to see something good. I want to see the results of a cinematographer and a director pushing the limits of their art, not just some nerds wagging their big, fast computer graphics in the air.

Some scenes were very well done though. The Balrog looked excellent and Gandalf's dialogue on the bridge was one of the few scenes which were dead on. This scene really makes me look forward to "The Two Towers" when we will see the battle of Helm's Deep and the Seige of Isengard where there should be tons of similarly well done CG creatures (Ents in this case) doing battle.

Overall it is a good movie that you should go see (hopefully without a bunch of screaming homophobes in the theater laughing the whole time Frodo and Sam are together), but don't expect to be thoroughly moved by the picture as a whole.

On a different note, the reaction of IMDB users to this movie really amazed me. As I write this it is 6 days after the film came out, and 9662 users have voted with over 78% of them voting 10. This has resulted in the film being rated as the #1 movie of all time. It is incredible. As history has shown, though, movies tend to move to more reasonable positions over time, such as The Matrix being in or near the top 10 when it came out but being #38 now. I believe this film will stay in the top 50, mabye even in the top 30 for quite a long while, but I would venture to guess that it will be out of the top 10 by Summer 2002.

Thanks for listening to my opinion,

Jarrod Lombardo

title: Cinematic Adaption of Books 1&2 Certainly Impresses.
review:
This film had been hyped up huge amounts by various people. So is it all it's cracked up to be? Well yes actually. Infact it's better than I expected. I'm not going to say it lives up to the hype because if wizards, orcs and the like have never done it for you before, then there's nothing here to convert you. If you do like mythic fantasy adventure type things then this is a must see.

The only other group of people who may not like the film are the diehards as there has been some changes and ommissions. But any film fan will realise that these have been nessecery. This, "The Fellowship of the Ring", brings to the screen the first two LOR books "The Ring Sets Out" and "The Ring Goes South" so even if your film is three hours long, you'll never get two books worth into it without some triming. The thing that did surprise me (but if I'd thought about it wouldn't have) was how most of the cutting and altering of material was from "The Ring Sets Out". Tom Bombadil, and the scenes he's in, are left out and other trimmings mean that the Hobbit's journey to Rivendell is now much shorter and is intercut with the growing dark menace. In fact whereas in the book it was a slow moving affair in the film we find we are rushed from A to B in no time at all. Subsequently when we reach the end of Book One we are not half way through the film. The other (major) change agin from book one is of course is that Arwen Undómiel now saves Frodo, not that this matters. Either this version of the scene or the one written in the book would have worked fine. It is purely because now you have to have the obligitory strong female in any film. Some people will moan about it but anything that gives Liv Tyler more screen time is fine by me.

Peter Jackson is on fine form directing this so called "impossible-to-make" film. All shots remain interesting and the New Zealand landscape is just amazing. I'm not usually impressed by landscapes but wow. The fast and frantic cutting together of the battle scenes make them at time hard to follow but they still impress. Music perfectly compliments the on-screen images and the film is perfectly cast.

In summary this film is fantastic and will entertain lots of people. As I said at the start of this (longer than intended) review if you don't like the sound of it please don't watch it. I'd hate to see lots of bad reviews from people who 'don't get it'. Likewise if you've made the book your life the changes will annoy you and you too should avoid. Everyone else sit back and enjoy.

5/5

title: Amazing! Awesome! Exactly as I pictured it would be...**SPOILERS**
review:
Going into this movie, having read the LOTR twice a long time ago, and the FOTR again just recently, and having seen the trailers, I was expecting the movie to be visually stunning, but was worried how Peter Jackson and crew could turn the epic novel (even just the first part of the trilogy) into a movie of only three hours. Well I needn't have worried. I was absolutely blown away.

I felt like everything I was watching was real, like I was right there watching it all unfold. The scenery was spectacular, the acting was intense and believable and the pacing of the events (with the going back and forth between the hobbits travels to Rivendell and Gandalf's capture and escape from Isengard and Saruman's creation of the Uruk-hai army) kept the story moving without getting too slow. The special effects were awesome and every scene was just as I had pictured it when reading the books - this in particular was very pleasing when watching the movie. The Shire, Bree, Rivendell, Isengard, Mordor, the Mines of Moria, the Bridge at Khazad-Dum, Lothlorien were just as I pictured they would be...

(Spoiler) It is also understandable that minor events such as the Barrow-wights and Tom Bombadil had to be cut out in order to fit the movie into just three hours. I can even forgive alterations in events such as Arwen rescuing Frodo at the ford, and the development of a romantic interest between Arwen and Aragorn. Even the somewhat goofy fight between Gandalf and Saruman was not too distracting. The trick that Peter Jackson was able to achieve was to keep the events moving along, thus not allowing these minor quibbles to become to annoying or distracting.

I give this movie the highest rating possible - it's the best Fantasy movie I have ever seen - and probably the best movie period. (I'm sure die hard Star Wars fans would disagree - I liked Star Wars, but I wouldn't rate any of the Star Wars movies anywhere near the LOTR - FOTR as far as Sci-Fi/Fantasy goes).

(Spoiler) Best Scene - Galadriel's reaction to her temptation of the Ring by Frodo. Don't take the kids - they'll have nightmares after seeing it....

title: A Lesson to Hollywood that Big Does Not Equals Bad
review:
This is my first comment ever for a movie, although i have previously read hundreds of them. I fell like a first time director doing his very first commentary in a DVD, i guess.

First of all i want to say that i loved Lord Of The Rings (LOTR). I've read the book some 12 years now (was it that long ago?). I'm not fanatic about it, but i liked it a lot. And for the general quality standards of fantasy that exists nowdays, it's still towers high and above all. Of course this book is the inspiration for all those tonnes of eroic epic quest-for-the-magical-amulet-or-whatever fantasy crap that is sold today. It ruined fantasy and made it guettizised. But is it truly Tolkien's fault? he just wrote a book that was his message to his children about the world has he saw it, and was writen while WWII was happening. He always denied that WWII had any influence on the book, but who can seriouly believe that? LOTR is a book about how the world is changing. Subtly that mensage come across, and it's a love letter to a time when things were easier and better, a longing for a pastoral past being ruined by modern industrialization. No wonder Mordor and Isengard are descripted as huges fountries. And those images are some of the greatest in the movie. It was the first that truly made me sense of awe that was so absent this year in movies. Truly the first battle in the movie prologue beetween the numanarians and the elves against the Sauron hords are great, but the industrial images made me remind all again what LOTR was about. Of course, the movie is mainly an entertainment feist, and in that it delivers totaly. I was very entertained,and what's better, was not treated as an imbecile for it, unlike Tomb Raider or Pearl Harbour. That movie brough back a true sense of wonder, the joy of discovering minute by minute a new region or aspect of this world, at the same time making me remember that long ago first read and also seeign it for the first time though my eyes. It's like all those images complementary to the text had gained live. The casting is dead right, no actor is miscasted, all are correct and they give greatperformances, never for once playing as if they were just making a kid's movie and nothing is to be taken seriously. Until now i totaly agree with the filmmakers choices and i think thatLOTR:Fellowship Of The Ring is the best entertaining movie of 2001. I know, with the lame competition that showed up this year it's not saying much, but in general i truly believethat this movie is a great one, and it will be remembered in the future,and it will be the comparison point to all the future fantasy movies. title: A decent film, but still disappointing. (spoilers)
review:
I watched this movie three times on opening day, starting with a midnight screening, and have very mixed feelings.

Visually, this is a gourmet feast; no question about it. The geographic youth of NZ, combined with an even-handed use of effects works tremendously well. Casting is for the most part dead-on, though I thought Galadriel and Celeborn were extremely disappointing. I loved Hugo Weaving as Elrond.

I really do think, though, that the ball was dropped in writing the screen play. Let me say that, yes, I am a bit of a Tolkien fanatic. It is probably impossible for that not to influence my views on the movie, but I have tried as much as possible to be fair.

Too many of the characters were simply dropped into the story with no real background or introduction. Merry and Pippin seem to serve as nothing more than comic relief. Hasn't the moviegoing public had enough of Jar-Jar and his ilk? Legolas and Gimli are dropped in to fill a quota established in the book. All I gained from the movie was that Legolas knows Aragorn, Gimli reallyreallyreallyreally wants to go through Moria and his dad is named Gloin; oh, they are both really good at killing orcs, too.

I also have some issues with the way Aragorn's royal lineage is introduced. You will have to excuse me as my first objection harkens back to the book, but Aragorn's ancestry is a secret and for good reason. Sauron is, understandably, not a fan of Isildur and his family, and actually believes he has successfully eradicated the line. The movie treats Aragorn's identity as common knowledge. That's problematic, for me at least. Boromir's reaction to Aragorn's identity is puzzling. He knows _exactly_ who Aragorn is and is apparently bitter at him for abandoning Gondor. Later, he asks if Aragorn has ever been to Gondor (the city of Minas Tirith, at least). This is almost contradictory and leaves me scratching my head. Aragorn leaving Gondor for a self-imposed exile makes for some potentially interesting stuff, but nothing else is said about the exile. I find that extremely frustrating.

Gollum is introduced as a player in the story in Moria. No problem with that. The way it is done, though... "Oh, look, Gollum's chasing after us and the Ring. Isn't that sweet..." Bwah?! No more Gollum, after that. This introduction smacks of nothing more than lipservice, no real enhancement of the story.

Personally, I think too much time was spent at Isengard -- time that could have been better used fleshing out characters and expanding the Council of Elrond; maybe explaining why Boromir made the trip to Rivendell?

The Lothlorien sequence was atrocious. Celeborn came off as petulant and effeminate and completely superfluous. Blanchet pretty much phoned in her performance as Galadriel. Of all things she reminded me of the drugged up Monty Burns in the Simpsons episode where Mulder and Scully investigate Homer's alien sighting. I think Lothlorien was included because it was the "safehouse" after Moria. Again, filling a quota established in the book. Oh, Galadriel's line, "He will try to take the Ring." That was just hamfisted. From Rivendell on, it was obvious that Boromir was set up as succumbing to the lure of the Ring. Unnecessary.

Aragorn having full knowledge of Frodo's decision to leave for Mordor alone strained credibility. "Have fun storming the castle!" The whole purpose of the Fellowship was to get Frodo to Mordor and destroy the Ring. I don't buy them quitting the way they did.

Finally, the lame one-liners.... Are these really necessary? I'll stick to addressing the biggest offender. Everyone is sitting at the council in Rivendell. Elrond declares the Fellowship and its purpose. The whole group is gathered in for a nice photo-op. The music is rising to a noble crescendo. Pippin asks "Where are we going?" I can hear the needle scratching across the record each time that line is uttered. You have a good, compelling scene with some power and nobility to it, and it is completely derailed by a cutesy oneliner. I don't get it.

The ball was dropped. This movie could have been a 9 or 10-out-of-10. The pieces were there. Instead, shoddy writing brings it down to a 7 at best. I find that inexcusable, considering the material, actors, and time with which they had to work.

title: Unsubtle
review:
Yes this film is visually impressive and quite grand. Some of the acting, especially Ian McKellen's rendering of Gandalf, is very good. I have no argument with the many parts of the original story that had to be compressed or trimmed in order to fit the material from the book into even a three hour movie.

However several fundamental areas of the story were changed in ways that are distracting and even distressing to one who has recently re-read the LOTR books--and that don't contribute to fitting the story in the time available or improve on or clarify it in the least.

For example Gandalf never revealed to Saurman that the Bilbo or Frodo possessed the One Ring. Gandalf was suspicious of Saurman's motives for long before the events of the story. Saurman suspected that Gandalf knew of the Ring and imprisoned him in an attempt to extract information and impede Gandalf's influence on events. Saurman didn't know of the Fellowship, it's mission or it's travels at the time they attempted the mountain pass and failed. It was the pure malice of the mountain that forced them to retreat and enter Moria. A better adaptation would have been to skip the attempt at the mountain pass entirely to save time in the film. Also, Saurman was never in direct league with Sauron, though he was beguiled by Sauron through his use of the Palantir and became the Dark Lord's unwitting agent. The film is overly willing to dispense with these subtleties of plot and dialog so it can make extra room for special effects and action scenes.

The Council of Elrond doesn't bear the even faintest resemblance to Tolkien's narrative, and is terribly muddled. This scene was so completely different and wrong that I won't even attempt a comparison.

The film's treatment of Galadriel's revelation to Frodo of how the One Ring would make her "terrible and worshipful" was unintelligibly overdone and lacked the subtlety of the original exchange--Galadriel was not severely tempted by the One Ring and mainly wanted to convey the danger it presented to her. What happened to Galadriel's revelation to Frodo that she wielded Nenya, one of the Three Rings of the Elves? "I pass the test" was her wistful expression of how she would prefer the fading of her Ring's power and her people over the twisting evil and terrible doom that the One would lay upon them, not that she had somehow overcome an unbearable temptation to take the Ring at the moment of their conversation.

I'm not simply griping out of plot purism. I would have been happier if the story was even more reduced, but managed hang together cleanly, found a manner of expression that conveyed something more akin to the spirit Tolkien's subtle storytelling, and spent more time on developing the characters, particularly the members of the Fellowship.

I have to admit though, I did like the Balrog.

title: this moview kicks ass
review:
I decided to write the review after the second viewing, which was a good idea because the movie hit me harder the second time around.

This may well be one of the best book to movie adaptations ever. Yes certain scenes are missed, but the movie loses little and the non book reader will not miss the loss.

Everything in the movie is near perfect, humble beginnings to wisened traveller - the movie simply rocks the modern Earth. Sure there are flaws, less character development than one might expect, even here I saw more of this the second time.

One word of warning this IS NOT Harry Potter. As a parent of a 9 and 6 year old I was amazed nay shocked at the number of kids under 10 at this movie with parents. By the time they had gotten through Moria the parents in front of me were covering up the eyes of their kid more times than he could see. And by the head lopping shot both parent were covering up the kids eyes. I made the comment "didnt see that in Harry Potter" ! [just loud enough for the parents to hear me]. The book is not for kids, neither is the movie.

I plan to see it at least a few more times. I saw Titanic 5 times and LOTR is way better.

title: All YOU NEED TO KNOW ABOUT LotR IN FIVE STATEMENTS
review:
1. They did a damn fine job translating it to film, especially this book which has been round for ages. FIlm and Lit. is definantly two differet genres, so you can expect it to be a little varied. Of course this is bad because most people already have the idea of how Middle Earth looks in their minds and that this is a story that shouldn't be changed or altered in any way, but alas, it still is wonderful.

2. The effects are better than you would think. Sure they still look shaky in lots of areas, but think about this. All those 80s movies you watch now that have horrible effects didnt look any better back then. And you can still watch and enjoy those movies. Effects unfortuanly can look good but never perfect, and its the same with CGI animation. Some people expect too much.

3. For those who havent read the series, or don't enjoy this kind of movie and think a lot of it was too vauge. Well let me tell you something. You have no imagination at all. Why does everything have to be laid out and explained for you in a film? Using your imagination wouldn't hurt, or even reading the hobbit or waiting for the rest of the films to come out. Again you expect too much, and then again this is why so many good films flop and are never touched again.

4. The makers poured their heart and soul into this film. It has been one of the films that have stood out in the past few years, and has actually been carefuly made and crafted. You can shout out a hll yeah to your Gladiators and Titanics, but in the LOTR we can see how careful they where to attempt to make it perfect. Unfortuantly i believe if JRR Tolkien was still alive he would disagree about the making of this film, but anything has to be better than that wretched cartoon.

5. All in all its good, its really good, it stands out, it surpasses many movies in a different kind of way. I dont believe in rankings of movies, but i do belive that this one is something special. It in no way should replace the book, in fact it should spark your ambitions to read it if you haven't yet. Above all if you have a strong imagiation,the film shouldnt overtake your current visions. The film is nothing more than an addictive to the book, and its a glorius film, with flaws of course, but you cant make everyone happy, and films will always have their flaws.

title: Enthralling
review:
It has been over thirty years since I first read The Lord Of The Rings. At the time I can distinctly remember reflecting what an incredible series of films this trilogy would make. I have had to wait all these years and you can be sure I was the first in line at the first showing last Wednesday. In one word I can sum up my experience as enthralling. For the uninitiated the movie would lose a lot of its punch but for us die-hard fans what a thrill to see finally on celluloid such an incredible world...such a real world....such a complex world. Who cares if a significant amount of detail was left out. For those familiar with the story it did not present a problem. For those unfamiliar, it still spins one heck of a story. I sat there for three hours and became totally engrossed in this world. And to think this work of fiction was completed 50 years ago!

This is what movie making is all about and I can't wait until part two comes out. In the meantime, I'll be back for repeated viewings and thankful someone had the vision and know-how to pull off the essential essence of what this entire story is all about. Great Christmas bonus!!!!

title: Fantastic!!
review: After waiting for many years and reading the wonderful novels many, many times, there is finally a movie.....and it is nothing short of fantastic. Normally the movie that follows a book will be a disappointment, but the producers, directors and casting agents (in addition to the prop/computer/model makers of course!) have done a great service by rendering the book, in all of its detail, true to the screen. This movie will surely take its place as one of the best movies to hit the screen anywhere, and anytime. Both fans of the Tolkien tradition and those that have not yet been introduced will find this film to be an adventure in the grandest scale!

title: Can't stop thinking about what I've seen
review:
When I first heard of Lord of the Rings being put on the big screen, I scoffed because I just KNEW it was going to end up as a horrible made-for-tv-type movie starring Kevin Sorbo or a 2 1/2-hour schmaltzfest with Danny DeVito and Sean Connery. It was neither. It was amazing. I haven't been this enthusiastic about cinema since the first Jurassic Park, and before that the Indiana Jones trilogy and Star Wars.

The wonderful scenes (brilliant and deftly composed) play in my mind and I scan my memory for more that I can relish: *spoilers* - The Ringwraiths, Sauron's "eye", Gandalf's innumerably subtle facial expressions, Gollum's eyes, the insects and spiders crawling away from the Rider as he peers over the edge of the road, The Mines of Moria, the fight in Weathertop - God I could go on, but I can't say much more than what so many other people have been saying about the movie. The only fault I've found in the movie is that it needs to be longer, and since the DVD will be out soon, we can all expect an expanded director's cut in the future ---- 10/10 - I love this film -----

title: No. 1 it is not
review:
For more than a year I've used the IMDB's top 250 movies of all time list as my 'canon' for great movies. And 95% of the time I agree fully with it and the ratings people collectively give the films on it. But this movie fits in that 5% that I just can't agree with. Don't get me wrong, I saw this movie the first day it came out, and was very enthusiastic to see it. My friends I saw it with had read all the books, but I had not. By this time it was #53 on the IMDB just from it's non-American release. And after seeing it I truly thought it was a great epic adventure. I thought "This is an instant classic. Sort of a second Star Wars trilogy (I don't count episode 1)." BUUUUUUUUUUT..... When I checked it's rating today, I was, well, just disappointed. THIS MOVIE DOES NOT DESERVE THE #1 SPOT ON THE IMDB LIST. It is a great movie, and never before had I enjoyed a whole 3 hour film like this, but their are a lot more films that are JUST SO MUCH BETTER! Schindler's List! Memento! The Usual Suspects! American Beauty! Pulp Fiction! American History X! Fight Club! Even The Matrix! These movies are all spectacular masterpieces that grip your mind and spirit, and blow LOTR away. It should also be noted that It's always been my view that The Godfather should not be #1 either, but should be right below The Shawshank Redemption. I can only hope that over the next few months the hype will diminish and FOTR will go to it's proper place somewhere in the teens or twenties. See this movie. Enjoy it. But do not forget that it is not perfect.

And it is DEFINITELY not deserving of the #1 place

title: Strikingly Inspiring
review:
So, I read the books in the 70's. More precisely, I read the Hobbit and the Lord of the Rings in the Summer between 3rd and 4th grade. I read them again a few years later. I am a fan.

I snuck into Star Wars when it first came out. I was 11. I still remember 'feeling the force' for weeks after that. The most impressive movie for an impressionable boy.

Where am I going with this?

The Fellowship of the Rings brings me back to the visual images I created for myself when, as a boy, I read the series. It brings me to a place where I can feel the importance of the journey that Frodo is forced out of honor, dedication, and fear to endure. I felt, while in that theatre, the same feelings that 27 years ago chilled me in an embrace that forced me to continue reading, late at night, with a flashlight under the covers. It may not have included every single detail of the novels and it may not have had the seamless effects that everyone craves, but it gave me everything that is required to journey back to Tolkein's world.

This movie is as good as Star Wars. This movie may not be the best written or the most seamlessly edited but it is important: Important in the way that a great story conveys a mood, a story, and a journey of imagination so poignant that for weeks after the experience one recalls, during the day or more importantly, the night; the feelings of desperation, fear, and awe that were part of the experience.

The feeling is true and the story is sound. I loved it and only by making it twice as long could those details that others complain about be corrected.

I loved it!

Bravo!

title: Pretty good film
review:
I have just seen FOTR tonight and have immensely enjoyed said experience! I can not understand how any adult who says that they have enjoyed Harry Potter over this superb film.

I have read all of the LOTR but was still on the edge of my seat for all the action / surprise sequences during the film. I could not expect a better film been made of a complex book. In my opinion people who are obsessed by the book should not watch the film as the imagination is always greater than any visual image on a celluloid film. The film is always going to leave parts out to make a smooth transition from book to film and it achieves it in a relaxed and enjoyable way. The film will also become greater with the next 2 chapters of the book. People who have not read the book I recommend watching the film a few times to take in it's details and intricacies that makes the film grow.

I await the next two films with anticipation.

david.

title: Stunning, value for money, a believable fantasy
review:
This is a visually stunning and thoroughly entertaining version of the classic novel. Oddly, none of the veteran actors steal the film (surprising, given the presence of Ian McKellen as Gandalf, Christopher Lee as Saruman and John Rhys-Davies as Gimli). Cate Blanchett makes a poor and uncharismatic Galadriel, with an almost husky voice (nothing like the melodic voice she is supposed to possess).

Apart from Sean Bean, who is perfect as Boromir (what did they feed this guy?), it is the new actors and actresses who shine. Elijah Wood makes a wonderful and sensitive Frodo, Billy Boyd's true Scottish accent makes for a warming Pippin and Sean Astin plays the Samwise Gamgee character as it was meant to be. Hugo Weaving makes a dark Elrond (he is a cross between his Agent Smith in The Matrix, Professor Snape in Harry Potter and the Scorpion King in The Mummy 2). Viggo Mortensen is a believable Aragorn, straight from the pages of the novel, and Liv Tyler makes a surprisingly good and likeable Arwen, with an elevated role. I hope she appears in the next 2 films. I also can't wait to see Andy Serkis in the next film as Gollum.

The scenes are beautiful, not least Hobbiton itself, though Galadriels' forest scene was rushed and it is shame the Barrow Downs were left out. Moria is chilling, though the Balrog encounter could have been better choreographed. The fight sequences are excellent, particularly the Sauron Battle at the beginning of the movie. The photography is wonderful.

The music is, sadly, not memorable. There is an inevitable Carol Orf-style battle theme and, even though other music was provided by Enya, I feel the film was let down a little here. A hobbity theme music with pipes and lyres would have gone down well.

Don't get me wrong - I loved the film. My criticisms are minor and I would easily rate this a 10 out of 10. For value for money, this 3 hour epic is simply unbeatable and the only real downside is the 12 month wait for part 2.

title: A rampaging epic that will stand next to Star Wars for all time!
review: This is the best movie of the year. Forget about AI. Forget about Memento. Forget about the box office blockbusters that deserve to have stones thrown at them. We have gone through a rough year at the movies, and at the very end, when we think that we have been totally jipped, along came the genius Peter Jackson and his historic masterpiece, The Fellowship of the Ring.

title: Pinnacle of cinematic achievement.
review:
The greatest film in the history of the art of cinema.

Breathtaking.

It's been out 4 days, and I've seen it 3 times already, including the first showing in the UK.

Usually I never see a film again until it's released on DVD, and what's more I'll be seeing LotR again quite a few times yet before its run in the cinema is over.

title: Reasonable, but far from perfect.
review: Before I explain why I don't think this is worthy of much of the praise it's been given here, I'll point out that I haven't read any of the Lord Of The Rings books, so that may affect my judgement. The main reason I didn't like the film much was that I don't think many of the characters were very well developed. Once the fellowship was formed, it seemed that I was supposed to sympathise with the members, when there was barely any information given about them. From then the film became repetitive, moving from one fight sequence to the next, with emotional interludes that didn't involve me much. I lost most sense of excitement at the battles because in many cases we didn't know anything about the adversary - the name of something was mentioned and a fight began with little explanation. There were good points to the film - generally good acting, great scenery and special effects. Many films would get away with a procession of action set-pieces, but I don't think this does, because most of the fights are not well filmed. There are fast cuts and camera movements, presumably intended to make it feel more exciting, but I felt they simply confused and reduced the freedom to watch what was actually meant to be going on. My enjoyment of this film may have been affected by the huge hype. If I hadn't been expecting so much, I might've liked it simply as a fun sequence of battles and scenery. As it is I can say it was not bad, but I certainly don't reccomend it highly. The final thing that disappointed me was the ending. I know it's leaving it open for a sequel, but I still think the ending was disappointing. For a film with a sequel already planned, there should at least be something which appears to be an ending, or there should be a cliffhanger. Fellowship Of The Ring just seemed to stop in a random place. 5/10

title: A wonderful experience roll on next December
review: Having read the book two or three times, how could one hope for a director to get such good detail into a film just three hours long. The Hobbits were wonderful, so realistic, the scene as you entered Hobbiton for the first time brought a lump to my throat.I felt I had been there, it was so familiar. The New Zealand scenery was stunning, the mines of Moria stunning, however it wasn't just about visual effects, the performances by Gandalf, Aragorn, Boromir, Frodo, Sam all were stunning and at times so captivating and emotional. I sat there at the end of the film wishing my life forward to December 2002.

title: in 3 words...: "WOW,WOW,WOW"
review:
after seeing lord of the rings twice in a single weekend i am left speechless...

after watching it for the 1st time i could only count the seconds till i got to watch it again...

this movie is amazing on so many levels,most of the viewers will undoubtedly stall over the eye popping f/x and/or the battle scences (especially the one in the begining of the movie,which is frightfully short & yet manages to capture you instantly)...

i for one stalled on the magnificent attention to detail. while it is true that the film ad-libs A-lot of the book it manages to remain VERY close to the spirit of the original(with the above mentioned slight varations),but what caught my eye was the simple fact that for the first time (in my mind at least) elves looked the way that elves are supposed to look,same for the hobbits and orcs and every other creature for that matter,heck...even gollum looked the way i pictured him...i mean the attention to detail gets so sickening when you actualy get to see that hobbits have hairy feet!!! i would have never thought they would pay that much attention to it,let alone show it on-screen...

title: Endlessly Fascinating
review: The first installment of The Lord of the Rings trilogy arrived amid so much hype and anticipation, I did not possibly think it could live up to it's own lofty expectations. However, within the first ten minutes of the movie, I was proven wrong. It is, without question, the single most enjoyable movie experience I have ever had. Now, I must admit that I was already familiar with the Tolkien and the inhabitants of Middle-Earth, having read the trilogy several times. It has been noted by others reviewing this film that it is not a perfect adaptation. That is true and it is perfectly fine with me. Adapting any book to film oftens changes the overall feel of the story and leads to some creative changes. Adapting this particular book, which is filled with some of the most creative characters and situations ever printed, must have been even harder.  Director Peter Jackson and company got it right on this one. I would suggest fans (or fanatics) of the book approach the movie as an entirely different entity from the book. I don't think even the most die-hard fan could be disappointed in this film. You'll want to pin your eyelids open and allow your eyes to soak up every second of the wonderful visuals. Jackson shot the movie in impossibly beautiful New Zealand and then added to that the best CGI scenery and effects I have ever seen. Ian McKellen, and Ian Holm, (who are great in everything), are amazing here as Gandalf the Grey and Bilbo Baggins respectively. Elijah Wood does a nice job as Frodo and I suspect we will see more out of him in the sequels as Frodo's roll is expanded. The rest of the cast including: Sean Astin, Viggo Mortensen, Liv Tyler, Kate Blachett, and Sean Bean are also top notch. The original music by Howard Shore becomes a character of its own. Take the time and escape to Middle-Earth, and enjoy this film. Just don't, for the love of God drink a Biggie-sized Coke while you do. At nearly 3 hours, the last hour can be tough, especially when they keep showing so much water on the screen!

title: In defense of the fighting
review:
I have read Lord of the Rings only once, about ten years ago, but am quite familiar with the whole realm of Middle Earth from childhood readings of The Hobbit and so forth... so for me it was great to see the whole thing brought to life. Even the CGI, unlike recent installments of Star Wars, didn't let it down. Die-hard fans of the novel have their own issues - if you can't handle the fact that it doesn't adhere to every single punctuation mark in the book, simply don't go and see it - but for those people who had previously believed that the book was the preserve of fey hippies, Stonehenge types and spotty schoolboys, this adaption shows it to be a much earthier and gutsier (and darker) tale than many of its fans may let on.

In defense of the fighting, to compare it to The Matrix or Crouching Tiger is to miss the point. Those two films are centred around the grace and fluidity of very precise martial arts skills; they're show-cases for almost balletic action. Lord of the Rings is closer to films like Braveheart or even, in a different context, Saving Private Ryan. You are not supposed to gasp at the skill of the fight choreographer, you are supposed to *feel* the fighting - confusion and half-seen glimpses are a well-worn technique for portraying a combatant's-eye-view of battle which the protagonists have no control over, the terror and mayhem of warfare rather than the grace and skill of martial artists in full control of the game.

Apart from a slightly slow bit in the Council of Elrond, a great piece of cinema - can't wait till Christmas 2002!

title: Surprisingly, no Amazingly, well done.
review: The film makers did a genuinely splendid job on this first installment on the saga. The only film adaptations of great novels that  are in the same league, IMHO, would be Apocalypse Now and Gone With The Wind. And neither had to face up to the passionate following of this one. FotR manages to squeeze in virtually every important element of the book, while its breakneck pace, and clear narrative makes a nearly three hour running time practically unnoticeable. The special effects manage that knife-edge balance that lets you simply experience the reality of the story which we've seen in 2001 and Star Wars: A New Hope. It avoids the problems of an Independence Day or Phantom Menace where your enjoyment of the story is molested by all the "Gee Whiz" moments. But what really makes this film stand out among blockbuster-type films is the acting. These guys are good, and are allowed to be good. There is no scene-chewing in the action-filled scenes, and more importantly, the quiet times are crafted just as meticulously, and treated as the important moments they are, rather than as the simple, wooden exposition that infests most of even the best action adventures.

title: WOW!! MOVIE OF THE CENTURY!
review: wow, where can i start about this absolutely AMAZING movie?? The plot? The special effects? The scenery? The character? A SOLID 10 for EVERYTHING!! I strongly recommend everyone to see this movie. Whether you like action, romance or adventure... I thought this was going to be a guy thing but was I WRONG!! title: Brilliant
review:
It is, one would think, impossible for a movie with this level of anticipation and expectation associated with it to actually achieve any sort of respect. How can it but fail? Making a movie from one of the deepest, most intricately woven stories of the last century seems like a effort in futility. You cannot possibly fit everything in, and without everything, the film will be less and the experience will disappoint. Right?

Maybe not. A perfect example of how this film plumbs the depth of Tolkien's masterpiece can be found in the short introductory sequence at the start of the film. We see a shot of Bilbo, upon finding the ring, or putting it in his pocket. All things considered, to someone who has not read the Hobbit, this might seem like an odd waste of 3 seconds of film. Why show it?

But to those of use who know the tale, that briefest of shots is enough to incorporate the entire riddle game that Bilbo and Gollum played, and freshens your memory of Bilbo's all important POCKET.

The story has been altered somewhat. The time line in particular undergoes a rapid acceleration. Those 17 years from Bilbo's party to Frodo's departure? Not there. In essence though, the tale is there in all its grandeur. The characters I've known most of my life simply step off the page and onto the screen. The only character with any significant change is Arwen, and her changes make her, frankly, a more interesting character than she was. Well, at least more interesting from the point of view of a film.

My only minor (very minor) complaints are with the elves and the appearance of Rivendell and Lothlorien, which somehow come off looking a little too much like an outlet mall in a trendy resort area. Otherwise, the film is as close to perfect as I could have imagined it being without being 9 hours long.

title: A Worthy Adaptation
review: I'll keep this short as many people have already expressed my exact opinions. This is a superb adaptation of the ABRIDGED Lord of the Rings.The casting, location and much of the feel of the book is perfect, and while I agree the Fellowship weren't introduced strongly at all during the Council of Elrond, I do believe that on average many of the characters showed a much greater depth than the relatively flat characters in the book. However, it is widely known that the story and novel itself were simply a means of Tolkien bringing his fantasy mythology and love of language to an audience.But in a film showing to a popular audience character and defined plot and structure are essential. Well Done to Peter Jackson and his crew for bringing this story to a commercial audience in the form of a commercially structured film, and hopefully it will inspire generations who would never even have considered reading a "thick book" to pick it up and experience the complete Lord of the Rings

title: A great movie, but it still was lacking...
review:
Let me just state for the record that I have not read the LOTR books, though I really want to. Therefore I have nothing to measure this movie up to (as far as how it relates the books).

Let me start by saying that this was a very good movie. The action sequences were incredible (the fight in the mines was simply fantastic), and the special effects were amazing. I do like the story, the acting was great, and the cinematography was better then expected.

All of this has been said by plenty of people before, so there's no use in rehashing why the movie is good. Therefore, what follows is my critique about its failings.

There are three to be precise. First of all, I did think that the movie dragged on a bit in certain points. I understand that the movie has a lot of background and character development to do, but I found myself shifting in my seat on more then one occasion.

Secondly, I didn't like the way that 9 people could so easily cut through several armies of orcs and goblins. The whole story is built upon how the elves, dwarves, and humans would be toast when Sauron came to power, but they seem to have no problems with the enemy. Just send 20 guys in and they appear to be more then enough to kill thousands of orcs. The Ring Wraiths were turned away by a single human in one encounter, and a single elf in another. That doesn't inspire fear...

Third, the ending leaves a lot to be desired. Why did Frodo decide that he did not want to travel with the Fellowship anymore? How come the ending showed that the Fellowship does not work? It left me thinking that SOME kind of event should have happened. Yes, I know its a trilogy, but so was Star Wars, and they were able to destroy the Death Star in the first movie. Especially since part two is a year away.

With all of those short-comings, I cannot give this movie a rating higher then 7/10. Perhaps the next two will improve this.

title: Great, Great Movie
review:
Let's get one thing straight. This is a three hour and fifteen minutes long movie. They cannot fit everything from the book into a movie of this size, and to lengthen would make it cumbersome and completely alienate anyone who has not read the books. Someone unfamiliar with the story already would watch the Tom Bombadil sequence (FYI, this sequence is not in the movie), and wonder, "Why?" Sure, some things could have been done differently, but one has to feel the sweat forming on their brow when the always wonderful Ian Mackellen comes on screen as Gandalf. Seeing the character being embodied on the big screen. I have heard little gripes like, "Why not call him Gandalf the Grey?" Well, if you'll remember, in the books no one really refers to him as such except for the narrator and off and on some characters refer to him as such if they have no personal connection with him. Plus, how odd would it be if Frodo said, "It's safe, isn't it Gandalf the Grey?"***WARNING SPOLIERS AHEAD**** Or, when Gandalf falls into the pit at the Bridge of Kahzad-Dum, if they yelled out, "Nooooo, Gandalf the Grey!!" See my point.

You have to take this adaptation for what it is, and what it is is a good old swords and sorcery flick with excellent acting, great plot, great characters and awesome visuals. Not to mention a score that would rival John Willams' for Star Wars. Jackson has brought to life the world all Tolkien readers know and love. He has taken great care in having Hobbits run around barefoot, even including the gift of Mithril Chain Mail from Bilbo to Frodo. A story inclusion that could have been completely cut. But it wasn't. Scenes like these were meant for the fans. Did Frodo really have to wake up and go to the mirror with Galdriel? Of course not, Jackson could have left that on the editing room floor as well. But he didn't. I say count your blessings, because this is simply the most stunning visual representation one will ever see of Middle Earth and all it's inhabitants.

The only thing that I have to fault with the film is two things. A few things could have been included that weren't, and some of the Fellowship aren't quite as developed as one would like. But also think of this. This is only the first film of a TRILOGY! Think people, there will be around 7 more hours of film left to make Gimli, Legolas, and Merry and Pippin more interesting. (Side Note: After seeing what was done with this film, I cannot wait to see what they did for the battle for Gondor in Return of the King.) And the things that weren't included will probably be picked up off the cutting room table for the DVD coming out next year, so just calm your selves down. (Note: The DVD's may come in two versions, one as a regular set with the theatrical movie and special features and one as a two or three DVD set with both the theatrical AND a Director's cut. Again, this is just my guess, DON'T START SPREADING RUMORS!!!!)

But the movie that we have for now is virtually flawless. And the flaws you may find within are extremely exscusable. Forget the fact that the acting is brilliant, the special effects are mind-blowing, that the visual representation of the world will blow you away, and you have a awesome experience. Just the feeling a fan will get when seeing the opening scenes will be worth the price of admission, and a feeling he/she will never forget. Go see it. You'll love it. You may not like a few things they did, but you will forgive them in the long run and be singing praises for Jackson and his heroic team by the time the movie's credits roll.
