review: I have never been much of a person that liked the world of elves, dwarves, orcs or wizards, but this movie sure changed my mind.  The only time I've seen these sorts of things, was from Warcraft (video game by Blizard Entertainment) and although I liked the game, I never really got into the whole thing behind it.  I had many friends online that were into elves and fairy tale type things, and I just didn't understand.  Now I am one of them. This movie couldn't have been better than my mind would have let it.  When it started out, everything was dark, and we were forced to listen, but we were treated to a back story.  I'm glad that was there for the people like me who haven't read the novels or anything like that.  I DID get to see a video that my friend had, and I enjoyed that, since I didn't really know what was going on.  It was interesting hearing them talk about things that happened in the video I saw. I was hooked to every part of the movie, and I couldn't look away.  There could have been a fire right behind me, and I wouldn't even know, unless they shut the movie off. The only problems I had with the movie is the fact that the theatre screwed up, and when the second reel started, it was upside down and backwards. There was a half-hour delay after that.  The only other thing was the sudden ending.  I guess they can do that, since there ARE two other movies coming, but I just didn't really see it coming. I'll have to suggest you see this movie, it's really good!  I enjoyed seeing all the actors I know in this movie, but I regret not seeing Brad Dourif. I'll have to catch him the second time around.

title: Middle Earth is alive...and why some people love to hate it.
review:
[Caution: may contain spoilers. You have been warned.]

In film, there exists, always, a certain sense of denial, when it comes to big screen literary adaptations; to say that a movie, any (adapted) movie is "true to the book ", is absurd. To directly transplant a novel to the local megaplex is impossible, and there are constant reminders of what can happen should you fail (remember Battlefield Earth? A two-thousand page book cannot be transposed into a movie with a total runtime of 117 minutes; too much will be lost in the story, and in ticket revenues.) And " The Lord of the Rings " is no exception. To Xerox " The Fellowship of the Ring " into a movie would be comical. The film would be 5-7 hours long with too much focus on sensory background. A film must be retouched for film, because film is a visual art form, while the written word is left more to the imagination. They are not interchangeable.

Tolkien's " The Lord of the Rings ", a whimsical adventure into the land and the hearts of those that inhabit Middle Earth, is considered by many to be one of the finest literary works of the 20th century, and therefore since its conception, has been awaiting a movie deal (and aside from the choppy 1978 cartoon, it waited.)

The first chapter of the Lord of the Rings, " The Fellowship of the Ring ", has just taken this step, and it is one of the best transitions of this sort in history, on par with The Godfather, and a narrow foothold higher than Gone With The Wind, but that doesn't make it a carbon copy of the novel. Most of the songs and poetic interludes have been cut out, certain passages, like the Hobbits' encounter with Tom Bombadil in the Old Forest, and the discovery of the Trolls from Bilbo's escapades in " The Hobbit ", are missing entirely. On the other hand, changes were added to help make the film move more smoothly, like Arwen's delivery of a wounded Frodo to Rivendell, and the unusual ending, which intermeshed the end of " Fellowship ", with the beginning of the second chapter of the saga, " The Two Towers. "

In the end, however, this matters not, because most of the people whom this will bother are the Tolkienites, who can never be completely pleased, because they each has a different perception about what each thing in Middle Earth should be like. And aside from everything else, The Fellowship of the Ring is a simply enchanting cinematic experience, with a scope and vision that hasn't been seen since Star Wars, and a well crafted story that would put the most gifted scriptwriter to shame. Brimming with action sequences rivaling Braveheart and Saving Private Ryan in their magnitude, and shot with intense care that puts you in the shoes of Aragorn, or Legolas, or whomever is battling it out with the forces of evil at the moment (and the forces of evil are truly that, thanks to the special effects crew: whether its the fiendish Orc-soldiers, or the enhanced Orc race, the Uruk Hai, the once innocent Stoor, Gollum, who slithers like snake in pursuit of his " precious ", and the most grandly designed creature of them all, the Balrog who haunts the caverns of Moria.)

All in all, Peter Jackson's first installment of " The Lord of the Rings ", is wondrous achievement that will remain a classic for years to come, and has (more importantly) done the epic novel justice.[Caution: may contain spoilers. You have been warned.]

title: Despite some problems, a great film
review:
"Fellowship of the Ring" is a great movie. Yes it has a few problems, but do a few corny CGI shots really detract from a good movie? I don't think so.

I have seen a lot of complaining from people about characters being cut out, or changed, or undeveloped. I can agree that it might be hard to understand the relationships between some of the characters, mostly between all of the hobbits. However, Gimli and Legolas have a very complex relationship, but this doesn't begin to manifest itself until the second book, and so, the second movie. I thought that the view that Elves and Dwarves don't get along was covered well at the Council of Elrond. I also see the feud simmering between Aragorn and Boromir, in that Boromir really has no interest in Aragorn's standing.

As far as the rest, I have no problem with the omissions of Tom Bombadil and Glorfindel, two characters from the books. The only important thing that happens with Bombadil is the hobbits pick up their swords, which was handled easily enough by Aragorn. And Glorfindel finds the hobbits and Aragorn heading to Rivendell and lets Frodo use his horse to get there faster, and then vanishes from the story. Now we have Arwen carrying Frodo, establishing a character that does show up later in the story. She doesn't have a big "Xen-arwen" fight like fanatics whine about, she just rides as fast as possible to get away from the Ringwraiths, JUST LIKE FRODO IN THE BOOK!

The only problem I really have is, where did all the companions come from, anyway? If you haven't read the books, you have no idea why they came, or where from. As is, they just seem to happen to be there at the right time (which really isn't far from the book, but still leaves a lot unanswered)

It is hard for me to be objective however, because I am such a fan of the books. I know the answers to the plot-hole questions, so some probably won't even occur to me-I just fill in the blank automaticaly.

Still, this as is close as I can imagine anyone could come to making this story well, and think Peter Jackson and Company did a superb job. Thanks, and way to go guys!!! If you like fantasy or drama or swordfighting or anything else, go see this. Get up now and go see it!

title: On the mark!
review: It was with more than a little trepidation that I sat down to watch this latest adaptation of the greatest book I've ever read. The trailers and commercials had made me very nervous. It looked like it might be a modern action adventure flick with lots of smart aleck lines and cartoon violence (never mind a plot or drama!) but I was wrong thank the Vala! Indeed it was true to the spirit of the book very much of the time and all the alterations and variations were generally necessary and well integrated. Thankfully a good bit of Tolkien's classic dialogue was incorporated. (Alas, some of the Alas' and ere's seem to have been dropped) The weakest part of the film was where they had cut out the chapters of Bombadil. The lack shows. Between the Shire and Rivendell are the poorest scenes. Also the action scenes were all vastly amplified and elaborated upon which I am somewhat ambivalent about. The action comes in books II and III! But enough nit picking! It was awesome. I could go on with further superlatives but you get the idea. :)

title: The best film for many years
review:
The responsibility, nay fear, of tackling a project like Lord of the Rings must have been nearly over overwhelming for Peter Jackson, when faced with this kind of film Directors often tend to stick religiously to the source material or they just fluff it completely. And yet this film manages to both be different enough from the book that it works cinematically while also leaving diehard fans of the novel ecstatic.

The film screams epic from start to end, with a multitude of wide-angled shots to leave you breathless, the film looks stunning throughout and does well to portray Middle Earth as a living breathing and believable place, everything just looks right. Places such as Rivendell and the halls of Moria are stunning and location shooting is mixed with CG to stunning effect.

The music is stably operatic, it's used masterfully throughout to heighten tension and emotion.

The acting too is almost consistently excellent Ian McKellen plays a superb Gandalf full of strength along with age and wisdom and that bit of quirkiness that fans of the novel know so well. Ian Holme has Bilbo as a wonderful mix between a skittering Hobbit and someone haunted by life. The entire fellowship hangs together well though Gimli comes off a bit `Scotty' and is therefore a bit more amusing than he necessarily should be especially since humour is already well taken care of by Merry and Pippin.

Essentially the film is an Action orientated drama and many of the quieter scenes from the book are omitted in order to do justice to the real crowd pleasers, and justice is indeed done, the scene with the Balrog is from begging to end one of the greatest moments in cinema history, it's powerful dramatic and emotional and leaves audiences stunned, and there are great scenes like this throughout, the ringwraiths approaching the hobbits, the chase on horseback, the battle a the end with Boromir all of them captivating.

This emphasis on action does have a few drawbacks however, Rivendell it hardly seen beyond the council of Elrond and fails to come over as the accommodating place it is in the novel, the greatest injustice however is to Lorien which comes off as a somewhat fearful place rather than one which turns even Gimli into an admirer of elves, speaking of which much of the fellowships character is lost and the strange love-hate friendship between Legolas and Gimli is not played upon.

These are minor quibbles however, much of what was cut eg. Tom Bombadil is not missed and what is in the film is uniformly excellent, over three hours there was not one moment I particularly disliked and there were a countless number of times I was simply blown away. This is the best film for many, many years and easily rivals the greatest films ever.

title: Thank you, Peter Jackson, for bringing Middle Earth to life.
review: As one who knows the trilogy almost by heart, I appreciate how Jackson has rendered Middle Earth and awakened the characters. The changes necessary for the film version were wise and sensitive to the original. I'll get the DVD version as soon as possible so I can play it over and over. Waiting for parts II and III will be very difficult.

title: Excellent! Well worth the wait.
review:
This is one of the best movies I've seen in years, maybe ever. The story remains faithful enough to the book so that you aren't thinking about how it's different here and there, yet isn't so full of "too many" details as to be boring. This movie is fast-paced, despite it's 3 1/2 hour run time. Of course, I imagine it helps to have read the book(s) or at least be familiar with the story, but I've heard from people that haven't read them that they also thought it was a fantastic flick.

In addition to the wonderful effects and excellent pacing, the casting of this film was no less than perfect. I have to admit that when I first heard Elijah Wood was to be Frodo, I was quite skeptical. However, I now have no doubt as to his perfection for the role. All the roles seem to have been perfectly cast, with my favorite being Hugo Weaving as Elrond. I would never have thought of him myself, and yet I cannot picture anyone else as Elrond. He is EXACTLY as I always imagined Elrond to be - EXACTLY. In addition to perfect casting, the acting itself is superb. I never saw the actors, just the characters brought to real, live-action life.

It's a shame that we have to wait for the follow-up movies, but if they are this good, they will be well worth the wait.

Definitely a KEEPER!

title: An artful film rendering of a literary masterpiece
review:
I was introduced to JRR Tolkien in the 1970's at the ripe old age of 30. I read The Hobbit and The LOTR trilogy as a bookseller for the Logos Bookstore chain. The adventures of Bilbo, Frodo, Gandalf and gang kindled a love for Fantasy Adventure stories I did not know I had. My love for these books and respect for Prof. Tolkien was passed on to my kids (now grown).

On Wednesday, 12/19, the 3 of us got together and saw LOTR - The Fellowship of the Ring. What a marvelous experience! Peter Jackson's reendering of Tolkien's masterpiece did not disappoint us. True, there were a few lovable scenes omitted (i.e. Tom Bombadil) and Arwen's role was expanded (more screen time for Liv Tyler?), but the changes from the book did not detract from our enjoyment of the film.

Adapting a novel to the screen will never be a perfect process. Novels and Film are different means to the same end - tell a story that the readers/viewers will find enlightening and enjoyable. Mr. Jackson and company did as good a job adapting LOTR to film as my family and I could have hoped for.

The casting was superb! I never expected Elijah Wood to bring life to Frodo as well as he did. A pleasant surprise there! Ian McKellan is now forever etched in my mind as Gandalf. Sean Astin played awkward but devoted Samwise Gamgee superbly. My last viewing of Mr. Astin's work was in the film "Rudy" where he played another awkward but devoted role. AS an actor, he has matured significantly since 1993. Viggo Mortensen played Strider/Aragorn was understated excellence. I last saw him in "28 Days" as a Baseball pitcher in a rehab clinic. I was afraid they would cast a musclebound hunk (ie Arnold) for this role and was a bit skeptical when Mr. Mortensen was cast. My compliments to him for his performance.

I was in awe of the convincing scenery and sets. I do not think that filming in England would have been appropriate. I cannot imagine Prof. Tolkien looking out his bedroom window and writing about what he saw when he described Middle Earth in his novels. The vistas in New Zealand matched the images created in my mind far more exact than England's would have.

The CGI effects are almost indistinguishable from the live sets. My only minor disappointments here were the long range views of Rivendell and surrounding gorge, and the Fireworks shots in the Shire. Otherwise, the CGI effects definitely deserve an Oscar nomination.

All in all, LOTR is the best Fantasy movie and literary adaptation I have watched in many years. In time, it will rank up there with Wizard of Oz, E.T., and the first three Star Wars movies. Not only will today's young people watch the films and read the books, but they will pass on these immense pleasures to their kids....and probably generations to come.

Well done, Peter Jackson, cast and crew!!!

review:
This was a great movie. Period.

The character development, granted, was not as much as that in other movies, but remember that this is the first third of a TRILOGY. Remember, the Empire Strikes Back had a heck of a lot more character development than Star Wars.

The action scenes were breathtaking. Since the Matrix was released, most action scenes have been pretty much the same. The action in this movie, however, is a little more old-school.

Also, for those of you complaining about how high the user rating for this movie is... It's rating from the top critics is 97% positive, so don't be so shocked. Also, don't assume Tolkien fans are stacking the vote. This is a GREAT movie, people. Not perfect, no. But darn close.

title: A fine but flawed film
review:
For anyone who does not want to read a long report on a strangers feelings about this film - don't bother reading this review.

I felt overall that although there were a few important defects in this film - the good that was in it very much outweighed the bad. Unfortunately - when the film did go wrong, it did so in fairly spectacular style.

The two scenes with which I have huge quibbles with were unfortunately - two scenes which I deem to be extremely important. The first of these was the Council of Elrond - which was I'm afraid, a shambles. I didn't want a complete parrot of the books text - but in this case, it would have been far superior to what was done. There was no real sense of the huge importance of this Council - or what anyone was doing there - Gloin (or Gimli - it doesn't matter which does it) never explained his presence there - a seeking of council from Elrond as to what should be done with the black rider that had visited the dwarves three times, seeking Baggins and the ring.

Legolas just appeared - without bringing the news that Gollum had escaped from Mirkwood - although this is less important. The only one I felt given any justice there was Boromir - although I do not remember him as being so outraged at the revealing of Aragorn as Isildur's heir. However - let that pass. The massive fight that ensued however was terrible, a bad idea - although it set up quite nicely the distrust between dwarves and elves - maybe too well, as it is difficult to see how Gimli and Legolas will strike up their great friendship.

The second really bad moment of the film was Lothlorien and the Mirror of Galadriel. I have heard great praise for Cate Blanchetts performance - I thought it to be awful, lacking in any subtlety and giving no indication as to the power of the three elvish rings. If the one ring goes into the fire of Mt. Doom, then Lothlorien, and all things made with the power of the three Elvish rings will fade. This was never explained.

These were the only large quibbles I had with scenes. Character wise - most were done exceptionally well - I thought Vigo Mortensons slightly unsure Aragorn to be slightly more interesting then the one in the book - Sean Bean was magnificent as Boromir as were Ian McKellen, Elijah Wood and Ian Holm. Gimli was a non-entity for this film - however this may change as he has much more time in The Two Towers. Merry and Pippin were done quite nicely - although I think it a mistake to have them joining by accident - they knew full well what they were doing and where they were going. This is however unimportant.

Lurtz - was appalling. A character created for the film - and when he was on screen, I felt myself wondering whether I was watching Lord of the Rings or Predator 3. Never mind.

On the whole this was an exceptional film, directed and shot beautifully by Peter Jackson - and he can recieve full credit for a film which on its own, is a masterpiece. Only when compared with the book does it start to come slightly short. I wait in eager anticipation of The Two Towers.

To all those who (somehow) have been bothered to read this incredibly boring review to the end - thankyou.

title: One of the Best
review: Has some part where fans of the books can nit-pick, but even so among the most entertaining movies ever.  The sets are awesome, the action is great, it is well acted, and even with some humor.  Liv Tyler is worthless, but she is only on screen a couple of minutes.

title: Sheer brilliance
review:
It isn't one of the greatest sci-fi/fantasy films ever  it is the greatest. It beats Star Wars to a bloody pulp, and I really like Star Wars.

Warning you now, this review is full of SPOILERS, so be warned.

Having read the books several times, there are a few things that I would have liked to have seen in the film, like Tom Bombadil, but I knew that this would be left out, as it is not essential to the story. However, the biggest sore points with me were the lack of time spent in either Rivendell or Lothlorien. The forming of the Fellowship was handled not as well as it could have been, but for those unacquainted with the books it probably was a good thing that it was quickly done, and if you are familiar with the books, then you know what was left out, so it doesn't really matter. Galadriel did come off badly, as she was made to look like some horrible demon on a par with Sauron, when in the books she isn't, she is just scared of the power of the One Ring, like everyone.

However, the biggest things that I should have been put into the film were to do with Aragorn, as you don't get the sense of his importance, and also, in the books, he is torn between going to Mordor, or going to Gondor, and there is none of this in the film. Also tied in to this is the importance of The Sword That Was Broken, which barely gets a mention, and yet is pivotal to the following films, particularly the final one. In the books it was actually re-forged in Rivendell, but this was not done in the film. I can't think of why this was, but hopefully it will be explained in the following parts of the adaptation.

But all of this aside, it is a great film. I'll say it again, it is a GREAT film. Possibly the greatest ever, although maybe Godfather still takes that honour. The actors were well chosen, and really brought the characters to life. The battle scenes were amazing, and I thoroughly enjoyed them, even though others have criticised them mercilessly. One of the best thing about the film, I think, was the use of the score, particularly in the fight scenes in Moria, when the score was suddenly; abandoned, so you could here the clinking of swords and heavy breathing of the Fellowship, as they were hemmed in by the Orcs.

It is a work of cinematic brilliance, and if The Two Towers, and Return Of The King are better than this, then they will undoubtedly be the greatest films ever.

title: Blimey, crikey, wow, strewth, god damn amazing.
review: if you have read the book or not, go and see this epic collaboration of imagination and pure undiluted fantasy. George Lucas take notes, lots of them. Combines the magic of fantasy, modern film making, superb acting and a unique vision. The effects and reality blend seamlessly. The continuous urge and fluidity of the movie is ceaseless even for well over 3 hours. This is one of the very few movies that must be seen on the big screen. Staggeringly beautiful, every frame is nothing short of a masterpiece. I am running out of adjectives that do this movie justice. Suffice to say its just truly wonderful.

title: Can you say "Best Picture" Oscar?
review: OMG! This was and is the best movie of 2001! Peter Jackson has done a fantastic job of bringing the novel to the screen! He's remained faithful a lot more than Chris Columbus did! The effects dazzled the entire audience, they were cheering for Strider in battle, AND surprisingly, some people (including myself) were actually frightened. It was the simple things like ringwraiths and urik-hai. To sum it up LOTR: Fellowship is the best movie I've seen this year and deserves to win the BEST PICTURE at the Oscars

title: I love the movie as well as it deserves...
review:
Which happens to be all the praise I, myself, can give. I am writing this in response to those people who are so upset that this movie is #1 on the IMDB Top 250... This is not the AFI Top 100 Films of All Time, this is a list voted by people (many of whom are like me, 18 year old film majors who use a computer constantly) that are not critics. But they love a good adventure and know one when they see it. Yes, 'The Godfather' is one of the greatest, best reviewed films ever, and it still is. It is still #3 on the AFI List, just because TFOTR is #1 on this list, does not take away from Coppola's masterpiece. If you believe 'Lord of the Rings' is the greatest film of all time (I gave it a 10, but it is behind only 2001 and the Star Wars saga in my list), say so, call it out from the rooftops and the streets. If not, do the same. But the votes are tallied and it has taken the top position, so what? Is your anger that petty that you will hate this movie because it took a spot it "does not deserve"?

I have read the books, a few times, starting when I was 10. Plus, I have heard the BBC production, which is very similiar to the movie, and is great. And I always wished they would make a live action movie out of my favorite books, and now they have and it is more than I could ever imagine in my wildest dreams. I can find nothing wrong (and I've seen it four times already, don't worry, I didn't pay for them all). Everything in my heart and my mind, tells me this is a movie we have all been waiting for, especially in these dark days. Here is an adventure to let loose the hearts of men on the greatest trip imaginable.

This is not the greatest movie of all time, you know why? Because it still has two more to go. The book was written as one complete thing, as was the movie (filmed all at once), so this will not be complete until 2003. Then, maybe then, it will overtake 'Star Wars' on my list. Until then, I will sing the praise of this movie and the name Peter Jackson, for he has made me believe in film as entertainment (for that is what it is meant to do) and art, as well.

On a four star scale, it is unratable. It is 11 out of 10. An A++, it fits no realms of scale. It simply is what it is: incredible, wonderful, powerful, moving, gripping, emotional and violent. We have not seen a movie like that for a long, long time. I hope Chris Columbus takes a note on how to adapt a book (you have to love it) and to George Lucas, I hope this movie makes Episode II incredible. I believe in all of you. Do not let me down.

title: Love it!
review: This is the most fantastic movie I have ever seen. Peter Jackson really has done a great job by making a film of a book that is almost impossible to put down on a screen. The movie takes you away on a journey to Middle-Earth so you never will leave it again. I think everybody in the film has done a great job in being the character of the book (they are Frodo, Sam, Merry, Pippin, Gandalf, Aragorn, Gimli, Boromir and Legolas - who I think was wonderful-) I can't wait tot see the Two Towers. In the meanwhile I go and see the Fellowship of the Ring lots of times...

title: This movie should win best picture
review:
At the end of each year, I always enjoy naming one movie that truly stands out as a fantastic movie. In 2000, I felt that honor went to Gladiator. So far, in the year 2001 I had yet to see a movie that truly captivated me...until now. Ladies and gentlemen, my choice for the best movie of 2001 goes to the Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring. This movie had everything you could want.

First off, the visual effects and costume design were amazing. The best example of this was the opening sequence with the battle between the forces of elves and men, and the forces of Mordor. It was amazing to see thousands of armor clad soldiers fight on a stormy, desolate battlefield. The costume design of the Dark Lord Sauron can only be described by one word...whoa. Also, the costumes of the Ringwraiths were fairly simple, yet they were striking at the time. The acting in the movie was top notch. Elijah Wood played a convincing Frodo Baggins. But, the stand out actor in this movie would be Ian McKellen, who played Gandalf the wizard. He made the character act in such a way, that it made me believe he was a wise, intelligent, and powerful wizard. As for the storyline itself, it is filled with drama, fights to the death, perilous journeys, and even a little humor. And, while it does not exactly follow the novel it is based on, the movie follows the novel closely enough so people who have never seen the movie can understand what is going on, while satisfying die hard fans of the novel.

You know, I have talked to many friends who have seen the movie. Some of them have read the novel, while others have not. But, overall, they enjoyed watching the movie. The fact is whether like the fantasy genre or not, Lord of the Rings is a movie that can appeal to everyone. So in conclusion, I urge you to go see this one of a kind film. And, you can bet that I will be first in line when the next Lord of the Rings movie comes out.

title: An instant classic. An all-time great.
review:
I can't imagine how this could have been better, except if it could have been long enough to include the whole book. Of course, that's completely impractical.

I loved almost all the changes from the book and understood why they were necessary. The prologue is admirably understandable for the uninitiated and grandly cinematic in itself. Howard Shore's score is terrific. The acting, however, is the best special effect. It makes the movie surprising moving for everyone.

Certainly and instantly one of the best movies of all time. A masterpiece.

title: Worthy of EVERYONE's Respect
review:
As always, I've skimmed through the first few dozen reviews posted on LOTR and have become annoyed by people's lack of comprehension.

All this talk of LOTR not being worthy of #1 on the 250 list, or not being as good Godfather or Star Wars or blah blah blah is insane.

If everyone could stop comparing one film to the other and try to think of the piece on its own, then I can't see how anyone couldn't see LOTR for anything other than simply fantastic.

When you consider the sheer amount of time, engery, blood, sweat and tears that have quite obviously been poured into this film and think about what it takes, and what it means to adapt one of the world's greatest literary achievements into a film, you must come to realize that a film like LOTR commands your respect.

Obviously its not a flawless movie, but guess what, THERE's NO SUCH THING!!!! I challenge anyone to go out and find a movie that everyone on the planet enjoys. There are a million different opinions out there ladies and gentlemen, and a million different ways to voice them. If you didn't enjoy LOTR I suggest you take a closer look at the films you DO enjoy, and then think about what makes those films great. I can assure you that those same qualities abound in this film, they're just executed differently. LOTR is a truly stunning accomplishment, and I feel awfully sorry for those that think it fell short.

Finally, let me leave you with this: "Don't you think we're lucky to be in a world where literary dreams as epic as Lord of the Rings can be made into a 3 hour film for the masses to appreciate? Think about how far we've come!"

title: I was impressed.....
review:
Okay, I'm not a Tolkien fan. I've never read The Lord of the Rings or even the Hobbit for that matter. I went to the theater yesterday to see a matinee of this film. I had no high expectations of what I thought it should look like or be like or anything like that. I went in there with an open mind not knowing anything about Tolkien's world.

I was quite impressed. The film was able to capture my attention for the entire 3 hours and I was able to understand what was going on even though I knew nothing of the characters, places or events. Some of the editing was questionable, but it's not going to be the downfall of Peter Jackson.

I realize that something were left out and somethings were changed. I know that Tolkien fans can be very die hard and scrutinizing when it comes to their favorite characters. But in a normal adaptation of a book only five to ten original scenes from the book are used and everything else is created by the screenwriter. Taking that into account, I think Peter Jackson and the screenwriters did a fabulous job keeping the majority of the story together while getting rid of things that were not integral to the movement of the story.

I've heard some negative comments about the fighting. In a previous review a good point was raised, while we are use to high tech fight sequences like in the Matrix and Crouching Tiger the fighting style in this film is totally different. Think of how upset Tolkien fans would be if they used the same fight choreography in LOTR as they did in The Matrix, this would have been just another kung fu movie set in a time when there was no kung fu (anyone remember The Musketeer). The fighting was meant to resemble that of mideval style, basically the smash and grab tactic.

As a non-Tolkein fan I loved the movie and I will see many more times, and I might even read the books.

title: This is the best movie ever
review:
There Are NO Spoilers, so don't get your panties in big wad!

This movie was awesome. There was only one problem with the movie, it was too short. It had good cinematography, good special effects, good costume design, good makeup. This movie will win best cinematography, best special effects, best visual effects, best costume design, best makeup, best director (Peter Jackson), best Picture.

If this movie was nominated for Golden Globe Awards it Might as well be nominated for Academy Awards.

People of all ages will love this movie. Elijah Wood was awesome. Liv Tyler was cool.

This is the perfect holiday movie. IT may 3 hours but it's worth it.

I give this wonderful, action packed epic a 10 out of 10.

title: It was EXACTLY as I pictured it!
review:
Well, I went last night... This is THE movie of the year, hands down. What can I say about this movie without sounding like a total fanboy... Probably nothing, so I'm going to jump directly into fanboydom now...

This film had me spellbound. Every scene was crafted from the stuff of dreams. The CGI was seamless. None of it was inapropriate or out of place. The hobbits look like hobbits in comparison with the humans, instead of humans shrunk down with a computer effect. Every overland shot conveyed the sense of a huge world, filled with endless adventure. (Warning, spoiler ahead)...

I cried when the Fellowship lost Gandalf, even though I've read the story and I know what REALLY happened...

My only complaint was that the combat scenes were too rushed and chaotic to follow the action very well. This was ok, though because the chaos was the thing they wanted to achieve, I'd imagine.

I wanted to write a long thing here, but I was just too amazed.

Go see this film

title: A feast for the eyes, a banquet for the heart
review:
They can stop making movies after this; everything a film can be has been accomplished here. Sure, I've read the book (thirteen times, actually) and I had great qualms about the monumental effort of bringing such an epic to celluloid, especially a book which has touched so many so deeply and on such profound levels.

The film is not "perfect" (whatever that means), but it is splendid. The visuals (a hearty cheer for Alan Lee, the film's conceptual designer) are stunning, the pace breathtaking, the characterizations warm and surprisingly humorous. There are depths in the book that the movie cannot reach, of course, given the constraints of time, but there are actually some ways in which the movie tops the book, in that Jackson has the ability to show us many things that Tolkien could only have his characters relate at second- or third-hand.

I feel the same way I feel after Thanksgiving, as though I may never have to eat again. This feeling will pass as well, I'm sure, but I have never been so replete from watching a movie. Deeply satisfying, beautiful, lovingly made. Go see it, you won't be sorry.

title: The Fantasy Trip of a Lifetime!
review:
We have witnessed a fantasy masterpiece, the likes of which has never been displayed on the silver screen.

I left the theater in absolute awe. For 3 hours I was swept away into the most beautiful fantasical world of pure magic.I can't say enough good things about this film.

This is by far the finest fantasy film ever made. It's in a league of it's own, and will undoubtedly go down in cinema history as one of the most groundbreaking films.

Peter Jackson is now my new favorite director. 10/10!!

title: worthy of #1
review:
Having seen this movie twice now, yes, there are inconsequential inconsistencies with the first book in the LotR trilogy, but they do not detract from the film's greatness. Judged as a movie by itself, I can think of no finer example of cinematic achievement.

Mr. Jackson, your love for the material and attention to detail were not missed by this viewer. Congrats for such a masterpiece!

And to the reviewers who can't believe this movie is currently #1 on the IMDB Top 250, get used to it. I could say far more negative things about Citizen Kane, The Godfather, Schindler's List, Star Wars and The Shawshank Redemption, and they are all in my "top 10" list.

title: One of the best movies I've ever seen!
review: A must see. Might not be like the books but very close. A lot of fun to watch. Most people that I saw it with were wishing there was more to see, even though it was 3 hours long. That, I think, says a lot for a movie.

title: GREAT!
review: i have to say that this is one of the best movie-interpretation-of-book i've ever seen. it has a smooth pace and i thought that the scenery looked like something right out the book. i understand why some changes were made; tom bombadill bit was erased to allow it to fit into its time span and arwen (liv tyler) never really saved the hobbits but was made to, to even out the importance of female characters. i thought gandalf, pippin and boromir were excellent. they looked and acted exactly how i thought they would. yet, obviously since ive read the book there are some things i wish i could change. the lothlorien bit for example. in the book lothlorien was a refuge for the fellowship after the moria ordeal but it seemed darker in the movie. in the book, galadriel was kinder, beautiful in a sweet way, in fact gimli asked for a lock of her hair for a present, which he would 'cherish forever'. in the movie she was dark, almost witch-like. that was one of the things that annoyed me. another was the fact that the legolas-and-gimli and the frodo-and-sam friendship was played down. in the book legolas and gimli become firm friends, comrades-of-war, in the movie legolas talks more to aragorn. it shows no dialogue between the two. also in the book sam seems to look upon frodo as a master, utterly devoting his life to him, but in the movie it seemed that the tie wasn't that strong. i can only hope that the two friendships are played upon more in the coming two parts. other than that though, it was fantastic. it kicked potters ass any day.

title: An excellent achievement and magical movie
review:
LOTR: THE FELLOWSHIP OF THE RING

Growing up in a non-English speaking country, I had only first heard of 'Lord of the Rings' during my tertiary studies overseas. A Malaysian good friend of mine told me how good the books were, but I never really got to know what the story was. That is until I came to New Zealand and had some local friends who enthusiastically filled me in with the main plots of the books. Only then I realized how great Tolkien's imagination was and how his writings had influenced our modern conception of sword and sorcery tales.

Having seen the movie and becoming more familiar with the detailed narration of Tolkien's masterpiece and symbolism, I realized that his story had been adapted into many books, games, films and toys around the world. From US's Dungeons & Dragon to Japan's Record of Lodoss War, LOTR is definitely the prime source material. And as such, the world described by Tolkien is richer, with superior story-telling and grandeur in scope. Director Peter Jackson with his excellent cast and crew and New Line Cinema backing, had done justice to the first chapter of the books. The Fellowship of the Ring itself is a loyal movie adaptation of the books, which I understand are great achievements in the English literary world.

One of the most important instrinsic aspects of the movie is the beautiful terrains of Tolkien's world, transformed vividly into celluloid, courtesy of the beautiful and diverse New Zealand's topography. Credits must also go to those hundreds of New Zealand Army members who joined the movie as Orcs and Goblin warriors. I also liked how the each characters from the books, were brought to life by such great performances. While wacthing the movie, I can see that the movie staff had selected thespians who would embody the essences of the protagonists and antagonists, and NOT the other way around as we have seen done in some great but disappointing sci-fi movies lately. Because of this careful selection and respect towards the integrity of the characterization, we are awarded with a well-chosen international cast. Each person brings his/her own charisma and personality that is magically entwines with the others', as the story progresses and takes us from one action to another, rendering a powerful and entertaining fairy tale.

Sean Bean has always been a fav. actor of mine, his portrayal of Boromir is very humane, complete with its strength, despair and sympathy. Elijah Wood's Frodo is sweet and a bit on the wimp side, with a child-like innocence. Merry, Pippin and Samwise characters were performed with genuine care, stereotyped at times but always courageous, and not the regular stupid or useless sidekicks. I guess Mortessen's voice is less charismatic although he definitely has that wild edge and devilishly handsome. My favourite character has to be Legolas, one cool elf-dude, complete with bow&arrows and two short scimitars. He has a remarkable speed, wisdom beyond his age, a sleek and eco-friendly costume and most of all a graceful appearance and manner. When he engages in a battle, he fights elegantly with wit and agility; light as a feather and fast as fury.

It's funny to see Liv Tyler as an elf, because that was my first impression of her when I first saw her in one of those Aerosmith's video clips. Blanchett's Galadriel is another gift, she has always been alluring and elegant in most films, and there is just something sensual about her features. It is a pity that Gimli is not as menacing as he should have been, but nevertheless when he fights, axes are bound to be flying. The digital effects were smartly controlled and used when necessary, so they wouldn't jeopardized the narration, as it did in The Phantom Menace. Lucas take notes!

At the end of this three-hour of pure entertainment and amazement, I was so mesmerized and fulfilled that I give 10 out of 10 for this movie. The movie just delivers, nothing is disappointing. I've heard several people complained that the movie was overlong and boring. Now when I watched the film, half of the audience clapped their hands at the end of the show, while most of the other half walked out with satisfied grins and began to 'wow'. The only person who said how boring it was, was this 5 year old girl who was sitting next to me and couldn't wait for the movie to finish.

title: Superb but not the best film ever (I think?!)
review:
I know more people that have tried reading The Hobbit and didn't complete it that actually made it to the end of the book (myself included). The book can be quite hard going in places and I think the same is true of the movie. The fantasy genre is begging for the Star Wars treatment but this film doesn't attempt that - and rightly so many of you would say.

The film is technically awesome. Probably the most amazing epic spectacle I've ever seen. It's wonderfully directed by the man who brought us the hilarious Braindead (Peter Jackson) but it's not the thrilling, non stop adventure that some might be (perhaps foolishly) expecting.

The film takes pains to build ambience and I think in this aspect it's very successful. The problem is that in many places we're wading through an awful lot of dialogue that isn't really that theatrical or tension building. I didn't laugh or cry or feel a shiver down my spine as a result of any speeches, monologues or exchanges. Ultimately, despite great casting and acting, a few scenes are left slightly flat due to the nature of the script. I mean, they could have got Quentin Tarantino to write a few scenes of dialogue, say - but I guess they ought to keep faith to the original book of course. I don't know whether the language or tone of the books is quite so unimaginative or not.

Despite this, and the fact that some cinemas still have less than comfy seat cushions which aren't suitable for 2 hour movies (let alone 3 hours like this one), the film is superb.

I will need to watch it again (I'll take a cushion this time) to fully bed down my opinion.

One thing is certain. So well crafted is this movie, from the costumes, the photography, the acting, the sets, the music, the effects and the make-up that it will doubtlessly stand the test of time. It will now be a classic trilogy of movies as well as novels.

My only concern is that this film didn't quite hit the spot I was looking for. You won't get a Star Wars buzz out of this film (come to think of it - I didn't out of Episode I either). You'll get an all together more measured and scrupulous sense of entertainment, but, by the time the third film is released, there will be no room left in the genre for the more thrilling and epic action adventure that the world of elves, dwarfs and magic users deserves. Still, I can't complain too much. I'll give it 9 out of 10.

title: I haven't read the books...
review:
There have been many reviews discussing the good and bad points of the LOTR, but most people seem to be giving a comparison to the books. I have never read them, so here's a point of view of the film.

It's long. Probably too long. That's not to say they could, or even should, have made it any shorter but somehow you don't feel as though time is passing as quickly as you would hope when watching a movie of such epic proportions.

For me, the film felt a little "flat". There were a few action, emotional and creepy scenes, but generally I never really felt a sense of excitement or tension. That is not to say I got bored, but I would have liked to feel stronger rushes.

People seem to have been disappointed by the lack of or portrayal of some characters, but I thought the actors (and special effects) did their job brilliantly. Gandalf truly comes across as a wise sage with deeper power, the hobbits seem like innocent children, and the other members of the "Fellowship", I thought came across very well. Yes, you don't see enough of Gimli, and perhaps Boromir (Sean bean) could have appeared more but I would say the point was made on the purpose and role of each and every character. Legolas/Orlando Bloom was a particularly likeable character.

My main comment, though, on the film is that it feels as though the entire plot of the trilogy has been condensed within this one movie, and the following two films are about resolving all that has happened in Fellowship. From the point of view of someone who doesn't know the story, like me, this is very important. I think LOTR *will be* a truly fantastic and wonderful trilogy, but Fellowship, certainly, on it's own feels as though too much is yet to be done and almost as though no enough has happened - bizarre as that may sound.

To give you a comparison, of you say Star Wars: A New Hope, and never saw the others, it wouldn't really matter. The story within that one movie has a beginning, middle and an end, and the audience is left satisfied. However, had you only ever seen Empire Strikes Back, you would be almost *too* interested in knowing what happens next, where the characters will go etc..

It is like this that Fellowship leaves an audience. I didn't think it was a story that was any more than a beginning - and since it's a trilogy, it obviously isn't meant to be any more than that, but it is a feature that I felt was abundently clear when leaving the cinema.

Still, all that aside, if you're the sort of person who is looking for an easy way to know what happens in the book (with slight alterations I would guess), or are looking for a highly impressive visually feast, then LOTR: Fellowship of the Ring will take you the first steps on a larger journey, then leave you, probably wanting to read the second book to know what happens...

title: THE film I´ve waited for
review:
This is THE film for me. Partly since I´ve waited over 20 years for it to become a film, but also because it gets better with each viewing.

So much detail so lovingly displayed. And, very much like the books, with each new viewing/reading you get new detail and new understanding.

THANKS to all involved in the quest to make this movie!

title: A film that can stand up with Apocalypse Now, or Brazil, or Citizen Kane, or Ran as a classic
review:
So that's why I go to the cinema. I have not felt as much anticipation and fulfilment when going to the cinema since I was a child. This film gave me the feeling I get when I see a good play at the theatre, but rarely get from a film. It made me realise how average films like Gladiator, Phantom Menace and the Matrix are. We've been conned all these years into accepting less than we deserve because these insignificant words have been shouted at us. This film is a classic in the way that Apocalypse Now, or Brazil, or Citizen Kane, or Ran are classics. It did not merely entertain me, or make me go 'Wow', I was INVOLVED in the film. I really did care what happened to the characters. Hell, I was even worried for people that I knew made it to the end of the story.

The fight scenes were some of the best I have seen (especially on Amon Hen), they were dirty, nasty and scary, like fight scenes could be. The heroism was in the self-sacrifice in the face of danger, not in meat-headed Conan twirlings.

The interpersonal relationships were wonderful. Especially, Gandalf with Bilbo, Gandalf with Frodo, Frodo with Bilbo, Gandalf with Saruman, Aragorn with Boromir, Aragorn with Arwen, Elrond with Gandalf, are we seeing a pattern here? Yes this is not a film about EVENTS - some of the events were missed out of the film and some were changed but the film was none the worse for it - this was a film about PEOPLE. The glory of the story is that all people (I use the term loosely, including Hobbits, Dwarves etc) have the potential for real heroism; the tragedy of the story is that all have the capacity for evil, to be tempted or corrupted. The film highlights this point so poignantly that I was in tears a number of times. We all know that even the smallest person can be heroic when the time comes, but it is interesting to see how even someone as powerful has to face their own fears.

Weaknesses? Well it was too short. Yes too short. I remember getting to the part when the fellowship left Lothlorien and thinking `Oh we must be near the end'. It really did fly by and sometimes a little too fast. One minute they say `we can't go through the Gap of Rohan' in sunshine, the next there in thick snow on Caradhras. A minor gripe, and one which may be corrected on the DVD.

Celeborn's acting was terrible and it stuck out like a sore thumb. It's one thing being self-centred' and other worldly' its another being cardboard.

The voice effect on Galadriel when she was tempted was just plain naff. It was like something from an old Doctor Who episode. In fact the whole Lothlorien section suffered from the time constraint. Time does not seem to exist here.' Too right, you were only there five minutes and then you left!

But these gripes are so minor as to be trivial. Its like saying Ferraris are not very fuel efficient or the perspective isn't perfect on the Last Supper.

Taken as a fantasy action film, this is something that is equal to Star Wars. But it is so much more. The fantastic effects - I was so worried about Isenguard, but it is simple magnificent  merely compliment the story, they are merely (merely!) creating an alternative reality, that is they create a reality not an alternative to reality. George Lucas could learn a thing or two from Peter Jackson, the so-CGI CGI in the Phantom Menace and the re-edits of the earlier Star Wars films look positively amateur in comparison. Unlike Star Wars (even the first two) there are real characters here, people that one could believe existed and one cares about. In this respect it is more like a classic historical drama.

This is truly one of the greatest films ever made. Like a great piece of literature, one must return to it again and again to get the most out of it. This is partly because with each revisit we cast off more of our preconceptions or because we change in our self and thus what we bring to it or how we perceive it changes, but mostly because there are so many layers to it that one cannot appreciate them all at once.

Thank you Peter Jackson, for reminding us that film can be art as well as being entertaining.

title: A faithful, excellent adaptation
review:
Keep in mind as I write that I grew up with the Lord of the Rings. So I suppose I am another one of these "fan boys" that loved it to death simply because it's any nerd's wet dream to see the books come to life.

However, the books were flawed greatly. Basis of all modern fantasy or not, Tolkien rambles, and is not the most intriguing writer of his generation, contrary to what many say.

That said, Peter Jackson's Fellowship of the Ring is a brilliant movie. Gone are long, dragging scenes from the novel, like the one in Mirkwood. Even without such excess baggage, the film still runs 3 hours, which means that enough of the novel is retained to satisfy all but the most rabid fans.

But let me skip the know-it-all perspective and get down to what you want to know. The fight scenes are wonderfully choreographed, the acting ranges from acceptable to great, the special effects are good, the film's pacing is excellent considering its length, and yes, every important scene in the book is preserved and represented well. Certain things are explained numerous times so as to get the casual fans to understand; others are not explained enough, but overall I had no problem with how much history was divulged. Keep in mind that I read the books. I cannot tell you if a virgin-Tolkeinite would understand this film fully.

I suppose the most impressive thing about Jackson's Fellowship of the Ring is the pervading feeling of desperation and abject terror. Most movies are content to tell you that the characters are scared of something. The Fellowship of the Ring draws you in and frightens you too. There were scenes when my muscles were clenched throughout, hoping desperately that my heroes would escape, despite technically already knowing what happens. The orcs and other evil forces are mostly convincing. The power of the ring, shown in various scenes throughout the movie, is downright terrifying. Those with children be warned: this movie is not to be confused with Harry Potter. The epic, seemingly hopeless battle between good and evil is likely to much for many small children to handle.

Overall, The Fellowship of the Ring is a very faithful adaptation of the novel. After the movie was over I was already giddy with anticipation of the next installment. You'd better believe that before that happens, I will see The Fellowship of the Ring again, and perhaps read through the books a third time if I have a chance. A thrilling epic, I rate this a 9/10.

title: voicing some frustrations with an overall great film
review:
I'm going to take some time to point out some flaws that I haven't seen others mention. these are flaws that, in my opinion, negatively affect the story. my biggest complaint, which will be backed by several examples, is that gandalf's power, reputation, etc. were EXTREMELY downplayed through omission of key actions, and changing of storyline. here is a list of examples:

1. when bilbo disappears gandalf makes a little explosion of smoke so the hobbits won't be so freaked out and will come to the conclusion it was simply some trick of gandalf's rather than thinking anything really mischievous was going on. this was omitted. it would've added another ten seconds to the movie.

2. gandalf was originally responsible for the white horses seen riding on the water. one simple line in the rivendell scene could've kept this a part of the story.

3. gandalf seen bickering with the rest of the council over what should be done with the ring? come on!

4. during the journey over caradhras saruman, seemingly knowing gandalf's thoughts, says gandalf is afraid to go to moria. not so. in the book he simply understood that the danger there should be the last route, when all others have failed.

5. at the gates of moria...and this is a big one...frodo, not gandalf, solves the riddle of the door? give me a break.

6. omitted is a scene after the fight with the orcs in moria in which gandalf puts a spell on the door and is met with a counterspell from the balrog, then gandalf counters and the door explodes from all the force, caving in the passage between the enemies and the fellowship, buying them some time, not to mention showing the power of gandalf.

7. when the fellowship reaches lothlorien and galadriel hears the tidings of the fall of gandalf and that saruman has turned from the path, she states that had she had her way gandalf the grey would have been the head of the wizards' council from the getgo. one small line that could've hinted at his wisdom and power.

i think that is sufficient supporting evidence. gandalf is a bad ass. the reader is only given hints of his power throughout the book, and his wisdom is fairly obvious. but these things are not even hinted at in the movie. he's made to seem a lesser wizard. shame on the scriptwriters.

also, aragorn is made to seem less of a man than he is. afraid of his birthright? where'd that come from? i see no need for that in the story.

i was disappointed the reforging of his sword was omitted as well. although i have a feeling that will be included in the latter films.

why was there mention of a palandir in the first film? not necessary. could've cut that section of the saruman scene to make more time for some of the more important stuff that was omitted. like the battle with the ringwraiths at the ford. could've used a little more action there.

i personally don't think cutting glorfindel was a good move, it only added a minute or two more screen time for arwen and we didn't get to see the wrath of an elf-lord because of it. i can live with it though.

would it have hurt to have sam look into the mirror as well in lothlorien? frodo saw the stuff sam was supposed to see, so they may as well have had sam there.

finally, boromir's death...the funeral scene should've been more of a focal point. with all the changes that were made in the name of film adaptation to hold the audience, etc. they certainly could've had the film end with boromir going over the falls instead of frodo and sam walking down a hill. where were the weapons of boromir's defeated enemies beneath his feet in the boat to show that he had conquered and was above them? i think the ending would have been more dramatic (which is what moviegoers want) had we seen the frodo and sam walking off scene, then aragorn pushes the boat out, they have their little talk about what they are doing as the boat drifts off, then it goes over and they dart off. end.

with those things said, let me get to the praise.

the acting is phenomenal. bilbo being of key note here. very well done. i don't think there was a bad performance in the film. legolas rocked as well. aragorn was to a t, save the doubt about his ability, which was a script error, not an acting error.

the visual imagery is breathtaking and unmatched. here's the best way i can think to put it...i've read all the books and any reader knows how they get a mental picture of the places being described, etc. every place in the film was above and beyond my imagination's picture of the land. the shire was beautiful beyond imagination. the argonath, the pillars of the kings on the river were awesome to behold. rivendell was incredible...the twilight of lothlorien was breathtaking. mordor...scary. isengard, fallen from grace with excellent imagery.

the still scene in moria where the fellowship is waiting for the orcs to breakthrough is worthy of posters.

in the book legolas can pull and aim an arrow without you seeing him move, i was quite pleased with the inclusion of a scene during the forest battle with the orcs where legolas pulled and fired 3 arrows, killing three orcs all in different lines of sight in no time at all. very well done. also, his walking out on the chain to the back of the troll, showing the grace of an elf...nicely done. he shouldn't have made a sound when he jumped down though. elvish feet fall silent on the ground.

also, while i could've sat through 2 more hours of film the time management of this film was great. had i not known the story and the length of the film beforehand i would've had no concept of time. that movie went quick.

i had great expectations of this film (i'm hoping it will surpass titanic at the box office [i hate titanic]). considering that, i was bound to be hard to please. even so, i walked away awestruck with all i had just seen. i saw it twice within twelve hours of it's release. i am going to give this movie a 10 when i vote here in a minute. straight to #1 on the top 250?!?! incredible. i don't know how i'm going to wait a year for the second movie. i've been waiting for this movie to come out for over two years now. now i have to wait a year before i can get more!

go see this movie. at least five times.

title: Brilliant in Every Capacity
review:
Perhaps there are those who would claim that Peter Jackson's monumental project's debut is only "ok", and while there opinion is noted, it should be completely disregarded. This amazing 'motion picture' (I feel this phrase, as opposed to 'film' is appropriate...doesn't it just feel bigger?)requires more than one or two viewings to fully absorb the magnitude of its theatrical merit. One can not even concieve of the huge task Jackson's took upon himself some 6 years ago, but the end result is well worth conception. While I have read its prequel, The Hobbit, I have not read TLOTR, and so am fully aquainted only with the prior story of Bilbo, not Frodo. Without spoiling the film for any, let me comment that the film contains amazing landscapes, beautiful music, comprehensive plots, mindboggling special effects, and most importantly, impeccable acting. Both McKellan and Wood give INCREDIBLE performances, not to mention Mortenson, who was fantastic as Aragorn. Several seens were beyond breathtaking, and a perfect mix of fast paced action as well as touching moments between characters keeps the audience both entertained and emotionally involved (one scene in particular from Frodo brought tears from many...kudos to orchestration for composing such soulful melody). After sitting through 2 hrs. and 45 min, I feel the only appropriate response is "wow". Wow. I can foresee some might be disappointed in the lack of resolution in the film. Unlike trilogies before it (Star Wars, Godfather) this film ends with much up in the air, leaving closure-obsessed moviegoers somewhat wanting. This, however, has little to do with the film, but more to do with the novel and the MONUMENTAL task which converting to the screen has been.

Leaving the theatre I was overcome with intense sadness, knowing that I must wait for an entire year to see the next installment. However, The Fellowship of the Ring is fantastic on its own merit, and will be one film I'll watch repeatedly until the next film is released. 10/10

title: A marvelous adaptation!
review:
I was soooo afraid that this film would be lousy and ruin Middle Earth for me forever! But it's fantastic. The director has managed to accomplish the seemingly Herculean feat of adapting a beloved, epic story in a respectful manner, only omitting parts that really wouldn't work in a film. That's the tricky thing about adaptations; they are not merely one-to-one translations of the original; they entail a complete re-imagining of the story in order to tell it via a different art form. I'm amazed at how well this was done. I was so engrossed in the story that I didn't notice the missing parts until after the movie was over, and I found that I really didn't "miss" them. Plus, people I saw the film with, who had not read the books, also loved it. The filmmakers are obviously doing something right. I can't wait to see the next installment!

Long live Frodo!

title: I'm sorry, Mr. Jackson...
review:
Look out, mini-spoilers!

I, like many, read the books when I was younger and loved them. It has been several years, so I am not nit-picking details of the story. However, this film has problems.

I'll start off with the good, of which there was, to be fair, much. The acting was above average with standout performances by Ian McKellan as Gandalf and Cate Blanchett as Galadriel (She has such great presence! I was mesmerized whenever she was on the screen.). The locations and sets were lush and lavish. The action sequences were amazing in many parts. Stylistically, the director was hit and miss. Often Jackson's shots were wonderfully realized, well framed, capturing a moment beautifully. At other times they seemed to take more of a "here's a thing" approach (just point the camera at it) with all the style of an ambitious home movie (tilt the camera slightly and zoom in  I'm thinking of the goblin and dwarf skeletons mostly here). Positive stylistic standouts include Frodo's world when he dons the ring and Galadriel's moment of temptation to take the ring of power. The changes in the story only added drama and character. The subplot between Arwen and Aragorn is quite stirring. The themes of the corrupting power of the ring played prominently in the film, which fueled an effective moral struggle throughout.

To be fair, Mr. Jackson took on a colossal task that could never be perfect. The books are large and packed with characters and action. Even a three-hour movie was bursting at the seams to contain what Jackson included. Another element that soured my experience is that I viewed this movie at what may be the worst movie theater of its kind in the world, the AMC 20 in Independence, Missouri, at which I have never viewed a movie I wanted to see without some kind of problem. This go-around involved idiocy in the projection booth as the first half of the movie was framed so that we could only read the top half of the subtitles ("maybe Elven only uses the top half of words" remarked one of my friends), then it was "fixed" to show us the top part of the next frame at the bottom of the screen during the crucial Council of Elrond scene, and later adjusted to show only the top half of subtitles again.

It has long been my contention that good movies take their time, an option that may have been unavailable to this film due to the incredible scope of its story. But Jackson showed he could do this for the introductory Shire sequences, probably some of the more unimportant exchanges in the story. Once Gandalf goes to visit Saruman, however, the movie is off at breakneck speed, barely stopping to just be with its characters once in a while. Even rare moments of character development seem rushed as our heroes are quickly whisked away to the next chase/fight/escape. For instance, as a reader, my version of meeting Strider is far different than the film's. This is a scene that requires time. We need a moment free of rising action to hear the sounds of the barroom, feel Frodo's tension, take note of the mysterious man in the corner. Jackson's version runs in fast forward. It goes like this (to be read at high speed with no breaths): Hey, who's that guy, he's been staring at us all night, oh him he's a ranger, call him Strider, hey you guys are calling attention to yourselves, let's get out of here, I'm Strider *running*.

Obviously, going in, any director/writer/editor would know that time is a commodity in this story. This being the case, I have issue with some of the decisions made in this film. Much of the time, Jackson seems to be too in love with his sets and locations. Countless are the sweeping, spinning shots of characters trekking across ever-changing terrain or taking in magnificent vistas. With such a crunch for screen time, there were far too many. For instance, I counted three separate sweeping/spinning shots of the monolithic Gondor King statues (Yeah, Pete, we see 'em). Less is more. Give us a quick establishing shot and then be with your characters in their environment. We will figure out where they are, that it is beautiful and get more `precious' time with the characters.

The key to good moviemaking is providing information. Not too much or too little. Too little information: The Fellowship's trek. To the unread moviegoer, where is Rivendell in relation to Mordor? Where's Saruman? Where are the Misty Mountains or the random passes debated as possible routes in the film? A simple, quick lay-down-the-map scene would have provided this and created a real sense of quest for the audience. For such an awesome undertaking there was no beginning, no moment of anticipation of the long road ahead or the adventures to come, just a random scene with Bilbo and Frodo at Rivendell, and "we're walking."

Too much information: Reactions after escaping the mines. Two or three tear-streaked faces are enough (e.g. everyone's sad). An inventory of weeping characters we barely know set to melodramatic music is too much. As a side note, scores never bother me, but this one intruded into nearly every scene. It only works once with a soft melody offsetting a grisly slow-motion action sequence.

In summary, I found the direction to be oft inspiring, but at times heavy-handed (the score was perpetually so). An example is Jackson's repetitive trading of shots back and forth between the Fellowship paddling and uruk hai warriors running.

I probably took this movie more seriously than I should have, as I'm apt to do when presented with the screen adaptation of one of the greatest novels of our time. Most people that I've talked to found it `awesome!' I'll give it a `good,' a `worth seeing,' and a `better luck next time.'

title: A Beautiful Film

title: Well done adaptation of the book
review:
Lord of the Rings: Just the name of it conjures up memories for those of us who read the books voraciously in our youth. Several attempts have been made to try an make a visual presentation out of this mountain of words, but none captured the full flavor. Clocking in at 400 pages of small type per book, the three books of JRR Tolkien's masterpiece are a daunting task for any film maker. The slavish attention to detail among the readers of the series is something to reckon with as well. They will be very unforgiving of any glaring errors, and no doubt will still sharpshoot even the small ones.

I believe that Peter Jackson's monumental task of filming all 3 movies together, and then staging them a year apart will go down in history as a pivotal film making event in the 2000s. The audacity of tying up several noted and hundreds of lesser actors for a year and a half(ling) of principal photography took a lot of pull. The expenditure of money (approaching $300 million), the scope of the material and scale of the production and sets are all grand.

Now enough back story, what about the movie?

Several points of the story have been cut and rearranged to make the narrative flow to the point. Tolkien was nothing if not verbose, so to eliminate Tom Bombadil, or compress several of the events of the hobbits leaving the Shire was not too distracting. I took exception to the scene famous from the trailer of Arwen (Liv Tyler), dubbed "Xenarwen" by some 'net wag (because of her transformation from a shy elf daughter of Elrond to a sword swinging "if you want him, come and claim him" vixen on screen) because she was such a minor character in the first book. I suppose it was to "punch up" her character a bit and make her presence more known, and to have a strong female character in an otherwise male dominated cast. Still, the changes wrought in the narrative were but little distraction. The majority of the narrative strings together and follows the book closely, even using much of the dialog, where appropriate. I can't really complain about what was left behind given the movie's gargantuan 178 minute running time. Trust me, get snacks at the concessions stand, you will be in it for the long haul. Step out for a quick break, and you could well miss something important.

The scope and scale of the film is grand. The whole of principal photography was shot in New Zealand, and they were able to replicate Middle Earth quite well. The scenes of the various towns and the townsfolk were well done and believable. The out of doors, the woods, mountains, meadows and forests had a lifelike look to them, well lit without being too bright.

Forced perspective as well as CGI tricks were used to differentiate between the sizes of the different races, with hobbits coming in at waist high to Men, with Dwarves and Elves filling the gaps. I thought Gimli was quite small, being, um, dwarfed by Legolas.

Much scenery was filled in with CGI in order to create the huge stonework and the terrible landscapes of some of the settings. The underground scenes of the Mines of Moria had a bit of flat CGI hangover that comes from inventing the whole of the scenery from the heart of a computer. Still, the CGI scenery had less sheen and artifacts to it than Star Wars' CGI, so the state of the artform is improving, even if the pace of the change has slowed.

There was an unholy host of horrors animated with CGI, and they appear to best the Lucas creations by showing thousand strong armies gathering and working and forging weapons in the dark of their underground lairs. The animated characters were well done, without many cheap effects.

The acting in general was well done, without some of the leadenness that often pervades costume dramas. I am not a fan of Elijah Wood as Frodo, but he plays the role with the right gravity and reluctance. Viggo Mortensen was spot on for Aragon, once you got used to the haunted look that he brings to his character. Sean Bean as Boromir was perfectly cast, and there were no real glaring errors or standouts in the remainder of the cast. Little scenery was chewed, and events were articulated and feelings shown with honesty.

The pace of the film is not always even, but tends to build as the film progresses. If you are not familiar with the narrative, the long walks across the meadows or hills appear agonizingly slow, but when you realize they are covering for months of travel, they can be excused their slowness. I felt the balance of voiceover vs live action to carry the narrative was very well done, with much of what was spoken about at Rivendell in the book as stories are instead shown as live action events in a more or less time line sequence, rather than just as flashbacks.

The combat scenes are fast paced and excellently choreographed, without any Matrix-like camera chicanery, just good classic swashbuckiling. The portrayal of archery is well shot, as I am a former archer myself, and could feel the expectation of the shots, and the rain of the arrows as they fell. Headbutting is a worthless exercise unless you have no other choice, it invariably hurts both combatants equally, yet it crops up again and again in the combat sequences here as well as many many other recent Hollywood films. Anyone who has actually headbutted another person in anger will soon realize that action movie's over reliance on this trick is just eyecandy. Still the rest of the swordwork and so on were well done. The orcs were appropriately scary in kind of a Predator sort of way.

I believe that this is the first film to truly live up to such an expansive book as The Fellowship of the Ring. You will not want to miss this portrayal if you are a fan of the LOTR book series, and you will probably want to see it anyway just because it is so well staged. It is a masterwork, and while not the best movie of the year, it is one of the most ambitious and one that lands closest to the mark it aimed for. The tenor of the film, the acting, the pace and the story are all compelling and well played considering the gargantuan task they undertook to film. Definitely worth a look.

title: It took me two viewings to separate the film from my expectations
review:
During my first viewing of the film, the expectations and the experience surrounding the film didn't allow me to lose myself in the film. I recognized that what I was seeing on the screen was brilliantly executed, but I wasn't involved.

My second viewing was wholly different and quite exceptional. I was swept up in the action and emotion, the scope and the characterization. There are plenty of reviews from plenty of people with plenty to say, but if the film didn't quite resonate with you the first time, a second viewing just might change everything.

title: nice piece
review:
This is a very good movie, and quite possibly one of my favorites ever (that is different, however than being one of the BEST ever). I wish deeply for a touch more character depth, and a few extra seconds for scene transition to make the movie flow a little better.

The evil in the evil characters is too simple and one-sided, and arwen's magic does seem a tad out of place- though I don't mind her getting a little more screentime. Battles were tremendous, though felt a teensy bit unrealistic (like the orcs shooting only before and after the jump over the pit, allowing the fellowship about a minute or two to focus on the jump- etc). As a martial artist, I can say it would have helped the top fighting actors (legolas, gimli, aragorn) to get some more fighting training a.k.a matrix- They were impressive, don't get me wrong, but they were asked to be superhuman fighters in a way that their skill levels didn't quite seem to fit with- for example- cutting down 10 orcs without getting your head split in two or even winded would require such finesse and skill- efficiency of each cut and proper footing, few of which were in place for any given scene. the special effects largely made up for it though- so we can still believe. In fact, you can't even really tell where reality ends and the special effects begin.

LOR was beautiful and elegant, had good acting overall, and was very exciting. It really did seem a lot shorter than 3 hours- maybe more like 1. The above complaints are nit picky, and this movie does deserve some oscars. I wouldn't call it the number one of all time.. but quite possibly best of the year- and its broad appeal does not surprise me in the least.

Not for little children- some of the adults were even quite frightened by a few of the scenes, and it is somewhat graphic at times. Highly recommended for everyone else though. There was crying, gasps and laughter in the audience throughout the movie- hallmarks of a quality film. I give it a 95/100.

The one thing that struck me was the use of subtle effects (like the size differences between hobbits and men).
