title: The things wrong with this movie are overwhelmed by what is right about it.
review:
I have never written a movie review before, but Peter Jackson's `Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring' has inspired me to make a few comments. As of this writing I have seen the movie three times. Each time it keeps getting better. Things that were big problems for me on the first viewing didn't matter on the second and were irrelevant by the third. To summarize my review with one sentence, the things wrong with this movie are overwhelmed by what is right about it.

First, a point that should be obvious in this case needs restating: This movie is Peter Jackson's `Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring', not J.R.R. Tolkien's. This does not make the movie illegitimate, but it does mean that it will not be the same. Retelling a story has a long established history in both literature and film. How many versions of the Dracula story are there? How many times has Hamlet been altered and remade? How about the Arthurian legends? There are many examples where a storyteller has been inspired by an earlier work and sought to express their vision of the story with their own images and own words. Sometimes this retelling is done so well it is better than the original; other times it is done poorly and is forgettable; sometimes - as is the case in this movie - the retelling is both better and worse than the original, improving some sections at the cost of others.

The scenes of the journey from Hobbiton to Bree to Weathertop to Rivendel are rushed and condensed. Much of the drama and character development is lost in the movie. The introduction of Strider is so truncated that you cannot help but feel you missed something. These scenes are to the eyes and ears what junk food is to the mouth and stomach - tasty, but not terribly satisfying. Tolkien was much better.

The end of the movie is powerful, dramatic, and emotional. Frodo's fear is tangible, the corrupting influence of the ring is clear, the depth of Sam's loyalty and love brought the audience to tears. I could go on an on about it. Suffice it to say that every character had his moment; the ending was sad and uplifting at the same time; it was film-making at its finest. Tolkien's ending was good, but Jackson's was better.

I could go on with a laundry list of comparisons, but that would not evaluate the movie in any meaningful way. Instead, I shall talk about what was right and wrong about the movie in and of itself.

One thing that did really bother me was the music score. During the fight scenes the music ran the gauntlet between fine and inspired, but during the quite emotional scenes it was often annoying, intrusive, and stifling. The music when Boromir fights alone against the orcs is terrific. I do not, however, need or want music playing while Aragorn and Arwen stare into each other's eyes and whisper terms of endearments to tell me they are in love. That is what acting is for. The music often made the softly spoken word hard to hear, and most of the Elvish dialogue is spoken softly. From what little I could make out the language sounded like it was beautiful, but I can't be certain because of the overused background music. Now to be fair, I have talked with many people about this movie and so far I seem to be the only one who feels this way. Maybe it is just me, but with each viewing I kept wishing that the music would just stop while the characters were having deep and serious conversations. It would have been more dramatic; it would have been better.

The cast is excellent. Ian McKellen is perfect as Gandalf. His performance is Oscar worthy. Ian Holm as Bilbo is a joy to watch. Elijah Wood portrayal of Frodo is rich with emotion and complexities. Sean Bean's Boromir is a deep and troubled man, noble at heart, capable of both corruption and redemption. Orlando Bloom's Legolas is frighteningly deadly in battle and conveys the deep ties Elf's have to the world around them with his ever-alert sense for approaching danger. I could go on, but the gist is that the casting was inspired and performances more than merely memorable.

Some of the fight scenes could have been better filmed. At times the camera is so close to the whirling combatants and is jerking around so much that it is impossible to tell what is happening. It is much better when they pull back a little and either hold steady on a scene or sweep over the battlefield. At those times, the battles seem epic and powerful.

Some of the special effects are awe-inspiring. The Balrog simply must be seen to be appreciated. The cave troll is frightful and deadly. The Nazgul that Frodo sees when he puts on The Ring are terrifying and horrific. The watcher at the gate is powerful and huge. Other times the effects are more mundane and in certain moments the quick eye will see things that just don't look right. One image that struck me as just wrong was when the orcs come scaling down the pillars like spiders. It was unnecessary and inappropriate for these creatures. The birth of the Uruk-Hai is gross and more properly belongs in a Wes Craven horror flick. In the end, the mistakes (if mistakes' is the right word) are fleeting and - for the most part - irrelevant.

The sets are well done. Hobbiton is beautiful, Bag-End is the example of what a Hobbit hole should be. The ruins are old and scary. Rivendel is peaceful and elvish. Lothlorian is built around trees so large that they beggar the imagination. Moria is creepy, dark, and huge. Isengard starts out as beautiful and is transformed into the place of nightmares. Could they have been done better? Maybe, but give them their due. Each set is rich in detail, full of culture and heritage. Each feels like a place that has existed for thousands of years. Not a bad achievement.

I could go on and on and on. There are hundreds of different elements that have to come together to make any movie. Any one of those elements if done poorly can turn a potentially great movie into something merely mediocre. Is Peter Jackson's `Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring' a great movie? It tries to be, and in many ways it succeeds. Its failures are not large, but they are enough to make one stop and think. I do believe this is the best fantasy movie ever made. Greatness is something I think time will have to decide.

title: Yawn!! Zzzzzzz
review: Three hours! Three entire hours of boredom; for me that is. I can definitely see why people would thoroughly enjoy this film, but I sure didn't.  I think that I should have read the books first. However for the first half hour of the movie I did know exactly what was going on, I did read the Hobbit. This film was definitely overrated, and I expected better, which is what caused part of my boredom. The fight scenes were very good and exciting.  Although I would have preferred a very long nap(which i did take several times throughout the movie) I am glad I saw it so I can discuss it and see what all the hype was about. title: Lord of the under achievers (small spoiler)
review:
Well I really, really, really wanted to like this film. But unfortunately I didn't. If you have read the book you will probably be dissapointed, if you haven't you will probably love the film. It seems to make any sense to me when you adapt a books and then change bits of it. I see Peter Jackson as being a very talented writer and I wish he had written a fantasy film but not an adaption of Lord of the Rings.

The acting is fine, with more good performances than bad, the effects are wonderful, better than anything in harry Potter, or the Star Wars Episode 1. The film score is fine, but in my view not very original or exciting. I found several very annoying things about the film though, firstly the use of blue filters took away much of the wonder of the film. secondly, I found the editing to be terrible at times especially during the battle scenes, which have no sense of feeling. Fast cutting and medium shots are meant to show pace and chaos during battle and can work when done will i.e Gladiator, which is saved by its battle scenes. Lord of the Rings fails to put any feeling into most of the fight scenes which did look chaotic but not in a good way. Also the battle scene between Gandalf and Saruman to be very dissapointing, more like a bad wrestling match with staffs, than a fight between two of the most powerful wizards on middle earth.

Hopefully, My expectations were to high and I may grow to like the film over time, but for the moment I feel both cheated and frustrated with the film.

title: Good God Y'all.
review:
I've been just a teeny bit skeptical of all the people who are freaking out over this movie. Now I'm about to do it myself. Stand back.

I just got done watching FOTR two hours ago, and I still haven't calmed down yet. For me, it was every bit as amazing as everyone's been saying. I want to laugh now, when I think of how I tried not to get too excited on the way to the theater for fear of being disappointed. I needn't have worried. It was breath-taking. Captivating. The perfect movie. I just cannot say enough good things about it.

The scenery, effects, story, etc. were all first rate. The Ring Wraiths were horrifying, the orcs gut-churning, and the troll was just....huge. The sword-fighting, archery, and action in general were exceptionally well handled. Not a single false step that I could see. And Arwen's chase on horseback? Jesus. My hair stood right on end.

But what really REALLY knocked me out were the characters themselves. Usually in movies of this type and scale, the characters are secondary to the story/action/CGI/you name it. Not so in this case. The characters are the reason to see this film. All were right on the money. I think this was made possible by the simple fact that the cast was made up of ACTORS instead of MOVIE STARS. They were able to melt into their roles. Become the characters. Instead of watching Arnold or Julia or Stallone, I was watching hobbits, elves, and wizards. My favorites were: 1. Frodo. Elijah Wood nailed it, right down to the ground. With his soft voice and slightly askew beauty, he is a wonder as the courageous, selfless, and to his knowledge, probably doomed hero. I can't wait to see what happens to him next. 2. Aragorn. God Almighty! Will you marry me Aragorn? Viggo Mortensen is simply stunning as the noble but reluctant king-in-disguise. Tender hearted and loyal, but a ferocious, relentless fighter as well. Speaking of loyal.... 3. Sam. His part is fairly minor in this first part of the series, yet Sean Astin manages to make him stand out with his touching and emotionally open performance. Sam is the perfect best friend. Unquestioningly faithful, and always there in a pinch. 4. Boromir. He hasn't been getting quite as much attention as some of the others, but to me, he was the most tragic and heart-breaking of them all. A good person, possibly even a great one, his intentions are nothing but honest. But his own indecision and lack of confidence are his undoing. That he is suspect throughout most of the movie, but ultimately dependable, is what makes his fate in the end so terribly, utterly sad. Sean Bean is fascinating from beginning to end. Warm and friendly with his companions one minute, cold and calculating with the ring the next. One of his best performances ever.

This is getting long (grin), so let me finish it off by saying that I thought FOTR was screechingly, mind-bogglingly good. I want to put my shoes on and go see it again right now. I will think and think and think about it until I do go again. Marvelous. An absolute success. Turn off your computer and go NOW.

title: They said no one could do justice to LOTR - they were wrong!
review:
The successful adaptation of a best-selling novel to the big screen is a monumental undertaking with many variables to take into account. The first obstacle is the nature of the novel - while books allow for a virtually unrestricted level of depth, detail and perception the bounds of cinema are far more constrained, especially with regards to time. Another concern is how the story is told - should the director opt for a mirror telling of the (a la "Harry PotterÂ…") or create his or her own interpretation and risk alienating the fans. There is also the matter of casting - every reader has their own preconceived ideas of what their favorite characters look like and who should play them - recall the imbroglio over the casting of Tom Cruise in "Interview With The Vampire". If the task does not yet seem daunting enough, imagine that you've chosen to film The trilogy that formed the keystone of the fantasy genre as we know it today, a series which has been read by over 100 million people over the past five decades. I'm sweating just thinking about it.

When Frodo a young, carefree Hobbit, receives a ring as a "gift" from his uncle, he has no idea of it's significance: forged in the furnaces of Mount Doom, the ring will bestow unimaginable powers upon those who know its secrets and bend their will to evil. Frodo learns that the ring's creator, the dark lord Sauron, has risen again and has dispatched his forces over the land to find it. The only way to halt Sauron's reign is for the ring to be cast into the fires of Mount Doom and thereby destroyed. Thus, Frodo, with the help of his eight companions - wizards and warriors, of differing kinds and kin- embark on a perilous journey to save Middle Earth.

Peter Jackson's plans to develop "The Fellowship of the Ring" into a movie began over six years ago. He shopped the idea around Hollywood, but was repeatedly turned down by every major studio. When he approached New Line, he expected little more, and was told that not only could he make his film, they wanted the whole trilogy. Jackson was both astounded and ecstatic, and set to work, filming all three films simultaneously in order to ensure continuity among the cast and scenery, resulting in a grueling 18-month shoot. The effort was well worth it.

****** Be warned - gushing & potential spoilers ahead*****

From the opening narrative, explaining the history of the ring you get the feeling of an epic unfolding before your eyes and the battle scene depicting the initial defeat of Sauron is phenomenal. The film then switches to the story of the passing of the ring, introducing several of the main characters and the Shire, and I felt as though Jackson knew the visions that I had in my head when reading the book.

I don't know much about Elijah Wood's past performances, but he is excellent as Frodo - from his facial expressions, to his happy-go-lucky naivete and cheery voice he nails Frodo on every level, and continues to do so as the story progresses. I cannot think of anyone else who could have captured his essence so purely. Ian McKellen is superb as Gandalf, the world-weary wizard, although he is a tad more lighthearted than his character in the book. McKellen shines (literally in at least one scene) in every scene, but his steadfast defiance in his battle against the Balrog sent shivers down neck ("being sniffed by the devil" as my mother used to say) . The scenes between Frodo and Gandalf are amplified by the difference in height between the two which are exaggerated for the film. Outstanding performances abound.

Viggo Mortenson is brilliant as Aragorn the ranger (he literally went native during the film, sleeping in the woods to get into his character), the scruffy warrior/savior with a secret. Liv Tyler is luminous as the almost ethereal female warrior Arwen and her lines, delivered almost exclusively in Elvish (the language was actually constructed for the film) are a melodic singsong. Christopher Lee, the classic Hollywood bad guy, is positively wicked and foreboding as the traitorous Saruman. Ian Holmes' conflicted Bilbo was somewhat tragic to behold, as you could see how his character had been eroded by the dark calling of the ring. The rest of the Fellowship also deliver thoroughly engaging performances. I would be remiss if I neglected to mention the hideous marauding orcs, the monstrously powerful Uruk Hai and the faceless ringwraiths with their hair-raising banshee-like wails which would give nightmares anyone unlucky enough to encounter them (that's if they live to tell about it). The lands of Middle Earth are as integral to the story as are characters that dwell within them and as diverse.

The lush greenery of the Shire with it's warren of hill holes looks so natural that it only follows that hobbits must live there - it is simply beyond question. Likewise, Rivendell and Lothlorien's serene settings are such that only a race as delicate and ageless as the Elves could be their inhabitants - anyone else would soil their purity. Balancing the beauty is the stark, terrifying ugliness of the Mines of Moria, with it's labyrinthine passages, and halls hewn from stone, which have been infested with the loathsome, scurrying creatures in the service of Sauron. The rendering of the scenes is, for lack of a better word, breathtaking. Then there is the netherworld of phantasms that Frodo enters whenever he puts on the ring - both mystical and terrifyingly beautiful. There are however some concerns lurking amongst this perfection.

The overall special effects are extremely well done, so much so, that the few scenes that aren't, notably the caverns of Isengard, and the burial of Boromir, are glaring. I was also curious why several sequences appeared milky and somewhat washed out, much like the look of the fantasy films of the 80's, as I did find it somewhat distracting. Finally, the film does plod on in certain sections, but mercifully only for short segments.

These minor quibbles aside, I would not hesitate to recommend this film to anyone who enjoys good cinema. It is outstanding. Mr. Jackson has done what no one thought he could do - bring a masterpiece of literature to life. Kudos. I only regret that I'll now have to wait another year for the sequel.

title: Fantastic
review: The movie, although missing some things from the book (which is unavoidable when making a movie from a book) is just spectacular. Even if you've read the book, and know what will happen, it's still exciting, and amazing to watch!

title: I am astounded.
review: I actually went to see this movie by myself two days after it came out. Then, as soon as it was over, I got a call from my roommate wanting to know if I wanted to see it again. So, off I went. It is, without hyperbole, one of the finest movies I have ever seen. And I'm shocked, but not totally surprised at how quickly it shot up to the top of the IMDB Best Movies List. The direction was excellent, the acting top-shelf, music set the perfect mood. I also have never seen a movie audience (or two, in my case) react so much to the action on screen. They laughed, they winced, they cheered. I heard people sobbing behind me at certain points in the movie. I hope this wins some awards, and I have no doubt that it will soon be very hard to find any available copies of the next book in the series, or perhaps any of the trilogy's volumes. Go see this. Now. Twice.

title: Incredible Book Becomes Incredible Screenplay
review:
WARNING: SPOILER INFORMATION AT END (additional warning below)

"The Fellowship of the Ring" movie is excellent in many ways, but what impressed me the most was the quality of the conversion from novel to screenplay.

The Harry Potter movie stands in my mind as a great example of how to keep a movie faithful to the plot of a book, but nonetheless, it lacked in several areas. The movie was too concerned with covering as many details as possible, so it tended to jump around from piece to piece. If you were to make a general outline of the book, you could then use it as a checklist of what to expect next in the movie. That ensures an accurate telling of the story, but that doesn't always translate well to the screen.

On the other hand, "The Fellowship of the Ring" defines how a book should be presented on screen. The plot remains completely intact, with details changing only when they enhanced the visual telling of the story. Having recently read the book, I was a bit disappointed in the exclusion of certain major events, but such omissions were necessary given the movie's epic running time of nearly three hours. Tolkien filled his story with an incredible number of elements that recur throughout the trilogy, and Frances Walsh did a flawless job of relating only those elements essential to the plot.

The overall perfection of this movie left me with only two minor gripes, the first of which is the casting of Elrond. Hugo Weaving has appeared in many movies, and he performed superbly in this one, but having seen him only in "The Matrix" before now, I had a hard time seeing him as anything other than Agent Smith.

WARNING: SPOILER INFORMATION BELOW!!!

My second gripe is the change in Frodo's actions at the end. The book has him trying to sneak off without being noticed, for fear that others will want to follow him into impending doom. But the movie has him telling everyone of his decision. The end result remains the same as the book (he and Sam leave together), but the way he handles his decision changes the mood and tone of the other characters. It also eliminates what I deem to be one of the first key elements in the shaping of Aragorn. The book leaves Aragorn torn between wanting to aid Frodo in his quest and wanting to rescue Merry and Pippen from the Orcs. In my mind, that decision marks the culmination of the Fellowship's progression under his leadership, and is a major step in his life as he develops into a king.

Beyond those two gripes, this movie is almost without flaw. The combination of exceptional work by Writer Frances Walsh and Director Peter Jackson solidly upholds Tolkien's desire to not only tell an epic story, but to also create and describe a whole new world.

title: A work of art.
review: Word cannot express how I feel about this movie... I am completely honored to have lived to see one of greatest films of all time in the theater when it first came out. This has been an experience I'll never forget. I have nothing else to say.

title: Overrrated but still great
review:
The overabundance of 10 ratings shows the bias of the reviewers, who like me, were so excited to finally get this movie. But perfect? forget it. The movie has some major problems.

***Spoiler Alert***

First off, the technique of telling us all the information about the characters or items, ie that Strider is Aragorn the King-to-be, what the Pilatir are, the whole history of the ring, all at the beginning, is foolish. It takes away a lot of the great drama that was in the book. Second, the choice of scenes is too biased toward violence and not enough toward drama. The Nazgul are nowhere near as fearsome as they should be as a result. Third, what's with the arbitrary changes? Why have Frodo find the password instead of Gandalf? That makes Gandalf less important and therefore the drama of his death is minimized. Why does Gimli not know that the dwarfs of Moria have been detroyed? That makes him seem foolish. Why take away the entire Buckland drama and replace it with a chance meeting in a field? Merry and Pippen are portrayed as idle thieves rather than noble friends.

Please. Much of this could have been done better. But the scenery and casting is spectacular (though I thought Aragorn should be heavier), and the sound alone makes it necessary to see this on the big screen. a solid 7/10.

title: Hard to describe the joy....
review: Briefly, it seems to be a near impossible job to convert Tolkein to the screen. Reading the Tolkein novels is an intensely personal experience that I'd recommend to all. After that, I'd recommend the Jackson film. Jackson has deftly avoided nearly all of the potential traps could have sunk such a movie. In a sentence, it FEELS like Middle Earth!

title: OK, so it's not the book. It's still incredible!
review:
Ignore the complaints of the anal retentives and fanboys who spit idiocy like, "Well, in Book 1, page 76, paragraph 3 of the first US edition, Frodo didn't say that. He said...blah blah blah blah." It's true that the movie takes some liberties with the text. It's also true that I might not have made some of the same choices had I been making the film myself. But fans of the Ring books should relax and allow themselves to become swept away by this awesome presentation.

The Fellowship of the Ring is the LotR movie we've been waiting all our lives for - for over three hours tonight, I wasn't sitting in a darkened theatre, I was in Middle Earth with the Nine Walkers. And when the lights came back up at the end of this first installment, my daughter summed up the feelings of everyone in the theatre when she said, "It's OVER?? Already?? I don't want to wait a YEAR for the next one!!"

title: The best book ever is now the best movie ever too!
review: Simply amazing!  Peter Jackson did an incredible job of bringing Tolkien's world to life!  The casting was perfect, and the acting amazing.  The scenery was unbelievable and the action scenes and special effects were stunning!  The only problem was that at 3 hours, it was not long enough and some scenes had to be rushed and others omitted.  Hopefully, additional scenes will be added to the DVD.  Nonetheless, it was as good as I imagined it could possibly be!  Weathertop was thrilling and the scene with the Balrog on the bridge of khazad-dum will leave you breathless!  Jackson did a great job of including a lot of detail that Tolkien fans could pick up on, and still making the movie very easy to follow for those that haven't read the books (yet).  I will have to see this several more times and now I can't believe I have to wait a year to see the Two Towers.

title: Stunning visual effects and cinematography aid in creating a sensational interpretation of the epic novel.
review: This movie is one of the best interpretations of a great novel to the big screen that I have ever seen. This is not an easy feat, being that we are talking about a science fiction/fantasy novel with characters such as hobbits, elves, dwarves, wizards, orcs, etc. But the use of special effects is (nearly) flawlessly applied in the director, Peter Jackson's, interpretation of the different races depicted in Tolkien's epic novels. Along with the stunning New Zealand landscape, which lends its own unique visual appeal, Jackson has created visual effects so astounding and so appealing that one is quickly drawn into the story, yet I did not feel overwhelmed. The screenplay does an excellent job of methodically telling the story of Frodo Baggins and the dilemma into which he is suddenly and mysteriously thrown. The movie left me with a feeling of satisfaction and a sense that I had been thoroughly entertained, but also with an intense desire to see those next two episodes which we know will be coming out in the next two years. In other words, the movie did what it was supposed to do, and did it splendidly! Now, I think it's time I go pull those books off my dusty bookshelf and.....

title: Good, not like the book, but covers the essentials
review: Good movie, not quite like the book, but covers the most important parts. Good special effects (the Balrog was incredible), excellent music, and great fights (the first one with Sauron, and the one at the end), overall, nice movie, to be seen maybe twice or even three times in the movies.

title: Someone finally got it right!
review: I've been a fan of the Lord of the Rings since I first read the books over 30 years ago.  I have watched with great anticipation as film makers throught the years have attempted the story.  I am very pleased that Jackson has brought Middle Earth to life.  He achieves all the intimacy that I felt when I read the books.  I don't know of anything that could have been done better.  And that's unusual since I am very critical.

title: Among the best of "fun" movies . . .
review: A great deal of skill and talent went into this production.  However, this movie is a spectacle; it is meant to thrill its audiences--which it does quite well.  All the actors are capable of exploring the nuances of character development, but this movie, however skillfully adapted, is not concerned with such matters.  I did not identify with any of the characters, although I did feel some sympathy, enough to remain interested for the three hours.  It could have been even better if it had more fully tapped into the myth of good, evil, and the battle of the will.  I rate LOTR: 8 out of 10, by far my highest score of any movie released this year.

title: even my stepmom liked it!!!
review:
everything I could say has probably been mentioned by at least two or twelve others in the hundreds of comments listed in the past ***THREE*** days...Three days and this movie has almost 7,000 votes and 600 comments, I've been using IMDB for years now and I've never seen a phenomenon like this. Of course, you have to consider the subject of all this.

All I have to say is this: Peter Jackson kept to the heart of the book which is simply that no one knows what strength lies within until one is asked to step foward. To me this movie comes at a time when we all need to be reminded that even though Bad Things happen and exist, anyone can have the strength and courage to stand up to the challenge. Cliche? Simplistic? Yeah, well it also didn't have a jamacian amphibian or a toddler yelling "Yippie" throughout. This movie could well become a classic for the simple fact that it has no pop culture references to bog it up, producers should take this as a sign that a fantasy movie doesn't need big guns,a wayans(or some other comedic ploy) to have a successful fantasy film.Let the story do the work, don't try to sell it to a demographic, peter didn't. And you know what, it worked. People that didn't enjoy the books enjoyed the movie, people that don't like fantasy liked the movie, kids, their parents and their grandparents liked the movie.And why? Because all the direction was focused on the story rather than trying to make everyone happy. "Love, a laugh, and some bit with a dog...that's what people want" Obviously not. Thank you Peter Jackson for bringing dignity to a genre that greatly needed it. Hope you shake it up the next three years.

title: Perfection?
review: Let's not beat around the bush here.  Anyone who's read J.R.R. Tolkien's Lord of the Rings trilogy will agree that it's quite simply the best work of fiction ever.  The many layers of Tolkien's tale, ranging from the story of an unlikely hero to the struggle of a world forced to change the nature of it's existence, it's magnificent grandeur and it's subtle beauty, are what make it possible for almost every reader (and now viewer) to become ensnared in the magic of Middle Earth.  This film respects its source in ways that few movie adaptations have.  It also respects the fact that not everyone is familiar with the tale of the One Ring of power.  Director Peter Jackson therefore crafts a film that for the virgin viewer will tell almost the entire story, and for the rest of us Tolkien readers he gives us little things like offhand comments made by the characters or stone trolls in the background that symbolize entire chapters of the books.  One of the most marvelous things about this film is the way the grand scope of the changing Middle Earth is juxtaposed with the little world of Frodo and the Fellowship, Jackson is absolutely artful in this and the feelings of intimacy and of magnificence work off of each other so well that at times they seem to be dancing.  Because of this, the audience is forced to feel the pressures that are on each member of the fellowship.  This adds to another one of the films great triumphs, which is the sensation that each moment in the story leads directly to the next and each decision affects the outcome of the quest completely.  Do not be afraid if you have never read the books.  Jackson, along with absolutely brilliant performances by Ian McKellen, Ian Holm, Christopher Lee, Sean Astin, and Elijah Wood make the story completely understandable and allow you to concentrate on the beauty of the world they have created rather than worrying if you've just missed something that a reader understood.  That said, you probably have, but it's most likely simply a small detail of Tolkien's fantasy world that incidentally is probably more complex than the human genome code.  Tolkien and Jackson seem to understand the human genome code as well, for their creative forces have come together and produced a nearly perfect film that will appeal to the hero in all of us.

title: My imagination came to life.
review: I was sceptical in the beginning, I didn't even want to go to watch it. However I had rare chance to be in USA at the time of opening and luckily I did go... I was amazed... it was almost like I had imagined it to be. This story has always been very close to me, NOW it is absolutely wonderful to see it while it resembles so much my imagination. I hope all of you can have similar experience. I wish I could see the next book tomorrow.

title: Impressive, Most Impressive
review:
I just came back from the cinema, having watched the first part of the Lord of the Rings trilogy, and i must say, it's even better than i thought!

Starting with the history of the ring, this movie grabs you, and won't let go untill the end-credits.

I've read the trilogy (and the Prequel The Hobbit) a few years back, and i must say this movie follows the book perfectly.

Of course the director had to make some adjustments, but the movie never seems illogical, like some part of the also excellent cartoon has.

The characters were also cast very good. From Elijah wood as Frodo, to Gimli played by one of my favorite actors John Rhys-Davies.

The humour is also well placed and never seems forced!

I'll definitely go see this movie a second time this week, and probably a third.

Everyone who likes movies should go see this one, i took my grandmother with me, who hadn't read any of the books, and even she found it a teriffic experience.

I almost can't wait untill christmas 2002 at least we have spiderman,attack of the clones, and maybe Terminator 3 to keep us occupied this year!!

title: Dazzling in its simplicity.. the best move I've seen.
review: Lord of the Rings doesn't struggle to live up to its own hype... nor does it strain to appeal to a market audience. Instead, it is a movie crafted very simply to tell a grand story, and bring the characters from the pages of a much loved book to life after so many years. There was no flashy, obviously inserted ILM computer work, no Skywalker sound to deafen the audience. Instead it was simple... and in its simplicity it became a masterpiece, towering over movies that died trying to be more than they were.. trying too hard to wow and amaze. Future directors need to review Jackson's methods, and learn that this is how movies should be made.

title: Better then Sex!
review: This is the best movie ever.. too bad I had to watch it so early in the morning.. but its better then sex and lasts longer.. AMAZING.. I played Everquest right after I watched the movie.. This is because I had a renewed interest in dwarfs and gooooooodddddd this is the best movie ever!!!!

title: I gave it a 10 because 9.0 just doesn't do it justice...
review:
...but the movie definitely has flaws, and 9.5 wasn't an option.

However, I'll hold off on that for a minute. If you appreciate the fact that movies - and any other visual medium - are, by definition, VISUAL, then you MUST go see Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Rings. It is, without a doubt, one of the most beautifully filmed movies in cinematic history. That fact alone is worth the price of admission. However, thanks to the eternally enlightening 'script' provided by the Professor J.R.R. Tolkien, this film succeeds far beyond the single dimension of sight.

There's no need to go into the story line or plot details, as virtually all here will know such things (or can easily read them by those more qualified to present that sort of stuff then I). The acting is superb - for a fantasy genre film. Ian McKellan *is* Gandalf, and should be at least nominated for a supporting actor award (or even a best actor nomination). Sean Bean, Liv Tyler, Elijah Woods, Viggo Mortenson, Ian Holm and Christopher Lee are all dynamic and perfectly cast. The sets are astounding, the special effects mind boggling, and Howard Shore's score will leave you humming the main theme as you walk out the theater.

There are problems. The editing is choppy - given the daunting task of taking 450 pages of highly expositional text and turning it into a coherent 3 (!) hour film. Because of Peter Jackson's style, the 'dark' definitely 'outshines' the 'light' in this film (its PG-13 rating is generous, in my opinion). Some scenes should have been clean lifted entirely, but look like they were added to please the Tolkien Faithful, to the detriment of the movie.

But those are minor quibbles. This movie is without a doubt one that should be on your 'to do' list before 2001 expires. I personally have placed it on my top 10 list of all time favorite films (which, coincidentally, are all 'epic genre' type films).

title: Jackson has cinematically matched the genius of JRR Tolkien
review: This film has soul, Character, wonder, scope . Truly a wondrous achievement capturing the spirit of nearly 500 pages of dense text in under 3 hours. In time this masterwork will clearly be on almost everyone's top 100 films, and many top ten lists. If next 2 films match the first will be as beloved as wizard of Oz. Truly magnificent lighting in a bottle.

title: This film surpasses the capability dreams
review: I am in shock.  I have never seen such an incredible display of the art of film making in my thirteen years on this earth.  I have seen many, many movies in my short life so far.  None even come close to comparing with this one.  The musical score was the best I have ever heard.  The sound effects were the best I have ever heard.  The visuals were the best I have ever seen.  Words cannot describe my feelings for this masterpiece.  I laughed, I cheered, and I watched in awe as I witnessed the greatest accomplishment in film making history.  And when it was over, I rose to my feet, thanked Mr. Tolkein, and left before I broke out in tears.  Please.  I am in a giving, kind mood right now.  Do yourself a favor and spend the $8.50 to watch this film.  You won't regret it.  I promise.

title: It took a Kiwi to make Hollywood look lazy.
review:
Yes, a little-known New Zealand Director with a passion for Fantasy, Horror and movies.

*MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD*

With "The Fellowship of the Ring", we get the definitive Fantasy film, but more than that, something that has never been seen before - a Fantasy film with great performances. All actors simply ARE their characters, McKellen's Gandalf is Obi-Wan, Merlin and Tolkien himself (according to Jackson and McKellen) rolled into one. Frodo, Bilbo and Aragorn come to life, every nuance of their performances adding a kind of depth to Tolkien's characters that makes you feel like you are watching real people, not actor's.

I cannot say enough about how proud Peter Jackson has made New Zealanders. His courage with such a production, and the effortless way he respectfully captures Middle Earth would have surely put a few grins on Tolkien's lips if he had lived to see it. The attention to detail is staggering from Hobbit-hole green doors, to Gimli's bouncing bedroll under his backpack, to the glowing, fiery script engraved on the One Ring - it's all there.

As Jackson co-wrote the script, it puts him in the best possible position to tell the story in three hours without losing any of the book's integrity. In fact, Jackson surpasses the Professor on occasion, adding much-needed depth to the characters of 'Boromir', 'Arwen' and 'Saruman', while giving the audience something they never really get from Tolkien - awesome and intense fight sequences. Tolkien glosses over such details, he is more concerned with describing every pebbly rock formation, every verse of every song, every speech and expositional account, leaving out all the meaty PHYSICAL action. Not so with Jackson, who puts you right there in amongst the fray with a kind of random, unrehearsed feel to the battles without adding the frustrating 'strobing' effect that "Gladiator" used constantly.

And unlike a certain other bearded Trilogy filmmaker, Jackson knows how to get the best out of his actors, letting the camera linger on pained expressions, and twinkling eyes, providing powerful close-ups.

It's masterfully filmed, skillfully written, impeccably acted and stunningly presented. Oh, and the music is pretty darn good too. The fact is, that it's not just the best fantasy film ever made, to leave it there would be an insult to Jackson and his hard-working team. Neither is it just the best film I have seen this year. Jackson has set a new benchmark for 'blockbusters' in general, living up to it's hype and then re-defining it, restoring the hopes of film buffs all over the globe, to send a message to Hollywood that simply says: "It's time to give audiences a reason to go to the movies again."

title: A marvelous achievement
review:
As a movie critic: This is a truely excellent epic adventure film. Engaging story, wonderful acting, breathtaking visuals, heart wrenching moments, and consistent pacing.

As a Tolkien fan: It's a valiant attempt that is faithful in intent with varying degrees of success. The film succeeds in action sequences, character interpretation, epic scope, and attention to detail. The film's main fault is that of ommision. The scenes in Bree, Rivendell, and Lorien could have been greatly expanded.

title: I had to see it again that night.
review: I saw the movie at a decent theatre in Bangor Maine (about 200 or so miles away).  I had very high expectations, as I have followed the progress of the film on the Internet.  It exceeded my expectations.  It was a wonderful piece of filming.  Everyone has raved about the looks, the pace and the chemistry of the cast, and rightly so.  The fellowship really comes across as loving and caring about each other.  Merry and Pippen steal many scenes. However, something that really stood out was the sound quality.  I saw it first in a surround sound theater and then in an older stereo theater in Calais, Maine.  It was a different movie.  See it with the best sound system you can!  The way the breathing, the arrows flying, just everything about the sound was so much more alive the first time in a good theater.  Shore did a good job on the Soundtrack by the way.  I was worried about the changes from the book.  I have to say that PJ did a fantastic job. Everything that was cut out would have lost many audience members.  I still wish that Elijah would have cried out "Go back to the land of Mordor and follow me no more!" at the ford.  Oh well.  I have to wait another year for the Two Towers.

review:
it is now 23 hours since i began to see this epic and still i don't know what to say, I just want to see it again and again and again and again....

two problems: it was too short and there is a whole year to "the two towers"

title: A Modern Mythology
review:
This movie excels in every aspect--acting, special effects, music. Best of all, because it is based on a great collection of literature by J.R.R. Tolkien, it inherits great themes, characters, and an incredible plot. Tolkien spent a good deal of his life developing an alternate world in his books, borrowing heavily from earlier stories and mythologies. Because the movie taps into this rich work, it has a deepness and sense of reality to it that would be impossible to create in a movie put together from scratch.

Speaking as a Tolkien fan, I thought the movie did a good job staying faithful to the book. I would give the movie a 10 as a film and a 9 as an interpretation of Tolkien's works. I would have liked to see Tom Bombadil, but I can understand that some parts of the book had to be cut out if the movie was going to have a reasonable length. But my major gripe about the movie was that it never touches on the conspiracy Sam, Merry, and Pippin made to stick with Frodo no matter what. Although the movie gives the sense that these three really care about Frodo, it seems like they get caught up in Frodo's ordeal without really knowing what's going on. In the book, they may not have fully realized what they were up against when they first started out, but by the time they got to Rivendale they had a good idea of the danger they were facing by joining Frodo. This contrasts sharply with the movie, where they volunteer to join the fellowship before they even know what the mission is. But I'm nit-picking. Overall, I thought the movie did a great job recreating Tolkien's world.

One criticism I've seen by some devout Tolkien fans is that the movie makes a lot of minor changes from the book, and who is this Peter Jackson fellow to think he can do that. Although it's true that a lot of minor changes were made in the movie, I think Jackson captures the essence of Tolkien well. If minor changes are made to distill the essence, then has blasphemy occurred? I don't think so. Also, Tolkien himself stated that his purpose in writing the Lord of the Rings was to update the mythologies for modern man. He took what antiquity had to offer, he gleaned the best parts, added some ideas of his own, and weaved it together into a rich tapestry relevant to us today. Jackson has employed Tolkien's method on Tolkien's works. Tolkien's books and Jackson's movies present us with a modern mythology.

title: See what happens?
review: This is what happens when you make something the way it's supposed to be made. Sure, it takes more time and effort and money. You also take a chance that many people in our Britney Spears infected, must be patronize at all times, one size fits all society won't get it. But if it is done right...you have something that's very special.

title: do not overlook the artistry of this film
review:
Let me start by saying that if I could pay IMDB more money to rate this movie higher than a 10, I would certainly do it. The movie is utterly deserving of praise.

In doing a film-adaptation of a book that is beloved by so many, you run two major risks: adhering too closely to the book (in which case, you don't really get to express much of your own creativity) or not adhering to the book enough (which could lead to losing the spirit of the book). Peter Jackson has found the happy middle-ground in glorious fashion. He is able to depict events and experiences from the book and fresh and original ways that, at the same time, give you the fullness of feelings that Tolkien meant to inspire.

Even if this film wasn't a film adaptation, it would still be a great movie because the artistry with which it is made. Let me mention just a few scenes:

-Gandalf's stand a Khazad-dum. The power with which Ian McKellan delivers his lines is unforgettable. In addition to his acting, other elements of the shot are incredibly well done. As he delivers those lines with strength and rage, the light of the Balrog's fire illuminates his dirtied face, reinforcing the feeling of rage.

-The various scenes of Frodo wearing the ring. The chaotic influence of the ring on its wearer is presented with incredible originality. I want to know who thought up this effect. Whoever you are, you are a GENIUS!

-Galadriel's temptation. A lot of people have complained about this scene, but I think it was superb. The transformation that takes place properly conveys the great power of Galadriel. In the original text, Tolkien hints at her power, but he keeps it a mystery. Given the time constraints of a film, Jackson didn't really have time to go into dialogues concerning Galadriel and her power. Instead, he tries to show us her power (and the threat it could potentially be) through a physical transformation. Jackson took a gamble that not everyone appreciates, but I certainly think it was an incredibly creative interpretation.

-Sam following Frodo into the river. No where on film have a witnessed a scene that better captures an individual's devotion to his friend. Despite knowing he can't swim, Sam wades into the river after Frodo, not even considering the danger. Astin plays this part with a moving childlike innocence. The slow underwater shots of Sam emphasize his unconditional devotion, as there are no looks of anger or panic on his face; only a look of longing to be with his friend.

I could go on and on about this film. There are so many scenes that are cleverly done and I commend the filmmakers for such refreshing creativity. I've seen it twice already, and I plan to see it many more times.

title: Great CGI and Scenery. Good Story. LOTR Fans BE QUIET! during the movie.
review:
The scenery was better than expected, I only recognised a few locations, the CGI enhancements were enough to keep me believing it was middle earth, and not too much to be obvious.

The story moved well, but one cut, a fly by just before viewing Gandalf and the good turned evil wizard in the gardens of Isanbard. (You can tell I am not a huge fan of the books, forgetting places and names already.) But that may be well the splicing of the theatre I was at.

I have been twice now and the second time was more exciting than the first. On my original viewing I found the start slow moving, I guess I was being impatient to see more of the mountainous scenery than Hobbiton as I originally come from the South Island. The second viewing I found the beginning wizz by and it was the ending before I knew it.

One warning, I got a sore backside both viewings, might bring a cushion next time.

There were a few bits I found a bit disappointing, very minor, but enough to stop me giving the film a 10. One was the CGI of the nine running from orcs in the mines of Moria. I would have preferred them to have miniaturised live action here as the characters looked like they were out of a cheap video game intro. But that was only 2 seconds out of a majestically CGI'd scene and the balrog must be the best CGI creature ever, for that scene it is worth the ticket fee alone.

My other grump is the audience, the first time I had a young lady who had obviously read the books discuss every scene to her mum. The second time I chose a later viewing in the hope of achieving a more mature audience. Nah two guys in front of me had obviously studied the books and had to discuss right there and then their views. Have I been spoilt by the silence of my flat while watching videos, or is it too much to expect people to be quiet in the theatre these days? PLEASE LEAVE YOUR "INTELLECTUAL" DISCUSSIONS for the trip home!

Thankfully the movie is engrossing enough that both times I hardly noticed the continual babble around me, and managed to become one with the story.

title: As a film - GREAT, as a book to celluloid - OOOOPS!!!!!
review:
Taken as if the book did not exist then this is a truly great film, with some of the best cinematography and special effects I have ever seen on the big screen. It will claim Oscars galore especially in the technical areas. No-one lets themselves down in the acting stakes, Ian McKellen is Gandalf, Sean Astin is Sam, and Christopher Lee is Saruman. 168 minutes flew by in all but the bladder. GO SEE THIS MOVIE.

BUT!!!!!! and it is a pretty big but, as an avid Tolkien fan I exited the cinema thinking not what was right with the film, but what was wrong, what was missing, what went against the spirit of Tolkien. The book is much more complex than this. It has more parallel storylines, more inter weaving of both plots and characters and a bigger vision. What Peter Jackson has dismissed as unnecessary to the telling of the story is the exact same thing that is vital to suck you in to the book. That makes the middle earth believable, that makes you care and what makes you want to know more. When New Line told Mr. Jackson, no not two films but THREE!!! Maybe He missed his opportunity to say "Well if your that keen let's make the ultimate interpretation, - make it six films"

IF ONLY!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

title: Can I move there?
review:
This has to be the most amazing fantasy movie of all time. After spending the first 5 minutes trying to figure out how Jackson accomplished the special effects, I gave up convinced that Middle Earth truly exists and I want to live there.

The majesty of the cinematography coupled with the special effects make this movie, uh, er, experience, uh, epic, uh, okay I give up, escapist alternate reality three hour getaway. And, the acting was exceptional. The credits should have read "Gandalf as himself," "Bilbo Baggins as himself," "Frodo Baggins as himself." You get the drift. Poor Elijah (Don't call me Frodo) will forever be known as Frodo Underhill - much the way Leonard Nimoy was forever known as Spock.

*** WARNING ***

If you see this movie, you will never settle for the tripe Hollywood produces every year. How can anyone ever expect to compete with Tolkien's genius rendered impressively by the most impressive fantasy director of all time. Comparisons to Harry Potter are laughable and comparisons to Star Wars are humorous - don't forget Tolkien had completed The Hobbit and much of the Trilogy before Lucas was born.

*** SPOILER ***

When the credits start rolling, you'll wonder if you can simply take a potty break and come back to watch the next 3 hours of what will undeniably be known as the greatest movie trilogy of all time. That I must wait for nearly a year to see the Part II is my only complaint. (Can I buy my tickets now?)

If you can see only one movie this Christmas, see something else, because if you watch this, you will want to go back and see it over and over again - thus, blowing your budget entirely. I know, I'm going back tomorrow for my fourth viewing!

title: The One Film
review: It may has been made better... but not by human. This is The One Film. There are a lot of good films, there are many very good films, there are some almost perfect films ("The Godfather", "Metropolis" etc.) but never before in more than 100 years of cinema history there has been a perfect film. Until now. It may be reached twice in the next two years, but that´s it. (I want to apologize if my English sounds gaga, but I´m still very impressed) 10/10, even 100/100...

title: see it - then see it again!
review: what can i say that hasn't been said? I'll try - it made the star wars 2 trailer on before it look awful, the first star wars 'epic' ws more of a memory of a bad star trek episode. LOTR had almost perfect casting (poor liv tries her best), perfect effects and design, a fine telling of the tale and for the sheer drama nothing tops it since i saw Magnolia. The sense of awe and wonderment of the hobbits, the tension and sense of threat from the utterly evil creatures were truly horrifying. Christopher and Ian as evil/good wizards WERE their characters, in fact once on screen the sense of character was overwhelming and you really grew to care for them - Sean Bean hit a personal best in this movie. The scenery was astonishing - it was impossible to tell where New Zealand ended and the effects began - they were flawless and no matter the scale of the statues or castles, never lost a sense of solidity, and each long shot drew an astonished breath. Finally where most films featuring fx creatures fail miserably, the creatures in LOTR were truly novel, with a sense of purpose and the fights were very strong on drama and tension, the threat to the characters felt real and emotional and even if I cannot recall half of what i might have read as a boy of the novel, Jackson has surpassed what I expected of a fantasy movie. A superb movie going experience, one for the first time I want to see again - and am willing to pay at the cinema to do so to get the full big screen effect once more. For sheer spectacle this beats Gladiator, beats Saving Private Ryan, Star Wars is lost to memory and fantasy is the king.I had faith that Peter Jackson would be honest in his story telling and give good cinema, but he really surpassed my expectations of a movie - this intelligent movie makes Hollywood look like an inbred idiot with a camera, producing trashy moneyspinners while the independents STILL create wonders, before Hollywood tries to water them down. Hopefully Jackson stays in New Zealand and continues to amaze us all - and for the next few years I think we will be. Thanks Peter!

title: A Must See! Spellbinding, Riveting, A Film-Making Achievement!
review: Many times, a movie review will depend on whether the reviewer read the book first or saw the film first.  For those who have read the book, the film usually is a letdown as there just aren't enough minutes to accurately depict all the action of the movie.  Additionally, if the filmmaker did not create the scenes as you, the reader, visualized them, it doesn't work. The first installment of Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, succeeds in every manner imaginable of re-creating Tolkien's middle-earth...from scenery, to special effects to a perfect cast. I was one of many who read these books in my youth, and waited many years to see the films bring the story to life.  It was worth the wait, as I cannot imagine the film without today's special effects knowledge.  The film is a guaranteed winner come Academy Award time for costume design, with the Orcs and Urik-hai topping the list. The limited criticisms I have read referred to a lack of characterization, an untidy ending and a departure from the books of Tolkien.  As far as the lack of characterization, remember this is the first installment of three.  Characters will develop more as the plot thickens. I was riding along in Middle-earth from the first moment of the film, and felt all the characters compelling.  In response to those who wrote of an untidy ending, this was the ending of the novel.  Those who feel cheated to wait a year for another taste, the same happened when Tolkien's books were released.  Lastly, as far as differences in the book and film, they are minimal and done creatively to not detract from the story.  In fact, Peter Jackson has used these differences to further develop the characterization consistent with Tolkien. The film is nearly 3 hours in length.  I attended the midnight showing on opening night and had to arise for work at 6 a.m.  Still, I found myself looking at my watch throughout the movie...not to see how much longer it was going to drag on but to see how much more I would get to see.  It was the shortest three-hour film I have ever seen.  When it ended, I was exhilarated, exhausted and ready for more. "Fellowship of the Ring" is an epic of the scale of "Lawrence of Arabia," special effects on the level of "The Matrix," and a filmed version of a novel as well-done as "To Kill A Mockingbird." Don't miss it.

title: A cinematic masterpiece-Great workmanship and plot.
review: As stated in my title, this is a great work, that whoever made should be proud of. The plot can be attributed to Tolkien, and the film-makers worked very hard to make sure that it was in accordance with the books. The set design was magnificent, and there was a marvelous performance by Hugh Weaving (officer smith in the matrix), as Elrond of Riverdell. This will be a movie that I, among many others, I suspect, will look back upon as one of the great works of our childhoods, or even lives. This is the next Star Wars.

title: A missed opportunity
review:
Contains Spoilers I was frankly disappointed. Visually and technically the film was great. The acting, particularly Gandalf, Frodo and Sam was fabulous. McKellen deserves Best Actor, he was flawless. However the screenplay and directing fall well short of what Tolkien's story deserves.

The film lacked the feeling of the books. Too much action/adventure, and not enough emotional balance. Clearly this is for the benefit of the audience who haven't read the books. I found the battle scenes rather boring; not a surprise when you know who is going to die when. I mean, they weren't going to kill off anyone but Gandalf in Moria, or Boromir at Amon Hen, were they? And neither Gandalf or Boromir was going to live through those scenes, no matter how heroically they fought. Of course, these scenes are important to the story, but they are not the story themselves, and the movie shouldn't lean so heavily on them at the expense of screentime for other things. There's no real suspense. The only suspense was: what are they going to change next in the story line...

Many changes to the story, purportedly made in the interests of time, seemed idiotic to me. In the book, Frodo resists the Nazgul ALONE at the Ford. Instead, in the movie, this heroic act was sacrificed to allow a minor character the opportunity to do something heroic. For all the hoopla over Arwen's expanded role, she is still little more than a cameo, and that at the expense of a fairly important moment (when Frodo resists the Nazgul) and who knows what else in the next films. And at the same time, they ignored the opportunity to bring out the tension between Aragorn and Elrond over Arwen's fate. This would have been dramatically compelling, and would have required less mutilation of the story.

Likewise, I found the changes to the Breaking of the Fellowship rather jarring. Here I'm afraid they succumbed to the need for some kind of perceived closure by giving Frodo and Aragorn a farewell scene. Rather than, in the book, Sam being the only one who figures out that Frodo is leaving, in the movie he's the last one to actually find him. It could have been done better by sticking closer to the book, even within the action/adventure framework. Imagine Boromir desperately fighting off the orcs as we cut back and forth to Aragorn, Gimli and Legolas racing to the scene - will they get there in time or not? Meanwhile cut to Frodo sadly preparing to leave and Sam racing back to the boats - will HE get there in time or will Frodo really go off alone? All we would have had to do without was the invented scene where Aragorn is almost killed by an Uruk-Hai - hello? He more or less waded into their ranks and slew them with impunity at Helms Deep (and most of them were so terrified of the very sight of him that they ran away). Here again, a sacrifice for mass-market appeal - the Uruk-Hai has killed one of our heroes, so we need to see another hero get revenge on-screen so that everything turns out neat and tidy, Hollywood-style.

The most disappointing character portrayal for me was Aragorn. I thought Viggo Mortensen definitely looked the part, but lacked any hint of the strength of personality and nobility which defined Aragorn in the book. Sure, he plunges into battle with gusto, but when there isn't a battle going on he seems almost indifferent to what's going on around him. After Gandalf falls, he starts telling people what to do, but it isn't clear why (on the strength of his determination and experience) he is CLEARLY the leader of the fellowship after Gandalf. They make him out to be somehow uncertain of whether to take up his heritage as heir of Isildur, when in the book there is no doubt in his mind or anyone else's. There ARE episodes in the book where Aragorn questions his own decisions - most notably at the end of Fellowship/beginning of Two Towers, but this doesn't come out in the movie since he more or less deliberately sends Frodo off to Mordor alone.

When I saw the movie a second time, I noticed that when Boromir inspects the shards of the magical sword which Aragorn is supposed to carry in Rivendell, Narsil has a sort of ring or open circle on the hilt. I also noticed that the sword that Aragorn uses at Amon Hen does NOT have the same hilt. It's possible this was just an oversight (they used a different prop in that battle), but with the attention given to detail, I doubt it. I'm afraid they are going to trample the story again and have Arwen bring it to him or something - otherwise how can they work her into the second movie...? It's also possible that I just saw it from the wrong angle, but if Aragorn had used a magic sword, they probably would (and SHOULD) have added effects to indicate that. Part of the wimpy Aragorn portrayal is due to lacking that sword, and the power it represents in the hands of Elendil's heir. It is supposed to be like a flame when wielded. Nobody else carries around swords like that, hence Aragorn is supposed to be uniquely powerful. In the movie, it's a toss-up whether he could even take Boromir one-on-one...

Most disappointing scene was in Lorien, of course. I didn't mind the Mirror scene and Galadriel's momentary transformation, per se except that Sam was excluded. For instance, in the (dare I mention it...) Bakshi version, I thought they went to the other extreme and downplayed the "edge" on Galdriel's character too much. In that version, she was just a goody-two-shoes, who sort of chuckled at the idea of taking the ring. But Lorien was spoiled in this film by the important character development which was left out. The interplay of Galadriel with Sam and Gimli are very important in the book, yet we see none of it. Sam's gift wasn't mentioned, so one has to worry about the ending of the trilogy in the Shire as well. What a pity that now we won't see Gimli almost starting a fight with Eomer over Galadriel! Or if we do see it, it won't make any sense. That would have been such a great scene, perfectly in line with Gimli's quirky portrayal in the film. Also missing was the CRUCIAL point that destruction of the ring will mean the end of both Rivendell and Lorien. There was some lame, unexplained voiceover about "footsteps of doom", but it wasn't brought out in any understandable way. Since we don't see that Rivendell and Lorien are unique places anyway, I guess it won't matter...

I have to agree with Roger Ebert's review that the hobbits are given short shrift. Merry and Pippin don't conspire to join Frodo because they are his friends and afraid for him, they do it by accident and being in the wrong place at the wrong time. The hobbits actually do fairly well for themselves by evading the Black Riders in the book before Strider shows up. Merry goes off in Bree and after seeing a Black Rider snooping around, actually tries to follow it. Strider can't believe that he didn't simply run away, and it shows that hobbits (not just Frodo and Sam) possess a sort of naive fearlessness that is crucial to their significance in the story.

I don't deplore the changes in the story because there is anything sacred about the text (for instance, I'm glad they left out the bizarre Bombadil episode, which couldn't have made any more sense in the movie than it does in the book). Rather, I think the movie could have been better by sticking closer to Tolkien's story, while preserving much more of the feeling.

The part that I liked best was the opening of the movie in the Shire. Here, we saw the actual characters that we love, not the 1-dimensional "Die Hard" versions they fall into when the action scenes begin. If the rest of the film had been done with the same love that the first scenes are, we would have had the movie I was hoping for.

title: Oh my dear God
review:

title: This is different than other situations
review:
There are plenty of other comments about the film and its qualities and drawbacks here, though make no mistake I've got plenty of opinion about that.

If you're familiar with the story, go see the movie without hesitation. I'm extremely familiar with it, so I don't think it was possible for me to get lost in it or confused.

If you're FANATIC about the story, well, you'll find lots of Tolkien fans that are ready to rip this film for its departures from the text, and just as many movie fans that are ready to defend Peter Jackson for the decisions he has to make to turn this into a film, epic or no.

The comments I've read from people who don't know the story run the gamut.

But there is something to keep in mind: This isn't one of three, any more than the book was one of three. It's the beginning of a very long tale. The book has action, yes, but also a lot of walking around and conversation and reflection. No matter how brief Peter Jackson makes the action scenes, he probably isn't going to have enough screen time to develop everything all at once.

Those familiar with the story know all the back-end relationships already. They hold them near and dear to their hearts. We have to trust that Jackson will develop them over the course of three movies.

The same can be said of those that find the ending anticlimactic. It isn't an ending. It's a convenient stopping point. Think back to Star Wars, which could have been its own standalone movie with enough climax to never go on to

Empire. Lucas didn't know if it would be a hit. If it was, great, let's continue (he had the whole story mapped out anyway). If it wasn't, well, on to the next project.

Of course, ESB was clearly to be followed up, so he had the liberty of leaving a lot of things hanging.

Well, we all know that movies 2 and 3 are coming. Jackson doesn't have to provide true climax here--only in the last installment will that be necessary.

title: The best.
review: Written as a novel, and masterfully played as a movie.  I have to give it a ten.  It's been long over due for a film of this quality to come. The actors & actress were very enlightening, and the story line itself, brought the books out from the 2 dimensional state into a 3D motion picture of an enchanting tale. A must see.

title: Fantastic, Mystic!
review:
I have just returned from the cinema. I saw Lord of the Rings and I must say it is one of the best movies I have ever seen. From the first minute on I felt like I was there in Middle-earth. I have read the first two books and I am still reading the last one. The world and the characters in the movie are nearly that what I imagined by reading the books, even better. GREAT ACTORS, GREAT SCENERY, GREAT STORY...JUST A GREAT MOVIE!

title: Sensational!
review: This film blew me away! The acting is magical(no pun intended). Everything about it is amazing! Sir Ian McKellen and Elijah Wood are amazing along with the backround cast of Sean Bean, Liv Tyler, Christopher Lee, Cate Blanchett, Viggo Mortensen. And the cinematography is also amazing. title: Amazing!
review: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Rings is perhaps one of the best movies ever made.  Mere words really cannot express how much I enjoyed this movie, but they will have to suffice.  From the very beginning, I was dazzled by not only the special effects, but by the sheer power of the camera-work, story-line, and fabulous acting.  This is one of few movies in which every single part was perfectly cast.  First off, Ian McKellen as Gandalf was absolutely perfect.  Without a doubt, he was the best character in the movie.  Ever since I read the books, Gandalf was my favorite character, and Ian did an outstanding job bringing the wizard to life. Cate Blanchett was also one who really stood out in my mind.  After I saw her as Galadriel, it was as if she was born to play that part, she fit it so well. Elijah Wood did a great job as Frodo Baggins.  The emotion and energy he put into his character is immense, and it definitely shows.  There were some discrepancies between the movie and the book.  They didn't, however, detract from the story, and all of them worked very well.  All in all, this is a must-see movie with a stellar cast, great story-telling and believability, and beautiful shots.  If you only saw one movie this Christmas, then this would definitely be the one.  It's just that good.  By the way, it's just as good the second time.  :?)

title: Acting impressions
review: Like many others, I was nearly speechless during the film, due to its imagery and epic storyline. However, the feature that most impressed me was the acting of Ian McKellum as Gandalf and his interaction with Elijah Wood's character, Frodo.  His face, with its twinkling eyes and slight turns of the lips, displayed an intense understanding of the character and convinced me that he was Gandalf indeed.  If he is not nominated for best supporting actor, I would be shocked.

title: A masterful movie, as good as the book.
review:
it's just beautiful. whereas the book's got some really wonderful passages, i do think they're surpassed by mr jackson's perfect scenography. what else can i say? three hours weren't long enough for such a powerful translation. since almost all i've got to say is compliments, i'll just mention the few things i didn't like:

-merry and pippin were reduced to comic relieve, specially pippin became an idiot.

-the final cut did look a bit rushed. i appreciatted that in the prologue (the last alliance battle was a bit too shadowy to my taste) and in the gap between bree and rivendell.

-i think the balrog was best introduced in the book. not that i complain about the even_the_goblins_got_scared introduction, but in the book it had a mistery element around who broke gandalf's spell and nearly destroyed him. and i loved gandalf's final helplessness, "and i'm already weary".

i can't think of anything else even remotely negative to say. i was fascinated by the evil nature of the ring and the "presence" of sauron throughout the entire film, as well as the effective use of flashbacks.
