title: A Movie as fully realized as The Book
review:
Dare I opine that the effects in this movie are unequalled in modern film-making? To wit: the magnificent, subterranean Goblin Hall (a CGI architecture masterpiece, 200-foot pillars stretching into shrouded distance); the hybrid orc at the tomb of Balin (a giant lumpy thing with the speed of a train and the relentlessness of Herpes Simplex B); the crumbling stone stairs, (a gratuitous flexing of effects muscle, which leaves one to assume that it was created merely to annoy George Lucas); Bilbo's initial meeting with Gandalf (a masterful handling of double-camera technique so subtle that it took a few moments to even realize your eyesight was being exploited); and so it went, each effect only enhancing the credibility of this incredible tale, paradoxically making this Fantasy World seem more 'real', rather than a CGI glut-fest: camera panning through vast caverns aflame with activity, as if they really existed; giant sculptures from antiquity adorning the countryside; wizardry, beasts, Vallejo-esque structures.

The movie being named The Lord Of The Rings, it was imperative to keep reminding the suburbanite viewer what all the running and screaming and poking was over. Consequently, there were 3 million close-ups of a filth-encrusted hand opening around a gold ring. Like Rocky Horror fans emulating their film heroes, people arrive at screenings having not washed their hands or hair for weeks. If you can make a person puke by letting them smell your hand, you get in for free.

ELIJAH WOOD, not having reached puberty yet at 22, played wide-eyed, bushy-footed hobbit hero, Frodo, cerulean-blue peepers and cheeks as-yet-unscarred by the Gillette Corporation. Urged by Gandalf to journey afar to destroy the Ring Of Power, Frodo embarks with three idiot friends. At an inn of disrepute, Frodo inadvertently rings his finger with this talisman and is assaulted by high-decibel shockwave static, out-of-focus fuzzheadedness and time-dilatory slow motion, a sum effect not unlike having way too much tequila with the boys the night before and going home with a fat stripper named Belulah and waking up with your face buried firmly between elephantine cheeks. (How I miss those days.) Here, the Hobbits ally with -

VIGGO MORTENSEN, as Strider/ Aragorn/ Euro Guy Compleat, the unshaven rockstar Hero. Always looking like he's just stepped out of a shower that didn't clean him, wet-haired Viggo lends his mighty sword to the quest in the hope that Wizard Gandalf might one day conjure up some soap. As the Hero Who Gets The Girl, on his first day of shooting, Viggo started making out with -

ORLANDO BLOOM, until someone told him that wasn't the girl. Bloom, whose name is perfectly congruent with the prim, blond elfin archer he played, Legolas, was responsible for holding up shooting for days on end when camera lenses would crack under the spell of his haunting boy-face. Constantly knocking on his trailer door, begging for beauty tips, was -

LIV TYLER. A goddess. The sensual electricity is headily apparent between her and Viggo, even though he hasn't washed since 1437 and his musky shirt is now stuck to his back with sweat. Some chicks just dig the rugged outdoorsy type, I guess. Anyone got her number? Certainly not -

SEAN ASTIN, who, having reached puberty and finding that he didn't like it, reverted back to dull, ambiguous child actor. Playing Frodo's sidekick, Sam-I-Am, most notably from Dr. Seuss's classic tale of Wizardry and Demonology, Green Eggs And Ham, Sam-I-Am is entrusted by Gandalf to ward Frodo. His one attempt at poignancy (`If I take one more step, it's the farthest I've ever been from home') is slamdunked by two hobbits from the East End, who join the quest to travel to the farthest reaches of the land, which was about ten miles down the road. Led by -

IAN MCKELLEN, renowned rille-faced veteran of stage, film and backdoor-mannery, as the stringy-haired, hessian-robed wizard Gandalf The Grey, hard-pressed curbing his desire to touch Elijah Wood's Golden Ring, dusky whispers taunting him whenever the candy-skinned man-boy would saunter near. One face-crease away from being Patrick Stewart's doppelganger, McKellen leads a ragtag expedition (did I just say 'ragtag'?) into special effects flummery, from the Elfin City, run by -

HUGO WEAVING, whose thespian prowess successfully melded two of his most famous roles: that of Agent Smith in The Matrix and the drag queen in Priscilla, Queen Of The Desert. Told by Peter Jackson, to `wear something from Priscilla', he did, perfectly befitting his role as the Elfin Queen. But can there be anyone more fey than the ORIGINAL Lord Of The Wings -

CHRISTOPHER LEE, aka Dracula (pronounced 'Drah-kyule', which lends it more legitimacy for some reason), playing the treacherous Saruman, Gandalf's Human Resources Manager. Enrobed in startling white, snowy mane cascading to his lower back, beard grown down to big-ass medallion (that was how he turned up on set every day - before makeup), Wahmpyre Christopher is testament to the rejuvenative diet of worms and virgin blood. Considering his mortal body died 35 years ago, Lee continues to make onscreen cameos with as much verve as undead people half his age, like -

THE BALROG, undoubtedly the COOLEST daemon to stalk cloven-hoofed and flame-chiaroscuroed across a screen, stage or pentacle EVER! This torn-winged, hell-blackened, ram-horned apotheosis of Evil Incarnate (how I love him so!), faces off with The Great Gandalf in a cinematic sequence so astounding, breath-stopping and power-hammering that George Lucas is *still* trying to re-write Star Wars Episode Three.

There are two more Rings movies on the way, each, so we hear, as monumentally staggering as this one - Good Luck, George!

title: A proper evaluation
review:
I never fail to be amazed at how gullible some people are with respect to movie promotion. That anyone intelligent would care for their asinine views is lamentable. Fortunately, I am an expert in film analysis and critique, and I've decided to take a little time out from my busy schedule in order to treat you to a proper, well-measured and meaningful evaluation. I insist you read it carefully and completely; it may be worthwhile to acquire a good dictionary now.

Reading film is a skill that takes time and practice to achieve. Few people other than myself achive mastery of it. Reading into "Fellowship of the Ring" leaves many questions unanswered. This would not be the case had the director been a great Frenchman like Truffaut or Bertolucci. They must be rolling in their graves. Peter Jackson is obviously on the learning curve of the directorial apprenticeship - I feel somewhat aggrieved that I could not go back in time and spare him some free consultancy. The film is worsened for this. However, there are other merits, notably the incredible array of special effects and camera trickery on display. All the stunts, scenery and effects (such as reducing character's size) were actually filmed inside a computer.

The film's main plot theme is basically about a boy called Frodo who finds a ring imbued by magical powers by an evil wizard called Saraman who has a large eye of fire. Upon finding this out he asks a wizard called Gandalf how to destroy it - he has to walk into a distant land called Mordor and throw it into a river. This may be read as a blunt analogy to nuclear proliferation, and makes for some intriguing possibilities in the sequels that will inevitably follow if this film is a success. I recommend that you watch this film.

I noticed that this film occupied position 6 in the IMDB top 250. Whilst the film admittedly has numerous merits, I graded it a '1' to bring it down to a more reasonable rank. I will be reviewing other movies soon, and I recommend you take the time and effort to consult my wisdom. If you would like to express your gratitude to me for this review, please feel free to place an entry in the messageboards.

review:
The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring. A purely amazing film. Peter Jackson has directed a new masterpiece. Truly outstanding. I give it 10/10 stars. A great triumphant picture.

It starts off by telling the tale of the creation of an amazing instrument of pure evil, known as the one ring. I tells of how the rings existence causes absolute corruption. A very touching film, filled with everything associated with fantasy. Prepare to be amazed when you see this film.

title: Spellbinding. As close to perfection as a movie could be. This is what cinema is all about.
review: I went to see this at 9.30 on a cool Sunday morning the week it was released. I had always promised myself that I would someday get around to reading The Lord of the Rings, so when I heard there was a movie on the way, I figured that was a good time to start. So I've read the books, and now I go to see how Peter Jackson has dealt with the story. And boy, what a ride! There is nothing I didn't like about this film, from the casting, acting, scenery, special effects and music. For three hours I was swept away into another world, not even noticing how much time had passed. When it finished, I was left sitting there, mouth open, wondering how I could ever come to the movies again. Although the story was somewhat altered, I think that the changes made enhanced a wonderful story. Cutting out the whole Tom Bombadil bit was, for me, the master stroke, as it was the one part of the book that almost made me put it down. Tolkien purists may not like some of the changes, but they are relatively a small group compared to the millions that have seen the film with no previous experience of Tolkien's work. Some allowances have to be made for storytelling's sake, and for clarity's sake. The cast: Wow. Not only were the characters exactly as I had pictured them when reading the book, but the performances, no exceptions, were top notch. I couldn't single out any one above the others, all were exceptional. Astin, Bean, Blanchett, Bloom, Boyd, Holm, Lee, McKellan, Monaghan, Mortenson, Rhys-Davies, Tyler, Weaving, Wood. What can I say? The work each actor put in to make their character believable is evident in the film. Kudos to all. Seamless special effects, in places that I didn't spot until I watched the DVD documentaries. The Moria scenes even had CGI Fellowship members running around....I hadn't even noticed! The opening scenes, with the siege of Barad-Dur, took my breath away. The New Zealand scenery is just incredible to behold. As a backdrop to one of the greatest (in my humble opinion!) films ever made, it adds a touch of mystery and awe to an already wonderful tale. But the finishing touches, for me were put in by Howard Shore. The Music: Words fail me. For me, the final piece of the puzzle. When you take a perfectly cast film, with great performances, fantastic scenery, and great special effects, you think you have it in the bag. But then along comes Howard Shore, and raises it to a whole new level. From the opening New Line Cinema logo, before we ever see what Jackson's Middle Earth looks like, we are transported to a new world through the sense of sound. The music of the elvish scenes is achingly beautiful with a sense of tragedy about it. We instinctively know that there is something going on here, that they are declining, before anyone mentions it. We feel the darkness of the opening scene, followed by the jolly, rustic Shire music to introduce us to all things Hobbit, then all along the journey we are treated to amazing pieces that enhance the mood every scene. I could go on for hours about Rivendell, Many Meetings, Aniron, A journey in the Dark, The Bridge at Khazad Dum, The Uruk-Hai theme, but I think I've made my point. Shore says in a documentary on the DVD that he saw this as his chance to write an opera. Well, act one is in the bag. Let's have the rest of it! Closing comments: Something that will be talked about for years to come. I think this is a cinematic masterpiece, and will rightly earn its place among the greatest films of all time. Peter Jackson, if you read this, please accept my heartfelt thanks for the experience you gave me on that Sunday morning. I have had some good movie experiences in my almost three decades, a few wow experiences, but only one Lord of the Rings experience. I grade this film 10/10, in every category.

title: This couldn't have been made any better!
review:
Before I saw this movie, I knew vaguely about the world of 'Middle-Earth' and what happened in The Lord of the Rings. After seeing it, it has driven me to finding out everything about Tolkien and this universe!

It is the best movie I have seen in a long time, and the second one is even better! The acting, and directing, the music, everything is the best it could possibly be! Peter Jackson did great on this movie, and I'm planning to see many of his movies in the future!

The story is based around the one ring, made by the evil lord Sauron in the fires of Mount Doom in Mordor. This ring could give him the power to enslave the world forever! But when Sauron was destroyed, the ring, after many centuries, found it's way into the hands of a Hobbit, (small human-like creatures), called Bilbo Baggins. Bilbo kept this ring for 60 years, with no-one knowing about it. Then his long-time friend Gandalf the Grey, a wizard, suspects that the ring has re-woken. Bilbo decides, after his 111 birthday, (which even for a hobbit, whose life-span is over 100, is getting on a bit), that he must leave Hobbiton, (the village where Hobbits live), and the Shire, (where Hobbition is.) He leaves the ring with his nephew and heir Frodo Baggins, along with his house. Gandalf releases that the ring has to be destroyed now or never. But to destroy it, they would have to go for many hundreds of miles to Mordor, and throw it into the fires of Mount Doom. Frodo volunteers to take the ring, seems it is his now. But he doesn't go alone. He takes his best friends Samwise, (or Sam), Gaggee, Meridoc, (or Merry), Brandybuck, and Perigrin, (or Pippin), Took. Meanwhile, Gandalf goes to Isengard to see the head of his counsel, Saurman the White, only to find out that he has turned evil, and now wants to join Sauron in his quest to find the ring. Eventfully, the hobbits and Gandalf see each other again in the elf city of Rivendell, where the Fellowship of the Ring, (hence the title), is formed. The Fellowship includes the 4 hobbits, Gandalf, 2 men, (Aragorn and Boromir), 1 dwarf, (Gimli), and 1 elf, (Legolas). The soul purpose of the Fellowship is to protect the Ring bearer, (Frodo), and make sure the quest to destroyed the ring does not fail.

This film was done the best it could be done! I couldn't imagine someone else doing a better re-make of it!

Well, an excellent book makes an excellent film!

I give this film, a non-mistakable: 10/10

~Becki

title: THIS FILM BELONGS NOWHERE NEAR THE TOP 10 MOVIES OF ALL TIME, AND NEITHER DOES THE SEQUEAL
review:
After reading my opening sentence, I'm sure there is a large offended group of people so let me clarify. I enjoyed the movie. It was fun to watch, good entertainment and decent action. However it is lacking in a few key areas. As I list them, I consider the two movies as one so keep that in mind.

Most importantly for me, very few of the characters show any depth. The guy that plays Alec Trevlyn in GoldenEye (I forget his characters name and the name of the actor but I'm sure you all know who i'm talking about) was one of the few who did exercise multiple levels of character and demonstrated internal conflict. Deep down he really wanted the ring and the associated power, but he over came this and ended up dying nobely for the survival of Frodo and the success of the destruction of the ring. Golem projected a similar struggle, but at this point we (the movie goers and not the book readers) are unsure of weather he does succede in snuffing his desire. All the other members of the fellowship had their personalities shaped early on and their actions are becoming painfully predictable; espicially Frodo.

Acting is often regarded as "brilliant" or "stunning" by the members of the cast. But as mentioned above, the hobbits, elves, men, wizards and so forth are not multilayerd. "Superficial" isn't the right word, but it's the first to come to mind. Honestly, I care much more about a character who is dealing with internal conflict as well as external. Undoubtedly, our "wee people of the Shire" face extreme conflict from other sources, but little from them selves. (The struggle with desperation over the ring could be labeled as "internal" but I got the impression the ring's power was too much for most beings. But feel free to place it where you like.)

Another common speaking point for LOTR fanatics is the cinema-tography. Aside from a few too many (although impressive arials backed by strong music) nothing comes directly to mind as good camera work, mainly because there is far too much computer generation. I understand that the effects are necessary for the credibilty of the film, but it loses cinematic appeal in the process becasue, as of yet, CG scenes are still quite evident.

There are parts of the film that are exceptionally strong. The story speaks for it self as one of the greatest adventures I'm aware of. But you all know as well as I, that the story does not make the movie. However, little of this credit can go to any one involed with the film becasue it is a very near and accurate account of the novels.

Maybe every thing I've written is wrong and out of line. Maybe I just did this because I'm bitter that these two movies keep other films out of the high ranks tey deserve. (ie. Memento, Dr. Strangelove, Pulp Fiction etc.)

Overall, 6/10

review: I loved the theatrical release of "Fellowship," but I REALLY loved the special extended edition. It didn't feel overlong, only richer, and more cohesive. Beautiful cinematography, direction, costumes, action, romance, and drama, this movie, and The Two Towers are full of magic. These two films have become modern classics, and have rightly crushed any recent fantasy trilogies (Star Wars prequels, especially) under foot. It's rare that a film can be so beautiful and touching to so many people, but be a fantasy film, too, typically tossed into some genre ghetto by critics who don't know better. title: A good extraction
review:
I thought LOTRTFTR (Lord of the Ring The Fellowship of the Ring) was an accurate overview of the book itself. Although some details were left out, the movie turned out to be quite a show.

I thought there was a transition throughout the movie. LOTRTFTR started out bright and full of life, this of course being with the shire. As the movie goes on I noticed it turning into a sort of roleplaying game, for we are always following Frodo's story. That's what most of the book is about as well, but it would have been nice to branch off into the other characters' stories as well but the movie would have been too long i suppose. Towards the end of the movie i thought it got quite dark and hopeless and the ending wasnt one that i would have chosen to cut back on in length, even though the book ended in a like wise manner, i would have prefered if the writers added a little bit more to it.

Over all i think this movie is worth its time in watching value, very good visuals and excellent sounds make this movie a standard for fantasy movies to come.

title: A treasure of unimaginable value.
review: This movie could not get any better than it is.  Peter Jackson is a wonderful director who caught the true essence of the book series and brought it to life with a talented cast and crew who were, fantastical. Every minute detail was used to create a film unlike no other that, as I see it, has changed the way every other filmmaker makes films.  Not only has this changed the film industry, but it has also changed the way many people look at everything.  After reading the books, they ultimately became my favourite, I was worried about how the movie would turn out, what with the time involved and the exclusion of Tom Bombadil, but now the movies have become my favourite movies as well. Each time I read even a page of the book or watch a scene from the movie I feel that I'm actually in Middle-Earth, and to create the same sense with two different mediums is utterly awe-inspiring! However they did it, it worked.  I cannot even write a grammatically correct paragraph about it without pausing to remember the words I want to say about it, but in any case I thank anyone who even had the smallest of part in making this trilogy.  I don't know any of them, I haven't met them, but wherever they are, thank you.  Gratias tibi ego.

review: I wasn't at first interested in seeing this film until people convinced me that this film was wonderful; not to mention it took home a lot of awards, including MTV Best Movie. This is just like any ordinary story about good vs. evil and the sacrifices it challenges. Lord or the Rings: Fellowship of the Ring is about an evil spirit resurrected and it is after a ring. title: Outstanding, Brilliant, Perfect, etc.
review:
The Lord of the Rings has finally made its way to the big screen, and has arrived in a brilliant, stunning fashion. The story, which follows the journey of the all-powerful One Ring, is driven astonishingly by incredible acting from everyone involved. title: Exceptional
review:
Spoilers Herein.

Those informed souls who have read the Lord of the Rings books should acknowledge that the Fellowship of the Ring is the least enjoyable, to the extent that one is, because of the 100 pages of description that begins the tale. Knowing this going into a movie makes a person wonder if the movie will share the same downfall and leave the audience bored for an hour while everyone is introduced. The answer is a resounding no, as the viewer is thrown into the story rather quickly, introducing the characters and the setting as the story progresses.

Peter Jackson does a marvelous job of staying true to the original books, while still maintaining the audience's interest for the entire 3 hours of the viewing. The cinematography and directing of the movie is nothing less than exceptional. This is complemented by the magnificent score that only serves to accentuate the marvelousness of the movie.

There are not any noticeable holes in the acting. Everyone from Frodo to Arwin, and everyone in between is well portrayed. Ian McKellan is absolutely incredible as Gandalf. I normally try to refrain from commenting on things like this, but he was robbed at the Oscars and deserved the best supporting actor award.

The action in the movie is well done and powerful, but it does not take over the course of the movie or the plot, and because of this, these two elements intermingle in harmony. After such an exceptional movie going experience, the cliff hanger at the end does not really disapoint a viewer that much because of the incredible movie they have just viewed. Those who have not read the books previously will be in for several twists and turns while those Tolkien fanatics will be pleased with the outcome of the story.

This is true cinematic brilliance and it rarely gets better than this. Kudos to Peter Jackson for a job well done.

title: The biggest thrill ride of 2001
review:
Rated PG-13

Chihiro_Sen15's Score: 9.6 out of 10

J.R.R. Tolkien still remains one of the best fantasy authors of the 20th century and "The Fellowship of the Ring" has now become one of the best fantasy film of all time. After reading "The Lord of the Rings" about 3 months before the movie was released, it still amazes and surprises me, both novel and film. Peter Jackson is one brave filmmaker and proved to be an excellent one at that after this beautiful movie.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" tells of the hobbit Frodo Baggins (Elijah Wood) who inherits a ring from his elderly cousin Bilbo (Ian Holm). However, this is no ordinary ring. It's the One Ring, forged by the Dark Lord Sauron to control Middle-Earth. But the Ring was taken from him and he is searching far and wide for the ring that'll help him enslave the world. Guided by the wizard Gandalf (Ian McKellan), Frodo recruits a fellowship of men, a dwarf, an elf and three fellow hobbits to help him against Sauron and his minions.

"The Fellowship of the Ring" does complete justice to Tolkien's original work. Jackson flawlessly combines Tolkien's themes with all the important story elements (Fans will notice Bombadil is missing) but knows how to make a great movie out of them, compared to the more workmanship job on the fluffier fantasy "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone". As far as the script goes, there are one or two scenes which I would stray away from dialogue. They're a bit over-scripted, particularly in Hobbiton. But this is only 1/3 of the trilogy, and there's quite a lot of exposition here.

Acting wise, the film does what it needs to do. Wood's Frodo is very good, and did better than what I expected him to do. One awkward line somewhat hurts him a bit. But Ian McKellan's Gandalf, on the other hand, is worth the money you spend to see this movie. His performance as Magneto in X-Men gave audiences the assurance that he can play fantasy characters, but Gandalf was just stunning. The cast also includes Viggo Mortensen as the human Aragorn, and Sean Bean as Boromir. The human characters are fleshed out real well, and Boromir particularly was more of a three-dimensional character than in the books. Others include Orlando Bloom as the elf Legolas, John Rhys-Davies as Gimli the dwarf and Sean Astin, Billy Boyd and Dominic Monaghan as Frodo's hobbit friends. All of these actors portray their characters extremely well.

Visually, the film is a grand feast. "The Fellowship of the Ring" won the Best Visual Effects Oscar and there's no denying it's win. It is a great mix of live action and CGI, some of the best I've ever seen. "Fellowship" is simply beautiful in visual effects and in it's production. The sets and the scenery have a certain realistic texture to it that seperates it from many other movies. Jackson has created a world that is totally believable and feels like you're actually there. And that is probably the highest compliment I can give the visuals.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" works wonderfully, on a technical level and on adapting Tolkien's original novel to the screen. It's entertaining and enthralling as it is deep, perfectly translating Tolkien's themes on screen. It isn't the best movie I've ever seen, due to some pacing problems, but what is one screen works on the whole, and Jackson does a near perfect job at a first time live-action "Lord of the Rings" film. But this is only 1/3 of the way there, and I'm extremely anticipating the final hour.

title: I beg to differ, sir
review:
Okay, I was sceptical about this 'masterpiece' before I even saw it, so no surprise that I am not jumping on the bandwagon. This is not a fantastic movie, in film-making terms. It is, however, a fantastic cult for those obsessed fans to indulge & immerse themselves in.

I may be a hypocrite because I am a huge Star Wars fan, but whereas SW was, in its time, quite in its own league, with LOTR I see many different influences, such as Excalibur (the Arthurian legend) and most of course many biblical similarities. It presents in an overblown way a very tired genre & very tired themes which are no longer exciting or unique.

The special effects in LOTR are, admittedly, spectacular, as was also the cinematography. But these elements alone cannot make for a great, landmark film, as so many people suggest. My comments may be wasted as I am absolutely in the minority - those people, like me, who know that LOTR is not for them usually don't bother to see the movie, let alone vote for it, which is why this film has such a ridiculously high rating.

LOTR is certainly not as good as SW, let alone better. Consider also the 30 years which have elapsed in cinematic progress & advances in technology. What's more, LOTR drags on needlessly & ends abruptly in an obvious promotional ploy to get viewers to see the next film. The cast-list may look impressive, but I found some of the acting (most notably from Lee & Holm) to be rather too much overacting and, as others have said, almost in the comic-book league. Credit though to Viggo Mortensen who, well, provided the film's only backbone & something to make you keep watching.

I perhaps would not be so critical, was it not such an overhyped film which seems to ensnare its victims like flies. Once somebody considers themself a fan, as I have so found out, it is frankly impossible to make them look at it objectively & regain their common-sense. In my opinion, it is a fairly likeable & almost exciting adventure film, 6/10 at the most.

title: The Rough Guide to Middle Earth
review:
Tolkein's epic fantasy novel had long been considered unfilmable, on account of the richness of the imaginative landscape described in his prose and occasional, vertiginous drawings. So the first thing to say about Peter Jackson's film is that it looks (i) amazing and (ii) exactly as you expected it to look. New Zealand and computer graphics have combined to create a visual extravaganza wholly true to the original's aesthetic. But the replacement of words by images in itself is merely a prerequisite for a successful film. And the words are largely, sadly, replaced: little of the text survives, and even in the beginning, when Galadriel gives us an introduction to then history of the ring, Tolkein's own various accounts have been discarded (arguably necessarily) in place of a softer, more matter-of-fact overview. None the less, the main details of the story survive. Scriptwriter Frances Walsh has simplified in places but has not shied away from the essential complexity and richness of the tale. Of course one has quibbles: we lose the subtlety of Saruman (a shame, when Christopher Lee is the perfect casting); all the hobbits, Bilbo excepted, seem about half a generation too young; the re-invention of Arwen as a warrior princess is dull, obvious and anachronistic; Hugo Weaving's Elrond is slightly camp and his council lacks due solemnity; and however often Viggo Mortenson flashes his cheekbones, Aragorn was surely never such a pretty boy. But compared with what seems right, what seems wrong is surely trivial by contrast. And yet the film still fails to really capture the magic of the book.

The problem is that a lot of the strength of the book is what happens when nothing is happening. A few examples suffice to illustrate the point. Headed towards Weathertop, Aragorn tells the hobbits fragments of ancient legends; by the time the party arrives, their destination is established as a place of wonder and history. But in the film, we leap there straight from Bree: Aragorn points out the ruined fortress as if he had never mentioned it previously, in the manner of a tour guide pointing out the sights. The subsequent flight to the ford is notable in the book as a time when the heroes are waiting, day after day, for inevitable attack, which when at last it happens has a much more powerful impact than the simple chase scene rendered here; while the attempted passage of the mountains, grimly familiar in prose to anyone who has battled the elements at altitude, is reduced to a single dramatic scene, that makes the point (that the pass will not be crossed) but wholly fails to suggest that the characters might die here (and slowly), defeated by nothing more magical than weather and cold. In consequence the film becomes a mere sequence of dramatic challenges: fight the orcs, flee the balrog, meet Galadriel, etc., etc., etc. The sense of time, and of the characters' changing perceptions of their mission as it passes, is lost. Instead, the battle scenes, which in part one are merely skirmishes, are played up. In spite of its great length, this film lacks patience. Everything is amazing; and so in a sense nothing is. Each landmark, so hard-earned in the primary text, comes quickly after the one before, like a sequence of edited highlights. Overall, the effect is that of a three hour trailer.

For devotees of the book "The Fellowship of the Ring" is fascinating but flawed. It's far from clear that it could have been better. But maybe film is simply too literal a medium to capture a vision that as literature is always more than the sum of its parts.

title: Raising the bar...
review: Based on the first volume of J.R.R. Tolkien's trilogy, Lord of the Rings is truly a spectacular display of how important a good cast and script is, even with state-of-the-art special effects. Rolling Stone had no doubt about their feelings on the matter- 'a movie epic that pops your eyes out, piles on thrills and fun, and yet stays intimately attuned to character'. The special effects are dazzling, particularly the firework display in the shire and the numerous fight scenes, justifying the $109 million budget. However it's the inspired cast who have been much celebrated, Elijah Wood gives a likeable, genuine performance with depth and complexity as Frodo and won the Empire best actor award for it, and the reliable Ian McKellen was Oscar worthy for his performance as Gandalf. However less well known, Viggo Mortensen gives the best performance in the cast and is strongly supported by Brit, Orlando Bloom and other compelling cast members Sean Astin, John Rhys-Davis and Christopher Lee. Please don't mention Cate Blanchett or Liv Tyler to me, although they do alright they are in no way worthy of their sixth and third credit postions respectively- why Jackson? why? The mesmerising cinematography by Andrew Lesnie combined with the eloquent musical score by Howard Shore creates a mise-en-scene of luxury and beauty. The New Zealand locations selected by Jackson were truly breathtaking and that alone leaves a lasting impression on the audience. However the underlying essence of the film is the importance of self-belief and the ability to trust others. This could have been mishandled into a mushy and disingenuous flop, however the script is executed with the utmost integrity by the cast to create a future classic. The final scene of intimacy between Sam and Frodo exemplifies the talent Jackson possesses to touch on intricate human emotion and yet still wow the audience in his visual feast. Lord of the Rings will be celebrated for many more years as one of the greatest fantasy movie epics of all time.

title: How many times must I yawn?
review:
Let me start out by saying that The Fellowship of the Ring is just boring. There were so many scenes that could have been taken out without harming the storyline at all, and so many scenes that WERE taken out that really damaged it.

I was excited to see The Fellowship of the Ring in theaters when it first came out. I heard it was a long movie, but I figured it could still be good. Which, yes, it was. But it was NOT good, too.

The plot is really cool, however. Sauron is returning to the world, and Frodo must take the ring back to the Land of Mordor and destroy the ring. It's really a great idea, and I've always loved fantasy. But this was just a little too long.

The special effects are pretty impressive. I really liked the ringwraiths and the galloping horses in the river. The Balrog was impressive, too.

Through all of this, The Fellowship of the Ring still fell short. Any of the action scenes are either too short or too repetitive. The movie consists of the main characters being chased by the villains, escaping, then being chased again. It's annoying.

I can't compare it to the books since I've never read them. I have heard that, for the most part, they stayed true. I'm just wondering if they could have stayed true without going for three hours. That is really a long time to sit and watch a movie. Seriously, who actually wants to sit that long? And for a movie that's kind of boring? Apparently many people do, since this movie has gotten such high undeserved ratings. I think people are saying it's good only because it's based on the books they love. If The Fellowship of the Ring didn't have any fans before it was released, I'll bet it wouldn't have done so good in the box offices.

Character development is poor. I never even knew the names of the dwarf, the elven archer, and two of the hobbits until I watched The Two Towers. That's pretty bad.

The Fellowship of the Ring could have done much better. But it just can't match up to other fantasy realms or other movies.

title: I'd rather have the Lord of all Ringworms...
review:
...than watch this overrated guff again. Fair enough, I haven't read any of the books so I don't gain any pleasure from seeing a favorite fantasy bought to screen, but X-men, Batman, Superman, Spiderman and even the BBC television series "The Lion the Witch and the Wardrobe" have all shown how to adapt texts in a way that satisfies fans and newcomers alike, so why couldn't this? It felt like a rush job with the director hoping that we'd be so dazzled by the (admittedly striking) special effects and scenery not to notice the holes in continuity, the awful dialogue, convienient changes in character and lapses in logic. I'm more than willing to suspend disbelief, but this film didn't give me any reason to do it. Here are just a few reasons why

XXXXX Warning: Possible spoilers ahead XXXXXXXXXXX

Shields seem to be in such short supply in Middle Earth that all you need to win battles is a bow and arrow. Which begs the question, why use swords at all?

Why is it that the "super-orcs" were just as easy to dispatch as ordinary orcs? Why waste so much time showing their creation and leading us to think they would be a real challenge to the fellowship?

The fight with the rock troll was daft. I know Frodo was wearing magical chain mail but didn't he actually get spiked?

How can someone with Gandalfs intelligence not know that the inscription above the tunnel door was a riddle?

No one warned me beforehand that Frodo would look so much like a hairy-footed version of a young Michael Jackson (although Frodo is admittedly darker). I kept expecting the slain orcs to rise up and all start dancing in a tribute to thriller...

The warriors are arguing at full pitch round the table. And little Frodo quiets them with his high-pitched squeaking? Please.....

Like I said, those were just a few reasons. I think the worst thing about the film was that it didn't try hard enough to make me care enough about any of the characters. I can't fault the actors for this as it was clearly the material. Sean Bean's death should have meant something, instead it just led to me thinking about the merits of of projectile weapons over blades.

I will see LOTR2, but only because it can't be worse than this.

title: Good, but not THAT good
review: I used to think "Dances With Wolves" was the most overrated movie of all time.  It wasn't bad, per se, but it was certainly not deserving of its Best Picture Oscar (Should've been GoodFellas).  The three hour+ movie can be summed up thusly:  white man bad, red man good.  OH, and the cinematography was gorgeous. And perhaps it is the cinematography that suckered so many into believing LOTR was so amazing.  It works as a very effective commercial for New Zealand tourism.  However, as a film, it breaks no new ground. Elijah Wood spends three hours looking like a deer caught in high beams. It gets annoying about 45 minutes in.  Merry and Pippin, the two pointless sidekick hobbits, are the equivalent of Disney's stereotypical comic relief fuzzy sidekicks (see: Timon and Pumbaa (Lion King), Sebastian and Flounder (Little Mermaid), etc.) The battle scenes are fairly typical for the genre: overwhelming odds, poor shooting bad guys, perfectly accurate good guys, false alarm main character "death", dramatic actual death scene of semi-major character. I do realize it is simply part one of three, so I won't criticize the non-ending.  However, I do not expect much more from the second installment.

review: This is the most overrated movie of all time. Okay, I have to give respect to it because it's always hard to make a movie out of a book, especially of a legendary series like LOTR. However, the actors weren't that great, especially Frodo is just awful. He has always the same expression on his face, no matter what happens. Fifth best movie of all time? Come on folks...the problem is that people come home from the movie theatre, and they still think of the landscapes and the fantasy world, give it a ten and bam - there you go. After they've watched the movie a second or third time, or even if they think about it for a while without being influenced by the ambiance of the cinema, they wouldn't give it more than 7 or 8 points.

title: Don't waste (a considerable amount) of your time...
review:
possible spoilers--but I don't think much could spoil this stinker.

I was actually sucked in by the hype and paid good money to see this. How a supposedly elite audience such as the IMDB member base could rank this film (at the time of my comment) as the #6 best movie of all time is more a comment on the IMDB member base--at least those who vote--than it is the film. This first installment is the last one I'll see, thank you, and I'll admit to being charmed by it up until we left the Shire.

After that, it was one special effects horror after another trying to finish off Frodo and his friend. Don't get me wrong. I love movies and will do anything to suspend my disbelief to be entertained and taken to another mystical place--but special effects just don't make a movie--(See The Perfect Storm, for example)--and they had everything but the tiger from "Gladiator" in this movie. Maybe the tiger would have helped.

Early into the second hour, I was hoping something, anything, would succeed in killing Frodo so I could leave. But no, I stayed right to the end, thinking "How could a movie with so much buzz be bad?"---but it was.

Boring. 3 out of 10, save yourselves while you can. And if you can't, well, at least you won't have me in front of you in line this Christmas (or next!) to see any more of of this foof. #6 indeed!

title: Well For a Person waiting for something to happen
review:
Sorry guy...There is No Stallone or Van Dame to make something happen.

This is a true top of the line beginning of an epic trilogy. I am sure I am not overstating this either. I never saw LOTR in the theatre because I was skeptical of it. I bought the DVD and must say it was a GREAT film and I can not wait to see The Twin Towers come December. My GF and I will be there this time to see it. She loved LOTR as well ( and no, we are not nerds or geeks or anyone who plays RPG's) We are just people who notice great films. I watch IFC all the time....

title: Maybe I just don't get it...
review:
Everybody loved this movie. So why do I think it's 3 hours of boring, driveling poop? I didn't read the novels, so I had no previous knowledge of the story outside the basic premise. Having seen the movie, I really don't know that much more. The entire movie was a bunch of people running around looking at things, being amazed at things, surprised at others, and overall just, well, walking around. The vast majority of the cinematography focused on panning out on all these vacuous people walking around, showing the very intriguing sites of the world in which these characters were manipulated. And that's just what happened; the characters were manipulated. They didn't grow on me, set themselves apart from each other, make me care for them, or even cause me to have slight interest in their lives, passions, or quest. I didn't care. Not one bit. I don't know. Maybe I just don't get it.

5/10

title: Snoozer
review: This is a film consisting of fluff and stuff with little more than pretty pictures and music, and a chance to catch some zzz's while the kids are entertained with another epic "action" drivel. In there somewhere, fortunately well hidden, or botched, as the case may be, is an anti-industrial message -- weren't the good olde middle ages so great. Boring, boring, boring.

title: Good, but not _that_ good
review:
I am so sick of the hype surrounding this movie. Sure, it was a good fantasyflick. But it also had more money, better actors and the advantage of having a huge crowd of fans that wouldn't admit that the movie was bad even if it was.

The movie has mood and sometimes it captured Tolkiens visions(what i think is the Tolkien vision, at least) pretty ok. But it still had a huge number of flaws. The 8.9-rating here at IMDB is ridicolous, it is NOT that good. And it's not fair to put it up among The Godfather and such movies.

It's something about this movie that i really don't like. Something that i can't put my finger on..

title: Not unwatchable, but OK
review: I'm sorry--I know that all of the big Lord of the Rings fans out there will hate me for this, but I did not like this movie that much.  It was about halfway through that I started to realize that about half the battle scenes could have been out and nothing would have been lost in the movie.  This movie was too long and could have easily fallen below two hours if they edited better.  The acting was also not the best (with an exception given to Ian McKellan).  Everyone says that Lord of the Rings was better at setting up at atmosphere than Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone, but the whole movie looked like it was shot in Ireland.  Harry Potter was a better movie and Lord of the Rings was definitely not the best of the year as many critics have said.  Not unwatchable, but also not worth my money to go to the theater.  An OK movie.

title: Overrated Movie Camouflaged by Acting/Scenery/Special Effects
review:
Most of you will think this a great movie and walk out of the theatre satisfied. Then a few years later, will have forgotten it completely, like "Willow" or "Legend". However, if your tastes run towards quality, then you will get bored after the 1st 10 minutes, and either walk out or stay to see if it gets better, like I did. It doesn't. Why?

1. Don't read the book!!! If you do, you'll see how superior it is to this film in every way and you'll feel ripped-off for purchasing a ticket.

2. The love scene sucked!

3. The beginning party for Frodo works in the book. In the movie, it is a big bore.

4. The constant similar struggles that don't lead to a climax work in the book, but not in the movie! How many times must I see Elija Wood get into a "deer-caught-in-the-headlights" look before you go "Enough already". Plus, the crisis don't lead to any sort of character development at all. Elija's character is still the same at the end as he was in the beginning - he has not changed a bit!

5. The movie was just too long - with lots of slowness to it. No drama, just action, great for a 10 year old, bad for someone needing to care about the characters before were going to be interested in their plight. Put these characters in today's world, and the film is unvieled for what it really is - a stinking bore.

6. The Ending Sucks. You know it, I know it, that's all there is to it.

7. "Star Wars One" was barely better than this movie. This movie was barely better than the awful "Harry Potter" movie. Even "Planet of the Apes", the bad one (Tim Burton) was better than Lord of the Rings.

8. Again, character development sucked. Who cared about these guys? Not I.

9. Etc, etc, etc.

Go see "The Last of the Mohicans" for a far better film. Or "Monster's Ball". Or anything. As long as it's not this movie.

title: Toss it into the fires of Mount Doom!
review:
Middle Earth is a wacky place with bizarre cultures co-existing illogically without any kind of interacting economic/political or social structure. Ruling Wizards just live in big dark fortresses and have armies who do their bidding on a whim. Orc soldiers need their general to be born in a puddle of lava-like ooze, and then run for miles non stop in heavy black armor on sunny days only to get promptly dispatched by two warriors' ho-hum display of Errol Flynnery. Elves have beautiful digs but no hint of how they built them or maintain them. Wringwraiths, about the most inept posse of idiots since the Keystone Cops, looked like they'd have done better to steal that farmer's scythe and fight over who should stand in line for the grim reaper's job after he meets himself. The hobbits all look like they fell out of Dickens while the tavern/inn scene looks like something out of a 17th century pirate movie. This as the rest of the film's look is ostensibly dark ages when not outright fairy-tale. There is A LOT wrong with this picture!

I never read Lord of the Rings all the way through (never held my interest) but I agree with others who say a movie should stand on its own. If the story can't make a decent three act movie, why bloody adapt it. Harry Potter is another example of a wildly successful book turned into a completely plotless movie. Hasn't anyone learned anything after Dune was adapted into a slow moving incomprehensible mess in 1984?

To say the three Lord of the Rings films can't be condensed into a shorter running time is bosh. This first film is a sprawling bore and explains nothing about the characters and cultures it insists we meet. A little bit of back story, sub text and a less lazy writer could have fashioned something more concise, logical and entertaining. As it is this movie is not good. It has its moments, but moments don't make a worthwhile experience at the cinema.

It's a mystery to my why the Lord of the Rings is such a popular literary work in the same why I never understood the Dungeons and Dragons phenomenon. This might make me sound like a hater of fantasy but I'm not. I love good fantasy stories which are done well. This is just a good looking coffee table fable with no substance.

When you take away the beautiful locations, fantastic imagery and CGI what are you left with? Just another extremely cheesy wizard against wizard story like something Jack Palance used to headline. Instead of being Excalibur (which Jackson steals from on more than one annoying occasion) or Dragonslayer this film is Hawk the Slayer or The Sword and the Sorcerer wrapped in gorgeous cinematography.

As good as Ian McKellen is in this film he cannot match the brilliance of Nicol Williamson and Ralph Richardson in Excalibur and Dragonslayer respectively. And Christopher Lee as a wizard we can remotely take seriously? Please.

This film is just not worth its praise. The acting is fine. The look of it as Ive said is at times fantastic. But the script is just aimless, choppy and devoid of clever story-telling.

Another addition to the bad movie file. Even that gawdawful Willow was better than this.

title: A masterpiece of movie making!
review: Absolutely the finest movie ever made. After having read the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy at least 20 times, I had been nervously anticipating the release of the movie, and hoping it would not portray the characters in a cheap, comical method as many artists have done so in still paintings. Upon my first viewing of the movie, I was blown away with the settings, acting, costumes, cinematography, music, and screenplay. All of these were far better than I could have imagined! Many Tolkien hardliners did not like the liberties with the changes in story and characters, but I saw a better movie because of it. How would Tom Bombadil have been added without destroying the intensity and dramatic chase scenes? I saw the movie 8 times in theaters and bought the DVD on opening day and am anxiously awaiting "The Two Towers". I was sadly disappointed when it did not win the oscar for best movie of the year, considering it won the award from the American Film Institute, and had much better reviews from professional critics and fans alike than the winner. Maybe "The Two Towers" will do better!

title: Cinema History
review: I first saw Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring a few weeks after its release.  I had read the books but didn't (I'm ashamed to say) rush to see the film.  I don't think I can stress how amazed I was by this modern masterpiece! Although I do not want to take credit away from JRR Tolkien for his wonderful piece of literature, I felt that the film brought the tale of Frodo Baggins and his companions to life like I had never imagined!  This first installment of the trilogy has a terrific cast of both established stars who further guarantee their places in cinema history (Ian McKellen, Elijah Wood, Cate Blanchett, Viggo Mortensen...) to newcomers (Billy Boyd, Dominic Monaghan, Orlando Bloom...) who will hopefully light up our screens for years to come! This is a piece of film magic with two more glorious chapters to come! With the three films made in one go over the course of two years the entire cast and crew should be incredibly proud that they have been involved in making epic cinema, the likes of which have never been seen before!

title: Don't believe the hype. 6 out of 10.
review:
This movie is WAY overrated. After sitting through 3 hours of this sludge, I failed to see what all the hype was about. Sure the special effects and cinematography are above average, but that's where it ends. The dialogue is weak, convoluted, and at times verges on hilarity. For example, the last line of the film, SPOILER (and I use this term very loosely) `Sam, I'm glad you're with me.' Give me a break! I waited 3 hours for this ending? There is absolutely no payoff for the viewer; it's just a longwinded journey with a fizzle for an ending.

I understand that this movie is based on a book and that it's the first part of a trilogy, but movies should be judged as single entities. For a movie to be considered a classic, it should be able to stand on it's own two feet. Example: `The Godfather II' is still a great film even if you've never seen `The Godfather' or know who Mario Puzo is. `Lord of the Rings' fails to transcend without the help of a series of books, and the rest of a trilogy of movies (which haven't come out yet). The plot just moves from one occurrence to another, there is little cohesion here. Some events are just completely irrational. SPOILER Why didn't anyone reach out a hand to Gandalf when he was hanging on the ledge? He's just hanging there for a while, and no one even makes a minor attempt to help him up. Why?

The character development is also terrible. Little time is spent in letting the audience get to know these individuals. Maybe they should have cut a few of them out. They tried to cram too much into 3 hours (a fourth of which was spent repeating the scene with the finger getting chopped off over and over and over.). The acting is decent though Elijah Wood just has the same troubled, incredulous expression on his face the whole time. Does this guy ever blink? And also, why didn't Frodo just put the ring on, become invisible, and take the darn thing to the dumping point. He could have skipped the whole way whistling Dixie. Can I get a witness? So anyway, I rate this movie a 6 out of 10. It would have been more suitable as one of those 3-part TV mini-series, and doesn't deserve to be rated as high as the classics. Don't believe the hype. Peace.

title: Better than Harry Potter but.....
review:
...the end was very disappointing. Why director Peter Jackson cut brutally the end without giving us an answer what the hell finally happened to the ring and the people? There I am to watch with my wife for nearly three hours an entertaining film but at the end we said no that cannot be possible. One year is too long to wait for the second part and I assure you that for all this reasons I will not see the second one. I have to admit that the special effects were super and the story better than Harry Potter because this movie has more adventures. The music remembered me to Titanic and Terminator and that's too pity for such a blockbuster. I liked very much the horse scenes (don't miss "SLEEPY HOLLOW") and the nice pictures from New Zealand.

I recommend to rent it before you buy it. I think this film is too long and too overrated. I give maximum 5/10.

title: What are you all thinking?
review:
Ok, this is really not a review as such, so I'll keep it brief.

At the time of writing, the IMDb users have this movie voted as the #4 best movie of all time.

Why? Are you all out of your minds? To me it's riddled with problems. Sure it has some nice cinematography, but the character development is incredibly superficial (and I mean down to the point that if you hadn't read the book, you probably wouldn't even remember who some of the major character's names were until you'd been watching the movie for 2 hours).

Jackson has 3 hours to try to convey Sam's devotion to Frodo, and the individual pesonalities of the other three young Hobbits, but by the end of the movie Sam is only just beginning to fill out as a character, and the other two are just cardboard cutouts.

To be fair, the film begins well, is often glorious visually, and ends well, with some great action sequences in the last 45 minutes, but well before then I was getting bored and losing interest in the lethargic middle section, which seemed to contribute nothing much of value except some plot details which could have been revealed far more quickly.

It's not a bad movie at all - I gave it 6 out of 10 - but you blokes have it rated above dozens of cinema's all time greats. Come on, you've got to be kidding. There's no way a movie this imperfect deserves to be in the top 100, let alone the top 4.

At least it's way better than Ralph Bakshi's atrocious 1980 attempt, but for me this movie just proves what I suspected all along. No film is ever going to do justice to the book.

title: A very tiresome nerd flick, that does not appeal to everyone. Bad movie!
review:
Wow, I was pretty excited about seeing this movie. The previews looked impressive and convincing, and most of my friends told me that this movie is awesome. So, I decided to give go watch it myself.

Oh my gosh, what a dissapointment! What a boring movie! Why was this movie even nominated to the Best Picture Category. Here are my reasons that this movie totally stunk!

1. The Dialogue- Ok...now, the dialogue is my biggest criticism for this movie. All the characters seemed like they were acting from script, not true to their character. Also, the dailogue was so nerdy and unappealing. Dialogue is the reason why Star wars episode 4, 5, 6 was so awesome and terrific!! We can really believe and enjoy the conversations of Princess Leia, Han solo, and luke skywalker. But, never could I enjoy the dialogues of loser Froto, Gandolf, etc. etc.

2. Unappealing- This movie is very unappealing. The dialogue stunk, and the movie fails to touch our hearts or actually make us care about this movie!!! I was bored, i hated the characters, and i tuned out of the movie fast and wanted to leave the movie theatre!! it was torture

3. The static, unchanging characters- Wow, what a horrible job of having good characters in this movie. What makes movies great is when the director allows the audience to identify themselves with the characters (this is the reason Spiderman was such a success!) Yet, let's take our supposed "protagonist" Froto, the loser kid who always freaks out about the ring. He had to have been one of the worst protagonists i have ever seen. I never rooted for him once in the movie. He never appealed to me. and most of all, He did nothing to make me care about him. All he did was whine whine whine. ok, Gandolf was descent, but no, he was no mentor like Obi Wan Kanobi. Now, the villain stunk!! he fell flat. We don't know enough about him. He's nothing compared to Darth Vader for that matter.

Three big criticisms, please consider them. People praise this movie, but i don't. It was a huge dissapointment, and i do not know what the hype is all about. If you want to see a good trilogy that appeals to everyone, go watch Star wars episode 4, 5, 6.

Bad movie. Falls flat. 2 out of 10 stars!

title: A film that I think is overated!
review: This film I thought was truley overated. I didn't know what the big deal was. The movie was just plain stupid and really really boring. I would probably never say this but Harry Potter was better than this trash. I'm not looking forward to see the next two installments because this one was really bad. I didn't like the action or the story. I would for sure not give this film any higher than a C-

title: Overrated
review: Well I was excited when I heard all my friends telling me how great this movie was. So when I got the chance to see it no one could stop me! But after 1/2 an hour I was yawning!! It was very dull to say the least! I know Tolkien fans say it is great! It is almost a point by point depiction of the book, but then again the book is not very interesting either. So to enjoy this movie you should either be: A) Tolkien fan or b) a girl (a combination of both would be the best!!) But for someone who hasn't read Tolkien, there is nothing new here, it is just an ok story based on folklore,and so while you watch this looong film, you start to get the feeling that it is actually quite overrated. It is like the movie Wyatt Earp, starring Kevin Costner. The film is a very detailed depiction of the wild west, but one thing was forgotten, the script! And that is the way I feel about LotR. It is so true to Tolkien, but it is never exciting enough for you to care.

title: most wonderfully executed movie I've ever seen
review:
I saw The Fellowship of the Ring at a theatre on New Year's Day of 2002 and was amazed. I had barely heard of Tolkien before hearing of the production of this movie, and even then, I dismissed it as mere pop-culture hype, similar to the likes of Harry Potter. Only until a few weeks before seeing the film did I begin to become really interested. I'm pretty sure that by the time I was walking into the theatre, I was expecting to see the best movie ever, and by the time I walked out three hours later, I think I was right.

I am glad that I didn't take any drinks into the movie, because looking back, I would have been disappointed to have missed one minute of it due to a bathroom break. The landscapes of Middle Earth were beautiful, the music was wonderful (I didn't realize this until listening to the score independent of the film seven months later, however.), and now that I've started reading the books and building my own mental images of them from Tolkien's writings, I can see for myself how correct the hard-core Tolkien fans were who said that the movie followed the book almost perfectly.

Not only in action and dialogue, but in the representation of personalities and character. Gandalf and Bilbo were perfect. The hobbits in general were great, though I must complain about Elijah Wood's being cast as Frodo. Sorry, I just don't like him.

When my brother popped CD of the original score into our CD player last week, I could see the movie play out as I heard the music. When I also started reading him the track names, he (who is currently reading The Fellowship) replied that the track names directly coincide with the chapter names in the book-another hint that the producers of the movie cared about following the book, something that I greatly appreciated.

I was pretty much a stranger to fantasy before seeing this movie and reading The Hobbit (I had only read C.S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia in grade school), so I feel that almost anyone who enjoys adventure films or a classic storybook-style tale will definitely enjoy this movie, and those that are fans of the genre should simply not do without.

10/10

title: The best movie of all time!!!!!!!!!!
review: The Lord of the Rings:The Fellowship of the Ring is the best movie of all time!!!!!!! It has something for everybody. There are some battle sequences for guys or people who just happen to like them. There is also a love story and a lot of really hott guys(Elijah Wood) for the girls. I would give this movie a 20 if I could. If anybody hasn't seen this movie I defintally recommend this movie to you. You won't be disappointed.

title: A long, boring video game.
review:
This movie is like watching your roommate play one of those stupid, neverending Final Fantasy games while for him to get killed so you can use the TV to actually watch something interesting. There's some cool stuff to look at here and there, and I was happy to see Sean Astin in a significant role, but after about an hour of watching little disfigured people running away from computer graphics, I'd had about enough. My guess is you'd like this a lot better if you're into the extremely long and thoroughly uninteresting books that accompany this particular series. The fonts are too small!

Nearly everything else I saw this year was better than this.

title: You want more after 3 hours
review: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring would make the late author very proud. It is extremely well done with a great cast of actors. There are not enough female roles in this story and it is a great story. Who would have thought that Sean Astin grew up to be a hobbit from his days as a "goonie" and Tobey Maguire who was best known for his role in the Ice Storm as Mike. Now he is the star of the film. He plays beside the wonderful attractive Orlando Bloom, John Rhys-Davies, the magnificent Christopher Lee as the dastardly wizard gone arye, Sir Ian McKellen as the wonderful charming gandalf(Sure he could play Macbeth and Shakespearan role but he certainly can play his friend, Dame Maggie Smith, in a Saturday Night Live appearance. He was just perfect and now he plays with his action figures. Then there is wonderful Sir Ian Holm (Just imagine two Sir Ians on the set, what are the chances). The film is about 3 hours and after all that there is still more and you want more. I only wished that they would finally give knighthood to Christopher Lee and John Rhys-Davies.

title: BORED OF THE RINGS (Yeah I know hardly original, but true!)
review: Yet again Im completed mystified why a film is so popular.  This was so s-l-o-w.  This seemed to drag on forever and by about halfway through I was becoming extremely restless.  It started off promising enough, but after that it just seemed to be endless shots of our heroes walking.  Where was the action? Where was the excitement?  Yes the bit in the Mines was good, but there was little else to get the pulse racing.  Sure some of the acting was top notch, particularly McKellen, and the scenery, both digital and real, was very pretty, but I just came out of this completely underwhelmed. Sure I'll go and see The Two Towers, but not because I'm gagging to find out what happens next, but simply to see if Jackson can come up with something better second time around.

title: not all that
review: I cannot believe all the gleaming reviews here. #3 movie of all time? I saw this 6 months after release because of all the hype. Bad idea. The effects are great but that's about all there is. I found myself looking at my watch every 15 minutes. By the second hour I was thinking why don't they just go to maldor and throw the ring in the fire so I can leave. It's way too long. And then to end the movie with a trailer for part 2?? That's just an insult to the audience. I thought this would be a good movie but it's just typical over-produced hollywood fare.

title: Good adaptation but boring movie
review:
I have read the books 3 times at around age 15, 25 and 33. I enjoyed them immensely. The movie was a good adaption of the book following the story well, with only a few key segments deleted. The one I most missed was Tom Bombadil and the barrow-wights. The acting was OK and camera work to make the hobbits appear smaller than humans was clever. The FX for the fights,etc was good and like others have said the landscape was well chosen. With the positives out of the way, I can now begin my rant.

Firstly maybe I have more imagination than some but in my minds eye I saw a hobbit differing more from humans than simply having a few hairs on its toes and having all that coffee stunt its growth. With todays FX alot more could have been done to make them seem less human and more middle earthy.

Second of all the movie was boring as snot!! Of the 3 books I think the fellowship was the weakest, but in context of the trilogy it was but the introduction to a bigger story (fortunately you can begin the next book right away or possibly tomorrow cause I gotta work in the morning and I need to get some sleep :). As a movie unto itself it simply doesn't cut it. Three hours and no real climax. If you compare this to Star Wars, Indiana Jones, the Matrix or other multiple part movies you can really see the difference. For those trilogies each movie was a complete story unto itself in addition to being a step in a larger journey. I think the anticipation and the hype made this much more than it really was. Something akin to Blair Witch which was interesting, innovative, nauseating and amusing but not even remotely scary and heavily over-hyped. Finally i am amazed that this film could break the top 250 films let alone the top 5. I suspect the other 2 parts of the trilogy will make for much more interesting fare and in comparison will make this film look like the dull yawner that it is.

P.S. I mentioned that the 1st book was an intro, in large part it was providing character development for the books to come and to be honest a 3 hour movie based primarily around developing characters for later films just can't be all that interesting.

title: Perfection on a screen
review: Words fail me, it's SO awesome !  It's a must-see for everybody - there's no getting around this one. Seen with sci-fi/adventure eyes :  This one will never ever be topped !  ...unless Tolkiens two sequels by some miracle manage to impress us even more, in which case we'll need an 11 on the rating scale !

title: Nothing spectacular...
review:
I was disappointed with this movie. It's not that I 'disliked' it, but it all seemed so ordinary, and typical. Nothing really inventive or spectacular. Fight some orcs, carry around a ring, whisper to each other about strange portents and impending evil, travel around a bit, fight some more orcs... For a three-hour movie, it left me with very, very little that was memorable. I thought the smoke ship going through the smoke ring, and Gandalf's fireworks were creative, and gave a sense of wonder, and I expected more of the same after that, but didn't get it. Some fantastic scenery, but does that really give credit to a film, or to God?? Elijah Wood, as Frodo, had the same pained expression on his face the whole movie. Vitto Morgenson and Ian MacKellen were both fitting for their roles, as were others, but there wasn't all that much to the roles themselves. I suppose that's the problem of trying to condense an epic story into a comparatively brief movie. One thing I found annoying is how everyone seemed to whisper their lines, especially during what would seem to be the important conversations. That seems to be a convention of acting and films these days, and it's baffling. It's as if everyone has laryngitis, or is in a library. The fight scenes were, well, fight scenes. Again, nothing special or different than what might be expected. Good guys kill everyone with one blow, and can take several blows themselves and survive. And when the two wizards fight each other, what could have been an interesting confrontation seems unfulfilled. My wife commented that the sound effects for the orcs sounded as if they were pulled from a stock sound effects CD or something.

I don't mean to totally bash the film, but it's as though it would have made an incredible TV miniseries, but not a great FILM series. For something that should have been REALLY COOL, it just misses the mark of ever reaching that. Sadly, in the preview for the next film (attached onto the end - the first time I've ever seen that!), it doesn't look like we're in for much better next time. Looks about the same, which is not surprising, as they were all filmed together. Perhaps the story might be more interesting, and they might do more, instead of just evading orcs, so that might be good.

That this has been ranked #3 of all time is truly astounding. I'm just glad it has now been bumped down from #2. Shawshank Redemption deserves that place much more than this movie.

title: Why Has This Lasted So Long?
review: I work at a movie theater, and we carried Lord of the Rings for over five months.  Now, I have read the book, and thought it was the most boring thing ever written, but after carrying the movie for so long, I figured that it had to be at least decent.  Boy, was I wrong.  Not only is the movie just as bad as the book, there are some parts that don't even follow the text, making the movie even worse.  After reading it, I didn't think that was possible, but I was definitely proven wrong.  I can see this franchise becoming long, drawn-out, and beaten senseless just to turn a bigger profit, just like the Star Wars saga (which should have never continued after the original three).  If you're movie theater it still beating this dead horse, don't waste your money, see something worth seeing in theaters, such as Spider-man.

title: Nothing happens
review: This is not a film, it is a 3-hour trailer.  Full of scenes that do not develop the story or the characters, developments that are never referred to later in the film, and events that are never explained.  I came out of this film feeling totally ripped-off.

title: Boo.
review:
what a boring movie.

i was warned it's not for people who haven't read the books -- and have no interest ever doing so. i should have heeded those warnings.

i wish i could see him again to ask him what he thought of the script.

the good: Elijah Wood (vastly underrated as an actor; he carried this), Ian McKellan (i have long suspected and am now convinced that he can play any role, in any movie), production value, and Gollum (just as i imagined, so creepy!)

the bad: i could go on for a while. i'm still p***ed they didnt do the hobbit in live-action. its the only one i read, and i thought (im clueless) thats what this was. aside from that personal problem...where was the plot? i mean god. how many times did we have to watch the same scene...fix, six? gandalf waxing poetic about the evil (insert place) of so-so inhabited by the terrible (insert obstacle0 so-and-so. its like watching dungeons and dragons, except they never die and have to start over.
